title.de: Garden in Bordighera, Impression am Morgen

'Garden_at_Bordighera,_Impression_of_Mor.story: Monet only meant to stay three weeks on the Ligurian coast. He stayed nearly three months. Durand-Ruel had pulled strings to get him into the private garden of Francesco Moreno in Bordighera, thick with palms and citrus and that pink Alpine light he couldn't stop writing about - 'I set up in a fairyland. It would take a palette of diamonds and precious stones,' he told the critic Theodore Duret. The canvas went into Otto Krebs's German collection, was seized as trophy art in 1945, and only resurfaced at the Hermitage in 1995, half a century after anyone had seen it.

source.canonical_title: File:'Jupiter and Antiope', oil on canvas painting by Hendrick Goltzius.Jpg
source.credit: Sotheby's New York, 28 January 2010, N08610, lot 167

'Jupiter_and_Antiope',_oil_on_canvas_pai.story: Goltzius only took up oil painting at forty-two, after decades as the most celebrated engraver in the Low Countries - a draughtsman who'd taught himself virtuoso burin work with a hand crippled in childhood. This late canvas is Jupiter visiting the sleeping Antiope disguised as a satyr: she lies across a heap of pillows and yellow silk, he leans in shaggy-legged with a handful of fruit while a grinning Cupid draws a bow from the shadows. The handling is smoother than you'd expect from a printmaker; the leer is pure Mannerism.

'Plage_de_Juan-les-Pins'_by_Claude_Monet.story: Monet spent four grumpy months on the Riviera in early 1888, complaining to Alice that the southern light was impossible to bottle — 'pink, blue, gold.' This beach at Juan-les-Pins, a scrap of pines leaning toward the Mediterranean, is one of the results. He worked fast, chasing weather, writing that his moods shifted faster than the sky. The 73 × 92 cm canvas belongs to a cycle of roughly 36 paintings he brought back from that Antibes campaign.

source.credit: Hohenbuchau Collection, on permanent loan to Liechtenstein, The Princely Collections, Vienna

'Still_Life_with_Fruit,_Dead_Game,_Veget.story: Chaos on a sideboard. Grapes glow, peaches bruise, and a felled swan drapes across the table, but the drama is elsewhere: a monkey has stolen a pear, a squirrel gnaws a nut, and a cat has just noticed both. Snyders specialized in these pantry riots, where luxury and larceny share a surface. The title lists the cast like a playbill because that's how buyers ordered them in 1635 Antwerp, pricing the painting by how many creatures it contained.

'Taj_Mahal'_by_Charles_W._Bartlett,_1916.story: The mausoleum and its flanking mosque and jawab float on the far bank of the Yamuna, rendered in the pale sand and dove-grey of a cool morning. The lower half is all river: a glassy, near-symmetrical reflection broken only by a small boat and a single figure in a red robe and white turban seated on the near shore. You can see the CWB cartouche and 'Taj Mahal 1916' block-printed in the lower left. Bartlett cut this in Tokyo with the shin-hanga publisher Watanabe Shozaburo during a round-the-world trip.

'The_Beach_at_Étretat'_by_Claude_Monet,_.story: Monet came back to Étretat in autumn 1885, staying at the Hôtel Blanquet through the stormy season. The cliffs in this canvas lean into a low winter sun, the Porte d'Aval arch cutting its famous silhouette. He painted from a rented fisherman's hut on the shingle, stove burning, doors open to the spray. The picture entered Sergei Shchukin's collection and is now at the Pushkin Museum in Moscow.

'The_Grand_Quay_at_Havre'_by_Claude_Mone.story: Back in his birthplace in autumn 1874, Monet set up at the working quay among bales of merchandise and moored ships, with the port's administrative buildings stacking up behind. He never finished it. Left rough and streaky in places, it went on to live in Otto Krebs's collection, seized by the Red Army in 1945, and is now in the Hermitage. One of four Le Havre port views from that trip.

source.canonical_title: File:'The Tea Service' oil on canvas painting by Claude Monet, 1872.jpg

'The_Tea_Service'_oil_on_canvas_painting.story: Painted in 1872, the year Monet and Camille settled into Argenteuil on the Seine and the first proper Impressionist summer began. A domestic moment: teapot, cups, folded cloth, light catching china. No drama. It's mostly a painter trying out what light does to glazes and silver reflections, the same attention that would within a couple of years be turning up in the poppy fields and regatta scenes that made his name.

title.avk: Fentugalaf miel koe Ekely (trutca ke Munch)

'Winter_Night,_Ekely'_by_Edvard_Munch,_1.story: Painted from the garden at Ekely, the property outside Oslo where Munch spent his last two decades mostly alone. A bare thicket of saplings rises dead-centre, blue-black against snow that goes pale green and violet in the fading light; a red farm building glows behind the ridge. This is late Munch, loose and almost scribbled, the paint thinly scrubbed so the weave of the canvas shows through. No scream, no anguish - just an old man at his studio window, watching his own trees, still interested in what winter does to colour.

(Barcelona)_Apullia_in_Search_of_Appullu.story: Turner's sly answer to a Royal Academy prize he felt snubbed by. In 1814 he submitted this canvas to the British Institution's landscape competition, lifting the composition almost directly from a Claude Lorrain the judges had praised. The trees, the gold light, the tiny figures searching for the shepherd Appullus, all Claude in costume. The judges rejected it anyway. It now hangs in Tate Britain.

(Barcelona)_Shipping_-_1825-30_-_William.story: Masts dissolve into weather. Turner spent the late 1820s losing interest in the edges of things, and this small unfinished study shows it, ships half-born out of a bruised sky. No drama, no shipwreck, just the sea doing its daily work. The canvas sat unexhibited in his studio until his death in 1851, when the Turner Bequest delivered nearly 300 oils to the nation.

(Barcelona)_Story_of_Apollo_and_Daphne_1.story: Apollo chases, Daphne flees, and Turner barely cares about either of them. The real subject is a hazy Italian valley liquefied by late afternoon sun. The myth supplies only the excuse. He exhibited it at the Royal Academy in 1837, the same year Victoria took the throne, and critics complained as usual that his figures looked like smears.

01_-_Ichikobu_Bridge.jpg.story: Ikkoku Bridge crosses a moat in Edo; beyond it, Fuji rises pale against a graded sky. Samurai residences line the water, their whitewashed walls catching the light. Hiroshige loved this trick of using a city bridge as a stage for the distant mountain. This is sheet one of his vertical Thirty-six Views of Mount Fuji, published in 1858 — the year he died of cholera at sixty-one. The series came out in the fourth month, posthumously completed.

07leucip.jpg.story: One horse rears, the other stays put. Two brothers, Castor and Pollux, swing the daughters of Leucippus up onto the saddles, and two putti grin from below. Rubens freezes the whole spiral at its most wound-up moment, diagonal limbs locking everyone into the knot. Jan Wildens did the sliver of landscape. Painted around 1618, it hangs in Munich's Alte Pinakothek, where generations of students have used it to argue about how Baroque composition actually works.

09_-_The_Teahouse_with_the_View_of_Mt._F.story: A teahouse perches on a hill; patrons lean on the railing to catch the best view of Fuji across the bay. It's the kind of scene Hiroshige witnessed a thousand times — travelers pausing for hot tea and a moment of the mountain. The composition stacks beautifully: roof, figures, pine, sea, Fuji. From the 1858 vertical Thirty-six Views of Mount Fuji, the last great series he completed before his death that same year. Edo teahouses charged a few mon; the view was free.

0_Entrevue_du_roi_et_de_Marie_de_Médicis.title: The Meeting of Marie de' Medici and Henry IV at Lyons

source.canonical_title: File:0 Entrevue du roi et de Marie de Médicis à Lyon - P.P. Rubens - Louvre 2.JPG
source.permission: This illustration was made by Jean-Pol GRANDMONT Please credit this : Jean-Pol GRANDMONT An email to Jean-Pol GRANDMONT would be appreciated.

title.fr: Entrevue du roi et de Marie de Médicis à Lyon le 9 novembre 1600.

0_Entrevue_du_roi_et_de_Marie_de_Médicis.story: Marie de' Medici wanted her life painted as myth, so Rubens obliged. Here she and Henry IV meet at Lyon disguised as Juno and Jupiter, peacocks and eagle in tow, while the city herself kneels below in a lion-drawn chariot. The couple had actually married by proxy in Florence months earlier and met for the first time at Lyon in December 1600 — hardly the divine summit shown. Rubens received the commission in autumn 1621 and delivered 24 canvases for the Luxembourg Palace by 1625. They now hang together in the Louvre's Galerie Médicis.

0_Le_Sultan_Mulay_Ahmad_de_Tunis_-_Ruben.title: Portrait of Ahmed III al-Hafsi Sultan of Tunis Alternative title(s): Portrait of Mulay Ahmad
0_Le_Sultan_Mulay_Ahmad_de_Tunis_-_Ruben.artist: Peter Paul Rubens / After Jan Cornelisz Vermeyen

0_Le_Sultan_Mulay_Ahmad_de_Tunis_-_Ruben.story: Rubens painted this copy around 1613 from a portrait by Jan Cornelisz Vermeyen, who had actually travelled to Tunis with Charles V in 1535. Mulay Ahmad — the Hafsid sultan deposed in that campaign — stands in a deep green robe cinched by a red-and-gold baldric, a curved dagger slung at his waist, the ruined Roman amphitheatre at El Djem rising behind him. Rubens clearly relished the turban's white architecture and the sheen of the silk, treating the commission less as ethnography than as a chance to study a great early Netherlandish source firsthand.

100_views_edo_063.jpg.story: Koi streamers snap above the rooftops for Boys' Day while Mount Fuji sits small and snowy in the gap between them. Below, the Suidobashi bridge and the Surugadai bluff — a samurai neighborhood — go about their business. Hiroshige likes this scale game: a paper fish looming bigger than a sacred mountain. From One Hundred Famous Views of Edo, the summer section, printed in 1857. The carp banners were meant to give sons the strength to swim upstream; Tokyo families still fly them every May 5th.

100_views_edo_076.jpg.story: Rafts of bamboo poles float at Kyobashi, stacked so thick they look like a second bridge. A line of travelers crosses overhead under a full moon; beneath, a boatman poles past the yards. The print is almost monochrome — deep indigo water, pale moon, the ochre bamboo — and it's one of Hiroshige's most restrained compositions. Autumn entry in the One Hundred Famous Views of Edo, published in 1857. Kyobashi's bamboo market supplied scaffolding and blinds to the whole shogunal city.

10_The_Prodigal_Son.jpg.title: Prodigal Son amid the swine

source.canonical_title: File:10 The Prodigal Son.jpg

title.nl: De verloren zoon bij de zwijnen
title.de: Der verlorene Sohn bei den Schweinen

10_The_Prodigal_Son.jpg.story: Dürer engraved this around 1496, just back from his first Italian trip and showing off. The prodigal son kneels in the muck of a German farmyard — not a biblical Judea but the wood-and-wattle buildings Dürer knew from Franconia — while the pigs crowd a trough at his knees. What made it famous in his own lifetime was the precision: every shingle on the roof, every bristle on the sow, the exact way light catches the young man's clasped hands. Dürer chose the moment of the parable nobody else was painting — not the homecoming, but the hinge, when the son realizes he has to go home.

11_-_Wild_Goose_Hill_and_the_Tone_River..story: Kōnodai sits above a bend in the Tone River, and Hiroshige perches us right on its grassy edge. Barges drift below, sails slack, while Fuji floats across the plain like an afterthought in pale blue. The title, literally 'Wild Goose Hill,' hints at the migrating flocks locals once watched here. This is one of the 36 vertical views Hiroshige designed in his final year; Tsutaya Kichizō published the series in 1858, the year the artist died of cholera in Edo.

1280px-Arcimboldo_Winter_1563.jpg.title: Allegory of Winter

source.canonical_title: File:Arcimboldo Winter 1563.jpg

1280px-Arcimboldo_Winter_1563.jpg.story: The most unsettling of Arcimboldo's four seasons: a gnarled old man made entirely of dead wood, his cheek a fungal burl, his lips a split mushroom, ivy trailing from the crown of his skull like unwashed hair. A straw mat wraps his shoulders against the cold, and the only living colour is a lemon and orange hanging from a broken twig at his chest, Medici fruits flattering the emperor who commissioned the set. It's a portrait as botanical joke, and yet the face is genuinely sad, the way an old tree in January is sad.

1280px-De_schovenbindster_(naar_Millet)_.title: Peasant Woman Binding Sheaves (after Millet)

source.canonical_title: File:De schovenbindster (naar Millet) - s0172V1962 - Van Gogh Museum.jpg

1280px-De_schovenbindster_(naar_Millet)_.story: Shut inside the asylum at Saint-Rémy through the winter of 1889, van Gogh had no models and bad weather, so he asked Theo to send black-and-white prints after Millet and set about 'translating' them into his own colour. The peasant woman stoops to bind wheat under a sky of molten yellow, her body all curves and torque. He called these copies his 'improvisations', like a musician playing another composer's score. They're some of his most tender works — a homage to the painter he'd revered since he was a Dutch preacher sketching miners.

1280px-Eugène_Ferdinand_Victor_Delacroi.title: Arab saddling his horse

source.canonical_title: File:Eugène Ferdinand Victor Delacroix 025.jpg
source.credit: 1. The Yorck Project (2002) 10.000 Meisterwerke der Malerei (DVD-ROM), distributed by DIRECTMEDIA Publishing GmbH. ISBN : 3936122202 . 2. artclon.com , image 3. The Hermitage, St. Petersburg

1280px-Eugène_Ferdinand_Victor_Delacroi.story: Two decades after Morocco, Delacroix was still mining the sketchbooks. A lone figure cinches a saddle against a stormy sky, a sword lying at his feet, the horse clearly on edge. The landscape is more stage set than geography — the picture is really about the tension between the calm, deliberate hands and the thunder gathering behind. Hermitage, St Petersburg.

1280px-Gericault_Theodore_1819-20_Portra.title: Portrait Study of a Youth

source.canonical_title: File:Gericault Theodore 1819-20 Portrait eines Jungen mit langem blonden Haar.jpg

description.de: Porträt eines Jungen mit langem blonden Haar

1280px-Gericault_Theodore_1819-20_Portra.story: A study rather than a finished portrait: a young sitter, long blond hair, face caught in a soft unguarded light. Gericault painted dozens of these close-range heads — models, friends, studio assistants — as exercises in character before they slid into more ambitious pictures. The handling is quick and direct, paint worked wet into wet. Done in 1819 or 1820, around the whirlwind of the Medusa Salon, it shows the side of Gericault that wasn't chasing scandal: an attentive, almost tender portraitist.

1280px-Gérôme-Black_Bashi-Bazouk-c._18.title: Bashi-Bazouk

source.canonical_title: File:Gérôme-Black Bashi-Bazouk-c. 1869.jpg
source.credit: Metropolitan Museum of Art, online collection (The Met object ID 440723)

1280px-Gérôme-Black_Bashi-Bazouk-c._18.story: A single figure, a Black bashi-bazouk, stands against a dark ground in a turban and embroidered silk tunic. Bashi-bazouks were the Ottoman Empire's notorious irregulars, paid in loot rather than salary; Gérôme painted them repeatedly after his travels in Egypt and the Levant. The sitter here was most likely a Parisian model dressed from the artist's own collection of costumes and weapons. Stripped of narrative and setting, the portrait lands somewhere between ethnographic study and character head, more interested in the fall of striped fabric and the lift of the chin than in telling any story.

1280px-Giuseppe_Arcimboldo_-_Four_Season.title: Four Seasons in One Head

source.canonical_title: File:Giuseppe Arcimboldo - Four Seasons in One Head - Google Art Project.jpg
source.credit: WwHACWGI-pgLUQ at Google Cultural Institute maximum zoom level

1280px-Giuseppe_Arcimboldo_-_Four_Season.story: A late, darker self-reflection. Painted around 1590, near the end of Arcimboldo's life, this single head crams all four seasons into one gnarled tree-man: a bare winter branch for the skull, summer cherries and plums cascading as hair, autumn grapes at the cheek, a few green spring shoots at the neck. The mood is wintry; the grin almost wry. Many scholars read it as a veiled self-portrait. It now hangs in the National Gallery of Art in Washington.

1280px-Giuseppe_Arcimboldo_-_La_Primaver.title: Primavera

source.canonical_title: File:Giuseppe Arcimboldo - La Primavera - Google Art Project.jpg
source.credit: iwHATomxJenU4w at Google Cultural Institute , zoom level maximum

1280px-Giuseppe_Arcimboldo_-_La_Primaver.story: Spring in full bouquet. Her cheek is a pink rose, her eyes budding flowers, her teeth the pale petals of a lily, and her whole torso blooms from collar to shoulder. Arcimboldo painted this version in 1573 for Emperor Maximilian II, a revisit of a theme he'd first tried a decade earlier. Botanists have counted roughly eighty identifiable plant species packed into her. She's now in Madrid's Real Academia de Bellas Artes de San Fernando.

1280px-Giuseppe_Arcimboldo_-_Summer_-_Go.title: The Summer

source.canonical_title: File:Giuseppe Arcimboldo - Summer - Google Art Project.jpg
source.credit: EAHRfTFyVNYeEA at Google Cultural Institute maximum zoom level

1280px-Giuseppe_Arcimboldo_-_Summer_-_Go.story: A portrait you can eat. Summer's cheek is a ripe peach, her nose a cucumber, her ear a split eggplant, her lips a pair of cherries, and her straw jacket is literally woven straw. Arcimboldo painted her in 1563 for the Habsburg court in Vienna, where Emperor Maximilian II loved a good visual riddle. Look at the collar of the Louvre version and you'll spot 'GIUSEPPE ARCIMBOLDO F' and '1563' stitched into the weave. The Vienna original is plainer around the edges, no floral frame.

1280px-Gustave_Caillebotte_-_The_Orange_.title: The Orange Trees

source.canonical_title: File:Gustave Caillebotte - The Orange Trees - Google Art Project.jpg
source.credit: 3QHnQ99LLC7m3A at Google Cultural Institute maximum zoom level

1280px-Gustave_Caillebotte_-_The_Orange_.story: An August afternoon at the family estate in Yerres, just southeast of Paris. Caillebotte's brother Martial lounges in a cane chair with a book, back to us, while their cousin Zoé stands primly under a parasol. The orange trees are pruned into neat compact balls, very Caillebotte: he loved manicured geometry where his Impressionist friends loved wildness. He painted it outdoors in 1878. The canvas is over five feet tall, and it now hangs at the Museum of Fine Arts, Houston.

title.fr: Vente esclave / Marché d'esclaves dans la Rome antique

1280px-Jean-Léon_Gérôme_-_Slave_Marke.story: On a stone platform in a Roman forum, an auctioneer hoists a naked woman above the bidding crowd. Gérôme painted several slave-market scenes — Roman, Ottoman, Egyptian — and they tended to outsell everything else in his studio. The archaeological trim is meticulous; the moral posture is harder to pin down. Critics then and now have argued over whether the pictures indict the trade or simply package it for bourgeois consumption. The Hermitage version, from around 1884, is the most clinical of the set.

1280px-Jean_Léon_Gerome_1896_La_Vérite.story: The full title is gloriously unhinged: Truth Coming Out of the Well Armed with Her Whip to Chastise Humanity. A naked woman hauls herself over the stone rim, cat-o'-nine-tails in hand, ready to deal out lashings. Gérôme made at least four Truth-in-a-well pictures in the 1890s, riffing on Democritus's line that truth lives at the bottom of one. Writers love to tie it to the Dreyfus affair, but Gérôme signed the anti-Dreyfus petitions — scholars now read it more convincingly as his ongoing scourging of the Impressionists. It hangs in Moulins, at the Musée Anne-de-Beaujeu.

1280px-John_Constable_-_The_Vale_of_Dedh.title: The Vale of Dedham

source.canonical_title: File:John Constable - The Vale of Dedham - Google Art Project.jpg
source.credit: 3wH6bKPjBycRxg at Google Cultural Institute maximum zoom level

1280px-John_Constable_-_The_Vale_of_Dedh.story: Constable's own childhood valley, seen from above. The Stour winds out to the sea at Harwich, his father's mills are tucked in among the trees, and a little gypsy encampment smoulders in the left foreground, a kettle propped over the fire. He had sketched this view in oil twenty years earlier; now, settled and grieving after Maria's death in 1828, he worked it up into a full Royal Academy picture for 1828. The National Galleries of Scotland bought it in 1944.

1280px-Nihon_fūkei_senshū,_Okayama_Uch.story: Uchisange is a central district of Okayama, the approach to the castle where daimyō retainers once kept their residences. Hasui drew it in 1923 for the ongoing Selected Views of Japan series, focusing on everyday roofs and a quiet intersection rather than the fortifications nearby. The timing matters: the same year, the Great Kantō earthquake destroyed his publisher Watanabe Shōzaburō's Tokyo workshop, taking most of the series' original blocks and 188 sketchbooks with it. Many late prints in the set, including this one, exist only in first impressions made before the fire.

Peter_Paul_Rubens_-_Old_Woman_and_Boy_wi.story: A boy leans in to light his candle from an old woman's, cheeks lit from below, her mouth slightly open as she steadies the flame. It is Rubens in Caravaggesque mode, a single wick doing all the illumination, shadows pooling in every wrinkle. The composition descends from a famous lost Gerard Dou-style tronie tradition, but Rubens paints it with buttery oil and real warmth. It hangs in the Mauritshuis in The Hague.

1280px-Pierre_Puvis_de_Chavannes_-_Young.title: Jeunes filles au bord de la mer

source.canonical_title: File:Pierre Puvis de Chavannes - Young Girls by the Seaside - Google Art Project.jpg
source.credit: CAGcDHZdQpElXA at Google Cultural Institute maximum zoom level

1280px-Pierre_Puvis_de_Chavannes_-_Young.story: Three women on a bare shore, doing almost nothing. One combs her hair, one stares at the sand, one has her back turned. There's no story here — just pale skin, cool sea, and the hush of Puvis de Chavannes's muted palette that looks like fresco even though it's oil. The Symbolists adored him for exactly this: mood instead of narrative. Painted in 1879 and now at the Musée d'Orsay. Seurat kept a reproduction pinned up in his studio.

1280px-Retrato_de_la_esposa_del_artista_.title: Portrait of the painters' wife and their two oldest children
1280px-Retrato_de_la_esposa_del_artista_.description: The portrait was most probably painted shortly after Holbein's return to Basel from England in 1528. Based on an entry in the Amerbach inventory of 1587, it is believed to show his wife, Elsbeth (born Binzenstock, and previously wife of the deceased tanner Ulrich Schmid), whom he had married in 1519. Also in the picture are his two eldest children, Philipp, born around 1522, and Katherina, born around 1526. Holbein's two youngest children, Jakob and Küngold, were born around 1529 and 1530. Originally the figures were painted on paper. Subsequently, they were cut out round the outlines and stuck to a dark panel. Part of the fringes of the picture were lost in the cutting, including the full date (bottom right corner). Scholars have called this work, which was influenced by the religious iconography of the madonna, one of the most personal of Holbein's portraits. (References: Buck, pp. 75–76; John Rowlands, Holbein: The Paintings of Hans Holbein the Younger, Boston: David R. Godine, 1985, ISBN 0879235780 , p. 31; Christian Müller; Stephan Kemperdick; Maryan W. Ainsworth; et al ,. Hans Holbein the Younger: The Basel Years, 1515–1532, Munich: Prestel, 2006, ISBN 3791335804 , pp. 403–405.)

source.canonical_title: File:Retrato de la esposa del artista con sus dos hijos, por Hans Holbein el Joven.jpg

title.es: Retrato de la esposa del artista con sus dos hijos
title.ja: 画家の家族の肖像 (ホルバイン)
title.de: Bildnis der Frau des Künstlers mit den beiden ältesten Kindern
title.nl: Portret van de vrouw van de kunstenaar met hun twee oudste kinderen

1280px-Retrato_de_la_esposa_del_artista_.story: Holbein came home to Basel in 1528 after two years in England and painted his wife Elsbeth with their two oldest children, Philipp and Katherina. He doesn't flatter her. Her eyes are red-rimmed, her mouth set; the little girl in the apricot smock looks away from him, the boy up at her. The composition borrows the shape of a Madonna and Child, which makes the frankness of the faces hit harder. The figures were originally on paper, later cut out and pasted to this dark panel - which is why the edges look slightly ragged.

1280px-Rocky_Landscape_in_the_Elbe_Sands.title: Rocky ravine in the Elbe Sandstone Mountains
1280px-Rocky_Landscape_in_the_Elbe_Sands.description: Dargestellt ist die Felsengruppe des Neurathener Felsentores (heute: Kleine Steinschleuder)

source.canonical_title: File:Rocky Landscape in the Elbe Sandstone Mountains - Caspar David Friedrich - Google Cultural Institute.jpg

1280px-Rocky_Landscape_in_the_Elbe_Sands.story: The rocks Friedrich piles up here are real — the Neurathen gate in Saxon Switzerland, a famous sandstone formation southeast of Dresden — but he stitched them together with peaks from entirely different sketches, because topography was never the point. A dead fir lies across the foreground, splintered stumps bracket the gorge, and the far summits dissolve into a bright haze. Painted around 1822-23 and now at the Belvedere in Vienna, it is one of his most concentrated sermons in stone: a ravine of death below, the unreachable divine above.

1280px-Suzuki_Harunobu_-_Evening_Snow_on.story: One of Harunobu's cleverer domestic inventions. The 'Eight Parlour Views' series transplants the classical Eight Views landscape tradition into a woman's room; here, a white cotton cloth tossed over the kotatsu heater becomes the 'evening snow.' The whiteness is embossed — gauffrage, pressed without ink — so the cotton really does seem to mound up off the page. A private joke about domesticity standing in for grand scenery, executed with the technical refinement that makes a Harunobu print feel almost tactile.

1280px-The_Chess_Game.jpg.title: The Chess Game

source.canonical_title: File:The Chess Game.jpg

1280px-The_Chess_Game.jpg.story: Two men bent over a chessboard in a tiled Cairo interior, a third watching from the side. Deutsch loved this kind of subject — quiet, contained, entirely about the play of light on costly surfaces. Every inch of the room is worked up: the glazed tiles, the inlaid table, the striped silk of the robes, the Qurans and brass lamps on the shelves behind. The game itself barely matters; what matters is the hush. Painted at the height of his powers, it is the sort of picture that sold immediately to a European collector who wanted a corner of Cairo hung on a Paris wall, and got it in almost hallucinatory detail.

1280px-Théodore_Géricault_-_Evening,_L.story: Part of a trio of monumental landscapes Gericault painted in 1818, each tuned to a time of day. 'Evening' goes for the heroic late-afternoon sublime: a crumbling Roman aqueduct cutting across a darkening valley, tiny figures dwarfed by storm light and ruin. Gericault isn't usually thought of as a landscapist — he's the Medusa guy — but these canvases show him chasing Poussin and Salvator Rosa, working out how to make nature itself theatrical. Painted the year before the Salon bombshell that made his name.

1280px-Thomas_Gainsborough_-_Clayton_Jon.title: Clayton Jones

source.canonical_title: File:Thomas Gainsborough - Clayton Jones - Google Art Project.jpg
source.credit: JgGJdiwSpAGoIA at Google Cultural Institute maximum zoom level

1280px-Thomas_Gainsborough_-_Clayton_Jon.story: A young Welsh gentleman in a powder-blue coat, painted when Gainsborough himself was barely seventeen. The brushwork is already confident but the face is still a student's, a little stiff around the mouth. Clayton Jones of Henllys was a neighbour in Suffolk, roughly the same age, and the portrait feels like two teenagers trying to look grown up. Gainsborough was apprenticed in London at the time and picked up commissions on visits home. It's one of his earliest surviving works, dated around 1744–45, now in the Yale Center for British Art.

1280px-Thomas_Gainsborough_-_The_Marsham.title: The Marsham Children

source.canonical_title: File:Thomas Gainsborough - The Marsham Children - Google Art Project.jpg

1280px-Thomas_Gainsborough_-_The_Marsham.story: Four siblings caught mid-scamper: the eldest girl steadies her little brother on a slope while the middle boy stretches up to gather nuts from a tree and his sister reaches into his apron for one. Gainsborough painted the Marsham children of Norfolk in 1787, the year before he died of cancer. The brushwork is feathery, almost gestural, the kids in powder-blue silk sashes. He boasted to a friend that he'd taken great trouble over it. It's now in the Gemäldegalerie, Berlin.

1280px-Van_Gogh_-_Das_Restaurant_Rispal_.title: The restaurant Rispal in Asnières

source.canonical_title: File:Van Gogh - Das Restaurant Rispal in Asniéres.jpeg
source.credit: 1. repro from art book 2. Google Art Project works from the Nelson-Atkins Museum of Art

1280px-Van_Gogh_-_Das_Restaurant_Rispal_.story: Asnieres, summer 1887. Van Gogh walked out along the Seine with his friend Emile Bernard and painted the riverside restaurants the Parisians took the train to on Sundays. Rispal's is caught in broad daylight, awning out, facade broken into flecks of clean colour — pure proof that the Paris year has done its work. The brown Dutch palette is gone; in its place, that peculiar Van Gogh mid-tone sunshine. Bernard remembered them arguing about Seurat the whole way home.

1280px-Van_Gogh_-_Garten_des_Hospitals_S.story: The walled garden of the Saint-Paul-de-Mausole asylum was one of the few subjects he was allowed to paint from life during his year at Saint-Rémy. Here a single small figure stands among massive pines whose trunks twist and flame upward, dwarfed by vegetation that feels half-alive. The raked path, the bench, the low wall — the whole enclosed world he could actually walk through. He described the garden to Theo as melancholy but beautiful, and you can sense both: a sick man finding Romanesque grandeur inside the exercise yard.

1280px-Van_Gogh_-_Weizenfeld_mit_Blick_a.story: Summer 1888, the first Arles wheat harvest, and Van Gogh is painting at full throttle. A field of cut stubble stretches to the little town on the horizon, roofs and church tower low against a hot sky. He loved the flat Provence light — he told Theo it was as clean as a Japanese print — and the canvas has the same cropped, high horizon he'd admired in Hokusai. Pure working country, painted fast, and one of the cornerstones of the great Arles summer.

1280px-Vincent_van_Gogh_-_Head_of_a_skel.story: A grinning skull clamps a cigarette between its teeth — smoke still curling up, one good ember at the tip. Van Gogh painted it in Antwerp in the winter of 1885–86 while enrolled at the art academy, where students drilled for hours copying plaster casts and skeletons. The joke is partly on that dry training, partly on his own habits: he was chain-smoking a pipe, losing teeth, and living on coffee. It's a small panel, barely 32 cm tall, now a star piece at the Van Gogh Museum in Amsterdam.

1280px-Vincent_van_Gogh_-_The_Postman_(J.title: The Postman (Joseph-Étienne Roulin)

source.canonical_title: File:Vincent van Gogh - The Postman (Joseph-Étienne Roulin) - BF37 - Barnes Foundation.jpg

1280px-Vincent_van_Gogh_-_The_Postman_(J.story: Roulin wasn't a postman, strictly speaking — he worked the Arles train station sorting mail — but van Gogh latched onto him as a steady, republican, drink-sharing friend during a very lonely year. He painted Roulin six times; this Barnes version catches the full splendour of the blue uniform with its gold braid, the forked Socratic beard, the wary-but-patient eyes. Van Gogh told Theo he painted it in a single sitting. Roulin kept visiting him in the hospital after the ear incident and helped move his things out of the Yellow House.

1280px-Wilhelm_von_Kobell_-_Reiter_am_Te.title: Riders at the Tegernsee

source.canonical_title: File:Wilhelm von Kobell - Reiter am Tegernsee - Google Art Project.jpg

1280px-Wilhelm_von_Kobell_-_Reiter_am_Te.story: Two riders have reined in above the Tegernsee, and Kobell paints the moment as if the air itself were holding still. The lake glints below, the Alps crease the horizon, and every button on the officer's jacket catches sun. It's oil on panel, 1832, now in Berlin's Alte Nationalgalerie. Kobell was sixty-six by then, and his late style hardened into this crystalline clarity, figures and landscape coexisting without blending. The horses barely breathe.

1280px-Zelfportret_als_schilder_-_s0022V.title: Self portrait as a painter

source.canonical_title: File:Zelfportret als schilder - s0022V1962 - Van Gogh Museum.jpg

1280px-Zelfportret_als_schilder_-_s0022V.story: Painted at the very end of the Paris years, winter 1887-88, just before Arles. Van Gogh shows himself at the easel in working clothes, palette loaded, brush in hand — no romantic flourishes. The face is gaunt, the beard red, the eyes wary. He wrote to his sister that he wanted a portrait that showed 'a deeper likeness than the photographer's.' It was the last self-portrait he did in Paris and, in a way, his farewell to the city. Van Gogh Museum, Amsterdam.

1280px-Zelfportret_met_grijze_vilthoed_-.title: Self-Portrait with Grey Felt Hat

source.canonical_title: File:Zelfportret met grijze vilthoed - s0016V1962 - Van Gogh Museum.jpg

1280px-Zelfportret_met_grijze_vilthoed_-.story: Paris, winter 1887. Van Gogh in a grey felt hat, set against a halo of short divided strokes — his quick, half-digested answer to Seurat and Signac. The face itself is painted looser, ruddier, with the familiar wary blue eyes. He made more than twenty self-portraits in Paris, partly because models cost money and partly because he was teaching himself, head by head, how to handle colour. One of the sharpest of the series. Van Gogh Museum, Amsterdam.

1529_Cranach_Allegorie_auf_Gesetz_und_Gn.title: Allegory of Law and Grace
1529_Cranach_Allegorie_auf_Gesetz_und_Gn.description: Allegory of Law and Grace. Painting on beech, later sawn into two panels. This Lutheran allegory teaches how the salvation of mankind is attained through the grace of God. On the left Death and the Devil drive the sinner into Hell. The law of the 10 Commandments cannot help him at the Last Judgment. The tree has withered. By contrast, on the right, John the Baptist points to Christ, who has died for mankind. The Resurrection and the leafy crown of the tree signify life, which the grace of God bestows on the faithful. This depiction of Lutheran theology long belonged to the Protestant canon of images.

source.canonical_title: File:1529 Cranach Allegorie auf Gesetz und Gnade anagoria.JPG

1529_Cranach_Allegorie_auf_Gesetz_und_Gn.story: A Lutheran diagram disguised as a painting. On the left: a naked sinner driven into hell by Death and the Devil, the Ten Commandments useless, the tree withered. On the right: John the Baptist points to the crucified and risen Christ, the same tree now leafy, salvation arriving by grace alone. Cranach painted it in 1529 on a single beech panel that was later sawn in two. The image was so clean a translation of Luther's theology that it became a Protestant icon — reproduced, adapted and copied across Germany for the rest of the century.

1596_Caravaggio,_The_Lute_Player_New_Yor.title: The Lute Player

source.canonical_title: File:1596 Caravaggio, The Lute Player New York.jpg
source.credit: Wildenstein Collection de:Image:1596 Caravaggio, The Lute Player Wildenstein Collection.jpg

1596_Caravaggio,_The_Lute_Player_New_Yor.story: The New York version of the Lute Player — Wildenstein Collection, long on loan to the Met — puts a Turkish carpet under the instruments and a caged songbird in the shadows. A tenor recorder and a small spinetta crowd the table. The boy's shirt has an odd broad yoke, almost dress-like, one reason early viewers took him for a girl. The music set in front of him includes pieces by Francesco de Layolle and Jacquet de Berchem, madrigals built on Petrarch's sonnets about longing.

15_Qian_Xuan_Eight_Flowers_National_Pala.title: Eight Flowers
15_Qian_Xuan_Eight_Flowers_National_Pala.description: Qian Xuan, Eight Flowers , Palace Museum, Beijing.

source.canonical_title: File:15 Qian Xuan Eight Flowers National Palace Museum Beijing.JPG

15_Qian_Xuan_Eight_Flowers_National_Pala.story: A handscroll that unrolls as eight discrete flower studies — narcissus, peonies, camellia, a branch of plum, pear blossom — each isolated against bare silk, nothing holding them together except the viewer's moving gaze. Qian Xuan was one of the Eight Talents of Wuxing and a Song loyalist who refused to serve the Mongol Yuan court after 1279. He retreated into painting and deliberately revived older, pre-conquest styles; this meticulous, unshowy approach to bird-and-flower work is part of that quiet protest. Each blossom reads less as botany than as a small act of remembering.

1627_Rubens_Maria_mit_dem_Kind_anagoria..title: Madonna and Child
1627_Rubens_Maria_mit_dem_Kind_anagoria..artist: Peter Paul Rubens / Jan Brueghel the Younger

source.canonical_title: File:1627 Rubens Maria mit dem Kind anagoria.JPG

1627_Rubens_Maria_mit_dem_Kind_anagoria..story: A true studio collaboration: Rubens paints the figures, Jan Brueghel the Younger handles everything green and growing. Mary in her red dress leans toward the nursing child, one hand steadying an illuminated book on the carpet-draped table. A fruit basket spills peaches and grapes at her elbow; roses cascade down the left side like a curtain pulled open. The younger Brueghel had inherited his father's Antwerp workshop only two years earlier, in 1625, and kept the Rubens partnership running for another decade. The seam between the two hands is almost invisible, which was the point.

1665_Girl_with_a_Pearl_Earring.jpg.story: Not a portrait — a tronie, Dutch for a study of a type or expression rather than a specific person. The turban is exotic costume, the pearl impossibly large (likely glass or tin, given the size). Recent scanning at the Mauritshuis found what the naked eye misses: eyelashes Vermeer painted in around both eyes, and a green curtain behind her head that has faded away as the copper-based pigment broke down over three centuries. The blue of the headscarf is natural ultramarine, ground from Afghan lapis lazuli — in Vermeer's Delft, worth more by weight than gold.

17_-_The_Sea_off_the_Miura_Peninsula.jpg.story: Pink clouds wrap Fuji's waist like a scarf, and a pine-studded cliff juts into Sagami Bay while three sails push out past the rocks. Hiroshige layers the view in bands, near pines, middle cliff, distant peak, so your eye steps out to sea one plane at a time. The Miura Peninsula was a real landmark for ships rounding toward Edo. The print belongs to his final Fuji series, vertical ōban format, roughly 36 by 24 cm, published by Tsutaya Kichizō in 1858.

1813_Schinkel_Blick_auf_den_Mont_Blanc_a.title: View of Mont Blanc" Alternative title: " Blick auf den Mont Blanc aus einem Hochgebirgstal mit Bauernhof im Vordergrund " and " Landschaft im Charakter des Montblanc

source.canonical_title: File:1813 Schinkel Blick auf den Mont Blanc anagoria.JPG

1813_Schinkel_Blick_auf_den_Mont_Blanc_a.story: A Savoyard chalet hunches on a bluff in the foreground, goats picking their way down a dirt path, a stone bridge arcing over a river, and Mont Blanc floats pink and unreal on the horizon. Schinkel painted it in 1813 - the year Prussia was still fighting Napoleon and his architectural career had not yet taken off - and the whole thing reads more like a staged scene than a topographical study. Which fits: he was designing opera sets around the same time. The working title admitted as much, calling it a landscape 'in the character of' Mont Blanc, a mood rather than a record.

1815_Schinkel_Mittelalterliche_Stadt_an_.title: Medieval City on a River

source.canonical_title: File:1815 Schinkel Mittelalterliche Stadt an einem Fluss anagoria.JPG

1815_Schinkel_Mittelalterliche_Stadt_an_.story: Schinkel's 'Medieval City on a River' is a Romantic fantasia more than a real place: a rose-coloured Gothic cathedral shoots up behind a wooded ridge, flanked by a rainbow arcing out of retreating storm clouds, while a procession of banners and horsemen winds toward the west portal and a dreamy city of spires stretches to the horizon. Painted in 1815, the architect-painter fused his two obsessions — idealised Gothic and post-Napoleonic national hope. The canvas hangs at the Alte Nationalgalerie in Berlin; this high-resolution capture comes via the Commons photographer anagoria.

1836_Heimkehr_des_Palikaren_anagoria.jpe.title: Palikare Return Home

source.canonical_title: File:Eduard Magnus - Heimkehr des Palikaren, 1836.jpg

1836_Heimkehr_des_Palikaren_anagoria.jpe.story: A Palikar - one of the Greek irregular soldiers who fought in the War of Independence - is coming home at sunset with his wife, children and a slung musket. Magnus paints him bearded and travel-worn, cradling a sleeping baby while a toddler clings to his leg and an older girl looks up adoringly. Behind them, mountains go pink in the last light and a caïque waits on the shore. It's pure philhellene kitsch from 1836, when every educated Berliner had opinions about Greek liberty, but Magnus is a good enough portraitist that the faces stay specific rather than generic.

1859_Menzel_Studentenfackelzug_anagoria..title: Student Torchlight Procession

source.canonical_title: File:1859 Menzel Studentenfackelzug anagoria.JPG

1859_Menzel_Studentenfackelzug_anagoria..story: A small oil on cardboard, 31 by 54 centimetres, and essentially a painted flare. In February 1858 Berlin students marched by torchlight to greet Crown Prince Friedrich Wilhelm and his English bride Victoria, a demonstration of liberal hopes dressed up as a wedding tribute. Menzel — always interested in what crowds and artificial light do to a street — turns the whole thing into smoke, sparks and jostling silhouettes, the faces dissolving into orange. Now in the Nationalgalerie, Berlin, acquired in 1971.

1866_Gustave_Courbet_-_Woman_with_a_Parr.title: Woman with a Parrot

source.canonical_title: File:1866 Gustave Courbet - Woman with a Parrot.jpg
source.credit: Metropolitan Museum of Art, online collection (accession number 29.100.57)

1866_Gustave_Courbet_-_Woman_with_a_Parr.story: A nude sprawls on a rumpled bed, her dark hair fanned across the sheets, a brilliant parrot balanced on her upraised fingers. Critics huffed about the "ungainly pose" and the disheveled clothes tossed aside, but the Salon of 1866 accepted it — Courbet's first nude to make it past the jury after his 1864 rejection. A younger generation, including Manet, took notice. It's at the Metropolitan Museum of Art.

1869_Courbet_Die_Woge_anagoria.JPG.title: The Wave

source.canonical_title: File:1869 Courbet Die Woge anagoria.JPG

1869_Courbet_Die_Woge_anagoria.JPG.story: Summer 1869, Étretat: Courbet set up in front of the Channel and painted waves obsessively — by his own count, around sixty of them. He wanted the sea's violence, not its postcard side. Here a green swell rears up, curls, and collapses into churning foam under a bruised sky. He built it in thick, knifed-on strokes, the paint almost sculptural. This version hangs at the Städel Museum in Frankfurt.

1871_Vereshchagin_Apotheose_des_Krieges_.title: Apotheosis of war

source.canonical_title: File:1871 Vereshchagin Apotheose des Krieges anagoria.JPG

1871_Vereshchagin_Apotheose_des_Krieges_.story: A pyramid of skulls on a yellow plain, crows picking through the sockets, a dead city behind. Vereshchagin had first thought to call it The Apotheosis of Tamerlane — the conqueror who built towers from his enemies' heads — but he widened the dedication on the frame: "to all great conquerors, past, present and future." Finished in Munich in 1871, it was received in Russia as something close to treason. The tsarist military banned his work from barracks. The picture has never stopped being current.

1872_Vereshchagin_Praesentation_der_Trop.story: The Emir of Bukhara receives the trophies of a victorious campaign in the tiled courtyard of his palace — and the trophies, piled at the base of the columns, are severed heads. Vereshchagin built the scene from what he had seen and heard during the Turkestan wars, and he refused to soften it. The contrast is the whole argument: exquisite architecture, attentive courtiers, a heap of human remains treated as accounting. Painted in Munich in 1872, it belongs to the same bleak sequence as Apotheosis of War.

1872_Vereshchagin_Triumphierend_anagoria.title: They are triumphant
1872_Vereshchagin_Triumphierend_anagoria.description: Central Asia , Samarkand , Registan . A celebration of victory over an enemy. The Emir of Bukhara and the notables of the city watch how the heads of Russian soldiers are impaled on poles.

source.canonical_title: File:1872 Vereshchagin Triumphierend anagoria.JPG

1872_Vereshchagin_Triumphierend_anagoria.story: Samarkand, the Registan. The Emir of Bukhara and his notables are gathered in celebration, and the poles rising above the crowd carry the heads of Russian soldiers. Vereshchagin had survived the 1868 siege of Samarkand himself and came away with the Cross of St George and a cold clarity about what conquest looked like from the other side of the wall. He painted the tilework behind the crowd with the same care he gave the heads on the spikes, letting the beauty and the barbarism share one canvas without apology.

1873_Monet_Houses_at_Argenteuil_anagoria.title: Houses at Argenteuil

source.canonical_title: File:1873 Monet Houses at Argenteuil anagoria.JPG

1873_Monet_Houses_at_Argenteuil_anagoria.story: Argenteuil, just downriver from Paris, is where Monet became Monet. He lived there from 1871 to 1878, buoyed by Durand-Ruel's cheques and painting almost every roof, sail and towpath in sight. This 1873 view of neighbourhood houses — pitched roofs, vine-draped walls, a church spire — is one of the quieter fruits of the period: no family members, no regatta, just the town sitting in its own summer light. A painter finally at ease with his landscape and with his bank balance.

1878_Vereshchagin_Schlachtfeld_am_Schipk.title: Battlefield at the Shipka Pass

source.canonical_title: File:1878 Vereshchagin Schlachtfeld am Schipkapass anagoria.JPG

1878_Vereshchagin_Schlachtfeld_am_Schipk.story: January 1878, the Shipka Pass. General Skobelev rides along the front congratulating his men on their victory over the Ottomans, sabre raised, cossacks cheering. In the foreground — the cost of it. Russian corpses frozen into the snow, stretching toward the viewer in the carpet Skobelev is riding past but not looking at. Vereshchagin was on Skobelev's staff during the battle. He paints the triumph and the bill for it in the same frame, and lets the viewer decide which one the painting is about.

source.canonical_title: File:1887, Renoir, Nu Dans un Paysage.jpg

1887,_Renoir,_Nu_Dans_un_Paysage.jpg.story: A small panel, barely the size of a magazine, with a seated nude half-lost in a thicket of green and gold. Renoir painted it around 1887 in his tight 'Ingres' manner, the figure outlined crisply against a landscape built from quick dabs. It is in the Henry and Rose Pearlman Foundation collection, on long-term loan to the Princeton University Art Museum, and measures only 21 by 31.7 centimeters.

18_-_The_Sagami_River.jpg.story: Two raftsmen pole logs through reeds so thick they almost swallow the boats, while a thin curl of smoke rises from a cooking fire on deck. An egret lifts from the rushes. Fuji sits pale behind a green hill, almost shy. The composition is unusual for the series because it leads with working people, not tourists. Hiroshige was probably still finishing designs when he died in 1858; his pupil Hiroshige II completed the series for publisher Kichizō of Kōeidō.

1902_Monet_Die_Waterloo-Brücke_anagoria..title: Waterloo-Bridge

source.canonical_title: File:1902 Monet Die Waterloo-Brücke anagoria.JPG

title.fr: Le pont de Waterloo, matin brumeux

1902_Monet_Die_Waterloo-Brücke_anagoria..story: From a fifth-floor balcony at the Savoy Hotel, Monet looked left to Waterloo Bridge and right to Charing Cross Bridge. Between 1899 and 1901 he painted forty-one canvases of Waterloo alone, drawn by the coal-smoke fog that turned the Thames into shifting veils of mauve, orange and green. He worked on multiple canvases at once as the light changed, then shipped the lot back to Giverny to finish from memory. 'I cannot send you a single canvas,' he wrote Durand-Ruel. 'I develop them all together.'

1993-151-1-pma2018.jpg.title: 1993-151-1-pma2018
1993-151-1-pma2018.jpg.story: 'Sous les pins, soir' — Under the Pines, Evening. Monet set his easel among the umbrella pines outside Antibes in early 1888 and came back at dusk again and again, watching the trunks darken to rust while the sea behind them turned lilac. He groused in a letter that painting the south was 'fencing with the sun.' The canvas, catalogued as W1191, has lived at the Philadelphia Museum of Art since its 1993 accession.

19_-_The_Seven_Ri_Beach.jpg.story: Shichirigahama means 'seven-ri beach', and a ri is about 3.9 km, so the name stretches along with the sand. The dark grains you'd see underfoot come from iron, which drew blacksmiths to the area. Hiroshige lets Enoshima hump up out of Sagami Bay on the right while Fuji cools the horizon behind it. Travelers in the foreground are dwarfed by both. It's one of his last vertical Fuji designs, published by Tsutaya Kichizō in 1858, the year Hiroshige died.

2022-06-24_at_13-35-16_Pêches_(C_Monet_-.title: Peaches

source.canonical_title: File:2022-06-24 at 13-35-16 Pêches (C Monet - W 952).png

2022-06-24_at_13-35-16_Pêches_(C_Monet_-.story: Catalogued as Wildenstein W952, this small still life of peaches dates to 1885, when Monet had newly settled at Giverny and was raiding his own kitchen for subjects. The fuzzed skins catch a side-light, each piece of fruit a soft bruise of pink and apricot. Monet once grumbled that still life was the painter's finger exercise — something to do when the weather made landscape impossible. The peaches are three, the brushwork quietly luxurious.

2022-06-24_at_13-41-59_W_967_Monet_-_L'E.title: Entrance to Giverny in Winter, 1885
2022-06-24_at_13-41-59_W_967_Monet_-_L'E.description: L'Entrée de Giverny en hiver 1885 W967

source.canonical_title: File:2022-06-24 at 13-41-59 W 967 Monet - L'Entrée de Giverny en hiver 1885.png

2022-06-24_at_13-41-59_W_967_Monet_-_L'E.story: The road curves into town under a sky the color of skimmed milk. Bare trees rake the air, hedges crust with frost, and every footprint in the crust looks like a tiny blue shadow. Monet had only just moved his household to Giverny in 1883, and this winter canvas is one of the first times he painted the place that would hold him for the rest of his life. It's catalogued as Wildenstein 967.

20_-_The_Entrance_Gate_at_Enoshima.jpg.story: Three women in matching kimonos pause at the torii, and if they look straight through it they frame Fuji dead center, mountain inside shrine. That's the visual joke and the devotional point at once. The pilgrims are a kō, a lay group bound for Enoshima Shrine, where Benzaiten is worshiped; legend says the goddess raised the island from the seabed in the sixth century. Hiroshige dated the design to the fourth month of 1858, months before cholera killed him.

21_-_Lake_at_Hakone.jpg.story: No people. No boats. Just Lake Ashi glassy and still, Mount Komagatake to one side, and Fuji rising cold and exact above a belt of mist. Hiroshige empties the famous resort town of Hakone completely, which is almost the point; the composition lets the mountain breathe. It's a quieter design than most in the series, and it's one of the vertical ōban prints Tsutaya Kichizō published in 1858, the final year of Hiroshige's life.

23_-_The_Sea_off_Satta.jpg.story: A huge wave curls toward you, its crest feathered into spray, while Fuji stands unbothered in white behind it. Critics always mention Hokusai's Great Wave here, but Hiroshige's version is looser, more rhythmic, more water than violence. The viewpoint is Satta Pass, a famous stretch of the Tōkaidō road where travelers climbed a cliff and got the whole of Suruga Bay in one look. Published in the 1858 Fuji series by Tsutaya Kichizō.

24_-_The_Pine_Forest_of_Mio.jpg.story: The Miho pine grove hooks out into Suruga Bay in a long sandy spit, and Fuji rises directly across the water like a partner. Locals still point to a pine called Hagoromo no Matsu, said to be where a heavenly maiden left her feathered robe, the legend behind the Noh play Hagoromo. The grove is now part of a UNESCO World Heritage site tied to Fuji. Hiroshige's print is from his final series, published by Tsutaya Kichizō in 1858.

2560px-Bonaparte_ante_la_Esfinge,_por_Je.title: Bonaparte ante la Esfinge

source.canonical_title: File:Bonaparte ante la Esfinge, por Jean-Léon Gérôme.jpg

2560px-Bonaparte_ante_la_Esfinge,_por_Je.story: 1798, the Egyptian campaign: Bonaparte on horseback faces the half-buried Sphinx, staff arrayed behind him at a respectful distance. It never happened — Gérôme invented the encounter — but the image stuck, and it's the one most people picture when they think of Napoleon in Egypt. Also titled 'Œdipe' by Gérôme, after the riddle-solver. Man versus monument, empire meeting older empire, both squinting at each other across the sand. Hearst Castle has it.

2560px-Courbet_LAtelier_du_peintre.jpg.title: The Painter's Studio

source.canonical_title: File:Courbet LAtelier du peintre.jpg

2560px-Courbet_LAtelier_du_peintre.jpg.story: Courbet called it a real allegory summing up seven years of his artistic and moral life. The canvas is enormous, nearly six metres across, and shows the artist at his easel painting a landscape, flanked on one side by his friends and patrons (Baudelaire reads in the corner, the critic Champfleury sits listening) and on the other by the anonymous poor, priests, hunters, a beggar. A nude model watches over his shoulder. Rejected from the 1855 Paris Universal Exposition, Courbet responded by building his own pavilion next door and charging admission. It now hangs at the Musee d'Orsay.

2560px-De_heuvel_van_Montmartre_met_stee.title: The Hill of Montmartre with Stone Quarry

source.canonical_title: File:De heuvel van Montmartre met steengroeve - s0012V1962 - Van Gogh Museum.jpg

2560px-De_heuvel_van_Montmartre_met_stee.story: Van Gogh's first Paris summer, 1886, and Montmartre is still half-village, half-city — allotments, windmills, and a working quarry gouged into the hill. The palette is still Dutch-dark, browns and greys warming toward the sky; the Impressionist colour riot is a year away. A figure in the foreground stoops over his tools. Vincent had just moved in with Theo and was walking the Butte daily, teaching himself to look like a Parisian. Van Gogh Museum, Amsterdam.

2560px-Edgar_Germain_Hilaire_Degas_031.j.title: le tub

source.canonical_title: File:Edgar Germain Hilaire Degas 031.jpg

2560px-Edgar_Germain_Hilaire_Degas_031.j.story: One of Degas's pastels of a woman washing herself in a shallow zinc tub - the kind of tub every Parisian apartment kept for bathing before plumbing arrived. She is crouched, reaching for her neck with one hand, steadying herself with the other; a dressing-table on the right holds a pitcher, a copper pot, brushes. The viewpoint is from above and behind, unflattering and matter-of-fact. Degas said he wanted to show women 'as if you were looking through a keyhole.' The coloured chalk is built up in scratchy, overlapping layers that catch light like dry skin.

2560px-Gustave_Courbet,_1857,_Le_Pont_d'.story: A Roman bridge near Lunel, stranded halfway across the Vidourle after centuries of floods knocked out the rest. Courbet painted it in 1857 while staying with the collector François Sabatier, working fast on paper later mounted to wood. No shepherdesses, no picturesque ruin dressing — just mottled stone, scrub, and the hard shadow of the surviving arch. That blunt refusal to prettify is exactly what he meant by Realism. Now at the Musée Fabre in Montpellier, where it slipped into the collection by 1892.

Hiroshi_Yoshida_-_Kumoi-Zakura_(Kumoi_Ch.title: 雲井櫻
Hiroshi_Yoshida_-_Kumoi-Zakura_(Kumoi_Ch.artist: Hiroshi Yoshida (1876 - 1950) (Japanese) Details on Google Art Project

source.canonical_title: File:Hiroshi Yoshida - Kumoi-Zakura (Kumoi Cherry Trees) - Google Art Project.jpg
source.credit: 2wHA6qvg4l6i2g at Google Cultural Institute maximum zoom level

Hiroshi_Yoshida_-_Kumoi-Zakura_(Kumoi_Ch.story: Moonlight, mist, and a wall of cherry blossom at Mount Yoshino; two small figures in kimono look up. Yoshida, trained as a Western-style oil painter before he turned to woodblock at forty-four, supervised every cut and every pull himself. The sheet is huge, almost 60 by 75 cm, printed from three separately carved sections aligned by hand. The women in the foreground are the daughters of his friend Kawai Shinzo. Yoshida made the edition in 1926 and stopped after fifty impressions.

2560px-Hiroshige24_shimada.jpg.title: Shimada-juku
2560px-Hiroshige24_shimada.jpg.description: wood-block print, reproduction from a miniature edition by Takamizawa, Japan Title: Shimada

source.canonical_title: File:Hiroshige24 shimada.jpg
source.credit: The fifty-stree stages of Tokaido (one of 53 prints, +2 for start and terminus)

2560px-Hiroshige24_shimada.jpg.story: Station 24 of the Tōkaidō: Shimada, on the near bank of the Ōi River. The Ōi had no bridge and no ferry by shogunal decree — a security measure that stranded travellers for days when the water ran high. Hiroshige shows the crossing in progress, bearers wading a daimyo's palanquin through the shallows while porters shoulder baggage on platforms. It's one of the quietly political prints in the series: the river is a border, the crossing is a ritual, and everyone in the picture is wet up to the thigh.

2560px-Hiroshige_Fishing_boats_on_a_lake.title: Hiroshige Fishing boats on a lake
2560px-Hiroshige_Fishing_boats_on_a_lake.description: 8 Views of Omi - #6. Descending Geese, Katata

source.canonical_title: File:Hiroshige Fishing boats on a lake.jpg

2560px-Hiroshige_Fishing_boats_on_a_lake.story: From the Eight Views of Ōmi, a print set Hiroshige lifted from Chinese landscape convention and re-seated on the shores of Lake Biwa. This is Katata, with geese descending at dusk — one of the oldest poetic images in East Asian art, a flock cutting down through cold air toward water. Hiroshige keeps it sparse: a dark spit of land, a few fishing boats, the lake going silver, the birds arranged like brushstrokes. The whole thing is held together by negative space.

2560px-Jean-Leon_Gerome_-_Souvenir_of_Ac.title: Souvenir of Achères

source.canonical_title: File:Jean-Leon Gerome - Souvenir of Acheres (1903).jpg

2560px-Jean-Leon_Gerome_-_Souvenir_of_Ac.story: One of the last things Gérôme ever painted — he died a few months later, in January 1904. No gladiators, no harems: just a stag and a doe picking their way through a flat Île-de-France clearing at Achères, autumn light washing through the trees. It's memory painting, the title says so outright. The Columbus Museum of Art holds it. An odd, gentle coda from the man who spent sixty years polishing spectacle.

2560px-Jean_Léon_Gérôme_-_Chariot_Rac.title: Chariot Race

source.canonical_title: File:Jean Léon Gérôme - Chariot Race - 1983.380 - Art Institute of Chicago.jpg

2560px-Jean_Léon_Gérôme_-_Chariot_Rac.story: The Circus Maximus, mid-lap: four quadrigas thundering toward the spina, dust pluming, horses stretched flat. Gérôme had already mined Roman spectacle with Pollice Verso four years earlier, and here he works the same archaeological playbook — exact harnesses, correct monuments, a crowd bleached to a pale smear by distance. The painting is less about any rider than about the machine of the games itself, the engineered thrill. Chicago's Art Institute holds it now. You can almost hear Ridley Scott and every sword-and-sandal director since taking notes.

2560px-Jean_Louis_Théodore_Géricault_0.title: The Epsom Derby

source.canonical_title: File:Jean Louis Théodore Géricault 001.jpg
source.credit: The Yorck Project (2002) 10.000 Meisterwerke der Malerei (DVD-ROM), distributed by DIRECTMEDIA Publishing GmbH. ISBN : 3936122202 .

2560px-Jean_Louis_Théodore_Géricault_0.story: The Epsom Derby, painted during Gericault's 1820-21 stay in England, where he became obsessed with horses, racing and the damp open country. The composition shows four thoroughbreds at full gallop, all legs stretched fore and aft — the old 'flying gallop' convention that photographers would later prove biomechanically impossible. No matter; what Gericault wanted was the velocity, the blur of turf and cloud, the jockeys leaning into the wind. It became one of the defining images of Romantic horseflesh.

2560px-NDL-DC_2586549-06_Kawase_Hasui_S0.story: A single farmer heads home with a hoe over the shoulder, a white sleeve flaring against the earthen embankment, while behind her the sun drops red between tall evergreens at the edge of what looks like tea fields. Ikegami in 1928 was still countryside on the southern edge of Tokyo; today the same view is dense housing. That documentary pull is part of why Twenty Views of Tōkyō has lasted — Hasui was sketching corners of the capital he knew were already slipping, rebuilt and rebuilding after the 1923 earthquake.

2560px-NDL-DC_2586549-07_Kawase_Hasui_S0.description: Akashi-chō after Rain (Akashi-chō no ugo), from the series Twenty Views of Tōkyō (Tōkyō nijūkei)

2560px-NDL-DC_2586549-07_Kawase_Hasui_S0.story: Akashichō sat on the Sumida estuary, the old foreign settlement, and Hasui frames the view from the dog's-eye level: a small animal staring out across wet pavement toward harbour ships and a factory smokestack beyond. Yellow lights from the far shore smear on the water; it's dusk, just after rain. The composition exists in two color states — a darker first printing and a lighter one with the Watanabe seal at right, produced in the 1930s. A detailed preparatory sketch survives in one of Hasui's sketchbooks at the Ōta City Folk Museum.

2560px-NDL-DC_2586549-12_Kawase_Hasui_T1.description: Ryuga Island, Oga Peninsula (Oga Hantō, Ryūgashima), from the series Souvenirs of Travel III (Tabi miyage dai sanshū)

2560px-NDL-DC_2586549-12_Kawase_Hasui_T1.story: The Oga Peninsula juts into the Sea of Japan from Akita, a moody coast of cliffs and caves. Ryuga Island — Dragon Island — sits just offshore. Hasui traveled there in June 1926 and made several prints for Souvenirs of Travel III, including this one. Blue-green water, stacked basalt, a stillness that suggests he waited for the right light. It was far from Tokyo and still felt remote in the 1920s, which is exactly why Hasui kept going back to places like it.

2560px-Nihon_fūkei_senshū,_Hizen_Kazus.title: Nihon fūkei senshū, Hizen Kazusa by Kawase Hasui
2560px-Nihon_fūkei_senshū,_Hizen_Kazus.description: Kazusa Village in Hizen Province (Hizen Kazusa ), from the series Selected Views of Japan (Nihon fūkei senshū), woodblock print

source.canonical_title: File:Nihon fūkei senshū, Hizen Kazusa by Kawase Hasui.jpg

2560px-Nihon_fūkei_senshū,_Hizen_Kazus.story: Kazusa is a small port on the Shimabara Peninsula in old Hizen Province — present-day Nagasaki Prefecture — on the Ariake Sea. Hasui included it in Selected Views of Japan (Nihon fūkei senshū), the 1922 series that turned his sketchbook travels into a more deliberate national survey. The project was unusual for its scope: not the famous stations of the Tōkaidō but obscure fishing towns and provincial harbors, chosen for weather and mood rather than fame. A woodblock print in the full shin-hanga manner, published by Watanabe Shōzaburō.

2560px-Ondergesneeuwd_veld_met_een_eg_(n.title: Snow-Covered Field with a Harrow (after Millet)

source.canonical_title: File:Ondergesneeuwd veld met een eg (naar Millet) - s0175V1962 - Van Gogh Museum.jpg

2560px-Ondergesneeuwd_veld_met_een_eg_(n.story: One of the last Millet copies, painted in early 1890 while van Gogh was still shut inside Saint-Rémy recovering from another attack. A harrow abandoned in a snow-covered field, a distant farmhouse, crows. He translated Millet's monochrome print into a bleached palette of lilac shadows and ivory white — winter as colour rather than absence of colour. There is almost no event in the picture; the abandoned tool does all the work. A quiet, resigned painting from a man getting ready to leave the south.

2560px-Pieter_Bruegel_the_Elder_-_Hunter.title: monthly cycle, scene: The Hunters in the Snow (winter)
2560px-Pieter_Bruegel_the_Elder_-_Hunter.description: " The Hunters in the Snow " by Pieter Bruegel the Elder . 1565. oil on panel , 117 cm × 162 cm. Kunsthistorisches Museum , Vienna

source.canonical_title: File:Pieter Bruegel the Elder - Hunters in the Snow (Winter) - Google Art Project.jpg
source.credit: WgFmzFNNN74nUg at Google Cultural Institute maximum zoom level

title.de: Zyklus der Jahreszeitenbilder, Szene: Heimkehr der Jäger (Winter)
title.nl: De seizoenen van het jaar: De terugkeer van de jagers (winter)
title.fr: Cycle des mois:Les chasseurs dans la neige (hiver)

2560px-Pieter_Bruegel_the_Elder_-_Hunter.story: One of six panels Bruegel painted for Niclaes Jongelinck, an Antwerp merchant who wanted the seasons to ring his suburban dining hall. Five survive; this is winter. The hunters come home from the left with a single scrawny fox, dogs nosing the snow with their tails down. In the valley below, a woman beats laundry; villagers skate and spin tops on the frozen millponds. A chimney fire is being put out on the far left — look for the ladder against the wall. Within a year of delivery, Jongelinck went bankrupt and the city of Antwerp seized the paintings for unpaid taxes.

Saint_Francis_of_Assisi_in_Ecstasy-Carav.title: Francis of Assisi in Ecstasy

source.canonical_title: File:Saint Francis of Assisi in Ecstasy-Caravaggio (c.1595).jpg

Saint_Francis_of_Assisi_in_Ecstasy-Carav.story: No stigmata bleeding here, no ecstatic swoon in a rocky grotto — just a tired man cradled in the dark by a boy with wings. It's Caravaggio's first religious commission, painted soon after Cardinal Francesco Maria del Monte took him into his household. Some have noted Francis's face resembles del Monte's own. Behind them an unearthly glow breaks over the night landscape; the rest is shadow. It hangs in Hartford now, at the Wadsworth Atheneum — a long way from a Roman palazzo.

Saint_Jerome_Writing-Caravaggio_(1605-6).story: A bald old scholar, naked from the waist up except for a blood-red cloak, leans across a table strewn with books and a skull. His quill is poised mid-word — probably translating the Vulgate. Painted around 1605-6 for Scipione Borghese, probably, though oddly it doesn't show up in his 1613 inventory. For nearly two centuries the Borghese catalog credited it to the Spaniard Jusepe de Ribera instead; it wasn't returned to Caravaggio until 1893.

source.credit: Photo by Szilas at the Van Gogh, My Dream Exhibition in Budapest, 2013

title.de: Die Brücke von Langlois in Arles mit Dame mit Regenschirm

2560px-The_Langlois_Bridge_at_Arles_-_My.story: A little wooden drawbridge on the canal south of Arles, the kind Dutch engineers had built across Provence. Van Gogh painted it obsessively in spring 1888 — four oils, watercolours, drawings — because it reminded him of home. In this version a carriage clatters across and a woman with a parasol walks the towpath; the water is hard cobalt, the grass a chemical green. He wrote to Theo that he wanted paintings you could send as postcards of happiness. The real bridge was destroyed in WWII; a replacement stands a few kilometres upstream.

The_Taking_of_Christ-Caravaggio_(c.1602).story: Judas's kiss lands just as the soldier's steel gauntlet comes down on Christ's shoulder — one gesture completing the other. At the right edge a man lifts a lantern to light the scene; he's almost certainly Caravaggio, stuck inside his own picture. Commissioned in 1602 by Ciriaco Mattei, it disappeared for two centuries and was found in 1990 hanging in a Jesuit dining room in Dublin, written off as a copy. It's now on long loan to the National Gallery of Ireland.

Van_Dyck,_Sir_Anthony_-_Venetia,_Lady_Di.title: Venetia, Lady Digby, on her Deathbed
Van_Dyck,_Sir_Anthony_-_Venetia,_Lady_Di.artist: van Dyck, Sir Anthony (1599 - 1641) – Artist Details on Google Art Project

Van_Dyck,_Sir_Anthony_-_Venetia,_Lady_Di.story: Venetia Stanley, celebrated beauty of the Caroline court, died in her sleep at thirty-two. Her husband Sir Kenelm summoned Van Dyck the next morning and had him paint her while she was still in bed — a single pink rose wilting by her pillow stands in for her fled life. Kenelm later wrote that the picture was "the only constant companion I now have." Van Dyck finished it in 1633; it hangs today at the Dulwich Picture Gallery in London.

2560px-Van_Gogh_-_Acker_mit_pflügenden_.title: Field with plowing farmers

source.canonical_title: File:Van Gogh - Acker mit pflügenden Bauern.jpeg
source.credit: 1. Copied from an art book 2. bing.com

2560px-Van_Gogh_-_Acker_mit_pflügenden_.story: From the window of his asylum room at Saint-Rémy, van Gogh watched a farmer plough the field beyond the wall through the autumn and winter of 1889. He painted the view over and over as the light and crops changed. In this canvas the furrows run in violent diagonals of violet earth, the horse and ploughman tiny against the ridge of the Alpilles. He told Theo the window gave him subjects enough for a lifetime. It's labour seen from confinement — a man in a cell watching someone else do the honest work.

2560px-Van_Gogh_The_Olive_Trees..jpg.story: The MoMA canvas from June 1889, painted a few weeks after he arrived at Saint-Rémy. Van Gogh decided the olive groves were the equivalent in Provence of what orchards had been for him in Arles — a subject he could hammer at from every angle. Here the silver trees writhe above pink earth; the Alpilles heave up behind them like a breaking wave under a cloud that answers the mountain's shape exactly. He wanted to paint olives, he said, because no one had done them properly — not even the Impressionists.

2560px-Vincent_van_Gogh_-_Grapes,_Lemons.title: Grapes, Lemons, Pears, and Apples

source.canonical_title: File:Vincent van Gogh - Grapes, Lemons, Pears, and Apples - 1949.215 - Art Institute of Chicago.jpg

title.de: Stillleben mit Trauben, Äpfeln, Zitronen und Birne

2560px-Vincent_van_Gogh_-_Grapes,_Lemons.story: Autumn 1887, a studio still life loud with new colour theory. Van Gogh piles up fruit — yellow lemons, violet grapes, a few pears and apples — on a bright yellow ground, and lets every object sit in a pool of its complementary. He signed and dedicated it to Theo. It is a laboratory picture, almost a chart of what he had learned from the Parisian Impressionists, and a direct rehearsal for the sunflowers coming the following summer in Arles. Art Institute of Chicago.

2560px-Vincent_van_Gogh_-_House_at_Auver.title: House at Auvers

source.canonical_title: File:Vincent van Gogh - House at Auvers - Google Art Project.jpg
source.credit: RwFvYmUb77JK5g at Google Cultural Institute maximum zoom level

2560px-Vincent_van_Gogh_-_House_at_Auver.story: A thatched roof, a chimney trailing nothing, a wedge of orange tile — Vincent painted this old Auvers cottage shortly after arriving in the village in May 1890. He'd fled the south looking for "the real country," and found it in these peasant houses he told Theo were "old thatched roofs that are becoming rare." The brushwork is almost choppy, the greens impatient. He had about two months left to live. It now hangs at the Museum of Fine Arts, Boston.

2560px-Vincent_van_Gogh_-_The_siesta_(af.title: Noon – Rest from Work (after Millet)

source.canonical_title: File:Vincent van Gogh - The siesta (after Millet) - Google Art Project.jpg
source.credit: LwFmpmDARcicFQ at Google Cultural Institute maximum zoom level

title.fr: La Méridienne oú La siesta, d'apres Millet

2560px-Vincent_van_Gogh_-_The_siesta_(af.story: Snowbound in the Saint-Rémy asylum in the winter of 1889-90, Vincent translated a black-and-white print of Millet into full Provençal heat. Two peasants nap in the shade of a haystack, boots off, sickles down, the air yellow as a lion. He called these copies "improvisations" on another composer's theme, not imitations. Theo's wife Jo would later donate this one to the French state. It hangs at the Musée d'Orsay in Paris.

2560px-Vincent_van_Gogh_-_Vineyards_at_A.title: Vineyards at Auvers / Vineyards with a View of Auvers

source.canonical_title: File:Vincent van Gogh - Vineyards at Auvers (1890).jpg
source.credit: Saint Louis Art Museum, online collection

2560px-Vincent_van_Gogh_-_Vineyards_at_A.story: One of the Auvers vineyard canvases from the last summer. Neat rows of vines curve across a low hillside toward pale village roofs; a woman in a straw hat bends among the leaves. The brushwork has loosened from the Saint-Rémy tightness — longer, calmer, rolling strokes — as if the northern light had unwound something in him. He painted roughly a picture a day in Auvers, some seventy canvases in ten weeks, before he walked out with a revolver. Hard to look at this peaceful green slope and remember that.

2560px-Vincent_van_Gogh_-_Vissersboten_o.title: Fishing boats on the beach at Les Saintes-Maries-de-la-Mer

source.canonical_title: File:Vincent van Gogh - Vissersboten op het strand van Les Saintes-Maries-de-la-Mer - Google Art Project.jpg

title.nl: Vissersboten op het strand van Les Saintes-Maries-de-la-Mer

2560px-Vincent_van_Gogh_-_Vissersboten_o.story: In late May 1888, Van Gogh took a stagecoach from Arles down to the Mediterranean fishing village of Saintes-Maries-de-la-Mer and stayed a week. He loved the boats: painted bright blues, greens and reds, pulled up on the sand like beached dragonflies. He did the drawing on the beach and finished the oil back in his yellow house in Arles. You can read their names on the sterns if you look closely. It's in the Van Gogh Museum.

2560px-Vincent_van_Gogh_-_Wheat_Fields_w.title: Wheat Stacks with Reaper

source.canonical_title: File:Vincent van Gogh - Wheat Fields with Reaper, Auvers - Google Art Project.jpg
source.credit: nAEx7tuIXuWdGQ at Google Cultural Institute maximum zoom level

2560px-Vincent_van_Gogh_-_Wheat_Fields_w.story: Painted in June 1890, not 1888: this is Auvers-sur-Oise, the village north of Paris where Van Gogh spent the last two months of his life under Dr Gachet's care. The reaper recurs in his late letters as a figure of the final harvest, mankind cut down like ripe wheat, though he insisted to Theo there was nothing sad in it, just a thing seen in full sun. Six weeks after finishing the picture he shot himself in a field like this. It's at the Toledo Museum of Art.
2560px-Vincent_van_Gogh_-_Wheat_Fields_w.year_note: Painted June 1890 in Auvers-sur-Oise (Toledo Museum of Art, F559), not 1888. Source metadata was incorrect.

2560px-William_Holman_Hunt_-_The_Scapego.title: The Scapegoat

source.canonical_title: File:William Holman Hunt - The Scapegoat.jpg

2560px-William_Holman_Hunt_-_The_Scapego.story: Hunt dragged his easel out to the poisonous salt flats of the Dead Sea in 1854, set up under an armed guard, and painted a goat from life as it slowly died in front of him. It is Leviticus in oil: the ram driven out bearing the sins of Israel, red wool around its horns, bones and mountains behind. Critics hated it. Hunt was unrepentant — for him, Pre-Raphaelite truth meant truth to the actual ground on which scripture happened.

title.zh-hant: 北宋 徽宗 竹禽圖 卷

北宋_徽宗_竹禽圖_卷-Finches_and_bamboo_MET_DP151.story: Huizong ruled Northern Song from 1100 until 1125, founded the imperial painting academy, and invented the wiry "slender gold" calligraphy that still bears his name. Two years after he abdicated, the Jurchen Jin armies sacked his capital and carried him off as a prisoner; he died in captivity in 1135. This small handscroll, ink and colour on silk, was painted when he still ruled: two finches balancing on a thin bamboo stem, feathers finely stippled, each claw placed with the same precision he brought to his calligraphy. It reads right to left, and the Met acquired it from the Crawford collection.
北宋_徽宗_竹禽圖_卷-Finches_and_bamboo_MET_DP151.year_note: Same object as the 2560px duplicate; Met dates it early 12th century. 1100 is the accession year / placeholder, corrected to c. 1110.

25_-_Fuji_on_the_Left_of_Tokaido_Road.jp.story: Walking from Edo to Kyoto on the Tōkaidō, you expect Fuji on your right the whole way. Near Yoshiwara the road bends and puts the mountain on your left instead, which is why this spot earned the nickname Hidari Fuji, 'left-hand Fuji.' Hiroshige had already made the bend famous in his Hoeido Tōkaidō decades earlier; this late vertical version, from the 1858 series published by Tsutaya Kichizō, revisits the trick with pine-lined road and travelers dwarfed by a pale cone.

26_-_The_Oi_River_Between_Suruga_and_Tot.story: The shogunate banned bridges over the Ōi, partly to slow any army marching on Edo, so crossing meant hiring porters. Hiroshige stacks them in tiers of luxury: a woman rides a palanquin up front, others sit on a plank, and in the far distance one traveler simply clings to a man's shoulders. Fuji floats serenely above the muddle. The river was notorious for sudden torrents. Print from the vertical 1858 Fuji series, published by Tsutaya Kichizō the year Hiroshige died.

31-_The_Otsuki_Plain.jpg.story: Wild grasses and autumn flowers crowd the foreground so tightly they nearly shoulder Fuji out of frame on the left. It's an extreme close-up, a trick of scale Hiroshige favored in his late work, and collectors rank this one among the six best designs in the series. The Ōtsuki Plain lies in Kai Province, west of Edo. Scholars now think Hiroshige used guidebooks rather than traveling the road himself. Published by Tsutaya Kichizō in 1858, the final year of his life.

32_-_Dog_Eye_Pass.jpg.story: Inume Tōge, literally 'dog eye pass,' snakes through the mountains of Kai Province. Hiroshige shows travelers hunched along its edge on a cold autumn day, a skein of geese unspooling across the sky in front of Fuji. Hokusai had already used the same pass in his own Fuji series; Hiroshige responded with a cooler, more melancholy version. The artist actually visited this corner of Kai in spring 1841 and wrote admiringly about it in his diary. Print published by Kichizō in 1858.
