33_-_Kogane_Plain.jpg.story: Horses graze loose on the Kogane Plain in Shimōsa, tails swishing, while the sky behind them warms toward sunset and Fuji holds the far horizon. The plain was a shogunal pasture where military horses were bred, so Hiroshige's grazing animals are more official than pastoral. Recent research suggests he never actually walked the road and worked from guidebooks instead, which is a little heartbreaking and a little impressive. From the 1858 vertical Fuji series, published by Tsutaya Kichizō.

3415_María_Magdalena_como_melancolía.jpg.title: Mary Magdalene as the Melancholy

source.canonical_title: File:3415 María Magdalena como melancolía.jpg
source.credit: Museo Soumaya Donation link to the image painting

3415_María_Magdalena_como_melancolía.jpg.story: The Magdalene slumps, reddened eyes closed, her cheek pressed into the heel of one hand in the classic posture of Melancholia — a saint caught less in penance than in plain exhaustion. A small perfume jar glints on the table beside her. Mary Garrard argues Artemisia later cannibalized this face for her London Self-Portrait as La Pittura; the canvas now lives at the Museo Soumaya in Mexico City.

34_-_Kuroto_Bay.jpg.story: Kuroto Bay bites into the coast of Kazusa Province, on the Bōsō Peninsula across the water from Edo, and Hiroshige uses its curve to carry the eye straight to Fuji. The peninsula was a popular detour for Edo travelers wanting a sea view with their mountain. This is print 34 in the series of 36, one of the last designs Hiroshige sent to publisher Tsutaya Kichizō before his death from cholera in Edo in the autumn of 1858.

36_-_The_Hoda_Coast.jpg.story: Print 36 and the series closes on the Bōsō Peninsula, looking across the water at Fuji from the rocky Hoda shore in Awa Province. Hiroshige finishes the set the way he opened it, with a long view over water and a single, patient mountain. He wouldn't live to see the finished set in shops; cholera killed him in Edo in 1858, and his pupil Hiroshige II helped Tsutaya Kichizō bring the remaining prints to market that same year.

4344-vis_Print_14762kopie.jpg.description: Peter Paul Rubens, Studie van een oude vrouw, 1615-1620, olieverf op eiken paneel, 50,2 x 40,6 cm.

source.canonical_title: File:4344-vis Print 14762kopie.jpg

4344-vis_Print_14762kopie.jpg.story: An old woman looks sideways, her skin creased like soft leather, the light catching the bridge of her nose and the damp rim of her eye. Rubens used studies like this as a library: faces he could pull into altarpieces and mythologies whenever he needed a weathered saint or a witness at the Cross. Oil on an oak panel just 50 by 40 centimeters, painted between 1615 and 1620, the head is less a portrait than a tool of the workshop.

500px-Gipsen_vrouwentorso_-_s0199V1962_-.title: Plaster Cast of a Woman's Torso

source.canonical_title: File:Gipsen vrouwentorso - s0199V1962 - Van Gogh Museum.jpg

500px-Gipsen_vrouwentorso_-_s0199V1962_-.story: A plaster cast from the studio, painted in Paris around 1887. Van Gogh owned a small collection of these academic casts — torsos, hands, a horse — and used them to practise on when models were out of reach. The treatment is odd and affecting: the cool white body set against rough, coloured brushwork that refuses to behave like a background. More than anatomy drill, it is a quiet argument with the academy, translating plaster into paint on his own terms. Van Gogh Museum, Amsterdam.

500px-Kuniyoshi_Utagawa,_Tiger.jpg.story: A tiger striding through wind, fur and whiskers bent sideways as if the whole print were weather. Kuniyoshi loved big cats — he kept several as pets and studied their shoulders and paws the way his rivals studied kabuki actors. By 1842 he was already famous for warrior prints, but the Tenpo reforms had just banned depictions of courtesans and actors, pushing ukiyo-e artists toward animals, landscapes, and history. The tiger, in that climate, reads as a swagger: a subject the censors couldn't touch, drawn with all the muscular bravado Kuniyoshi usually reserved for Suikoden heroes.

960px-03_-_Sukiyagahsi.jpg.story: Not Hokusai's — Hiroshige's own Thirty-Six Views of Mount Fuji, made near the end of his life in 1858. Sukiyagashi was the embankment of the outer moat in central Edo, close to what is now Ginza. Fuji sits small on the horizon; the foreground belongs to city life — the moat, a bridge, the wooden frontage of the warehouses. It's the Edo answer to Hokusai's series: less theatrical weather, more everyday glimpses of the mountain between buildings.

960px-13_-_The_Tama_River.jpg.story: Plate 13 of Hiroshige's late Thirty-Six Views of Mount Fuji. The Tama River ran west of Edo through farmland and was associated with cloth-bleaching — women spreading long strips of dyed cotton in the shallows, a sight old enough to be in Heian poetry. Hiroshige keeps Fuji as a pale cone at the horizon and lets the foreground do the work: figures at the river, pale sky, a low cut of bank. Understated, almost Whistler-ish, a quarter-century before Whistler got there.

Evening_Snow_at_Terashima_Village.jpg.title: Evening Snow at Terajima Village (Yuki ni Kururu, Terajima-mura) from the series Twelve Subjects of Tokyo

source.canonical_title: File:Evening Snow at Terashima Village.jpg

Evening_Snow_at_Terashima_Village.jpg.story: Hasui called Terajima a favorite: a long, gentle slope in the Mukōjima district north of the Sumida, a few telephone poles, houses going dark on either side of a drainage ditch. In the print a single figure trudges off into snow that thickens and turns a bruised purple toward dusk, the only warmth leaking from paper screens. Terajima has since been absorbed into Sumida ward; the village he knew is gone. From the 1920 Twelve Scenes of Tokyo — the design Narazaki picked for the cover of his 1979 monograph, and one of the most-reproduced Hasui prints there is.

960px-Fox_Hunt_1893_Winslow_Homer.jpg.story: A red fox pushes through deep snow along the Maine coast, and crows are diving at him out of a dark sky, one shape already huge in the upper right. The ocean is a dim blue strip behind. Homer painted this at Prouts Neck in 1893; it was the largest canvas he ever made. The usual relationship of fox to prey is inverted - this time he's the hunted one, slowed by the drifts while the birds, starving in a hard winter, go for his eyes. Not sentimental nature, but the sort Homer actually saw from his studio window.

960px-Hanagami_Danjo_no_jo_Arakage_fight.story: Kuniyoshi's warrior prints were Edo's action cinema — muscular, tattooed, usually fighting something biblically large. Here Hanagami Danjō-no-jō Arakage is shown wrestling a giant salamander in the Tontagawa River in Izumo, a minor legend Kuniyoshi seems to have picked mostly because it let him draw a thrashing amphibian the size of a man. The composition is all diagonals and churning water. This is the late 1820s-30s vein that made samurai tattoos briefly the fashion in the capital.

960px-Hiroshige,_Futamigaura_in_Ise_Prov.title: 'Ise Futamigaura'
960px-Hiroshige,_Futamigaura_in_Ise_Prov.description: Ise futamigaura (Futami Bay in Ise Province). Ukiyo-e print shows the two large rocks ( Meoto Iwa or "wedded rocks") just off the shore at Futamigaura, with a network of ropes, torii gate and shrine, with a view of Mount Fuji in the background. No. 27 in the series Fuji sanjūrokkei (Thirty-six views of Mount Fuji) , 1858.

source.canonical_title: File:Hiroshige, Futamigaura in Ise Province, 1858.jpg
source.credit: This image is available from the United States Library of Congress 's Prints and Photographs division under the digital ID jpd.01320 . This tag does not indicate the copyright status of the attached work. A normal copyright tag is still required. See Commons:Licensing .

960px-Hiroshige,_Futamigaura_in_Ise_Prov.story: The Meoto Iwa, or 'wedded rocks,' off the coast of Futamigaura in Ise — two sea stacks lashed together by a ceremonial shimenawa rope, a torii on the taller one, and, on clear dawns, Mount Fuji just visible a hundred and fifty miles across the water. Number 27 in the late Fuji series. Hiroshige tilts the rocks slightly and sizes Fuji down to a ghost, so the shrine ropes do the compositional heavy lifting. The rocks are still roped today; the priests replace the hemp three times a year.

960px-Hiroshige,_Sunset_Hill,_Meguro_in_.title: Hiroshige, Sunset Hill, Meguro in the eastern capital, 1858
960px-Hiroshige,_Sunset_Hill,_Meguro_in_.description: Tōto meguro yuhhigaoka (Sunset Hill, Meguro in the eastern capital). Ukiyo-e print shows a view of Mount Fuji from Meguro in Tokyo, with red maple trees in the foreground. No. 10 in the series Fuji Sanjūrokkei (Thirty-six views of Mount Fuji) , printed by Tsuta-ya Kichizō, Tokyo, 1858.

source.canonical_title: File:Hiroshige, Sunset Hill, Meguro in the eastern capital, 1858.jpg
source.credit: This image is available from the United States Library of Congress 's Prints and Photographs division under the digital ID jpd.01307 . This tag does not indicate the copyright status of the attached work. A normal copyright tag is still required. See Commons:Licensing .

960px-Hiroshige,_Sunset_Hill,_Meguro_in_.story: Yuhigaoka — Sunset Hill — in Meguro, then a rural fringe of Edo. In Hiroshige's day people walked out here in autumn for the maples, the way Kyotoites went to Takao. He frames Fuji through flame-red foliage with the sun going behind it, one of the show-off colour prints in the late Fuji set. The neighbourhood is now dense Tokyo suburbs and the hill itself is gone, smoothed out by twentieth-century roads, but the print is why Meguro still trades on the name.

960px-Hiroshige_II_Suō_Iwakuni.jpg.story: The Kintai Bridge at Iwakuni under thick snow, its five wooden arches stepping across the river like a row of hooped kilns. Hiroshige II made this for his series One Hundred Famous Views of the Provinces, picking up where his teacher and father-in-law left off. A small red cartouche in the upper right holds the title. The composition is almost stark: white snow, blue water, the geometry of those arches. Built in 1673 and famously reconstructed after typhoons, the bridge was already a tourist draw by the time this print appeared in 1859.

960px-Hiroshige_Mt_fuji_4.jpg.story: Misaka Pass, on the old road between Kai Province and the Kofu basin, with Fuji reflected in Lake Kawaguchi below. The view from Misaka is one of the canonical 'mirror-Fuji' sites — the mountain and its inverted double stacked on the lake's surface. Hiroshige handles it flatly, like two symmetrical triangles of blue, with a twist of travellers on the pass road for scale. Hokusai had painted the same view thirty years earlier; Hiroshige's is quieter, the joke of the reflection played straight.

960px-Jean-Léon_Gérôme_002.jpg.title: Napoleon in Egypt

source.canonical_title: File:Jean-Léon Gérôme 002.jpg
source.credit: The Yorck Project (2002) 10.000 Meisterwerke der Malerei (DVD-ROM), distributed by DIRECTMEDIA Publishing GmbH. ISBN : 3936122202 .

960px-Jean-Léon_Gérôme_002.jpg.story: A slender, thoughtful Napoleon on horseback, alone against the pyramids and a pale stretch of desert. Gérôme painted several versions of this encounter, recasting the 1798 Egyptian campaign as a solitary meditation rather than a military parade. The general is dwarfed by the monuments, but the composition clearly flatters him: here is a conqueror measuring himself against the Pharaohs. Gérôme had made his own first trip to Egypt only seven years earlier, and the sun-bleached light and scrupulous topography carry the conviction of someone who had squinted at that horizon in person.

960px-Lofty_Mt.Lu_by_Shen_Zhou.jpg.story: Shen Zhou painted this towering hanging scroll in 1467 as a birthday gift for his old teacher Chen Kuan, who came from the Mount Lu region. He had never actually visited the mountain. Instead he built it out of literary memory and the landscape tradition he had spent a lifetime absorbing, stacking ridges and pine groves up the silk until the tiny scholar at the bottom of the path looks ant-sized. The dense, patient brushwork and the crown of poem-inscriptions at the top are the Wu School ideal in one picture. National Palace Museum, Taipei.

960px-Museo_del_Prado_-_Goya_-_Caprichos.story: An artist slumps asleep at his desk while owls, bats and a lynx close in behind him. The inscription on the desk reads: "The sleep of reason produces monsters." Goya meant it as the hinge of the whole Caprichos — plate 43 of 80, originally intended as the frontispiece. The etching-and-aquatint was published in Madrid in 1799; Goya pulled it from sale days later, nervous about the Inquisition. He handed the plates to the king in exchange for a pension for his son.

960px-Robert_Delaunay,_1926,_Tour_Eiffel.title: Tour Eiffel

source.canonical_title: File:Robert Delaunay, 1926, Tour Eiffel, oil on canvas, 169 × 86 cm, Musée d'Art Moderne de la ville de Paris.jpg

960px-Robert_Delaunay,_1926,_Tour_Eiffel.story: A narrow vertical, 169 by 86 centimetres, shaped like the tower itself. By 1926 Delaunay had been returning to figuration for five years and the destructive fractures of 1911 are long gone. The lattice stands whole, framed by a patchwork of flat coloured rectangles that read simultaneously as Parisian street grid and as homage to the abstract disc paintings he had lately set aside. Hanging now at the Musée d'Art Moderne de la Ville de Paris, it is the same obsession revisited with a lighter hand, the painter in his forties revisiting the monument that had made his name at twenty-four.

960px-SesshuToyo.jpg.title: SesshuToyo

source.canonical_title: File:SesshuToyo.jpg
source.credit: Emuseum Original uploader was ToraryuKawabata at en.wikipedia
source.permission: PD-ART.

960px-SesshuToyo.jpg.story: Autumn Landscape, companion to Sesshu's famous Winter. The eye enters along a wedge of rock in the foreground, climbs through brushwood and crooked pine, and comes to rest on a distant pavilion tucked between hills where a tiny boatman is poling across shallow water. The brush is drier and calmer than the winter scroll beside it, but the same muscular draughtsmanship is there, the same refusal to prettify. Sesshu was a Zen monk first and a painter second, and you can feel the discipline in every stroke. Tokyo National Museum.

960px-Tokyo_junidai,_haru_no_atagoyama_b.title: Tokyo junidai, haru no atagoyama by Kawase Hasui
960px-Tokyo_junidai,_haru_no_atagoyama_b.description: Atagoyama in Spring (Haru no Atagoyama), from the series Twelve Scenes of Tōkyō (Tōkyō jūnidai), woodblock print

source.canonical_title: File:Tokyo junidai, haru no atagoyama by Kawase Hasui.jpg

960px-Tokyo_junidai,_haru_no_atagoyama_b.story: Mount Atago is a modest rise in central Tokyo — small enough to be a hill, steep enough to have a shrine on top and a famously punishing stone stairway up to it. Hasui made this sheet in 1921 to close out the Twelve Scenes of Tokyo series Watanabe had been issuing since 1919. Spring shows up as pale blossom and soft haze rather than any explicit cherry-tree drama. Signed Hasui, red Kawase seal, oban format. One of the last designs in the series before the 1923 earthquake changed what could still be drawn from life.

960px-Van_Gogh_-_Le_Moulin_de_la_Galette.story: Not Renoir's dance garden but the actual working windmill on top of Montmartre, painted from below in 1886. Van Gogh did a whole small series of the Moulin de la Galette in his first year in Paris — scruffy fence, bare trees, a couple of Parisians on a Sunday walk. The colour is muted, the brushwork still tight; he is watching Impressionism from across the street, not yet inside it. A transitional picture, half Brabant peasant painter, half future Arles firework.

A_Friendly_Call.jpeg.story: Chase's wife Alice receives a visitor in the bright Shinnecock sitting room, parasol still in hand as if the call might not last. It's a showpiece of reflected light — mirrors multiply the room, the cushions are a riot of pattern, and every surface is crammed with the Japanese prints, fans, and textiles Chase compulsively collected. Critics at the time read it as a quiet answer to Sargent and the European interior painters: American domestic life could be just as sophisticated. Now a highlight of the National Gallery of Art in Washington.

source.canonical_title: File:A Hippopotamus and Crocodile Hunt P5296.jpg

A_Hippopotamus_and_Crocodile_Hunt_P5296..story: Spears bristle, a horse rears, dogs lunge, and the hippo twists open a pink cavern of a mouth while a crocodile thrashes underfoot. Rubens had never seen either animal alive; he worked from Albrecht Durer's rhinoceros woodcut and from stuffed specimens in Mantua. Commissioned by Maximilian I of Bavaria around 1615 for his Munich residence, the painting now hangs in the Alte Pinakothek. The whole mass of bodies corkscrews into a single diagonal of violence.

A_Parisian_Lady_(Édouard_Manet)_-_Nation.title: A Parisian Lady
A_Parisian_Lady_(Édouard_Manet)_-_Nation.description: This painting shows a fashionable Parisienne in casual clothes. She is wearing a black dress with an accentuated waistline and a draped bustle, a hat, gloves, a handbag and black lace-up boots. The quality, trimmings and style of the clothes showed the social and economic status of the wearer. The model is the actress Ellen André. But above all, this is a picture of a modern woman, not a portrait of a particular individual. Prominent men and women were traditionally portrayed in full length. Here, a new powerful agent and status symbol is portrayed – the woman as consumer and the woman as commodity.

source.canonical_title: File:A Parisian Lady (Édouard Manet) - Nationalmuseum - 19127.tif
source.permission: The author died in 1883, so this work is in the public domain in its country of origin and other countries and areas where the copyright term is the author's life plus 100 years or fewer . A_Parisian_Lady_(Édouard_Manet)_-_Nation.story: The actress Ellen Andrée, head to toe in street black: bustled dress, little hat, gloves, umbrella, laced boots. She stares past you as if she's late for something. Manet wasn't painting Ellen so much as painting a type, the modern Parisienne who shops, who is shopped for, who moves through the city alone. The full-length format was traditionally reserved for royalty and generals. Manet gave it to a woman going out. The canvas hangs at the Nationalmuseum in Stockholm.

A_Sunday_on_La_Grande_Jatte,_Georges_Seu.title: A Sunday on La Grande Jatte

source.canonical_title: File:A Sunday on La Grande Jatte, Georges Seurat, 1884.jpg

title.fr: Un dimanche après-midi à l'Île de la Grande Jatte

A_Sunday_on_La_Grande_Jatte,_Georges_Seu.story: Look closer and the park dissolves into dots. Seurat spent two years placing tiny touches of pure color side by side, trusting your eye to mix them into sunlight, shade, and starched Sunday cotton. The scene is an island in the Seine where Parisians came to stroll, fish, and show off hats the size of dinner plates. Everyone faces forward like figures on a Greek frieze; no one speaks. He even added a painted border of dots so the picture couldn't sit in an ordinary frame. It's almost seven feet tall and ten feet wide.

A_View_of_the_Archbishop's_Palace,_Lambe.title: A View of the Archbishop's Palace, Lambeth
A_View_of_the_Archbishop's_Palace,_Lambe.description: This watercolour was Turner's first to be accepted for the Royal Academy's annual exhibition in April 1790, the month he turned fifteen. The watercolour showcases Turner's progress in mastering perspective, showing several buildings at dramatically different angles.

source.canonical_title: File:A View of the Archbishop's Palace, Lambeth.jpg

A_View_of_the_Archbishop's_Palace,_Lambe.story: Lopsided rooflines, a Gothic gatehouse, a sliver of the Thames: Turner's first watercolour accepted by the Royal Academy, hung in April 1790, the month he turned fifteen. He was still a pupil of Thomas Malton and it shows, a teenager trying to fit three different viewing angles into one sheet and almost pulling it off. The palace still stands on the south bank of the Thames opposite Westminster.

A_colored_version_of_the_Big_wave_from_1.title: A colored version of the Big wave from 100 views of the Fuji, 2nd volume
A_colored_version_of_the_Big_wave_from_1.description: It is a mirrored version of the famous great wave of Kanagawa from the 36 views of the Fuji. There are no boats and the wave crests are birds.

source.canonical_title: File:A colored version of the Big wave from 100 views of the Fuji, 2nd volume.jpg

A_colored_version_of_the_Big_wave_from_1.story: Hokusai revisited his own Great Wave near the end of his life, in the second volume of One Hundred Views of Mount Fuji (1835), as a small black-and-white book illustration — flipped left-to-right, with the boats gone and the foam crests breaking into flocks of birds. This is a later coloured impression of that cut, the blue laid in by hand or by recut blocks. Compared to the 1831 print it's quieter, stranger, more dreamlike: the wave has become a bird in itself. Mount Fuji is still waiting in the gap.

A_female_martyr_saint,_probably_Saint_Ca.title: A Female Saint and Martyr (St. Catherine of Alexandria?)

source.canonical_title: File:A female martyr saint, probably Saint Catherine of Alexandria.jpg

title.avk: Caterina tumtikya ke Aliskandarya (2) (trutca ke Gentileschi)

A_female_martyr_saint,_probably_Saint_Ca.story: A young woman turns her gaze upward, a palm of martyrdom in her fingers — likely Catherine of Alexandria, though no spiked wheel anchors the identification. Artemisia painted female martyrs repeatedly after her 1612 rape trial, in which she was tortured with the sibille cords to verify her testimony against Agostino Tassi. The canvas is one of several unassigned Catherines moving through the attribution literature.

A_sketch_of_the_Mitsui_shop_in_Suruga_st.story: Fuji hovers over a Tokyo rooftop and a kite hangs in the same blue, while down on Suruga Street the Mitsui dry-goods emporium hums along: tilers patching a roof, clerks in the shadow of the eaves, a delivery boy hurrying past. This is the second print in Hokusai's Thirty-six Views of Mount Fuji, around 1830. The Mitsui shop shown here became, eventually, the Mitsukoshi department store, which is still trading in the same part of Tokyo.

Accolade_by_Edmund_Blair_Leighton.jpg.title: The Accolade

source.canonical_title: File:Accolade by Edmund Blair Leighton.jpg

Accolade_by_Edmund_Blair_Leighton.jpg.story: A queen in white satin lowers a sword to a young knight's shoulder, and a whole hall of onlookers holds its breath. Leighton painted this in 1901 and it became the image of medieval knighting, endlessly reproduced on biscuit tins, greeting cards, and paperback covers ever since. The historical accuracy is frankly invented; women rarely performed the accolade. But look at the fall of her sleeve and try to care.

Adachi_Moor.jpg.title: Adachi Moor
Adachi_Moor.jpg.artist: Artist Yoshitoshi Tsukioka (1885), photgrapher Bruce Argue (myself)
Adachi_Moor.jpg.description: Photo of The Lonely House on Adachi Moor. Some extra information: https://cs.nga.gov.au/Detail.cfm?IRN=183100

source.canonical_title: File:Adachi Moor.jpg
source.credit: Photograph of an original print dated 1885 owned by me

Adachi_Moor.jpg.story: A demon-hag crouches by a fire pit at the bottom of the sheet, knife bared, her victim — a pregnant woman in a red robe — dangling by the ankle from the rafters, upside down and impossibly limp. Yoshitoshi's 'Lonely House on Adachi Moor' (1885) illustrates the grisly folktale of the Kurozuka ogress who killed travellers for her daughter's medicine. It's one of the last masterpieces of ukiyo-e, printed in the ghostly palette of red, ink-black and paper-white that the aging Yoshitoshi made his own. This photograph is by Bruce Argue.

AdamEveParadiseCranach.jpg.title: Adam and Eve in Paradise

source.canonical_title: File:AdamEveParadiseCranach.jpg
source.credit: Fine Arts Museums of San Francisco

title.es: Adán y Eva en el Paraíso

AdamEveParadiseCranach.jpg.story: A small, dark-ground cabinet picture — Cranach's first crack at the subject he would paint for the rest of his life. Adam and Eve stand on either side of the Tree of Knowledge, the serpent coiled above, creatures of the garden scattered around them. Tiny (under 60 cm tall), intimate, meant for close looking. It became the template for dozens of later Wittenberg-workshop variants, all sharing the same black backdrop and slim, almost weightless nudes. The original lives today at the National Museum in Warsaw.

Admiral_of_the_White_by_Thomas_Gainsboro.title: Admiral Rodney at the Battle of the Saintes
Admiral_of_the_White_by_Thomas_Gainsboro.description: Behind is the French fleur de lys naval ensign from the captured Ville De Paris

source.canonical_title: File:Admiral of the White by Thomas Gainsborough.jpg

Admiral_of_the_White_by_Thomas_Gainsboro.story: George Brydges Rodney, painted the year after he broke the French line at the Saintes and saved Jamaica for the Crown. Gainsborough hangs the fleur-de-lys ensign behind him — captured from the Ville de Paris, the flagship Rodney took — as a kind of painted trophy. Rodney himself wears the blue-and-gold of an Admiral of the White and looks tired, which he was: he'd been hauled home over a prize-money scandal before the victory rehabilitated him. The portrait is more restrained than Gainsborough's society flourishes. It has a job to do.

Adolph_Menzel_-_Bauplatz_mit_Weiden_-_Go.story: Berlin in the 1840s was swallowing its own outskirts — new tenements rising on fields that last year had been pasture. Menzel painted this small oil, barely forty centimeters tall, of one such raw lot: scaffolding going up, fresh-dug earth, and a stand of willows that haven't yet been cleared. No workmen, no drama, no moral. Just the odd quiet of a weekday afternoon on a site mid-construction, the trees casting shadows on planks that will outlast them by about a week.

Adolph_Menzel_-_Das_Balkonzimmer_-_Googl.title: The Balcony Room

source.canonical_title: File:Adolph Menzel - Das Balkonzimmer - Google Art Project.jpg

Adolph_Menzel_-_Das_Balkonzimmer_-_Googl.story: Menzel had just moved his mother and sisters into a new apartment off the Anhaltische Tor in Berlin, a few weeks before he set up this canvas. The room is nearly empty — a sofa, a mirror, two chairs pushed aside — because the family hadn't unpacked. What he wanted was the light. A breeze catches the white curtains and puffs them into the room; sunlight throws their shape onto the bare floorboards. He signed it, but most scholars think he never finished it, and never meant to show it. It was an exercise, a private study of what light does when nobody is watching.

Adolph_Menzel_-_Eisenwalzwerk_-_Google_A.title: The Iron Rolling Mill (Modern Cyclopes)

source.canonical_title: File:Adolph Menzel - Eisenwalzwerk - Google Art Project.jpg

Adolph_Menzel_-_Eisenwalzwerk_-_Google_A.story: In 1872 Menzel went to the Königshütte rail works in Upper Silesia and filled sketchbooks — over a hundred pencil studies of men swinging tongs, a furnace's mouth, the shape a body makes when it braces against heat. Three years later he delivered this: workers wrestling a white-hot ingot while others eat lunch in the shadows at left and a shift changes at right. The subtitle — Modern Cyclopes — is his joke, and also not a joke. The banker who bought it went broke almost immediately and sold it to the National Gallery at a profit of nineteen thousand thaler.

Adolph_Menzel_-_Flötenkonzert_Friedrichs.story: Menzel worked on this for two years, 1850 to 1852, obsessively. Frederick the Great had been dead seventy years, but Menzel knew his Sanssouci — he had been drawing the king's world for a decade, from uniform buttons to silverware. So the room is accurate: the rococo gilding, the candles in their branching sconces, C.P.E. Bach at the harpsichord. Frederick plays his own composition while his sister Wilhelmine listens from a pink sofa. The chandelier is the only real light source, and Menzel makes you squint into it — the whole painting hums around that glow.
Adolph_Menzel_-_Flötenkonzert_Friedrichs.year_note: Painting is dated 1850-1852; completion and conventional date in museum records (Alte Nationalgalerie, Google Arts & Culture) is 1852, not 1850.

Adoration_of_the_Magi_by_Artemisia_Genti.story: One of three huge canvases commissioned by Bishop Martín de León Cárdenas for the choir of Pozzuoli Cathedral, more than three metres tall — Artemisia's biggest public platform in Naples. The 1964 cathedral fire scorched the upper register irreparably, especially the face of the Moorish magus. After half a century of conservation in Naples, the painting returned to its original wall in May 2014.

Adoration_of_the_Shepherds,_Murillo_(Pra.story: One of Murillo's earliest major commissions, painted around 1650 for the Franciscan convent of San Francisco in Seville, where he was still in his early thirties and sharpening his style on Ribera's deep browns. A shepherd leans in with a trussed lamb, a barefoot woman brings a basket of eggs, and the infant Christ — pale, naked, held up by the Virgin — catches the only real light in the room. It went from the convent to the Spanish royal collection after the Peninsular War and has hung in the Prado ever since.

After_Rubens_-_Anne_of_Austria,_Queen_of.story: Anne of Austria was Spanish, not Austrian — the name came from her Habsburg mother's line — and she married Louis XIII at fourteen. Rubens painted her from life during one of his three Paris visits in the 1620s, probably the 1625 stay when he was negotiating the Luxembourg cycle with her mother-in-law. The original is lost; this version at the Louvre is a studio copy, one of several that survive. The lace ruff is the real subject: a cartwheel of starched linen that cost a small estate and took a full-time laundress to maintain.

After_the_Battle_of_Grunwald_-_Alfons_Mu.story: The morning after 15 July 1410: the Teutonic Knights are broken, the field is a carpet of corpses, and the Polish king Władysław II Jagiełło stands in the middle of it with a hand across his face, refusing to look. Mucha painted this the tenth of twenty panels in his Slav Epic, subtitled The Solidarity of the Northern Slavs — Poles, Lithuanians, Russians and Bohemian mercenaries all on the same side. It's 405 by 610 cm, egg tempera and oil on canvas, completed in 1924 and now with the National Gallery in Prague.

After_the_attack._Plevna,_1877-1878.jpg.story: A field dressing station behind the Plevna lines. Wounded men lie on the grass in rows, some propped against each other, some already beyond help, while tents receive the worst cases and smoke from the battle still drifts on the horizon. Vereshchagin had been at Plevna himself — wounded there, and his brother killed. He researched the canvas obsessively once he got back to Paris, refusing to repeat a pose or a face. Every soldier on the ground is a specific man. That was the whole point.

Albinus_skeleton_w_less_muscles.jpg.story: The Dutch anatomist Albinus wanted his atlas to outlast every rival, so he hired the engraver Jan Wandelaar to draw the skeleton standing upright, in landscape, next to a live Indian rhinoceros named Clara who was touring Europe at the time. The conceit is absurd and it works. The bones are measured from a real cadaver using a grid system Albinus designed himself; the rhino lends scale and a kind of pastoral calm. Plate IV of the 1749 Tabulae, later reissued in London by Castigne, whose name sits at the bottom.

Albinus_skeleton_w_muscles.jpg.story: Companion to plate IV, now with the superficial muscles laid back onto the skeleton. The figure still stands in the same contrapposto, right arm out, but a storm is rolling in behind instead of a rhino, and a leafy branch fills the space where Clara stood. Albinus insisted his anatomies be shown outdoors, in dignified poses, because he thought a body stripped of skin still deserved to look like a person. Engraved by Wandelaar, published at Leiden 1749, re-issued in London.

Albrecht_Altdorfer_-_Schlacht_bei_Issus_.story: Duke William IV of Bavaria wanted a suite of eight battle scenes for his Residenz, and Altdorfer took Alexander's victory over Darius at Issus in 333 BC. Count the soldiers if you can — there are thousands, tiny as pinheads, and each tiny helmet catches its own glint. But Altdorfer wasn't thinking only of antiquity. The year was 1529, and Suleiman's Ottoman army was at the walls of Vienna. The Persians wear turbans and Turkish battle dress. Above it all, a swirling sky cracks open over the curve of the Mediterranean — one of the first paintings to show weather as cosmic drama.

Albrecht_Dürer,_Adam_and_Eve,_1504,_Engr.title: Adam and Eve
Albrecht_Dürer,_Adam_and_Eve,_1504,_Engr.description: Adam and Eve standing on either side of the tree of knowledge with the serpent.After introduced to the canon of proportions—a mathematical system designed to depict the ideal human body—by Jacopo de' Barbari , an Italian artist visiting Nuremberg in 1500, Dürer used the technique to create Adam and Eve. He paired their flawless physiques with an emphasis on perfect temperament. Erwin Panofsky argued that the animals embody the balance of bodily fluids believed to determine personality, called humors, and were associated with particular traits, for example, elk (melancholy), rabbit (sensuality), cat (cruelty), and ox (sluggishness). Praising Dürer's couple, contemporary poet Caspar Velius wrote, "When the Angel saw them, he said with amazement: 'You were not yet this beautiful when I drove you out of Paradise.'" (Morgan Library & Museum)

source.canonical_title: File:Albrecht Dürer, Adam and Eve, 1504, Engraving.jpg

title.uz: "Odam Ato va Momo Havo" Dyurer oʻymakorligi

Albrecht_Dürer,_Adam_and_Eve,_1504,_Engr.story: Dürer signed this plate prouder than any other: ALBERT[US] DVRER NORICVS FACIEBAT 1504, inked on a tablet dangling from the branch Adam grips. Four animals crouch at their feet — elk, ox, cat, rabbit — the four humours, in balance for one last second before the bite. A parrot chatters on the branch above. He had been working out ideal human proportions from Vitruvius and Jacopo de' Barbari, and the couple stands in careful contrapposto, each polished curve built from measurement. The Fall, handed down through the burin in lines so fine you can count the hairs.

Albrecht_Dürer,_Selbstbildnis_mit_26_Jah.story: Dürer was twenty-six, back from Venice with Italian ideas about what a painter was, and tired of being treated in Nuremberg like a glorified cobbler. So he painted himself as a gentleman: kidskin gloves, silk-striped cap, a blue-and-white cord across the chest, and an open window behind him showing snow-capped Alps he'd crossed on foot. The gloves are the point — these are hands that don't have to work. On the ledge he wrote, in his own hand: 'I painted this from my own likeness. I was twenty-six years old. Albrecht Dürer.'

Albrecht_Dürer_-_Adam_and_Eve_(Prado)_2..story: Back in Nuremberg after his second Venetian trip, Dürer painted what are generally considered the first life-size nudes in German art — two narrow panels, each well over two metres tall, on separate planks so they could face across an open doorway. Adam glows in warm light; Eve cools toward silver. She already has the apple, handed down by a serpent; he reaches for a branch of the tree of knowledge with its label bearing Dürer's signature. The panels went to Prague for Rudolf II, were looted by the Swedes in 1648, and were gifted to Philip IV of Spain in 1654. They have been in Madrid since 1827.

Albrecht_Dürer_-_Barbara_Dürer,_die_Mutt.title: Barbara Dürer, the Artist's Mother

source.canonical_title: File:Albrecht Dürer - Barbara Dürer, die Mutter des Künstlers (1514).jpg

title.de: Barbara Dürer, geb. Holper / Barbara Dürer, die Mutter des Künstlers

Albrecht_Dürer_-_Barbara_Dürer,_die_Mutt.story: Charcoal on paper, March 1514. Barbara Dürer, née Holper, is sixty-three, ill, and two months from death. Her son draws her without flinching: sunken cheek, hollow temple, the thin ridge of the nose, one eye already shadowed. He inscribed it later, above the head, noting her age and — after her death that May — her passing. In his family chronicle he wrote that she 'died hard' and that he felt for her more than he could say. Held today by the Kupferstichkabinett in Berlin, which acquired it at auction in Paris around 1877.

Albrecht_Dürer_-_Der_Flügel_einer_Blaura.title: Wing of a European Roller

source.canonical_title: File:Albrecht Dürer - Der Flügel einer Blauracke (ca. 1500).jpg

Albrecht_Dürer_-_Der_Flügel_einer_Blaura.story: Dürer painted the wing from a dead bird — a European roller, a dove-sized cousin of the kingfisher with turquoise primaries that keep their color long after the bird stops breathing. He worked on vellum, in watercolor and gouache heightened with gold, feather by feather, until the gradation from teal to cobalt to near-black at the tips comes out right. The filename says 1500 but the painting is signed and dated 1512, made during the stretch when Dürer was amassing reference for his theoretical treatises. It now sits in a dim drawer at the Albertina; color that fragile doesn't belong in daylight.
Albrecht_Dürer_-_Der_Flügel_einer_Blaura.year_note: The watercolor is signed and dated 1512 on the sheet; Wikipedia and the Albertina date it to 1512. The ca. 1500 in the filename appears to be an older guess now superseded.

Albrecht_Dürer_-_Hare,_1502_-_Google_Art.title: Young Hare
Albrecht_Dürer_-_Hare,_1502_-_Google_Art.description: Die Werkstattfenster spiegeln sich in den Augen des Hasen.

source.canonical_title: File:Albrecht Dürer - Hare, 1502 - Google Art Project.jpg

Albrecht_Dürer_-_Hare,_1502_-_Google_Art.story: Look close at the hare's right eye and a tiny cross-barred window floats inside it — the reflection of Dürer's Nuremberg workshop, painted in at roughly the size of a pinhead. Watercolour and gouache on paper, heightened with touches of white, every whisker laid down individually. He signed and dated it with his famous AD monogram in the shadow beneath the belly, as if the creature had just wandered over it. No one knows whether he sketched a dead hare, a live one, or stuffed a specimen for the sitting. The Albertina has kept it ever since.

Albrecht_Dürer_-_Head_of_an_Old_Man,_152.title: Head of an Old Man

source.canonical_title: File:Albrecht Dürer - Head of an Old Man, 1521 - Google Art Project.jpg

title.de: Bildnis eines 93-jährigen Mannes (Studie für das Gemälde "Der Heilige Hieronymus")

Albrecht_Dürer_-_Head_of_an_Old_Man,_152.story: Brush, black and grey ink, heightened with white body colour on grey-violet prepared paper — a virtuoso head study Dürer made in 1521, the year of his Netherlandish journey, when he was hunting models in Antwerp and sketching anyone who would sit. The old man's skin reads almost as sculpture: every wrinkle cut, the beard modelled strand by strand, the prepared ground doing the middle tone while the white lifts the forehead and nose into daylight. He signed it with the familiar AD and the date at upper right. The sheet is at the Albertina in Vienna.

Albrecht_Dürer_-_Melencolia_I_-_Google_A.title: Melencolia I

source.canonical_title: File:Albrecht Dürer - Melencolia I - Google Art Project (427760).jpg

Albrecht_Dürer_-_Melencolia_I_-_Google_A.story: A winged figure slumps against a stone block, compass slack in her hand, surrounded by the tools of geometry — polyhedron, sphere, scale, hourglass, bell, a beautifully wrong-looking solid no one has quite identified. A putto scribbles on a slate. A starved hound sleeps. Over the sea, a comet and a rainbow. On the wall, a magic square whose bottom row reads 1514, the year Dürer engraved the plate and the year his mother died. The title MELENCOLIA § I hangs from a bat-like creature in the sky. Scholars have argued about every object in this print for five centuries.

Albrecht_Dürer_-_Praying_Hands,_1508_-_G.title: Praying Hands
Albrecht_Dürer_-_Praying_Hands,_1508_-_G.description: detail study for the " Heller Altarpiece "

source.canonical_title: File:Albrecht Dürer - Praying Hands, 1508 - Google Art Project.jpg

Albrecht_Dürer_-_Praying_Hands,_1508_-_G.story: Brush and grey ink, heightened with white, on blue paper Dürer tinted himself — a working study for a kneeling apostle at the foot of the Heller Altarpiece in Frankfurt. The altarpiece burned in a Munich fire in 1729; only copies remain, which makes this surviving scrap of preparatory drawing weirdly precious. The sheet once had a matching study of the apostle's head; someone cut the two apart long ago. Scholars now think Dürer may have finished the hands to this pitch partly as a showpiece for clients. The drawing lives at the Albertina.

Albrecht_Dürer_-_The_Expulsion_from_Para.title: The Expulsion from Paradise, from The Small Passion

source.canonical_title: File:Albrecht Dürer - The Expulsion from Paradise (NGA 1943.3.3634).jpg

Albrecht_Dürer_-_The_Expulsion_from_Para.story: A pocket-sized woodcut, barely five by four inches, cut for the devotional book Dürer called the Small Passion — thirty-seven scenes running from the Fall to the Last Judgment, printed in Nuremberg in 1511 with Latin verses by Benedictus Chelidonius on the back of each sheet. An angel wields a fiery sword; Adam steps out already clutching a spade; Eve turns her face away, a pose that shifts the emphasis from seduction to shame. Dürer packaged the whole series as a book ordinary readers could afford, a new commercial idea for a major artist.

Albrecht_Dürer_-_The_Large_Piece_of_Turf.title: The Large Piece of Turf

source.canonical_title: File:Albrecht Dürer - The Large Piece of Turf, 1503 - Google Art Project.jpg

Albrecht_Dürer_-_The_Large_Piece_of_Turf.story: A scrap of weedy ground nobody would have bent down to look at — cock's-foot, dandelion, yarrow, greater plantain, a daisy — raised to the dignity of a finished picture. Dürer worked it in watercolour and gouache on paper, eye level with the soil, so the grasses tower and the clay bank behind them feels like a cliff. Botanists have identified at least nine species in the tangle. Nothing is arranged; nothing is idealised. In 1503 this choice of subject was almost unheard of. It hangs today at the Albertina in Vienna.

Albrecht_Dürer_-_The_Men’s_Bath_-_Google.title: Bath House

source.canonical_title: File:Albrecht Dürer - The Men’s Bath - Google Art Project.jpg

Albrecht_Dürer_-_The_Men’s_Bath_-_Google.story: Six naked men around a wooden tub: one leans on a water spigot shaped suspiciously like what you'd expect, two more play flute and fiddle, another drinks from a tankard. The rotund one is said to be Willibald Pirckheimer, Dürer's best friend; at least one of the others may be Dürer himself. The woodcut came out in 1496 or 1497, just as Nuremberg was closing its public baths to stop an outbreak of syphilis — which probably helped sales. It's one of the first Northern European prints of male nudes with no saint, no myth, no excuse.

Albrecht_Dürer_Druckplatte_Christus_am_Ö.title: Christ on the Mount of Olives (Printing Plate)
Albrecht_Dürer_Druckplatte_Christus_am_Ö.description: Albrecht Dürer, Christ on the Mount of Olives, 1515, the only surviving copper printing plate, Bamberg State Library

source.canonical_title: File:Albrecht Dürer Druckplatte Christus am Ölberg.jpg

Albrecht_Dürer_Druckplatte_Christus_am_Ö.story: The only surviving Dürer printing plate — iron, 22 by 15.5 cm, etched in 1515. Christ kneels in the olive grove; the apostles sleep; Judas and the soldiers approach through a gate at the back. Dürer experimented with etching just six times. He couldn't control the acid bite and disliked the limited tonal range, and he abandoned the medium entirely soon after. Every other plate he worked has been lost. This one — pitted, oxidised, no longer printable — is kept at the Bamberg State Library, where it was recently digitised as part of the 'Bamberg Treasures' collection.

Alexander_III_reception_by_Repin.jpg.title: Aleksander III receiving rural district elders in the yard of Petrovsky Palace in Moscow.

source.canonical_title: File:Alexander III reception by Repin.jpg

title.es: Alejandro III recibiendo a los decanos de los distritos rurales en el patio del palacio Petrovski en Moscú.
title.ru: Прием волостных старшин Александром III во дворе Петровского дворца в Москве.
title.de: Alexander III. empfängt eine Delegation von Landvogten

Alexander_III_reception_by_Repin.jpg.story: On 21 May 1883, just after his coronation, Tsar Alexander III stood in the yard of Moscow's Petrovsky Palace and lectured five hundred village elders: obey your landlords, the law will not be softened. Repin was commissioned to record the speech and shows the tsar planted square in the middle of a sea of kaftans and grey beards, the peasants kneeling in the dust. The painting is unusually flat and official by Repin's standards — a commission, not a cause. Delivered in 1886, it hangs today in the Tretyakov.

Alexandra_and_Elena_Pavlovna_of_Russia_b.title: Портрет дочерей императора Павла I

source.canonical_title: File:Alexandra and Elena Pavlovna of Russia by E.Vigee-Lebrun (1796, Hermitage).jpg

Alexandra_and_Elena_Pavlovna_of_Russia_b.story: Vigée Le Brun had fled the Revolution and by 1796 was in St Petersburg painting Catherine the Great's granddaughters, Alexandra and Elena Pavlovna. She first dressed the girls in Grecian tunics with short sleeves, which Catherine found obscene: all that bare arm on Romanov children. The empress made her paint them over. In the finished Hermitage canvas the tunics are now demure muslin with long sleeves, the classical fantasy half-swallowed by propriety. Both girls would be married off in their teens as instruments of dynastic policy. Alexandra died at seventeen; Elena at nineteen.

Alfons_Mucha_-_1896_-_Autumn.jpg.title: Autumn

source.canonical_title: File:Alfons Mucha - 1896 - Autumn.jpg

Alfons_Mucha_-_1896_-_Autumn.jpg.story: One of four decorative panels Mucha designed in 1896 for the Parisian printer F. Champenois — his first set of Seasons, and the one that fixed the formula for a thousand later posters. Autumn stands in a grove hung with ripe grapes, reaching to taste one, a wreath of chrysanthemums on her hair. Colour lithograph, about 103 by 54 cm. Champenois had commissioned personified Seasons from others before, but Mucha's panels outsold every rival; the printer had him redo the series in 1897 and again in 1900. Autumn is the sultry, fruitful one — pitched, deliberately, against her sister Winter.

Alfons_Mucha_-_1896_-_Spring.jpg.title: Spring

source.canonical_title: File:Alfons Mucha - 1896 - Spring.jpg

Alfons_Mucha_-_1896_-_Spring.jpg.story: A slender young woman on a flowering branch, making a lyre out of twigs and her own hair, while small birds perch close enough to listen. This is one of the four 1896 Seasons panels Mucha designed for the Paris printer F. Champenois — decorative colour lithographs about 103 by 54 cm, the set that launched the 'Mucha style' as a mass-market product. Spring is the innocent of the four; her palette is pale green and cream, her pose deliberately weightless against Summer's heat and Winter's huddle. Champenois reprinted the concept twice more, in 1897 and 1900.

Alfons_Mucha_-_1896_-_Summer.jpg.title: Summer

source.canonical_title: File:Alfons Mucha - 1896 - Summer.jpg

Alfons_Mucha_-_1896_-_Summer.jpg.story: Summer dangles her feet in a pool, a poppy wreath slipping on her brow, eyes half-lidded against the heat — the sultry panel in the 1896 Seasons series Mucha designed for F. Champenois in Paris. Colour lithograph, about 103 by 54 cm, one of four decorative panels sold together and separately. It was Mucha's first set of such panels and became one of his best-selling works; Champenois asked him for fresh Seasons sets in 1897 and 1900 on the strength of it. The idea of personifying the seasons was old; the langour, the whiplash hair, the ornamental arch behind her — those were new.

Alfons_Mucha_-_1896_-_Winter.jpg.title: Winter

source.canonical_title: File:Alfons Mucha - 1896 - Winter.jpg

Alfons_Mucha_-_1896_-_Winter.jpg.story: Wrapped in a pale cloak against the cold, Mucha's Winter huddles beside a snow-laden bush, breath visible, a small bird cupped in her hands. She's one of four panels in The Seasons, the first decorative series Mucha made for the Paris printer Champenois in 1896 and the one that cemented his formula: a single idealised woman, a halo-like arc, a slice of nature doing the talking. Champenois sold these as affordable wall-pieces for middle-class apartments — art you could pin up rather than inherit. The set did so well that he commissioned two more Seasons cycles, in 1897 and 1900.

Alfons_Mucha_-_1898_-_Dance.jpg.title: Dance

source.canonical_title: File:Alfons Mucha - 1898 - Dance.jpg

Alfons_Mucha_-_1898_-_Dance.jpg.story: Dance is one of four panels in Mucha's 1898 series The Arts, where he ditched the traditional props — no tambourines, no lyres, no brushes — and let each art be personified by a woman responding to a moment of nature. Dance gets the morning breeze: her hair and gauze whipped sideways, autumn leaves scattering across a rising-sun disc behind her head. Champenois printed the set on vellum in an edition of 1,000, with 50 deluxe copies on satin. Poetry, Music and Painting are her sisters in the series.

Alfons_Mucha_-_1898_-_The_Flowers_Lily.j.title: Series The Flowers, "Lily"

source.canonical_title: File:Alfons Mucha - 1898 - The Flowers Lily.jpg

Alfons_Mucha_-_1898_-_The_Flowers_Lily.j.story: Lily belongs to Mucha's 1898 quartet The Flowers — Rose, Iris, Carnation, Lily — four women posed as the blooms themselves. She stands ankle-deep in a bed of white lilies, arms raised in a near-liturgical gesture, her halo a single opened flower. Mucha pushed the Art Nouveau whiplash curve as far as it would go here: stem, sleeve and hair all read as one continuous line. The panels were printed by Champenois in Paris and sold as unframed decorative lithographs, a format Mucha had more or less invented two years earlier.

Alfons_Mucha_-_The_Moon,_1902.jpg.title: Alfons Mucha - The Moon, 1902

source.canonical_title: File:Alfons Mucha - The Moon, 1902.jpg

Alfons_Mucha_-_The_Moon,_1902.jpg.story: One of four panels in Mucha's Moon and the Stars set — the others are Morning Star, Evening Star and Pole Star. Each personifies a heavenly body as a woman suspended in a dark sky; The Moon is lunar, silver-cool, eyes half-closed, a crescent at her back. By 1902 Mucha was already famous for Sarah Bernhardt posters and in flight from his own commercial style, and this series is visibly more meditative than the sparkling-water and cigarette-paper work of the 1890s. A quieter Mucha, still unmistakable.

Amsterdam_musee_van_gogh_monet_tulipes_m.story: Monet spent about a month in Holland in spring 1886, travelling between The Hague, Rijnsburg and Sassenheim in search of the bulb fields in full bloom. He wrote to a friend that the colour was 'impossible to convey with our poor palettes.' He produced five canvases of tulip rows and windmills. This one, now at the Van Gogh Museum, was sold through the Paris dealers Boussod, Valadon & Cie, where Theo van Gogh worked — Vincent almost certainly saw it there.

An_Afternoon_Stroll_by_William_Merritt_C.title: An Afternoon Stroll

source.canonical_title: File:An Afternoon Stroll by William Merritt Chase, San Diego Museum of Art.JPG

An_Afternoon_Stroll_by_William_Merritt_C.story: A woman in white, parasol raised, walks a sandy path through the Shinnecock dunes — possibly Chase's wife, possibly a student posed in passing. The picture is almost all sky and scrub, the figure a vertical accent in a landscape built from washy horizontal bands. Chase taught his summer students to work fast and trust the first impression, and this canvas shows him doing exactly that. Now in the San Diego Museum of Art, it's one of the clearest examples of his Long Island manner at full stride.

An_Experiment_on_a_Bird_in_an_Air_Pump_b.title: An Experiment on a Bird in an Air Pump by Joseph Wright 'of Derby', 1768. The original is in The National Gallery, London .

source.canonical_title: File:An Experiment on a Bird in an Air Pump by Joseph Wright of Derby, 1768.jpg

An_Experiment_on_a_Bird_in_an_Air_Pump_b.story: A travelling lecturer has pumped the air out of a glass globe and a white cockatoo is slumping inside it. Wright arranges the room around that single candle: the showman's theatrical stare, the father explaining, the girls refusing to look, the boy at the window reaching for the cage cord, the full moon outside as a cool counterweight to the flame. It is Enlightenment science staged as a parlour drama, and Wright doesn't tell you whether the bird will be revived or left to die. The painting treats a scientific demonstration with the gravity a previous century reserved for altarpieces.

title.vi: Sự tôn thờ của các hiền sĩ giữa tuyết

Anbetung_der_Könige_im_Schnee.jpg.story: Bruegel pushes the Adoration into the far left corner and buries it behind a snowstorm. The Magi arrive almost unnoticed while villagers haul firewood, break ice, and trudge past frozen houses in what may be the first depiction of actively falling snow in Western painting. The flakes are flicks of white added on top of a finished scene, as if the storm rolled in while he worked. The inscribed date was long read as 1567 but recent technical examination argues for 1563. It lives in the Oskar Reinhart Collection at Winterthur and tends to strike modern viewers as a weather report first and a nativity second.

title.pt: A lamentação sobre o Cristo morto

Andrea_Mantegna_-_The_Lamentation_over_t.story: Few paintings in the Renaissance are as physically shocking as this. Mantegna shoves the viewer right up against Christ's pierced soles, dragging the eye along the sheeted torso to the hollow face. Two weeping mourners crowd in at the left — the Virgin's creased cheek, John's open mouth — but the real subject is foreshortening as grief: no middle distance, no escape. The ochre-grey palette is almost monochrome, like carved stone. Found in Mantegna's studio after his death in 1506, it now hangs at the Pinacoteca di Brera in Milan.

Andrea_Mantegna_014.jpg.title: St. Sebastian

source.canonical_title: File:Andrea Mantegna 014.jpg
source.credit: The Yorck Project (2002) 10.000 Meisterwerke der Malerei (DVD-ROM), distributed by DIRECTMEDIA Publishing GmbH. ISBN : 3936122202 .

Andrea_Mantegna_014.jpg.story: Mantegna's second Saint Sebastian lashes a marble-pale martyr to a fluted Corinthian column among the ruins of a classical arch, arrows punching through him from every angle while a vine creeps over shattered entablature. In the lower-right corner, two archers — one turning his bald head away — ground the horror in matter-of-fact craft. The distant road winds up to a hilltop fortress under scudding clouds. It's the Louvre's version, painted around 1480, and pure Mantegna: antiquarian archaeology, anatomical showmanship, and cool Paduan severity all at once.

Anna_Alexandrovna_Galitzin,_nee_Gruzinsk.story: By 1797 Vigée Le Brun had reached St Petersburg, and her prices had reached the stratosphere. No obstacle for Princess Anna — great-granddaughter of the last king of Kartli and reputedly one of the wealthiest women in Russia. She sits on a lavishly upholstered green sofa in what was probably at-home dress; the sheer sleeves appear to have been added afterwards, since the Russian aristocracy preferred a little less skin on the wall. Baltimore Museum of Art.

Anna_Hillmayer_1829,_by_Joseph_Stieler.j.title: Portrait of Anna Hillmayer (1812-1847)
Anna_Hillmayer_1829,_by_Joseph_Stieler.j.description: Tochter des Wildprethändlers Hillmayer im Rosental 2, München, gemalt 1829 für die Schönheitengalerie

source.canonical_title: File:Anna Hillmayer 1829, by Joseph Stieler.JPG

Anna_Hillmayer_1829,_by_Joseph_Stieler.j.story: Anna Hillmayer was seventeen, the daughter of a Munich game-meat dealer on Rosental 2, when Stieler set her in front of the Frauenkirche in traditional Munich dress with a prayer book in her hands. Ludwig I wanted his Gallery of Beauties to mix aristocrats with shoemakers' daughters, and Anna is the proof of the idea. She never married. She died on her thirty-fifth birthday in 1847, but in the painting she stays seventeen, local, composed, completely at home in her city.

Annibale_Carracci,_Pietà,_Kunsthistoric.title: Pietà with two angels

source.canonical_title: File:Annibale Carracci, Pietà, Kunsthistorichen, Vienna.jpg

Annibale_Carracci,_Pietà,_Kunsthistoric.story: A small oil on copper, dated by scholars around 1603, now at the Kunsthistorisches Museum in Vienna. The dead Christ stretches along a white shroud, his head and shoulders fallen into the lap of a Virgin who has half-fainted; two putti lean in from behind, one crying, the other trying to hold her up. Annibale squeezes a monumental composition onto a plate barely bigger than a book. The copper support gives the flesh an enamel-like glow. A surviving letter suggests he gave a version of this Pietà to his doctor, Giulio Mancini, in lieu of a fee.

Annibale_Carracci_-_Christ_Wearing_the_C.title: Christ wearing the Crown of Thorns, supported by Angels

source.canonical_title: File:Annibale Carracci - Christ Wearing the Crown of Thorns, Supported by Angels - WGA04427.jpg
source.credit: Web Gallery of Art : Image Info about artwork wga QS:P11807,"c/carracci/annibale/1/thorns"

title.de: Christus mit der Dornenkrone, von Engeln gestützt

Annibale_Carracci_-_Christ_Wearing_the_C.story: Painted in Annibale's Bolognese years, roughly 1585-1587, well before he left for Rome. Christ slumps forward under the weight of the thorns while two small angels press in from behind to keep him upright, one cupping his shoulder, the other dabbing at blood. The mood is quiet rather than theatrical, more devotional image than altarpiece. Light rakes in from the left across exposed skin, leaving the angels' feathers almost transparent against deep brown. The panel belongs to a group of intimate Passion scenes now associated with Parma and Naples collections.

Annibale_Carracci_-_River_Landscape_-_Go.title: River Landscape

source.canonical_title: File:Annibale Carracci - River Landscape - Google Art Project.jpg
source.credit: WAHqTJM81QDcpw at Google Cultural Institute maximum zoom level

Annibale_Carracci_-_River_Landscape_-_Go.story: Around 1590, while most Italian painters still used landscape as a backdrop for saints or satyrs, Annibale Carracci made it the whole point. A fisherman hauls a net, a ferryman poles travellers across a shallow river, distant hills blue out at the horizon — and that's the picture. No miracle, no myth, no hovering god. It's a founding moment for what becomes the ideal classical landscape a century later with Claude and Poussin. The oil-on-canvas, almost five feet wide, now hangs in the National Gallery of Art in Washington, part of the Samuel H. Kress bequest.

source.canonical_title: File:Annibale Carracci - The Butcher's Shop - Google Art Project.jpg
source.credit: fwE_t62Eg-rHIQ at Google Cultural Institute maximum zoom level

Annibale_Carracci_Susanna.jpg.title: Susanna and the Elders

source.canonical_title: File:Annibale Carracci Susanna.jpg

Annibale_Carracci_Susanna.jpg.story: A lesser-known treatment from Annibale's Bolognese-Roman middle years, usually dated around 1590. Susanna sits nude at the rim of a stone basin, twisting sharply when two elders crane over a low fence to leer. Annibale keeps it domestic rather than operatic: the grain of the stonework, the rumple of a dropped linen, a single bare foot still dangling in water. The pose plants the kind of muscular, grounded naturalism his academy in Bologna was teaching as an antidote to Mannerist twist. A related etched version entered circulation in the same years.

Anonymous-Ten_Thousand_Miles_of_the_Yang.title: Myriad Miles of the Yangtze River
Anonymous-Ten_Thousand_Miles_of_the_Yang.description: Ten Thousand Miles of the Yangtze River , scroll, Color on silk, 26.8cm x 11.153m. Located at the National Palace Museum , Taipei.

source.canonical_title: File:Anonymous-Ten Thousand Miles of the Yangtze River.jpg

title.zh: 宋夏圭長江萬里圖 卷

Anonymous-Ten_Thousand_Miles_of_the_Yang.story: An eleven-metre handscroll of ink-washed mountains and river that unrolls like travel footage shot from a boat. The attribution to Xia Gui is traditional rather than secure; the National Palace Museum dates this version to the Ming. Still, it inherits the Ma-Xia playbook: economy over detail, axe-cut brushstrokes, huge reserves of empty silk standing in for mist and water. You read it the way you'd read a long walk, a few metres at a time, settlements thinning into crags and back into river again. The Yangtze itself is mostly negative space.

Anonymous_-_Brustbild_eines_jungen_Manne.title: Bust Portrait of a Young Man

source.canonical_title: File:Anonymous - Brustbild eines jungen Mannes - 4641 - Österreichische Galerie Belvedere (cropped).jpg

Anthonis_van_Dyck_016.jpg.title: Marchesa Elena Grimaldi Cattaneo

source.canonical_title: File:Anthonis van Dyck 016.jpg

title.de: Porträt der Marchesa Elena Grimaldi, Gattin des Marchese Nicola Cattaneo.
title.zh: 埃萊娜·格里馬爾迪·卡塔內奧侯爵夫人肖像畫

Anthonis_van_Dyck_016.jpg.story: Painted in Genoa in 1623, during Van Dyck's Italian years, and now at the National Gallery of Art in Washington. The Marchesa steps forward onto the terrace of her palazzo in head-to-toe black silk, her lace-cuffed hand holding a sprig of orange blossom, the traditional sign of chastity. Behind her, an African attendant raises a bright red parasol that cuts a clean shape against a grey sky. The scale and swagger borrow directly from Rubens's Genoese portraits of a decade earlier. It hung with portraits of her two children, Filippo and Maddalena, still together in Washington.

Anthonis_van_Dyck_054.jpg.title: Drunken Silenus supported by Satyrs

source.canonical_title: File:Anthonis van Dyck 054.jpg

Anthonis_van_Dyck_054.jpg.story: A crowd of boozy satyrs and maenads hauls a vast pink-bellied Silenus through the dappled edge of a wood — flutes piping, grapes pressed to his mouth, a leering faun whispering at the right, two cherubs tussling over a bunch of grapes below. The scene is pure Rubens in spirit and once bore his name; it's now usually given to the young Van Dyck working inside Rubens's studio around 1620, before he'd fully found his own sharper line. The panel hangs at the Gemäldegalerie Alte Meister in Dresden.

Anthony_van_Dyck_-_Mary_Ruthven,_Lady_va.title: Portrait of Mary Ruthven, Lady van Dyck

source.canonical_title: File:Anthony van Dyck - Mary Ruthven, Lady van Dyck.jpg

Anthony_van_Dyck_-_Mary_Ruthven,_Lady_va.story: Painted around 1639-1640 in London, now at the Prado in Madrid. Mary Ruthven, from a Scottish noble family, had recently married Van Dyck; the knighthood he'd received from Charles I made her Lady van Dyck. She sits in a shining blue silk dress cut low at the neckline, pearls at her throat, fingering a bracelet on her wrist with a relaxed, half-distracted gesture. In her hair, a wreath of oak leaves puns on his surname - Dutch for oak. She gave birth to their only child, Justina, just eight days before Van Dyck's death in 1641.

Anthony_van_Dyck_Rachel_de_Ruvigny.jpg.title: Rachel de Ruvigny, Countess of Southampton
Anthony_van_Dyck_Rachel_de_Ruvigny.jpg.artist: After Anthony van Dyck / Anthony van Dyck
Anthony_van_Dyck_Rachel_de_Ruvigny.jpg.description: Rachel de Ruvigny, Countess of Southampton

source.canonical_title: File:Anthony van Dyck Rachel de Ruvigny.jpg

title.de: Rachel de Ruvigny, Gräfin von Southampton

Anthony_van_Dyck_Rachel_de_Ruvigny.jpg.story: Rachel de Ruvigny floats on clouds in icy-blue satin, a pearl choker at her throat and one hand resting on a great bronze globe while a skull peeks from the hem of her gown. The allegorical reading is Fortune, or perhaps Fortune tamed by Virtue — the sphere rolls, the skull reminds, the sunburst breaks through. Van Dyck painted the original for her husband, the 4th Earl of Southampton, around 1640, shortly before his own death; this version is the Fitzwilliam Museum's fine early copy after a composition that exists in several hands.

Anton_Van_Dyck_-_Anton_Giulio_Brignole-S.title: Anton Giulio Brignole-Sale on horseback

source.canonical_title: File:Anton Van Dyck - Anton Giulio Brignole-Sale on horseback - Google Art Project.jpg
source.credit: kQG1dKzvnwCU7g at Google Cultural Institute maximum zoom level

Anton_Van_Dyck_-_Anton_Giulio_Brignole-S.story: Anton Giulio Brignole-Sale was twenty-two, rich, a budding writer, and wanted to be painted like a prince — so in 1627 the Brignole-Sale family account books record a payment to Van Dyck for exactly that. The young Genoese nobleman wheels a grey charger through a stage-set arch, baton in hand, plume at his hip, plainly modelled on Titian's equestrian Charles V. Van Dyck was finishing his six-year Italian tour and had the swagger of the Genoese elite down cold. The portrait still hangs in Palazzo Rosso, the Brignole family's own house on Via Garibaldi.

Anton_van_Dyck_-_Samson_and_Delilah_-_Go.title: Samson and Delilah

source.canonical_title: File:Anton van Dyck - Samson and Delilah - Google Art Project.jpg
source.credit: ggFmBL7gYcnEbg at Google Cultural Institute maximum zoom level

Anton_van_Dyck_-_Samson_and_Delilah_-_Go.story: Van Dyck painted this Samson and Delilah around 1628-30, after his Italian years, and he rewrote the story. Rubens, his old master, had shown Delilah as a cool operator pocketing her fee. Van Dyck gives her a face full of regret — she reaches toward Samson even as the Philistine soldiers seize him, and Samson, in a quote lifted from Titian, clutches at her leg on the way down. The canvas is nearly two and a half metres wide and now hangs in the Kunsthistorisches Museum in Vienna.

Aphonse_Mucha_-_Rose_1898.jpg.title: Aphonse Mucha - Rose 1898
Aphonse_Mucha_-_Rose_1898.jpg.description: A reproduction of the 1898 painting "Die Rose" by Alphonse Mucha

source.canonical_title: File:Aphonse Mucha - Rose 1898.jpg

Aphonse_Mucha_-_Rose_1898.jpg.story: Rose is the warm counterpart to Lily in Mucha's 1898 series The Flowers. She leans against a trellis of pink roses, one bloom tipped into her hair, another between her fingers, the whole panel bathed in a sunset wash. What looks effortless was carefully staged — Mucha photographed models in his Paris studio and drew from the prints, layering the posed figure over a flat arabesque of stems and petals. Champenois printed the four panels as colour lithographs and sold them as inexpensive wall decor, no frame required.

Apparatus_and_Hand.jpg.title: Apparatus and Hand

Arabian_nights_3_by_John_Frederick_Lewis.title: Arabian nights 3 by John Frederick Lewis

source.canonical_title: File:Arabian nights 3 by John Frederick Lewis.jpeg

Arabian_nights_3_by_John_Frederick_Lewis.story: Two women in an upper room in Cairo - one reclining on a divan in striped silks, another standing in a red doorway. Carved mashrabiya screens filter white daylight; a framed panel of Arabic calligraphy hangs on the yellow wall. Lewis had spent the 1840s living in a Mamluk house in the old city and he knew this light intimately. His interiors aren't quite harems - they're harem fantasies, respectable enough for the Royal Academy, but the pattern-work and the granular attention to floor tiles and textile weave were something English watercolour had never seen before.

Arcimboldo_Air_(copy).jpg.title: The Air

source.canonical_title: File:Arcimboldo Air (copy).jpg
source.credit: Arcimboldo. 1526-1593. Ausstellungskatalog des Kunsthistorischen Museums Wien 2008, p. 147. ISBN 978-3-85497-118-4 , Scanned by uploader

Arcimboldo_Air_(copy).jpg.story: Arcimboldo painted the Four Elements in 1566 for Emperor Maximilian II, and Air was the one composed entirely of birds — a peacock for the chest, a pheasant tail making a goatee, a duck's bill curled into an eyelid, with the Habsburg eagle perched at the shoulder. The original is lost or at least never firmly identified; what circulates instead are early copies and variants of the invention, this being one of them. Read it as a sixteenth-century in-joke about a court that prized ingenuity over decorum, preserved in a later hand.

Arcimboldo_Earth.jpg.title: The Earth

source.canonical_title: File:Arcimboldo Earth.jpg
source.credit: Arcimboldo. 1526-1593. Ausstellungskatalog des Kunsthistorischen Museums Wien 2008, p. 1152. ISBN 978-3-85497-118-4 , Scanned by uploader

Arcimboldo_Earth.jpg.story: Earth is a tightly packed zoo. An elephant's trunk becomes an ear, a deer's head the jaw, a ram curls into the brow, and a lion's pelt drapes the shoulder like a little Habsburg trophy. Arcimboldo painted it in 1566 as part of a Four Elements series for Emperor Maximilian II, a companion set to his Four Seasons. The more you stare, the more animals surface. Count carefully and you can find over fifty species tucked into a single profile, from a boar and a donkey to a tiny monkey riding the neck.

Arcimboldowater.jpg.title: The allegory of Water

source.canonical_title: File:Arcimboldowater.jpg
source.credit: Arcimboldo. 1526-1593. Ausstellungskatalog des Kunsthistorischen Museums Wien 2008, p. 1152. ISBN 978-3-85497-118-4

Arcimboldowater.jpg.story: Water is a glittering heap of marine life stacked into a face. A crab forms the chest, an octopus curls across the shoulder, a shark's open jaw becomes the mouth, and pearls drip as earrings. Arcimboldo painted it in 1566 alongside Fire, Earth, and Air as an allegorical set for the Habsburg court. Every creature here, rays, eels, lobster, turtle, squid, would have been familiar to court naturalists cataloging the emperor's expanding world. The picture now lives in Vienna's Kunsthistorisches Museum, where the whole imperial series was eventually gathered.

Argenteuil_A14692.jpg.title: Argenteuil

source.canonical_title: File:Argenteuil A14692.jpg

Argenteuil_A14692.jpg.story: Monet had just moved his family to Argenteuil, a riverside town fifteen minutes by train from Paris, and he couldn't stop painting the view from the embankment. Sailboats tick against their moorings, the Seine goes pearly under a high sky, and the opposite bank lies flat as a ribbon. Everything here is weekend weather. He would paint this stretch of water dozens of times over the next four years, but the 1872 canvases have a particular lightness, as if he's still surprised the place is his. It now hangs at the National Gallery of Art in Washington.

Ariko weeps on her boat.jpg.title: Ariko weeps on her boat

Arnaut_and_his_dog_by_Jean_Leon_gerome.j.title: Arnaut Blowing Smoke at the Nose of His Dog
Arnaut_and_his_dog_by_Jean_Leon_gerome.j.description: Arnaut is oriental name for Albanian - This Arnaut warrior fought for Muhamed Ali (an Albanian), founder of modern Egypt.

source.canonical_title: File:Arnaut and his dog by Jean Leon gerome.jpg

Arnaut_and_his_dog_by_Jean_Leon_gerome.j.story: The joke is in the dog's face. An Arnaut, one of the Ottoman empire's Albanian mercenaries, leans down and blows a long plume of tobacco smoke straight into the nose of his greyhound, which is recoiling in disgust. Gérôme called the picture Une Plaisanterie, 'A Joke,' and sometimes added the subtitle 'A greyhound who does not like the snuff.' It's a rare moment of pure domestic comedy from a painter usually after grandeur and cruelty. Painted in 1882, oil on canvas, now in a private collection.

Artemisia_Gentileschi_-_Danaë.jpg.title: Danae

source.canonical_title: File:Artemisia Gentileschi - Danaë.jpg

Artemisia_Gentileschi_-_Danaë.jpg.story: Artemisia's Danaë sprawls across crimson and white drapery, arms flung back, golden hair unspooling, as Jupiter's shower falls in a scatter of actual coins — a maidservant in blue and white catches them in her gathered skirt at the right. The flesh is ivory against almost black shadow; the erotic charge is startlingly direct, the trick with the purse faintly wry. Long given to Orazio and now generally accepted as young Artemisia's from around 1612, the small panel belongs to the Saint Louis Art Museum.

Artemisia_Gentileschi_-_Madonna_con_Bamb.title: Virgin with the Child

source.canonical_title: File:Artemisia Gentileschi - Madonna con Bambino (1609-1610).jpg

Artemisia_Gentileschi_-_Madonna_con_Bamb.story: One of Artemisia's earliest surviving works, painted around 1610-1611 when she was about seventeen, now at the Galleria Spada in Rome. The Virgin has just finished nursing: her breast is still uncovered, and the Child, cheek pressed to her shoulder, reaches up to touch her face in a slow, satisfied caress. The colour is almost entirely warm - ochre drapery, amber flesh - against a shadow that her father Orazio would have recognised from their shared Caravaggesque vocabulary. It is contemporary with her Pommersfelden 'Susanna,' her first signed canvas.

Artemisia_Gentileschi_Cleopatra2.jpg.title: Death of Cleopatra

source.canonical_title: File:Artemisia Gentileschi Cleopatra2.jpg

Artemisia_Gentileschi_Cleopatra2.jpg.story: A heavy nude stretched on bone-white linen, deep red curtain behind, the asp already coiling around her slack fingers — Artemisia gives Cleopatra none of the operatic theatrics later painters loved. The body is weighty and unidealised, the face already turning away. The attribution bounces between Artemisia and her father Orazio; the picture, dated around 1613 and in a Milanese private collection, is one of several Gentileschi Cleopatras, and the closest thing early Baroque Rome produced to a study of a woman choosing her own death without witnesses.

Artemisia_Gentileschi_Judith_Maidservant.title: Judith and Her Maidservant
Artemisia_Gentileschi_Judith_Maidservant.description: Judith and her servant pause, seeming to hear a noise outside Holofernes’ tent. The shadowy interior is theatrically illuminated by a single candle. Judith’s hand shields her face from the glow, drawing attention to Holofernes’ discarded iron gauntlet. The viewer’s eye travels to the object in the maidservant’s hands: Holofernes’ severed head.

source.canonical_title: File:Artemisia Gentileschi Judith Maidservant DIA.jpg

Artemisia_Gentileschi_Judith_Maidservant.story: A candle does all the work: Judith's raised hand throws a hard shadow across her cheek, her maid is a mass of brocade bent over the severed head, and Holofernes' discarded iron gauntlet glints on the carpet. Both women have paused, alert to something in the dark beyond the tent. Collector Leslie H. Green bought the picture in 1952 and gifted it to the Detroit Institute of Arts.

Artemisia_Gentileschi_Mary_Magdalene_Pit.title: Penitent Mary Magdalene

source.canonical_title: File:Artemisia Gentileschi Mary Magdalene Pitti.jpg

Artemisia_Gentileschi_Mary_Magdalene_Pit.story: Painted during Artemisia's Florentine years, around 1616-1618, and still in the Pitti. Mary Magdalene sprawls in a huge saffron-yellow silk dress, one hand clutching her chest, the other pushing away a small mirror engraved with 'Optimam partem elegit' - 'she has chosen the best part.' The hair is loose, almost tangled, lit from the right by a narrow, sharp beam in the Caravaggesque manner. The commission likely came through Grand Duchess Maria Maddalena de' Medici, whose name the saint shared. Artemisia signed it 'Artemisia Lomi,' the surname she used while working in Florence.

Artgate_Fondazione_Cariplo_-_Hayez_Franc.title: The Last Meeting between Jacopo Foscari and his Family Before Being Sent into Exile
Artgate_Fondazione_Cariplo_-_Hayez_Franc.description: The painting was commissioned in 1838 by Emperor Ferdinand I , who had arrived in Milan for his coronation as king of Lombardy and Veneto , and it was destined for the Belvedere Gallery in Vienna. On its completion in 1840 the work was valued at the extremely high price of five thousand florins by the Commissione Permanente di Pittura dell’Accademia di Brera , which thus recognized its exceptional quality. In 1928 this large canvas was auctioned at the Galleria Scopinich in Milan, together with other valuable Italian paintings from the imperial collections, where it was bought by Antonio Bernocchi an important member of the rising entrepreneurial middle class, who was active in the textile sector and became senator of the Kingdom of Italy in 1929. The painting entered the Cariplo Collection from this prestigious private collection in 1989. Histoire de la République de Venise by the French historian Pierre Daru is the literary source of this episode regarding the Doge, who was forced to accept that his son Jacopo was sentenced to exile after being unjustly accused of treason. This subject had also been formerly addressed by Lord Byron in 1821 in his tragedy The Two Foscaris , which inspired the opera of the same name in 1844 by Giuseppe Verdi . The critics immediately recognised the theatrical appeal of history painting that often chose the same subjects as the more popular operas. The general public readily identified with the events depicted on canvas because of the precise reconstruction of settings, costumes and gestures, but also because they included portraits of their contemporaries as historical figures. In this canvas in the Collection the Doge is an older self portrait of Hayez himself, and with a dramatic gesture he forces his son to respect the decision of the Council of Ten, as he leans on his stick trembling with emotion. The differing reactions of the figures around him are evident: the silent suffering of the women; the icy expression of Jacopo’s enemy Loredano standing beside him, as the condemned son stretches out his hands towards his father; the various emotions of the children. Jacopo’s leavetaking of his family is rendered even more agonising by the allusion to his imminent departure from his homeland evident in the view of the lagoon with the ships about to set sail, which can be glimpsed through the portico of the Ducal Palace. The myth of Venice and the loneliness of the powerful are condensed in this episode, which Hayez treated repeatedly in several versions, including the famous canvas commissioned by his friend and adviser Andrea Maffei and executed between 1852 and 1854 (Florence, Galleria d’Arte Moderna Palazzo Pitti). The artist’s dramatic sensibility and the similarity between his painting and Verdi’s opera, was further confirmed when he was asked to revise the costume-sketches for the staging of The Two Foscaris in 1858.
