title.it: L'ultimo abboccamento di Jacopo Foscari con la propria famiglia (I due Foscari)
title.de: Das letzte Zusammentreffen zwischen Jacopo Foscari und seiner Familie vor der Vertreibung ins Exil

Artlib_gallery-13875-o.jpg.title: Artlib gallery-13875-o

source.canonical_title: File:Artlib gallery-13875-o.jpg

Artlib_gallery-13875-o.jpg.story: "The Vanquished. Requiem." A field stretches to the horizon under a heavy sky. What looks at first like ploughed earth resolves into the bodies of Russian soldiers, barely covered, going on and on. A priest swings a censer over them. Vereshchagin painted this after the siege of Plevna, where his own brother had been killed, and Petersburg generals accused him of empathising with the Turks and insulting the army. The painting answers them without answering — there is nothing in it but the dead and the service being read for them.

As_the_Old_Sing,_So_the_Young_Pipe,_by_J.title: As the Old Sing, So the Young Pipe
As_the_Old_Sing,_So_the_Young_Pipe,_by_J.description: As the Old Sing, So the Young Pipe oil on canvas 155 × 180 cm 1638-1640 inscribed t.c.: Ut genus,est genius concors consentus ab ortu

source.canonical_title: File:As the Old Sing, So the Young Pipe, by Jacob Jordaens.jpg

As_the_Old_Sing,_So_the_Young_Pipe,_by_J.story: The proverb goes: as the old sing, so the young pipe — children copy their elders, for better or worse. Jordaens made the subject his own, painting the scene at least a dozen times. A loud multi-generational family crammed around a table, grandmother leading a song from a sheet, parents joining in, a toddler blowing on a recorder, a dog underfoot. The Latin inscription up top translates roughly as like breed, like disposition. This is one of the finest versions, with the line the young pipe doing double duty: charming picture of domestic music-making, and deadpan warning that bad habits run in the blood.

Asakusa_Honganji_temple_in_th_Eastern_ca.story: Hokusai shoves the temple roof so close to the picture plane it nearly crowds Fuji out. Workmen crawl across the tiles, mending something; a kite tugs at its string in the winter wind, telling you it's probably New Year's Day. The roof's triangle rhymes with the mountain's. Beneath it, Edo's busiest neighborhood goes about its morning, oblivious. The Higashi Hongan-ji branch temple that anchors the view had stood in Asakusa since 1657.

At_first_glance_he_looks_very_fiarce,_bu.story: One of Kuniyoshi's famous 'body-puzzle' prints: a glowering giant who, on closer inspection, is built entirely out of contorted naked men piled together. The face, the topknot, even the scowling eyebrows are limbs and torsos. The title — roughly, 'looks scary, actually a nice guy' — is the whole joke. Prints like this were Kuniyoshi's end-run around the Tenpo censorship laws: too playful to ban, too crowded to summarise. Children loved them, adults bought them, and the inspector shrugged.

At_the_beer_garden_(1883)_-_Adolf_Friedr.story: Tiny — about 13 by 18 centimetres — and done in gouache, which Menzel loved for its chalky, quick response. He was pushing seventy and still sitting in Berlin beer gardens filling notebooks: waiters' aprons, hats, the geometry of a crowded table under trees. The picture isn't posed for anything; it's the kind of note he made by the hundreds. Now at the Museum Georg Schafer in Schweinfurt.

Auguste_Renoir_-_En_été_-_La_bohémienne_.story: Lise Tréhot, Renoir's lover and favorite model of the late 1860s, sits in a striped dress against green foliage, arms bare, eyes heavy-lidded. He called it 'En été' — In Summer — and subtitled it 'La bohémienne' for the Salon of 1868. The critics were underwhelmed; the painter Théodule Ribot was one of the few who praised it. It's loose, almost unfinished around the leaves, flesh painted with a freedom Renoir hadn't quite shown before. Now at the Alte Nationalgalerie in Berlin.

Auguste_Renoir_-_La_Grenouillère_-_Googl.title: The Frog Pond

source.canonical_title: File:Auguste Renoir - La Grenouillère - Google Art Project.jpg

Auguste_Renoir_-_La_Grenouillère_-_Googl.story: Summer 1869, Renoir and Monet set up their easels side by side at La Grenouillère, a floating restaurant and swimming spot on the Seine at Croissy. They painted the same view on the same afternoons — the tiny tree-topped island nicknamed 'the camembert,' the rowboats, the bathers — and between them cracked Impressionism wide open. Light became broken strokes; water became dashes of blue and white. This version hangs at the Nationalmuseum in Stockholm. Monet's hangs in the Metropolitan.

source.canonical_title: File:Autoportrait au turban (Perpignan).jpg

title.fr: Autoportrait dit au turban de Hyacinthe Rigaud

Autoportrait_au_turban_(Perpignan).jpg.story: Rigaud spent his life painting other people in ermine and brocade; here, at thirty-nine, he turns the brush on himself and swaps the state-portrait pomp for a loose oriental turban. The fur-trimmed wrap, the half-smile, the sidelong glance — he looks less like the Sun King's official portraitist than a working painter caught between commissions. The canvas hung in his own studio for decades before reaching his native Perpignan, where the Musée Hyacinthe Rigaud still keeps it. He signed and dated it 1698, three years before the Louis XIV portrait that would make him famous.

Ave_Caesar_Morituri_te_Salutant_(Gérôm.title: Hail Caesar! We Who Are About to Die Salute You

source.canonical_title: File:Ave Caesar Morituri te Salutant (Gérôme) 01.jpg

B159_Rembrandt.jpg.title: The Shell (Conus Marmoreus)

source.canonical_title: File:B159 Rembrandt.jpg

B159_Rembrandt.jpg.story: Rembrandt kept a room of curiosities in his Amsterdam house, and somewhere on those shelves sat this marbled cone, a rare import from the Indian Ocean that the Dutch called hertshoren, stag's horn. He drew it straight onto the copper plate, so the printed shell spirals the wrong way, counter-clockwise, which no real Conus marmoreus ever does. Three states exist: first a bare drypoint shadow, then an etched dark box behind it, then the tip sharpened with burin. Catalogued as B.159 and dated 1650, it is the only still life Rembrandt ever etched.

B320_Rembrandt.jpg.title: Self portrait in a cap, with eyes wide open

source.canonical_title: File:B320 Rembrandt.jpg

title.de: Selbstporträt mit Mütze und aufgerissenen Augen
title.nl: Zelfportret met baret en opengesperde ogen

B320_Rembrandt.jpg.story: Rembrandt is twenty-four, still working in Leiden, and obsessed with his own face as a laboratory. Here he catches himself mid-startle: brows hiked, eyes flung open, mouth slightly parted, as if someone just slammed a door behind him. The cap swallows his hair in shadow; a single wire of light traces the tip of his nose. It's less a portrait than an acting exercise in copperplate, one of roughly two dozen self-portrait etchings he made before leaving for Amsterdam. He signed the tiny plate with his early monogram, RHL.

Back_View_of_Fuji_from_Dream_Mtn_in_Kai_.title: Back View of Fuji from Dream Mtn in Kai Province (Hiroshige, 1852)
Back_View_of_Fuji_from_Dream_Mtn_in_Kai_.description: Back View of Mt.Fuji from Dream Mountain in Kai Province (Japanese: 甲斐夢山裏富士, Kai yumeyama urafuji ). No. 33 [1] (or No. 6 [2] ) in the series Thirty-six Views of Mount Fuji (first version).

source.canonical_title: File:Back View of Fuji from Dream Mtn in Kai Province (Hiroshige, 1852).jpg

Back_View_of_Fuji_from_Dream_Mtn_in_Kai_.story: Hiroshige turns the usual postcard around: we're behind Fuji, looking at its less-photographed flank from Yumeyama — Dream Mountain — in Kai Province. The foreground tumbles with pines and cliff; the mountain itself is almost demure, a pale cone in the distance. This is the horizontal first version of his Thirty-six Views of Mount Fuji, issued in 1852, six years before he'd do the whole series again in vertical format. The 'back view' was its quiet joke: Fuji has a rear elevation, and it's beautiful too.

Baglione.jpg.title: Sacred and Profane Love

source.canonical_title: File:Giovanni Baglione - The Divine Eros Defeats the Earthly Eros.jpg
source.credit: Web Gallery of Art : Image Info about artwork wga QS:P11807,"b/baglione/sacred2"

title.fr: Victoire de l'Amour sacré sur l'Amour profane

Baglione.jpg.story: Baglione painted this version of Sacred and Profane Love specifically to upstage Caravaggio's Amor Vincit Omnia, and the whole thing reads like a courtroom exhibit. A fully armoured angel of Divine Love descends in a storm of metallic wings to catch a naked, flailing Cupid in the act; behind him a dark, horned demon with Caravaggio's own features snarls from the shadows. It is an extraordinary picture and also a petty one, painted by the man who would soon sue Caravaggio for libel in Rome's most famous artists' feud.

Baigneurs_a_Asnieres.jpg.title: Seated Nude: Study for 'Bathers at Asnières'

source.canonical_title: File:Baigneurs a Asnieres.jpg

Baigneurs_a_Asnieres.jpg.story: Factory smokestacks puff on the far bank while working-class Parisians loaf by the river in their underwear. Seurat was twenty-four. He painted the figures solid and sculptural, like a Piero della Francesca fresco dragged out to the suburbs, then dotted highlights on top after discovering pointillism. The Salon jury rejected it in 1884, so he hung it at the scrappy new Salon des Indépendants instead, catalog number 261. That orange hat on the boy in the water was one of his first experiments with the optical-mixing technique that would define the rest of his short career.

Baldassare_Castiglione,_by_Raffaello_San.story: Castiglione wrote The Book of the Courtier, the bestselling sixteenth-century manual on how to be elegant without looking like you're trying, a quality he called sprezzatura. Raphael, his close friend, paints him exactly that way: grey-blue velvet and lynx fur, a soft black beret, quiet eyes that miss nothing. Finished around 1514-15, it became a portrait template copied by Rembrandt, who did a pen sketch of it at auction in 1639, and echoed by Matisse. It hangs in the Louvre. Castiglione mentioned the painting in a Latin elegy written after his wife's death.

Bartolomé_Esteban_Murillo_-_Saint_Rose_o.story: Rose of Lima, the first person born in the Americas to be canonised, was made a saint in 1671 — which is almost certainly why Murillo painted this around 1670, riding the Sevillian enthusiasm for the new Dominican intercessor. She kneels in her black-and-white habit beside a sewing basket, and the Christ child is sitting in the basket on a little cushion, chatting to her as if nothing could be more natural. The oil is now in the Museo Lázaro Galdiano in Madrid.

Bartolomé_Esteban_Perez_Murillo_008.jpg.story: Mary pauses her sewing; Joseph leans in from his carpenter's bench; the child Jesus dangles a small bird before an eager little dog, who rises on its hind legs in anticipation. The honeyed Sevillian light that made Murillo the darling of later Grand Tourists bathes a cluttered workshop floor of shavings and cloth. Painted around 1650, near the start of his mature phase, it now hangs in the Prado, Madrid.

Basket-fishing_in_the_Kinu_River_(Kinuga.title: Basket-fishing in the Kinu River (Kinugawa hachifuse) -- Hokusai
Basket-fishing_in_the_Kinu_River_(Kinuga.description: Hokusai Basket-fishing in the Kinu River (Kinugawa hachifuse) , Oceans of Wisdom series

source.credit: Original publication : Japan, 1830s Immediate source : https://ukiyo-e.org/image/mfa/sc145753

Basket-fishing_in_the_Kinu_River_(Kinuga.story: Two fishermen wade into the Kinugawa clutching a circular bamboo trap, the river's current cut into Hokusai's signature curling whitecaps. The print comes from his Oceans of Wisdom (Chie no umi) series of around 1833, a set of ten views celebrating regional fishing techniques. Hachifuse, "eight-fold cover," refers to the woven basket itself, dropped over a patch of shallow water to trap sweetfish. Hokusai was in his early seventies when he cut the series, and the sheet is printed in the deep Prussian blue he had only recently adopted.

Bathsheba_(c.1827),_by_Francesco_Hayez.j.title: Bathsheba

source.canonical_title: File:Bathsheba (c.1827), by Francesco Hayez.jpg
source.credit: Christie's , LotFinder: entry 6510043 (sale 22691, lot 25, London, 3 December 2024)

Bathsheba_(c.1827),_by_Francesco_Hayez.j.story: Bathsheba steps from her bath with her hair down, unaware that King David is watching from a rooftop across the way. Hayez painted her around 1827 as the plump, pearly Venetian type he had grown up studying, less a biblical warning than a nude excuse. A maid kneels to dry her feet; a second peers off toward the distant palace.

Bauernfeind,_Gustav_-_At_the_Entrance_to.title: At the Entrance to the Temple Mount, Jerusalem

source.canonical_title: File:Bauernfeind, Gustav - At the Entrance to the Temple Mount, Jerusalem - 1886.png

Bauernfeind,_Gustav_-_At_the_Entrance_to.story: Bauernfeind sets up before one of the gates into the Haram al-Sharif, with stone, shadow, and a slow stream of worshippers and tradesmen passing beneath the arch. The picture is almost unreasonably exact: every joint in the ashlar, every fold in a robe, every sun-bleached tone of Jerusalem limestone. He spent months on each of these canvases and kept returning to the Temple Mount gates as a subject. Twelve years after this, he gave up Germany and moved his family permanently to Jerusalem.

Bazille_and_Camille_(Study_for_Déjeuner_.title: Bazille and Camille (Study for "Déjeuner sur l'Herbe")

source.canonical_title: File:Bazille and Camille (Study for Déjeuner sur l'Herbe) A35075.jpg

Bazille_and_Camille_(Study_for_Déjeuner_.story: A woodland clearing, quick strokes, two figures mid-stroll: Monet's tall friend Frédéric Bazille, caught in the gesture of turning, and Camille Doncieux in a pale dress beside him. It's a study for a vast canvas Monet hoped would dethrone Manet's scandalous picnic painting. The big version never made it to the Salon and was eventually cut up and abandoned in a cellar. This fragment-scale sketch, painted outdoors in the forest of Fontainebleau, now hangs at the National Gallery of Art in Washington.

Beardsley-peacockskirt.png.title: Beardsley-peacockskirt
Beardsley-peacockskirt.png.description: “The Peacock Skirt”, illustration by Aubrey Beardsley for Oscar Wilde 's play Salomé (1892)

source.canonical_title: File:Beardsley-peacockskirt.PNG

Beardsley-peacockskirt.png.story: Pure black ink on white, no half-tones, no shading. Salome advances on a slender dandified John the Baptist, her train ballooning into a colossal peacock fan whose eyed feathers are the only thing holding the left half of the composition together. The line is impossibly thin where it wants to be and drops into flat black where it wants weight. Drawn for the 1894 English edition of Wilde's Salome, which John Lane published with Beardsley's illustrations; Beardsley was 21, and dead of tuberculosis four years later.

Bemberg_Fondation_Toulouse_-_Bateaux_sur.story: Monet went to Etretat in the winter of 1883 partly to get out of Paris and partly to paint the same cliffs Courbet and Boudin had worked before him. Here the famous arch of the Porte d'Aval sits quietly in the middle distance while a long row of beached fishing boats takes the foreground - blunt wooden hulls, tarred and patched, hauled up above the tideline. The sea is calm and silvery, the beach a scatter of tiny figures. Less a grand motif than a working shore, caught on a bright, chilly day.

The rest dissolves into an unmodulated dark ground. He was twenty-four when he painted it in 1860 and would spend the next decade assembling the group portraits of Manet's circle that made his name. The panel hangs in the Fondation Bemberg in Toulouse.

Besneeuwde_ochtend_in_Koishikawa-Rijksmu.story: A waitress on a teahouse balcony leans out and points. Follow her finger past the sloping tile roofs, over snow still fresh on the pines, and there's Fuji: pale, exact, composed. Her guests, wrapped against the cold, tilt their heads to look. It's a small, quiet theater of seeing, staged in a rectangle of veranda. The print is scene 11 in a series that was first issued for the New Year of 1831.

By 1908 the water carrier had become almost a brand for him, endlessly repeated for an international market that couldn't get enough. The picture makes a domestic chore look like a fashion plate, which was precisely the point.

BodhidharmaYoshitoshi1887.jpg.story: From the 1887 run of the Hundred Aspects series. Bodhidharma - Daruma in Japanese, the Indian prince who brought Zen to China - sits wrapped in his robe in the cave at Shaolin, where legend says he faced a wall for nine years until the wall began to crumble. Yoshitoshi draws him hunched and intense, vines creeping through the broken masonry, the moon visible through the gap. The title cues the reading: the crumbling window is the mind giving way, and the moon coming through is what's on the other side of it.

Bonneville,_Savoy_by_Joseph_Mallord_Will.story: Turner crossed into Savoy on his 1802 Alpine trip and kept the little town of Bonneville, tucked under the Môle, as one of his favourite motifs - he painted it several times. This version, exhibited 1803, is classical in its bones: a Claudean valley, trees framing a middle distance, figures on a road. But the light on the distant peak is already unmistakably his, cool and high and particular.

Botticelli,_annunciazione_di_cestello_02.story: Gabriel has just landed. His knee touches the tiled floor, lily in hand, while Mary sways back in a near-swoon — her body curving away from the news, her hand echoing his in a gesture suspended between refusal and acceptance. Through the arched window, a walled garden and a distant tree anchor the miracle in a specific, breezy afternoon. Botticelli painted it in 1489 for the Cestello church in Florence, now Santa Maria Maddalena dei Pazzi. The floor tiles have been worked out mathematically to produce perfect perspective — his math teacher was reputedly the great mathematician Luca Pacioli.

Botticelli,_incoronazione_della_vergine,.story: John sits exiled on Patmos, rocky crag under him, eagle at his shoulder, the Aegean slate-grey beyond. He stares straight up — the Apocalypse is beginning to unroll in the sky. This small panel is one of four predella scenes that ran along the bottom of Botticelli's Coronation of the Virgin altarpiece, painted around 1490 for the goldsmiths' chapel in the Florentine church of San Marco. The main panel shows Christ crowning Mary in a gold-streaked heaven; the predella grounds the ecstasy in narrative. Today the whole assembly is in the Uffizi.

Botticelli_-_A_Virgem_e_o_Menino_com_um_.story: A grave young Madonna balances the Christ Child while an angel offers a bowl of grapes and wheat, Eucharist food dressed up as a snack. The pale faces, almond eyes, and high foreheads owe everything to Botticelli's master Filippo Lippi, who trained him while this tempera panel was being worked out. It now hangs at the Spedale degli Innocenti in Florence, the foundling hospital designed by Brunelleschi, which feels right: a painting about a mother and a fed child in a building built for abandoned ones. Botticelli was born in 1445, so the Innocenti itself now dates this panel around 1465-1467.
Botticelli_-_A_Virgem_e_o_Menino_com_um_.year_note: Year 1450 is impossible (Botticelli was born 1445). Spedale degli Innocenti dates this panel c. 1465-1467; using midpoint 1466.

Botticelli_04_Louvre.jpg.story: The young John the Baptist, in his rough camel-hair tunic, crowds in at the Virgin's knee to adore the sleeping Christ Child, who is collapsed across Mary's lap like a baby who just gave up on being fed. Botticelli paints Mary's fingers long and nervous, and her gaze goes nowhere in particular, the first flicker of the melancholy he would perfect in the Uffizi Madonnas. The tondo-adjacent composition was widely copied by his workshop. Tempera on panel, painted in Florence around 1470-1475, it hangs in the Louvre.

Bouquet_of_Mallows.jpg.story: Monet started this lush vase of wild mallows around 1880, got stuck, and shoved it to the back of the studio. Forty years later — forty — he dragged it out and finished it. You can see where the old paint had dried flat and the late brushwork sits on top in some of the petals. He finally signed and sold it around 1920. The off-centre vase and high tipped-up viewpoint give the whole thing a strange tilting feel. It hangs at the Courtauld in London.

Boy_with_a_Basket_of_Fruit-Caravaggio_(1.story: Lean in close and you can see the fungal spots on the grape leaf, the wormholes on a peach, a cluster of insect eggs on another leaf. Caravaggio, barely in his twenties and scraping by in Rome, painted the basket as carefully as he painted the boy holding it — Mario Minniti, his Sicilian friend, about sixteen, shoulder bared. The canvas sat in Cavaliere d'Arpino's workshop until 1607, when Cardinal Scipione Borghese strong-armed the whole hoard out of him and stuffed it into his own collection.

Brooklyn_Museum_-_Snow_Scene_-_Utagawa_T.story: Kunisada — signing, as he usually did by this point, as Toyokuni III — working in the snow-scene tradition that ukiyo-e designers treated as a test piece. Snow in a woodblock print is mostly absence: the unprinted paper, carefully reserved by the block-cutter, left to do the work. Figures bundled in straw capes pick across a white landscape. Kunisada ran the biggest ukiyo-e studio in Edo, outsold Hokusai and Hiroshige in his lifetime, and turned out pieces like this between the kabuki actor prints that were his bread and butter.

Brooklyn_Museum_-_Study_of_a_Girl_in_Jap.story: Japonisme was everywhere in 1890s New York and Chase, an obsessive collector of kimonos and Asian props, leaned in harder than most. Here a young model — likely one of his daughters — stands in a patterned robe against a shadowy studio wall, more study than finished statement. The paint is loose, the face barely resolved; what Chase cares about is the fall of silk and the quiet drama of silhouette. The Brooklyn Museum holds it as a record of how deeply Japanese design had seeped into American studio practice.

Brooklyn_Museum_-_Tabi_Miyage_Dai_1_-_Sh.story: An inn in the mountains of northern Honshu, one building, evening, rain. Hasui's own notes describe an unbearable loneliness there — cedars blurred by the shower, lamps glowing through wet paper screens. Published in summer 1919 by Watanabe Shōzaburō as part of the first Tabi Miyage (Souvenirs of Travel) series, it's an early landmark of shin-hanga: ukiyo-e craft, Western atmosphere, and the sort of quiet that only shows up when you're the one person still awake.

Byam_Shaw_-_Omphale,_1914.jpg.story: The Lydian queen Omphale, who bought Hercules as a slave and had him spin wool while she wore his lion skin. Byam Shaw gives her the hide as hood and cape, a length of the hero's club under her arm, and sets her against a wall of Celtic-looking roundels. The amber necklace and turquoise bangle feel like studio props. It's a late work - he died in 1919 - and there's something tired and defiant about it, a Victorian imagination refusing to let go. The gaze is straight at you, slightly mocking.

CLAUDE_MONET_1840_-_1926_LE_GIVRE_À_GIVE.story: Painted in 1885, Monet's second winter at Giverny, before the famous garden existed. He had rented the pink house two years earlier and was still learning the valley: its fogs, its meadows, the way hoarfrost silvered the grass at dawn. Fifty-four by seventy-one centimeters, signed lower left, the whole canvas tuned to a chalky blue-white with a single pinkish-ochre streak of earth. It surfaced at auction and now hangs in Hasso Plattner's collection at the Museum Barberini in Potsdam, accession MB-Mon-18.

CLAUDE_MONET_1840_-_1926_NYMPHÉAS_AVEC_R.story: Two meters wide, painted between 1914 and 1917 in the huge studio Monet had built for exactly this kind of canvas. The Great War was on. His son Jean had just died. Clemenceau was visiting and pushing him to keep working. Tall grasses at the pond's edge mirror down into the water, breaking the lily-pads into a vertical tremor. The signature is a studio stamp rather than a brushed name — Monet never finished reworking it. It sold at Sotheby's in 2013.

source.canonical_title: File:Caillebotte, L'Homme au balcon, boulevard Haussmann - Christie's.jpg

Caillebotte,_L'Homme_au_balcon,_boulevar.story: A man stands at a wrought-iron balcony, his back to us, looking down at the boulevard Haussmann. That is it, that is the picture, and it's one of Caillebotte's quiet masterpieces of 1880. The balcony railing slices the canvas like a grid; the figure is anonymous, well-dressed, turned away. It is the same apartment at 31 boulevard Haussmann where the artist lived, and several of his balcony pictures are set here. Caillebotte treats modern Paris the way nobody else in the Impressionist group did: from above, through iron, with a cool architect's detachment.

Caillebotte_Gustave_Femme_Nue_Etendue_Su.story: This startling pastel of a woman stretched out on a rumpled couch is believed to be Caillebotte's earliest dated work, made in 1873 when he was twenty-five. It looks nothing like the cool, rain-slicked boulevards he became famous for: the flesh is pinkish and alive, the drapery is messy, the pose is frank rather than idealized. A gift to the Metropolitan Museum from collector Iris Cantor, it's a reminder that before Caillebotte became the Impressionists' banker and urban geometer, he was a young man figuring out what to do with a nude.

source.canonical_title: File:Canestra di frutta (Caravaggio).jpg

Canestra_di_frutta_(Caravaggio).jpg.story: A wicker basket sits on the edge of a shelf as if about to fall into your lap. The peach has a wormhole; an apple is gnawed; a grape leaf curls and browns at the tip. Around 1599 Caravaggio made this nothing-subject — no saint, no sitter — and Cardinal Federico Borromeo of Milan ended up with it by 1607. He hung it in his new Ambrosiana library, where it still is. The flat cream-colored background was painted in later by another hand.

title.th: นักดนตรี

Caravaggio_-_I_Musici.jpg.story: Cardinal del Monte loved music and kept expensive instruments on hand — Caravaggio borrowed them. Four boys in loose classical drapery tune up, pass madrigal sheets, and ignore each other in the way real musicians do between entries. The lutenist is Mario Minniti again; the dark-eyed boy looking straight out is almost certainly Caravaggio himself. A small Cupid reaches for grapes at the left edge. The Met bought it in 1952, battered and overcleaned, the music on the sheets half-scrubbed away.

Caravaggio_-_La_Deposizione_di_Cristo.jp.title: The Entombment of Christ

source.canonical_title: File:Caravaggio - La Deposizione di Cristo.jpg

Caravaggio_-_La_Deposizione_di_Cristo.jp.story: Nicodemus crouches at the bottom edge and stares straight at us over Christ's lolling knees — a heavy old man with Michelangelo's face, quoted on purpose. The body isn't being lowered into a tomb so much as held out toward the viewer over a slab of stone, like an offering at an altar. Painted 1603-4 for the Vittrice chapel in the Chiesa Nuova in Rome, it was carted off to Paris by Napoleon in 1797 and came back to the Vatican in 1816, where a copy now stands in the chapel.

Caravaggio_-_Medusa_-_Google_Art_Project.title: Medusa

Caravaggio_-_Medusa_-_Google_Art_Project.story: Painted on a convex wooden jousting shield, not a flat canvas — Leonardo had done something similar a century earlier, and del Monte wanted Caravaggio to match the trick. Medusa's face, frozen mid-scream, is Caravaggio's own. Blood ropes from the severed neck; the serpents still thrash. Del Monte sent the shield to Ferdinando I de' Medici in Florence around 1598, and it has stayed in the Medici collections ever since. Today it hangs in the Uffizi.

title.ja: 慈悲の七つの行い (カラヴァッジョ)

Caravaggio_-_Sette_opere_di_Misericordia.story: Pio Monte della Misericordia in Naples wanted seven panels, one per corporal work of mercy. Caravaggio gave them one canvas instead, all seven acts happening at once in a cramped nighttime street: a young woman nurses her jailed father through a grate (that's 'visit the imprisoned' and 'feed the hungry' in a single image, lifted from the Roman Charity story), a deacon tears his cloak for a beggar, Samson drinks from a jawbone. Painted in 1607, it still hangs above the church's altar, where they built it for.

Caravaggio_Judith_Beheading_Holofernes.j.title: Judith Beheading Holofernes

source.canonical_title: File:Caravaggio Judith Beheading Holofernes.jpg

Caravaggio_Judith_Beheading_Holofernes.j.story: Painted in Rome around 1599 for the Genoese banker Ottavio Costa, who prized it so highly he kept it behind a silk curtain and forbade its sale in his will. Caravaggio gives Judith a clean white blouse and a look of slight revulsion, as if the general's blood might spatter the linen — she's keeping her arms straight, leaning back from the work. The crone beside her, Abra, watches with a butcher's patience, holding out the sack. Holofernes is alive at the moment of the stroke: eyes wide, mouth open, one hand still pushing against the mattress. The painting vanished for three centuries and was rediscovered in a Roman attic in 1950.

Carl_Friedrich_Seiffert_-_Die_Blaue_Grot.title: The Blue Grotto on Capri

source.canonical_title: File:Carl Friedrich Seiffert - Die Blaue Grotte auf Capri (1860).jpg

Carl_Friedrich_Seiffert_-_Die_Blaue_Grot.story: Seiffert ducks inside the famous Capri grotto and paints what the guidebooks promised: water lit from below in that impossible cobalt, the low stone arch framing a scrap of Mediterranean daylight, a small rowboat drifting in from the glare. The Berlin-trained Late Romantic went to Italy in search of exactly this kind of luminous set-piece. He signed and dated the canvas 1860.

Carl_Spitzweg_-_Das_Auge_des_Gesetzes_(J.title: Justitia
Carl_Spitzweg_-_Das_Auge_des_Gesetzes_(J.description: "a sculpture of Lady Justice with cracks at its foundation, Justitia holding broken scales and wearing a somewhat disarranged blindfold, while a soldier hides behind a wall" sold under duress by Jewish collector Leo Bendel (who later died in a concentration camp) bought by the Nazis after WW II hung in a presidential estate until 2006 restituted to its rightful heirs in 2019 sold for $773,000 at auction, 6 May 2020

source.canonical_title: File:Carl Spitzweg - Das Auge des Gesetzes (Justitia) - 1857.jpg

Carl_Spitzweg_-_Das_Auge_des_Gesetzes_(J.story: A pocket-sized allegory with a long shadow. Spitzweg's Lady Justice stands on a cracked pedestal, her scales broken, her blindfold askew, while a soldier skulks behind the wall — the painter's wry verdict on a law that looks the other way. The painting's own afterlife caught up with its subject: sold under duress in the 1930s by the Jewish collector Leo Bendel, who later died at Buchenwald, it was bought by the Nazis, hung in a postwar presidential residence, and only returned to his heirs in 2019. It fetched $773,000 at auction the following spring.

Carl_Spitzweg_-_Der_Briefbote_im_Rosenth.title: The courier in the Rosenthal

source.canonical_title: File:Carl Spitzweg - Der Briefbote im Rosenthal.jpg
source.credit: Joachim Nagel: Carl Spitzweg. Belser, Stuttgart 2008, S. 31

Carl_Spitzweg_-_Der_Briefbote_im_Rosenth.story: The postman turns into a narrow old-town alley and the whole street comes alive. Heads appear at windows, women lean from doorways, a prettily wrapped parcel and what looks very much like a love letter are the day's real event. Spitzweg painted this tall, crowded little scene — the Rosenthal being a quiet lane in his native region — around 1858 and it hangs today in Marburg's university museum. It is pure Spitzweg: small-town curiosity dressed up as high drama, affection and mockery in the same brushstroke.

Carl_Spitzweg_-_Der_Maler_auf_einer_Wald.title: The Painter Resting Under an Umbrella in a Forest Clearing
Carl_Spitzweg_-_Der_Maler_auf_einer_Wald.description: Der Maler auf einer Waldlichtung, unter einem Schirm liegend . Ca. 1850. Oil on canvas. 49.5 × 30.2 cm.

source.canonical_title: File:Carl Spitzweg - Der Maler auf einer Waldlichtung, unter einem Schirm liegend.jpg
source.credit: Joachim Nagel: Carl Spitzweg. Belser, Stuttgart 2008, S. 11

Carl_Spitzweg_-_Der_Maler_auf_einer_Wald.story: A young painter has downed tools and stretched out under a green umbrella in a forest clearing, hat tipped forward, sketching pad idle on the moss. A butterfly has settled on the half-finished drawing; a blackbird eyes him from the umbrella's rim. Spitzweg, who often painted himself as exactly this kind of happy idler, worked it up around 1850 on a narrow canvas just under 50 by 30 centimetres.

Carl_Spitzweg_-_Der_arme_Poet_(Neue_Pina.title: The poor poet

source.canonical_title: File:Carl Spitzweg - Der arme Poet (Neue Pinakothek).jpg
source.credit: 1. The Yorck Project (2002) 10.000 Meisterwerke der Malerei (DVD-ROM), distributed by DIRECTMEDIA Publishing GmbH. ISBN : 3936122202 . (the version fom Berlin, Nationalgalerie) 2. Wichmann, Siegfried: Carl Spitzweg , München 1990, S. 57 ISBN 3-7654-2306-8 3. Cybershot800i , Own work , Taken in 17 June 2011

Carl_Spitzweg_-_Der_arme_Poet_(Neue_Pina.story: Bundled in a threadbare coat and nightcap, the poet props an umbrella against the leaking roof and scribbles on, oblivious; a stovepipe wanders off to nowhere, manuscripts insulate his mattress. When Spitzweg showed it at the Munich Kunstverein in 1839 critics read the irony as an insult to poetry itself. The jilted early masterpiece is now among the most-reproduced pictures in Germany; this version, 36 by 45 centimetres, hangs in the Neue Pinakothek.

source.canonical_title: File:Carl Spitzweg - Der eingeschlafene Einsiedler.jpg

Carl_Spitzweg_-_Im_Dachstübchen_(v.1849).title: In the Attic Room, c. 1849
Carl_Spitzweg_-_Im_Dachstübchen_(v.1849).description: The Garret or The Attic (c. 1840s). Private collection

source.canonical_title: File:Carl Spitzweg - Im Dachstübchen (v.1849).jpg

Carl_Spitzweg_-_Im_Harem.jpg.title: In the Harem

source.canonical_title: File:Carl Spitzweg - Im Harem.jpg
source.credit: The Yorck Project (2002) 10.000 Meisterwerke der Malerei (DVD-ROM), distributed by DIRECTMEDIA Publishing GmbH. ISBN : 3936122202 .

Carl_Spitzweg_-_Im_Harem.jpg.story: A Spitzweg harem is, of course, a joke on orientalism: a dozing eunuch, a slim woman peering from behind a grille, ornament piled on ornament with the same sly fondness he brought to provincial bookworms. Painted about 1855 on a small canvas 38 by 31 centimetres, it belongs to the Munich painter's late vein of imagined Easts he never actually visited.

Carl_Spitzweg_-_In_the_Alpine_High_Valle.title: In the Alpine High Valley (Landscape with Mt. Wendelstein)

source.canonical_title: File:Carl Spitzweg - In the Alpine High Valley (Landscape with Mt. Wendelstein) - Google Art Project.jpg
source.credit: ywEgUz_pmN9_IA at Google Cultural Institute maximum zoom level

Carl_Spitzweg_-_In_the_Alpine_High_Valle.story: Spitzweg is best known for droll little bookworms and grumpy scholars, so this looming Alpine cliff comes as a jolt. Painted around 1871, the canvas is unusually large for him, and it dispenses with the jokes: grey rock walls close off a shaded valley beneath the Wendelstein, a Bavarian peak Spitzweg knew well from walking tours. Figures, if you can find them, are specks. The real subject is the weight of the mountain and the cold light sliding off wet stone. It now hangs in the Museum Kunstpalast in Dusseldorf.

Carl_Spitzweg_013.jpg.title: The intercepted love letter

source.canonical_title: File:Carl Spitzweg 013.jpg
source.credit: 1. The Yorck Project (2002) 10.000 Meisterwerke der Malerei (DVD-ROM), distributed by DIRECTMEDIA Publishing GmbH. ISBN : 3936122202 . 2. Wichmann, Siegfried; Carl Spitzweg , München 1990, S. 114

Carl_Spitzweg_013.jpg.story: From an upper window a student in his duelling cap lowers a sealed letter on a thread toward the open casement below, where a young woman bends so intently over her needlework she misses it entirely — while her sharp-eyed aunt, two panes over, has just spotted the whole scheme, mouth falling open. The narrow sandstone facade drops an oblique shadow across the wall. The painting is now at the Museum Georg Schäfer in Schweinfurt.

Carl_Spitzweg_036.jpg.title: The Sunday Stroll

source.canonical_title: File:Carl Spitzweg 036.jpg
source.credit: The Yorck Project (2002) 10.000 Meisterwerke der Malerei (DVD-ROM), distributed by DIRECTMEDIA Publishing GmbH. ISBN : 3936122202 .

Carl_Spitzweg_036.jpg.story: A rotund paterfamilias strides ahead through tall grass with his top hat balanced on his walking stick for shade; behind him his wife and daughters bob along under bonnets and parasols, a dachshund bringing up the rear. Spitzweg catches the whole Biedermeier family outing in one wry silhouette. The oil on panel measures about 41 by 53 centimetres and is dated 1841.

Carl_Spitzweg_Der_Schmetterlingsjäger_18.title: The Butterfly Hunter

source.canonical_title: File:Carl Spitzweg Der Schmetterlingsjäger 1840.jpg
source.credit: The Yorck Project (2002) 10.000 Meisterwerke der Malerei (DVD-ROM), distributed by DIRECTMEDIA Publishing GmbH. ISBN : 3936122202 .

Carl_Spitzweg_Der_Schmetterlingsjäger_18.story: A stout gentleman tiptoes through high summer ferns, umbrella in one hand, comically small net in the other, kitted out as if for a safari rather than a meadow. Spitzweg skewers the Biedermeier craze for butterfly-collecting with genuine affection — the man is absurd, but the slanting light on his enormous hat is tender. The little oil on panel, 31 by 25 centimetres, is today in the Museum Wiesbaden.

Carl_Spitzweg_Ständchen_c1854.jpg.title: The Serenade

source.canonical_title: File:Carl Spitzweg Ständchen c1854.jpg
source.credit: The Yorck Project (2002) 10.000 Meisterwerke der Malerei (DVD-ROM), distributed by DIRECTMEDIA Publishing GmbH. ISBN : 3936122202 .

Carl_Spitzweg_Ständchen_c1854.jpg.story: A violinist has shinned halfway up a ladder below a latticed window, serenading whoever may be inside; the alley is all moonlit stucco and long diagonal shadow. Spitzweg loved the Ständchen theme for exactly this lighting problem — how little silver you need to model a face out of the dark. The oil on panel, 39 by 22 centimetres, dates to about 1854 and remains in private hands.

Carlos_V_en_Mühlberg,_by_Titian,_from_Pr.title: Equestrian Portrait of Charles V
Carlos_V_en_Mühlberg,_by_Titian,_from_Pr.description: Portrait of Charles V on horseback, painted by Titian in Augsburg (1548) to celebrate the Battle of Mühlberg, located in the Museo del Prado of Madrid.

source.canonical_title: File:Carlos V en Mühlberg, by Titian, from Prado in Google Earth.jpg
source.credit: The Prado in Google Earth: Home - 7 th level of zoom, JPEG compression quality: Photoshop 10.

title.es: Carlos V en la batalla de Mühlberg
title.de: Kaiser Karl V. nach der Schlacht bei Mühlberg
title.it: Ritratto di Carlo V a cavallo
title.fr: Charles Quint à cheval à Mühlberg
title.pl: Karol V po bitwie pod Mühlbergiem

Carlos_V_en_Mühlberg,_by_Titian,_from_Pr.story: Charles V, Holy Roman Emperor, rides out of a German dawn in black and gold armour, lance couched, to commemorate his crushing victory over the Protestant Schmalkaldic League at Mühlberg on the Elbe in April 1547. Titian painted it in Augsburg the following year, inventing the European equestrian portrait as we know it. Charles was gouty, exhausted, and at the peak of his power; within a decade he'd abdicate and retire to a monastery. Scorched by fire in 1734, it still hangs in the Prado.

Carlyle_Maclise_Original.jpg.title: Carlyle Maclise Original
Carlyle_Maclise_Original.jpg.description: Portrait of Carlyle, full length. He is leaning with crooked right elbow against a pillar, a hat in his left hand.

source.canonical_title: File:Carlyle Maclise Original.jpg

Carlyle_Maclise_Original.jpg.story: A pencil study, not a finished painting: Thomas Carlyle leans full-length against a fluted column, right elbow crooked up behind his head, a soft bowler hat dangling from his left hand. Tight frock coat, narrow trousers, dandyish at the ankles. Maclise drew him like this around 1830 for the Fraser's Magazine celebrity series he signed 'Alfred Croquis'; the lithograph that appeared in 1833 was based on exactly this pose.

CarnegieMuseumofVincentGoghAfterRain.jpg.title: Wheat Fields after the Rain
CarnegieMuseumofVincentGoghAfterRain.jpg.description: Photo of Vincent Van Goghs' Wheat Fields after the Rain (The Plain of Auvers)

source.canonical_title: File:CarnegieMuseumofVincentGoghAfterRain.jpg
source.credit: Photo I took of Vincent Van Goghs' Wheat Fields after the Rain (The Plain of Auvers) from 1890. Carnegie Museum of Art

title.fr: Champs de blé après la pluie

CarnegieMuseumofVincentGoghAfterRain.jpg.story: Painted in Auvers-sur-Oise in July 1890, just weeks before his death, this is the Oise valley scrubbed clean. The wheat is bright, the distant houses tiny, the whole plain breathing after a downpour. Vincent's brush chops the field into thousands of short green and gold strokes — no drama, just wet air and working land. The Carnegie Museum of Art in Pittsburgh acquired it in 1958.

CasinCaillebotte.jpg.title: Portraits in the Countryside
CasinCaillebotte.jpg.description: Caillebotte's mother along with his aunt, cousin, and a family friend

source.canonical_title: File:CasinCaillebotte.jpg

CasinCaillebotte.jpg.story: Four people in a garden on a summer afternoon, and not one of them is looking at another. Caillebotte's mother reads, his aunt sits stiffly, his cousin Marie bends over her needlework in the foreground, and a family friend occupies her own private orbit. The setting is the family property at Yerres. Caillebotte picked this canvas as one of his six submissions to the Third Impressionist Exhibition in 1877, and then gave it to his cousin Zoe as a wedding present, which is how it ended up at the small museum in Bayeux rather than in Paris.

Caspar_David_Friedrich's_Chalk_Cliffs_on.title: Chalk Cliffs at Ruegen

source.canonical_title: File:Caspar David Friedrich's Chalk Cliffs on Rügen.jpg
source.credit: The Yorck Project (2002) 10.000 Meisterwerke der Malerei (DVD-ROM), distributed by DIRECTMEDIA Publishing GmbH. ISBN : 3936122202 .

title.fr: Falaises de craie sur l'île de Rügen
title.ja: リューゲン島の白亜岩
title.avk: Afoltafa kiria moe Rügen ewala (trutca ke Friedrich)

Caspar_David_Friedrich's_Chalk_Cliffs_on.story: Three figures peer over a vertiginous drop, framed by leaning trees, the Baltic glittering improbably far below. Friedrich painted this soon after his marriage to Caroline Bommer in 1818, and many read the trio as the painter, his wife, and his brother — the clothes colour-coded in faith, love, and hope. The thin man in blue, his hat laid aside in humility, is almost certainly a self-portrait. For once Friedrich's mood is bright rather than funereal, though the cliff edge does its usual Romantic work: life on solid green, death in the white chalk, eternity out at sea.

Caspar_David_Friedrich_-_Abtei_im_Eichwa.title: The Abbey in the Oakwood

source.canonical_title: File:Caspar David Friedrich - Abtei im Eichwald - Google Art Project.jpg

title.fr: L'Abbaye dans une forêt de chênes
title.el: Μονή στο δάσος με τις βελανιδιές

Caspar_David_Friedrich_-_Abtei_im_Eichwa.story: A funeral procession winds through snow toward the broken gothic portal of a ruined abbey. Two candles, a coffin, bare oaks, a thin crescent moon - that's the whole show. Friedrich based the ruins on Eldena Abbey near his hometown of Greifswald, wrecked in the Thirty Years' War, and asked that the picture hang beneath The Monk by the Sea at the 1810 Berlin Academy. Frederick Wilhelm III bought the pair straight off the wall for the royal collection. They still hang together in the Alte Nationalgalerie, Berlin.

Caspar_David_Friedrich_-_Das_Kreuz_im_Ge.title: Cross in the Mountains (altarpiece Tetschen)

source.canonical_title: File:Caspar David Friedrich - Das Kreuz im Gebirge.jpg
source.credit: 1. The Yorck Project (2002) 10.000 Meisterwerke der Malerei (DVD-ROM), distributed by DIRECTMEDIA Publishing GmbH. ISBN : 3936122202 . 2. nevsepic.com.ua

title.fr: ‚Croix dans la Montagne‘ dit aussi Le Retable de Tetschen
title.de: Tetschener Altar, Szene: Das Kreuz im Gebirge

Caspar_David_Friedrich_-_Das_Kreuz_im_Ge.story: Friedrich finished this in 1808 for Count Franz von Thun-Hohenstein's castle chapel in Tetschen, Bohemia - and promptly caused a scandal. Critics howled that you couldn't put a landscape on an altar. Friedrich painted one anyway: a rocky peak, a few dark firs, and Christ on a gilded crucifix caught in the last rays from a sun that's already set. The viewer sees the cross from behind and below, the way a pilgrim would. He even designed the carved gilt frame himself, with palm fronds and a wheat-ear eye of God. It's now in the Galerie Neue Meister, Dresden.

Caspar_David_Friedrich_-_Der_Mönch_am_M.title: The Monk by the Sea

source.canonical_title: File:Caspar David Friedrich - Der Mönch am Meer - Google Art Project.jpg

title.fr: Le Moine au bord de la mer
title.es: Monje a la orilla del mar

Caspar_David_Friedrich_-_Der_Mönch_am_M.story: Nearly four feet of canvas, and maybe a tenth of it is monk and dune. The rest is Baltic sea and weather. Friedrich painted over two sailing ships he'd already put on the horizon, leaving nothing for the eye to grab. When it was shown at the Berlin Academy in 1810, the critic Heinrich von Kleist wrote that looking at it felt "as if one's eyelids had been cut away." King Frederick Wilhelm III bought it for the royal collection anyway. It still hangs in the Alte Nationalgalerie, Berlin, beside its pendant.

Caspar_David_Friedrich_-_Der_einsame_Bau.title: Solitary Tree

source.canonical_title: File:Caspar David Friedrich - Der einsame Baum - Google Art Project.jpg

Caspar_David_Friedrich_-_Der_einsame_Bau.story: A battered old oak, its crown already dead, stands over a shepherd and his drowsing flock as morning mist lifts off the meadow. The banker Joachim Heinrich Wagener commissioned it in 1822 as one half of a pair - this is "morning," its companion Moonrise over the Sea is "evening." The mountains in the distance are the Riesengebirge, sketched on Friedrich's hiking trips. Wagener left his whole collection to the Prussian state in 1861, founding the Nationalgalerie. The tree has been in Berlin ever since.

Caspar_David_Friedrich_-_Die_Lebensstufe.title: Life stages

source.canonical_title: File:Caspar David Friedrich - Die Lebensstufen (ca. 1834).jpg

Caspar_David_Friedrich_-_Die_Lebensstufe.story: Five ships at five distances from shore, five people at five ages of life. The setting is Utkiek near Wieck, the promenade where Greifswalders went to watch boats come in - Friedrich's hometown. The old man in the foreground, back turned, is often read as the painter himself, around sixty; the children playing with the little Swedish pennant are his own son Gustav Adolf and daughter Agnes Adelheid. Greifswald had belonged to Sweden in Friedrich's childhood before passing to Prussia in 1815. Painted around 1835, now in the Museum der bildenden Kunste, Leipzig.
Caspar_David_Friedrich_-_Die_Lebensstufe.year_note: The Stages of Life is generally dated 1835, not 1834.

Caspar_David_Friedrich_-_Mondaufgang_am_.story: Two women in silk and a young man perch on a rocky shore, backs to us, watching a full moon lift over the Baltic. Two sailing ships glide in. The whole canvas is only 55 by 71 centimetres, small enough to lean close and catch the violet bloom Friedrich laid into the water. Painted in 1822 for the Berlin banker Wagener alongside The Solitary Tree - morning and evening, earth and sea, a matched pair. Wagener's bequest started the Nationalgalerie in 1861, and it still hangs there.

Caspar_David_Friedrich_-_Wanderer_above_.title: The hiker above the sea of fog
Caspar_David_Friedrich_-_Wanderer_above_.description: The hiker stands as a back figure in the center of the composition. He looks down on an almost impenetrable sea of ​​fog in the midst of a rocky landscape - a metaphor for life as an ominous journey into the unknown.

source.canonical_title: File:Caspar David Friedrich - Wanderer above the sea of fog.jpg
source.credit: The photographic reproduction was done by Cybershot800i . ( Diff )

Caspar_David_Friedrich_-_Wanderer_above_.story: The peak under his boots is real — the Kaiserkrone in the Elbe Sandstone Mountains southeast of Dresden, where Friedrich walked with a sketchbook for years. The jagged crag behind his right shoulder is the Zirkelstein. Friedrich built the composition from studies drawn separately and stitched together, the way you'd assemble a dream. The figure wears a dark green Altdeutsche coat, a nationalist fashion after the Napoleonic wars — some have read him as a memorial to a fallen officer. The picture stayed in private hands until 1970, when the Hamburger Kunsthalle finally bought it for its permanent collection.

Cassatt_Mary_Lydia_at_the_Tapestry_Loom_.title: Lydia at the Tapestry Loom

source.canonical_title: File:Cassatt Mary Lydia at the Tapestry Loom c. 1881.jpg

Cassatt_Mary_Lydia_at_the_Tapestry_Loom_.story: Cassatt's older sister Lydia, bent over a tapestry frame, pink dress catching the studio light, hair pinned up, hands working without looking up. Lydia was already ill with Bright's disease and would be dead within a year; Cassatt painted her constantly in those last months, at tea, reading, driving a pony cart, always absorbed in something ordinary. The brushwork here is fast and loose where it needs to be, the loom and chair-back slashed in with a few strokes, but the face is held still. It is a sister's picture first and an Impressionist exercise second.

Cassatt_Mary_Maternite_1890.jpg.title: Motherhood

source.canonical_title: File:Cassatt Mary Maternite 1890.jpg

Cassatt_Mary_Maternite_1890.jpg.story: A mother in a dusky-pink wrap holds her baby to the breast, and Cassatt handles the moment without a drop of sentiment. The pastel sits close to the skin: loose hatching across the mother's sleeve, a flat cream of the infant's shift, cheeks blurred into warmth. The baby is heavy, wide-awake, grabbing one foot. Cassatt had watched Degas draw bathers this way for a decade by 1890, and you can feel that training in how the shoulders turn and the eyes stay down. Not a Madonna. Just a tired, tender afternoon.

Cats_suggested_as_the_fifty-three_statio.title: 'Cats Suggested as The Fifty-three Stations of the Tōkaidō'

source.canonical_title: File:Cats suggested as the fifty-three stations of the Tokaido.jpg

Cats_suggested_as_the_fifty-three_statio.story: Kuniyoshi was a famous cat person, and in 1850 he turned the fifty-three post stations of the Tokaido highway into a triptych of cats. Each little animal is a visual pun on a place name, labelled in red cartouches along the top. Some are just cats being cats, curled, washing, swatting, fighting over a fish; others are wearing collars or doing something faintly human. The joke only lands if you know the stations, but the drawing is so quick and affectionate it works even if you don't. Straightforwardly one of the friendliest prints in ukiyo-e.

Cawing_crow_by_Ohara_Koson.jpg.title: Cawing crow by Ohara Koson
Cawing_crow_by_Ohara_Koson.jpg.description: Cawing crow by Ohara Koson, c. 1900s

source.canonical_title: File:Cawing crow by Ohara Koson.jpg

Charing_Cross_Bridge,_Monet.jpg.title: Charing Cross Bridge

source.canonical_title: File:Charing Cross Bridge, Monet.jpg

Charing_Cross_Bridge,_Monet.jpg.story: Monet checked into the Savoy Hotel in autumn 1899 and set up his easel at a fifth-floor window, looking downriver toward Charing Cross Bridge. The fog was the point. He'd later say he loved London only in winter, because the fog gave the city its mass and weight. Trains ghost across the iron span here; smoke and steam blur into river mist until bridge and sky barely separate. He'd return in 1900 and 1901, and keep finishing the canvases back in Giverny for years. The Thames series eventually reached around 100 paintings of Charing Cross, Waterloo, and Parliament.

Charing_Cross_Bridge,_Reflections_on_the.title: Charing Cross Bridge, Reflections on the Thames

source.canonical_title: File:Charing Cross Bridge, Reflections on the Thames.jpg

Charing_Cross_Bridge,_Reflections_on_the.story: Same Savoy window, same iron railway bridge, entirely different weather. Monet complained in letters home that the light changed every few minutes and he could barely keep up, shuffling between canvases as conditions shifted. Here the bridge is almost a rumor, a pale bar floating above its own smeared reflection. He'd begun this view in autumn 1899 and kept hauling these canvases back to Giverny each spring, refining them from memory and photographs. The whole Thames project, begun that year, eventually ran to around 100 paintings.

Charlotte_Dubourg_par_Fantin-Latour.jpg.title: Charlotte Dubourg par Fantin-Latour
Charlotte_Dubourg_par_Fantin-Latour.jpg.description: Charlotte Dubourg, par Henri Fantin-Latour (1836-1804); Musée d'Orsay, Paris

source.canonical_title: File:Charlotte Dubourg par Fantin-Latour.jpg
source.permission: Public domain

Charlotte_Dubourg_par_Fantin-Latour.jpg.story: Charlotte was the painter's sister-in-law — sister of his wife Victoria, herself a flower painter — and she sat for him at thirty-two, in 1882. There's no charm offensive here: the black dress blots into the background, the hands lie quietly folded, and Charlotte looks past you with the mild impatience of someone who has sat too long already. Fantin could paint roses that felt exhaled; with family he went bone-dry and still. The canvas entered the Musée d'Orsay's collection and remains one of his sharpest likenesses.

Chase_William_Merritt_A_Sunny_Day_at_Shi.title: A Sunny Day at Shinnecock Bay

source.canonical_title: File:Chase William Merritt A Sunny Day at Shinnecock Bay c1892.jpg

Chase_William_Merritt_A_Sunny_Day_at_Shi.story: Shinnecock Hills, on the south fork of Long Island, was where Chase ran his pioneering outdoor summer school from 1891 to 1902 — America's first serious plein-air academy. He painted its low dunes, bayberry scrub, and huge sky obsessively, often with his own daughters as quick figures anchoring the composition. This view across the bay is pure Chase: thin, confident strokes, a horizon band of water, and the bleached greens of east-end Long Island in midsummer. Teaching by demonstration, he would knock out paintings like this while students watched.

Chase_William_Merritt_James_Abbott_McNei.title: James Abbott McNeill Whistler

source.canonical_title: File:Chase William Merritt James Abbott McNeill Whistler 1885.jpg
source.permission: PD-Art

Chase_William_Merritt_James_Abbott_McNei.story: Chase sailed to London in the summer of 1885 intent on painting the famously prickly Whistler, and the two agreed to portray each other. Chase finished his; Whistler never did. The result shows the older painter as a dandy in a long black coat and top hat, wand-like cane in hand, pale face floating against shadow — more caricature than homage, and Whistler hated it. Their friendship cratered on the spot. The picture is now at the Met, a record of a collaboration that ended in mutual insult rather than the dual portraits both men had planned.

Chase_William_Merritt_Portrait_of_Miss_D.title: Portrait of Dora Wheeler

source.canonical_title: File:Chase William Merritt Portrait of Miss Dora Wheeler 1883.jpg

Chase_William_Merritt_Portrait_of_Miss_D.story: Dora Wheeler was a former pupil of Chase and the daughter of Candace Wheeler, Louis Tiffany's collaborator in the Associated Artists decorating firm. Chase sets her in her mother's studio surrounded by the company's embroidered hangings and blue-and-white porcelain — a full-length aesthetic-movement portrait that won a medal at the Munich Exhibition of 1883. She looks up from her book as if the viewer has just walked in.

Chase_William_Merritt_Self_Portrait_1915.title: Self Portrait in 4th Avenue Studio

source.canonical_title: File:Chase William Merritt Self Portrait 1915.jpg
source.credit: 1. Upload Bot (Cobalty), possibly from a Art-CD-Rom 2. Richmond Art Museum, online collection

Chase_William_Merritt_Self_Portrait_1915.story: Chase was sixty-five and a year from death when he painted this — standing in his Fourth Avenue studio in a dark suit, brush in hand, the familiar clutter of his collections just barely indicated behind him. He looks tired. After four decades as America's most visible painter-teacher, he had watched Modernism arrive, sneered at the Armory Show, and lost students to movements he couldn't follow. The self-portrait is plain, even stark. No props, no flourish — just the painter and his tools, summing up.

Chase_William_Merritt_Still_Life_With_Wa.title: Still Life With Watermelon

source.canonical_title: File:Chase William Merritt Still Life With Watermelon 1869.jpg

Chase_William_Merritt_Still_Life_With_Wa.story: An early student work by the twenty-year-old Chase, painted in Indianapolis before he left for his formative years in Munich. The sliced melon, the brass bowl, the dark background — it is squarely in the Dutch still-life tradition his first teachers pushed him toward, and already shows the confident wet-in-wet handling that would become his signature.

Chase_mrs_meigs_piano_organ_1883.jpg.title: Chase mrs meigs piano organ 1883

source.canonical_title: File:Chase mrs meigs piano organ 1883.jpg

Chase_mrs_meigs_piano_organ_1883.jpg.story: Mrs Meigs, wife of a New York architect, at her pipe organ — an oddly intimate music-room portrait in the crowded aesthetic taste of the 1880s. Chase loved these dense interiors stuffed with rugs, brass, and tapestries, painting them as much for the textures as for the sitter. The keyboard catches a narrow band of studio light; the rest of the room recedes into warm, lived-in gloom.

Chen_Rong_-_Nine_Dragons.jpg.title: Nine Dragons 九龍圖 九龙图
Chen_Rong_-_Nine_Dragons.jpg.artist: Chen Rong 陳容 陈容

source.canonical_title: File:Chen Rong - Nine Dragons.jpg

Chen_Rong_-_Nine_Dragons.jpg.story: A long handscroll, unrolled here as one horizontal strip: columns of Chinese colophon text on the left give way to ink clouds, rock, and surging water out of which dragons twist, chase a flaming pearl and dive back into mist. The ink is extraordinarily wet where the storm gathers and bone-dry where scales catch light. Chen Rong finished it in 1244; it carries inscriptions and seals from centuries of later owners and now lives in the Museum of Fine Arts, Boston.

Chichester_Canal_(1828).jpg.title: Chichester Canal

source.canonical_title: File:Chichester Canal (1828).jpg

title.ro: Canalul Chichester (pictură de J. M. W. Turner)
title.ja: チチェスター運河 (絵画)
title.de: Abendlandschaft, wahrscheinlich der Kanal von Chichester

Chichester_Canal_(1828).jpg.story: Painted for the 3rd Earl of Egremont, who had sunk fifteen thousand pounds into building the canal and wanted a picture to hang at Petworth. Turner gave him pure stillness: a becalmed ship, a glassy cut of water, a Sussex sunset spreading like spilled honey. He made two nearly identical versions around 1828. This one stayed in Turner's own hands and came to Tate through the 1856 bequest; the other still hangs in the panelled Carved Room at Petworth.

Childe_harold.jpg.title: Childe Harold's Pilgrimage

source.canonical_title: File:Childe harold.jpg
source.credit: 1. abcgallery.com 2. Sotheby’s (not for sale, only as a reference image)

Childe_harold.jpg.story: Turner exhibited this at the Royal Academy of 1832 with four lines of Byron pinned to the frame: 'and now, fair Italy! / Thou art the garden of the world…' The poet had died eight years earlier at Missolonghi, and the picture is partly an elegy — broken columns, goatherds, a dreamy Claudian distance standing in for the whole sweep of Italian ruin. Visitors loved it; critics grumbled about the colour. It hangs at Tate Britain, where it arrived with the 1856 Bequest.

Chinese_Warship_Ting_Yuang_Visiting_Japa.title: Chinese Warship Ting Yuang Visiting Japan
Chinese_Warship_Ting_Yuang_Visiting_Japa.description: The Ting Yuang was the flagship of Chinese fleet and the biggest warship of the Far East. Built in Germany in 1881, it was seriously damaged in 1895 during the Sino-Japanese war. This print depicts one of its visits in the Japanese ports of Nagasaki and Yokohama in 1886 and 1891.

source.canonical_title: File:Chinese Warship Ting Yuang Visiting Japan.jpg

Chinese_Warship_Ting_Yuang_Visiting_Japa.story: A triptych ukiyo-e from 1895 showing the Qing ironclad Ting Yuen - German-built, 7,000 tons, at the time the heaviest warship in East Asia - anchored off Japan with local sampans crowded around her hull. By the time Koitsu designed the print, the Ting Yuen was no longer a dignitary in Japanese waters but a sunken wreck: scuttled at Weihaiwei that February after being torpedoed in the Sino-Japanese War. The work is a nostalgic postcard of two peacetime visits, Nagasaki 1886 and Yokohama 1891, retold for an audience that had just beaten her.

Christ_on_the_Cross_-_Peter_Paul_Rubens_.title: Christ on the Cross
Christ_on_the_Cross_-_Peter_Paul_Rubens_.description: Christ on the Cross - Peter Paul Rubens

source.canonical_title: File:Christ on the Cross - Peter Paul Rubens (unframed).jpg

Christian_IX_of_Denmark_with_family_(Tux.title: Christian IX of Denmark with his family
Christian_IX_of_Denmark_with_family_(Tux.date_created: between 1883 and 1886 date QS:P571,+1883-00-00T00:00:00Z/8,P1319,+1883-00-00T00:00:00Z/9,P1326,+1886-00-00T00:00:00Z/9 ( Prince Valdemar of Denmark (Christian's son) married Princess Marie of Orléans on 20 October 1885. If she is not here, the painting should have been made before that date.)
Christian_IX_of_Denmark_with_family_(Tux.description: Painting of Christian IX of Denmark with his large family of European royalty gathered in the garden hall at Fredensborg Palace.

source.canonical_title: File:Christian IX of Denmark with family (Tuxen).jpg

title.pt: A Família de Cristiano IX da Dinamarca
title.th: พระบรมวงศานุวงศ์ในพระเจ้าคริสเตียนที่ 9

Christian_IX_of_Denmark_with_family_(Tux.story: Five by seven metres of European royalty crammed into one room. Tuxen painted this colossal group portrait between 1883 and 1886, during the so-called Fredensborg Days when Christian IX — the "father-in-law of Europe" — and Queen Louise summered with their children, in-laws and grandchildren at Fredensborg Palace. Thirty-two sitters, including the future Tsar Nicholas II and a cluster of British, Greek and Russian royals. Tuxen lived at the palace to study them all. The commission launched his forty-year run as go-to portraitist for the crowned heads of Europe, and hangs today at Christiansborg.

Circle_of_Pieter_Bruegel_the_Elder_-_Win.title: Winter Landscape with a Bird Trap
Circle_of_Pieter_Bruegel_the_Elder_-_Win.description: Rund 100 Kopien sprechen für die außerordentliche Beliebtheit dieser Komposition nach Pieter Bruegel dem Älteren. Man hat vermutet, dass der ungewöhnlich strenge Winter des Jahres 1564/65 auslösendes Moment für Bruegels zweimalige Beschäftigung mit dem Thema der Winterlandschaft gewesen sein könnte. Der Vogelfalle (rechts) und den Eisläufern wurde sprichwörtlicher bzw. moralisierender Hintersinn unterlegt (Ermahnung zur Wachsamkeit, Schlüpfrigkeit der Lebensbahn), doch ohne überzeugenden Beweis. Diese Kopie gilt als eines der ältesten und qualitätvollsten Exemplare.

source.canonical_title: File:Circle of Pieter Bruegel the Elder - Winter Landscape with a Bird Trap.jpg

title.fr: Paysage d’hiver avec un piège à oiseaux
title.pl: Pejzaż zimowy z łyżwiarzami i pułapką na ptaki

Circle_of_Pieter_Bruegel_the_Elder_-_Win.story: Bruegel the Elder's 1565 composition, one of his most copied, survives in roughly a hundred versions turned out by sons, workshop, and followers. This one, from the circle around the family business, is considered among the earliest and best. Villagers skate on thin ice while, almost too casual to notice on the right, a heavy door is propped over scattered seed: a bird trap. Contemporary viewers would have read it as a warning about slippery footing, snared souls, and the ordinary dangers of being alive. The harsh winter of 1564-65 probably set Bruegel on the subject in the first place.

ClaudeMonetBanksoftheSeine.jpg.title: Banks of the Seine at Lavacourt

source.canonical_title: File:ClaudeMonetBanksoftheSeine.jpg
source.credit: Photo I took at the Frick Art Museum

title.fr: Bords de la Seine à Lavacourt

Claude_Monet,_1867,_Regatta_at_Sainte-Ad.title: Regatta at Sainte-Adresse

source.canonical_title: File:Claude Monet, 1867, Regatta at Sainte-Adresse, Metropolitan Museum of Art.jpg

title.ja: サン＝タドレスのレガッタ

Claude_Monet,_1867,_Regatta_at_Sainte-Ad.story: High tide, stiff wind, white sails crowded against a flat horizon. Monet spent the summer of 1867 broke and living with his aunt at Sainte-Adresse, grinding out twenty paintings at once. On June 25 he wrote to Bazille that he was working on "regattas at Le Havre with many figures on the beach." This sunny scene was conceived as a pair with a gray, low-tide beach painting now at the Art Institute of Chicago.

Claude_Monet,_1875,_Train_in_the_Snow,_o.title: Train in the Snow

source.canonical_title: File:Claude Monet, 1875, Train in the Snow, oil on canvas, 59 × 78 cm, Musée Marmottan Monet.jpg

Claude_Monet,_1875,_Train_in_the_Snow,_o.story: Monet stood on the platform at Argenteuil station with snow coming down and painted the locomotive as it hissed toward him, headlamp a single yellow smear. It was his commuter stop: the train to Paris left from here. The whole winter of 1874-75 he worked the snow around Argenteuil obsessively. The canvas was donated to the Musée Marmottan Monet in 1940, where it still hangs.

Claude_Monet,_Adolphe_Monet_in_the_Garde.title: Adolphe Monet in the Garden of Le Coteau at Sainte-Adresse
Claude_Monet,_Adolphe_Monet_in_the_Garde.description: Adolphe Monet in the Garden of Le Coteau at Sainte-Adresse

source.canonical_title: File:Claude Monet, Adolphe Monet in the Garden of Le Coteau at Sainte-Adresse, 1867.jpg

title.fr: Adolphe Monet lisant dans un jardin

Claude_Monet,_Adolphe_Monet_in_the_Garde.story: An old man in a straw hat, dozing or reading, lost among climbing roses and foxgloves. This is Adolphe Monet, the artist's father, in the garden of Le Coteau, the summer house of the well-off Lecadre cousins who were putting up the family during Monet's broke summer of 1867. Camille had just given birth to their illegitimate son Jean back in Paris, and Adolphe had all but disowned him over it. The canvas remains in private hands.

Claude_Monet,_Fishing_Boats_Leaving_the_.title: Fishing boats leaving the harbor, Le Havre

source.canonical_title: File:Claude Monet, Fishing Boats Leaving the Harbor, Le Havre.jpg

title.fr: Le Havre, bateaux de pêche sortant du port
title.de: Fischerboote verlassen den Hafen, Le Havre

Claude_Monet,_Fishing_Boats_Leaving_the_.story: Dawn at Le Havre, and the fleet is already sliding past the jetty. Monet's brush runs the ink-blue water over with a dirty pink; the smokestacks smudge their own weather. He'd grown up staring at this harbour, and came back in 1874 with an eye sharpened by three years in Argenteuil. The scene is the outer basin of his hometown, the same water that two years earlier gave him 'Impression, Sunrise'.

Claude_Monet,_Le_Grand_Canal.jpg.title: The Grand Canal

source.canonical_title: File:Claude Monet, Le Grand Canal.jpg

Claude_Monet,_Le_Grand_Canal.jpg.story: Monet swore he'd never paint Venice — too famous, too done. Then in October 1908 Alice dragged him there as guests of Mary Young Hunter at the Palazzo Barbaro, and he cracked on the second morning. This is the Grand Canal looking toward Santa Maria della Salute, her dome smudged pink in the lagoon haze, gondola mooring posts jutting like crooked teeth. He worked frantically for three months, produced thirty-seven canvases, then never returned. Alice died in 1911 before he could.

Claude_Monet._Die_Weide._Frühling_an_der.description: Das Bild zeigt eine Weide im Frühling am Fluss Epte, in der Nähe von Giverny. Die morgendliche, kühle Stimmung hält Monet in Pastellfarben fest.

Claude_Monet_(French_-_Still_Life_with_F.title: Still Life with Flowers and Fruit

source.canonical_title: File:Claude Monet (French - Still Life with Flowers and Fruit - Google Art Project.jpg
source.credit: cAEQBxyETd21jQ at Google Cultural Institute maximum zoom level

Claude_Monet_(French_-_Still_Life_with_F.story: Painted in the studio, but the summer showing through. Monet was living at Bougival on the Seine in 1869, chasing light outdoors all season, and it shows up in the tablecloth: broad flat washes next to apples jotted in a few sketchy strokes, petals built from short dense dabs. Each surface treated like its own little experiment in how color behaves under shifting light. The same restlessness would, over the next decade, harden into Impressionism. It hangs at the Getty in Los Angeles, accession 83.PA.215.

Claude_Monet_-_A_Corner_of_the_Apartment.title: A Corner of the Apartment

source.canonical_title: File:Claude Monet - A Corner of the Apartment - Google Art Project.jpg

Claude_Monet_-_A_Corner_of_the_Apartment.story: Monet pulls the curtain back on his own home. Little Jean stands alone in the middle of the floor, a small dark figure in a long smock, while Camille hovers half-lost in shadow near the back. Potted plants spill from the ceiling and a lamp glints between them, turning the Argenteuil apartment into a kind of stage set. The light pulls you toward the sunlit window at the rear. Painted in 1875, it now hangs in the Musee d'Orsay, Paris.

Claude_Monet_-_A_Seascape,_Shipping_by_M.title: A Seascape, Shipping by Moonlight

source.canonical_title: File:Claude Monet - A Seascape, Shipping by Moonlight - Google Art Project.jpg
source.credit: IAGkIdZveew5CQ at Google Cultural Institute maximum zoom level

Claude_Monet_-_A_Seascape,_Shipping_by_M.story: A nocturne, which is unusual for Monet - he later admitted moonlight was punishingly hard to paint from life. This one shows the harbour at Honfleur, close to his boyhood Le Havre, with sailing boats and a steamer cut into dark silhouettes against the moonlit water. He worked it up around 1864 with an unusual combination of palette knife and brush, a full decade before the first Impressionist exhibition. It now hangs in the Scottish National Gallery in Edinburgh.

Claude_Monet_-_A_Walk_in_the_Meadows_at_.title: A Walk in the Meadows at Argenteuil

source.canonical_title: File:Claude Monet - A Walk in the Meadows at Argenteuil - 1998.107 - Rhode Island School of Design Museum.jpg

title.fr: La Promenade dans les prairies à Argenteuil

Claude_Monet_-_A_Walk_in_the_Meadows_at_.story: Two women and a child wade through hip-high grass under a breezy summer sky. You can practically hear the grasshoppers. Monet worked this field outside Argenteuil again and again in the summer of 1873, but this version is the airiest, with a low horizon and an enormous pillowed cloud above. The women's dresses are almost lost in the meadow, a deliberate dissolve: figures as texture, not focus. The painting was a 1998 gift of Houghton P. Metcalf Jr to the RISD Museum in Providence, Rhode Island.

Claude_Monet_-_Alice_Hoschedé_au_jardin..title: Alice Hoschedé in the Garden

source.canonical_title: File:Claude Monet - Alice Hoschedé au jardin.jpg

Claude_Monet_-_Alice_Hoschedé_au_jardin..story: Alice is thirty-seven, seated in a white dress under a tree in Monet's Vétheuil garden, needlework in her lap, the Seine a blue smudge behind her. She and her husband Ernest had moved in with the Monets in 1878 after Ernest went bankrupt; when Camille Monet died in 1879, Alice stayed on and something shifted. This canvas dates from 1881, right before the affair became impossible to hide. Monet picked it as his single image of that year for his big 1889 retrospective with Rodin at Galerie Georges Petit.

Claude_Monet_-_Antibes.jpg.title: Claude Monet - Antibes
