Claude_Monet_-_Antibes.jpg.story: The old town of Antibes sits on its spit of rock, bleached by winter sun, while a single wind-bent pine anchors the foreground. Monet painted this in January–April 1888, one of around three dozen canvases from a campaign he hated and loved in equal measure. The pink walls, blue sea, and bleaching mistral light would show up a year later at Theo van Gogh's gallery in Paris, where ten of the Antibes pictures sold for 11,900 francs.

source.canonical_title: File:Claude Monet - Argenteuil - 1872 - Musée d'Orsay.jpg

Claude_Monet_-_Arrival_of_the_Normandy_T.title: Arrival of the Normandy Train, Gare Saint-Lazare

source.canonical_title: File:Claude Monet - Arrival of the Normandy Train, Gare Saint-Lazare - Google Art Project.jpg

title.ro: Sosirea trenului din Normandia, gara Saint-Lazare
title.fr: Arrivée du train de Normandie, gare Saint-Lazare
title.hu: A Normandiai vonat érkezése, Gare Saint-Lazare
title.fa: ورود قطار نورماندی به ایستگاه گار سو لازار
title.zh: 到達諾曼地的火車，聖雷札火車站

Claude_Monet_-_Arrival_of_the_Normandy_T.story: A Normandy train noses into Paris under a cathedral of iron and glass, steam and smoke curling up into the triangular vault. Tiny figures wait on the platform, almost dissolved in the haze. Monet signed it 'Claude Monet 77' in the lower left and showed it at the third Impressionist exhibition that April. The industrialist Martin A. Ryerson bought it in 1911 for $7,000 and bequeathed it to the Art Institute of Chicago in 1932.

Claude_Monet_-_Automne_sur_la_Seine_Arge.title: Autumn on the Seine, Argenteuil

source.canonical_title: File:Claude Monet - Automne sur la Seine Argenteuil (1873).jpg

Claude_Monet_-_Automne_sur_la_Seine_Arge.story: Autumn at Argenteuil, the river running between two walls of yellowing trees that double themselves on the water. Monet has tipped the palette warm: ochre, copper, a little smoky blue. It's probably late October; you can feel the bite coming on. He painted from a small studio-boat he'd bought that year, which let him drift into exactly the motif he wanted. Manet later painted Monet painting from that boat. This canvas belongs to the High Museum of Art in Atlanta.

Claude_Monet_-_Camille_Monet_sur_son_lit.title: Camille Monet on her deathbed

source.canonical_title: File:Claude Monet - Camille Monet sur son lit de mort.JPG

title.fr: Camille Monet sur son lit de mort

Claude_Monet_-_Camille_Monet_sur_son_lit.story: Camille Doncieux — Monet's first wife, the woman in the green dress, the parasol, the poppy field — died at thirty-two on 5 September 1879. Monet painted her that same morning. The brushwork is stricken: short, dabbing strokes, a pale violet cast, her face half-lost in the bedclothes. He later admitted, to his own horror, that even then part of his eye was analysing the colours of death on the skin he had loved. He never signed the canvas; a stamped signature was added after his own death. It is now in the Musée d'Orsay.

Claude_Monet_-_Champ_de_blé.jpg.title: Wheatfield

source.canonical_title: File:Claude Monet - Champ de blé.jpg

Claude_Monet_-_Champ_de_blé.jpg.story: A wheatfield under a flat summer sky, the grain already turned gold, brushwork so dense the canvas feels like a woven thing. Monet painted several of these around Vétheuil in 1881, small and fast, no figures to slow him down. The horizon sits high, forcing your eye to stay in the field itself, in the quick ticks of yellow and ochre and green. No haystacks yet, no series, no program, just a patch of ripe wheat on a warm afternoon.

Claude_Monet_-_Champ_de_coquelicots_près.title: Poppy Field near Vétheuil

source.canonical_title: File:Claude Monet - Champ de coquelicots près de Vétheuil.jpg
source.credit: 1: Unknown source Unknown source 2: Stiftung Sammlung E.G. Bührle 3: ArtDaily.com

title.de: Champ de coquelicots près de Vétheuil
title.ja: ヴェトゥイユ近郊のひなげし畑

Claude_Monet_-_Champ_de_coquelicots_près.story: Summer 1879. Monet's wife Camille was dying, money was gone, and he walked out into the fields above Vétheuil and painted this. The clouds are laid on in broad slabs; the poppies are quick red jabs of a loaded brush. A dealer bought it that November for pocket money. It later passed through Durand-Ruel, Bernheim-Jeune and several Berlin collectors before landing where it is now: the E.G. Bührle Foundation in Zürich.

Claude_Monet_-_Cliff_Walk_at_Pourville_-.title: Cliff Walk at Pourville

source.canonical_title: File:Claude Monet - Cliff Walk at Pourville - Google Art Project.jpg
source.credit: Google Arts & Culture: Home - pic Maximum resolution.

title.ro: Plimbare pe o stâncă la Pourville
title.ja: プールヴィルの断崖の上の散歩
title.ca: El passeig del penya-segat a Pourville

Claude_Monet_-_Cliff_Walk_at_Pourville_-.story: Two women in summer whites stand on a grassy cliff edge while the English Channel stretches out below, flecked with sailboats. Monet spent the summer of 1882 in Pourville, a small Normandy fishing village, painting the coast in every weather. One of the figures is probably Marthe Hoschedé, daughter of his future second wife Alice. The wind is doing most of the work in this painting: it flattens the grass, tugs the parasol, puffs the sails. The Art Institute of Chicago has owned it since 1933.

source.canonical_title: File:Claude Monet - Dahlias (16035439250).jpg

Claude_Monet_-_Der_Koch_(Le_Père_Paul)_-.title: Portrait of Père Paul

source.canonical_title: File:Claude Monet - Der Koch (Le Père Paul) - 540 - Österreichische Galerie Belvedere.jpg

Claude_Monet_-_Der_Koch_(Le_Père_Paul)_-.story: Meet Paul Antoine Graff, Alsatian cook and landlord of the Hôtel À la Renommée des Galettes in Pourville, where Monet lodged in 1882. Père Paul's galettes — crusty Breton cakes — got top billing on the signboard. Monet painted him in gratitude, white toque, white jacket, face floating out of a grey oval like a warm biscuit. It was a gift, never sold. Today it hangs in Vienna's Belvedere, a rare Monet portrait from a painter who mostly looked at water. Paul died in 1893.

Claude_Monet_-_Entrée_du_port_de_Trouvil.title: en

source.canonical_title: File:Claude Monet - Entrée du port de Trouville.jpg

Claude_Monet_-_Entrée_du_port_de_Trouvil.story: Summer 1870 at Trouville, Monet working alongside his old mentor Boudin. Nine canvases came out of that stay, and this harbor-mouth view was one of them. It also matters for another reason: Paul Durand-Ruel bought it, beginning a dealer-artist partnership that would run for the rest of Monet's life and effectively bankroll Impressionism. Wildenstein catalogued it as number 154.

Claude_Monet_-_Flowered_Riverbank,_Argen.title: Flowered Riverbank, Argenteuil

source.canonical_title: File:Claude Monet - Flowered Riverbank, Argenteuil.jpg

Claude_Monet_-_Flowered_Riverbank,_Argen.story: Wild dahlias and tangled grasses swallow the bottom two-thirds of the canvas, shoved so close you can almost pick them. Above, far off, a factory chimney leaks smoke into the sky, the tidy horizon line pushed right up to the top edge in a cropping trick borrowed from Japanese ukiyo-e. Painted in 1877 as Monet's years at Argenteuil wound down, it belongs now to the Pola Museum of Art in Hakone, Japan.

Claude_Monet_-_Flowering_Plum_Trees_-_Go.title: Plum Trees in Blossom

source.canonical_title: File:Claude Monet - Flowering Plum Trees - Google Art Project.jpg

Claude_Monet_-_Flowering_Plum_Trees_-_Go.story: Spring 1879, near Monet's rented house at Vétheuil. You glimpse the village roofs and the hill of Chênay through a haze of pale-pink blossom. The painting is almost unreasonably cheerful given what was happening inside the house — Camille Monet was in the last months of her illness and would die that September. It now hangs at the Museum of Fine Arts in Budapest.

Claude_Monet_-_Graystaks_I.jpeg.title: Grainstack (Sunset)

source.canonical_title: File:Claude Monet - Graystaks I.JPG

title.fr: meule de paille au coucher du soleil

Claude_Monet_-_Graystaks_I.jpeg.story: Between August 1890 and February 1891 Monet painted twenty-five canvases of the grainstacks in the field behind his Giverny garden. They were his first proper series — the same two stacks, worked over at different hours, seasons and weathers, treated as a single decorative ensemble rather than individual pictures. When Durand-Ruel exhibited fifteen in May 1891 they sold within days and made him famous. This sunset version, now at the Museum of Fine Arts in Boston, burns at the horizon while the stack itself sinks into cold blue shadow.

Claude_Monet_-_Houses_of_Parliament,_Sun.title: Houses of Parliament, Sunlight Effect

source.canonical_title: File:Claude Monet - Houses of Parliament, Sunlight Effect (Le Parlement, effet de soleil) - Google Art Project.jpg
source.credit: ogHX89fG0cGJxQ at Google Cultural Institute maximum zoom level

Claude_Monet_-_Houses_of_Parliament,_Sun.story: Same terrace at St Thomas' Hospital, same Parliament silhouette, but here the sun has punched a hole in the fog and ignited the water. Monet chased these effects across roughly nineteen Parliament canvases, each labeled for a specific atmospheric condition — effet de brouillard, effet de soleil, trouée de soleil. He worked from the terrace between 1900 and 1901, then finished this one in Giverny and signed it 1903. It was one of thirty-seven Thames views unveiled at Durand-Ruel's Paris gallery in May 1904, the first time the public saw any of the series.

Claude_Monet_-_Hôtel_des_roches_noires._.title: Hôtel des Roches Noires, Trouville

source.canonical_title: File:Claude Monet - Hôtel des roches noires. Trouville - Google Art Project.jpg
source.credit: lAEswCWla3bwcw at Google Cultural Institute maximum zoom level

Claude_Monet_-_Hôtel_des_roches_noires._.story: Summer 1870, newlywed Monet is at Trouville with Camille, the war about to break any week. On the seafront promenade stands the Hotel des Roches Noires, flags snapping in the wind off the Channel. Look at those flags: red-and-white stripes laid down in a few brusque, almost careless strokes, same restless touch animating the wispy clouds above. A Second Empire pleasure palace caught at its high-water mark. Later, Proust would use this hotel as one of his models for the Balbec in the Search. Musee d'Orsay, Paris.

Claude_Monet_-_In_the_Woods_at_Giverny-_.title: In the Woods at Giverny: Blanche Hoschedé at Her Easel with Suzanne Hoschedé Reading

source.canonical_title: File:Claude Monet - In the Woods at Giverny- Blanche Hoschedé at Her Easel with Suzanne Hoschedé Reading - Google Art Project.jpg
source.credit: 5wF3eJ0lvxhbeg at Google Cultural Institute maximum zoom level

Claude_Monet_-_In_the_Woods_at_Giverny-_.story: Dappled sunlight drops through Giverny oaks onto two young women: Blanche at her easel, Suzanne curled on the grass with a book. Blanche Hoschedé later married Monet's son Jean and became the family's archivist of his late work. The painting belongs to the Los Angeles County Museum of Art, a 1964 gift from Mrs. Fred Hathaway Bixby.

Claude_Monet_-_Intérieur,_Après_dîner.jp.title: Interior, after Dinner

source.canonical_title: File:Claude Monet - Intérieur, Après dîner.jpg

Claude_Monet_-_Intérieur,_Après_dîner.jp.story: Lamplight pooling onto a dark table, a woman in gray (Camille) still seated, a man at the mantelpiece (possibly Bazille), a servant clearing. Painted in the winter of 1868–69 at Étretat, where Monet had holed up with Camille and their infant son Jean, broke and sponging off friends. It's an unusually quiet, almost Dutch-feeling interior for him — all firelight and hanging oil lamp. Now at the National Gallery of Art, Washington.

Claude_Monet_-_Jardin_à_Sainte-Adresse.j.title: Garden at Sainte-Adresse

source.canonical_title: File:Claude Monet - Jardin à Sainte-Adresse.jpg

Claude_Monet_-_Jardin_à_Sainte-Adresse.j.story: Red gladioli, striped parasols, and two tricolor flags snapping in the breeze over the Channel. Monet's father sits in the foreground; his cousin-in-law Jeanne-Marguerite leans at the rail. Renoir called it "the Japanese painting" for its high, flattened viewpoint, clearly borrowed from the ukiyo-e prints flooding Paris. The Met bought it at auction in 1967 for a then-record $1.4 million.

Claude_Monet_-_Jean-Pierre_Hoschedé_and_.title: Jean-Pierre Hoschedé and Michel Monet on the Bank of the Epte

source.canonical_title: File:Claude Monet - Jean-Pierre Hoschedé and Michel Monet on the Bank of the Epte.jpg

Claude_Monet_-_Jean-Pierre_Hoschedé_and_.story: Two boys lie belly-down in summer grass above the river Epte, shirts bright against the green, peering at something in the current. Jean-Pierre was Alice Hoschedé's son, Michel was Monet's youngest — they grew up as brothers in the Giverny household. The painting is in a private collection, and the patch of riverbank is a short walk from Monet's garden gate.

Claude_Monet_-_L'Été_-_Google_Art_Projec.title: Summer

source.canonical_title: File:Claude Monet - L'Été - Google Art Project.jpg

Claude_Monet_-_L'Été_-_Google_Art_Projec.story: A field blazing with light, and buried in it: Camille and little Jean, barely more present than the trees. Émile Zola singled this one out for praise when it showed at the 1876 Impressionist exhibition at Nadar's. The figures don't matter more than the grass, and that was the whole point. Oil on canvas, 57 by 80 cm, hanging today at the Alte Nationalgalerie in Berlin.

Claude_Monet_-_L'été_-_Champ_de_coquelic.title: Summer, Field of Poppies

source.canonical_title: File:Claude Monet - L'été - Champ de coquelicots.JPG

Claude_Monet_-_L'été_-_Champ_de_coquelic.story: One of four views Monet painted in the summer of 1875 of the plain of Gennevilliers, just across the Seine from Argenteuil. Wild poppies pepper a fallow field, a woman with a parasol and a child thread through the grass, a second pair follows behind them. The subject was already a Monet calling card — the famous Orsay Coquelicots dates from two years earlier — but here the brushwork is looser, the poppies almost vibrating. High summer painted from the inside out.

Claude_Monet_-_La_Corniche_near_Monaco_-.title: The Corniche near Monaco

source.canonical_title: File:Claude Monet - La Corniche near Monaco - Google Art Project.jpg
source.credit: QwEto4QimXEOzg at Google Cultural Institute maximum zoom level

Claude_Monet_-_La_Corniche_near_Monaco_-.story: On his way back from Bordighera in April 1884, Monet stopped along the Corniche — the cliff road hugging the coast above Monaco. He set up where the land drops hard into impossibly blue water and painted the heat shimmer straight on. Pink rock, silver olives, a sea the colour of a peacock's throat. Monet fretted in letters that the palette looked theatrical, but insisted it was exactly what he saw. The painting is in the Rijksmuseum.

Claude_Monet_-_La_Manneporte_(Étretat).j.title: The Manneporte (Étretat)
Claude_Monet_-_La_Manneporte_(Étretat).j.description: Monet spent most of February 1883 at Étretat, a fishing village and resort on the Normandy coast. He painted eighteen views of the beach and the three extraordinary rock formations in the area: the "Porte d'Aval," the "Porte d'Amont," and the "Manneporte."

source.canonical_title: File:Claude Monet - La Manneporte (Étretat).jpg

Claude_Monet_-_La_Manneporte_(Étretat).j.story: February 1883: Monet holed up at Étretat and painted the rock arches like a man possessed. The Manneporte is the biggest of the three — a limestone elephant wading into the Channel. He set up below tide line, got caught by a wave once and nearly lost canvas, easel, and himself. The result is all spray and shadow, the arch looming like a cathedral door. He finished eighteen Étretat canvases that winter.

Claude_Monet_-_La_Pointe_de_la_Hève_at_L.title: The Pointe de la Hève at Low Tide

source.canonical_title: File:Claude Monet - La Pointe de la Hève at Low Tide - Google Art Project.jpg

title.de: La Pointe de la Hève bei Ebbe
title.fr: La Pointe de la Hève à marée basse
title.hu: A Pointe de la Hève apálykor

Claude_Monet_-_La_Pointe_de_la_Hève_at_L.story: Wet sand, a low sky, tiny figures near beached boats. Monet grew up looking at this stretch of coast near Le Havre, and he painted the headland first outdoors at a portable size, then hauled the composition back to his Paris studio and enlarged it for the 1865 Salon. Viewers there kept mistaking his signature for Manet's, leading the older painter to track down the young upstart in person. The canvas measures about 90 by 150 cm and now lives at the Kimbell Art Museum in Fort Worth.

Claude_Monet_-_La_Seine_à_Vétheuil_(1881.title: The Seine at Vétheuil

source.canonical_title: File:Claude Monet - La Seine à Vétheuil (1881).jpg

Claude_Monet_-_La_Seine_à_Vétheuil_(1881.story: Monet painted the Seine from his Vétheuil bank obsessively, the same stretch of water in every weather. This is a summer version, 1881, poplars on the far shore doubling themselves in the mirror below, a small boat barely disturbing the surface. He was still living in the rented house with Alice Hoschedé and her six children; money was tight, but Durand-Ruel had started buying again. Within months the whole household would move downriver to Poissy, and this view would be gone for good.

Claude_Monet_-_Le_Palais_Ducal.jpg.title: The Doge's Palace

source.canonical_title: File:Claude Monet - Le Palais Ducal.jpg

Claude_Monet_-_Le_Palais_Ducal.jpg.story: The Doge's Palace seen from a boat bobbing in the lagoon, its pink-and-white stone dissolved into pure light on water. Monet painted the palace ten times during his 1908 Venetian stay, mostly from a gondola anchored off San Giorgio Maggiore. He hated it at first — wrote to a friend that the city was impossible, the motifs cliché — but by the end he was in tears at having to leave. This version now lives at the Brooklyn Museum, a 1920 gift from collector A. Augustus Healy.

Claude_Monet_-_Le_Parlement,_coucher_de_.story: A sunset over Westminster, dated 1904, but scaffolded on sketches Monet had made from St Thomas' Hospital in 1900 and 1901. The towers melt into their own reflection; the sun smolders like a coal through thick river air. By 1904 Monet had shown the Thames series at Durand-Ruel in May and could finally exhale — he'd written to his wife Alice that the London canvases were tormenting him, that he'd need another lifetime to finish them. This version hangs at the Kunsthaus Zürich.

He modeled the boat on one Charles-Francois Daubigny had built before him, and used it for years to paint sailing scenes at Petit-Gennevilliers otherwise inaccessible from shore. This 1876 version belongs to the Museum of Art and History in Neuchatel, Switzerland.

Claude_Monet_-_Le_pont_de_chemin_der_fer.story: Monet had a thing for the Argenteuil railway bridge, a severe slab of iron and concrete thrown across the Seine for the Paris commuter line. Where other painters might have hidden it, he made it the hero, painting the piers full-on with a train puffing across the top. The shock of modernity, softened by river light. He did at least four versions in 1873 alone, each with a different weather, different traffic. This one is in a private collection; the Musee d'Orsay holds the most famous sibling canvas.

Claude_Monet_-_Les_Pyramides_de_Port-Cot.story: Three jagged sea stacks burn orange under a high sun while the Atlantic heaves around them in streaks of teal and violet. Monet arrived on Belle-Île in September 1886 planning to stay ten days and stayed more than two months, lashed by storms he actually enjoyed. The "pyramids" at Port-Coton became his favorite motif there; he painted them at least six times.

Claude_Monet_-_Les_canotiers_à_Argenteui.story: Two young rowers in straw boaters lean into their oars, the Seine at Argenteuil flashing around them like hammered tin. Monet worked much of that summer from his floating studio, a converted boat he'd had built on Manet's advice. Sunday canoeing was the new Parisian obsession, the suburbs suddenly accessible by train. The painting now lives in the private Nahmad collection.

Claude_Monet_-_Neige_à_Argenteuil_(1874-.title: Snow at Argenteuil

source.canonical_title: File:Claude Monet - Neige à Argenteuil (1874-75).jpg
source.credit: Google Art Project works from the Nelson-Atkins Museum of Art

Claude_Monet_-_Neige_à_Argenteuil_(1874-.story: The winter of 1874-75 dumped snow on Argenteuil, and Monet painted it eighteen times. This one looks up the boulevard Saint-Denis with the local station at his back, flakes still falling: the sky and ground rhyme in the same dirty-mauve whites. He loaded the road with impasto you can almost step in. Now in the MFA, Boston.

Claude_Monet_-_Nymphéas_(1905).jpg.title: Water Lilies

source.canonical_title: File:Claude Monet - Nymphéas (1905).jpg
source.credit: Museum of Fine Arts, Boston, online database

Claude_Monet_-_Nymphéas_(1905).jpg.story: By 1905 Monet had been staring at his Giverny pond for years, and it shows. The horizon is gone. There's no bank, no sky, no far shore — just a patch of green-purple water with a scatter of lilies floating on top, as if the canvas itself were laid flat on the surface. He was sixty-five, obsessive, rising before dawn to catch the light before it changed. This painting belongs to the first big Nymphéas series he exhibited together in 1909 at Durand-Ruel, where forty-eight water lily canvases hung side by side.

Claude_Monet_-_Nymphéas_(W_1698).jpg.title: Water Lilies

source.canonical_title: File:Claude Monet - Nymphéas (W 1698).jpg

Claude_Monet_-_Nymphéas_(W_1698).jpg.story: 1907, and Monet has gone vertical. The pond elongates into a narrow tower of water, pink blooms stacked up the canvas like notes on a staff. He experimented with tall formats that year, rotating the usual landscape rectangle onto its short side to force the eye downward through reflection after reflection. The catalog number W 1698 is from Daniel Wildenstein's massive five-volume Monet catalogue raisonné, the scholarly map that tracks every surviving canvas.

Claude_Monet_-_Nymphéas_W1852_-_Musée_Ma.title: Water Lilies

source.canonical_title: File:Claude Monet - Nymphéas W1852 - Musée Marmottan-Monet.jpg

Claude_Monet_-_Nymphéas_W1852_-_Musée_Ma.story: A 1910 Nymphéas, and the pond is no longer just a pond — it's a slab of moving color that happens to have flowers in it. That winter the Seine had flooded Giverny and nearly wiped out the lily garden; Monet had to rebuild the banks and replant. This canvas hangs at the Musée Marmottan Monet in Paris, which holds the largest Monet collection in the world thanks to a 1966 bequest from his son Michel, who'd inherited the contents of Giverny after Monet's death.

Claude_Monet_-_On_the_Boat_-_Google_Art_.title: 舟遊び

source.canonical_title: File:Claude Monet - On the Boat - Google Art Project.jpg
source.credit: UQFKgSkcsCnEuQ at Google Cultural Institute maximum zoom level

Claude_Monet_-_On_the_Boat_-_Google_Art_.story: Two of Alice Hoschedé's daughters lean over the side of a skiff on the Epte, staring into water so green it looks carved from glass. Monet skipped the horizon entirely — there's no sky, no bank, just the hull, the reflections, and the girls' absorbed faces. It's a radical compositional move for 1887, closer to a Japanese print than a classic riverscape. Suzanne, the one on the left, would become Monet's most painted model in the coming years. The canvas hangs at Tokyo's National Museum of Western Art.

Claude_Monet_-_Pond_with_Water_Lilies_-_.title: Pond with Water Lilies

source.canonical_title: File:Claude Monet - Pond with Water Lilies - Google Art Project.jpg
source.credit: 7wFvMeHQCRDVEw at Google Cultural Institute maximum zoom level

Claude_Monet_-_Pond_with_Water_Lilies_-_.story: By 1907 Monet had been painting the same pond at Giverny for over a decade - rerouting a stream, importing Japanese lilies, hiring a gardener just to keep the pads clean of dust. This canvas is from the stretch where he stopped painting the bridge and the bank and let the surface do everything. No horizon. No sky, except as reflection. Just willow-shadow dragged vertically through floating clouds of pink. He was sixty-seven, his cataracts already thickening, and the water was starting to double as a mirror for a world he was losing the ability to see clearly.

Claude_Monet_-_Poplars_on_the_Epte_-_Goo.title: Poplars on the Epte

source.canonical_title: File:Claude Monet - Poplars on the Epte - Google Art Project.jpg
source.credit: tAF_YbFvVelS9Q at Google Cultural Institute maximum zoom level

Claude_Monet_-_Poplars_on_the_Epte_-_Goo.story: Monet bought these poplars. In 1891 the commune of Limetz put the trees on the Epte up for auction as timber; Monet partnered with a local lumber dealer so he could keep painting them until he was finished, then hand them over to be cut. This S-curve of trunks and their double in the water is one of about 24 canvases from the series. The painting is at the National Gallery of Scotland.

Claude_Monet_-_Poppy_Field_-_Google_Art_.title: Wild Poppies Near Argenteuil

source.canonical_title: File:Claude Monet - Poppy Field - Google Art Project.jpg

title.ja: アルジャントゥイユの��なげし

Claude_Monet_-_Poppy_Field_-_Google_Art_.story: A red tide of poppies cascading down a low hill, Camille and Jean walking ahead, a second pair (maybe the same pair, repeated) higher up. The painting is built on two diagonals and a riot of small red dabs. Monet showed it at the first Impressionist exhibition in 1874, where visitors argued about whether the flowers were flowers or just paint. They are, obviously, both. Renoir was a regular guest at Argenteuil that summer, and you can feel him hovering just off-canvas. The work is at the Musee d'Orsay.

Claude_Monet_-_Poppy_Field_-_Google_Art_.title: Champ de coquelicots

source.canonical_title: File:Claude Monet - Poppy Field - Google Art Project (430231).jpg
source.credit: hAFVe_EcSVyxCg at Google Cultural Institute maximum zoom level

Claude_Monet_-_Poppy_Field_-_Google_Art_.story: Red poppies scattered across a sloping field above Vétheuil, no parasol-twirling figures this time, just the flowers and the summer air. Monet painted the motif repeatedly in 1881, each canvas a slightly different angle or hour. The paint sits up off the surface in dabs; step close and the poppies dissolve into pure color. It's Impressionism at full confidence, no apology, no storytelling. Acquired by the J. Paul Getty Museum in 1985.

Claude_Monet_-_Red_and_Pink_Poppies_(115.title: Claude Monet - Red and Pink Poppies (11538159396)

source.canonical_title: File:Claude Monet - Red and Pink Poppies (11538159396).jpg
source.credit: Claude Monet - Red and Pink Poppies , Irina , 25 December 2013, 02:31

Claude_Monet_-_Reflections_of_Clouds_on_.title: Reflections of Clouds on the Water-Lily Pond

source.canonical_title: File:Claude Monet - Reflections of Clouds on the Water-Lily Pond.jpg
source.credit: Digital image, The Museum of Modern Art, New York

Claude_Monet_-_Reflections_of_Clouds_on_.story: MoMA's three-panel Monet, almost 13 metres long, wraps you in pond the way Monet always wanted. The horizon is gone; the clouds arrive only as reflections sliding between water lilies. Begun around 1920, it was one of the canvases Monet kept in the Giverny studio rather than sending to the Orangerie, reworking the surface through worsening cataracts right up until his death in 1926. MoMA bought the triptych with the Mrs. Simon Guggenheim Fund in 1959.

Claude_Monet_-_Regattas_at_Argenteuil_-_.title: Regattas at Argenteuil

source.canonical_title: File:Claude Monet - Regattas at Argenteuil - Google Art Project.jpg

title.ja: アルジャントゥイユのレガッタ

Claude_Monet_-_Regattas_at_Argenteuil_-_.story: A Sunday on the Seine, dinghies leaning into the wind, and Monet painting as if the whole thing might dissolve if he slowed down. The water is loud with reflections: the white sails sit twice, once in the air, once broken up in the current. Argenteuil had become the Parisian bourgeoisie's favourite sailing spot after the railway arrived, and Monet worked the scene for a decade. He used the broadest strokes here, almost careless, trusting the eye to reassemble them. The canvas is at the Musee d'Orsay.

Claude_Monet_-_Regnvær,_Etretat_-_Google.title: Rainy Weather, Étretat

source.canonical_title: File:Claude Monet - Regnvær, Etretat - Google Art Project.jpg
source.credit: hAGxTh_ktg_DlQ at Google Cultural Institute , zoom level maximum

Claude_Monet_-_Regnvær,_Etretat_-_Google.story: Rain blurs the arch of the Porte d'Aval into a soft gray ghost, and the sea slumps flat beneath it. "Regnvær" is Norwegian for rainy weather — the painting hangs at the National Museum in Oslo, which is why it wears that Scandinavian title. Monet chased weather like this on the Normandy coast in the mid-1880s specifically because it kept other painters indoors.

Claude_Monet_-_Road_at_La_Cavée,_Pourvil.title: Road at La Cavée, Pourville

source.canonical_title: File:Claude Monet - Road at La Cavée, Pourville - Google Art Project.jpg
source.credit: kAHKLO3n2oSnOQ at Google Cultural Institute maximum zoom level

Claude_Monet_-_Road_at_La_Cavée,_Pourvil.story: A hollow way — chemin de la cavée — cut between banks of grass, climbing up from the village of Pourville toward the cliff tops. Monet painted four versions of this lane in 1882 and sold the lot to Durand-Ruel on 10 October that year. Pink flowers flicker in the verge; the sea waits at the top of the slope, just a blue sliver. It's a landscape of anticipation: you haven't seen the Channel yet, but you can smell it. This canvas lives at Boston's Museum of Fine Arts.

Claude_Monet_-_Rocks_at_Belle-lle,_Port-.title: Rocks at Belle-lle, Port-Domois

source.canonical_title: File:Claude Monet - Rocks at Belle-lle, Port-Domois - Google Art Project.jpg
source.credit: HAHXgPLFma1p1Q at Google Cultural Institute , zoom level maximum

Claude_Monet_-_Rocks_at_Belle-lle,_Port-.story: Black basalt teeth bite up out of a sea that looks like hammered metal. Belle-Île's Atlantic coast shocked Monet — he'd painted the gentler Channel for years — and he stayed ten stormy weeks in the autumn of 1886 to wrestle with it. This view of the Port-Domois inlet is in the collection of the Cincinnati Art Museum.

Claude_Monet_-_Sailing_Boat,_Evening_Eff.title: Claude Monet - Sailing Boat, Evening Effect

source.canonical_title: File:Claude Monet - Sailing Boat, Evening Effect.jpg

Claude_Monet_-_Springtime_-_Google_Art_P.title: Springtime

source.canonical_title: File:Claude Monet - Springtime - Google Art Project.jpg
source.credit: pAEsabNHoa1naA at Google Cultural Institute maximum zoom level

Claude_Monet_-_Springtime_-_Google_Art_P.story: A woman reads in the orchard grass while blossom-light filters through new leaves onto her white dress. This is Camille, Monet's first wife, posed among the fruit trees behind the house at Argenteuil. The paint is thin and quick and the greens are half a dozen different greens. Monet loved spring for exactly this reason: the foliage is still patchy enough to let sunlight through, so every surface flickers. He made several versions that season, each cooler or warmer than the last. This one lives at the Walters Art Museum in Baltimore.

Claude_Monet_-_Still_Life_with_Pheasants.title: Still Life with Pheasants and Plovers

source.canonical_title: File:Claude Monet - Still Life with Pheasants and Plovers - Google Art Project.jpg

Claude_Monet_-_Still_Life_with_Pheasants.story: Game birds, feathers catching the studio light, laid out on a table like a hunter's trophy. Monet rarely painted dead birds, and this 1879 canvas shows him working harder at the feather detail than he usually bothered with for flowers or water. The plovers' speckled breasts get the same careful attention as the pheasant's coppery tail. It now belongs to the Minneapolis Institute of Art.

Claude_Monet_-_Street_in_Sainte-Adresse_.title: Street in Sainte-Adresse

source.canonical_title: File:Claude Monet - Street in Sainte-Adresse (1867).jpg

Claude_Monet_-_Street_in_Sainte-Adresse_.story: A woman and child paused halfway down a cobbled slope, other figures vanishing around the bend, chimney smoke smudging blue into the roofline. Monet painted this small upright view during the same prolific summer at Sainte-Adresse that produced the Met's Regatta and the flag-strewn garden. The composition leans on a steep diagonal of wall and cobble, the kind of framing he was picking up from Japanese prints. It hangs at the Clark Art Institute in Williamstown, Massachusetts.

Claude_Monet_-_Temps_calme_Pourville.jpg.title: Temps calme, Pourville

source.canonical_title: File:Claude Monet - Temps calme Pourville.jpg
source.credit: Artbook: Rudolf Staechelin’sche Familienstiftung Basel (Hrsg.): Nafea, die Sammlung Rudolf Staechelin, Basel .

Claude_Monet_-_Temps_calme_Pourville.jpg.story: Calm weather, Pourville. Monet rented a cottage on this Normandy coast in 1882 and fell hard for the chalky cliffs and flat gray sea. This one is the quiet mood, sea almost lilac, cliffs rising softly on the right, a boat or two hardly moving. He'd brought Alice and the kids for the summer. The weather obliged long enough for him to finish a handful of these before the wind kicked up and he started the rougher variants.

Claude_Monet_-_The_Argenteuil_Bridge_-_G.title: The Bridge at Argenteuil

source.canonical_title: File:Claude Monet - The Argenteuil Bridge - Google Art Project.jpg
source.credit: zAGt_suewfK9Qw at Google Cultural Institute maximum zoom level

Claude_Monet_-_The_Argenteuil_Bridge_-_G.story: 1874: the year the Impressionists first exhibited together, and the year Monet painted this bridge seven times. Orange masts and hulls sit hard against the blue-grey Seine, complementaries cranked up until the water almost rings. The bridge itself had been rebuilt after Prussian troops blew it up in 1870. The canvas is 60 by 80 cm and hangs at the Musée d'Orsay.

Claude_Monet_-_The_Artist’s_Garden_in_Gi.title: The Artist’s Garden in Giverny

source.canonical_title: File:Claude Monet - The Artist’s Garden in Giverny - 1983.7.12 - Yale University Art Gallery.jpg

Claude_Monet_-_The_Artist’s_Garden_in_Gi.story: Rows of irises surge diagonally across the canvas in bands of violet and rose, a narrow pink path threading between them toward a dappled line of trees. Monet was sixty when he painted this in 1900, already wealthy, already famous, and still treating his garden like a second studio. The Clos Normand — the formal garden on the house side of the road — was his first horticultural project at Giverny, begun when he moved there in 1883. This version hangs at Yale; a close sister painting is at the Musée d'Orsay.

Claude_Monet_-_The_Cliff_of_Aval,_Etréta.title: The Cliff of Aval, Étretat

source.canonical_title: File:Claude Monet - The Cliff of Aval, Etrétat - Google Art Project.jpg
source.credit: 7AFALGbV2i_P5w at Google Cultural Institute maximum zoom level

Claude_Monet_-_The_Cliff_of_Aval,_Etréta.story: A single arched fang of chalk wades into the Channel while the water chops green around its ankles. Monet painted the Falaise d'Aval again and again from the beach, hauling his easel across slippery shingle so the cliff leaned over him like a doorway. He told his dealer the sea at Etretat was "so beautiful" he couldn't tear himself away. This canvas lives in the Clark Art Institute.

Claude_Monet_-_The_Fort_of_Antibes.jpg.title: The Fort of Antibes

source.canonical_title: File:Claude Monet - The Fort of Antibes.jpg

Claude_Monet_-_The_Fort_of_Antibes.jpg.story: Fort Carré, the sixteenth-century star fort guarding Antibes harbor, squats on the horizon while a gnarled foreground tree does all the compositional work. Monet painted it in 1888 during his long, exasperating Riviera stay — he wrote that the colors were 'fairylike' and impossible. The fort hadn't changed much since Napoleon was briefly imprisoned there in 1794. Monet's version is far less about the stones than about the blast of Mediterranean blue behind them.

Claude_Monet_-_The_Gare_Saint-Lazare;_Ar.title: Claude Monet - The Gare Saint-Lazare; Arrival of a Train - 1877
Claude_Monet_-_The_Gare_Saint-Lazare;_Ar.description: The Gare Saint-Lazare: Arrival of a Train

source.canonical_title: File:Claude Monet - The Gare Saint-Lazare; Arrival of a Train - 1877.jpg

Claude_Monet_-_The_Gare_Saint-Lazare;_Ar.story: The biggest of Monet's twelve Gare Saint-Lazare canvases, all done in the first half of 1877. He'd moved from Argenteuil into an apartment near the station to paint them, working on several at once, sometimes leaning wet canvases against each other. Pigment sits in thick mounds here, hues jostling until they fuse at a distance. Seven of the twelve went straight to the third Impressionist exhibition. This one lives at Harvard's Fogg Museum.

Claude_Monet_-_The_Highway_Bridge_under_.title: The Highway Bridge under repair

source.canonical_title: File:Claude Monet - The Highway Bridge under repair.jpg

Claude_Monet_-_The_Highway_Bridge_under_.story: The old road bridge at Argenteuil had been blown up by retreating French troops during the Franco-Prussian War, and when Monet painted it in 1872 scaffolding still clung to the piers. It's an odd subject for an Impressionist, all struts and diagonals and sawed timber, but he treats the repair work as a gift: pure geometry stuck into the soft river light. A boat drifts past as if none of the damage matters. The bridge would be back in service within the year. The painting belongs to a private collection.

Claude_Monet_-_The_Houses_of_Parliament,.title: The Houses of Parliament, Sunset

source.canonical_title: File:Claude Monet - The Houses of Parliament, Sunset.jpg

title.fr: Le Parlement de Londres, soleil couchant

Claude_Monet_-_The_Houses_of_Parliament,.story: Another sunset from the same terrace, another variation on the same impossible problem — how to paint air. Monet finished this canvas in 1904 after four years of reworking, and it went into the thirty-seven-painting Thames show at Durand-Ruel that May. Critics loved it. Clemenceau, the future French prime minister and Monet's close friend, wrote a rave. The painter was sixty-four, already deep into his water-lily obsession, and this was effectively his farewell to urban subjects — he'd barely paint a city again for the remaining twenty-two years of his life.

Claude_Monet_-_The_Magpie_-_Google_Art_P.title: The Magpie

source.canonical_title: File:Claude Monet - The Magpie - Google Art Project.jpg
source.credit: rQGnadHwK8lSmg at Google Cultural Institute maximum zoom level

Claude_Monet_-_The_Magpie_-_Google_Art_P.story: One black bird on a wattle gate, sunlight raking across untouched snow, shadows cast in pale blue and violet rather than black. Painted near Étretat in the Normandy winter of 1868–69, it's one of the first places Monet let shadow carry color — a quiet bit of heresy that the Salon jury rejected in 1869. The canvas stayed in private hands for more than a century before the Musée d'Orsay bought it in 1984. It's now among the most-loved paintings in the collection.

Claude_Monet_-_The_Railway_Bridge_at_Arg.title: Railroad Bridge, Argenteuil

source.canonical_title: File:Claude Monet - The Railway Bridge at Argenteuil (Philadelphia).jpg

title.fr: Le Pont du chemin de fer à Argenteuil

Claude_Monet_-_The_Railway_Bridge_at_Arg.story: Same iron bridge, different angle. Monet has pulled back so the span stretches across the whole canvas like a ruler laid on water, a plume of steam rising from the crossing train. A sailboat slides underneath; the old world passing beneath the new. He painted this the summer Renoir and Manet were both dropping in, and the three of them spent days outdoors on the riverbank. The canvas is in the Philadelphia Museum of Art, part of the Mr and Mrs Carroll S. Tyson Jr collection.

Claude_Monet_-_The_Road_to_Vétheuil_-_Go.title: The Road to Vétheuil

source.canonical_title: File:Claude Monet - The Road to Vétheuil - Google Art Project.jpg
source.credit: 7wHPKlnfBc-apA at Google Cultural Institute maximum zoom level

Claude_Monet_-_The_Road_to_Vétheuil_-_Go.story: Monet painted at least five views looking back along this road toward Vétheuil, set up on the verge with the river behind him. This version is the bare-ground one, no snow, the poplars stripped, a figure on the path for scale. Duncan Phillips bought it for his Washington gallery in 1920 and it's been at the Phillips Collection ever since — one of the first Impressionist paintings to enter a public American museum.

Claude_Monet_-_The_Valley_of_the_Nervia..title: The Valley of the Nervia

source.canonical_title: File:Claude Monet - The Valley of the Nervia.jpg

Claude_Monet_-_The_Valley_of_the_Nervia..story: The Nervia cuts down from the Ligurian Alps to the sea at Ventimiglia, just across the French border from Menton. Monet painted this view during his 1884 Riviera campaign, drawn to the olive groves stacking up the valley walls in staggered silvers and greens. He complained in letters that the southern light 'drinks up' the colours, forcing him to mix pinks and blues he'd never have used in Normandy. The distant hills dissolve into lavender haze.

Claude_Monet_-_The_Water_Lilies_-_Clear_.title: Clear Morning with Willows
Claude_Monet_-_The_Water_Lilies_-_Clear_.description: Detail of Clear Morning with Willows of Monet's water lilies in the Musée de l'Orangerie

source.canonical_title: File:Claude Monet - The Water Lilies - Clear Morning with Willows - Google Art Project.jpg
source.credit: 7QHpOuLSwKTH8A at Google Cultural Institute maximum zoom level

Claude_Monet_-_The_Water_Lilies_-_Clear_.story: Two willow trunks split the water like dark pillars, with the pond glittering between them in dawn light. This is one of Monet's Grandes Décorations, the eight mural-scale Nymphéas he painted for France as a gift after the Armistice in 1918. He worked on them through cataracts and grief — his son Jean had died in 1914, Alice in 1911 — layering paint up to fifteen strokes deep. They were installed at the Orangerie in 1927, a few months after Monet's death.

Claude_Monet_-_The_Water_Lilies_-_Green_.title: Reflets verts

source.canonical_title: File:Claude Monet - The Water Lilies - Green Reflections - Google Art Project.jpg
source.credit: -wEwoHEvFukepQ at Google Cultural Institute maximum zoom level

Claude_Monet_-_The_Water_Lilies_-_Green_.story: Nearly twenty-six feet of canvas of almost nothing but green. No horizon, no bank, no sky — just reflected foliage and lily pads swimming in depth. Reflets verts hangs in the first oval room at the Orangerie, where Monet specified the curved walls and natural overhead light himself. He wanted viewers to feel submerged. The rooms opened on 17 May 1927, six months after his death from lung cancer at Giverny.

Claude_Monet_-_The_Water_Lilies_-_Mornin.title: Matin

source.canonical_title: File:Claude Monet - The Water Lilies - Morning - Google Art Project.jpg
source.credit: IAHgEdqp703amQ at Google Cultural Institute maximum zoom level

Claude_Monet_-_The_Water_Lilies_-_Mornin.story: Matin stretches more than forty feet across four joined panels in the Orangerie's first oval room. Pale pink blossoms drift against soft blue-green water, the willow's reflection swaying at the edges. Monet painted it in his huge new Giverny studio, built in 1915 specifically for these panels — a barnlike hangar with overhead skylights that horrified the locals. When President Clemenceau inaugurated the rooms in 1927, the press called it 'the Sistine Chapel of Impressionism.'

Claude_Monet_-_The_Water_Lilies_-_The_Cl.title: The Clouds

source.canonical_title: File:Claude Monet - The Water Lilies - The Clouds - Google Art Project.jpg
source.credit: YQEt9_UVgiL-Og at Google Cultural Institute maximum zoom level

Claude_Monet_-_The_Water_Lilies_-_The_Cl.story: One of the vast panels Monet built for his Grandes Décorations, the sprawling water lily cycle he dreamed of sinking viewers inside like a room made of pond. Here, the pond stops being water and becomes a mirror for sky: pale lavender clouds drift face-down across the surface, the lilies almost incidental. Monet was in his mid-seventies, his cataracts worsening, his son Jean recently dead. The painting now hangs in the first oval room of the Musée de l'Orangerie in Paris, where it stretches roughly 12.75 metres wide.

Claude_Monet_-_The_Water_Lilies_-_The_Tw.title: The Two Willows

source.canonical_title: File:Claude Monet - The Water Lilies - The Two Willows - Google Art Project.jpg
source.credit: 3AEQUJnQ8YnB_A at Google Cultural Institute maximum zoom level

Claude_Monet_-_The_Water_Lilies_-_The_Tw.story: The willows never appear as trees. Monet kept them offstage, letting their long green stripes fall into the pond as reflections while the real picture plane stays water, lilies, and drifting sky. It's one of eight panels he devoted to the Grandes Décorations at Giverny, working behind blackout curtains through the First World War with artillery audible from Paris. He signed the deed of gift the day after the Armistice in November 1918. The finished Deux saules panel runs 17 metres across the second oval room of the Orangerie.

Claude_Monet_-_The_Water_Lilies_-_Tree_R.title: Reflets d'arbres

source.canonical_title: File:Claude Monet - The Water Lilies - Tree Reflections - Google Art Project.jpg
source.credit: _QE0pUecImBBMQ at Google Cultural Institute maximum zoom level

Claude_Monet_-_The_Water_Lilies_-_Tree_R.story: A study for the Orangerie cycle, all verticals: dark tree reflections plunging straight down into the pond like ink dropped in milk. Monet started building his second, larger Giverny studio in 1915 just to house canvases like this one, some of them two metres tall. He painted standing on a platform with a cigarette usually going, dabbing on colour with brushes as long as his forearm. By the time he began the Grandes Décorations he'd been studying the same pond for thirteen years.

Claude_Monet_-_The_Windmill,_Amsterdam,_.title: The Windmill on the Onbekende Gracht, Amsterdam

source.canonical_title: File:Claude Monet - The Windmill, Amsterdam, 1871.jpg
source.credit: 1. Bridgeman Art Library : Object 129973 2. Museum of Fine Arts, Houston, online collection

Claude_Monet_-_The_Windmill,_Amsterdam,_.story: The old Zaandam mill ground coloured woods for yellow, red and blue dyes, right there on the Onbekende canal. Monet sketched it during his Dutch escape from the Franco-Prussian war in 1871 and worked it up later, at Argenteuil. Good thing he did. The mill was torn down in 1876, and the canvas now hangs at the Museum of Fine Arts, Houston.

Claude_Monet_-_Tulip_fields_in_Holland_(.title: Tulip fields in Holland

source.canonical_title: File:Claude Monet - Tulip fields in Holland (Musée d'Orsay).jpg
source.credit: The Yorck Project (2002) 10.000 Meisterwerke der Malerei (DVD-ROM), distributed by DIRECTMEDIA Publishing GmbH. ISBN : 3936122202 .

Claude_Monet_-_Tulip_fields_in_Holland_(.story: Red, yellow, and pink stripes of tulip run flat to a windmill on the horizon, with a ditch of blue sky doubled in the water up front. Monet spent about two weeks near Sassenheim in April and May 1886 at the invitation of a Dutch diplomat, and came home with five canvases. This one went to the Musée d'Orsay via the 1906 Camondo bequest.

source.canonical_title: File:Claude Monet - Vase of Tulips (14300279725).jpg
source.credit: Claude Monet - Vase of Tulips , Irina , 2014-05-29 23:25

Claude_Monet_-_View_of_Vétheuil.jpg.title: View of Vétheuil

source.canonical_title: File:Claude Monet - View of Vétheuil.jpg

Claude_Monet_-_View_of_Vétheuil.jpg.story: The summer of 1880 broke early and hot, and Monet responded with a burst of sun-filled canvases of Vétheuil and its gardens. This one shows the village from across the Seine, built up out of fragmented strokes of pure colour — jewel yellows, iridescent blue, a blood-red roof or two. The Metropolitan Museum of Art in New York bought it in 1956 and hangs it in Gallery 818.

Claude_Monet_-_Villas_à_Bordighera.jpg.story: Bordighera's villas pop out of Monet's 1884 canvases like sugar cubes in a jungle — pale ochre walls, red-tiled roofs, half-swallowed by date palms. He'd wangled access to the Moreno gardens and painted from inside the greenery looking out, chasing the moment a ray of sun hit stucco. He wrote Durand-Ruel that he'd need 'a palette of diamonds and jewels' to do the place justice. He settled for cadmium and cobalt.

Claude_Monet_-_Voir_le_d'Argenteuil_(187.title: View of Argenteuil - Snow

source.canonical_title: File:Claude Monet - Voir le d'Argenteuil (1874-75).jpg
source.credit: The Nelson-Atkins Museum of Art, Kansas City

Claude_Monet_-_Voir_le_d'Argenteuil_(187.story: A big snowfall has muffled Argenteuil. Dark silhouettes of travelers trudge toward the little pink railway station, their bodies almost cut from paper against the violet and lavender snow. Monet had been devouring Japanese prints, and you can see it in the flat shapes and the cool, strange palette. He sold this one at his own Hotel Drouot auction on March 24, 1875, listed simply as 'effet de neige.' It lives today at the Nelson-Atkins Museum of Art in Kansas City.

Claude_Monet_-_Vétheuil_-_Google_Art_Pro.title: Vétheuil

source.canonical_title: File:Claude Monet - Vétheuil - Google Art Project (427751).jpg

Claude_Monet_-_Vétheuil_-_Google_Art_Pro.story: A 1879 view of the village from across the Seine, sixty by eighty-one centimetres, painted in the nervous short strokes Monet was using during his hardest year. The water takes up almost half the canvas, churned into flickering horizontal dashes; the houses and church tower sit low on the far bank. This one made its way to Australia: it's now at the National Gallery of Victoria in Melbourne.

Claude_Monet_-_Vétheuil_en_hiver.jpg.title: Vétheuil in Winter

source.canonical_title: File:Claude Monet - Vétheuil en hiver.jpg

Claude_Monet_-_Vétheuil_en_hiver.jpg.story: The winter of 1878–79 was brutal on the Seine. Monet, short on cash and with a dying wife at home, hauled his gear out anyway and painted the ice floes grinding past Vétheuil. The medieval church tower on the far bank floats above a river flecked with pale blue and pink. He may have worked from his studio boat, a flat-bottomed skiff with just enough room for an easel. Dr Georges de Bellio, an early collector, snapped it up and wrote Monet in December 1879 that this canvas would never leave his hands. It now hangs at the Frick Collection in New York.

Claude_Monet_-_Water_Lilies,_1917-1919.j.title: Water Lilies

source.canonical_title: File:Claude Monet - Water Lilies, 1917-1919.JPG

Claude_Monet_-_Water_Lilies,_1917-1919.j.story: By 1917 Monet was seventy-seven, working on the huge Orangerie decorations and half-blind with cataracts he refused to have operated on. Around the big Grandes Décorations he also painted nineteen smaller square-format Nymphéas between 1917 and 1919, most of which he kept in the studio. Four went to the dealer Bernheim-Jeune in November 1919. Pond surface fills the entire canvas — no sky, no bank, just reflected clouds and blossoms floating free, an almost abstract window laid flat.

Claude_Monet_-_Water_Lilies_-_1906,_Ryer.title: Water Lilies

source.canonical_title: File:Claude Monet - Water Lilies - 1906, Ryerson.jpg

Claude_Monet_-_Water_Lilies_-_1906,_Ryer.story: A bruise of violet, a smear of rose, and the pads drift as if someone nudged the water a minute ago. Monet painted this at Giverny, working from a small flat-bottomed boat he'd had built specifically for the pond. He complained constantly in letters — the flowers wouldn't hold still, the light was all wrong, he'd scraped another canvas — and yet he kept at it. This one landed in Chicago via Martin A. Ryerson, a Gilded Age lumber heir who filled the Art Institute with French paintings before his death in 1932.

Claude_Monet_-_Waterlilies_-_Google_Art_.title: Waterlilies

source.canonical_title: File:Claude Monet - Waterlilies - Google Art Project.jpg
source.credit: EQEY9dAnBaXfnQ at Google Cultural Institute maximum zoom level

Claude_Monet_-_Waterlilies_-_Google_Art_.story: Look closely: the lily pads don't sit on the water, they sit in it, half-submerged, caught mid-float. Monet's trick here is the reflection — clouds and trees hover beneath the surface while the pads float above, so the eye can't tell up from down. He'd enlarged his lily pond twice by 1906, diverting water from the Ru (a branch of the Epte) despite protests from his Giverny neighbors, who were convinced his exotic plants would poison the local cattle.

Claude_Monet_-_Waterlilies_-_Google_Art_.title: Waterlilies

source.canonical_title: File:Claude Monet - Waterlilies - Google Art Project (hgEnPzjBK2STHg).jpg
source.credit: hgEnPzjBK2STHg at Google Cultural Institute , zoom level maximum

Claude_Monet_-_Waterlilies_-_Google_Art_.story: Green on green on green, with sudden violet shadows where the pads interrupt the sky. By 1907 Monet was painting the pond almost every day the weather allowed, chasing what he called the envelope — the shimmer of air between the motif and the eye. He'd had cataracts coming on for years, though he'd refuse surgery until 1923. Some scholars argue the deepening reds and murky greens of these late Nymphéas trace the progression of his failing vision.

Claude_Monet_-_Waterlilies_-_Nympheas_(1.title: Water Lilies

source.canonical_title: File:Claude Monet - Waterlilies - Nympheas (1908).jpg

Claude_Monet_-_Waterlilies_-_Nympheas_(1.story: A rounder, softer Nymphéas from the summer just before Monet left for Venice. The pads sit in loose rings on water the color of an overcast sky, with a few pink blossoms holding the middle. He'd nearly destroyed a whole group of these that year — scraped or slashed fifteen canvases he judged failures — before finally letting Durand-Ruel show the survivors at the 1909 exhibition, which sold out within days of opening.

Claude_Monet_-_Waterloo-Brücke_-_1903.jp.title: Waterloo Bridge. Effect of Fog

source.canonical_title: File:Claude Monet - Waterloo-Brücke - 1903.jpeg

title.fr: Le Pont de Waterloo. Effet de brouillard

Claude_Monet_-_Waterloo-Brücke_-_1903.jp.story: Waterloo Bridge sat directly across from Monet's Savoy suite, and he painted it roughly forty times. This one, now in the Hermitage, carries the date 1903 — meaning he'd hauled the unfinished canvas back to Giverny and kept pushing it long after the last London trip in 1901. Barges chuff past in muted orange and violet. The bridge dissolves into its own steam. Monet wrote that without the fog, London wouldn't be beautiful — and he only exhibited the Thames series in 1904, after four years of studio work.
Claude_Monet_-_Waterloo-Brücke_-_1903.jp.year_note: Filename indicates 1903 and the Hermitage/WikiArt catalogue this as 1903; input JSON had 1899.

Claude_Monet_-_Windmills_Near_Zaandam_-_.title: Windmills Near Zaandam
Claude_Monet_-_Windmills_Near_Zaandam_-_.description: Following his exile in England during the Franco-Prussian War (1870-71), Monet stopped in Zaandam, a picturesque town near Amsterdam, from May through October of 1871. During his stay, he painted about 20 small views of the town and its environs. In this example, a lone girl walks along the footpath between Oostzaan and Zaandam. By limiting the range of colors, Monet conveys the atmosphere of an overcast day. Similar muted colors were found in the works of the contemporary Netherlandish landscape painters known as The Hague school.

Claude_Monet_-_Windmills_Near_Zaandam_-_.story: After the Franco-Prussian War forced him into exile in London, Monet drifted home via Holland and stayed in Zaandam, a little Dutch town near Amsterdam, from May to October 1871. About twenty small views came out of it. Here a lone girl walks the footpath between Oostzaan and Zaandam under a gray, low sky; Monet dials the palette down to convey the damp, overcast air, echoes of the Hague School. Oil on canvas, 40.6 by 72.4 cm. Walters Art Museum, Baltimore, 37.894.

Claude_Monet_-_Woman_with_a_Parasol_-_Ma.story: Camille looks down at you from a low grassy rise, her white dress and veil snatched sideways by the wind. The parasol's green underside echoes the grass; little Jean stands further back, half in shadow. Monet painted the whole thing outdoors, chasing the summer sky. It went to the second Impressionist exhibition at Durand-Ruel's gallery in April 1876 and now hangs in the National Gallery of Art, Washington, a 1983 gift from Paul Mellon.

Claude_Monet_-_Église_de_Varengeville,_e.story: The little thirteenth-century sailors' church at Varengeville, perched on its cliff, bathed in early sun. Monet stumbled onto it by accident walking the coast in 1882 — and then painted it at least seven times. For this morning view he scrambled onto rocks only exposed at low tide, working fast while the tide was out. The church is still there, and still slipping: coastal erosion has been eating the cliff for a century. Part of a campaign that produced nearly a hundred canvases in one Normandy year.

Claude_Monet_-_Étretat,_The_Beach_and_th.title: Étretat: The Beach and the Falaise d'Amont

source.canonical_title: File:Claude Monet - Étretat, The Beach and the Falaise d'Amont - 1964.204 - Art Institute of Chicago.jpg

title.fr: Étretat: La Plage et la Falaise d'Amont

Claude_Monet_-_Étretat,_The_Beach_and_th.story: Dark dabs of beached fishing boats cluster on the pebbles, dwarfed by the green flank of the Falaise d'Amont rising at the right. Monet worked this view during a long, storm-haunted stay in February 1885, writing Alice Hoschedé about gales that nearly blew him off the shingle. The picture has lived at the Art Institute of Chicago since 1964, accession 1964.204.

Claude_Monet_021.jpg.title: Fishermen on the Seine at Poissy

source.canonical_title: File:Claude Monet 021.jpg
source.credit: The Yorck Project (2002) 10.000 Meisterwerke der Malerei (DVD-ROM), distributed by DIRECTMEDIA Publishing GmbH. ISBN : 3936122202 .

title.fr: Pêcheurs sur la Seine à Poissy
title.de: Fischer auf der Seine bei Poissy

Claude_Monet_021.jpg.story: Winter on the Seine at Poissy, where Monet had moved the household in December 1881. He hated Poissy — wrote that the town had nothing to offer a painter — but he still went out on the riverbank with his easel. A boat, a fisherman, bare trees, the water flat and grey. He'd be gone within two years, upstream to Giverny. In the meantime this 1882 canvas, now in Vienna's Belvedere, is a small act of professional stubbornness: paint the place anyway.

Claude_Monet_022.jpg.title: Jeanne-Marguerite Lecadre in the Garden Sainte-Adresse

source.canonical_title: File:Claude Monet 022.jpg

Claude_Monet_022.jpg.story: Jeanne-Marguerite Lecadre, the wife of Monet's better-off cousin Paul-Eugène, stands in a pale dress at the garden fence, a path of red geraniums and roses running away from her. Monet painted it outdoors at Le Coteau in Sainte-Adresse, the family's country place, in the summer of 1866. The handling is still tight and descriptive, years before he loosened into true impressionism. It hangs at the Hermitage in Saint Petersburg.
Claude_Monet_022.jpg.year_note: Hermitage dates this painting to 1866, not 1867.

Claude_Monet_023.jpg.title: Study of a Figure Outdoors: Woman with a Parasol, facing left
Claude_Monet_023.jpg.description: The pictured woman is Suzanne Hoschedé, daughter of Hoschedé, second wife of Claude Monet (1868-1899)

source.canonical_title: File:Claude Monet 023.jpg
source.credit: The Yorck Project (2002) 10.000 Meisterwerke der Malerei (DVD-ROM), distributed by DIRECTMEDIA Publishing GmbH. ISBN : 3936122202 .

Claude_Monet_023.jpg.story: A young woman on a grassy ridge, parasol tilted, dress and scarf snapping in the breeze so hard you can almost hear it. The sitter is Suzanne Hoschedé, Monet's future stepdaughter. He painted a companion version with her facing right the same summer of 1886. Both hang together at the Musée d'Orsay, and neither has a face — Monet left it deliberately blank.

Claude_Monet_029.jpg.title: The Fisherman's House, Varengeville, 1882

source.canonical_title: File:Claude Monet 029.jpg
source.credit: The Yorck Project (2002) 10.000 Meisterwerke der Malerei (DVD-ROM), distributed by DIRECTMEDIA Publishing GmbH. ISBN : 3936122202 .

Claude_Monet_029.jpg.story: One of the stone cabins above Varengeville, built in the Napoleonic era to watch for British ships and repurposed by fishermen as a storage shed. Monet turned it into a face: door for a mouth, two windows for eyes, orange roof ringing against the blue Channel behind. Painted in 1882 during his long Normandy campaign, it now hangs at Museum Boijmans Van Beuningen in Rotterdam. The cabin is tiny, the cliff enormous — and yet the composition lets the little house win.

Claude_Monet_044.jpg.title: Water-Lilies

source.canonical_title: File:Claude Monet 044.jpg
source.credit: 1. The Yorck Project (2002) 10.000 Meisterwerke der Malerei (DVD-ROM), distributed by DIRECTMEDIA Publishing GmbH. ISBN : 3936122202 . 2. [1]

Claude_Monet_044.jpg.story: Two metres square of pond and nothing else. Painted in 1916, this canvas puts you directly over the water, close enough that the lilies tilt toward your feet and the reflected willows plunge downward into unreachable green. It entered the collection of Japanese industrialist Kōjirō Matsukata, was sequestered by the French government during the Second World War, and finally arrived in Tokyo in 1959 as part of the founding gift to the National Museum of Western Art.

Claude_Monet_051.jpg.title: Stilleben mit Chrysanthemen

source.canonical_title: File:Claude Monet 051.jpg
source.credit: The Yorck Project (2002) 10.000 Meisterwerke der Malerei (DVD-ROM), distributed by DIRECTMEDIA Publishing GmbH. ISBN : 3936122202 .

Claude_Monet_051.jpg.story: An avid gardener even in his poorest years, Monet cranked out about twenty floral still lifes between 1878 and 1883 — they sold more reliably than landscapes. This bronze-and-copper pile of chrysanthemums is one of them, painted in 1878 on a 54-by-65 cm canvas. The brushwork is loose and quick; you can almost smell the wet stems. The Musée d'Orsay owns it.

Claude_Monet_052.jpg.title: Bouquet of Sunflowers

source.canonical_title: File:Claude Monet 052.jpg
source.credit: The Yorck Project (2002) 10.000 Meisterwerke der Malerei (DVD-ROM), distributed by DIRECTMEDIA Publishing GmbH. ISBN : 3936122202 .

Claude_Monet_052.jpg.story: A fat bouquet of sunflowers, pulled from the path outside his Vétheuil door, stuffed into a Chinese vase and painted fast. The paint goes on thick enough to cast its own shadows, ridges of yellow catching the real light in the room. When Monet showed it at the 1882 Impressionist exhibition, critics praised the brio. Years later Van Gogh saw it in Paris and wrote home that Monet's sunflowers were something to beat. The Met acquired it in 1929 from the Havemeyer bequest.

Claude_Monet_Camille_au_métier.jpg.title: Camille at the Loom

source.canonical_title: File:Claude Monet Camille au métier.jpg

Claude_Monet_Camille_au_métier.jpg.story: Monet lugged the easel inside for this one. Camille sits bent over her embroidery loom on a veranda, surrounded by potted greenery, light leaking in from the side and flickering across the front of her dress in little white strokes. It's a quiet borrowing from the 17th-century Dutch interiors that were back in vogue in Paris. Painted in 1875, 'Madame Monet Embroidering' now belongs to the Barnes Foundation in Philadelphia.

Claude_Monet_Le_bateau_atelier.jpg.title: The Studio Boat

source.canonical_title: File:Claude Monet Le bateau atelier.jpg

Claude_Monet_Le_bateau_atelier.jpg.story: Monet painted himself at work inside the cabin of his studio boat, brush in hand, Camille reading beside him, sunlight skidding across the water outside. Art historians flag this 1876 canvas as a turning point: he couldn't possibly have painted the scene purely from observation, so he's stepping, consciously, past strict plein-air Impressionism. The painting is in the Barnes Foundation in Philadelphia.

Claude_Monet_Nympheas_1915_Musee_Marmott.title: Water Lilies
Claude_Monet_Nympheas_1915_Musee_Marmott.description: Seerosen 1915 Öl auf Leinwand 130 x 153 cm

source.canonical_title: File:Claude Monet Nympheas 1915 Musee Marmottan Paris.jpg

Claude_Monet_Nympheas_1915_Musee_Marmott.story: Not a decoration, not a commission, just Monet alone with the pond in 1915 while the war ground on a hundred kilometres east. The lilies cluster on a surface where violet, green, and dusk-blue keep trading places, and the horizon is missing entirely. He was seventy-four and had just lost his stepdaughter Suzanne's husband at the front. The painting reached the Musée Marmottan in Paris through the 1993 bequest of Annie Rouart, and measures 130 by 153 centimetres.

Claude_Monet_The_Cliffs_at_Etretat.jpg.title: The Cliffs at Etretat

source.canonical_title: File:Claude Monet The Cliffs at Etretat.jpg

Claude_Monet_The_Cliffs_at_Etretat.jpg.story: Two great chalk headlands shoulder into a pale sea, the famous Manneporte arch cut clean through the farther one like a keyhole. Monet's strokes are short and dry here, the kind of brushwork that makes the cliff face feel actually crumbly. The painting now hangs at the Clark Art Institute in Williamstown, Massachusetts, donated by Sterling and Francine Clark in 1955.

Claude_Monet_The_Duck_Pond.jpg.title: The Geese

source.canonical_title: File:Claude Monet The Duck Pond.jpg
source.credit: 1. Unknown source Unknown source 2. Clark Art Institute

Claude_Monet_The_Duck_Pond.jpg.story: A pond, a few startled geese, the water a shudder of green and grey. Despite the English title 'The Duck Pond', Monet called these birds geese and they belong to the Argenteuil years, when he was painting his own backyard as if it were a world. Quick, wet brushwork. The whole thing feels painted in the minute before a bird takes off.

Claude_Monet_Vetheuil_01.jpg.title: Vétheuil

source.canonical_title: File:Claude Monet Vetheuil 01.jpg

Claude_Monet_Vetheuil_01.jpg.story: Painted in 1880, the year Monet finally started pulling out of the Vétheuil years. The village sits on the far bank of the Seine, its cluster of roofs and church tower mirrored in water that Monet has worked into dozens of tiny broken reflections. The canvas is almost square, sixty by eighty centimetres. It now lives at the Kelvingrove Art Gallery and Museum in Glasgow.

Claude_Monet_Water_Lilies_1908.jpg.title: Water-Lilies

Claude_Monet_Water_Lilies_1908.jpg.story: The surface reads like marbled paper: pale blue, silver, a whip of green, and the pink flowers almost shy, tucked between pads. 1908 was the year Monet's eyesight started seriously failing — he'd been seeing yellow-brown casts on everything — and also the year he finally made peace with leaving the pond unfinished. He'd sometimes stop mid-stroke and mutter that the water was the only thing he could still paint, because it was allowed to be vague.

Clearing_Sky_after_Snow,_Kannon_Temple,_.story: Fresh snow on the red pagoda and lantern at Asakusa's Sensō-ji, a few bundled figures crossing the precinct, the sky washing clean. Hasui caught Tokyo between eras — still pre-war, still full of wooden temples — in soft, layered woodblock printings that somehow feel wetter and colder than photographs. This one belongs to his Twenty Views of Tokyo series, published in 1926.

Cleopatra_and_Caesar_by_Jean-Leon-Gerome.story: The moment Plutarch describes: Cleopatra, smuggled into Caesar's quarters rolled in a carpet, unfurls herself at his feet. Caesar looks up from his papers, startled. A Nubian attendant watches from behind. Gérôme painted it in 1866, and the California banker Darius Ogden Mills bought it in the 1870s; the Mills family kept it for more than a century before it went to a private collector in 1990. The carpet-smuggling scene is a favourite of film, but Gérôme got there first.

source.canonical_title: File:Cliffs at Pourville A21450.jpg

Cliffs_at_Pourville_A21450.jpg.story: Monet worked the Pourville cliffs in 1882 as if running a science experiment on weather — same chalk wall, same tideline, different hour, different sky. Here the cliff shoulders in from the left, grass fizzing along its spine, the sea flat and pale below. He often juggled up to eight canvases in a single day, chasing the light from one to the next. One small village, one summer, roughly a hundred paintings. This is one of them.

Climbing_on_Mt._Fuji.jpg.story: This is the odd one out. Every other print in the series frames Fuji from a distance; here you're inside the mountain, hauling yourself up its flank. Pilgrims in white jackets pick their way over the rocks with wooden staffs. Others huddle in a cave, out of the wind, waiting for sunrise. No summit, no symmetry, no postcard view. The Japanese title is Shojin tozan, roughly 'pilgrims ascending'.

Confusion_of_Tongues_(89393754).jpg.story: Genesis 11. Work on the tower has just stopped: masons argue with words that don't line up anymore, God's shadow looms, the unfinished bricks stand against a brightening sky. Doré frames it as a thwarted engineering project as much as a theological event — scaffolding, pulleys, a crane mid-lift. It's one of the strongest plates in the 1866 Bible and a go-to image whenever anyone needs a picture of Babel, which turns out to be often.

Constable_-_Seascape_Study_with_Rain_Clo.title: Seascape Study with Rain Cloud ( Rainstorm over the Sea )

source.canonical_title: File:Constable - Seascape Study with Rain Cloud.jpg

Constable_-_Seascape_Study_with_Rain_Clo.story: A fast oil sketch, probably done at Brighton around 1824 while Constable's tubercular wife Maria was taking sea air. Almost no detail: a scrape of beach, two dark specks for a boat, and above them a shelf of storm cloud dragging a grey curtain of rain into the Channel. He worked these studies straight on paper, outdoors, chasing the weather. Maria would die four years later. The picture, barely bigger than a placemat at around 22 by 33 centimetres, is in the Royal Academy of Arts in London.

Constable_Salisbury_meadows.jpg.title: Salisbury Cathedral from the Meadows
Constable_Salisbury_meadows.jpg.description: en:Salisbury Cathedral from the Meadows by en:John Constable .

Constable_Salisbury_meadows.jpg.story: Constable called this one 'the Great Salisbury' and considered it his most important painting. He exhibited it at the Royal Academy in 1831, three years after Maria's death, with a black storm rolling over the cathedral and a hay wagon fording the river in the foreground. The rainbow arching to the spire seems to have been added later, probably after Archdeacon John Fisher, Constable's closest friend, died in 1832. A line from Thomson's 'The Seasons' hung beside it in the catalogue. The Tate acquired it for the nation in 2013.

source.canonical_title: File:Cornard Wood.png
