title.nl: Gezicht op Cornard Wood, bij Sudbury, Suffolk

Cornard_Wood.png.story: Gainsborough was twenty-one, newly back in Suffolk, and painting the woods he'd walked since boyhood. Cornard Wood is not a grand commission, just a tangle of oaks, a donkey, a peasant gathering sticks, a pond catching the sky. He later said he had 'very early from a little boy' imitated every hedge and tree he saw, and this painting shows it: the leaves feel handled rather than staged. It is the earliest surviving landscape he was proud of, the sort of thing he would rather have done all day than flatter another duchess.

Cornelia_Vetterlein.jpg.title: Portrait of Cornelia Vetterlein (1811-1862)

source.canonical_title: File:Cornelia Vetterlein.jpg

Cornelia_Vetterlein.jpg.story: Cornelia Vetterlein was sixteen when Stieler painted her in 1828 for Ludwig I's Gallery of Beauties. The daughter of an Upper Franconian state councillor and granddaughter of a Bayreuth court gardener, she gets something most of the gallery's women don't: a background. A castle stands behind her, meant to signal constancy. She wears the gentle uniform of the series, pale shoulders, dark ringlets, steady gaze, and later married into the Künsberg barony. One of thirty-six, painted to be compared.

Cornelis_Cornelisz._van_Haarlem_-_The_Fa.title: The Fall of Ixion.

source.canonical_title: File:Cornelis Cornelisz. van Haarlem - The Fall of Ixion - Google Art Project.jpg

Cornelis_Cornelisz._van_Haarlem_-_The_Fa.story: Ixion tried to seduce Hera. Zeus tricked him with a cloud-double, caught him mid-grope, and strapped him to a fiery wheel that would spin forever through the underworld. Cornelis van Haarlem paints the plunge: muscled limbs knotted into impossible angles, the wheel already burning. It's Haarlem Mannerism at full throttle, anatomy twisted for display rather than plausibility. Painted in 1588, the same year the Spanish Armada sank.

Cornelis_Cornelisz._van_Haarlem_-_The_Fa.title: The Fall of the Titans

source.canonical_title: File:Cornelis Cornelisz. van Haarlem - The Fall of the Titans - Google Art Project.jpg
source.credit: 2AEcYz8BknPYRg at Google Cultural Institute maximum zoom level

Cornelis_Cornelisz._van_Haarlem_-_The_Fa.story: A heap of rebel gods tumbling out of the sky, limbs tangled like a wrestling match that forgot which way was up. Cornelis treats the defeat of the Titans as an anatomy showcase, each buttock and bicep polished to porcelain. The figures barely fit the frame. It was painted in 1588 for the Prinsenhof in Haarlem, part of a series celebrating Dutch civic power through pagan myth.

Cornelis_Cornelisz_van_Haarlem_-_Een_mon.title: A monk and a nun [ 3 ]

source.canonical_title: File:Cornelis Cornelisz van Haarlem - Een monnik en een begijn - 1590.jpg

title.nl: Een monnik die in de borst van een begijn knijpt [ 2 ]

Cornelis_Cornelisz_van_Haarlem_-_Een_mon.story: A Franciscan in a grey habit slides one hand under a beguine's bared breast while the other gestures, eyes locked on hers; she half-smiles, beads dangling, eyes cast down. On the table: a glass of red wine, grapes, pears, a split pomegranate, a bread roll. Every symbol in the still life is doing anticlerical work. A 1591 Haarlem satire on the Catholic clergy, painted when Cornelis was in his late twenties and the northern Netherlands had just gone Calvinist.

Cornelis_de_Vos_-_El_triunfo_de_Baco.jpg.title: The Triumph of Bacchus
Cornelis_de_Vos_-_El_triunfo_de_Baco.jpg.description: The Triumph of Bacchus and Ariadne

source.canonical_title: File:Cornelis de Vos - El triunfo de Baco.jpg

Cornelis_de_Vos_-_El_triunfo_de_Baco.jpg.story: A grossly fat, pink Bacchus lolls on a gilded chariot pulled by two snarling tigers, waving a tambourine, crowned in vine leaves. A blonde nymph props him up; a goat-legged satyr leers behind; on the right an elderly Silenus slumps face-down against his donkey while a putto grabs at grapes. De Vos painted it as part of Philip IV's mythological cycle for the Torre de la Parada hunting lodge outside Madrid, following designs supplied by Rubens, and it still hangs in the Prado.

Corner_in_Voyer-d'Argenson_Park_at_Asnie.title: Square Saint-Pierre, Paris / Lane in Voyer d'Argenson Park at Asnieres

source.canonical_title: File:Corner in Voyer-d'Argenson Park at Asnières by Vincent van Gogh.jpeg

Corner_in_Voyer-d'Argenson_Park_at_Asnie.story: Summer 1887, the public park at Asnieres just outside Paris. Van Gogh painted several views here on outings with Bernard and Signac — allees, couples, bright grass. This one closes in on a quiet corner: a path turning between trees, dappled light, a small figure or two. The brushwork is already loose and directional, colour divided cleanly. It is the Van Gogh of Paris at his most un-Dutch, almost pastoral, pulling Impressionist technique toward something more personal.

Correggio,_Ritratto_di_dama,_c.1517-1518.title: Correggio, Ritratto di dama, c.1517-1518
Correggio,_Ritratto_di_dama,_c.1517-1518.description: Ritratto di dama , Olio su tela, 102 x 86 San Pietroburgo, Hermitage Il secondo periodo della vita del Correggio si apre con l’esecuzione, tra il 1517 e il 1520, di un’opera di elevata raffinatezza stilistica ma alquanto enigmatica: il Ritratto di dama (variamente identificata in Veronica Gambara o Ginevra Rangoni ), firmato con la colta latinizzazione del suo nome: Anton(ius) Laet (us)

source.canonical_title: File:Correggio, Ritratto di dama, c.1517-1518.jpg

Correggio,_Ritratto_di_dama,_c.1517-1518.story: A young woman in a broad silver-braided snood sits before a laurel or ivy thicket, steady-eyed and faintly smiling, holding a dark bowl in her lap. White lawn sleeves puff against a brown bodice; a view opens to blue hills on the right. The identification swings between Veronica Gambara and Ginevra Rangoni, and the picture is one of Correggio's rare secular portraits — signed with the Latin pun 'Antonius Laetus,' Antonio the Glad. Painted around 1517-18, at the start of his Parma years, it's now at the Hermitage in St Petersburg.

Correggio_-_Leda_and_the_Swan_-_Google_A.title: Leda and the Swan

source.canonical_title: File:Correggio - Leda and the Swan - Google Art Project.jpg

Correggio_-_Leda_and_the_Swan_-_Google_A.story: Correggio painted Leda and the Swan around 1530-32 for Federico II Gonzaga of Mantua, probably as a gift for Emperor Charles V — one of a set of Loves of Jupiter. The picture has had a rough life. In the 18th century, Louis, son of the Regent of France, decided Leda's expression of pleasure was obscene and took a knife to her face. The canvas was stitched back together and her head repainted three separate times, most recently by Jakob Schlesinger in 1830. It now hangs in Berlin's Gemäldegalerie, a masterpiece you are always looking at through other people's retouching.

Countess_Siemontkowsky_Bystry_by_Vigee_l.title: Portrait of Countess Siemontkowsky Bystry
Countess_Siemontkowsky_Bystry_by_Vigee_l.description: Exhibitor: Adam Williams Fine Art Ltd Portrait of the Countess Siemontkowsky Bystry (NOTE: no such noble family in Poland) In 1789 after fleeing France following the Parisian mobs march on Versailles, Vigée Le Brun set out for Italy on what would turn out to be twelve years of exile from France. There Count Wilczek, the Austrian ambassador to Milan, suggested she move to Vienna. Upon her arrival in 1792, she was warmly received in aristocratic circles, and she quickly received numerous commissions from distinguished Polish and Austrian nobles. This portrait of Countess Bystry is a wonderful example of the portraits she produced in Vienna.

source.canonical_title: File:Countess Siemontkowsky Bystry by Vigee le Brun.jpg

title.de: Bildnis von La comtesse Siemontkowsky Bystry
title.fr: Portrait de la comtesse Siemontkowsky Bystry
title.nl: Portret van La comtesse Siemontkowsky Bystry

Countess_Siemontkowsky_Bystry_by_Vigee_l.story: One of many commissions Vigée Le Brun took on during her flattering reception in Vienna, where Austrian and Polish nobles queued up after her 1792 arrival. The countess — Anna Rakowska, on her second marriage — is posed as Hebe, cupbearer of the gods, holding a goblet with the painter's signature warm and powdery palette. The family name "Siemontkowsky Bystry" has since puzzled researchers: no such Polish house is recorded, suggesting a transcription tangle somewhere along the way.

Courbet_-_L'Hallali_du_cerf.jpg.title: The kill of deer
Courbet_-_L'Hallali_du_cerf.jpg.description: It's a painting by Gustave Courbet in Museum of Fine Arts of Besançon. It's an oil on canvas of 11 x 16 ft. (355 x 505 cm)

source.canonical_title: File:Courbet - L'Hallali du cerf.jpg

Courbet_-_L'Hallali_du_cerf.jpg.story: A stag crashes to its knees in the snow, overwhelmed by hounds, the huntsman's horn about to sound the death-call — the hallali. Courbet worked on this monster through the winter of 1866–67; it's nearly seventeen feet wide, a scale the academy reserved for saints and Napoleons. Giving that treatment to a dying deer was, predictably, provocative. It hung at the Salon of 1869 and now lives at the Musée des Beaux-Arts et d'Archéologie de Besançon.

source.canonical_title: File:Courbet - The Sailboat (Seascape), c. 1869.jpg

Courbet_Autoportrait.jpg.title: Self-Portrait with Pipe
Courbet_Autoportrait.jpg.description: It is a relatively popular image of him; three copies were made​​. It shows him smoking pot, which was taboo at the time.

source.canonical_title: File:Courbet Autoportrait.jpg

title.avk: Ayikye dem plo, mivdelt (trutca ke Courbet)

Courbet_Autoportrait.jpg.story: Courbet at about thirty, head cocked, eyes half-lidded, pipe drooping from red lips: the picture of Bohemian swagger. He painted it in 1848 and 1849, a pivotal moment when he was inventing Realism and about to scandalize the Salon with The Stonebreakers and A Burial at Ornans. In a letter to his patron Alfred Bruyas he called the sitter 'the portrait of a fanatic, an ascetic, a man disillusioned with the stupidities that served as his education.' It hangs today at the Musée Fabre in Montpellier.

Courtyard_with_Lunatics_by_Goya_1794.jpg.title: Courtyard with Lunatics or Yard with Madmen
Courtyard_with_Lunatics_by_Goya_1794.jpg.description: In one of his letters, Goya describes the painting: "a yard with lunatics, in which two nude men fight with their warden beating them... [it is a scene I saw in Zaragoza]." [1]

source.canonical_title: File:Courtyard with Lunatics by Goya 1794.jpg
source.credit: The Meadows Museum's Permanent Collection , accessed 2010-03-20.

Courtyard_with_Lunatics_by_Goya_1794.jpg.story: Two naked men wrestle on the stone floor while a keeper rains down blows with a stick. Others huddle, rock, or stare into the middle distance. High walls trap the heat and the screams; a single shaft of sunlight slants in from above. Goya painted this small tin-backed panel in 1793–94, while recovering from the illness that left him deaf. He told a friend it showed "a yard with lunatics" he had seen himself in Zaragoza. It's one of the first works where the nightmare begins to leak in.

Cranach_Madonna_under_the_fir_tree.jpg.title: Madonna under the fir tree.

source.canonical_title: File:Cranach Madonna under the fir tree.jpg

Cranach_Madonna_under_the_fir_tree.jpg.story: Commissioned around 1510 for Wrocław Cathedral and hung there for over four centuries in the Chapel of St John — one of Cranach's most elaborate Madonnas, the fir tree a nod to Silesian landscape. It survived the Reformation, two world wars, and an astonishing act of thievery: in 1946 the priest hired to restore the damaged panel had a forgery made and slipped the real picture out to Berlin. The swap was only caught in 1960. The original finally came home to Wrocław in 2012 and hangs in the Archdiocesan Museum.

Cristo_en_casa_de_Marta_y_María,_by_Dieg.title: Kitchen Scene with Christ in the House of Martha and Mary
Cristo_en_casa_de_Marta_y_María,_by_Dieg.description: Jesus at the home of Martha and Mary

source.canonical_title: File:Cristo en casa de Marta y María, by Diego Velázquez.jpg

title.es: Cristo en casa de Marta y María

Cristo_en_casa_de_Marta_y_María,_by_Dieg.story: A young maid grinds garlic with a scowl, her fist red from work, while an older woman points over her shoulder to a framed scene of Christ scolding Martha for bustling. Velázquez was maybe nineteen when he painted this in Seville, already showing off the trick that would make him famous, a kitchen made of paint so thick you could eat the fish. The chili pepper on the table is one of the earliest in European art, painted around 1618.

Crossing_the_River_Styx.jpg.title: Crossing the River Styx

source.canonical_title: File:Crossing the River Styx.jpg

title.es: El paso de la laguna Estigia

Crossing_the_River_Styx.jpg.story: Patinir's most ambitious invention: a soul in Charon's little boat, drifting down the middle of the panel, forced to choose. To the left, a luminous Christian paradise with angels and bright sky; to the right, a smoking Hell with Cerberus at the gate and fires licking the hills. The figure leans toward Hell — a detail scholars have chewed on for a century. Mythology and Christianity yoked together without apology. The Prado bought it in 1933; it's arguably the single most important painting Patinir left behind.

Crow_and_blossom_by_Ohara_Koson.jpg.title: Crow and blossom by Ohara Koson
Crow_and_blossom_by_Ohara_Koson.jpg.description: Woodblock print by Ohara Koson (1887-1945) of a crow and blossom

source.canonical_title: File:Crow and blossom by Ohara Koson.jpg
source.credit: Woodblock print circa 1910 by Ohara Koson (1877-1945)

Crow_and_blossom_by_Ohara_Koson.jpg.story: A crow grips a thin cherry twig, head turned, one blue-clawed foot lifted. The blossoms are almost theatrical against the grey-green ground, and a few petals tumble past the bird's chest. Koson made hundreds of these bird-and-flower prints for Watanabe's studio, aimed squarely at the American export market that had fallen for Hokusai a generation earlier. This one has the restraint of his earlier Koson signature period: no gimmicks, just a heavy bird on a light branch.

Cult-of-beauty-001.jpg.story: Joanna Hiffernan again, this time in profile at a mantelpiece in Chelsea, examining a Japanese fan, her reflection floating in the mirror behind her. Whistler painted it in 1864 and kept fiddling with it for years. It's quieter than the first 'White Girl', more intimate, the white made of pinks and lilacs and greys when you actually look. The poet Swinburne wrote a sonnet about it that Whistler had pasted to the frame. It hangs at Tate Britain.

Dance-At-Bougival.jpg.story: A man in a yellow straw hat whirls his partner across a cafe terrace, her red bonnet tipping back, a cigarette butt and a bouquet trampled at their feet. Renoir painted the pair in 1883; the woman is Suzanne Valadon, then an eighteen-year-old model who would become a serious painter herself and the mother of Utrillo. Her partner is likely Paul Lhote, a journalist friend. The canvas is in the Museum of Fine Arts, Boston, bought in 1937.

Danceringreen.jpg.title: Danceringreen

source.canonical_title: File:Danceringreen.jpg

Danceringreen.jpg.story: Four dancers caught mid-pirouette on a green-lit stage, viewed from a box seat above, so the floor tilts up like a plate. One adjusts her shoulder strap, the others blur into motion. Degas worked the composition in pastel over monotype in 1877-79, showing it at the fourth Impressionist exhibition in 1879. It now hangs at the Thyssen-Bornemisza in Madrid.

Daniel_in_the_Lion's_Den_c1615_Peter_Pau.title: Daniel in the Lions' Den

source.canonical_title: File:Daniel in the Lion's Den c1615 Peter Paul Rubens.jpg
source.credit: 1. Web Gallery of Art : Image Info about artwork wga QS:P11807,"r/rubens/15biblic/07daniel" 2. National Gallery of Art, Washington D.C.

Daniel_in_the_Lion's_Den_c1615_Peter_Pau.story: Nine lions, life-size, drawn from beasts Rubens watched in the menagerie of the Archdukes in Brussels. Daniel kneels at dawn, hands clasped, rolling his eyes to heaven while the pride yawns and stretches around him, unbothered. Rubens kept the canvas for himself and later traded it to the English ambassador Dudley Carleton in 1618 for a pile of antique marbles. It passed through Charles I's collection and Blenheim Palace before the National Gallery of Art in Washington bought it in 1965. The painting is roughly three metres wide.

Dans-la-prairie-by-Claude-001.jpg.title: Dans la prairie
Dans-la-prairie-by-Claude-001.jpg.description: painting of the French artist's wife, Camille, reading in a meadow full of flowers. It was first exhibited in Paris in 1877.

source.canonical_title: File:Dans-la-prairie-by-Claude-001.jpg

Dans-la-prairie-by-Claude-001.jpg.story: Camille lies full-length in a field of wildflowers, a book held up to her face, her striped dress half-swallowed by the blooms. Signed 'Claude Monet 76' in the lower right, it was painted at Argenteuil and shown at the third Impressionist exhibition in April 1877. After a stint on loan to the National Gallery in London, it went under the hammer at Christie's London in February 2009.

Dans_la_forêt_de_Fontainebleau_1866.jpg.story: Renoir hauled his paints into the Fontainebleau forest in 1866 and painted what Corot and the Barbizon crowd had been painting for decades — but already you can see him fidgeting against their formula. The browns are warmer, the brushwork looser, sunlight breaks through the canopy in broken flecks instead of smooth washes. He was 25 and starting to bend the rules. Just three years later he'd paint La Grenouillère and burn them down entirely.

David_Brutus.jpg.title: The Lictors Bring to Brutus the Bodies of His Sons

source.canonical_title: File:David Brutus.jpg

David_Brutus.jpg.story: David exhibited this six weeks after the storming of the Bastille, and Paris read it instantly. Lucius Junius Brutus, founder of the Roman Republic, has just condemned his own sons to death for plotting to restore the monarchy. The lictors carry the bodies in from the right; Brutus sits rigid in shadow beneath a statue of Roma, his toes clenched, a decree gripped in his fist. His wife and daughters break down in full light. The Revolution had its icon of civic duty over family, finished on cue.

David_Wilkie_Chelsea_Pensioners_Reading_.title: Chelsea Pensioners Reading the Waterloo Dispatch

source.canonical_title: File:David Wilkie Chelsea Pensioners Reading the Waterloo Dispatch.jpg

David_Wilkie_Chelsea_Pensioners_Reading_.story: Wellington commissioned this in August 1816, barely a year after Waterloo, and Wilkie took six years to finish it. Veterans gather at a table outside the Duke of York pub in Chelsea while one reads aloud from the Waterloo Gazette — the dispatch Wellington had sent from the battlefield. When it went on show at the Royal Academy in 1822 the crowds were so dense that a protective rail had to be installed, the first time such a measure had been needed. Genre painting, not history painting, had suddenly delivered the nation's grandest public image of victory.

David_with_the_Head_of_Goliath-Caravaggi.story: The head David holds up by the hair is Caravaggio's own — older, bruised, mouth still open as if mid-curse. He painted it around 1609-10, a fugitive in Naples after killing a man in a Roman tennis-court brawl, and sent it to Cardinal Scipione Borghese in Rome as a plea for the papal pardon that would let him come home. He died on the coast at Porto Ercole before the pardon reached him. The painting hangs in the Galleria Borghese today.

De_Gion_brug_te_Hondo_in_Amakusa_Amakusa.story: A small, perfect scene on the Amakusa islands off Kyushu: a woman crosses the Gion bridge with a bundle of vegetables under her arm, pausing to watch ducks on the river below. Selected Views of Japan, 1924 — a reminder that his travel series was as much about ordinary errands as famous temples.

De_humani_corporis_fabrica_(24).jpg.title: On the Fabric of the Human Body, Plate 24

source.canonical_title: File:De humani corporis fabrica (24).jpg

De_humani_corporis_fabrica_(24).jpg.story: A plate from the muscle-man sequence of Vesalius's Fabrica, printed in Basel in 1543. Fourteen flayed figures strike theatrical, almost balletic poses through the book, losing a layer of musculature in each successive woodcut, so that the reader watches a single body progressively undressed. The letters scattered across the torso key to the anatomical text on the facing page. The drawings are usually attributed to a pupil of Titian.

De_humani_corporis_fabrica_(25).jpg.title: On the Fabric of the Human Body, Plate 25

source.canonical_title: File:De humani corporis fabrica (25).jpg

De_humani_corporis_fabrica_(25).jpg.story: Another of the fourteen muscle figures from Vesalius's 1543 Fabrica. Line them up in the order they're printed and the hills behind them join edge to edge into one continuous landscape — the Euganean Hills south of Padua, where Vesalius taught anatomy. Nobody noticed the panorama until the early twentieth century. The figures strut through it like actors who've forgotten they're being dissected.

De_humani_corporis_fabrica_(26).jpg.title: On the Fabric of the Human Body, Plate 26

source.canonical_title: File:De humani corporis fabrica (26).jpg

De_humani_corporis_fabrica_(26).jpg.story: From the same Padua muscle sequence, a few layers deeper. By this point in the Fabrica the skin and superficial muscles are gone; what's left are the deep attachments, the body becoming architectural. Vesalius was twenty-eight when the book came out, a Flemish anatomist who had insisted, against centuries of Galenic deference, on cutting the bodies himself. The woodblocks were cut in Venice and shipped over the Alps to Basel for printing.

De_humani_corporis_fabrica_(27).jpg.story: Another plate from the 1543 muscle-man series. The pose is deliberate — ecorche figures were expected to stand like antique statues, as if the dignity of the ancient body survived its own flaying. The Fabrica's 200-odd woodcuts, probably drawn by someone trained in Titian's workshop, turned medical illustration from schematic diagram into art, and every anatomical atlas since has been arguing with it.

De_pruimenboomgaard_te_Kameido-Rijksmuse.story: A single plum branch shoves itself right across the foreground, black and clawed, while a pink fog of blossom sprawls behind it and the sky burns red to green. The tree — called Garyūbai, the "reclining dragon" — was a real celebrity at the Kameido shrine outside Edo. Hiroshige printed it in 1857 as sheet 30 of One Hundred Famous Views of Edo. Thirty years later Van Gogh copied it in oils, keeping the audacious crop and even trying to letter the Japanese characters.

title.nl: Zittende vrouw naast een vaas chrysanten

Degas,_A_Woman_Seated_beside_a_Vase_of_F.story: An early Degas, painted when he was still finding his subject. The flowers - great shaggy asters and dahlias in a green vase - take up most of the canvas; the woman, pushed hard to the right edge, is almost an afterthought, chin on hand, looking away. The museum's label hedges on whether she is Madame Valpinçon, a childhood friend's wife. What matters is the off-centre composition, borrowed from Japanese prints and totally novel in 1865, and the sense that the real portrait is of the bouquet, with a human being for scale.

Delacroix-Marc_Aurèle-MBA-Lyon.jpg.story: Marcus Aurelius on his deathbed in 180 AD, commending his son Commodus to a circle of Stoic philosophers who already look like they know how that will turn out. Delacroix began it in 1843 while ill himself, left his pupil Louis de Planet to lay in the underpainting, then finished it the following year. The gloom is unusually heavy for him — more Poussin than Romantic fireworks. Musée des Beaux-Arts, Lyon.

Delaunay_ChampDeMars.jpg.title: Champs de Mars: The Red Tower
Delaunay_ChampDeMars.jpg.description: Graphic Champs de Mars: La Tour Rouge . 1911 - 1923 , Robert Delaunay . Oil on canvas. The Art Institute of Chicago .

source.canonical_title: File:Delaunay ChampDeMars.jpg

title.nl: Champs de Mars: de rode toren

Delaunay_ChampDeMars.jpg.story: The most famous of Delaunay's towers, started in 1911 and reworked as late as 1923 (he inscribed both dates on the stretcher, along with the phrase 'epoque destructive'). The tower pushes up through flanking apartment blocks in furnace reds and oranges, winglike clouds slicing past the summit. When he painted it, the real Eiffel Tower was still its original red-brown. Delaunay exaggerates the colour until the structure almost burns, then frames it with cool grey Haussmann façades tipped into multiple viewpoints at once. It entered the Art Institute of Chicago in the Winterbotham bequest and is arguably the single image that sells Orphism to modern eyes.

Delftsedonderslag.jpg.story: On 12 October 1654 the Delft gunpowder magazine exploded and took a quarter of the city with it. Van der Poel, who lost his young daughter in the blast, painted the aftermath more than twenty times. This version looks across the flattened northeast quarter toward the still-standing towers of the Oude and Nieuwe Kerk, under a heavy, bruised sky. In the foreground, survivors pick through rubble and a body lies half-covered in the dirt. The sky gets the whole top half of the picture - the real subject is the awful quiet that comes after.

Descente_de_croix_rubens.jpg.title: Descent from the Cross
Descente_de_croix_rubens.jpg.description: Peter Paul Rubens (1577-1640), Descent from the Cross, ca. 1617-18 St. Petersburg, Hermitage

source.canonical_title: File:Descente de croix rubens.jpg

Descente_de_croix_rubens.jpg.story: Another Descent, this one from about 1617 to 1618, a tauter, smaller cousin of the Antwerp altarpiece. Christ's body slumps across the white shroud in a single diagonal, Mary's face floods with grief, and a workman in red grips the corner of the cloth with his teeth. The panel ended up in Catherine the Great's Hermitage, where it still hangs in Saint Petersburg.

Despair_Edvard_Munch_1894.jpeg.title: Despair
Despair_Edvard_Munch_1894.jpeg.description: This is a painting featuring a figure standing on a bridge, gazing down, seemingly lost in thought. The background consists of a dramatic, swirling sky with striking red, yellow, and blue colors. The figure is dressed in dark clothing, and their posture and the expression on their face convey a sense of melancholy or introspection. The contrast between the vibrant sky and the subdued figure adds to the emotional impact of the scene. The artwork has an expressive, somewhat abstract style, characteristic of Edvard Munch's work.

Destruction_of_Leviathan.png.story: Isaiah 27: the Lord with his great and strong sword shall punish leviathan. Doré delivers the scene at maximum voltage — a serpent coiling through churned sea, a sword-bearing figure blazing down out of storm light. Engraved by H. Pisan for the 1866 Tours edition of the Bible, the project that made Doré a household name in English-speaking homes as well as French ones. Heavy-metal album covers owe this plate a royalty check.

Die_landschaft_mit_den_drei_baeumen.jpg.story: The most famous etched landscape in European art, and everything in it is weather. Three oaks hunch on a ridge on the right; on the left, rain sluices down in diagonal streaks over dimpled water; a tiny fisherman crouches on the bank, a couple of lovers nearly vanish into the grass. In the middle distance, Amsterdam's skyline broods under a break in the cloud. Rembrandt made it in 1643 with etching, drypoint and engraving all on one plate, and never made another print like it.

Don_Juan_by_Eugène_Delacroix.jpg.story: Straight out of Byron's poem: Don Juan and the other shipwreck survivors, adrift in the Mediterranean, drawing lots to decide who gets eaten. Delacroix gives us the moment the slip of paper is pulled — faces half in shadow, the sea a low green heave, sails gone. It is Géricault's Raft of the Medusa channelled through literature rather than journalism, and it has hung in the Louvre since 1883.

Don_Quijote_illustrated_by_Gustav_Dore_I.story: One of roughly 370 drawings Doré made for the 1863 French edition of Cervantes — the set that fixed Don Quixote's look for everyone who came after. Before drawing, he traveled La Mancha, sketching the dust, the inns, the bone-dry plains. What he brought back was a landscape with weight to it, Quixote a skinny silhouette lost in sweeping light. Disney animators, John Huston, every later illustrator — they were all working from Doré's template, whether they admitted it or not.

Dong_Yuan_rivers_detail.jpg.story: A detail from a tenth-century handscroll associated with the Southern Tang master Dong Yuan, now in Beijing's Palace Museum. You see the ingredients of the tradition he invented almost all at once: a bank of reeds in the foreground, a tiny boat with two figures, low wooded islets, and behind them hills built up from Dong's soft 'hemp-fibre' strokes - feathery, repetitive, almost dry. The silk has darkened to a warm tea colour over a thousand years. Later literati painters would look at exactly this kind of quiet riverbank and copy it for centuries.

Dore,_Gustave;_La_Sainte_Trinite.jpg.story: A nineteenth-century oil on board, roughly 63 by 51 centimetres, in which Dore copies a Rubens Trinity of around 1620 now in Antwerp. Dore made his fortune in wood engraving but painted all his life, often working after the old masters he'd been forced to reduce to black ink for mass-market Bibles and Dantes. Here he gets to keep Rubens's flesh and colour. Bequeathed to the Glynn Vivian Art Gallery in Swansea in 1911.

Dore-I_had_done_a_hellish_thing.jpg.story: Plate for the 1876 edition of Coleridge's Rime of the Ancient Mariner — the moment after the bird falls. Doré puts the sailor in the crows-nest, ratlines around him, the crossbow still in his hand, and leaves the albatross offstage. The sea below is vast and unbothered, which is the point: the Mariner has just crossed a line and the universe hasn't noticed yet. That edition sold out and went through thirty printings in twenty-five years.

Dragomirov_by_Repin.jpg.story: Dragomirov was the empire's most quotable general — a Suvorov scholar who commanded Russian troops crossing the Danube in 1877, ran the Nikolaev Academy, and was famous for plainspoken lectures arguing that morale and the bayonet mattered more than firepower. Repin paints him seated, in uniform, medals and all, but unstiffened: shrewd, tired eyes, a face that has done a lot of talking. It's one of a long run of portraits Repin turned out in the late 1880s of people he admired or was fascinated by — Tolstoy, Stasov, Mussorgsky on his deathbed — where the point was psychological fix rather than official likeness.

Duchess_of_Polignac_by_E.Vigee-Lebrun_(1.title: Yolande-Martine-Gabrielle de Polastron, Duchess de Polignac

source.canonical_title: File:Duchess of Polignac by E.Vigee-Lebrun (1787, Atheneum).jpg

title.fr: Yolande-Martine-Gabrielle de Polastron, duchesse de Polignac

Duchess_of_Polignac_by_E.Vigee-Lebrun_(1.story: Yolande de Polastron, Duchess de Polignac, was Marie Antoinette's closest friend and governess to the royal children — a position that made her one of the most resented women at court. Vigée Le Brun painted her more than once; this 1782 version, now at the Wadsworth Atheneum, dresses her as a courtier-shepherdess in the straw hat the queen's circle made fashionable. Warm light catches the face, the pose is relaxed almost to the point of informality, and the whole thing is calculated to look like it wasn't calculated at all.

source.canonical_title: File:Durer-ecureuil.jpg

Durer-ecureuil.jpg.story: Dürer kept a kind of menagerie on paper — a hare, a stag beetle, a roller's wing, this pair of red squirrels. He painted them on vellum in watercolor and gouache, one gnawing a hazelnut, the other alert, tail curled overhead like a question mark. The fur is built up whisker by whisker. He was about forty when he made it, at the height of his powers, working for his own study rather than any commission. The Albertina in Vienna holds it now, in a drawer that only opens on occasion — vellum and daylight don't mix.
Durer-ecureuil.jpg.year_note: Input year 1492 is unsupported. The Albertina and Wikipedia give 1512; 1492 would predate Dürer's mature nature-study practice and his use of signed vellum watercolors. 1512 is consistent with the Wing of a Roller and other late nature studies.

Duse_by_Repin.jpg.story: Eleonora Duse was then the most famous actress in Europe — d'Annunzio's muse, rival to Sarah Bernhardt, and notorious for refusing stage makeup. She was touring Russia in the winter of 1891 when Repin caught her. He worked in charcoal on a huge canvas, over 100 by 139 cm — almost life-size — and got her in a long dark dress, standing, hand at her chin. The sittings were short and reportedly tense; what he wanted was presence, not likeness. The drawing hangs in the Tretyakov and is usually cited as one of his best charcoal portraits of a sitter who barely sat.

Dürer_-_Académie_de_femme_debout,_de_dos.title: Academic Study of a Standing Woman, Seen from Behind

source.canonical_title: File:Dürer - Académie de femme debout, de dos, la main sur une hampe d'où part un voile, INV 19058, Recto.jpg

Dürer_-_Académie_de_femme_debout,_de_dos.story: Dürer had just come back from his first Italian trip and was trying to teach himself what Italian painters learned from live models — a discipline the German workshops didn't use. So he drew this woman from behind, standing, one hand gripping a pole from which a veil trails. Brush and pen on paper, barely larger than a sheet of notebook paper. The back and legs are rendered with real weight; the hair and drapery he flicked in almost as afterthought. It's a private sheet, the kind of drawing an artist makes when nobody has commissioned anything and he just wants to get better.

Dürer_-_Hieronymus_Holzschuher_(1469-152.story: Hieronymus Holzschuher was fifty-seven, a Nuremberg patrician and senator, when Dürer painted him in 1526 — one of a small group of late portraits of city fathers that also included Jakob Muffel and Johann Kleberger. Oil on linden panel, 51 by 37 cm, with a slide-on wooden cover that once protected the surface. The white curls corkscrew, the pale blue eyes cut straight out of the panel, the fur collar so specific you can count the guard hairs. Dürer inscribed HIERONIMVS HOLTZSCHVER ANNO DO[MI]NI 1526 ETATIS SVE 57 in the upper left. It hangs in the Berlin Gemäldegalerie.

E.V.Pavlov_by_Repin.jpg.story: Evgueni Pavlov was one of Russia's pioneering surgeons — a specialist in antiseptic technique who later treated Alexander III after the Borki train crash. Repin had personal reasons to paint him: his own wife Vera was in Pavlov's care for a liver ailment, and his student Veryovkina was being treated there for a broken arm. Repin sketched in the operating theater itself. He gives Pavlov in a white apron, hands working over the patient under the clinic lights, assistants ringed around — a documentary painting in the same realist spirit as Thomas Eakins' Gross Clinic, though less theatrical. Russian Museum, St. Petersburg.

E1924-3-16-pma2018.jpg.title: E1924-3-16-pma2018

source.canonical_title: File:E1924-3-16-pma2018.jpg

E1924-3-16-pma2018.jpg.story: A quiet bend of the Epte, the little tributary that threaded through Monet's Giverny property and fed the pond he'd later remake into a water garden. He painted this stretch of riverbank in 1888, with poplars and willows packed into a nearly abstract wall of greens. No figures, no weather event, no story — just the painter standing in the grass working out how water, leaves, and reflected sky fit together. It hangs in Philadelphia.

EL_JALEO-SINGER.jpg.title: The Ruckus (El Jaleo)

source.canonical_title: File:EL JALEO-SINGER.jpg
source.permission: Copyright has expired since it was registered in 1925 ( [1] ; registration number G76006)

EL_JALEO-SINGER.jpg.story: A dancer leans back mid-stamp while a row of musicians claps and growls along the wall behind her. Sargent had traveled through Spain in 1879 sketching flamenco in smoky tavernas, and he worked the canvas up at full length, nearly eleven feet wide, for the Salon of 1882. Isabella Stewart Gardner so adored it that she built a Moorish arch in her Boston museum specifically to frame it, where it still glares out at visitors today.

Eakins,_Thomas_-_Wrestlers_1899.jpg.title: Wrestlers

source.canonical_title: File:Eakins, Thomas - Wrestlers 1899.jpg
source.permission: Image source: Los Angeles County Museum of Art (LACMA) Image Library . LACMA has released this image as a " Public Domain High Resolution Image". Attribution is requested (see LACMA's terms of use ).

Eakins,_Thomas_-_Wrestlers_1899.jpg.story: Two wrestlers locked on the mat - one pinning, one pinned, faces squeezed sideways against the canvas-covered floor. In the background a rower works a sliding seat on a board, another figure stands off to the right in a loose jock. Eakins painted this at 55, three years after a 1899 photo session he arranged at a Philadelphia gym, and treated the grappling hold with the same forensic eye he brought to dissections. No drama, no flattery: just two male bodies under load, the low brown light of a working gym, muscle and vein reported exactly as seen.

Edgar_Degas_-_At_the_Races_in_the_Countr.story: Degas paints his friend Paul Valpinçon at the races near Argentan, but the horses don't matter. What matters is the baby. Paul's infant son Henri sleeps in the nurse's arms under a parasol, while the family bulldog stares out bored. The carriage gets sliced in half by the frame, a trick borrowed from Japanese prints and photography. He showed it at the first Impressionist exhibition in 1874.

Edgar_Degas_-_The_Orchestra_at_the_Opera.title: The Orchestra at the Opera.

source.canonical_title: File:Edgar Degas - The Orchestra at the Opera - Google Art Project 2.jpg
source.credit: Google Art Project: Home - pic Maximum resolution.

Edgar_Degas_-_The_Orchestra_at_the_Opera.story: Degas painted his bassoonist friend Désiré Dihau front and center, then filled the pit around him with other musicians who actually played there too, a private joke among Paris Opéra regulars. Above the stage lights, the ballerinas get decapitated by the frame, reduced to pink tulle legs. The painting was finished around 1870 and started Degas on the ballet subject that would consume the rest of his career.

Edgar_Germain_Hilaire_Degas_004.jpg.title: Ballettprobe

source.canonical_title: File:Edgar Germain Hilaire Degas 004.jpg
source.credit: The Yorck Project (2002) 10.000 Meisterwerke der Malerei (DVD-ROM), distributed by DIRECTMEDIA Publishing GmbH. ISBN : 3936122202 .

Edgar_Germain_Hilaire_Degas_004.jpg.story: A rehearsal room, not a stage. Dancers yawn, scratch, adjust a shoe while the ballet master taps his stick. Degas loved the backstage more than the performance, the moment before the illusion hardens. Morning light slides in from tall windows and catches dust. He painted this around 1873, one of dozens of rehearsal scenes he built in the studio from memory and hired models rather than life.

Edinburgh_NGS_Singer_Sargent_Lady_Agnew..title: Portrait of Lady Agnew of Lochnaw (1865-1932)
Edinburgh_NGS_Singer_Sargent_Lady_Agnew..description: Lady Agnew's direct gaze and informal pose, emphasised by the flowing fabric and lilac sash of her dress ensure the portrait's striking impact.

source.canonical_title: File:Edinburgh NGS Singer Sargent Lady Agnew.JPG
source.permission: photographical reproduction in the public domain

Edinburgh_NGS_Singer_Sargent_Lady_Agnew..story: Gertrude Agnew sinks sideways into a flowered bergere and fixes you with a look that is part amused, part appraising, as if she has already decided what she thinks of you. Sargent painted her in about six sittings in 1892, and you can feel the speed: the white chiffon sleeves are little more than flicks of loaded brush, the lilac sash drags in one wet stroke. After the Madame X disaster in Paris he needed London society to trust him again, and this canvas, shown at the Royal Academy, did the job. It made Lady Agnew famous and made Sargent the portraitist everyone wanted.

Edmund_Blair_Leighton_-_Abelard_and_his_.title: Abelard and his Pupil Heloise
Edmund_Blair_Leighton_-_Abelard_and_his_.description: Edmund Blair Leighton - Abelard and his Pupil Heloise .

source.canonical_title: File:Edmund Blair Leighton - Abelard and his Pupil Heloise.jpg

Edmund_Blair_Leighton_-_Abelard_and_his_.story: A book lies open between them, but neither is reading. Peter Abelard, the most feared logician in 12th-century Paris, has been hired to tutor his landlord's brilliant niece Heloise. You can see where this is going. Leighton paints the hush just before scandal: the careful distance, the slipped glance, the candle doing its work. History fills in the rest. Their affair produced a son, a secret marriage, a horrifying mutilation ordered by Heloise's uncle, and some of the most scorching love letters in medieval literature. Leighton exhibited this at the Royal Academy in 1882.

Edmund_Blair_Leighton_-_In_Time_of_Peril.title: In Time of Peril

source.canonical_title: File:Edmund Blair Leighton - In Time of Peril - Google Art Project.jpg
source.credit: 9gF4Die6xd2HeQ at Google Cultural Institute maximum zoom level

Edmund_Blair_Leighton_-_In_Time_of_Peril.story: A nun's robe hides a noblewoman and her infant; the prioress turns them toward a staircase as armed men pound at the gate. Leighton builds the whole drama out of fabrics, the rough wool of the sisters against the silks still peeking from the fugitives' sleeves. Is it the Wars of the Roses? The English Civil War? He deliberately keeps it vague so the tension does the talking. Exhibited at the Royal Academy in 1897.

Edmund_Blair_Leighton_-_My_Next-Door_Nei.title: My Next-Door Neighbour

source.canonical_title: File:Edmund Blair Leighton - My Next-Door Neighbour.jpg

Edmund_Blair_Leighton_-_My_Next-Door_Nei.story: Two Georgian gardens, one shared wall, and a conversation you could time with a sundial. She leans on the parapet with a book; he leans from his side with his hat off. Nothing is happening and everything is. Leighton specialized in these flirtations-in-slow-motion, where a glove, a ribbon, or the angle of a shoulder does more work than a speech would. Painted in 1894, when Regency revival was in full swoon across English parlors.

Edmund_Blair_Leighton_-_Ribbons_and_Lace.title: Ribbons and Laces for Very Pretty Faces

source.canonical_title: File:Edmund Blair Leighton - Ribbons and Lace.jpg

Edmund_Blair_Leighton_-_Ribbons_and_Lace.story: The full title is the street-seller's cry: "Ribbons and laces for very pretty faces." A peddler has set down his tray in a sunlit courtyard and two young women are rummaging through it while a third hangs back, already in love with something. Leighton dates the costumes to the Regency and lights the whole scene like a candy-shop window. Painted 1902.

Edmund_Blair_Leighton_-_The_Dedication_(.title: The Dedication
Edmund_Blair_Leighton_-_The_Dedication_(.description: (See source) « The Dedication is an important rediscovery in Edmund Blair Leighton 's oeuvre . Known only through a black and white photogravure published in 1908 it has not appeared on the open market for over seventy-five years. [...]»

source.canonical_title: File:Edmund Blair Leighton - The Dedication (1908).jpg
source.credit: Christie's , LotFinder: entry 5755480 (sale 1177, lot 49, London, King Street, 12 December 2013)

Edmund_Blair_Leighton_-_The_Dedication_(.story: A Templar kneels at a country altar, sword held out flat in both hands, asking a blessing on the steel before he rides to war. His lady kneels beside him, eyes closed, hands folded. Leighton loads the chapel with tapestries and stained glass so the light does the praying. Shown at the Royal Academy in 1908 and bought out of the show by a Captain Mendoza, it then vanished into private hands for over seventy years.

Edmund_Blair_Leighton_-_The_Elopement_-_.title: The Elopement

source.canonical_title: File:Edmund Blair Leighton - The Elopement - 1893.jpg

Edmund_Blair_Leighton_-_The_Elopement_-_.story: A rope ladder, a waiting horse, and a bride-to-be swinging one slippered foot over the sill. Leighton loved this kind of breath-held moment, and he rigged it for maximum suspense: her lover steadies her, a servant holds the lantern low, and somewhere in the house a father is still asleep. The 18th-century costume dates the runaway couple with satisfying precision, down to the buckled shoes. He showed it at the Royal Academy in 1893.

Edmund_Blair_Leighton_-_The_End_of_the_S.title: The End of the Song
Edmund_Blair_Leighton_-_The_End_of_the_S.description: [...] Although The End of the Song illustrates no specific incident in history or literature, it recalls two well-known literary subjects, Tristram and Iseult and Paolo and Francesca . [...] (Christie's)

source.canonical_title: File:Edmund Blair Leighton - The End of the Song (1902).jpg

Edmund_Blair_Leighton_-_The_End_of_the_S.story: A lute has just gone quiet in a tower chamber; the singer and his listener are still looking at each other. Leighton said the painting illustrated no specific story, but anyone who knew their Dante or their Malory filled in Paolo and Francesca, or Tristan and Iseult, without being asked. The Christie's catalogue makes exactly that point. 1902, oil on canvas.

Edmund_Blair_Leighton_-_The_Hostage.jpg.title: Edmund Blair Leighton - The Hostage

source.canonical_title: File:Edmund Blair Leighton - The Hostage.jpg

Edmund_Blair_Leighton_-_The_Hostage.jpg.story: An aristocratic young woman stands at the center of a group of very polite captors, everyone pretending this is a civilized arrangement. Leighton's genius was staging coercion without violence: the guards' hands rest on sword hilts, a retainer offers her a cup, and the whole room is a negotiation frozen mid-sentence. Painted in 1912, a decade before his death and deep in the Edwardian appetite for chivalric tableaux. Oil on canvas.

Edouard_Manet_-_At_the_Café_-_Google_Art.title: At the Café

source.canonical_title: File:Edouard Manet - At the Café - Google Art Project.jpg
source.credit: GgEZL0iu5Gl9FA at Google Cultural Institute maximum zoom level

Edouard_Manet_-_At_the_Café_-_Google_Art.story: Boulevard de Rochechouart, Brasserie Reichshoffen, around 1878-79. A top-hatted man nurses a beer, a woman in a peach bonnet turns to meet your eye, another waits for service. Manet went there often and sketched on the spot; the looseness is Frans Hals by way of a noisy bar. Behind them a mirror doubles the room and the ambient chatter. The woman's direct stare is the old Manet trick: you are not watching the scene, you are in it, being watched back.

Edouard_Manet_-_Olympia_-_Google_Art_Pro.title: Olympia
Edouard_Manet_-_Olympia_-_Google_Art_Pro.description: This is a derivative work based on the Google Art Project image (see gallery below). The flesh tone has been warmed.

source.canonical_title: File:Edouard Manet - Olympia - Google Art Project 3.jpg
source.credit: Google Art Project: Home - pic Maximum resolution. Colours edited by uploader

Edouard_Manet_-_Olympia_-_Google_Art_Pro.story: Manet painted her in 1863 but waited until the 1865 Salon to unleash her, and Paris lost its mind. A nude courtesan stares straight back at you, one hand planted firmly where a goddess would demure, a black ribbon at her throat, a startled cat at her feet. Critics called her a gorilla and a Queen of Spades; guards had to hang the canvas high to keep walking sticks from reaching it. She was modeled on Victorine Meurent. The flesh in this particular file has been warmed by a later editor.

Edouard_Manet_-_The_Plum_-_National_Gall.title: The Plum

source.canonical_title: File:Edouard Manet - The Plum - National Gallery of Art.jpg

Edouard_Manet_-_The_Plum_-_National_Gall.story: A young woman sits alone at a pink marble café table, chin in hand, an unlit cigarette between her fingers and a brandy-soaked plum untouched in its little glass. She's dreamy, not miserable. The model is again Ellen Andrée, and the painting reads as Manet's reply to Degas's bleaker L'Absinthe of the year before. He first painted a beer in that glass, then changed his mind. The date is around 1877. Paul Mellon gave it to the National Gallery of Art in 1971.

Edouard_Manet_031.jpg.title: At the Père Lathuille Restaurant

source.canonical_title: File:Edouard Manet 031.jpg
source.credit: The Yorck Project (2002) 10.000 Meisterwerke der Malerei (DVD-ROM), distributed by DIRECTMEDIA Publishing GmbH. ISBN : 3936122202 .

title.ru: У папаши Латюиля, на открытом воздухе

Edouard_Manet_031.jpg.story: Terrace of the restaurant Père Lathuille's, near the Clichy tollgate. A well-dressed woman has almost finished her lonely lunch when a young man in a beige suit leans in from behind, one arm around her chairback, eyes locked on hers. He's Louis Gauthier-Lathuille, the owner's son, and he turned up to pose in his dragoon's uniform before Manet made him change. She is smiling. The original female sitter was Ellen Andrée, who dropped out and was replaced by Mlle French. It hangs in Tournai.

Edouard_Manet_Boating.jpg.title: Boating

source.canonical_title: File:Edouard Manet Boating.jpg

Edouard_Manet_Boating.jpg.story: Summer 1874, Gennevilliers. Manet was crossing the Seine to visit Monet and Renoir at Argenteuil and came back with this: a boater in a flat straw hat, white shirt pulled tight across his back, steering a skiff whose varnished wood cuts one hard diagonal across a sheet of cobalt water. The sailor is Manet's brother-in-law Rodolphe Leenhoff. The cropping and flat planes are Japanese prints at work. The Salon of 1879 called it the last word in painting. It's at the Met.

Edvard_Munch,_1893,_The_Scream,_oil,_tem.title: The scream of nature

source.canonical_title: File:Edvard Munch, 1893, The Scream, oil, tempera and pastel on cardboard, 91 x 73 cm, National Gallery of Norway.jpg
source.credit: National Museum of Art, Architecture and Design

Edvard_Munch,_1893,_The_Scream,_oil,_tem.story: Munch wrote it down before he painted it. Walking a path above Oslo with two friends one evening, he felt suddenly tired and stopped. The sun was setting, the clouds over the fjord turned blood red, and he sensed — his words — a scream passing through nature. This is the National Museum version, the one he worked up in oil, tempera and pastel on a piece of cardboard. Up in the sky, in a tiny pencil inscription, someone (probably Munch himself) has written in Norwegian: 'Can only have been painted by a madman.' The two companions walk on, oblivious, along the rail of the path.

Edvard_Munch,_1922,_Starry_Night,_Munch_.title: Starry Night

source.canonical_title: File:Edvard Munch, 1922, Starry Night, Munch Museum, Oslo.jpg

Edvard_Munch,_1922,_Starry_Night,_Munch_.story: This isn't the famous 1893 Starry Night. By 1922 Munch had retreated to Ekely, his property on the edge of Kristiania, and spent the deep winter evenings at the top of his veranda steps painting the sky above his own garden. It belongs to a short, concentrated run of blue-tinted night pictures made between 1922 and 1924: same veranda, same railing, same hill, the stars placed like pinpricks over a snowfield. He was almost sixty, already deaf in one ear from an old hemorrhage, painting essentially alone. The silence is the subject.
Edvard_Munch,_1922,_Starry_Night,_Munch_.year_note: Munch Museum and Artsy date this Ekely Starry Night 1922-1924; 1923 used as the midpoint of the campaign.

Edvard_Munch_-_Bathing_Men_(Ateneum).jpg.title: Bathing Men

source.canonical_title: File:Edvard Munch - Bathing Men (Ateneum).jpg

Edvard_Munch_-_Bathing_Men_(Ateneum).jpg.story: Summer 1907, Warnemünde on the Baltic. Munch had moved into the quarters of a harbor pilot named Carl Nielsen and spent his days at the local nudist beach, painting the bathers at something like life size: the canvas is over two metres tall. Three men walk straight out of the surf toward the viewer, sunburn-ruddy, frankly naked, unapologetic. He conceived the picture as the central panel of an Ages of Life triptych flanked by youth and old age, and exhibited it that way in Helsinki in 1911. It scandalised viewers, then the Ateneum bought it anyway.

Edvard_Munch_-_Jealousy_-_MM.M.00864_-_M.title: Jealousy

source.canonical_title: File:Edvard Munch - Jealousy - MM.M.00864 - Munch Museum.jpg

Edvard_Munch_-_Jealousy_-_MM.M.00864_-_M.story: Munch came back to jealousy obsessively, painting the scene no fewer than eleven times over his lifetime. The setup is always the same: a green-faced man stares straight out at us in the foreground while behind him a woman in red offers an apple to another man, Eve and her suitor glimpsed over the cuckold's shoulder. This 1913 version from the Munch Museum turns the colour up; the man's complexion has gone almost gangrenous. The woman is usually read as Dagny Juel Przybyszewska, the woman Munch's friend Stanisław married, and whose name hangs over half his love pictures.
Edvard_Munch_-_Jealousy_-_MM.M.00864_-_M.year_note: MM.M.00864 is dated 1913-1915 by the Munch Museum; 1913 is the accepted start date and matches the filename.

Edvard_Munch_-_The_Brooch._Eva_Mudocci_-.title: The Brooch. Eva Mudocci

source.canonical_title: File:Edvard Munch - The Brooch. Eva Mudocci - Google Art Project.jpg

Edvard_Munch_-_The_Brooch._Eva_Mudocci_-.story: Eva Mudocci was a British violinist touring Europe with the pianist Bella Edwards when Frederick Delius introduced her to Munch in Paris. In 1903 Munch had the lithographic stone hauled up to her hotel room and drew her directly on it, long black hair spilling over her shoulders, one brooch pinned at the neck. He sent her a note along with the print: "Here is the stone that has fallen from my heart." The image earned her the nickname Madonna in Munch's circle. She kept the original stone for the rest of her life.

Edvard_Munch_-_Train_Smoke_-_Google_Art_.title: Train Smoke

source.canonical_title: File:Edvard Munch - Train Smoke - Google Art Project.jpg

Edvard_Munch_-_Train_Smoke_-_Google_Art_.story: A plume of white smoke drags across the Bunne Fjord south of Kristiania, softening into the winter air as if the train itself had already passed out of the frame. Munch painted this in 1900 from the Nordstrand side, the same stretch of coast that gave him Winter at Nordstrand and The Island. The brushwork is looser than the anguished 1890s work, more lyrical: lines roll in rhythmic bands, the water answers the sky. It's a Munch with no figures and no scream, just industrial breath hanging in a fjord.

Edvard_Munch_-_Two_Human_Beings_(The_Lon.title: Two Human Beings (The Lonely Ones)

source.canonical_title: File:Edvard Munch - Two Human Beings (The Lonely Ones) (1906-08).jpeg

Edvard_Munch_-_Two_Human_Beings_(The_Lon.story: Munch first painted this pair in 1892, then lost the canvas in 1901 when the ship carrying his exhibition exploded at sea. He kept the image alive in prints, famously a woodcut where he sawed the block into three pieces, one for the man, one for the woman, one for the beach and sky, inking each separately. This oil from 1906-08 rebuilds the composition from those prints, which is why the figures face the opposite way from the lost original. A man and a woman stand on the shore, shoulders almost touching, looking out. Nothing passes between them.
Edvard_Munch_-_Two_Human_Beings_(The_Lon.year_note: Dated 1906-08 by the Munch Museum; midpoint used.

Edvard_Munch_-_Vampire_(1895)_-_Google_A.title: Vampire

source.canonical_title: File:Edvard Munch - Vampire (1895) - Google Art Project.jpg

Edvard_Munch_-_Vampire_(1895)_-_Google_A.story: Munch called it Love and Pain. The vampire reading came later, courtesy of his friend the Polish critic Stanisław Przybyszewski, who saw a man submissive under a biting woman and never let the title go. Look at the picture itself and it's ambiguous on purpose: a red-haired woman leans into a man's neck in what could be a kiss, a consolation, or a bite. Munch worked the motif in six versions between 1893 and 1895, oils and prints, each one tuning the embrace a little differently. The name stuck because it was more marketable than tenderness.

Edvard_Munch_-_Weeping_Nude_-_Google_Art.title: Weeping Nude

source.canonical_title: File:Edvard Munch - Weeping Nude - Google Art Project.jpg

Edvard_Munch_-_Weeping_Nude_-_Google_Art.story: A woman kneels on a bed, head sunk into her hands, body turned in on itself. Munch painted her in 1913-14, one year before the war, in drenched carmine and cinnabar that pool across the coverlet like a blood-warm tide. Nobody knows who she is or what she is crying about. Softer pinks and yellow-greens push in from the edges of the room, almost kind, but the red refuses to let her up. He kept the canvas himself, and it stayed in Oslo with the rest of his estate after he died.
Edvard_Munch_-_Weeping_Nude_-_Google_Art.year_note: Munch Museum dates the canvas 1913-1914; corrected to 1914 as the completion year.

Edward_Hopper_-_Night_Shadows_-_Oct_1922.title: Edward Hopper - Night Shadows - Oct 1922 Shadowland
Edward_Hopper_-_Night_Shadows_-_Oct_1922.description: Etching "Night Shadows" by Edward Hopper, on page 23 of the October 1922 Shadowland .

source.canonical_title: File:Edward Hopper - Night Shadows - Oct 1922 Shadowland.jpg
source.credit: Shadowland (Sep. 1922 - Feb. 1923) on the Internet Archive

Edward_Hopper_-_Night_Shadows_-_Oct_1922.story: Hopper was nearly forty, still making his living as a commercial illustrator, and etching — not oil — was where he first found his subject. In Night Shadows, a single figure walks a pool of lamplight on an otherwise empty street, seen from an upper-window vantage that turns the viewer into a watcher. The composition already contains everything he would do in paint a decade later: isolation, geometric shadow, a whiff of menace. The plate was steel-faced for high-volume printing, and an impression was reproduced in Shadowland magazine in October 1922.

El_Beso_(Pinacoteca_de_Brera,_Milán,_185.title: The Kiss

source.canonical_title: File:El Beso (Pinacoteca de Brera, Milán, 1859).jpg
source.credit: Web Gallery of Art : Image Info about artwork wga QS:P11807,"s-e.html?/html/h/hayez/6hayez"

El_Beso_(Pinacoteca_de_Brera,_Milán,_185.story: A man in a plumed hat tilts a woman back against a stone step and kisses her as if the carriage is waiting. Her blue silk puddles onto the floor; his red tights flare like a flag. The shadow on the stair hints at someone lurking off to the left. Italians read it as a goodbye between a patriot and his sweetheart on the eve of war with Austria. Hayez painted it in 1859, the year French and Piedmontese troops marched into Lombardy. It now hangs in the Pinacoteca di Brera.

El_Greco_-_Christ_as_Saviour_-_Google_Ar.title: Christ as Savior
El_Greco_-_Christ_as_Saviour_-_Google_Ar.description: The work shows Jesus Christ as the Savior of the world, and is part of the Apostolate painted by El Greco that is preserved in the Museum of El Greco in Toledo .

source.canonical_title: File:El Greco - Christ as Saviour - Google Art Project.jpg
source.credit: JwG7tm_-gzOwJQ at Google Cultural Institute , zoom level maximum

El_Greco_-_Christ_as_Saviour_-_Google_Ar.story: El Greco ran a busy Toledo workshop at the end of his life painting sets of the twelve apostles for churches and private patrons. This Salvador, dated between 1610 and his death in 1614, is the head of one such Apostolado, now at the Museo del Greco in Toledo. Christ faces us frontally in the old Byzantine manner of El Greco's Cretan youth, right hand raised in blessing, left hand resting on the terra orbis. He's the only figure in the whole series who looks straight out; the apostles are painted turned toward him. The canvas is signed, and more carefully finished than any apostle beside it.
El_Greco_-_Christ_as_Saviour_-_Google_Ar.year_note: Museo del Greco dates the Salvador/Apostolado 1610-1614; 1612 used as the midpoint, and El Greco died in 1614 so the supplied year coincided with his death year.

El_Greco_View_of_Toledo.jpg.title: View of Toledo

source.canonical_title: File:El Greco View of Toledo.jpg

El_Greco_View_of_Toledo.jpg.story: One of only two surviving landscapes from El Greco, and unlike anything else in Spanish painting before it. The sky is doing the actual work here — a bruised, electric green-black shot through with broken cloud — while Toledo crouches below on its hill, rearranged from reality so the Alcázar and cathedral sit where he wanted them, not where they stood. The city becomes a state of mind rather than a survey. Painted around 1596-1600, late in his Toledo years, it reads less like a view than like weather pushed through a Byzantine icon: flat, charged, and slightly hallucinatory.

El_Jardín_del_Amor_(Rubens).jpg.title: The Garden of Love

source.canonical_title: File:El Jardín del Amor (Rubens).jpg
source.credit: Transferred from de.wikipedia to Commons by Outisnn . Original uploader was Nocturne at de.wikipedia . Later version(s) were uploaded by Louis le Grand at de.wikipedia .

El_Jardín_del_Amor_(Rubens).jpg.story: Rubens painted this around 1633, a few years into his late second marriage, and the mood shows it. Silk-draped couples lounge in a twilit garden while cupids shove them gently together, one brandishing Juno's peacock, another a torch. Helena Fourment, his teenage bride, turns up more than once; Rubens himself is said to be the man in black on the far left, escorting a woman in. Philip IV liked it enough to hang it in his bedroom at the Royal Palace of Madrid, where it was recorded in 1666. It's been in the Prado ever since.

source.canonical_title: File:El coloso.jpg
source.permission: PD-Art, PD-Old

El_coloso.jpg.story: A naked giant strides across a horizon while, in the foreground, a panicked crowd and its livestock scatter in every direction — a single bull bolts the wrong way. The Prado catalogued it as Goya for a century, then downgraded it in 2008 after infrared caught an 'AJ' monogram pointing to Asensio Juliá, his assistant. Debate continues; the painting has hung in the Prado since Pedro Fernández Durán bequeathed his collection in 1931.

El_dos_de_mayo_de_1808_en_Madrid.jpg.title: The Second of May 1808 or The Charge of the Mamelukes

source.canonical_title: File:El dos de mayo de 1808 en Madrid.jpg

El_dos_de_mayo_de_1808_en_Madrid.jpg.story: Madrid, around the Puerta del Sol, the afternoon of 2 May 1808. Napoleon's Mamelukes — Egyptian cavalry in turbans — charge into a crowd that has had enough, and the crowd stabs back with knives. A white horse rears, its rider already dying; a Mameluke topples from the saddle; blood pools on the paving stones. Goya painted it in 1814, six years after the fact, once the French were finally out. It hangs in the Prado as the pendant to The Third of May.

El_jardín_de_las_Delicias,_de_El_Bosco..title: The Garden of Earthly Delights
El_jardín_de_las_Delicias,_de_El_Bosco..description: In the open triptych three scenes are included. The left panel is dedicated to Paradise, with the creation of Eve and the Fountain of Life, while the right one shows Hell. The central panel gives its name to the ensemble, since in a garden are represented the delights or pleasures of life. Between Paradise and Hell, these delights are nothing but allusions to Sin, showing humanity given over to various worldly pleasures. The representations of Lust, with a strong erotic charge, are evident, together with others of a more enigmatic meaning. Through the fleeting beauty of flowers or the sweetness of fruits, a message of fragility is conveyed, of the ephemeral character of happiness and the enjoyment of pleasure. Certain groups seem to confirm this, such as the couple enclosed in a glass bubble on the left side, probably alluding to the Flemish saying: “Happiness is like glass, it breaks quickly.” The closed triptych represents in grisaille the third day of the creation of the World, with God the Father as Creator, according to the inscriptions on each panel: “He himself said it and everything was made” and “He himself commanded it and everything was created” Genesis (1:9–13). A work of moralizing character, it is one of Bosch’s most enigmatic, complex and beautiful creations, made in the last stage of his life. Acquired in the auction of the prior don Fernando, natural son of the great Duke of Alba, Philip II took it to El Escorial in 1593. ‎

source.canonical_title: File:El jardín de las Delicias, de El Bosco.jpg

El_jardín_de_las_Delicias,_de_El_Bosco..story: The triptych everyone knows and no one fully explains. On the left, Eden: God presenting Eve to Adam under a pink fountain teeming with odd fauna. In the centre, a vast pink-and-green garden crawling with naked figures riding birds, climbing into fruit, bathing in circular pools — pleasure taken to the point where it stops looking like pleasure and starts looking like a warning. On the right, a black, burning hell of musical-instrument tortures and bird-headed demons. Bosch painted this around 1500 for a Netherlandish patron; Philip II eventually shipped it to El Escorial. Five centuries on it still feels less like allegory than like someone else's fever.

Elisabeth-Louise_Vigée_Le_Brun_-_Portrai.title: Portrait of Marie Gabrielle de Gramont, Duchesse de Caderousse

source.canonical_title: File:Elisabeth-Louise Vigée Le Brun - Portrait of Marie Gabrielle de Gramont, Duchesse de Caderousse - Google Art Project.jpg
source.credit: _wHjP8UuQV3NbQ at Google Cultural Institute maximum zoom level

title.fr: Portrait de Marie Gabrielle de Gramont, duchesse de Caderousse

Elisabeth-Louise_Vigée_Le_Brun_-_Portrai.story: Vigée Le Brun talked her sitter out of the wig powder. The sitter, Marie-Gabrielle de Gramont, was a friend of Marie Antoinette and, in 1784, still a comtesse; she wouldn't become a duchess until 1800, which is why the label on the back of the panel is actually wrong about her title. Le Brun set her up as a fantasy peasant girl with a straw hat and a basket of fruit, riding the queen's own craze for rustic play-acting at the Petit Trianon. The hair, freed from powder, is the point: jet-black, natural, a little shocking at court. The picture is now in Kansas City.

Elisabeth-Louise_Vigée_Le_Brun_-_The_Mar.title: The Marquise de Pezay, and the Marquise de Rougé with Her Sons Alexis and Adrien

source.canonical_title: File:Elisabeth-Louise Vigée Le Brun - The Marquise de Pezay and the Marquise de Rougé with Her Sons Alexis and Adrien.jpg
source.credit: 1. www.ne.jp 2. National Gallery of Art, Washington, DC

title.fr: La marquise de Pezay et la marquise de Rougé avec ses fils Alexis et Adrien

Elisabeth-Louise_Vigée_Le_Brun_-_The_Mar.story: A group portrait of two friends and two small boys, hung at the 1787 Salon right next to Vigée Le Brun's huge state picture of Marie Antoinette with the royal children. Contemporaries read it as a hymn to friendship and maternal love. On the right, the young Marquise de Rougé leans into her sons Alexis and Adrien; on the left, the widowed Marquise de Pezay completes the circle. Two years before the Revolution swept this world away — the artist included. Now at the National Gallery of Art in Washington.

Elisabeth_Louise_Vigee_Le_Brun_-_Countes.title: Countess Anna Ivanovna Tolstaya
Elisabeth_Louise_Vigee_Le_Brun_-_Countes.description: Elisabeth Louise Vigee Le Brun - Countess Anna Ivanovna Tolstaya

source.canonical_title: File:Elisabeth Louise Vigee Le Brun - Countess Anna Ivanovna Tolstaya.jpg

Elisabeth_Louise_Vigee_Le_Brun_-_Countes.story: Painted in Saint Petersburg during Vigee Le Brun's long exile from revolutionary France, this is a young Russian countess softened into something between Arcadian nymph and fashion plate. The sitter leans her cheek on her knuckles beside a fed waterfall, white muslin gown loosened at the waist, a gold locket slung on a long chain. The Russian nobility ate up this kind of neo-classical pastoral; Vigee Le Brun gave them wet rocks, sharp silk and the steady, faintly amused eye contact she had perfected on Marie Antoinette.

Elisabeth_Vigée-Lebrun_-_Lady_Hamilton_a.title: Life Study of Lady Hamilton as the Cumaean Sybil
Elisabeth_Vigée-Lebrun_-_Lady_Hamilton_a.description: "Emma Hamilton (1765–1815) rose from the lowest rank of society to the peak of distinction by marrying, in 1791, Sir William Hamilton, English ambassador to Naples. There she was famous for her “attitudes”—tableaux vivants performed before swooning audiences who felt themselves transported back to antiquity. This study from life preceded a larger composition that Vigée Le Brun carried with her throughout Europe and Russia to promote her work." [1]

source.canonical_title: File:Elisabeth Vigée-Lebrun - Lady Hamilton as the Persian Sibyl.jpg

Elisabeth_Vigée-Lebrun_-_Lady_Hamilton_a.story: Emma Hamilton, once a blacksmith's daughter, had just married Britain's ambassador to Naples and was the talk of Europe for her "attitudes" — tableaux vivants staged before swooning audiences. Vigée Le Brun cast her as the Cumaean Sibyl, with plume and parchment, the prophetess of nearby Cumae. This life study preceded a larger finished version the painter lugged across Europe and Russia as a calling card to impress future patrons. Signed "a Rome 1792."

Elisabeth_Vigée-Lebrun_-_Portrait_of_Hya.title: Portrait of Hyacinthe-Gabrielle Roland

source.canonical_title: File:Elisabeth Vigée-Lebrun - Portrait of Hyacinthe Gabrielle Roland.jpg
source.credit: 1. ne.jp 2./3. Unknown source Unknown source 4. The AMICA Library

Elisabeth_Vigée-Lebrun_-_Portrait_of_Hya.story: A portrait of two émigrées who found one another in revolutionary Rome. Hyacinthe-Gabrielle Roland had been a Parisian actress and was then living unmarried with the Irish peer Richard Wellesley, with several children already. Vigée Le Brun paints her windswept against a stormy sky, hair tumbling over bare shoulders — no powder, no drawing room, none of the decorum that ruled her Versailles work. Scholars read the picture as a pivot in her career, the moment exile loosened her style. Fine Arts Museums of San Francisco.

Elisabeth_Vigée-Lebrun_-_Self-Portrait_w.title: Elisabeth Vigée-Lebrun - Self-Portrait with Her Daughter, Julie - WGA25082

source.canonical_title: File:Elisabeth Vigée-Lebrun - Self-Portrait with Her Daughter, Julie - WGA25082.jpg
source.credit: Web Gallery of Art : Image Info about artwork wga QS:P11807,"v/vigee/self_da"

Elizabeth_Vigee_Lebrun_-_Portrait_of_Moh.title: Portrait of Muhammad Dervish Khan

source.canonical_title: File:Elizabeth Vigee Lebrun - Portrait of Mohammed Dervish Khan 366N10007 B3Y2Q.jpg

Elizabeth_Vigee_Lebrun_-_Portrait_of_Moh.story: In summer 1788 three ambassadors arrived in Paris from Mysore, sent by Tipu Sultan to lobby Louis XVI against the British in India. Vigée Le Brun spotted the lead envoy, Muhammad Dervish Khan, at the Opera — 'so remarkably picturesque' — and a royal request secured sittings at his Paris lodgings. Full-length, sword in hand, landscape behind. When she sent for the finished canvas he tried to keep it, hidden behind his bed. The embassy failed; Tipu reportedly had the returning envoys executed. In 2019 the painting sold at Sotheby's for $7.18 million, a record for a pre-modern woman artist.

Enbu_by_Hayami_Gyoshu.jpg.title: Enbu by Hayami Gyoshu
Enbu_by_Hayami_Gyoshu.jpg.description: Hayami Gyoshu: Dance of Flames (炎舞 Enbu)

source.canonical_title: File:Enbu by Hayami Gyoshu.jpg

Enbu_by_Hayami_Gyoshu.jpg.story: A pillar of orange flame climbing a black ground, and seven moths circling the heat - some burnt brown, some pale as paper, one about to pitch into the fire. Gyoshu painted this in 1925 on silk with mineral pigments; it's Nihonga technique aimed at something almost abstract. He'd seen moths gather around a lamp at his summer house in Karuizawa. The painting is now an Important Cultural Property of Japan. Gyoshu kept pushing - flowers, gold screens, this - until typhoid fever killed him at forty.

title.fr: Enoshima dans la province de Sagami

Enoshima_in_the_Sagami_province.jpg.story: Twice a day the tide pulls back and a sandbar opens between Enoshima and the mainland. Hokusai catches that moment: a ribbon of wet sand, pilgrims already crossing, surf still foaming at the edges. The five-story pagoda of Ryukoji rises from the wooded island; far off to the right, Fuji keeps its distance. Enoshima was famous for its sea caves and its shrine to Benzaiten, goddess of everything that flows.

Entrée_de_cimetière_(1825)_-_Caspar_Da.title: The Cemetery Entrance

source.canonical_title: File:Entrée de cimetière (1825) - Caspar David Friedrich (Galerie Neue Meister, Dresden).jpg

Entrée_de_cimetière_(1825)_-_Caspar_Da.story: A crumbling wall, a sagging gate, two tiny figures hesitating at the threshold. Friedrich places the viewer in shadow and pushes all the light — the crosses, a small church, a tower — to the far side of the stone portal. The gate is Dresden's Trinitätsfriedhof, which Friedrich himself helped design and in which he would eventually be buried. Painted in 1825 and now in the city's Galerie Neue Meister, it is one of his most direct pieces of theology in oil: this side dark, the other side bright.

Erasmus_Quellinus_(II)-_El_Amor_dormido,.title: Amor Asleep
Erasmus_Quellinus_(II)-_El_Amor_dormido,.artist: After Peter Paul Rubens / Peter Paul Rubens / Erasmus Quellinus II

source.canonical_title: File:Erasmus Quellinus (II)- El Amor dormido, 1630.jpg

Erasmus_Quellinus_(II)-_El_Amor_dormido,.story: Painted around 1636-38, not 1630, for the Torre de la Parada — Philip IV's hunting lodge in the hills outside Madrid, for which Rubens's workshop turned out more than sixty Ovidian scenes on a galloping deadline. Quellinus worked from a Rubens oil sketch, now in the Musee Bonnat in Bayonne, and stuck close to it: a grown-up Cupid slumped in sleep, wings folded, quiver slack, a visual pun on the loss of vigilance that love demands. For two centuries the Prado kept it under Rubens's name; it was only reattributed to Quellinus in 1973.

Erasmus_Quellinus_(II)_-_The_Rape_of_Eur.title: The rape of Europa (Ovid, Metamorphoses, II, 868-875

source.canonical_title: File:Erasmus Quellinus (II) - The Rape of Europe.jpg

title.nl: De roof van Europa (Ovidius, Metamorfosen, II, 868-875)

Erasmus_Quellinus_(II)_-_The_Rape_of_Eur.story: Quellinus takes Ovid at a clip: Europa already up on the disguised Jupiter, red drapery snapping in the wind, the bull looking back at us with a startlingly soft, almost human eye. The composition is stripped down compared with his master Rubens, sea and sky barely sketched, the whole picture hanging on the torque of the girl's body against the white flank. Painted in 1635 when Quellinus was still orbiting the Rubens workshop, it is a quieter, more graphic take on a scene Antwerp was repainting every other year.

Escola_de_Atenas_-_Vaticano_2.jpg.title: Escola de Atenas - Vaticano 2
Escola_de_Atenas_-_Vaticano_2.jpg.description: A Escola de Atenas, afresco no Vaticano

source.canonical_title: File:Escola de Atenas - Vaticano 2.jpg

Escola_de_Atenas_-_Vaticano_2.jpg.story: The School of Athens, seen here in a tighter frame that keeps the painted architecture visible around the fresco. Raphael fills a vast coffered hall with roughly fifty philosophers: Plato and Aristotle walking toward us at the vanishing point, Plato pointing up, Aristotle pointing flat ahead. Pythagoras writes at the lower left, Euclid bends over a slate on the right, and a glum Heraclitus — the face is Michelangelo's — slumps on a block in the foreground. Painted 1509–11 for Julius II's private library in the Vatican, it's still the clearest picture anyone ever made of the Renaissance idea of philosophy as a shared room.

source.canonical_title: File:Eugen de Blaas The Flirtation.jpg
