Eugen_de_Blaas_The_Flirtation.jpg.story: Two seamstresses at a sunlit wall, needlework half-forgotten, a suitor leaning in with the grin of a man overplaying his hand. De Blaas stages the courtship as theatre: dappled light through vines, a crumbling stucco backdrop, costumes pressed and spotless. It is an 1904 fantasy of working-class Venetian life scrubbed free of poverty, painted for collectors who wanted charm without grit.

Eugen_von_Blaas_-_Plauderei_-_1905.jpg.title: Eugen von Blaas - Plauderei - 1905

source.canonical_title: File:Eugen von Blaas - Plauderei - 1905.jpg

Eugen_von_Blaas_-_Plauderei_-_1905.jpg.story: "Plauderei" is just German for a chat, and that is all this painting promises — two or three Venetian girls caught mid-conversation, probably about a boy, probably on a sunlit step. By 1905 De Blaas had been producing variations on this scene for decades and knew exactly what his buyers in London and New York wanted: pretty faces, clean linen, and the flattering suggestion that life in Venice was one long afternoon flirtation.

Eugen_von_Blaas_-_Sharing_the_News_1904..title: Sharing the News

source.canonical_title: File:Eugen von Blaas - Sharing the News 1904.jpg

Eugen_von_Blaas_-_Sharing_the_News_1904..story: Three young women cluster on a Venetian doorstep, one reading aloud, the others craning in. The news itself doesn't matter — De Blaas is painting the pleasure of gossip, the shared lean of the shoulders, the bright white apron catching the afternoon sun. It is his usual formula turned out with practised skill: a little narrative hook, a lot of polished surface, and everyone looking suspiciously well-dressed.

Eugen_von_Blaas_-_The_Spider_and_the_Fly.title: Eugen von Blaas - The Spider and the Fly - 1889

source.canonical_title: File:Eugen von Blaas - The Spider and the Fly - 1889.jpg

Eugen_von_Blaas_-_The_Spider_and_the_Fly.story: The old moralising nursery-rhyme title — "Will you walk into my parlour?" — turned into a Venetian flirtation scene. A young woman leans from a window; a suitor below plays spider. De Blaas signs 1889. An old Royal Albert Museum (Exeter) label once rode the reverse, so the picture toured British provincial galleries before drifting into private hands, where it remains.

Eugen_von_Blaas_-_Two_Venetian_Women.jpg.title: Two Venetian Women

source.canonical_title: File:Eugen von Blaas - Two Venetian Women.jpg

Eugen_von_Blaas_-_Two_Venetian_Women.jpg.story: Two sun-struck Venetian girls lean in close, one clutching a rose, the other smiling sidelong at a secret the viewer doesn't get to hear. It is exactly the kind of picturesque Venice the Anglo-American tourist trade adored in 1898: warm skin, starched collars, painted with De Blaas's tidy academic finish and not a ripple of modernist doubt. Hung in a London dealer's window, it would have sold by teatime.

Eugen_von_Blaas_Bildnis_Arthur_Graf_Berc.title: Eugen von Blaas Bildnis Arthur Graf Berchtold 1882
Eugen_von_Blaas_Bildnis_Arthur_Graf_Berc.description: Bildnis Arthur Graf Berchtold (1843-1929), erbliches Mitglied des ungarischen Oberhauses und ungarischer Reichstagsabgeordneter; signiert, datiert Eugen von Blaas 1882 (unter dem Rahmen)

source.canonical_title: File:Eugen von Blaas Bildnis Arthur Graf Berchtold 1882.jpg

Eugen_von_Blaas_Bildnis_Arthur_Graf_Berc.story: A break from the fisher-girls. Arthur Graf Berchtold owned the Palazzo Contarini degli Scrigni on the Grand Canal and served as a hereditary member of the Hungarian upper house and deputy in the Reichstag. De Blaas, who lived and worked in Venice, would have known the palazzo well. The portrait is straight formal commission work — dark ground, steady gaze, fine black wool — painted the year Berchtold turned 39.

Eugen_von_Blaas_Der_rote_Fächer_1892.jpg.title: The Red Fan, 1892

source.canonical_title: File:Eugen von Blaas Der rote Fächer 1892.jpg

Eugen_von_Blaas_Der_rote_Fächer_1892.jpg.story: Half-length of a blonde Venetian girl framed in a weathered stone window, a red, flower-painted fan in her left hand. Wide-necked blouse, brocade bodice, gold chain, creole earrings, cheeks just slightly rouged — the full de Blaas inventory. The trick of the picture is the contrast: immaculate skin against pitted, crumbling brick. Small panel, oil on wood, signed and dated 1892 lower right.

Eugene_de_Blaas_-_Curiosity_(1892).jpg.title: Eugene de Blaas - Curiosity (1892)

source.canonical_title: File:Eugene de Blaas - Curiosity (1892).jpg

Eugene_de_Blaas_-_Curiosity_(1892).jpg.story: A knot of Venetian women leaning in to overhear something just out of frame. The composition was reproduced in the Pears Annual Christmas supplement of 1892 — Pears being the soap empire whose seasonal gift-books did more than most galleries to circulate late-Victorian sentimental painting into ordinary living rooms. That provenance tells you everything about where de Blaas sat in the taste of his day: academically respectable, endlessly reproducible, aimed squarely at the parlour.

Eugene_de_Blaas_-_Daydreaming_by_the_sho.title: Daydreaming by the shore

source.canonical_title: File:Eugene de Blaas - Daydreaming by the shore (1895).jpg

Eugene_de_Blaas_-_Daydreaming_by_the_sho.story: A tall, narrow canvas — nearly 140 centimetres high — with a single barefoot Venetian girl standing against a lagoon horizon, lost in thought. De Blaas rarely worked at this vertical stretch, and the format lets him linger over the full length of skirt, shawl and bare feet on wet sand. Signed E de Blaas 1895. It spent the later twentieth century bouncing between Los Angeles and New York auction rooms before disappearing back into a private collection.

Eugene_de_Blaas_A_Pensive_Moment.jpg.title: A Pensive Moment

source.canonical_title: File:Eugene de Blaas A Pensive Moment.jpg

Eugene_de_Blaas_A_Pensive_Moment.jpg.story: Another of de Blaas's single-figure Venetian girls, this one caught mid-thought rather than mid-flirt. Oil on cradled panel, 85 by 53 centimetres, signed 1896. No grand narrative, no moral — just the careful rendering of pale skin, dark hair, a quiet tilt of the head, and the fabric and jewellery that signalled "Venice" to tourists shopping the Ponte di Rialto galleries. It sold at Christie's New York in 2000.

source.canonical_title: File:Eugene delacroix.jpg

Eugène_Delacroix_-_A_Mortally_Wounded_B.title: Wounded Brigand (Roman Shepherd)

source.canonical_title: File:Eugène Delacroix - A Mortally Wounded Brigand Quenches his Thirst - WGA06165.jpg
source.credit: Web Gallery of Art : Image Info about artwork wga QS:P11807,"d/delacroi/1/109delac"

Eugène_Delacroix_-_A_Mortally_Wounded_B.story: An early, modestly sized Delacroix from 1825, now in Basel: a dying bandit flat on his stomach, beard trailing in the puddle he's drinking from. No heroism, no clear landscape — just a body emptying itself into the dirt. The brushwork already has the Venetian warmth and Rubensian muscle that would carry him through the next forty years, applied here to a subject most Salon painters wouldn't have dared keep so small and squalid.

Eugène_Delacroix_-_Collision_of_Moorish.title: Collision of Moorish Horsemen
Eugène_Delacroix_-_Collision_of_Moorish.description: Delacroix described the spectacular and violent military pageantry at the court of Sultan Abd-er-Rahmen of Morocco (1778-1859), which he witnessed while accompanying Count Charles de Mornay on a diplomatic expedition on behalf of King Louis Philippe of France in 1832: "During their military exercises, which consist of riding their horses at full-speed and stopping them suddenly after firing a shot, it often happens that the horses carry away their riders and fight each other when they collide."

source.canonical_title: File:Eugène Delacroix - Collision of Moorish Horsemen - Walters 376.jpg

Eugène_Delacroix_-_Collision_of_Moorish.story: At the Moroccan sultan's court in 1832, Delacroix watched a fantasia — a ceremonial cavalry charge that ended with a synchronised gunshot. Sometimes, he noted, the horses panicked and slammed into each other. That is the instant he paints here: two riders and their mounts tangled mid-collision, dust and robes flying. Fluid, almost careless brushwork; no heroics, just the chaos he'd actually seen. Walters Art Museum, Baltimore.

Eugène_Delacroix_-_Les_Natchez,_1835_(M.title: The Natchez
Eugène_Delacroix_-_Les_Natchez,_1835_(M.description: Depicts Natchez Native American mother and father with their newborn child on the banks of the Mississippi River. Inspired by 1801 novel "Atala" by Chateaubriand, the setting is in French Colonial Louisiana; the Natchez couple have recently escaped upriver from a massacre. [ 1 ] ↑ MET Museum

source.canonical_title: File:Eugène Delacroix - Les Natchez, 1835 (Metropolitan Museum of Art).jpg
source.credit: 1. Web Gallery of Art : Image Info about artwork wga QS:P11807,"/d/delacroi/2/212delac" 2. Metropolitan Museum of Art, online collection (The Met object ID 110000620)

Eugène_Delacroix_-_Les_Natchez,_1835_(M.story: A young Natchez couple collapsed on a riverbank, the mother cradling a newborn, the father too exhausted to do more than watch the water. Delacroix had started the picture in 1823 after reading Chateaubriand's Atala, then set it aside for over a decade before finally showing it at the Salon of 1835. The family has fled upstream from the 1729 French massacre of their people in Louisiana. The baby, the catalogue note warned, would not survive.

Eugène_Delacroix_-_Shipwreck_on_the_Coa.title: Shipwreck on the Coast

source.canonical_title: File:Eugène Delacroix - Shipwreck on the Coast - Google Art Project.jpg
source.credit: 7QEvX2VgBvI66Q at Google Cultural Institute maximum zoom level

Eugène_Delacroix_-_Shipwreck_on_the_Coa.story: A smear of foam, a broken mast leaning seaward, figures too small to name clinging to the rocks. Delacroix painted it in 1862, a year before he died, working quickly with a loaded brush and almost no drawing underneath. By then his hand had loosened completely, closer to Turner's late gales than to the tight theatre of his Salon years. You can count the strokes in the cliffs. He signed the canvas in red at the lower right; the Museum of Fine Arts, Houston bought it in 2004.

Eugène_Delacroix_-_The_Fanatics_of_Tang.title: The Fanatics of Tangier

source.canonical_title: File:Eugène Delacroix - The Fanatics of Tangier - WGA06195.jpg
source.credit: 1. Web Gallery of Art : Image Info about artwork wga QS:P11807,"/d/delacroi/3/314delac" 2. [1]

Eugène_Delacroix_-_The_Fanatics_of_Tang.story: In 1832 Delacroix and his diplomat companion hid in an attic in Tangier and watched through shutters as the Aïssaoua brotherhood whirled through the street in ecstatic trance. Five years later he painted it from memory and sketches, pouring the crowd down a narrow lane in a flash of white robes and raised arms. It is Orientalism, yes, but also a genuine attempt to render a religious frenzy he found bewildering and unforgettable. Minneapolis Institute of Art.

Evening_landscape_at_moonrise_-_Van_Gogh.title: Evening Landscape at Moonrise
Evening_landscape_at_moonrise_-_Van_Gogh.description: Evening landscape at moonrise - Van Gogh

FRANCESCO_HAYEZ_-_Incontro_di_Giobbe_ed_.title: Meeting of Job and Esau
FRANCESCO_HAYEZ_-_Incontro_di_Giobbe_ed_.description: The painting illustrates Jacob's return to his homeland, asking forgiveness from his brother Esau for having deceived his birthright. Biblical subjects had a lot of luck around the mid-nineteenth century, as the suffering of the Jewish people recalled the Italian political situation.

source.canonical_title: File:FRANCESCO HAYEZ - Incontro di Giobbe ed Esaù (1844).jpg

Faded_Laurels_by_Edmund_Leighton.jpg.title: Faded Laurels

source.canonical_title: File:Faded Laurels by Edmund Leighton.jpg
source.credit: Bukowskis – Arts & Business, Important Spring Sale 649, 14 June 2023, lot 809

Faded_Laurels_by_Edmund_Leighton.jpg.story: An old harpist sits alone on the church steps while the crowd, king and queen included, presses inside to hear the younger musician. His laurel crown is brown; the new man's is green. Leighton lays the metaphor on thick and knows it. The Athenaeum's 1889 reviewer groaned that he was wasting his talent on a "sentimental anachronism," which rather misses that sentiment was the point. The painting hangs today in a private collection in Sweden.

Famille_de_paysans_dans_un_interieur.jpg.title: Peasant Family in an Interior
Famille_de_paysans_dans_un_interieur.jpg.artist: Attributed to Louis Le Nain / Antoine Le Nain

source.canonical_title: File:Famille de paysans dans un interieur.jpg

Famille_de_paysans_dans_un_interieur.jpg.story: A dim cottage interior that refuses to perform its own poverty. A woman in a grey kerchief sits front and centre holding a stoneware jug and a small glass of red wine, meeting the viewer head-on. A barefoot boy plays a pipe beside the table; a bearded man in a broad hat tears bread; a kitten noses at an overturned copper pot on the earth floor. The palette is mostly umber and ash with a few chalk-white linens doing the lighting. The Le Nain brothers shared a Paris studio and signed as one, which is why attribution of pictures like this still drifts between Louis and Antoine.

Femenine_wave.jpg.title: 'Feminine Wave'

source.canonical_title: File:Femenine wave.jpg

Femenine_wave.jpg.story: Hokusai painted this spiralling wave when he was 86 years old, one year before his death, as a ceiling panel for a festival float in the town of Obuse. Its pair, Masculine Wave, crashes in an opposing panel; together they were meant to swing overhead while the float was pulled through the streets. Unlike the woodblock Great Wave, this is a painting on wood, and the curl is rounder, more lunar. Dated 1845, the Kanmachi float ceiling panels are among the final works of his life.

title.fr: Les Femmes d'Alger dans leur appartement
title.it: Donne di Algeri nei loro appartamenti
title.nl: De vrouwen van Algiers in hun vertrek

Femmes_d'Alger_dans_leur_appartement,_Eu.story: Three women on cushions, a hookah between them, a servant glancing back as she leaves. The tiled floor glows; the slippers are embroidered in real silver. Delacroix had been smuggled into a harem in Algiers in 1832 by a sympathetic customs official and made frantic watercolor notes on the spot. Two years later, the finished canvas hung at the Salon of 1834. Cézanne later said every painter who came after owed something to those reds and greens.

Fernand_Khnopff013.jpg.title: Portrait of Marguerite Khnopff

source.canonical_title: File:Fernand Khnopff013.jpg

Fernand_Khnopff013.jpg.story: Khnopff painted his sister Marguerite many times, always as this smooth, sealed presence. Here she stands full length in a tight white tailor-made, high collar buttoned to the throat, one gloved hand resting lightly on her forearm, the other on what might be a door handle. The whole picture is pale grey and bone white; a small bronze disc floats on the wall beside her like a planet. Marguerite was her brother's private emblem of chastity and refusal, and this 1887 portrait is the quietest version of the cult.

Fernand_Le_Quesne_-_Les_deux_perles_(The.title: The Two Pearls, 1889

source.canonical_title: File:Fernand Le Quesne - Les deux perles (The two pearls) (1889).png

Fernand_Le_Quesne_-_Les_deux_perles_(The.story: The colour version of Le Quesne's 1889 Salon piece, and you can see why the sepia reproduction never did it justice. Glaucus is a warm dark silhouette against a pale Channel sea, the sailing boats picked out in cold white, while the nereid on her giant scallop shell glows pink against green-grey rock. The whole thing is tuned to that single gesture, his hand closing over hers around the second pearl. Academic to the bone, but genuinely beautiful in the colour as the figures meet at arm's length.

Félicien_Rops_-_Pornokratès_-_1878_(2).title: Pornocrates

source.canonical_title: File:Félicien Rops - Pornokratès - 1878 (2).jpg
source.credit: The Yorck Project (2002) 10.000 Meisterwerke der Malerei (DVD-ROM), distributed by DIRECTMEDIA Publishing GmbH. ISBN : 3936122202 .

Félicien_Rops_-_Pornokratès_-_1878_(2).story: Rops's most notorious print: a blindfolded woman in black stockings and opera gloves, naked apart from a blue sash, led across a plinth by a fat pig on a pink ribbon. Three winged cupids flutter around her in a starry sky. Along the base runs a frieze of the arts, Sculpture, Music, Poetry, Painting, crouched and dejected while Lady Vice parades above them. It is a flagrant piece of Belgian decadence, half satire of bourgeois morality, half straight erotic provocation, and it took Rops four days of drinking and drawing in 1878 to finish.

source.canonical_title: File:Flowers in a Rococo Vase A24470.jpg

Flowers_in_a_Rococo_Vase_A24470.jpg.story: Cezanne almost never painted cut flowers — they wilted faster than his working method, which required days of slow, chalky build-up per object. This one, around 1876, he pushed through anyway: zinnias, asters, a blast of pink, stuffed into a gilt rococo vase that clashes on purpose with the tight, hatched brushwork. He gave it to his friend Gustave Caillebotte, who kept it until he died. It reached Washington's National Gallery of Art in 1963 through Chester Dale's bequest.

Foggy_Morning_at_Pourville_-_Claude_Mone.title: Foggy Morning at Pourville

source.canonical_title: File:Foggy Morning at Pourville - Claude Monet.jpg

Foggy_Morning_at_Pourville_-_Claude_Mone.story: Le matin, temps brumeux, Pourville — morning, misty weather. Monet drains the palette to greys and soft lilac, smudges the horizon until sea and sky share a seam. No drama, just atmosphere: that Channel fog you could walk into and vanish. Painted in 1882 on one of his restless Normandy mornings, the canvas measures 61 by 74 centimetres and has hung at the Birmingham Museum of Art in Alabama since 1981.

Follower_of_Rogier_van_der_Weyden_(Nethe.title: The Deposition
Follower_of_Rogier_van_der_Weyden_(Nethe.artist: Follower of Rogier van der Weyden (Netherlandish, 1399/1400 - 1464) (1399 - 1464) – artist (Netherlandish) Details on Google Art Project

source.canonical_title: File:Follower of Rogier van der Weyden (Netherlandish - The Deposition - Google Art Project.jpg

Follower_of_Rogier_van_der_Weyden_(Nethe.story: Christ slumps from the cross into the arms of the mourners, his body drawn with the same translucent pallor Rogier van der Weyden had perfected a generation earlier. Mary faints; John steadies her. The painter, working in the Low Countries around 1490, borrowed the composition from the master but tightened the faces, adding real grief to the formula. The grainy wood panel remains an anonymous tribute to Rogier, who died in Brussels in 1464.

Fox_In_The_Snow_-_Courbet_(1860).JPG.title: Fox in the Snow

source.canonical_title: File:Fox In The Snow - Courbet (1860).JPG
source.credit: 1. dallasmuseumofart.org 2. The AMICA Library 3./4. Dallas Museum of Art, online collection

Fox_In_The_Snow_-_Courbet_(1860).JPG.story: A fox crouches low in white powder, jaws clamped on a rodent, a splash of red blood on the snow. No hunter, no moral, no picturesque wilderness — just one small animal eating another. That bluntness was the point. Courbet hung it at the Salon of 1861, part of his ongoing argument that ordinary life, claws and all, deserved the same canvas size as gods and generals. It lives at the Dallas Museum of Art.

Francesco_Hayez_-_Odalisca_che_legge,_18.title: Odalisque reading

source.canonical_title: File:Francesco Hayez - Odalisca che legge, 1867.jpg
source.credit: The Yorck Project (2002) 10.000 Meisterwerke der Malerei (DVD-ROM), distributed by DIRECTMEDIA Publishing GmbH. ISBN : 3936122202 .
source.permission: 10.000 Gemälde für Commons

Francesco_Hayez_-_Odalisca_che_legge,_18.story: Goya gets the swooning pose; Hayez gives us a woman who'd rather read. Propped on her elbow, cheek on one hand, she ignores the viewer entirely in favor of whatever's on the page. The satin slippers and the embroidered pillow sell the fantasy of the harem, but the book quietly deflates it. Hayez was almost eighty when he painted this odalisque in 1866, still producing the lush, eroticized orientalism that Milanese collectors couldn't get enough of.

Francesco_Hayez_-_Ritratto_di_Alessandro.title: Portrait of Alessandro Manzoni

source.canonical_title: File:Francesco Hayez - Ritratto di Alessandro Manzoni.jpg
source.credit: The Yorck Project (2002) 10.000 Meisterwerke der Malerei (DVD-ROM), distributed by DIRECTMEDIA Publishing GmbH. ISBN : 3936122202 .

Francesco_Hayez_-_Ritratto_di_Alessandro.story: Manzoni at fifty-six, in a dark coat and the faintest smile, hands resting on a closed book. Hayez painted him in 1841, the year Manzoni finally published the definitive Tuscan-rinsed edition of The Betrothed after rewriting it line by line. The two men were close friends in Milan; Hayez captured the novelist's long face and thinning hair without flattery. The portrait hangs in the Pinacoteca di Brera.

Francesco_Hayez_-_Self_Portrait_in_a_Gro.title: Francesco Hayez - Self Portrait in a Group of Friend - Google Art Project
Francesco_Hayez_-_Self_Portrait_in_a_Gro.description: Self-Portrait in a Group of Friends (1824 or 1827) by Francesco Hayez. Museo Poldi Pezzoli, Milan. Friends: Tommaso Grossi, Giuseppe Molteni, Giovanni Migliara and Pelagio Pelagi

source.canonical_title: File:Francesco Hayez - Self Portrait in a Group of Friend - Google Art Project.jpg
source.credit: bwFUwn2Et3dOjQ at Google Cultural Institute maximum zoom level

Francesco_Hayez_-_Self_Portrait_in_a_Gro.story: Four friends lean in over a table scattered with drawings, and Hayez slips himself into the huddle, second from the left. The others are all Milanese names worth knowing: the novelist Tommaso Grossi, the portraitist Giuseppe Molteni, the landscape painter Giovanni Migliara, and the decorator Pelagio Pelagi. It's a snapshot of the Romantic circle in 1820s Milan, painted around 1824 to 1827, the group that would shape Italian culture in the run-up to unification. The picture belongs to the Museo Poldi Pezzoli, which keeps it in Milan where it was made.

Francesco_Hayez_-_Susanna_at_her_Bath_(N.title: Susanna at Her Bath

source.canonical_title: File:Francesco Hayez - Susanna at her Bath (National Gallery, London).jpg
source.credit: 1. the second upload from File:Francesco Hayez 054.jpg 2. - 5. National Gallery, London - online catalogue .

Francesco_Hayez_-_Susanna_at_her_Bath_(N.story: Susanna steps into her bath unaware that two elders are peering through the shrubbery, ready to blackmail her. Hayez gives us the instant before she notices. Her skin catches a cool light; the linen falls away in a crumpled heap; one slipper still clings to her foot. Painted in 1850, this is one of Hayez's most polished nudes, all Venetian warmth and hushed erotic charge. He made several versions of the subject over a decade. This one hangs in the National Gallery, London.

Francesco_Hayez_-_The_Refugees_of_Parga_.story: On the beach at Parga, an Epirote family loads everything it owns into a boat while a man in the foreground digs up his ancestors' bones to take with him. When Britain ceded the town to Ali Pasha in 1819, thousands of Greeks fled rather than live under Ottoman rule. Hayez finished this huge canvas in 1831, more than a decade later, for a Brescian patron. It hangs today in the Pinacoteca Tosio Martinengo.

Francesco_Hayez_056.jpg.title: Samson and the lion

source.canonical_title: File:Francesco Hayez 056.jpg
source.credit: The Yorck Project (2002) 10.000 Meisterwerke der Malerei (DVD-ROM), distributed by DIRECTMEDIA Publishing GmbH. ISBN : 3936122202 .

Francesco_Hayez_056.jpg.story: Samson has the lion by the jaws and is ripping them apart with both hands, his cloak slipping, every tendon bright. Hayez painted the Old Testament episode in 1842, working at Brera in the full-blown history style Milan expected of him. The beast's hind legs already buckle. A broken honeycomb in the lion's carcass, Samson's riddle to come, is only hinted in the shadow at lower right.

title.it: Saturno che divora i suoi figli

Francisco_de_Goya,_Saturno_devorando_a_s.story: Saturn, wild-eyed and wild-haired, is eating his own child head-first. The god was meant to, according to the myth — he'd been warned a son would overthrow him — but Goya paints the thing as pure private horror. He brushed it straight onto the dining-room wall of his farmhouse outside Madrid, the Quinta del Sordo, sometime between 1820 and 1823. No one was meant to see it. After his death the murals were peeled off the walls, transferred to canvas, and eventually handed over to the Prado.

Francisco_de_Zurbarán_-_Christ_on_the_Cr.title: Christ on the Cross

source.canonical_title: File:Francisco de Zurbarán - Christ on the Cross - WGA26051.jpg
source.credit: 1. Art Institute of Chicago 2. Web Gallery of Art : Image Info about artwork wga QS:P11807,"z/zurbaran/1/christ_x"

Francisco_de_Zurbarán_-_Christ_on_the_Cr.story: Zurbarán was twenty-eight and barely launched when the Dominicans of San Pablo in Seville commissioned this Crucifixion. He gave them a Christ that looked carved rather than painted: pale body floating out of total darkness, feet nailed side by side rather than crossed, every fold of the loincloth starched into geometry. Visitors viewing it through a grille in a dim chapel reportedly mistook it for sculpture. Art Institute of Chicago.

Francisco_de_Zurbarán_006.jpg.title: Francisco de Zurbarán 006
Francisco_de_Zurbarán_006.jpg.description: Agnus Dei (c. 1635–1640), 38 cm × 62 cm. Oil on canvas. Museo del Prado

source.canonical_title: File:Francisco de Zurbarán 006.jpg

Francisco_de_Zurbarán_006.jpg.story: A single lamb, feet bound, lying on a stone slab against pure black. No cross, no altar, no saint. Zurbarán painted several of these in the 1630s and 40s, and they read simultaneously as quiet still lifes of a young merino and as the Agnus Dei, the sacrificial Lamb of God. The wool is painted so meticulously you can almost feel the lanolin. This version, now in the Prado, measures only about 38 by 62 centimeters. The tight crop and the refusal of symbolic props are what make it devastating. Counter-Reformation piety reduced to one animal, one plank, and the dark.

Francisco_de_Zurbarán_046.jpg.title: Saint Luke as a painter, before Christ on the Cross

source.canonical_title: File:Francisco de Zurbarán 046.jpg

Francisco_de_Zurbarán_046.jpg.story: Saint Luke — patron of painters, according to tradition a portraitist of the Virgin — stands at the foot of the Cross holding his brushes and looking up. Most scholars think the face is Zurbarán's own, a quiet late-career self-portrait folded into a devotional image. The Christ beside him has the same sculptural whiteness he'd been perfecting for thirty years. Prado.

Frans_Snijders_-_Keukenstilleven.jpg.title: Kitchen Still Life

source.canonical_title: File:Frans Snijders - Keukenstilleven.jpg

title.nl: Stilleven met groenten, fruit, wild en een kreeft

Frans_Snijders_-_Keukenstilleven.jpg.story: A skinned hare draped over a table, a dead swan with its neck spilling off the edge, a boar's head with its mouth open mid-grunt, artichokes, lobsters, a bowl of oysters — Snyders piled it on. Painted around 1614 in Antwerp, this is the kind of kitchen display a rich merchant commissioned to show off his table. Snyders had just come back from a spell in Italy and started collaborating regularly with Rubens; you can feel the Rubens muscle in the dead animals. The panel is in the Boijmans Van Beuningen in Rotterdam.

Frans_Snyders_-_A_Greyhound_Catching_a_Y.story: A single clenched moment: the dog's jaws close on the boar's flank, the boar twists mid-stride, and the underbrush blurs. Snyders painted hunts by the dozen for Flemish and Spanish patrons who wanted the thrill of the chase without the mud. He worked from studies of real hounds at the ducal kennels, which is why you can almost count the ribs beneath the greyhound's skin.

Frans_Snyders_-_Concert_of_Birds_-_WGA21.title: Concert of Birds

source.canonical_title: File:Frans Snyders - Concert of Birds - WGA21526.jpg

Frans_Snyders_-_Concert_of_Birds_-_WGA21.story: An owl grips a sheet of music in its talons and conducts. Around it, fifteen other birds — a hoopoe, a jay, a parrot, a bird of paradise from New Guinea — open their beaks and lean in for the chorus. Snyders painted several of these "bird concerts" in the late 1620s; this version, from 1629–30, now hangs in the Prado. The joke is old (birds trying to read music) and the painting is serious (Snyders knew his ornithology — most of these species are identifiable to this day).

Frans_Snyders_-_Cook_at_a_Kitchen_Table_.title: Cook at a Kitchen Table with Dead Game

source.canonical_title: File:Frans Snyders - Cook at a Kitchen Table with Dead Game.jpg

Frans_Snyders_-_Cook_at_a_Kitchen_Table_.story: Antwerp's larder in paint: a cook leans into a table groaning with a trussed swan, hare, partridge, and a spill of apples. Snyders was the go-to painter of flesh in seventeenth-century Flanders; Rubens routinely called him in to paint the birds and beasts in his own canvases. Note the cook's weary glance at the swan's long neck, and the cat slinking under the table with an eye on what it can steal. Snyders could render feather and fur in a single brushload, which is why kitchens like this one hung in the grandest dining halls of 1634.

Frans_Snyders_-_Lying_Lioness.jpg.title: Lying Lioness

source.canonical_title: File:Frans Snyders - Lying Lioness.jpg

Frans_Snyders_-_Lying_Lioness.jpg.story: A study, not a set piece. The lioness sprawls on her side, paws loose, ribs rising, and Snyders lavishes the same attention on her golden pelt that he gave to the swans and hares in his kitchens. He painted from menagerie animals kept in Antwerp, and sheets like this one circulated through his studio as reference for the big hunt commissions. The beast is the entire subject.

Frans_Snyders_-_Orpheus_and_the_animals..title: Orpheus and the animals

source.canonical_title: File:Frans Snyders - Orpheus and the animals.jpg

Frans_Snyders_-_Orpheus_and_the_animals..story: A classic Antwerp division of labour: Van Thulden, a Rubens pupil, handles the figure of Orpheus charming the beasts with his lyre, while Snyders — the city's great specialist in fur, feather and fang — crowds the canvas with lions, boars, deer, birds and exotic creatures listening in uneasy peace. Snyders' animals are never decorative; they watch, breathe, smell the air. The result is half myth, half menagerie, a reminder that in 17th-century Flanders a single picture was often the work of two very confident hands.

Frans_Snyders_and_workshop_-_The_boar_hu.title: The boar hunt
Frans_Snyders_and_workshop_-_The_boar_hu.artist: Frans Snyders and workshop – creator Born in Antwerp, Belgium. Details on Google Art Project

source.canonical_title: File:Frans Snyders and workshop - The boar hunt - Google Art Project.jpg
source.credit: jwHaDccc1u4Icg at Google Cultural Institute maximum zoom level

Frans_Snyders_and_workshop_-_The_boar_hu.story: A boar at bay, hounds in mid-leap, a hunter's spear just entering the frame. Snyders produced these hunts on a near-industrial scale from his Antwerp studio, with assistants blocking in landscape while the master handled the flashing teeth and wet nostrils. The composition radiates outward from the boar's bared tusks, so your eye never settles - exactly the point in a painting meant to hang opposite a dining table.

Franz_Von_Stuck_-_The_Struggle_for_Woman.title: The Struggle for Woman

source.canonical_title: File:Franz Von Stuck - The Struggle for Woman.jpg

Franz_Von_Stuck_-_The_Struggle_for_Woman.story: Two naked men wrestle on a rocky ledge while a woman watches, half-turned away, a picture of clinical detachment. Kampf um das Weib is Stuck's Darwinian gloss on desire: sexual selection staged as bloodsport, with no winner yet declared. He painted the subject more than once, tightening the composition each time into near-frieze flatness. By 1905 he was rich, ennobled, living in his self-designed Villa Stuck in Munich, and producing these mythic set pieces by the yard.

Franz_von_Stuck,_by_Franz_von_Stuck.jpg.title: Franz von Stuck, by Franz von Stuck
Franz_von_Stuck,_by_Franz_von_Stuck.jpg.description: Self-portrait oil on board 38.1 x 24.2 cm signed c.r.: FRANZ / VON / STUCK / 1923

source.canonical_title: File:Franz von Stuck, by Franz von Stuck.jpg

Franz_von_Stuck,_by_Franz_von_Stuck.jpg.story: Stuck at sixty, in a dark coat against a darker ground, looking out with the frank, slightly weary stare of a man who has been a baron for almost two decades. By 1923 the symbolist fevers were behind him; Kandinsky and Klee had long since left his Munich Academy classroom and gone abstract, and Stuck's own reputation was beginning its long slide. The small oil on board is signed and dated at lower right in his customary blocky capitals.

Franz_von_Stuck_-Wounded_Amazon,_1903.jp.title: Wounded Amazon (Original Title: Verwundete Amazone)

source.canonical_title: File:Franz von Stuck -Wounded Amazon, 1903.jpg

Franz_von_Stuck_-Wounded_Amazon,_1903.jp.story: An Amazon astride a rearing horse, arm flung up, a black-shafted arrow in her side, a second rider falling behind her. Stuck loved these muscular mythological skirmishes and returned to the Amazon subject repeatedly. The composition is all diagonals and backlit silhouettes; the palette is burnt and bronze, like something dug up from antiquity. He was by this date a baron, a professor at the Munich Academy, and about to have Kandinsky and Klee pass through his studio.

Franz_von_Stuck_004.jpg.title: The Sin

source.canonical_title: File:Franz von Stuck 004.jpg
source.credit: The Yorck Project (2002) 10.000 Meisterwerke der Malerei (DVD-ROM), distributed by DIRECTMEDIA Publishing GmbH. ISBN : 3936122202 .

Franz_von_Stuck_004.jpg.story: A pale woman emerges from darkness with a huge black serpent coiled around her shoulders, its head resting at her breast, its eyes two glinting points. Stuck made Die Sünde the sensation of the 1893 Munich Secession's first exhibition, painted it again at least a dozen times, and built his career on it. The thick gilded frame is part of the work, drafted by Stuck himself. The sin is Eve's, but the face belongs more to the femme fatale of 1890s Munich than to Genesis.

Franz_von_Stuck_Salome.jpg.title: Salome

source.canonical_title: File:Franz von Stuck Salome.jpg
source.credit: Eva Mendgen: Franz von Stuck 1863–1928. Benedikt Taschen Verlag, Köln 1994; ISBN 3-8228-8953-9

Franz_von_Stuck_Salome.jpg.story: Salome dances barefoot with her arms raised, bare-breasted, strings of pearls swinging, while a grinning attendant in the shadows holds the Baptist's severed head on a platter. The picture hit at the height of Salome-mania: Wilde's play had appeared in 1891, Strauss's opera premiered the year before Stuck painted this. Stuck gives her the cold athletic body he liked and a sky of deep indigo scattered with stars. The Städtische Galerie im Lenbachhaus in Munich holds the canvas.

Frederick_Law_Olmsted.jpg.title: Frederick Law Olmsted

source.canonical_title: File:Frederick Law Olmsted.jpg

Frederick_Law_Olmsted.jpg.story: Olmsted, the landscape architect behind Central Park and the Emerald Necklace, was 73, his memory already slipping, and deeply uncomfortable being painted. Sargent had him stand among his own plantings at Biltmore in North Carolina, cane in hand, dogwoods and rhododendrons at his feet, the great George Vanderbilt estate he had just designed spreading out beyond the frame. The result is half-portrait, half-garden. It was finished in 1895 and still hangs at Biltmore.

Fujiwara_no_Yasumasa_Playing_the_Flute_b.title: Fujiwara no Yasumasa Playing the Flute by Moonlight
Fujiwara_no_Yasumasa_Playing_the_Flute_b.description: Japan, 1883 Alternate Title: Fujiwara no Yasumasa Gekka Roteki zu Prints; woodcuts Triptych; color woodblock prints Image: 14 3/16 x 28 1/8 in. (36.0 x 71.4 cm); Sheet: 14 3/4 x 28 5/16 in. (37.4 x 72.0 cm) Herbert R. Cole Collection (M.84.31.137a-c) Japanese Art

source.canonical_title: File:Fujiwara no Yasumasa Playing the Flute by Moonlight LACMA M.84.31.137a-c.jpg
source.credit: Image: http://collections.lacma.org/sites/default/files/remote_images/piction/ma-31808204-O3.jpg Gallery: http://collections.lacma.org/node/191379 archive copy at the Wayback Machine

Fujiwara_no_Yasumasa_Playing_the_Flute_b.story: A court noble in brocade robes strolls through dry autumn grasses, playing his flute while a low full moon hangs at the left edge. The bandit lurking behind him has stopped dead, sword half-drawn, frozen by the music. Yoshitoshi loved these Heian-era ghost stories and tests of nerve, and the composition tells the whole legend at a glance: pursuer and prey sharing one long horizon of reeds. Printed in 1883, deep into the Meiji era, when woodblock was already giving ground to photography. The indigo night and that cold flat moon do all the heavy lifting.

FuseliArtistMovedtoDespair.jpg.title: The Artist Moved by the Grandeur of Antique Fragments

source.canonical_title: File:FuseliArtistMovedtoDespair.jpg
source.credit: Web Gallery of Art : Image Info about artwork wga QS:P11807,"f/fuseli/02antiqu"

FuseliArtistMovedtoDespair.jpg.story: A lone figure sprawls on the flagstones of a Roman courtyard, head in hand, weeping beside the colossal marble hand and foot of Constantine. The fragments dwarf him; the grief is theatrical and completely sincere. Fuseli had just left Italy in 1778 after nearly a decade studying the antique, and he came away convinced that ancient sculpture wasn't a model to copy but an emotional hammer. This red-chalk sheet became his most famous drawing, a manifesto of Romantic sublime, and now lives at the Kunsthaus Zürich.

Futsuka_Zuki_by_Kawai_Gyokudō.jpg.title: Futsuka Zuki by Kawai Gyokudō
Futsuka_Zuki_by_Kawai_Gyokudō.jpg.description: New Moon , Sumi and color on silk, hanging scroll, the first prize of Tokyo industry exhibition in 1907.

source.canonical_title: File:Futsuka Zuki by Kawai Gyokudō.jpg
source.credit: National Museum of Modern Art, Tokyo

Futsuka_Zuki_by_Kawai_Gyokudō.jpg.story: A two-day moon, thin as a fingernail, hanging over mountains at dusk. Gyokudo painted Futsuka Zuki on silk in 1907 and took first prize at the Tokyo industry exhibition that year; it was the picture that made his national reputation. The scene is quiet to the point of near-emptiness, the kind of compression nihonga allowed: ink, a breath of colour, a sliver of sky. He was thirty-four, still working out how to fold his Maruyama-Shijo training into something new. This is where it clicked.

G._Caillebotte_-_Homme_portant_une_blous.title: G. Caillebotte - Homme portant une blouse

source.canonical_title: File:G. Caillebotte - Homme portant une blouse.jpg

title.fr: Le Père Magloire sur la route entre Saint-Clair et Etretat

source.canonical_title: File:G. Caillebotte - Intérieur.jpg
File:G. Caillebotte - L'Yerres, pluie.jpg
source.credit: Sidney and Lois Eskenazi Museum of Art Provenance Project

title.avk: Yerres kuksa bak muvara (trutca ke Caillebotte)

G._Caillebotte_-_Le_jardin_du_Petit_Genn.title: The Garden at Petit Gennevilliers in Winter
G._Caillebotte_-_Le_jardin_du_Petit_Genn.description: Le jardin du Petit Gennevilliers en hiver (1894) Private collection.

source.canonical_title: File:G. Caillebotte - Le jardin du Petit Gennevilliers en hiver.jpg

title.fr: Le jardin du Petit Gennevilliers en hiver (1894)
title.ja: プティ・ジャンヌヴィリエの庭、冬（1894）.

G._Caillebotte_-_Le_jardin_du_Petit_Genn.story: This is one of the last things Caillebotte painted. The garden at Petit-Gennevilliers stripped down for winter: bare branches, cold light, the glasshouse shut up. In February 1894 he caught a chill working outdoors here, developed pulmonary congestion and died on the 21st, aged forty-five. He was the Impressionists' quiet benefactor; his Monets, Cezannes and Renoirs, bequeathed to the French state, became the seed of the Musee d'Orsay collection. This winter garden is a valediction he did not know he was writing.

G._Caillebotte_-_Nasturces.jpg.title: Nasturces (1892)

source.canonical_title: File:G. Caillebotte - Nasturces.jpg

G._Caillebotte_-_Nasturces.jpg.story: Nasturtiums, painted at Petit-Gennevilliers in 1892, two years before Caillebotte's sudden death. No figures, no architecture, just a close-up tangle of round leaves and orange-red flowers worked in short, dancing brushstrokes. By this point the one-time painter of rainy Parisian streets had turned almost entirely to his garden, and the canvases had shrunk and warmed. The picture has passed through private hands ever since.

G._Caillebotte_-_Un_balcon_(1880).jpg.title: Balcony, Boulevard Haussmann
G._Caillebotte_-_Un_balcon_(1880).jpg.description: Gustave Caillebotte: Un balcon au 31 Bd Haussmann, domicile du peintre

source.canonical_title: File:G. Caillebotte - Un balcon (1880).jpg

G._Caillebotte_-_Un_balcon_(1880).jpg.story: The other Haussmann balcony painting, made the same year. This time Caillebotte opens the view outward: the balcony frames the intersection below, trees soften the edges, and you can almost hear the traffic. The address was his own, 31 boulevard Haussmann. Together with its companion piece, this canvas belongs to a small Parisian project about what it feels like to stand six stories up and watch the city's new geometry unfold. Critics in 1880 were not sure what to do with pictures that had so much railing and so little anecdote.

G._Caillebotte_-_Villas_à_Trouville.jpg.title: Villas at Trouville

source.canonical_title: File:G. Caillebotte - Villas à Trouville.jpg

title.ja: トゥルヴィーユの別荘

description.ja: トゥルヴィーユの別荘

G._Caillebotte_-_Villas_à_Trouville.jpg.story: By 1884 Caillebotte had largely decamped from Paris to Petit-Gennevilliers, and he was spending parts of summer on the Normandy coast. From a cliff above Trouville he painted this plunging view of sea and sky, using the same steep, slightly vertiginous perspective he had invented for his city streets. The foreground is thickly loaded; the distant water is whispered on. It now hangs at the Cleveland Museum of Art. You can feel him applying Parisian tricks to pure landscape, and you can feel him starting to care less about people.

Gathering_Bamboo_Shoots,_by_Suzuki_Harun.title: Gathering Bamboo Shoots, by Suzuki Harunobu, 1765

source.canonical_title: File:Gathering Bamboo Shoots, by Suzuki Harunobu, 1765.jpg

copyright.usage_terms: Creative Commons Zero, Public Domain Dedication

Gauguin_-_Bretonne.jpg.title: Breton Girl

source.canonical_title: File:Gauguin - Bretonne.jpg

Gauguin_-_Bretonne.jpg.story: A young Breton girl in a stiff white coiffe and dark bodice, painted during Gauguin's first long stay in Pont-Aven in the summer of 1886. The brushwork is still Impressionist-loose, but you can already feel him reaching for something flatter and more iconic. He'd come to Brittany partly because it was cheap, partly because the peasant Catholicism felt, to him, primitive and unspoiled. Within two years he'd be painting those same coiffes in blazing unmodulated color. This one still keeps its feet in the 1880s.

Gauguin_Huttes_sous_les_arbres.jpg.title: Huts under the Trees

source.canonical_title: File:Gauguin Huttes sous les arbres.jpg

Gauguin_Huttes_sous_les_arbres.jpg.story: Huts, palm shade, a dog maybe, heat pressing down through the leaves. Gauguin painted this on Martinique in 1887, a detour he made with the painter Charles Laval after a miserable stint digging on the Panama Canal to pay their way. He caught dysentery and malaria and had to crawl back to France by autumn, but the handful of Martinique canvases changed him. The tropical palette and flattened foliage feed directly into everything that comes after. It's now in the Van Gogh Museum in Amsterdam.

General_Sir_David_Baird_Discovering_the_.title: General Sir David Baird Discovering the Body of Sultan Tippoo Sahib
General_Sir_David_Baird_Discovering_the_.description: Painting titled "General Sir David Baird Discovering the Body of Sultan Tippoo Sahib after having Captured Seringapatam, on the 4th May, 1799". Oil on canvas. 348.50 x 267.90 cm; Framed: 398.30 x 322.70 x 20.00 cm. Presented by Irvine Chalmers Watson, received 1985. Painted after Baird's death.

source.canonical_title: File:General Sir David Baird Discovering the Body of Sultan Tippoo Sahib.jpg

General_Sir_David_Baird_Discovering_the_.story: Wilkie's huge late history piece, painted for the Baird family four decades after the event. Seringapatam has just fallen in May 1799; Baird stands on the stone steps of the sally port in his white breeches and red-fronted coat, sword lowered, one arm flung wide as lantern-light picks out the corpse of Tipu Sultan at his feet. Wilkie goes full Rembrandt with the darkness, crowds the edges with looters, sepoys, a Highlander holding a torch, and a boy squinting up from the gloom. It is imperial propaganda, obviously, but painted with real theatrical conviction. National Galleries of Scotland.

Gentileschi,_Artemisia_-_Esther_before_A.title: Esther before Ahasuerus

source.canonical_title: File:Gentileschi, Artemisia - Esther before Ahasuerus - c. 1628–1635.jpg
source.credit: Metropolitan Museum of Art, online collection (The Met object ID 436453)

Gentileschi,_Artemisia_-_Esther_before_A.story: Queen Esther, mid-faint, sags into the arms of two maids as the Persian king rises from his throne — the instant she breaks protocol to plead for her people. Artemisia puts the court in contemporary Venetian dress and, X-rays revealed, painted out a boy with a restraining dog that would have echoed Veronese. Elinor Dorrance Ingersoll gave the canvas to the Metropolitan Museum of Art in 1969.

Gentileschi-Lucrezia-Potsdam.jpg.title: The Rape of Lucretia

source.canonical_title: File:Gentileschi-Lucrezia-Potsdam.jpg

Gentileschi-Lucrezia-Potsdam.jpg.story: Tarquin pins Lucretia's wrist as she twists away, the sword already half-raised — Artemisia painted the Roman matron three times, and this is the violent moment rather than the suicide. Frederick the Great bought it out of the Farnese holdings at Capodimonte in the 1750s for his Neues Palais. A 2019 restoration stripped back later overpaint and recovered Tarquin's original face.

Gentileschi-allegoria.jpg.title: Allegory of Painting

source.canonical_title: File:Gentileschi-allegoria.jpg

Gentileschi-allegoria.jpg.story: A nude woman sleeps on her side amid the apparatus of a studio — palette, brushes, compass, a theatrical mask for imitation — as if Painting itself had dozed off mid-shift. The canvas surfaced with an Artemisia attribution in 1988, but connoisseurs have wavered since; some now assign it to an anonymous Neapolitan of the mid-century. It hangs at the Musée de Tessé in Le Mans, quietly disputed.

Georges_Seurat,_Seated_Nude,_Study_for_U.title: Seated Nude: Study for 'Bathers at Asnières', 1883
Georges_Seurat,_Seated_Nude,_Study_for_U.description: Seated Nude, Study for Une Baignade by Georges Seurat, 1883, National Gallery of Scotland

source.canonical_title: File:Georges Seurat, Seated Nude, Study for Une Baignade, 1883, Scottish National Gallery.jpg

Georges_Seurat,_Seated_Nude,_Study_for_U.story: A study for one of the most famous paintings in London - Bathers at Asnières - made the year before Seurat finished it. The model is hunched, a working-class body rendered in soft crayon and chalk, the contours blurring into the paper's grain. Seurat made dozens of these preparatory studies in 1883; the Scottish National Gallery in Edinburgh holds this one.

Georges_Seurat,_c.1879-81,_Vase_of_Flowe.title: Vase of Flowers
Georges_Seurat,_c.1879-81,_Vase_of_Flowe.description: Georges Seurat, c.1879-81, Vase of Flowers ( Vase de Fleurs, Bouquet dans un Vase ), oil on canvas, 46.3 x 38.5 cm, Fogg Museum

source.canonical_title: File:Georges Seurat, c.1879-81, Vase of Flowers, oil on canvas, 46.3 x 38.5 cm, Fogg Museum.jpg

Georges_Seurat,_c.1879-81,_Vase_of_Flowe.story: Seurat rarely painted flowers, which makes this small bouquet a curiosity. The petals are loose, the background brushy, the whole thing feels closer to Manet than to the pointillist he was about to become. Painted around 1879-81, before the dots took over his practice. Oil on canvas, 46.3 by 38.5 cm, now at the Fogg Museum in Cambridge.

Georges_Seurat_-_Landscape_at_Saint-Ouen.title: Landscape at Saint-Ouen

source.canonical_title: File:Georges Seurat - Landscape at Saint-Ouen PC 7.jpg

Georges_Seurat_-_Landscape_at_Saint-Ouen.story: A palm-sized panel, painted along the Seine on the edge of Paris when Seurat was about nineteen. Warm brown wood grain shows through the brushstrokes because he hadn't primed it - speed mattered more than finish. He called these little boards croquetons and made roughly seventy of them, training his eye on light before he ever thought of dots. This one, from about 1878-79, now lives at the Met.

Georges_Seurat_-_Les_Poseuses.jpg.title: The Models

source.canonical_title: File:Georges Seurat - Les Poseuses.jpg

Georges_Seurat_-_Les_Poseuses.jpg.story: Critics sneered that pointillism was cold, mechanical, unable to paint a living body. So Seurat painted three nude models in the corner of his own studio, with La Grande Jatte propped against the back wall as a cheeky inside joke. Same model, three poses: standing, sitting, from behind. Stockings, a green umbrella, and a bright red parasol litter the floor. He worked on it from 1886 to 1888 and showed it at the fourth Salon des Indépendants that spring. It now lives at the Barnes Foundation in Philadelphia.

Georges_Seurat_-_View_of_Fort_Samson.jpg.story: Summer 1885. Seurat took the train to Grandcamp on the Normandy coast and painted this old fort perched above the Channel. The sea is a patient blue haze, the grass a weave of green and violet touches, and the whole thing feels less like a place than a vibration. He was refining the dot technique he'd tried out in Bathers at Asnières and would soon unleash on La Grande Jatte. Small canvas, big quiet. It now hangs in the Hermitage in St. Petersburg.

Georges_Seurat_019.jpg.title: The Circus

source.canonical_title: File:Georges Seurat 019.jpg
source.credit: The Yorck Project (2002) 10.000 Meisterwerke der Malerei (DVD-ROM), distributed by DIRECTMEDIA Publishing GmbH. ISBN : 3936122202 .

Georges_Seurat_019.jpg.story: A bareback rider springs off a white horse. A clown tumbles in the foreground. The audience sits stacked in tidy tiers, utterly still, as if watching a physics diagram. Seurat was chasing a theory that line direction controls emotion: upward strokes for joy, horizontals for calm. He died in March 1891 at thirty-one, probably of diphtheria, before finishing it. The unvarnished canvas went straight from the easel to that year's Salon des Indépendants, and now hangs at the Musée d'Orsay.

Georges_Seurat_026.jpg.title: The Seine at La Grande Jatte

source.canonical_title: File:Georges Seurat 026.jpg
source.credit: The Yorck Project (2002) 10.000 Meisterwerke der Malerei (DVD-ROM), distributed by DIRECTMEDIA Publishing GmbH. ISBN : 3936122202 .

title.fr: La Seine à la Grande Jatte - Printemps
title.es: El Sena en la Grande Jatte
title.de: Die Seine an der Grand Jatte, Frühling
title.zh: 春天，塞纳河上的大碗岛

Georges_Seurat_026.jpg.story: Back to the island, but quieter this time. No bustles, no top hats, just the Seine slipping past a bend of grass and a few sailboats leaning into the breeze. Seurat painted it in 1888, after he'd already made his giant Sunday statement; here he's letting the place breathe. The dots are tighter, the palette cooler, the mood closer to a held breath. Grande Jatte was still a working-class getaway on the edge of Paris, about four miles downstream from Notre-Dame.

Georges_Seurat_048.jpg.title: The Diggers

source.canonical_title: File:Georges Seurat 048.jpg
source.credit: The Yorck Project (2002) 10.000 Meisterwerke der Malerei (DVD-ROM), distributed by DIRECTMEDIA Publishing GmbH. ISBN : 3936122202 .

Georges_Seurat_048.jpg.story: Workmen breaking ground in a raw Paris suburb, shovels swinging, the earth turned over in broad flat strokes. Seurat painted Les Terrassiers around 1883, drawn to laborers the way Millet had been a generation earlier but flattening them into near-geometric blocks. It's a pre-pointillist canvas - no dots yet, just the patient crosshatched brushwork he called balayé.

Georges_de_La_Tour,_The_Fortune_Teller.j.title: The Fortune Teller

source.canonical_title: File:Georges de La Tour, The Fortune Teller.jpg

Georges_de_La_Tour,_The_Fortune_Teller.j.story: A rich young man has his palm read by an old gypsy woman while three of her accomplices quietly lift his purse, cut his medal, and pick his pocket. The inscription in the background gives La Tour's name and the town of Luneville. The picture's authenticity was fought over for decades after it surfaced in the 1940s; the Metropolitan Museum bought it in 1960 amid a public uproar in France over its export. Today nobody doubts it, and almost nobody can stop looking at the thief's sidelong eyes.

Georges_de_La_Tour_-_Newlyborn_infant_-_.description: Virgin and Child with Saint Anne

Georges_de_La_Tour_-_Rixe_de_musiciens_-.title: The Musicians' Brawl
Georges_de_La_Tour_-_Rixe_de_musiciens_-.artist: Georges de La Tour (French, 1593 - 1652) (1593 - 1652) – artist (French) Details on Google Art Project

source.canonical_title: File:Georges de La Tour - Rixe de musiciens - Google Art Project.jpg
source.credit: fgHS5adsdubLnw at Google Cultural Institute maximum zoom level

Georges_de_La_Tour_-_Rixe_de_musiciens_-.story: Two street musicians lunge at each other over a dropped hurdy-gurdy. One brandishes a knife; the other squeezes a lemon into his rival's eye. La Tour painted this about 1625, before his famous candlelit nocturnes, and the daylight is merciless - every wrinkle, every snarled tooth, every greasy strand of hair. It's at the Getty in Los Angeles, where the violence still reads across four hundred years.

Georges_de_La_Tour_-_Smoker.jpg.title: The Smoker with Pipe

source.canonical_title: File:Georges de La Tour - Smoker.jpg

Georges_de_La_Tour_-_Smoker.jpg.story: A man in a feathered cap blows on the embers of his clay pipe; the coal flares, his cheeks puff, and the light picks out the lit end, the ribbon at his throat, and the whites of his eyes. La Tour painted a handful of these single-figure genre pieces late in life. The flame here is tiny and the subject nothing at all, but the picture is almost a demonstration of what he had spent thirty years learning to do with a single point of fire.

Georges_de_La_Tour_-_The_Magdalen_with_t.title: The Magdalen with the Smoking Flame

source.canonical_title: File:Georges de La Tour - The Magdalen with the Smoking Flame - Google Art Project.jpg

Georges_de_La_Tour_-_The_Repentant_Magda.title: The Repentant Magdalen

source.canonical_title: File:Georges de La Tour - The Repentant Magdalen - Google Art Project.jpg
source.credit: 2QGwZrE8Px8k9A at Google Cultural Institute maximum zoom level

Georges_de_La_Tour_-_The_Repentant_Magda.story: Mary Magdalen, a skull in her lap, stares into a mirror lit by a single candle. The flame doubles in the glass, and her face is half shadow. La Tour painted several versions in the late 1630s; this one, at the National Gallery of Art in Washington, is dated around 1635-40. Look for the pearl necklace tossed aside on the table - the worldly life she's in the act of leaving.

Georges_de_La_Tour_009.jpg.title: Penitent Mary Magdalene (Magdalena Wrightsman)

source.canonical_title: File:Georges de La Tour 009.jpg
source.credit: The Yorck Project (2002) 10.000 Meisterwerke der Malerei (DVD-ROM), distributed by DIRECTMEDIA Publishing GmbH. ISBN : 3936122202 . https://www.metmuseum.org/collection/the-collection-online/search/436839

Georges_de_La_Tour_009.jpg.story: The Magdalene sits at a table, her hand resting on a skull, her face half-turned toward the flame of an oil lamp. A mirror doubles the light and the skull. La Tour painted at least four versions of the penitent Magdalene, of which this one, once in the Wrightsman collection and now at the Metropolitan Museum, is perhaps the most tender. Everything earthly has been set down: the jewellery on the floor, the hand on the bone. The silence is the subject.

Georges_de_La_Tour_022.jpg.title: The Dream of Saint Joseph

source.canonical_title: File:Georges de La Tour 022.jpg

Georges_de_La_Tour_022.jpg.story: An angel, lit from within, leans toward the sleeping Joseph and touches his arm; a single candle on the table behind supplies most of the visible light. La Tour strips the Nativity's supporting miracle to two figures, one flame, and a great black ground. For centuries the picture hung in Nantes as a Honthorst or an anonymous Caravaggist; only after Hermann Voss's 1915 rediscovery of La Tour did it return to its real author. The Musee des Beaux-Arts de Nantes owns it.

Georges_de_La_Tour_044.jpg.title: Job mocked by his Wife

source.canonical_title: File:Georges de La Tour 044.jpg
source.credit: The Yorck Project (2002) 10.000 Meisterwerke der Malerei (DVD-ROM), distributed by DIRECTMEDIA Publishing GmbH. ISBN : 3936122202 .

Georges_de_La_Tour_044.jpg.story: Job sits naked on his dunghill, hands bound, body blotched with sores; his wife looms over him by candlelight, a cup in her hand, mocking. The painting turned up in a village church in Epinal in the 1930s and became one of the anchors of the La Tour rediscovery. Art historians still argue whether she is tormenting her husband or offering him comfort. The flame, shielded by her fingers, throws a glow across her red dress and his stricken face and leaves the rest of the world black.

Gerechtigkeit-1537.jpg.title: Justice

source.canonical_title: File:Gerechtigkeit-1537.jpg

Gerechtigkeit-1537.jpg.story: Cranach paints Justice as one of his signature long-limbed nudes: a pale woman balancing on a dark ground, blindfold gone, holding sword and scales with almost casual ease. The allegory was a staple of German courts and council halls in the 1530s, a reminder to magistrates of what hung over their heads. Cranach's version trades civic gravity for his trademark cool sensuality — the transparent veil, the arch of the hip, the small head on the narrow shoulders. The winged serpent signature tucks into a corner. Virtue as pin-up, essentially, and the Wittenberg workshop could not make them fast enough.

Gerhard_von_Kügelgen_portrait_of_Friedr.title: The Painter Caspar David Friedrich

source.canonical_title: File:Gerhard von Kügelgen portrait of Friedrich.jpg
source.credit: 1. allposters.com 2. Bildindex der Kunst und Architektur : object 20146333 – image file XKH141499a.jpg 3. Bridgeman Art Library : Object 141499

Gerhard_von_Kügelgen_portrait_of_Friedr.story: Painted around the time the two men were neighbours in Dresden, this is the face behind every fogbound Rügen shore and ruined abbey. Kügelgen gives Friedrich a heavy greatcoat, an unruly red beard, a green waistcoat glimpsed at the throat, and eyes that don't quite meet yours. The background is bare, barely-there landscape, as though the sitter were already half dissolved into one of his own paintings. It has become the definitive image of German Romanticism's quiet monk, partly because so few other portraits of Friedrich survive.

GericaultHorseman.jpg.story: A cavalry officer wheels his terrified horse mid-charge, sabre up, smoke boiling behind him. Géricault was twenty-one and almost unknown when he submitted this to the 1812 Salon; it won him a gold medal. The diagonal is pure theatre: horse lunging one way, rider twisted the other, eyes locked on something off-canvas. Napoleon's Grande Armée was marching into Russia as visitors filed past it. Two years later Géricault painted the officer's broken counterpart, a wounded cuirassier limping from the field. The Charging Chasseur hangs in the Louvre.

Gerome--Haggin--Horse-Market.jpg.title: 'The Horse Market'
Gerome--Haggin--Horse-Market.jpg.description: The Horse Market (1867) by Jean-Léon Gérôme, Haggin Museum, Stockton, CA

source.canonical_title: File:Gerome--Haggin--Horse-Market.jpg

Gerome--Haggin--Horse-Market.jpg.story: A chestnut Arabian is trotted out for inspection, its polished coat catching the Cairo light. Gérôme built the architecture behind it by stitching together two photographs, both taken not in Egypt but in Yemen, one in Moka and one in Hodeidah. The latticed window he grafted on is Egyptian in style but sits on supports that look Indonesian. The whole scene is an invented composite, dressed to look real. It has lived at the Haggin Museum in Stockton, California, since the 1930s. Painted in 1867.

Gerome--Haggin--Saddle-Bazaar.jpg.title: 'The Saddle Bazaar, Cairo'
Gerome--Haggin--Saddle-Bazaar.jpg.description: The Saddle Bazaar, Cairo (1883) by Jean-Léon Gérôme, Haggin Museum, Stockton, CA

source.canonical_title: File:Gerome--Haggin--Saddle-Bazaar.jpg

Gerome--Haggin--Saddle-Bazaar.jpg.story: The star of the picture is a white horse with a henna-stained mane, its tail dyed the same rusty orange. It's being sold by a bashi-bazouk to a Jewish merchant in a corner of Cairo that Gérôme built out of memory and studio props rather than direct observation. Saddles and bridles hang on the walls; the light is the hard flat sun of North Africa. Painted in 1883, one of four Gérômes at the Haggin Museum in Stockton, California, a collection assembled by the museum's founders.

Gerome--Haggin--The-Artist-and-His-Model.title: The Artist and His Model
Gerome--Haggin--The-Artist-and-His-Model.description: The Artist and His Model (1895) by Jean-Léon Gérôme, Haggin Museum, Stockton, CA

source.canonical_title: File:Gerome--Haggin--The-Artist-and-His-Model.jpg

Gerome--Haggin--The-Artist-and-His-Model.story: Gérôme, in the later half of his career, turned sculptor and liked to paint himself at the chisel. Here he's tucked into his studio with his favourite model, Emma Dupont, shaping a tinted version of his Tanagra figure (the finished marble holds a little Hoop Dancer in her palm). The room is a clutter of plaster casts and studio kit, all the colours echoing in blues, pinks and whites. He was seventy-one and still insisting on working from life. Painted in 1895, now at the Haggin Museum in Stockton, California.

Gerome--Haggin--Unfolding-the-Holy-Flag..title: 'The Standing Bearer, Unfolding the Holy Flag'
Gerome--Haggin--Unfolding-the-Holy-Flag..description: The Standing Bearer, Unfolding the Holy Flag (1876) by Jean-Léon Gérôme, Haggin Museum, Stockton, CA

source.canonical_title: File:Gerome--Haggin--Unfolding-the-Holy-Flag.jpg

Gerome--Haggin--Unfolding-the-Holy-Flag..story: A doorkeeper in Tuareg robes stands before a carved door and shakes out a green banner inscribed with Arabic calligraphy, most likely verses from the Qur'an. Gérôme painted this in 1876, during years when French readers were absorbing accounts of Saharan explorers and missionaries being killed in the desert. The banner is a kind of threshold, and so is the doorway behind it. The canvas is small, about half a metre tall, and has lived at the Haggin Museum in Stockton, California, since the 1930s.

Gerome_-_An_Idyll,_1852.jpg.title: An Idyll (Daphnis and Chloe)

source.canonical_title: File:Gerome - An Idyll, 1852.jpg

Gerome_-_An_Idyll,_1852.jpg.story: Also called Daphnis and Chloe, after the Greek pastoral novel. Two shepherd lovers recline on a rock in a wooded glade; she leans into him, a small goat nuzzles their feet, a basket of fruit tips beside them. Sunlight filters through leaves, everything stilled to the softness of a tapestry. Gérôme was still in his late twenties, not yet the hard-edged Orientalist of the next decade; this is him doing Salon pastoral in the manner of his teacher Gleyre. The picture dates from 1852.

Gerome_venus.jpg.title: Gerome venus

source.canonical_title: File:Gerome venus.jpg

Gerome_venus.jpg.story: Venus breaks the surface on a foam-lit swell, and a whole traffic jam of putti tumbles around her. One clutches a golden apple, winking at the myth of Paris. Gérôme picked the instant of birth itself rather than the usual landfall-on-Cyprus routine favoured by Botticelli and company. The palette stays cool and pearly, the kind of dawn you see before the beach wakes up. Painted in 1890 on a tall, narrow canvas, it sold at auction in 1991 and hangs today in a private collection.

Gerrit_van_Honthorst_-_De_koppelaarster..title: The Matchmaker or The Procuress

source.canonical_title: File:Gerrit van Honthorst - De koppelaarster.jpg

Gerrit_van_Honthorst_-_De_koppelaarster..story: Honthorst stages this like a Caravaggio he half-remembers from Rome: a hidden candle throws gold across a grinning girl in plumes and a low bodice, while the old procuress leans from the shadows with a schoolmarmish finger-wag that really means get on with it. The lute on the right is the polite euphemism; the coins slid across the green baize are the transaction. What sells the picture is the faces. The client in feathered cap is still a silhouette, caught at the instant of being persuaded. A whole genre of Dutch brothel scenes lives in that pause.

source.canonical_title: File:Gérôme, Achat d'une esclave, 1857 (5613508015).jpg

Gérôme,_The_Two_Majesties_1883.jpg.title: The Two Majesties

source.canonical_title: File:Gérôme, The Two Majesties 1883.jpg

Gérôme,_The_Two_Majesties_1883.jpg.story: A lion on a rocky outcrop stares west at the setting sun — the two majesties of the title. Gérôme painted lions obsessively in his later career, often from specimens at the Paris zoo and from his own photographic studies, and he'd already turned to sculpture by this point, modelling the same beasts in bronze. The picture is almost kitsch and knows it: the animal's silhouette squared against a blazing sky, the romantic shorthand for sovereignty. Ponce Museum of Art, Puerto Rico.

Gérôme--Execution_of_Marshall_Ney--186.title: The Execution of Marshal Ney
Gérôme--Execution_of_Marshall_Ney--186.description: Jean-Léon Gérôme, The Execution of Marshall Ney, 1868, Graves Art Gallery, Sheffield.

source.canonical_title: File:Gérôme--Execution of Marshall Ney--1868--Sheffield.jpg

Gérôme--Execution_of_Marshall_Ney--186.story: Michel Ney, one of Napoleon's marshals, was shot in December 1815 for rallying to the returning Emperor during the Hundred Days. Gérôme shows the aftermath: Ney face-down in the Paris mud at the Luxembourg, his hat still beside him, the firing squad marching off in the distance. A scribbled Bonapartist graffito on the wall has already been half-erased. No speeches, no noble last words, just a body on wet stones and the executioners leaving. Critics found it shockingly cold; it remains one of the most unsparing execution pictures of the century. Sheffield's Graves Art Gallery now owns it.

Gérôme--Femme_circassienne_voilée--Ve.title: 'Veiled Circassian Beauty'
Gérôme--Femme_circassienne_voilée--Ve.description: Jean-Léon Gérôme, Femme circassienne voilée, or Veiled Circassian Beauty (1876), Qatar Museums Authority, Doha. Auctioned in 2008 at Christie's for 2,057,250 GBP.

source.canonical_title: File:Gér��me--Femme circassienne voilée--Veiled Circassian Beauty--1876.jpg

Gérôme--Femme_circassienne_voilée--Ve.story: A young woman in a fez and gauzy white veil meets the viewer's eye over the fabric she holds to her face. Circassian women — from the North Caucasus, often trafficked into Ottoman households — were a staple Orientalist fantasy in 19th-century Paris, and Gérôme knew exactly what he was selling. The picture is small, tight, and immaculate: just the head, the head covering, a blank backdrop. Qatar Museums bought it at Christie's in 2008 for over two million pounds. Centuries of projection, distilled into a single gaze.

Gérôme_-_Cave_Canem.jpg.title: Cave Canem

source.canonical_title: File:Gérôme - Cave Canem.jpg

Gérôme_-_Cave_Canem.jpg.story: 'Beware the dog' — the mosaic greeting at the threshold of a Pompeian house. Gérôme paints the famous doorway with a real chained dog barking beneath its tiled warning, collapsing two millennia into a single gag. He'd been to Pompeii, sketched the mosaics, and loved this kind of winking archaeology: the ancient world as something you could almost ring the doorbell of. Small, sharp, funny — and like most of Gérôme's late Roman scenes, obsessive about getting the tesserae right.

Gérôme_-_L'entrée_du_Christ_à_Jérus.title: Entry of the Christ in Jerusalem

source.canonical_title: File:Gérôme - L'entrée du Christ à Jérusalem - cadre.jpg

Gérôme_-_L'entrée_du_Christ_à_Jérus.story: Painted when Gérôme was in his seventies: Christ rides into Jerusalem on the donkey, palm-wavers press around him, but the mood is subdued rather than triumphant. The colonnaded street and the sun-bleached stone architecture are Gérôme's Middle East reconstructed from his many trips through Egypt and the Holy Land — he wanted the city to look like a place with dust in it, not a stage set. It lives at the Musée Georges-Garret in Vesoul, the town where he was born.

Gérôme_-_Painting_Breathes_Life_into_S.title: The Antique Pottery Painter: Sculpturæ vitam insufflat pictura (Painting Breathes Life into Sculpture)

source.canonical_title: File:Gérôme - Painting Breathes Life into Sculpture v1.jpg

Gérôme_-_Painting_Breathes_Life_into_S.story: The Latin motto running across the title — Sculpturae vitam insufflat pictura — was Gérôme's pictorial manifesto. A young woman in a Tanagra workshop paints color onto small terracottas of his own Hoop Dancer while customers browse the shelves. It's a dig at the whitewashed plaster-cast orthodoxy of his day: Greek statues, he insisted, were painted, and modern sculpture should follow. This is the first of two 1893 versions and now lives at the Art Gallery of Ontario. Every figure in the shop is female — artist, shopkeeper, clients — making the whole economy of small polychrome art a feminine affair.

Gérôme_-_Summer_Afternoon_on_a_Lake.jp.title: Summer Afternoon on a Lake

source.canonical_title: File:Gérôme - Summer Afternoon on a Lake.jpg

Gérôme_-_Summer_Afternoon_on_a_Lake.jp.story: A late, unusually quiet Gérôme — no gladiators, no harems, no marble girls waking up. Two figures drift in a skiff on glassy water with a wooded bank folding away behind them; the sun is low, the air hazy. The man who spent his career polishing archaeological tableaux is suddenly after the same hour Monet was chasing, only through an academic's precise eye. Painted around 1895, when Gérôme was in his seventies and splitting time between Paris and landscape sketching trips.

Gérôme_Eminence_grise_1873.jpg.title: The Grey Eminence
Gérôme_Eminence_grise_1873.jpg.description: Grey Eminence, François Leclerc du Tremblay (1577–1638), the right-hand man of Cardinal Richelieu

source.canonical_title: File:Gérôme Eminence grise 1873.jpg
source.credit: Scan from the original work : Richelieu: Art and Power , 2002 exhibition catalog, edited by Hilliard Todd Goldfarb, p. 381. Montreal : Montreal Museum of Fine Arts ; Cologne : Wallraf-Richartz-Museum – Fondation Corboud ; Ghent, Belgium : Snoeck-Ducaju & Zoon. ISBN 9789053494073 .

Gérôme_Eminence_grise_1873.jpg.story: On the grand staircase of Cardinal Richelieu's palace, a shabby Capuchin friar reads his breviary while courtiers bow and scrape on either side. This is François Leclerc du Tremblay — Père Joseph — Richelieu's confidant and the original 'grey eminence', the man pulling strings from behind the robes. Gérôme wrings the whole picture out of that contrast: sober brown habit against an avalanche of silk, feathers, and satin; downcast eyes against wary, hungry ones. The flattery is elaborate and the friar barely registers it. A tiny essay in how real power rarely announces itself.

Giaele_e_Sisara_(ca.1620)_-_Artemisia_Ge.title: Jael and Sisera

source.canonical_title: File:Giaele e Sisara (ca.1620) - Artemisia Gentileschi (Museum of Fine Arts, Budapest).jpg
source.credit: Web Gallery of Art : Image Info about artwork wga QS:P11807,"m/g/gentiles/artemisi/jaelsise"

Giaele_e_Sisara_(ca.1620)_-_Artemisia_Ge.story: Jael steadies a tent peg above the sleeping Canaanite general's temple, hammer cocked, her mouth set. Artemisia condenses the biblical killing to two bodies and a single decision, the drapery falling in hard diagonals across Sisera's inert arm. The Budapest Museum of Fine Arts acquired the canvas in 1975, where it carries inventory number 75.11.

Giorgione_-_Pala_di_Castelfranco.jpg.title: Madonna and Child between St. Francis and St. Nicasius

source.canonical_title: File:Giorgione - Pala di Castelfranco.jpg
source.credit: The Yorck Project (2002) 10.000 Meisterwerke der Malerei (DVD-ROM), distributed by DIRECTMEDIA Publishing GmbH. ISBN : 3936122202 .

title.it: Pala di Castelfranco: Madonna col il Bambino tra San Francesco e San Nicasio
title.de: Altar von Castelfranco, Szene: Thronende Madonna mit dem hl.Nicasius und dem Hl. Franziskus

Giorgione_-_Pala_di_Castelfranco.jpg.story: Giorgione's hometown altarpiece, commissioned for a chapel in Castelfranco Veneto, rewrites the sacra conversazione by pushing the Madonna up onto an improbably tall plinth so she seems to float against open sky. Below, a silver-armoured knight (often identified as St Nicasius) and a brown-robed Franciscan stand on checkered marble like chess pieces on either side of a patron's tomb. The landscape behind, a dreamy Venetian countryside of towers and hazy hills, is doing as much devotional work as the figures. It is one of the few paintings nobody tries to take away from him.

Giorgione_-_Sleeping_Venus_-_Google_Art_.title: Sleeping Venus
Giorgione_-_Sleeping_Venus_-_Google_Art_.description: Although nude figures (such as Botticelli's "Birth of Venus") had been painted before this one, this is probably the first nude to show a figure simply as a depiction of a nude. It is named "Venus" but has no traditional attributes (such as Cupid) to indicate that it represents a goddess. It was a break from tradition, and set a new subject for the artist, resulting in 20th century works such as the nudes of Francis Bacon and Henry Moore.

source.canonical_title: File:Giorgione - Sleeping Venus - Google Art Project 2.jpg
source.credit: Google Art Project: Home – pic Maximum resolution.

title.th: วีนัสหลับ

Giorgione_-_Sleeping_Venus_-_Google_Art_.story: A naked woman asleep in a meadow, pillowed on red silk, completely at ease under an open sky. Giorgione painted her around 1510 and died of plague before he could finish the landscape and drapery; his younger friend Titian stepped in to complete the picture. There's no Cupid, no shell, nothing to say she's a goddess at all except the pose. Every reclining nude that follows, from Titian's own Venus of Urbino to Manet's Olympia, is answering this quiet prototype. She's now in the Gemäldegalerie in Dresden.

Girl_Carrying_a_Basket_by_Winslow_Homer,.title: Girl Carrying a Basket

source.canonical_title: File:Girl Carrying a Basket by Winslow Homer, 1882.png
source.credit: National Gallery of Art, Washington DC

Girl_Carrying_a_Basket_by_Winslow_Homer,.story: A girl in a long dress carries a basket across her hip, walking through a field with the grave, self-contained look Homer gave his English fishing-village figures. He painted this in 1882 during his long stay at Cullercoats, a windswept fishing community on England's North Sea coast, where he lived from spring 1881 through late 1882. The Cullercoats year changed him: the figures got bigger, the palette cooler, the whole project heavier. Everything after this is the famous late Homer.

Giuseppe_Arcimboldo_Fire_Kunsthistorisch.title: Fire
Giuseppe_Arcimboldo_Fire_Kunsthistorisch.description: The allegory of Fire combines objects that are related to fire. The cheek is formed by a large firestone, the neck and chin are formed by a burning candle and an oil lamp, the nose and ear are contoured by firesteels; a blond moustache is formed by a crossed bundle of wood shavings for kindling, the eye is an extinguished candle stub, the forehead area is a wound-up fuse, the hair of the head forms a crown of blazing logs. The breast is composed of fire weapons: mortar and canon barrels together with the respective gunpowder shovel and a pistol barrel. Prominently positioned in the picture is the collar of the Order of the Golden Fleece , beneath which the imperial double-eagle can be seen: a clear reference to the Habsburg House and the beneficiary of the series, Emperor Maximilian II.

source.canonical_title: File:Giuseppe Arcimboldo Fire Kunsthistorisches Museum.jpg

Giuseppe_Arcimboldo_Fire_Kunsthistorisch.story: Fire is a face on the brink of combustion. A flint makes the cheek, a lit candle the chin, a burning oil lamp the throat, and the hair is literally ablaze. Across the chest Arcimboldo stacks cannon barrels, a mortar, and a pistol, with gunpowder shovels peeking out, an unmistakable nod to Habsburg military might. Hanging over it all is the collar of the Order of the Golden Fleece and the imperial double-eagle, dedicating the 1566 canvas to Emperor Maximilian II. A compliment with teeth.

Giuseppe_Bartolomeo_Chiari_-_Susannah_an.title: Susannah and the Elders
Giuseppe_Bartolomeo_Chiari_-_Susannah_an.description: The biblical book of Daniel tells of Susanna, a married woman who is spied upon by two old judges while bathing in her garden. They attempt to force themselves upon her, saying that if she does not submit, they will accuse her of adultery. With Daniel's assistance, Susanna's innocence is established, and the two elders are put to death. This painting depicts the unhappy woman as she tries to escape the advances and gazes of the men. The focus on her body testifies to her innocence and virtue, as truth was often symbolized by a nude woman, but was also meant to appeal to male patrons. The soft, luminous coloring is characteristic of the late Roman baroque style.

Giuseppe_Bartolomeo_Chiari_-_Susannah_an.story: Chiari takes the Old Testament shakedown and gives it the soft pink light of a Roman late-Baroque ceiling. The two judges loom from the left, one already grabbing Susanna's shoulder, the other hissing into his accomplice's ear while pointing off toward whoever might see; she twists away toward a trickling fountain, trying to hold her sheet. The story is about blackmail and false testimony, but Chiari is visibly more interested in the lit flesh and the cascading yellow satin than in the ethics, which is honest of him if not especially heroic.

Glazunov_by_Repin.jpg.story: Alexander Glazunov was twenty-two, already a published symphonist and the darling of St Petersburg's musical avant-garde, when Repin painted him in 1887. The composer slouches a little in his chair, hair tousled, gazing sideways with the half-distracted air of someone still hearing a theme. Repin liked to paint musicians he actually knew — Mussorgsky, Rubinstein, Borodin — and he and Glazunov moved in the same Mamontov-circle drawing rooms. The loose, almost sketchy brushwork of the jacket shows Repin at his most unbuttoned. The portrait is now held by the State Russian Museum.
