Goethe_Kügelgen.jpg.title: Portrait of Johann Wolfgang von Goethe

source.canonical_title: File:Goethe Kügelgen.jpg

title.de: Porträt von Johann Wolfgang von Goethe

Goethe_Kügelgen.jpg.story: Goethe at fifty-nine, painted in Dresden by his friend Kügelgen and not especially flattered for it. The poet looks tired, jowly, eyes slightly unequal, hair receding into a cloud. A crimson mantle is thrown over the dark coat, and the silver star on his chest is the Russian Order of St Anne, a reminder that Weimar's privy councillor moved in imperial circles. Goethe reportedly liked the picture; posterity has sometimes preferred the more idealised profiles, but this one has the honesty of a face seen across a dinner table.

Goltzius's_right_Hand.jpg.title: Goltzius's right Hand
Goltzius's_right_Hand.jpg.description: Goltzius's Right Hand, 1588 - Pen and brown ink ; 9 x 12 5/8 in. (23 x 32.2 cm) - Teylers Museum, Haarlem

source.canonical_title: File:Goltzius's right Hand.jpg
source.permission: Gemeinfreiheit

Goltzius's_right_Hand.jpg.story: Goltzius drew his own right hand — the one that made him famous across Europe — in pen and brown ink in 1588. The hand is visibly deformed: a childhood burn had fused the fingers, leaving it permanently clenched. He turned that disability into a flex, training the claw to produce some of the most virtuosic engraved lines of the sixteenth century. The drawing is at the Teylers Museum in Haarlem.

Gowy-atalanta-prado.jpg.title: Atalanta and Hippomenes (Ovid, Metamorphoses, X, 560-680)
Gowy-atalanta-prado.jpg.artist: After Peter Paul Rubens / Peter Paul Rubens / Jacob Peter Gowy

source.canonical_title: File:Gowy-atalanta-prado.jpg

Gowy-atalanta-prado.jpg.story: Philip IV wanted his new hunting lodge outside Madrid — the Torre de la Parada — papered with Ovid, and in 1636 he commissioned Rubens to design sixty-odd mythological scenes. Rubens, by then in his late fifties and riddled with gout, sketched the compositions on small oil panels and farmed the big canvases out to Antwerp's younger painters. Jacob Peter Gowy got Atalanta, caught mid-stride after Hippomenes has chucked the third golden apple — Aphrodite's trick to break her stride. Gowy signed it on the column at right. The panel Rubens painted for him to copy is in Rotterdam; this, the final version, hangs in the Prado.
Gowy-atalanta-prado.jpg.year_note: Rubens received the Torre de la Parada commission in 1636 and Gowy executed this canvas c. 1636-38 per the Prado catalogue. The input year 1635 predates the commission.

Goya_-_The_Garroted_Man.jpg.title: The Garroted Man

source.canonical_title: File:Goya - The Garroted Man.jpg

Goya_-_The_Garroted_Man.jpg.story: A man sits slumped against a wooden post, a crucifix clutched in stiffening fingers. The iron garrote has already done its work. A single tall candle burns at his feet, the only mercy in the cell. Goya etched this around 1778–1780, early in his career, long before the Caprichos or the Disasters. Spain still executed people this way into the 19th century. There's no title in elegant script, no moral caption — just the quiet, unglamorous fact of a state killing.

Goya_Maja_naga2.jpg.title: The Nude Maja

source.canonical_title: File:Goya Maja naga2.jpg
source.credit: The Nude Maja . On-line gallery . Museo del Prado (2012). Archived from the original on 2010-01-03 . Retrieved on 2013-04-07 .

title.th: La maja desnuda

Goya_Maja_naga2.jpg.story: She stares straight back at you, unembarrassed, arms folded behind her head on a rumple of silk. Goya made her around 1797–1800 for Manuel Godoy, the king's all-powerful minister, who kept her in a private cabinet paired with a clothed version that could be swapped in when company called. The model's identity has been argued over for two centuries; Pepita Tudó, Godoy's mistress, is the current best guess. The Inquisition later hauled Goya in to answer for her — specifically, for the pubic hair.

Goyō_Hashiguchi_(1915)_Yokugo_no_onna_(c.title: Goyō Hashiguchi (1915) Yokugo no onna (cropped and compressed) 01
Goyō_Hashiguchi_(1915)_Yokugo_no_onna_(c.description: Portrait of a Japanese woman after a bath. Colour woodcut print in the Shin-Hanga style, 40.1 x 26.1 cm

source.canonical_title: File:Goyō Hashiguchi (1915) Yokugo no onna (cropped and compressed) 01.jpg

Goyō_Hashiguchi_(1915)_Yokugo_no_onna_(c.story: Woman After the Bath, one of only fourteen prints Hashiguchi ever released. A young woman crouches on a low wooden platform, wringing a blue-patterned cloth into a red lacquer basin. Her hair is piled up in a loose knot, her skin flat and unshadowed in the shin-hanga manner, the background a single sheet of charcoal-grey textile. It is absurdly patient work: Hashiguchi supervised his own carvers and printers after falling out with the usual publisher, and he died at forty-one before most of his planned series ever left the studio.

Grant_Wood_-_American_Gothic_-_Google_Ar.title: American Gothic

source.canonical_title: File:Grant Wood - American Gothic - Google Art Project.jpg
source.credit: 5QEPm0jCc183Aw at Google Cultural Institute maximum zoom level

Grant_Wood_-_American_Gothic_-_Google_Ar.story: Wood spotted the house first — a little white frame cottage in Eldon, Iowa, with a pretentious pointed window lifted straight out of European Gothic. He sketched it on the back of an envelope, then went home to Cedar Rapids and cast the people he fancied ought to live there: his sister Nan, pinned into a colonial-print apron, and Dr. Byron McKeeby, the family dentist, clutching a three-tined hayfork that rhymes with the stitching on his overalls. They posed separately in Wood's studio, never together. When the painting won a bronze medal at the Art Institute of Chicago in 1930, Iowa farm wives were furious — they thought he was mocking them. Wood insisted he was painting his own people.

source.canonical_title: File:Guercino - Martirio dei Santi Giovanni e Paolo.jpg

Guercino_-_Martirio_dei_Santi_Giovanni_e.story: A quick pen-and-wash sketch rather than a finished painting - you can still see where Guercino dragged the brush and left the paper bare. An executioner stands back-to-us, sword dropped, hauling one kneeling saint forward by the hair while the other lies already beheaded in the corner. The squiggled curls and looping drapery are the shorthand of a draughtsman working at speed. Barbieri was nicknamed 'the squinter' after a childhood eye injury, and ran the leading Bolognese studio after Reni died; sheets like this are the private machinery behind the altarpieces.

Guo_Zhongshu-Traveling_on_the_River_in_S.title: Traveling on the River in Snow
Guo_Zhongshu-Traveling_on_the_River_in_S.date_created: latter half of the 10th century AD
Guo_Zhongshu-Traveling_on_the_River_in_S.description: Traveling on the River in Clearing Snow , by Guo Zhongshu (c. 910–977 AD). This painting shows a pair of Chinese cargo ships (with stern-mounted rudders) accompanied by a smaller craft. It is painted on silk and dated to the early Song Dynasty period (960–1279 AD).

source.canonical_title: File:Guo Zhongshu-Traveling on the River in Snow.jpg

Guo_Zhongshu-Traveling_on_the_River_in_S.story: A cargo junk in fine ruled line, its rigging drawn with the fussy precision of someone who actually understood how a stern-mounted rudder worked. Guo Zhongshu was a tenth-century scholar-official famous for jiehua - 'boundary painting' - the discipline of rendering ships and pavilions with a ruler and still making them feel atmospheric. The silk has darkened to the colour of old tea. A block of calligraphy and a cluster of red collectors' seals float beside the mast; the river itself is barely indicated, just a soft wash the boat seems to drift on.

Gustav_Bauernfeind_-_A_Street_Scene,_Dam.title: Gustav Bauernfeind - A Street Scene, Damascus (Sotheby's, ShafikGabrCollection) 001l2010
Gustav_Bauernfeind_-_A_Street_Scene,_Dam.description: A painting by Gustav Bauernfeind of a crowd in Damascus street.

source.canonical_title: File:Gustav Bauernfeind - A Street Scene, Damascus (Sotheby's, ShafikGabrCollection) 001l2010.jpg

Gustav_Bauernfeind_-_A_Street_Scene,_Dam.story: A Damascus souk under slatted wooden awnings: sunlight falling in bars across faces, vendors, and a wall of Ottoman stonework. Bauernfeind worked up scenes like this from on-the-spot studies, then built them in his studio with the precision of an architectural rendering. This canvas was in the Shafik Gabr collection of Orientalist painting and passed through Sotheby's in 2010. It is one of the pictures that, a century after his death in Jerusalem, pushed Bauernfeind's prices into the millions.

Gustav_Bauernfeind_-_At_the_Dome_of_the_.title: Gustav Bauernfeind - At the Dome of the Rock and the Fountain of Qayt Bay, Jerusalem (late 19thC) (Sotheby's) n11434-cwtmf-t1-02-a
Gustav_Bauernfeind_-_At_the_Dome_of_the_.description: A painting by Gustav Bauernfeind outside the Dome of the Rock in Jerusalem.

source.canonical_title: File:Gustav Bauernfeind - At the Dome of the Rock and the Fountain of Qayt Bay, Jerusalem (late 19thC) (Sotheby's) n11434-cwtmf-t1-02-a.jpg

Gustav_Bauernfeind_-_At_the_Dome_of_the_.story: By the time Bauernfeind painted this he was effectively a Jerusalem local, having moved his family there in 1898. The golden Dome of the Rock dominates the upper canvas; in front of it, the delicate fifteenth-century Fountain of Qayt Bay with its carved stone canopy breaks the plaza into something more human-scaled. Pilgrims and passers-by cluster in the shadow it casts. Bauernfeind's architect eye keeps the geometry razor-sharp, but the light is unmistakably Levantine, flat midday whites bouncing off the Haram esplanade. It is a late picture, and the painter has stopped being a tourist.

Gustav_Bauernfeind_-_Jerusalem_from_the_.title: Gustav Bauernfeind - Jerusalem from the Mount of Olives at Sunrise (c 1902) (Sotheby's) l20022-bl8tn-01
Gustav_Bauernfeind_-_Jerusalem_from_the_.description: A painting by Gustav Bauernfeind of Jerusalem viewed the Mount of Olives at Sunrise, around 1900.

source.canonical_title: File:Gustav Bauernfeind - Jerusalem from the Mount of Olives at Sunrise (c 1902) (Sotheby's) l20022-bl8tn-01.jpg

Gustav_Bauernfeind_-_Jerusalem_from_the_.story: Around 1902, two years before his death, Bauernfeind climbed the Mount of Olives at first light and painted what thousands of pilgrims before him had come to see: the walled city laid out across the Kidron Valley as the sun caught the Dome of the Rock. The view is hallowed almost to the point of cliche, but Bauernfeind refuses sentimentality. He paints it cold, clean, architecturally exact, with the pink dawn only just beginning to warm the stone. He was buried in Jerusalem two years later.

Gustav_Bauernfeind_-_The_Gate_Of_The_Gre.title: The Gate Of The Great Umayyad Mosque, Damascus

source.canonical_title: File:Gustav Bauernfeind - The Gate Of The Great Umayyad Mosque, Damascus.jpg

Gustav_Bauernfeind_-_The_Gate_Of_The_Gre.story: Bauernfeind trained as an architect before he trained as a painter, and it shows here: every course of masonry, every inlaid tile of the great Umayyad gate is rendered with a draftsman's patience. Painted in 1890 after repeated trips east from Stuttgart, the picture turns one of Islam's holiest thresholds into a working street scene, with worshippers, loungers and sellers arranged against that famous stone screen. The scale is intimate but the ambition is huge. A few decades later Bauernfeind would move to Jerusalem for good; this Damascus canvas belongs to the restless years leading up to that decision.

Gustav_Bauernfeind_-_Warden_of_the_Mosqu.title: Gustav Bauernfeind - Warden of the Mosque, Damascus (1891) (HQ image)
Gustav_Bauernfeind_-_Warden_of_the_Mosqu.description: Gustav Bauernfeind - Warden of the Mosque, Damascus (1891)

source.canonical_title: File:Gustav Bauernfeind - Warden of the Mosque, Damascus (1891) (HQ image).jpg

Gustav_Bauernfeind_-_Warden_of_the_Mosqu.story: A doorkeeper sits cross-legged on a stone bench outside the Umayyad Mosque, turbaned and unbothered, while the ornate doors behind him stand half open onto a glimpsed courtyard of fountain, carpets and kneeling worshippers. Bauernfeind painted this in 1891, and you can feel the architect in him lining up every mosaic tile and iron hinge. It's a small, patient picture about a single job and a single threshold, but it opens onto a whole world. His own letters describe sitting for hours with a sketchbook, waiting for the warden to settle back into his habitual pose.

Gustave_Caillebotte_-_Paris_Street;_Rain.title: Paris Street in Rainy Weather
Gustave_Caillebotte_-_Paris_Street;_Rain.description: Il s'agit de la place de Dublin vue depuis la rue de Moscou.

Gustave_Caillebotte_-_Paris_Street;_Rain.story: A wet cobbled junction in Baron Haussmann's brand-new Paris, seen through what feels like a camera lens. A couple in black strolls straight at us under a glossy umbrella, a top-hatted man crosses behind them, and the wedge-shaped building on the right slices the canvas like a knife. Caillebotte painted it in 1877 at age twenty-eight and hung it at the third Impressionist exhibition that spring. The spot is the Place de Dublin, near Gare Saint-Lazare. It's enormous, nearly seven by nine feet, and lives at the Art Institute of Chicago.

Gustave_Caillebotte_Boating_on_the_Yerre.title: Boating on the Yerres

source.canonical_title: File:Gustave Caillebotte Boating on the Yerres.jpg
source.permission: A painting that is in the public domain because of its age.

Gustave_Caillebotte_Boating_on_the_Yerre.story: Three sleek perissoires, kayak-like skiffs for one, glide down the Yerres on a summer afternoon. Caillebotte made at least seven boating pictures at the family estate between 1877 and 1878; this is among the largest and earliest. The riverbank tips forward, the water wedges off to the lower left, and only the hulls stay rigid and sharp while everything else dissolves. A rower himself, he was obsessed with the mechanics of small boats, and you can feel it in the way these three knife through the surface. It now hangs in the Milwaukee Art Museum.

Gustave_Courbet_-_Jo,_the_Beautiful_Iris.title: Jo, the Beautiful Irish Girl

source.canonical_title: File:Gustave Courbet - Jo, the Beautiful Irish Girl - Google Art Project.jpg
source.credit: 6wGkbiqb-8Vy9A at Google Cultural Institute maximum zoom level

title.sv: Jo, den vackra irländskan" Jo, the Beautiful Irish Girl

Gustave_Courbet_-_Jo,_the_Beautiful_Iris.story: Joanna Hiffernan — Whistler's redheaded muse, and possibly Courbet's lover — gazes into a hand mirror, fingers threading through a cascade of auburn hair. Courbet met her in Trouville in autumn 1865 and wrote excitedly about beginning the portrait of "a superb redhead." He liked the result so much he painted four near-identical versions for eager middle-class buyers. This one, dated 1866, is at the Metropolitan Museum of Art.

Gustave_Courbet_-_La_vague_-_Google_Art_.title: The Wave

source.canonical_title: File:Gustave Courbet - La vague - Google Art Project.jpg

Gustave_Courbet_-_La_vague_-_Google_Art_.story: Another of Courbet's Étretat waves from the summer of 1869 — same stretch of Normandy coast, same single-minded staring at breaking water. The horizon sits low, the wave rises to meet a storm-stacked sky, and the palette knife does most of the talking. This was the painter inventing "series" before Monet had the idea. The canvas entered the Alte Nationalgalerie in Berlin in 1906 from the collection of critic Théodore Duret.

Gustave_Courbet_-_Le_Désespéré_(1843).story: A young man clutches his hair and stares straight out of the canvas, eyes wide, mouth half-open, looking either terrified or electrified. It is Courbet, twenty-four years old, freshly rejected by the Salon, painting himself as if to test how much emotion a face could hold. The picture, begun in 1843, is tiny, 45 by 54 cm, and tight as a held breath. He kept it all his life; it hung in his studio through triumph, scandal and exile. In 2025 the Qatari royal collection bought it, with a five-year loan to the Musee d'Orsay first.

Gustave_Courbet_029.jpg.title: Gustave Courbet 029

source.canonical_title: File:Gustave Courbet 029.jpg
source.credit: The Yorck Project (2002) 10.000 Meisterwerke der Malerei (DVD-ROM), distributed by DIRECTMEDIA Publishing GmbH. ISBN : 3936122202 .

Gustave_Courbet_029.jpg.story: Autumn 1865: Courbet was in Trouville with Whistler, knocking out seascape after seascape — twenty-five in all, he bragged, "each more free and extraordinary than the last." In this one, a barefoot girl stands on the empty beach, seagulls wheeling at her feet, her long hair tumbling loose. Courbet loved pairing wild hair with wild creatures. The painting is known as Girl with Seagulls, Trouville, dated 1865.

Gustave_Courbet_038.jpg.title: The Sleeping Spinner

source.canonical_title: File:Gustave Courbet 038.jpg

Gustave_Courbet_038.jpg.story: A young woman has nodded off at her spinning wheel, chin sunk to her chest, a skein of wool still loose in her lap. Courbet paints her heavy peasant dress and the cat-curl of her posture with the same gravity academic painters reserved for saints. No moral, no lesson, just an afternoon swallowing someone whole. He sent it to the Salon of 1853, where a Montpellier collector promptly bought it. The painting has lived at the Musée Fabre in Montpellier ever since.

Gustave_Dore_-_La_Siesta,_Memory_of_Spai.title: ラ・シエスタ、スペインの思い出

source.canonical_title: File:Gustave Dore - La Siesta, Memory of Spain - Google Art Project.jpg
source.credit: GwHIUBydu4m7Ig at Google Cultural Institute maximum zoom level

Gustave_Dore_-_La_Siesta,_Memory_of_Spai.story: Doré is remembered for his black-and-white book engravings — Dante, Don Quixote, the Bible — but he painted too, and big. Here a Spanish woman dozes through the afternoon heat, lit in tawny golds and deep shadows. It's a memory piece, stitched together from his travels across Spain. The canvas is nearly ten feet tall. It's dated 1868 and now lives at the National Museum of Western Art in Tokyo.

title.fr: Le Mont Sainte-Odile avec le mur païen

Gustave_Doré-Mont_Sainte-Odile_avec_mur.story: Doré was born in Strasbourg and never let Alsace go — not after France lost it in 1871, not after Paris made him rich. Mont Sainte-Odile, the Alsatian pilgrimage peak ringed by a prehistoric drystone rampart (the Pagan Wall), gave him a subject that was home, history, and loss at once. The canvas now lives at the Musée d'art moderne et contemporain de Strasbourg, a short drive from the mountain itself.

Gustave_Doré_-_La_Vallée_de_larmes.jpg.title: The Vale of Tears

source.canonical_title: File:Gustave Doré - La Vallée de larmes.jpg

Gustave_Doré_-_La_Vallée_de_larmes.jpg.story: Thirteen feet tall, twenty feet wide, and finished the year he died. Doré painted it after his mother's death, taking the line from Matthew 11 (Come unto me, all ye that labour and are heavy laden) and staging Christ not at the center but small in the middle distance, a slow figure with a cross. The foreground is the point: a crush of the wrecked, the royal, the ragged, all moving toward him. Now at the Petit Palais in Paris.

Gustave_Doré_-_Landscape_in_Scotland_-_.title: Landscape in Scotland
Gustave_Doré_-_Landscape_in_Scotland_-_.description: As a native of Alsace in eastern France and lacking the formal training provided in Paris, Doré began his career as an illustrator and remained outside the mainstream of French painting. His dramatic landscapes, with their grand vistas and turbulent skies, reflect the Romantic movement that had prevailed in French art a generation earlier. Doré visited Scotland on a salmon-fishing expedition in 1873, and over the next eight years, he painted a number of scenes based on his sketches of the Scottish landscape. Doré is perhaps best known for his illustrated Bible (1866). This proved to be an important calling card for the artist, enabling him to open the Doré Gallery in New Bond Street, London, where this painting was probably originally exhibited.

Gustave_Doré_-_Landscape_in_Scotland_-_.story: Doré fell for the Highlands on an 1873 salmon-fishing trip and kept going back. In the studio he reworked his sketches into Romantic landscapes a generation late — turbulent cloud, stag-scale solitude, no village in sight. Landscape in Scotland probably hung at his own Doré Gallery in London, aimed at the same Victorians who bought his Bible. Now at the Walters in Baltimore, acquired in 1986.

Gustave_Doré_-_Roland,_Count_of_Mans.jp.title: Gustave Doré - Roland, Count of Mans
Gustave_Doré_-_Roland,_Count_of_Mans.jp.description: Roland, Count of Mans & knight of Blaives - image by Gustave Doré [1832-1883] from the book: "Days of Chivalry/ Legend of Croquemitaine" - Quatrelles 1866, p.15 https://archive.org/details/daysofchivalryor00quat/page/14/mode/2up

source.canonical_title: File:Gustave Doré - Roland, Count of Mans.jpg
source.credit: https://archive.org/details/daysofchivalryor00quat/page/136/mode/2up Days of Chivalry https://archive.org/details/AI156/page/n101/mode/2up Sagrada Biblia T1 https://archive.org/details/AI159/page/n331/mode/2up Sagrada Biblia T4

Gustave_Doré_-_Roland,_Count_of_Mans.jp.story: Not the famous Roland of Roncevaux but a supporting knight from a now-forgotten 1866 fable, 'La Légende de Croquemitaine' by Quatrelles. Doré gives him the full treatment anyway: plumed helm, kite shield, rearing warhorse in elaborate caparison, the rest of the company dissolving into dust and hatching behind him. It's a wood engraving the size of a book page, and it reads like a film still - everything posed for maximum silhouette, the horse's tossed mane matched by the smoke. Hack work produced at speed, but Doré at his most effortlessly theatrical.

Gustave_Doré_-_St._John's_vision_of_dea.title: Gustave Doré - St. John's vision of death
Gustave_Doré_-_St._John's_vision_of_dea.description: (La Muerte) Vision de San Juan image by Gustave Doré [1832-1883] from the book: "La Sagrada Biblia T.4" - Felix Torres Amat 1884, p.391 https://archive.org/details/AI159/page/n353/mode/2up

source.canonical_title: File:Gustave Doré - St. John's vision of death.jpg
source.credit: https://archive.org/details/daysofchivalryor00quat/page/136/mode/2up Days of Chivalry https://archive.org/details/AI156/page/n101/mode/2up Sagrada Biblia T1 https://archive.org/details/AI159/page/n331/mode/2up Sagrada Biblia T4

Gustave_Doré_-_St._John's_vision_of_dea.story: From a Spanish edition of Doré's Bible illustrations, this is Revelation 6: the pale horse, and he that sat upon him was Death. Doré draws the rider as a floating skeletal figure trailing drapery and a spectral horse's head, surrounded by a cloud of writhing souls that on close inspection turn into more bodies, more faces, all the way to the dark edges. Below, a tiny earthly landscape glows under the chaos. The whole thing is cut in wood, and the tonal range - from coal-black smoke to pure white paper - is what made Doré's Bible a bestseller across three continents.

Gustave_Doré_-_The_Holy_Bible_-_Plate_I.title: Gustave Doré - The Holy Bible - Plate I, The Deluge
Gustave_Doré_-_The_Holy_Bible_-_Plate_I.date_created: The first edition was 1866. This edition is probably from about that time - may well be a first edition - but in any case is certainly not later than 1900 or so.
Gustave_Doré_-_The_Holy_Bible_-_Plate_I.description: "The Deluge", Frontispiece to Doré's illustrated edition of the Bible. Based on the story of Noah's Ark, this shows humans and a tiger doomed by the flood futilely attempting to save their children and cubs.

source.canonical_title: File:Gustave Doré - The Holy Bible - Plate I, The Deluge.jpg
source.credit: The Holy Bible: Containing the Old and New Testiments, According to the Authorised Version. With Illusrations by Gustave Doré. ( Cassell / Company , Limited: London, Paris & Melbourne)

description.de: „Die Sintflut“, Frontispiz zu Dorés illustrierter Bibelausgabe. Basierend auf der Geschichte der Arche Noah zeigt es Menschen und einen Tiger, die vergeblich versuchen, ihre Kinder und Jungen vor der Flut zu retten.
description.fr: "Le Déluge", Frontispice de l'édition illustrée par Gustave Doré de la Bible. Basé sur l'histoire de l'Arche de Noé, la gravure montre des humains et un tigre tentant en vain de sauver leur progéniture.

Gustave_Doré_-_The_Holy_Bible_-_Plate_I.story: Doré's frontispiece to his 1866 illustrated Bible: the last rock above the floodwaters, and everyone who has scrambled onto it is already beyond saving. A tigress crouches at the summit guarding her cubs; below her a naked family hoists a baby up by the arms while the sea keeps climbing. The wood-engraving is almost theatrical in its gloom - gulls wheel, a corpse drifts in the foreground - and it fixed the 19th-century picture of Noah's flood for a generation of readers. This crisp version is a contemporary digital restoration by Adam Cuerden.

HENRI_ROUSSEAU_-_La_Encantadora_de_Serpi.story: A dark silhouette with pale eyes plays a flute at the edge of a moonlit river, and the snakes come: one curling around her shoulders, another rising from the reeds, a third threading the foliage behind. The commission came from Berthe, mother of the painter Robert Delaunay, who'd travelled in India and wanted something exotic for her salon. Rousseau, as usual, worked from the Jardin des Plantes greenhouse and his own imagination. Picasso admired it fiercely. It entered the Louvre in 1922 and now hangs at the Musée d'Orsay.

source.canonical_title: File:Harunobu 2 Pers.jpg

Harunobu_2_Pers.jpg.story: A quiet Harunobu encounter: two slender figures, doll-faced and impossibly graceful, caught in one of the small Edo moments he made his signature. The print dates from around the years he was refining the full-colour nishiki-e technique — cleanly registered blocks, soft palette, a sense that the page has been tinted by weather rather than ink. Harunobu had a gift for compressing a whole mood into two bodies and a few lines of floor. You don't get drama; you get atmosphere.

Harunobu_Bijin_sur_une_véranda.jpeg.title: Beauty on a Veranda
Harunobu_Bijin_sur_une_véranda.jpeg.description: Harunobu, nishiki-e print of unusual size of 13.6" by 21.3". Probably between 1760 and 1770. Museum of Fine Arts, Boston (cropped) : Parody of the Muken no Kane Scene in the Play Hiragana Seisuiki: Woman Standing on a Veranda outside a Room with a Party

Harunobu_Bijin_sur_une_véranda.jpeg.story: An unusually large nishiki-e, roughly fourteen by twenty-one inches, in which Harunobu stages a mitate — a playful parody — of the Muken no Kane scene from the puppet play Hiragana Seisuiki. A woman stands on a veranda outside a lit room where a party goes on without her. The theatrical reference would have been instantly readable to Edo viewers; today the picture works as pure atmosphere, the party warm and distant, the solitary figure just outside its glow. Harunobu loved this kind of literary double exposure.

Harunobu_Jouvenceau_aux_chrysanthèmes.j.title: Young Man with Chrysanthemums
Harunobu_Jouvenceau_aux_chrysanthèmes.j.description: Suzuki Harunobu : egoyomi, chûban size, unsigned (1765-1767).

source.canonical_title: File:Harunobu Jouvenceau aux chrysanthèmes.JPG

Harunobu_Jouvenceau_aux_chrysanthèmes.j.story: An egoyomi — a 'picture calendar,' one of the private deluxe prints Edo poets commissioned for the New Year with the month numbers hidden inside the design. Chuban size, unsigned, as these often were, made in the short burst between 1765 and 1767 when Harunobu was perfecting full-colour printing. A youth stands among chrysanthemums, the flower of autumn and long life. The refinement is typical of the egoyomi world: small editions, rich pigments, knowing viewers, little need to shout.

Harunobu_Kanzan_et_Jittoku.JPG.title: Harunobu Kanzan et Jittoku
Harunobu_Kanzan_et_Jittoku.JPG.description: Woodcut print by Suzuki Harunobu : egoyomi, aiban size, showing a mitate (parody) of Kanzan and Jittoku, the well known Chinese Buddhist monks (Jittoku is easily recognized, as he always holds a broomstick).

source.canonical_title: File:Harunobu Kanzan et Jittoku.JPG

Harunobu_Kanzan_et_Jittoku.JPG.story: Another Harunobu mitate, this one taking on Kanzan and Jittoku — the eccentric Chinese Zen poet-monks usually shown as wild-haired laughing hermits. Jittoku is, as ever, identifiable by his broom. Harunobu re-casts them in his own slim, youthful register, softening their scruffiness into something elegant and deadpan. An egoyomi in aiban size, it's a small print with a lot of cultural layering: Buddhist legend, poetic allusion, and the cheerful Edo habit of dressing up old icons in contemporary clothes.

Hasegawa_Tohaku_-_Pine_Trees_(Shōrin-zu.title: Pine Trees / right hand screen
Hasegawa_Tohaku_-_Pine_Trees_(Shōrin-zu.description: "Pine Trees" by Hasegawa Tōhaku (Japanese, 1539–1610). The painting has been designated as National Treasure in the paintings category .

source.canonical_title: File:Hasegawa Tohaku - Pine Trees (Shōrin-zu byōbu) - right hand screen.jpg
source.permission: Copyright expired.

Hasegawa_Tohaku_-_Pine_Trees_(Shōrin-zu.story: The right-hand screen of Tōhaku's pair - designated a National Treasure and one of the things Japanese ink painting is measured against. A pine stands in the centre, fully drawn; to either side the trees fade into mist so thinly laid down you can still see the paper's joins. No ground, no horizon, just trunks dissolving. Tōhaku made these around 1600, after moving to Kyoto from provincial Noto and setting out to rival the Kanō school; the screens feel like a private answer to the noisy gold-leaf rooms of his competitors.

Hashiguchi_Goyo_-_Woman_in_Blue_Combing_.story: Goyo only ever released fourteen prints. This 1920 sheet, Kamisuki, is the one people hang on the wall when they say shin-hanga. A woman in a blue-and-white kimono draws a comb through a dark rope of hair. Nothing else is in the room - no mirror, no window, just the cream ground of the paper. The restraint is the point: after one frustrating collaboration with the publisher Watanabe, Goyo oversaw every block, every pull, every pigment himself. A year after this print, meningitis killed him at forty-one.

Hatsuhana_doing_penance_under_the_Tonosa.title: Hatsuhana doing penance under the Tonosawa waterfall
Hatsuhana_doing_penance_under_the_Tonosa.description: 賢女烈婦伝 初花。初花は浄瑠璃『箱根霊験躄仇討』に登場する飯沼勝五郎（躄勝五郎）の妻。足が不自由になった夫の仇討ちを叶えるため箱根権現に願掛けする

source.canonical_title: File:Hatsuhana doing penance under the Tonosawa waterfall.jpg

Hatsuhana_doing_penance_under_the_Tonosa.story: Hatsuhana, heroine of the puppet-play Hakone Reigen Izari Adauchi, prays under the Tonosawa waterfall at Hakone for strength to help her crippled husband Katsugorō avenge his father. Kuniyoshi shows her kneeling in the white fall of water, hands pressed together, robes soaked and darkening. The series is 'Lives of Wise and Virtuous Women,' one of the moralising frames Kuniyoshi used to get past Tenpō-era censorship, which had clamped down on actor and courtesan prints. The water, as usual in his work, is the most alive thing in the image.

HavreMonet.jpg.title: The Bassin du Commerce, Le Havre

source.canonical_title: File:HavreMonet.jpg

HavreMonet.jpg.story: The commercial basin at Le Havre, seen from the quay: a forest of masts, fat cargo hulls, and the town behind it all going about its business. Monet had come home in autumn 1874, partly to prepare a future exhibition, partly to paint the working port that had shaped his eye as a boy. He made four views that trip; they're now scattered across Philadelphia, LA, the Hermitage and one private hand.

Hayez,_Francesco_–_Accusa_segreta_–_1847.title: Accusa segreta

source.canonical_title: File:Hayez, Francesco – Accusa segreta – 1847 1848.jpg

Hayez,_Francesco_–_Accusa_segreta_–_1847.story: A young Venetian woman in black pauses on a stair, a folded note in her gloved hand, on her way to drop it into one of the city's bocche di leone, the stone lion's mouths that swallowed anonymous denunciations. Her face is closed; her jewellery is too good. Hayez painted her between 1847 and 1848 as Venice itself was rising against Austria. The canvas is in the Musei Civici di Pavia.

Hayez,_Lot_con_le_figlie,_1833.png.title: Hayez, Lot con le figlie, 1833

source.canonical_title: File:Hayez, Lot con le figlie, 1833.png

Hayez,_Lot_con_le_figlie,_1833.png.story: Lot slumps back against a rock, wine cup tipped, while one daughter refills it and the other waits her turn. Sodom still burns in the distance, a thin orange line under heavy cloud. Hayez painted the Genesis episode in 1833 with all its uneasy intimacy intact, the older daughter's hand resting just where it shouldn't, the younger one's shoulder bare. Nobody looks anyone in the eye. The canvas shows Hayez at his most confident with flesh and drapery, already the house painter of Milanese history.

Hayez,_Tamar_di_Giuda,_1847.jpg.title: Tamar

source.canonical_title: File:Hayez, Tamar di Giuda, 1847.jpg

Hayez,_Tamar_di_Giuda,_1847.jpg.story: Tamar in a headscarf and a fall of heavy jewels, half-smiling as she hides the staff and seal she's just taken from her father-in-law Judah. Hayez painted the Genesis trickster in 1847 with all the Orientalist trimmings Milan was buying at the time, brass lamp, patterned cushion, slipping silk. The pledge in her hand will save her life when Judah tries to have her burned.

Hayez_-_Selbstporträt_im_Alter_von_78_Ja.title: Self-Portrait at the Age of 78, 1869

source.canonical_title: File:Hayez - Selbstporträt im Alter von 78 Jahren, 1869, GE 2578.jpg

Hayez_-_Selbstporträt_im_Alter_von_78_Ja.story: Seventy-eight years old and still sizing up the mirror. Hayez paints himself in black, a white collar and a crumple of neckcloth catching what little light there is. The eyes do the work: sharp, a bit tired, completely unflattering. No brush in hand, no studio props, just the face of the man who basically invented Italian Romantic history painting. This 1869 self-portrait ended up in the Hermitage in St. Petersburg, catalogued as GE 2578.

Head_of_Cyrus_Brought_to_Queen_Tomyris,_.title: Legend of Tomyris (the head of Cyrus brought to Queen Tomyris).

source.canonical_title: File:Head of Cyrus Brought to Queen Tomyris, Peter Paul Rubens.jpg

title.ru: Питер Пауль Рубенс. Царица Томирис перед головой Кира

Head_of_Cyrus_Brought_to_Queen_Tomyris,_.story: Queen Tomyris of the Massagetae lost her son to the Persian king Cyrus. When her army finally killed him, she had his severed head dunked in a wineskin of blood — "drink your fill," Herodotus reports her saying. Rubens paints the moment Cyrus's head arrives on a platter, Tomyris cool and composed in gold and ermine. Designed around 1622-23 and largely executed by studio hands, the picture likely flattered Archduchess Isabella, who was publicly likened to virtuous warrior queens. It's now at the Museum of Fine Arts, Boston, measuring over three and a half metres wide.

Hendrick_Goltzius,_Dutch_(active_Haarlem.title: Sine Cerere et Libero friget Venus (Without Ceres and Bacchus, Venus Would Freeze)
Hendrick_Goltzius,_Dutch_(active_Haarlem.description: Sine Cerere et Baccho friget Venus

source.canonical_title: File:Hendrick Goltzius, Dutch (active Haarlem) - Sine Cerere et Libero friget Venus (Without Ceres and Bacchus, Venus Would Freeze) - Google Art Project.jpg
source.credit: kgEEzyit7xGqTg at Google Cultural Institute maximum zoom level

Hendrick_Goltzius,_Dutch_(active_Haarlem.story: Terence's old line: without food and wine, love goes cold. Goltzius takes the proverb at face value, piling bread and grapes around a shivering Venus while Ceres and Bacchus do the warming. The technique is the real flex though, it's pen on canvas, inked like a monumental engraving, then tinted. He called it a 'penwerk' and it's the size of a proper history painting. Probably hung in Emperor Rudolf II's Prague collection before drifting through Swedish and English royal hands. The Philadelphia Museum of Art acquired it in 1990.

Hendrick_Goltzius_-_Farnese_Hercules_-_G.title: Farnese Hercules

source.canonical_title: File:Hendrick Goltzius - Farnese Hercules - Google Art Project.jpg

title.de: Hendrick Goltzius und Jacob Matham betrachten den Herkules Farnese

Hendrick_Goltzius_-_Farnese_Hercules_-_G.story: Most engravers showed the Farnese Hercules from the front, club and muscles out. Goltzius, fresh from a 1591 trip to Rome, circled around and drew the backside — the towering slab of shoulders and glutes — with two tiny gawking visitors at the base for scale. His trademark swelling-and-tapering lines wrap the flesh like contour maps. The print is dated 1592 and was unusually large and ambitious for a reproductive engraving.

Hendrick_Goltzius_-_Portrait_of_the_Haar.title: Portrait of Jan Govertsz. van der Aer (?-1612)

source.canonical_title: File:Hendrick Goltzius - Portrait of the Haarlem Shell Collector Jan Govertsen van der Aer - Google Art Project.jpg

title.de: Porträt des Muschelsammlers Jan Govertsen van der Aer (1545–1612)
title.nl: De Haarlemse schelpenverzamelaar Jan Govertsen van der Aer (1545-1612)

Hendrick_Goltzius_-_Portrait_of_the_Haar.story: Goltzius painted his friend Jan Govertsz. van der Aer in 1603 with a lapful of shells and not much fuss. The sitter was a Haarlem textile dealer, but the shells were the point. Around 1600, conch and nautilus shells from the new East India trade were the trophies of an early-modern nerd, pricier than paintings sometimes. One enormous spiral rests in his palm, catching the studio light against his black tunic. A globe sits behind him, which is how you signalled 'I know where this stuff comes from.' It lives at Museum Boijmans Van Beuningen in Rotterdam.

Hendrick_Martensz._Sorgh_001.jpg.title: The Lute Player.

source.canonical_title: File:Hendrick Martensz. Sorgh 001.jpg
source.credit: Web Gallery of Art : Image Info about artwork wga QS:P11807,"s/sorgh/luteplay"

Hendrick_Martensz._Sorgh_001.jpg.story: A young man in a feathered cap tilts back with his lute, half singing, half flirting, while a woman across the laid table props her chin on her hand and lets him work for it. The red curtain is pulled aside to show a sliver of Rotterdam canal; a spaniel dozes at his feet, a cat at hers. Sorgh spent his whole career in that city painting exactly this kind of compact, well-upholstered moment — fruit on pewter, a stoneware jug, the particular small vanities of the merchant class. Painted 1661, near the height of his run as headman of the local painters' guild.

Hendrik_Avercamp_-_Winter_Scene_on_a_Can.title: Winter Scene on a Canal

source.canonical_title: File:Hendrik Avercamp - Winter Scene on a Canal - Google Art Project.jpg

Hendrik_Avercamp_-_Winter_Scene_on_a_Can.story: Avercamp couldn't speak — he was known in Kampen as "de Stomme," the Mute — but he could pack a frozen canal with skaters, kolf-players, fallen drunks, sleighs, and peeping dogs, every tiny figure doing its own small thing. The Netherlands was in the grip of the Little Ice Age, and winters like this one, around 1615, really froze hard enough to skate on. He made a whole career out of painting them.

Henri-Julien-Félix_Rousseau,_French_-_Ca.title: Carnival Evening
Henri-Julien-Félix_Rousseau,_French_-_Ca.artist: Henri-Julien-Félix Rousseau, French, 1844–1910 (1844–1910) – Artist/Maker (French) Born in Laval, France. Died in Paris, France. Details on Google Art Project

source.canonical_title: File:Henri-Julien-Félix Rousseau, French - Carnival Evening - Google Art Project.jpg
source.credit: 3wFKsz9ULBaojw at Google Cultural Institute maximum zoom level

Henri-Julien-Félix_Rousseau,_French_-_Ca.story: Two Pierrot figures in costume stand at the edge of a black winter wood. The moon is a perfect disc. A street lamp glows where no street should be. A small face leers from a shed. Nothing explains itself. Painted in 1885-86, 'Carnival Evening' was Rousseau's first serious public painting, submitted at 42 by a tax clerk who taught himself to paint on weekends. Critics found it laughable, Signac defended it, Picasso later bought him dinners. The Philadelphia Museum of Art holds it now.

Henri_Fantin-Latour_-_A_Studio_at_Les_Ba.title: A Studio at Les Batignolles

source.canonical_title: File:Henri Fantin-Latour - A Studio at Les Batignolles - Google Art Project.jpg

title.ja: バティニョールのアトリエ

Henri_Fantin-Latour_-_A_Studio_at_Les_Ba.story: Manet stands at his easel painting Zacharie Astruc, who sits still in a coat. Behind them, crammed into the studio, are Renoir with a straw hat, Zola holding his glasses, Bazille (who'd be dead within months in the Franco-Prussian War), and Monet half hidden at the back. Fantin-Latour painted this group portrait in 1870 as an act of loyalty, Manet had been savaged for 'Olympia' and these were the painters and writers who stood with him. Shown at the 1870 Salon, it was Fantin's first real public hit. It hangs at the Musée d'Orsay.

Henri_Fantin-Latour_-_Flowers_and_Fruit_.title: Flowers and Fruit

source.canonical_title: File:Henri Fantin-Latour - Flowers and Fruit - Google Art Project (807372).jpg
source.credit: TwGqoeTbR6edeQ at Google Cultural Institute maximum zoom level

Henri_Fantin-Latour_-_Flowers_and_Fruit_.story: In 1866 the Greek merchant Michael Spartali commissioned four still lifes from Fantin-Latour to ship back to London, where flower pictures were selling fast. Fantin worked on them from March through September, tight little symphonies of petals, grapes and porcelain. He aimed to paint 'in the manner of Chardin,' meaning with patience and no drama. This canvas has no story to tell, no allegory, just the thing in front of him. It's at the Toledo Museum of Art in Ohio.

Henri_Fantin-Latour_-_Retrato_de_M._e_Mm.title: Mr and Mrs Edwin Edwards

source.canonical_title: File:Henri Fantin-Latour - Retrato de M. e Mme Edwards, 1875.jpg

title.pt: Retrato de M. e Mme Edwards

Henri_Fantin-Latour_-_Retrato_de_M._e_Mm.story: Edwin Edwards was a London lawyer turned etcher, and Fantin-Latour had promised him a double portrait in which Mrs Edwards would hover beside her husband's copper plate 'like a guardian angel.' The finished picture, painted during the couple's Paris sittings in February 1875, is stranger than that. Edwin bends over his work, oblivious; Ruth fixes the viewer with a level, almost challenging stare, her dark dress swallowing half the room. The Salon jury gave it a second-class medal that year. It now hangs at Tate Britain.

Henri_Fantin-Latour_-_Still_Life_with_a_.title: 花と果物、ワイン容れのある静物

source.canonical_title: File:Henri Fantin-Latour - Still Life with a Carafe, Flowers and Fruit - Google Art Project.jpg
source.credit: PgHDLISlX3RxkA at Google Cultural Institute maximum zoom level

Henri_Fantin-Latour_-_Still_Life_with_a_.story: Fantin-Latour was Manet's friend and Whistler's drinking companion, but on his own he painted quiet things: a glass carafe, a china bowl, a white cloth. In 1865 he was 29, already committed to the still-life as a serious object of attention. Everything here has a weight, the cold hardness of glass against the soft furred skin of a peach. No symbolism, no story, just looking. The painting belongs to the National Museum of Western Art in Tokyo, acquired in 1997.

Henri_Fantin-Latour_-_Vase_of_Flowers_wi.title: Henri Fantin-Latour - Vase of Flowers with a Coffee Cup (13648335833)
Henri_Fantin-Latour_-_Vase_of_Flowers_wi.description: Vase of Flowers with a Coffee Cup

Henri_Matisse,_1902,_Notre-Dame,_une_fin.title: Notre-Dame , ( A Glimpse of Notre Dame in the Late Afternoon )

source.canonical_title: File:Henri Matisse, 1902, Notre-Dame, une fin d'après-midi, oil on paper mounted on canvas, 72.4 x 54.6 cm, Albright-Knox Art Gallery.jpg
source.permission: {{{permission}}}

Henri_Matisse,_1902,_Notre-Dame,_une_fin.story: Painted from the window of his apartment at 19 quai Saint-Michel, this is Matisse at his most Cézanne-struck — and at his most anxious. The Humbert fraud scandal had just ensnared his wife's family, and the so-called Dark Period had him slogging through lawyers and journalists all spring. Notre-Dame sits across the Seine in slabs of smoky mauve and olive, the open shutter cropping the view like a bar. The strokes are blocky, untextured, and you can already feel him pushing toward the Fauve riot three years away. Buffalo's Albright-Knox has it.

Henri_Matisse,_1920-21,_Odalisque,_oil_o.title: Odalisque

source.canonical_title: File:Henri Matisse, 1920-21, Odalisque, oil on canvas, 61.4 x 74.4 cm, Stedelijk Museum.jpg
source.permission: {{{permission}}}

Henri_Matisse,_1920-21,_Odalisque,_oil_o.story: By 1920 Matisse had moved to Nice and turned his studio into a small theatre: striped hangings, a day bed, a model in a sheer chemise. The eyes close, the shoulders slip, and the whole room reads as pattern on pattern — a world away from the austere Notre-Dame of twenty years earlier. The painting belonged to the German textile magnate Albert Stern before a forced 1941 sale delivered it to the Stedelijk; in 2024 the Dutch Restitutions Committee ordered it returned to his heirs.

Henri_Meunier04.jpg.title: Henri Meunier04
Henri_Meunier04.jpg.description: "L'Heure du Silence", Poster by Henri Meunier (1873-1922), Belgian designer

source.canonical_title: File:Henri Meunier04.jpg

Henri_Meunier04.jpg.story: "L'Heure du Silence" — the hour of silence. A woman in a loose green robe lifts a finger to her lips against a flat orange sunset, the sun reduced to a glowing bar behind bands of cloud. Meunier has stripped out everything unnecessary: three colours, a handful of contours, Japanese-print economy pressed into service for a Belgian Art Nouveau poster. He was 24 when he made this in 1897, already known in Brussels for the same trick of bold outlines around a single quiet gesture. The image sells you a mood rather than a product, which was increasingly the Belle Epoque's idea of what a poster could do.

Henry_Fuseli_-_Titania_and_Bottom_-_Goog.title: Titania and Bottom

source.canonical_title: File:Henry Fuseli - Titania and Bottom - Google Art Project.jpg

Henry_Fuseli_-_Titania_and_Bottom_-_Goog.story: Shakespeare's fairy queen, drugged by Oberon, wraps herself around a weaver with a donkey's head. Fuseli painted it around 1790 for Alderman Boydell's Shakespeare Gallery, a publishing scheme meant to rival history painting with scenes from the bard. The canvas is enormous, nearly nine feet tall, and swarming with changelings, tiny goblins and a miniature old woman tugged along by what looks like a moth. Everyone is beautiful or grotesque, nothing in between. Titania's smile is a problem. It entered Tate's collection in 1887.

Het_Zojo_heiligdom_in_Shiba_Shiba_Zojoji.story: Zojoji in snow: the great red Tokugawa temple at Shiba, with a lone woman walking past under an umbrella. This is probably Hasui's most imitated composition — the red gate, the white snow, the tiny figure — and one reason his name travelled abroad so fast. From Twenty Views of Tokyo, 1925, published by Watanabe two years after the Great Kanto earthquake had flattened much of the city. A quiet print, but also a kind of reassurance.

Hieronymus_Bosch_-_The_Garden_of_Earthly.title: Creation
Hieronymus_Bosch_-_The_Garden_of_Earthly.description: Exterior (shutters) of The Garden of Earthly Delights . Dargestellt ist der Zustand der Erdkugel am Ende des dritten Schöpfungstages, wo die Trennung zwischen Licht und Finsternis, Himmel und Erde, Wasser und Land bereits vollzogen ist (Genesis 1,1-13). Der Maler sieht die Erdoberfläche als Scheibe, integriert diese aber schon in eine Kugel, wobei der untere Teil mit Wasser gefüllt ist.

source.canonical_title: File:Hieronymus Bosch - The Garden of Earthly Delights - The exterior (shutters).jpg
source.credit: Originally uploaded to the English Wikipedia by w:User:Blankfaze .

Hieronymus_Bosch_-_The_Garden_of_Earthly.story: Shut the triptych and this is what you get, the world on the third day of creation. No sun, no moon, no people yet. Bosch paints the earth as a flat disc inside a glass bubble, half filled with water, fringed with strange vegetation just starting to sprout. God watches from the top-left corner, Bible in hand, the size of a thumbnail. Everything's in grey-green grisaille, colour withheld until you pry the doors open and find paradise and hell inside. Currently dated to 1490-1510 by the Prado, which has owned it since 1939.

Hieronymus_Bosch_-_The_Trees_have_Ears_a.title: The Trees have Ears and the Field has Eyes

source.canonical_title: File:Hieronymus Bosch - The Trees have Ears and the Field has Eyes - Kupferstichkabinett Berlin KdZ 549.jpg

Hieronymus_Bosch_-_The_Trees_have_Ears_a.story: A Flemish proverb made visual: six open eyes stare up from the ground, two human ears sprout from tree trunks, an owl watches from a hollow. The lesson is keep your mouth shut, somebody's always listening. Bosch drew it around 1500 in brown ink on a small sheet barely eight inches tall. The Latin at the top reads, roughly, 'poor the mind that always borrows and never invents,' which is either a signature or a dare. Kupferstichkabinett in Berlin holds it, one of only three drawings scholars agree are truly his.

Hieronymus_Bosch_-_Triptych_of_Temptatio.title: Triptych of Temptation of St Anthony

source.canonical_title: File:Hieronymus Bosch - Triptych of Temptation of St Anthony - WGA2585.jpg

Hieronymus_Bosch_-_Triptych_of_Temptatio.story: Saint Anthony kneels in a burning landscape while demons hold a black mass, fish sprout legs, and a naked queen beckons from a hollow tree. Open the wings and the hermit gets no peace: flying frogs, a reading pig-priest, a crawling jug with human feet. Bosch piles hybrid on hybrid until horror becomes almost comic. The Lisbon triptych, oil on oak, came to Portugal's royal collection in the sixteenth century and now anchors the Museu Nacional de Arte Antiga, where conservators in 2015 confirmed its panels were felled from the same tree as another signed Bosch.

Hiroshi_Yoshida,_Hikaru_umi,_1926.jpg.story: Two sailboats lean into a breeze on a sea so bright the water reads almost white, the wake picked out in the thinnest grey line. Hikaru umi, "the sparkling sea," opens Yoshida's 1926 series of eight Seto Inland Sea views, all cut from the same six keyblocks and varied only by colour inking. He rated this version the most demanding of the group: to get the glitter, the printer had to leave large islands of paper completely untouched.

Hiroshige-53-Stations-Hoeido-01-Nihonbas.story: Dawn at the Nihonbashi bridge in Edo, and a daimyō procession is heading out on the long road south. Hiroshige opens his Tōkaidō series with the moment of departure: porters shoulder lacquered boxes, spear-bearers fall in line, a couple of dogs sniff the curb. This is print number one of fifty-five, published by Hōeidō around 1833, and it essentially launched Hiroshige's career. He had just walked the Tōkaidō himself the previous year. The road from here to Kyoto is 500 kilometres.

Hiroshige-53-Stations-Hoeido-14-Hara-MFA.story: Mount Fuji looms so large over the Hara station that Hiroshige lets its peak break the top border of the print. Three travellers trudge along a wetland path in the morning light, one of them a woman, which was rare to show on the road. The blues are doing all the work here, that imported Prussian blue pigment that made the Tōkaidō series look so fresh in 1833. Hara sits in present-day Numazu in Shizuoka prefecture, and the view of Fuji from there really is that commanding.

Hiroshige-53-Stations-Hoeido-16-Kanbara-.story: Three travellers bent against a blizzard, a village buried to its eaves, the whole print hushed in white and grey. Kanbara is one of the most famous images in the Tōkaidō series and also one of the strangest, because Kanbara sits on Suruga Bay and almost never gets snow like this. Scholars still argue whether Hiroshige was remembering somewhere else, inventing the scene outright, or just chasing a mood. He published it around 1833. The composition, all diagonals and empty space, is pure graphic invention.

Hiroshige-53-Stations-Hoeido-34-Futagawa.story: Three pilgrim women in braided hats trudge up a bleak stretch of moorland called Sarugababa, Monkey Plateau, while three teahouse keepers wave them toward a roadside rest stop serving kashiwa mochi. The scrubby pines and dry grass make this one of the loneliest stops on the Tōkaidō, and Hiroshige lets the flat yellow-brown of the plateau take up most of the page. Published by Hōeidō around 1833, it's station 34 of 53 on the old road between Edo and Kyoto.

Hiroshige-53-Stations-Hoeido-35-Yoshida-.story: Carpenters crawl over a scaffold strapped to Yoshida Castle, hammers out, while the Toyokawa Bridge stretches across the river below them with a traveller or two still making the crossing. Hiroshige loved a construction scene, and here he uses the scaffolding to frame the castle instead of just showing it. Yoshida is modern-day Toyohashi in Aichi prefecture. The print is number 35 in the Tōkaidō series published by Hōeidō around 1833. The Toyokawa Bridge was 120 metres long, one of the longest on the whole road.

Hiroshige-53-Stations-Hoeido-36-Goyu-MFA.story: A pair of innkeepers in aprons have grabbed a traveller by the sleeve and are physically dragging him toward their door while another yanks at his companion's arm. This was a real hazard at Goyu: the station was famous for its aggressive serving maids who doubled as prostitutes, and Hiroshige plays the scene half-comic, half-alarming. A delivery boy slips by in the background with dinner trays. Published by Hōeidō around 1833, the print is station 36 of 53 on the Tōkaidō road.

Hiroshige-53-Stations-Hoeido-37-Akasaka-.story: Inside an Akasaka inn: travellers soak their feet, eat, and get their heads shaved, while across the courtyard two serving women sit at mirrors doing their makeup for the evening shift. A sago palm grows in the garden between them. Hiroshige gives us a cutaway view of inn life you rarely see in the series, domestic and a little voyeuristic at once. Akasaka and neighbouring Goyu were only two kilometres apart, the shortest gap on the whole Tōkaidō. The print dates from around 1833.

Hiroshige-53-Stations-Hoeido-40-Chiryu-M.story: Early summer at Chiryū, and dozens of horses are loose in a meadow under pine trees, tails swishing, while dealers in wide straw hats inspect them from a tent set up for the fair. The Chiryū horse market was one of the three biggest in Japan, drawing buyers from across the country every April. Hiroshige fills the foreground with green and lets the horses dot the middle distance like a pattern. This is station 40 of 53 on the Tōkaidō, published by Hōeidō around 1833.

Hiroshige-53-Stations-Hoeido-44-Yokkaich.story: Wind is the real subject here. A traveler runs after his flyaway straw hat along the Mie River, robes whipped sideways, while a second figure bends low over a plank bridge clutching his coat shut. The reeds all lean one way; the pines do too. Hiroshige gives us no drama beyond weather, and that's the point. Yokkaichi was the 44th post station on the Tōkaidō, roughly halfway between Kyoto and Edo, and this sheet is one of the best-loved designs in the Hōeidō edition, published around 1833-34.

Hiroshige-53-Stations-Hoeido-53-Kusatsu-.story: Two kago-bearers sprint past each other outside a teahouse, their passengers pitched forward like cargo about to spill. A banner reads "Meibutsu ubagamochi" — the station's famous sweet rice cake. Kusatsu sat where the Tōkaidō met the Nakasendō, which is why everyone looks like they're in a hurry. The sign on the roadside post house advertises the specialty by name. This is the 52nd station (Kusatsu), printed by Hōeidō around 1833-34; the block carries the Takemago variant seal.

Hiroshige11_hakone.jpg.title: Hakone-juku
Hiroshige11_hakone.jpg.description: wood-block print, reproduction from a miniature edition by Takamizawa, Japan Title: Hakone

source.canonical_title: File:Hiroshige11 hakone.jpg
source.credit: The fifty-stree stages of Tokaido (one of 53 prints, +2 for start and terminus)

Hiroshige11_hakone.jpg.story: Hiroshige makes Hakone's mountains look like shattered jade — jagged facets of green, ochre and deep blue stacked impossibly steep. A tiny daimyō procession threads the pass single-file, dwarfed to ants. Far below, Lake Ashi gleams pale with Mount Fuji just peeking across it. The pass was the Tōkaidō's toughest checkpoint, and travelers genuinely dreaded it. This is the 11th station from the Hōeidō series of 1833-34, here reproduced in the miniature Takamizawa edition.

Hiroshige19_ejiri.jpg.title: Ejiri-juku
Hiroshige19_ejiri.jpg.description: wood-block print, reproduction from a miniature edition by Takamizawa, Japan Title: Ejiri

source.canonical_title: File:Hiroshige19 ejiri.jpg
source.credit: The fifty-stree stages of Tokaido (one of 53 prints, +2 for start and terminus)

Hiroshige19_ejiri.jpg.story: Miho no Matsubara curves off to the right like a green comma, its pine-clad spit poking into Suruga Bay. Sails crowd the harbor — dozens of them, so many you stop counting — while Mount Fuji looms over the whole scene in pale blue. Ejiri was a bustling port town as well as the 18th post station, and Hiroshige leans into that maritime bustle rather than the road. This print comes from the Hōeidō edition of 1833-34, here as a Takamizawa miniature reproduction.

Hiroshige20_fuchu.jpg.title: Fuchū-juku
Hiroshige20_fuchu.jpg.description: wood-block print, reproduction from a miniature edition by Takamizawa, Japan Title: Fuchu

source.canonical_title: File:Hiroshige20 fuchu.jpg
source.credit: The fifty-stree stages of Tokaido (one of 53 prints, +2 for start and terminus)

Hiroshige20_fuchu.jpg.story: Travelers wade the Abe River on the shoulders of porters, or ride on plank litters held high above the current. One passenger grips the sides of her kago looking distinctly unenthused. Fuchū (modern Shizuoka) was the 19th station, and the river crossing here was unbridged by shogunal decree — a security measure that kept ferrymen in steady work. Hiroshige designed this for the Hōeidō edition in 1833-34; this sheet is a later Takamizawa miniature reproduction.

Hiroshige22_okabe.jpg.title: Okabe-juku
Hiroshige22_okabe.jpg.description: wood-block print, reproduction from a miniature edition by Takamizawa, Japan Title: Okabe

source.canonical_title: File:Hiroshige22 okabe.jpg
source.credit: The fifty-stree stages of Tokaido (one of 53 prints, +2 for start and terminus)

Hiroshige22_okabe.jpg.story: A narrow mountain road threads between two steep, moss-dark slopes along the Utsu Pass, with a thin stream tumbling down the gorge. Tiny figures pick their way through — you almost miss them. Okabe sat at the foot of one of the Tōkaidō's loneliest stretches, the kind celebrated in the Ise Monogatari for its ivy-choked gloom. This is the 21st station, originally issued in Hiroshige's Hōeidō edition of 1833-34 and here reproduced in Takamizawa's miniature format.

Hiroshige25_kanaya.jpg.title: Kanaya-juku
Hiroshige25_kanaya.jpg.description: wood-block print, reproduction from a miniature edition by Takamizawa, Japan Title: Kanaya

source.canonical_title: File:Hiroshige25 kanaya.jpg
source.credit: The fifty-stree stages of Tokaido (one of 53 prints, +2 for start and terminus)

Hiroshige25_kanaya.jpg.story: The Ōi River sprawls across the foreground in a wide, pale ribbon, and a daimyō procession is literally wading it — porters hoisting palanquins overhead, banners held high. The Ōi had no bridge, again by shogunal rule, so delays were routine and sometimes stretched for days when the water rose. Kanaya was the 24th station, on the western bank. Hiroshige's Hōeidō design dates to around 1833-34; this print is the Takamizawa miniature reproduction.

Hiroshige28_fukuroi.jpg.title: Fukuroi-juku
Hiroshige28_fukuroi.jpg.description: wood-block print, reproduction from a miniature edition by Takamizawa, Japan Title: Fukuroi

source.canonical_title: File:Hiroshige28 fukuroi.jpg
source.credit: The fifty-stree stages of Tokaido (one of 53 prints, +2 for start and terminus)

Hiroshige28_fukuroi.jpg.story: A rest stop under a huge, spreading tree: a kettle hangs from a wooden frame over a small fire, and porters and travelers lounge around it, smoking and stretching. One man pokes at the coals. It's the quietest kind of scene Hiroshige ever made — no weather, no drama, just a breather. Fukuroi was the 27th post station on the Tōkaidō. The design appeared in the Hōeidō edition around 1833-34 and is reproduced here in the Takamizawa miniature set.

Hiroshige30_hamamatsu.jpg.title: Hamamatsu-juku
Hiroshige30_hamamatsu.jpg.description: wood-block print, reproduction from a miniature edition by Takamizawa, Japan Title: Hamamatsu

source.canonical_title: File:Hiroshige30 hamamatsu.jpg
source.credit: The fifty-stree stages of Tokaido (one of 53 prints, +2 for start and terminus)

Hiroshige30_hamamatsu.jpg.story: A bare, forked pine dominates the print, with travelers gathered at its base around a small fire — one warms his hands, another blows on the coals, smoke drifting sideways. The rest of the composition is almost empty: flat fields and a low castle wall in the distance. Hamamatsu was the 29th station and a castle town (the print's subtitle calls it "Winter Scene"). The original design is from Hiroshige's Hōeidō series of 1833-34; this is the Takamizawa miniature reproduction.

Hiroshige38_fujikawa.jpg.title: Fujikawa-juku
Hiroshige38_fujikawa.jpg.description: wood-block print, reproduction from a miniature edition by Takamizawa, Japan Title: Fujikawa

source.canonical_title: File:Hiroshige38 fujikawa.jpg
source.credit: The fifty-stree stages of Tokaido (one of 53 prints, +2 for start and terminus)

Hiroshige38_fujikawa.jpg.story: A daimyō procession crests a rise and bows have been ordered — three villagers prostrate by the roadside as the banners pass. A crow flies off unimpressed. Snow dusts the roofs and the stubbled fields. Fujikawa was the 37th Tōkaidō station, and this image captures the rigid etiquette of sankin-kōtai, the alternate-attendance travel that kept daimyō shuttling to Edo. Hiroshige's design appeared in the Hōeidō edition around 1833-34; this sheet is a later Takamizawa miniature reproduction.

Hiroshige39_okazaki.jpg.title: Okazaki-juku
Hiroshige39_okazaki.jpg.description: wood-block print, reproduction from a miniature edition by Takamizawa, Japan Title: Okazaki

source.canonical_title: File:Hiroshige39 okazaki.jpg
source.credit: The fifty-stree stages of Tokaido (one of 53 prints, +2 for start and terminus)

Hiroshige39_okazaki.jpg.story: The great Yahagi Bridge stretches almost the full width of the print — at around 200 ken (roughly 370 meters) it was said to be the longest on the Tōkaidō. A daimyō procession crosses in formal order, banners and palanquins catching the light, while Okazaki Castle sits behind on its low rise. This is the 38th station. Hiroshige issued the original in his Hōeidō series of 1833-34; the Takamizawa miniature reproduction keeps every figure on that long bridge.

Hiroshige45_ishiyakushi.jpg.title: Ishiyakushi-juku
Hiroshige45_ishiyakushi.jpg.description: wood-block print, reproduction from a miniature edition by Takamizawa, Japan Title: Ishiyakushi

source.canonical_title: File:Hiroshige45 ishiyakushi.jpg
source.credit: The fifty-stree stages of Tokaido (one of 53 prints, +2 for start and terminus)

Hiroshige45_ishiyakushi.jpg.story: A lonely temple roof pokes up from a grove of winter-bare trees, and a single traveler heads toward it along a muddy track. Behind, the Suzuka range rolls off in soft, cold blues. Ishiyakushi was the 44th station, named for the Ishiyakushi-ji temple honoring the Buddha of Healing. Hiroshige keeps it almost unpopulated — unusual for the series, and closer in mood to his later snow landscapes. The design was issued in the Hōeidō edition around 1833-34; this is the Takamizawa miniature reproduction.

Hiroshige47_kameyama.jpg.title: Kameyama-juku
Hiroshige47_kameyama.jpg.description: wood-block print, reproduction from a miniature edition by Takamizawa, Japan Title: Kameyama

source.canonical_title: File:Hiroshige47 kameyama.jpg
source.credit: The fifty-stree stages of Tokaido (one of 53 prints, +2 for start and terminus)

Hiroshige47_kameyama.jpg.story: A file of travelers trudges up a snow-covered slope toward Kameyama Castle, whose walls and tiled gates crown the hilltop in sharp white. The sky above is that deep graded blue Hiroshige reserved for cold, clear mornings. Kameyama was the 46th Tōkaidō station, and this print — often titled "Clear Weather After Snow" — is one of the most quietly dramatic in the whole series. The original belongs to the Hōeidō edition of 1833-34; this sheet is the Takamizawa miniature reproduction.

Hiroshige49_sakanoshita.jpg.title: Sakanoshita-juku
Hiroshige49_sakanoshita.jpg.description: wood-block print, reproduction from a miniature edition by Takamizawa, Japan Title: Sakanoshita

source.canonical_title: File:Hiroshige49 sakanoshita.jpg
source.credit: The fifty-stree stages of Tokaido (one of 53 prints, +2 for start and terminus)

Hiroshige49_sakanoshita.jpg.story: A knot of travelers rests at a cliff-edge teahouse, staring out at the jagged face of Fudesute-yama — "Brush-Throwing Mountain." The legend: a painter so despaired of capturing the peak that he flung his brush down the slope. Hiroshige's point is gently comic; his own version is beautiful anyway. Sakanoshita was the 48th Tōkaidō station, perched in the Suzuka range. The print comes from the Hōeidō edition of 1833-34, here in the Takamizawa miniature format.

Hiroshige50_tsuchiyama.jpg.title: Tsuchiyama-juku
Hiroshige50_tsuchiyama.jpg.description: wood-block print, reproduction from a miniature edition by Takamizawa, Japan Title: Tsuchiyama

source.canonical_title: File:Hiroshige50 tsuchiyama.jpg
source.credit: The fifty-stree stages of Tokaido (one of 53 prints, +2 for start and terminus)

Hiroshige50_tsuchiyama.jpg.story: Rain slashes down in the steep Suzuka Pass as a daimyō procession hunches along a bridge, spears and banners lashed by water, a swollen river roaring beneath. The whole print is greens and blacks, almost no sky. Tsuchiyama — the 49th station — was famous for rain; a local saying had it that the weather broke the moment you arrived. Hiroshige's design, one of the wettest in the series, appeared in the Hōeidō edition around 1833-34; this is the Takamizawa miniature reproduction.

Hiroshige_(1838)_Two_mandarin_ducks.jpg.title: Hiroshige (1838) Two mandarin ducks
Hiroshige_(1838)_Two_mandarin_ducks.jpg.description: Ukiyo-e print of two mandarin ducks by Andō Hiroshige, 1838

source.canonical_title: File:Hiroshige (1838) Two mandarin ducks.jpg

Hiroshige_(1838)_Two_mandarin_ducks.jpg.story: Two mandarin ducks tuck against the snow, the drake blazing with orange fan-feathers while his mate keeps her brown camouflage. A few narcissus push up beside them. In Chinese and Japanese tradition these birds mate for life, so painters slipped them into wedding gifts like a wink. Hiroshige cut this small print around 1838, a kachō-e — bird-and-flower print — meant for a fan or album. No landscape drama here, just two birds pretending it isn't cold.

Hiroshige_A_large_waterfall.jpg.title: Famous Views of the 60 Provinces - #23. Yoro Waterfall in Mino Province

Hiroshige_A_large_waterfall.jpg.story: Yoro Falls drops about 32 meters down a mossy cliff in Mino Province, and local legend says the water once turned to sake for a devoted son carrying his aging father up the path. Hiroshige doesn't illustrate the tale — he lets the fall do the talking, a long white ribbon between dark rock. Two tiny pilgrims at the base set the scale. From his Famous Views of the Sixty-odd Provinces, 1856. The falls are now the centerpiece of Yoro Park in Gifu.

Hiroshige_Atake_sous_une_averse_soudaine.description: Part of the series One Hundred Famous Views of Edo , no. 058 , part 2: Summer.

Hiroshige_Atake_sous_une_averse_soudaine.story: The sky cracks open over the Shin-Ohashi bridge and the rain comes down as hard diagonal lines, carved individually into the woodblock. Pedestrians scatter under hats, parasols, a straw mat. The Sumida River below has gone slate. This 1857 print — Sudden Shower at Ohashi — is the one Van Gogh copied in oils eight years later, meticulously reproducing every needle of rain. From Hiroshige's One Hundred Famous Views of Edo, it's arguably the most influential ukiyo-e print in the West.

Hiroshige_Full_moon_over_a_mountain_land.title: Hiroshige Full moon over a mountain landscape
Hiroshige_Full_moon_over_a_mountain_land.description: 8 Views of Omi - #3. Autumn Moon At Ishiyama Temple

source.canonical_title: File:Hiroshige Full moon over a mountain landscape.jpg

Hiroshige_Full_moon_over_a_mountain_land.story: The moon climbs over Ishiyama Temple and the whole scene goes quiet. Lake Biwa spreads out like cooled metal; pines hold their breath on the bluff. This is the autumn-moon entry in Hiroshige's Eight Views of Omi, a set he designed around 1834 riding the wave of his Tokaido fame. The temple below is where legend says Murasaki Shikibu began writing The Tale of Genji, gazing out at this exact moon. Hiroshige knew the story. He gave her the weather she would've wanted.

Hiroshige_Heavy_rain_on_a_pine_tree_2.jp.title: Hiroshige Heavy rain on a pine tree 2
Hiroshige_Heavy_rain_on_a_pine_tree_2.jp.description: 8 Views of Omi - #2. Night Rain In Karasak

source.canonical_title: File:Hiroshige Heavy rain on a pine tree 2.jpg

Hiroshige_Heavy_rain_on_a_pine_tree_2.jp.story: No people, no boats, no lamps — just one twisted pine on the Karasaki shore taking a beating. Hiroshige lays the rain down as sheets of grey ink, diagonal and relentless, and you can almost hear the needles hiss. The Karasaki pine was already a celebrity tree, propped up on wooden crutches so its enormous limbs wouldn't snap. That's the point: something ancient, stubborn, refusing to come apart in weather. From the Eight Views of Omi, published around 1834.

Hiroshige_View_of_a_long_bridge_across_a.title: Hiroshige View of a long bridge across a lake
Hiroshige_View_of_a_long_bridge_across_a.description: 8 Views of Omi - #7. Evening Glow In Seta

source.canonical_title: File:Hiroshige View of a long bridge across a lake.jpg

Hiroshige_View_of_a_long_bridge_across_a.story: Evening at Seta, and the Karahashi bridge stretches across the water in two graceful leaps, stepping from a little pine island. Boatmen drift home; the sky turns peach and mauve. Seta's bridge was the spot where Lake Biwa funnels into the Seta River — the only crossing south of the lake, and a poet's shorthand for journey's end. Hiroshige made it the seventh of his Eight Views of Omi around 1834. A samurai once said you couldn't claim to have seen Japan without crossing it.

Hodakayama,_from_the_series_Twelve_Scene.title: Hodakayama
Hodakayama,_from_the_series_Twelve_Scene.description: Hodakayama, from the series Twelve Scenes in the Japan Alps, Hiroshi Yoshida

source.canonical_title: File:Hodakayama, from the series Twelve Scenes in the Japan Alps, Hiroshi Yoshida.jpg

Hodakayama,_from_the_series_Twelve_Scene.story: Snow still clings to the ridges of Mount Hotaka as a climbing party picks its way up the scree in the foreground, their packs rendered in a handful of deft strokes. Yoshida, who led ascents in the Northern Alps nearly every summer, drew from memory and on-site sketches. The print belongs to his 1926 series Twelve Scenes in the Japan Alps, issued the year he also cut the Seto Inland Sea set, and is one of only a few Yoshida woodblocks to include identifiable human figures at work.

Hokusai_(1828)_Cuckoo_and_Azaleas.jpg.title: Hokusai (1828) Cuckoo and Azaleas
Hokusai_(1828)_Cuckoo_and_Azaleas.jpg.description: Ukiyo-e woodblock print of a cuckoo and azaleas by Japanese artist Katsushika Hokusai (1828)

source.canonical_title: File:Hokusai (1828) Cuckoo and Azaleas.jpg

Hokusai_(1828)_Cuckoo_and_Azaleas.jpg.story: Not Mount Fuji, not a wave. A small vertical print from around 1828: a little cuckoo drops past a branch of pink azaleas with a haiku tucked in beside it. Hokusai made a set of these bird-and-flower pieces in the middle of his landscape boom, tighter and quieter than the blockbusters. The poem is by an 18th-century poet named Hyakuchi; the bird is caught mid-dive.

Hokusai_1760-1849_Ocean_waves.jpg.title: 'Chôshi in Shimôsa Province'

source.canonical_title: File:Hokusai 1760-1849 Ocean waves.jpg

Hokusai_1760-1849_Ocean_waves.jpg.story: Hokusai was in his seventies when he cut this block, working alongside his more famous Great Wave. Choshi sits at the mouth of the Tone River in old Shimosa Province, notorious for the way ocean swells slam into outflowing current. He gives you a single fishing boat tipped on the lip of a wave, the crew mid-grip, the horizon shoved up high so the water does most of the work. It comes from Chie no umi, a ten-print set of fishing scenes whose title puns on 'oceans of wisdom.' The series was published by Moriya Jihei around 1832-34 and stopped abruptly, unfinished - one of Hokusai's rarest runs.

Hokusai_Manga_01.jpg.title: Hokusai Manga 01
Hokusai_Manga_01.jpg.description: A page from Hokusai Manga Volume I

source.canonical_title: File:Hokusai Manga 01.jpg
source.credit: Michener, James A. (1958) Hokusai Sketchbooks: Selections from the Manga , Rutland, Vermont & Tokyo: Charles E. Tuttle Company

Hokusai_Manga_01.jpg.story: Don't let the word fool you. Hokusai's manga meant brush gone wild, not comics, and this first volume came off the blocks in 1814 when he was 55 and short on money. The aim was practical: a sketchbook for students to copy from. He filled it with immortals, Buddhas, scholars, fishermen, wrestlers, grasses, birds, expressions of rage and boredom, all in black, grey, and a flush of pale pink. Fifteen volumes followed, over four thousand drawings in total.
Hokusai_Manga_01.jpg.year_note: Volume 1 of Hokusai Manga was published in 1814, not 1850.

Hokusai_Manga_02.jpg.title: Hokusai Manga 02

source.canonical_title: File:Hokusai Manga 02.jpg
source.credit: Michener, James A. (1958) Hokusai Sketchbooks: Selections from the Manga , Rutland, Vermont & Tokyo: Charles E. Tuttle Company

Hokusai_Manga_02.jpg.story: Volume two, same hungry eye. Hokusai's Manga was block-printed in only three inks, black, grey, and a dusty pink, and every page crams in dozens of figures, as if he couldn't waste the paper. Wrestlers bend, cranes preen, a scholar dozes, a child yawns. He called the project brush gone wild, and the second volume appeared in 1815, riding the runaway success of the first. The set eventually grew to fifteen volumes and around four thousand images, the last three published posthumously.

Holbein_Danse_Macabre_1.jpg.title: Danse Macabre. I. The Creation

source.canonical_title: File:Holbein Danse Macabre 1.jpg
source.credit: Taken from Die imposante Galerie , originally uploaded by Soilwork

Holbein_Danse_Macabre_1.jpg.story: The opening plate of Holbein's Dance of Death series, cut around 1526 when he was working in Basel and not yet the Tudor court painter he'd become in London. God the Father leans out of a cloud above Eden while animals mill in the foreground - a deer, a boar, a rabbit, fish in the stream. It's only the first plate: the skeletons, the pope, the emperor and the ploughman all come later. Small enough to hold in your palm, but the block-cutting is sharp enough that every leaf reads.

Homère_déifié,_dit_aussi_L'apothéose_d'H.title: The Apotheosis of Homer

source.canonical_title: File:Homère déifié, dit aussi L'apothéose d'Homère - Jean-Auguste Dominique Ingres - Musée du Louvre Peintures INV 5417 ; C 196.jpg

title.fr: Homère déifié, dit aussi L'apothéose d'Homère

Homère_déifié,_dit_aussi_L'apothéose_d'H.story: A state commission for a ceiling in Charles X's new Louvre galleries. Homer sits enthroned on the steps of a Greek temple, crowned by a winged figure of the Universe; the Iliad and Odyssey rest at his feet like twin daughters. Around him, the great men of every age jostle to pay respects: Raphael peeks out top left in black Renaissance dress, Dante, Poussin, Molière, Racine, all packed in like a class photo of civilization. Ingres made over a hundred drawings for it. It came off the ceiling in 1855.

Honjo_Tatekawa,_the_timberyard_at_Honjo..story: A lumberyard in Honjo, on the east bank of the Sumida. Tall planks stand stacked like a forest of right angles; one man saws, two more unload tiles, and the whole print becomes a lesson in geometry. Between the timbers, a small, polite Fuji. Hokusai loved these working-city views as much as the spectacular ones. Tatekawa literally means 'standing river' — the canal that floated the logs into town.
