Hugo_van_der_Goes_(Gand,_1440_circa_–_Au.title: Monforte Altarpiece

source.canonical_title: File:Hugo van der Goes (Gand, 1440 circa – Auderghem, 1482) Altare Monforte - Adorazione dei Magi (1470 circa) - Tecnica olio su tavola Dimensioni 147×242 cm - Gemäldegalerie, Berlin.jpg
source.credit: Flickr Raffaele pagani Taken on 22 August 2019

Hugo_van_der_Goes_(Gand,_1440_circa_–_Au.story: An Adoration staged like a solemn audience: the Virgin in deep blue holds a pale, alert Christ Child while the eldest king kneels at left, the second in red presses his palms together, and the third, a young Black king, stands at right with a jewelled crown held out. Behind them, through an archway, a receding miniature landscape — tiny riders, a village, shepherds being told the news. Van der Goes packs the surface with brocade, fur and wilting plants, all rendered with that cold Flemish precision that lets you count the threads. The panel once anchored a much larger altarpiece; the wings are lost.

Hugo_van_der_Goes_-_Vienna_Diptych.jpg.title: Vienna Diptych

source.canonical_title: File:Hugo van der Goes - Vienna Diptych.jpg

title.de: Diptychon mit Sündenfall und Erlösung (Beweinung Christi)

Hugo_van_der_Goes_-_Vienna_Diptych.jpg.story: Two small panels side by side. On the left, Adam and Eve stand under the fatal tree; the serpent, painted with a little human head and a lizard's body, reaches up for the apple. On the right, the body of Christ is being lowered onto the ground, Mary collapsed over him, the mourners jammed into the picture at every scale. Fall on one side, Redemption on the other — the oldest binary in Christian art, compressed by Van der Goes into something intimate enough to hold in your hands. He painted this in the last few years before his breakdown, and the Lamentation already feels dangerously close in.

Hungry_Ghosts_Scroll_Kyoto_5.jpg.title: Hungry Ghosts Scroll

source.canonical_title: File:Hungry Ghosts Scroll Kyoto 5.jpg

Hungry_Ghosts_Scroll_Kyoto_5.jpg.story: A section of the 12th-century Gaki Zoshi, a Buddhist handscroll depicting the realm of the hungry ghosts, one of the six paths of rebirth. Emaciated gaki with distended bellies grovel near a seated Buddha, while others writhe in flames at the right. The text alongside, in courtly kana, narrates their torments. Paint is worn and paper is foxed, which only adds to the unease. These scrolls were didactic: look at what greed in this life earns you in the next. Late Heian Japan took karma seriously enough to illustrate it in full color.

Hunt-AwakeningConscience1853.jpg.title: The Awakening Conscience

source.canonical_title: File:Hunt-AwakeningConscience1853.jpg

Hunt-AwakeningConscience1853.jpg.story: A kept woman rises abruptly from her lover's lap, something in the drawing-room song at the piano having startled her. Hunt crammed every surface with moral clues — the cat toying with a bird under the table, the tangled embroidery, the unmarked wedding finger — and insisted on a real room in a St John's Wood 'maison de convenance.' Ruskin wrote a long letter to The Times explaining every symbol. Hunt meant it as the secular companion to his Light of the World.

Hyacinthe_Rigaud_-_Gio._Francesco_II_Bri.title: Gio. Francesco II Brignole-Sale

source.canonical_title: File:Hyacinthe Rigaud - Gio. Francesco II Brignole-Sale - Google Art Project.jpg
source.credit: uAGQ6aZ0QZCs0A at Google Cultural Institute maximum zoom level

Hyacinthe_Rigaud_-_Gio._Francesco_II_Bri.story: The Genoese aristocrat Giovanni Francesco II Brignole-Sale swept through Paris in 1739 and sat for the eighty-year-old Rigaud, by then the grandest portraitist in France. Rigaud gives him the full royal treatment he had perfected on Louis XIV: scarlet drapery, a thundercloud, the heavy choreography of cuffs and wig. It was one of the last major commissions the painter would complete before his death in 1743. The portrait went back to Genoa with its sitter and still hangs in the Palazzo Rosso, part of the Musei di Strada Nuova.

Hyacinthe_Rigaud_-_Portrait_of_Cardinal_.title: Portrait of Cardinal Guillaume Dubois
Hyacinthe_Rigaud_-_Portrait_of_Cardinal_.description: Luxurious, flamboyant dress—a voluminous wrap of scarlet silk topped by a short fur cape—signals that the subject of Hyacinthe Rigaud’s portrait was clearly a man of consequence. Guillaume Dubois gained the favor of Louis XIV as tutor to his grandson, the future king Louis XV, and served as chief minister under Louis’s successors, the regent Duke of Orleans and Louis XV. Dubois was appointed a cardinal in the Catholic Church in 1721, a lofty aspiration at least partly motivated by political ambition: the title gave him the power to remove political adversaries with impunity. Dubois holds a letter with the words Au Roy (to the king), commemorating the moment he had the honor of proclaiming his former student as king.

source.canonical_title: File:Hyacinthe Rigaud - Portrait of Cardinal Guillaume Dubois - 1967.17 - Cleveland Museum of Art.jpg

Hyacinthe_Rigaud_-_Portrait_of_Cardinal_.story: Scarlet silk spills over the cardinal's shoulders in waves you can almost hear rustle. Guillaume Dubois had tutored the young Louis XV, and the letter in his hand — inscribed Au Roy — marks the moment he announced his former pupil's accession. Dubois had lobbied hard for the red hat he wears here; once a cardinal, he could expel rivals from office with ecclesiastical cover. Rigaud, now in his sixties, still knew how to make fabric carry the argument. Dubois died the same year the portrait was finished, 1723, barely enjoying the triumph it commemorates.

Hércules_lucha_con_la_hidra_de_Lerna,_po.title: Hercules Fighting the Hydra of Lerna
Hércules_lucha_con_la_hidra_de_Lerna,_po.description: En esta escena Hércules debe enfrentarse a un animal fabuloso que representa un peligro para los hombres y simboliza los males y los vicios a los que el hijo de Zeus y de Alcmena vence tras probar su astucia y fuerza. El mal aparece representado por una sierpe de extraña figura con muchas cabezas a la cual decían hidra y tenía tal naturaleza que por una cabeza de aquellas que le fuere tajada le nacían tres, en manera que cuanto más trabajaran en su muerte [...] tanto más ella por su naturaleza multiplicaba su vida. Así inicia Enrique de Villena el relato del terrible peligro que representaba la hidra, cuyo final habían intentado los habitantes de la pantanosa región de Lerna, cerca de Argos, donde no había descanso ni paz a causa del dañino monstruo. Para resolver esta situación, Hércules, cubierto con la piel del león de Nemea que ya había matado en el episodio anterior (P1243), tuvo que sustituir la fuerza por el ingenio. La hidra fue acorralada y destruida por medio del fuego y enterradas luego sus cenizas. En sintonía con otros de los cuadros de la serie, Zurbarán destaca la poderosa figura de Hércules en el centro de la escena, en plena ejecución del castigo al monstruo y fuertemente iluminado frente a la oscuridad que envuelve el fondo. De nuevo, el pintor se apoyó para resolver la composición en las estampas de Cornelis Cort, tomando aspectos de varios episodios de la serie flamenca, aunque especialmente de la del mismo tema, donde figura también el sobrino del protagonista, Iolao. Éste, apareciendo por la derecha de la escena, porta la tea encendida que consumaría la destrucción de la hidra. De la misma estampa se toma el cangrejo situado a los pies del héroe -en el grabado, asoman además una serie interminable de animales que incluía escorpiones-, y de cuya presencia encontramos una explicación en la obra de Baltasar de Victoria, quien cuenta que salió un cancro de la Laguna Lerna a dar ayuda a la portentosa Hidra. Las principales diferencias con la representación del grabador Cornelis Cort las hallamos en el escenario donde transcurre el episodio, cerrado y claustrofóbico en la pintura de Zurbarán, muy alejado del exterior luminoso de la propuesta del flamenco. Varían también los tipos humanos, revestidos en el lienzo de un carácter tosco y popular que quizás pretendía españolizar el mito. Las bruñidas cabezas, ejecutadas de una manera muy sumaria en relación con el modelado de los cuerpos, se destacan por su tono tostado, como si estuviéramos ante aldeanos que se hubieran desprendido de su vestimenta para la ocasión (Texto extractado de Ruiz, L. en: El Palacio del Rey Planeta. Felipe IV y el Buen Retiro, Museo Nacional del Prado, 2005, p. 149).

source.canonical_title: File:Hércules lucha con la hidra de Lerna, por Zurbarán.jpg

Hércules_lucha_con_la_hidra_de_Lerna,_po.story: Part of a ten-canvas Hercules cycle Zurbarán painted for the Hall of Realms at Philip IV's new Buen Retiro palace in 1634. Here the hero, wrapped in the Nemean lion's skin, torches the Hydra while his nephew Iolaus rushes in with a second brand. Zurbarán leaned on prints by Cornelis Cort for the composition but swapped the Flemish sunshine for his own claustrophobic gloom and gave Hercules the sun-browned face of a Spanish peasant. Prado.

Idylls_of_the_King_3.jpg.story: Plate III from Doré's plates for Tennyson's Arthurian cycle, first published 1867 — the humbled knight Edyrn, his lady, and his dwarf making their way toward Camelot to submit to the king. Doré gives it the melancholy hush he reserved for chivalric material: mist, a thin procession, the court somewhere ahead in the fog. The illustrated volumes were the must-have Christmas gifts of their year in London, and they sold Tennyson harder than any review ever did.

Ike_Taiga_-_Orchids_-_1975.268.94_-_Metr.title: Orchids

source.canonical_title: File:Ike Taiga - Orchids - 1975.268.94 - Metropolitan Museum of Art.jpg

Ike_Taiga_-_Orchids_-_1975.268.94_-_Metr.story: A few orchid leaves arc across the paper like flung calligraphy, a single blossom balanced at the tip. Taiga, a self-taught prodigy from Kyoto who could paint with his fingers, here uses the brush as a writer would, the stems practically a grass-script signature. Edo-period literati loved the orchid because it bloomed unseen in valleys, a Confucian metaphor for virtue without audience. The Met has held this hanging scroll since 1975 as part of the Harry G. C. Packard Collection.

Ildefonso-Altar_-_The_Holy_Family_under_.title: The Holy Family under the Apple Tree
Ildefonso-Altar_-_The_Holy_Family_under_.description: Ildefonso-Altar: the Holy Family under the appletree

source.canonical_title: File:Ildefonso-Altar - The Holy Family under the appletree, by Peter Paul Rubens.jpg

title.de: Ildefonso-Altar: Die Hl. Familie unter dem Apfelbaum (Außenseiten der Flügel)
title.nl: De heilige familie onder de appelboom met Johannes de Doper, Elisabeth en Zacharias

Ildefonso-Altar_-_The_Holy_Family_under_.story: This is the back. When the Ildefonso triptych closed in the court chapel of St. Jacob op de Coudenberg in Brussels, worshippers saw this: the Holy Family dozing under an apple tree, young John the Baptist wandering in with his parents, a domestic scene standing in for Eden's lost one. The apple is the point. Commissioned around 1630 by the governess Isabella Clara Eugenia, it panels out to 362 by 246 cm and now lives in Vienna's Kunsthistorisches Museum.

Ilia_Efimovich_Repin_(1844-1930)_-_Volga.title: Barge Haulers on the Volga

source.canonical_title: File:Ilia Efimovich Repin (1844-1930) - Volga Boatmen (1870-1873).jpg

Ilia_Efimovich_Repin_(1844-1930)_-_Volga.story: Eleven men in rags drag a barge upriver by a leather harness slung across the chest. Repin spent two summers on the Volga sketching the real haulers — the defrocked priest Kanin at the front, the sunburnt boy Larka in pink straightening against the strap. Dostoevsky worried the painting would be a protest tract; instead Repin gave each hauler a face, a history, a private exhaustion. It took three years to finish and made him famous at twenty-nine. Tsar Alexander III's brother bought it for 3,000 roubles.

Ilja_Jefimowitsch_Repin_-_Reply_of_the_Z.title: The Zaporozhye Cossacks Replying to the Sultan

source.canonical_title: File:Ilja Jefimowitsch Repin - Reply of the Zaporozhian Cossacks - Yorck.jpg
source.credit: The Yorck Project (2002) 10.000 Meisterwerke der Malerei (DVD-ROM), distributed by DIRECTMEDIA Publishing GmbH. ISBN : 3936122202 .

title.fr: Les Cosaques zaporogues écrivant une lettre au sultan de Turquie
title.de: Saporoschzen schreiben dem türkischen Sultan einen Brief

Ilja_Jefimowitsch_Repin_-_Reply_of_the_Z.story: A gang of Cossacks collapses in laughter around a scribe as they dictate a gleefully obscene reply to Sultan Mehmed IV, who had ordered their surrender. Repin worked on it for more than a decade, sketching Cossack descendants on trips to Ukraine and hunting down the right kind of laugh on every face. You can see the gap-toothed hetman Ivan Sirko at the centre, pipe in hand. Tsar Alexander III bought the finished canvas in 1891 for 35,000 roubles, then a record; this is the earlier 1878–1891 version now in the Russian Museum.

Ilya_Repin_-_Ceremonial_Sitting_of_the_S.title: Ceremonial Sitting of the State Council on 7 May 1901 Marking the Centenary of its Foundation.

source.canonical_title: File:Ilya Repin - Ceremonial Sitting of the State Council on 7 May 1901 Marking the Centenary of its Foundation - Google Art Project.jpg
source.credit: uAFzvVW61WKsPg at Google Cultural Institute maximum zoom level

Ilya_Repin_-_Ceremonial_Sitting_of_the_S.story: Eighty-one bureaucrats in gold braid, painted life-size, stretching across four by nearly nine metres of canvas. Nicholas II commissioned it to mark the Council's centenary on 7 May 1901, and Repin, nearly sixty and losing the use of his right hand, finished it in 1903 with help from his students Boris Kustodiev and Ivan Kulikov, who each took sections of the hall. The Emperor approved. Fifteen years later the regime it celebrated was gone; the painting survives in the Russian Museum.

Ilya_Repin_-_Cesar_Cui.jpg.story: César Cui was the odd man out of the Mighty Handful — by day a military fortifications engineer who lectured czars on siege warfare, by night a composer and the group's sharp-elbowed critic. Repin had already painted the rest of the circle; Cui sat for him in 1890, and Repin gives him in civilian dress, sidelong, pen or book in hand, looking less like a soldier than a quietly irritable man of letters. The portrait belongs to that long Repin project of fixing the faces of his generation's Russian cultural life — the same impulse behind his portraits of Mussorgsky, Borodin, Stasov and Rimsky-Korsakov.

Ilya_Repin_-_Dragonfly._Painter's_daught.title: Dragonfly. Painter's daughter portrait

source.canonical_title: File:Ilya Repin - Dragonfly. Painter's daughter portrait - Google Art Project.jpg

title.ru: Стрекоза. Портрет В.И. Репиной, дочери художника
title.avk: Delt va nazbeya ke Repin (trutca ke Repin)
title.pt: Libélula. Retrato da filha do pintor

Ilya_Repin_-_Dragonfly._Painter's_daught.story: Twelve-year-old Vera Repina perches on a wooden rail against a bleached summer sky, legs dangling, hat tilted, painted at the family's dacha in 1884. Repin catches her mid-fidget, half-grin half-squint, and the title sticks: she's a dragonfly on a stalk. No grand subject, no allegory, just the light through a straw hat and a father amused by his daughter. The canvas is 111 by 84 cm and has been in Moscow's Tretyakov Gallery for over a century.

Ilya_Repin_-_Sadko_-_Google_Art_Project_.title: Садко

source.canonical_title: File:Ilya Repin - Sadko - Google Art Project levels adjustment 2.jpg
source.credit: PgFUvF6cbe8PYQ at Google Cultural Institute maximum zoom level

Ilya_Repin_-_Sadko_-_Google_Art_Project_.story: The merchant-musician Sadko, from Russian epic poetry, stands at the bottom of the sea choosing a bride from the Tsar's undersea court. Repin, homesick in Paris, crowds the canvas with half-fish princesses parading past in greens and dirty golds; the rejected mermaids pout in the foreground. He painted the 322 by 230 cm canvas in 1876 and it won him membership in the Imperial Academy that same year. Tsesarevich Alexander bought it; it now hangs in the Russian Museum in St Petersburg.

Ilya_Repin_Unexpected_visitors.jpg.title: They did not expect him
Ilya_Repin_Unexpected_visitors.jpg.description: Shows the unexpected homecoming of a Russian revolutionary from exile in Siberia. The idea for ​the painting arose from the completion of the “Holy procession”. Here everything is seen right in front of the viewer. The artist is clearly present somewhere nearby, observing, listening, arguing. We find him on the right in the foreground by a characteristic head, familiar from his self-portraits of these years, and the equally characteristic slanting of the shoulders. It can be seen that the picture was painted over and over again, the role of each character clarified, their placement at the intersection of views and light rays; a free space preserved in front of them. Repin worked on the canvas twice as much as he did on the “Cross procession”, he felt his way to the “wandering”, elusive plot. “They did not expect him” was preceded by a trip to Spain, copying of Velazquez in the halls of the Museo Prado. Repin contrasted “cabinet theories” and “The Truth of Life.” This prompted him to blend the proportions of speculative and everyday, allowed him to combine the intellectual space of the plan with the interior of the house in Martyshkino, where he realized it. It is impossible to imagine that in the clear light of a quiet day, this strange phantom man appears timidly, uncertainly, that he has just walked along the sun-drenched grass greening through the balcony glass, that he will remain in this room where everyone except him has a place. There is a sad story about the returning, and not waiting, which is so difficult to understand each other.

source.canonical_title: File:Ilya Repin Unexpected visitors.jpg

Ilya_Repin_Unexpected_visitors.jpg.story: A revolutionary, released from Siberian exile, steps unannounced into the family drawing room. The mother half-rises from her chair; the wife at the piano turns in shock; the two children stare — the boy recognising his father, the little girl frowning at a stranger. Repin reworked the face of the returning man three times before he got the mixture of timidity and hope right. The room is drenched in ordinary afternoon sunlight, which is what makes the moment unbearable. Finished in 1884–1888 after a study trip to Spain copying Velázquez, it hangs in the Tretyakov Gallery.

Imaginary_tour_through_Xiao-xiang.jpg.title: Imaginary tour through Xiao-xiang
Imaginary_tour_through_Xiao-xiang.jpg.description: Part of the Imaginary tour through Xiao-xiang (紙本墨画瀟湘臥遊図, shihon bokuga shōshōgayūzu) by Li Shi (李氏) from the 12th century, Song Dynasty. Scroll, 30.3 cm x 400.4 cm. Ink on paper. Located at Tokyo National Museum , Tokyo .

Imaginary_tour_through_Xiao-xiang.jpg.story: A Southern Song handscroll, four metres of river in ink washes so pale they nearly evaporate. Low hills slide past, reed banks, a boat or two, the whole Xiaoxiang region imagined by a monk who never went. The painter signed only 李氏, Mr. Li, and vanished. What's extraordinary is how much the centuries added: every bright red square is a collector's seal, and the colophon at right gathers generations of commentary. The picture has been passed around, loved, stamped, argued over, and ended up in Tokyo. It is as much a record of viewers as of landscape.

In_the_Conservatory_-_edited.jpg.story: Manet's friends Jules and Jeanne Guillemet, who ran a fashionable clothing shop, in the glasshouse at 70 rue d'Amsterdam that Manet was borrowing as a studio. She sits on a bench in a grey dress; he stands behind, leaning over the back, cigar in hand. Their wedding rings catch the light and their fingers almost touch on the wood. Critics at the 1879 Salon found it unusually restrained for him. In 1896 the Berlin Nationalgalerie bought it, the first museum anywhere to acquire a Manet.

In_the_Water_by_Eugen_von_Blaas_(1843-19.title: In the Water by Eugen von Blaas (1843-1931)
In_the_Water_by_Eugen_von_Blaas_(1843-19.description: In the Water oil on canvas 80.3 x 45 cm signed l.l.: Eug de Blaas

In_the_Water_by_Eugen_von_Blaas_(1843-19.story: A startling outlier in de Blaas's output — the only nude he is known to have painted. A young woman stands mid-calf in shallow water, leaning to watch a school of small fish drift past her shins. Cloud covers the sky, but a gold light still catches on the surface. The canvas is signed and dated 1914; the dated file name is off by several decades. Everything else — the Venetian light, the attention to wet fabric and flesh — is pure de Blaas.

IngresOdipusAndSphinx.jpg.story: Ingres first wrestled this subject in Rome as a young academic exercise, then kept enlarging it for decades. Oedipus leans in close, almost eye to eye with the winged monster, his calf muscles catching the light while a terrified survivor flees into the shadow behind. The Sphinx is tucked into her rocky grotto, paws crossed, her breast half in darkness. A skull and a dropped foot lie among the rocks, warnings to travelers who guessed wrong. The version in the Louvre was reworked from a 1808 envoi Ingres sent from the French Academy.

Ingres_(atelier)_-_Angélique_-_Piscine_R.story: A studio version of Ingres' 'Roger Freeing Angelica,' the subject drawn from Ariosto: Angelica chained naked to a rock as the knight Roger swoops in on his hippogriff to kill the sea monster. Ingres painted the original in 1819 for Louis XVIII and returned to the motif for years, with pupils producing replicas under his eye. This one hangs at La Piscine in Roubaix, the converted art-deco swimming pool turned museum. The pose — Angelica's arched neck, closed eyes, impossible marble torso — is pure Ingres: erotic and glacial at once.

Ingres_-_estudo_de_nu_-_1801.jpg.title: Study of a Male Nude

source.canonical_title: File:Ingres - estudo de nu - 1801.jpg
source.credit: Web Gallery of Art : Image Info about artwork wga QS:P11807,"i/ingres/00ingres"

Ingres_-_estudo_de_nu_-_1801.jpg.story: Ingres was twenty-one and still an art student. In 1800 and 1801 he won the Academy's top prize for figure painting with studies like this one — a careful, contrapposto male nude painted from the life model at the École. The same year he took the Prix de Rome with a much larger mythological scene. The drawing here is cool, sculptural, already showing the silhouette-first instinct he'd carry into his portraits. Look how the weight shifts onto one leg, the other relaxed: pure classical contrapposto, learned from marble.

Ingres_Academic_study_of_a_male_torso.jp.title: Academic study of a male torso.

source.canonical_title: File:Ingres Academic study of a male torso.jpg

Ingres_Academic_study_of_a_male_torso.jp.story: A naked man, a north light, a charcoal stick: this was what art students did all morning at the École in 1801. Ingres did it better than most. He won the Academy's top figure-painting prize that year and the Prix de Rome on top of it, with studies no more elaborate than this one. He's not interested in character; he wants the long, unbroken outline. Today this particular study sits in the National Museum in Warsaw, one of a small group of survivors from his student years.

Ingres_Etude_Bain_Turc_Louvre_1859.jpg.title: Ingres Etude Bain Turc Louvre 1859
Ingres_Etude_Bain_Turc_Louvre_1859.jpg.description: Ingres, étude dessinée pour le Bain Turc 1859 cabinet des dessins musée du Louvre

source.canonical_title: File:Ingres Etude Bain Turc Louvre 1859.jpg

Ingres_Etude_Bain_Turc_Louvre_1859.jpg.story: A working drawing from the Louvre's cabinet des dessins, made while Ingres was wrestling his great late harem picture into its final round form. Pencil, chalk, the outlines of stacked nudes overlapping in the steam. He was 79, still drawing bodies from memory and from the squared-up tracings of figures he'd invented decades earlier. The sheet is dated 1859. Three years later he'd cut the painting down from a rectangle into the tondo we know now as Le Bain turc.

Ingres_Odalisque_esclave_Fogg_Art.jpeg.title: Odalisque with Slave
Ingres_Odalisque_esclave_Fogg_Art.jpeg.description: Ingres, L'Odalisque à l'esclave , 1839 Fogg art museum

source.canonical_title: File:Ingres Odalisque esclave Fogg Art.jpeg

Ingres_Odalisque_esclave_Fogg_Art.jpeg.story: A harem scene with the volume turned down. The odalisque lies back on cushions, one arm flung overhead, her eyes half-closed; at her feet, a slave in striped silks plays a long-necked tanbur while a Black eunuch keeps watch at the far door. Peacock feathers, a hookah, a small fountain in the garden beyond. The music is the whole point, even though you can't hear it. Ingres painted two versions; the Harvard Art Museums' Fogg holds this one, signed and dated 1839.

Iván_el_Terrible_y_su_hijo,_por_Iliá_Rep.story: Ivan IV has just struck his son with an iron-tipped staff; now he clutches the dying tsarevich to his chest, thumb pressed uselessly against the wound, eyes wide with the knowledge of what he has done. Blood soaks the carpet. Repin painted it after hearing a Rimsky-Korsakov symphonic movement and watching a bullfight in Spain, wanting, he said, to paint the colour of guilt. A viewer slashed the canvas with a knife in 1913; another attacked it with a security post in 2018. Still in the Tretyakov, still being restored.

J.L._Gerome_-_The_Wailing_Wall_-_Google_.story: Gerome, meticulous even by Orientalist standards, painted the great Herodian ashlar blocks of the Western Wall in Jerusalem so precisely you can count the weathering lines. A handful of worshippers lean into the stone; weeds sprout from the mortar. He traveled repeatedly to the region and worked from photographs as well as sketches. The canvas is dated 1880. It's now in the collection of the Israel Museum in Jerusalem, a few hundred meters from the wall itself.

JEAN_LOUIS_THÉODORE_GÉRICAULT_-_La_Bal.title: The Raft of the Medusa

source.canonical_title: File:JEAN LOUIS THÉODORE GÉRICAULT - La Balsa de la Medusa (Museo del Louvre, 1818-19).jpg

title.vi: Chiếc bè của chiến thuyền Méduse

JEAN_LOUIS_THÉODORE_GÉRICAULT_-_La_Bal.story: Fifteen survivors on a makeshift raft, after thirteen days of saltwater, sunstroke, mutiny, and cannibalism. Géricault interviewed two of them, built a scale model, sketched severed limbs in the morgue, and shaved his head so he wouldn't leave the studio. The moment he chose isn't rescue but the instant before it, when a tiny speck on the horizon might still ignore them. The 1816 wreck of the Méduse was a political scandal; Géricault made it a painting 23 feet wide. The Louvre has owned it since 1824.

Jacob_Jordaens_-_Naked_old_man,_standing.story: A life study — a standing nude of an old man, the slumped shoulders and loose skin observed with the same unglamorized interest Jordaens would bring to his satyrs and feast-table uncles a decade later. The 1600 date on this image is almost certainly wrong (Jordaens was seven years old) and it likely comes from his earlier working years, when he was still in Adam van Noort's studio alongside the young Rubens. Drawings and oil sketches of this kind circulated through Antwerp workshops as reference material; the same ungilded body type turns up again and again in his later mythologies.

Jacob_Jordaens_-_Prometheus_bound.jpg.title: Prometheus Bound

source.canonical_title: File:Jacob Jordaens - Prometheus bound.jpg

Jacob_Jordaens_-_Prometheus_bound.jpg.story: Prometheus chained to his Caucasus rock, the eagle at his liver — the punishment for stealing fire. Jordaens was following Rubens, who had painted a famous version of the same subject in 1611–12 with the eagle tearing at a very muscular Titan. Jordaens' take is darker and less operatic, with the figure sagging rather than writhing, the bird's wing crowding the upper frame. It belongs to a run of mythological pictures he made in the 1640s when his workshop was taking on the kind of classical commissions Rubens had formerly monopolized. Wallraf-Richartz Museum, Cologne.

Jacob_Jordaens_-_Psyche_receives_the_cup.title: Psyche receives the cup of immortality on the Olympus

source.canonical_title: File:Jacob Jordaens - Psyche receives the cup of immortality on the Olympus.jpg

Jacob_Jordaens_-_Psyche_receives_the_cup.story: The payoff of the Apuleius story: Jupiter has forgiven the mortal Psyche, and on Olympus the cup of ambrosia is passed to her — she becomes a goddess and is finally reunited with Cupid. Jordaens gives the gods in an unposed huddle of pink flesh and wine-colored drapery, less ceremonial than domestic. The canvas belongs to the great decorative cycle he produced for Huis ten Bosch outside The Hague, commissioned by Amalia van Solms after the death of her husband Frederick Henry — the Oranjezaal, where Jordaens painted several of the largest walls.

Jacob_Jordaens_-_Selbstbildnis_-_12876_-.title: Self portrait

source.canonical_title: File:Jacob Jordaens - Selbstbildnis - 12876 - Bavarian State Painting Collections.jpg

Jacob_Jordaens_-_Selbstbildnis_-_12876_-.story: Jordaens inherited Rubens's studio empire after 1640 and ran Antwerp painting for two decades. Here he is looking at himself around 1650, hair receding, gaze level, the collar a tired white against dark cloth. No allegory, no flourish, just a working painter in his fifties who still had commissions flooding in from Sweden to Spain. The portrait is in the Bavarian State Painting Collections in Munich.

Jacob_Jordaens_-_The_Feast_of_the_Bean_K.title: The Feast of the Bean King

source.canonical_title: File:Jacob Jordaens - The Feast of the Bean King - Google Art Project.jpg
source.credit: MwEBgGg74T1f2g at Google Cultural Institute maximum zoom level

Jacob_Jordaens_-_The_Feast_of_the_Bean_K.story: On Twelfth Night in Flanders, whoever found the bean baked into the cake became king for the evening, and everyone had to drink when he drank. Jordaens painted the scene more than once, and this riotous Vienna version is the grandest: a red-faced king in a paper crown, faces shining with wine, a dog, a baby, someone being sick in the corner. The Latin motto up top translates roughly as 'nothing resembles a madman more than a drunkard.' It hangs in the Kunsthistorisches Museum.

Jacob_Wrestles_with_the_Angel_(89394819).story: Genesis 32: Jacob, alone by the Jabbok, grapples all night with a stranger who turns out not to be a man. Doré stages it like a sculpture group — Jacob planted, the angel lifted on one wing, both locked until dawn. The plate appeared in the 1866 illustrated Bible, engraved by Laplante, and became a fixture of Sunday-school literature for a century. Doré's angel is strikingly physical: no glow, just muscle and a grip that won't let go until it does.

Jacopo_Tintoretto_-_Marriage_at_Cana_-_W.title: Marriage at Cana

source.canonical_title: File:Jacopo Tintoretto - Marriage at Cana - WGA22470.jpg
source.credit: Web Gallery of Art : Image Info about artwork wga QS:P11807,"t/tintoret/3_1560s/2cana"

Jacopo_Tintoretto_-_Marriage_at_Cana_-_W.story: Tintoretto hurls the wedding at Cana down a vertiginous receding table — figures small at the far end, serving-women enormous in the foreground handling amphorae. The miracle itself (water into wine) is half-hidden in the crush; Christ is small and distant, and what you notice first is the dinner service. He painted it for the refectory of the Santa Maria della Salute's predecessor, Santa Maria dei Crociferi, in 1561. The painting survived the fire that gutted the church in 1629 and is now in the sacristy of the Salute, alongside his later Old Testament scenes.

Jacopo_Tintoretto_-_The_Last_Supper_-_WG.story: Tintoretto's final Last Supper, painted 1592-94 for San Giorgio Maggiore, still hangs where he put it. He refused Leonardo's frontal symmetry: the table rockets back at a steep diagonal into the gloom of a Venetian inn, servants clearing plates, a cat sniffing a basket. Light comes from a smoky oil lamp and from Christ's own halo, which dissolves into a swarm of transparent angels overhead. The everyday and the supernatural share one room. He died two years after finishing it.

James_Abbot_McNeill_Whistler_006.jpg.story: Old Battersea Bridge was a creaking wooden thing by 1872, due to be torn down, and Whistler turned it into a Japanese print. The single pier looms like a Hiroshige pillar; fireworks flare in the distance; the water holds everything in a wash of blue. He painted it from memory after evenings on the river, and one critic joked that real bridges don't look like that. Ruskin would soon say much worse about a related Nocturne. This one now hangs at Tate Britain.

James_Abbot_McNeill_Whistler_011.jpg.story: The real title is Harmony in Pink and Grey: Portrait of Lady Meux. Valerie Meux had been a bartender and possibly a banjo-playing stage performer before marrying into a brewing fortune; polite society refused her, so she commissioned Whistler to paint her three times. She stands as if on a stage, chiffon train trailing pink. The two got on well until they didn't, and Whistler destroyed a third portrait after an argument. This one hangs at the Frick in New York.

James_Abbott_McNeill_Whistler,_Fishing_B.title: James Abbott McNeill Whistler, Fishing Boat, 1879-1880, etching on laid paper
James_Abbott_McNeill_Whistler,_Fishing_B.description: Fishing Boat by James Abbott McNeill Whistler, 1879-1880, etching on laid paper

source.canonical_title: File:James Abbott McNeill Whistler, Fishing Boat, 1879-1880, etching on laid paper.jpg

James_Abbott_McNeill_Whistler,_Fishing_B.story: Bankrupted by the Ruskin lawsuit, Whistler accepted a commission from the Fine Art Society and fled to Venice for what was supposed to be three months. He stayed fourteen. Fishing Boat belongs to the Second Venice Set, published in 1886, printed on warm laid paper so the drypoint burr glows. A narrow hull and mast cut across the middle, a single figure aboard, the water sketched in loose horizontal squiggles. A domed church hovers at the right edge, barely there. He came home solvent.

James_Abbott_McNeill_Whistler,_Rotherhit.title: James Abbott McNeill Whistler, Rotherhithe, etching, 1860, Dallas Museum of Art
James_Abbott_McNeill_Whistler,_Rotherhit.description: Rotherhithe is an etching by James Abbott McNeill Whistler that was completed in 1860. It is held by the Dallas Museum of Art.

source.canonical_title: File:James Abbott McNeill Whistler, Rotherhithe, etching, 1860, Dallas Museum of Art.jpg

James_Abbott_McNeill_Whistler,_Rotherhit.story: Whistler etched this from the balcony of the Angel Inn at Rotherhithe, looking across the Thames toward the City, with the dome of St Paul's just visible at the far left. Two men loaf in the foreground while a forest of rigging and warehouse roofs stretches beyond. It is one of sixteen plates that became the Thames Set, held back until 1871. Even Whistler's hardest critics conceded the etchings; Rotherhithe is the one collectors have always fought over, a working river seen by someone in no hurry.

James_McNeill_Whistler_-_Green_and_Silve.title: Green and Silver: Beaulieu, Touraine

source.canonical_title: File:James McNeill Whistler - Green and Silver- Beaulieu, Touraine - Google Art Project.jpg
source.credit: IQEu_qM6fwiCLQ at Google Cultural Institute maximum zoom level

James_McNeill_Whistler_-_Green_and_Silve.story: A riverbank in the Loire valley, reduced to a few bands of green and silver. Whistler made this on a painting trip in 1888, and kept the panel small so he could carry it in a pocket. There's a boy fishing, maybe, a strip of water, a slip of sky, the whole thing handled so thin you see the wood grain through it. He'd stopped calling these studies and started calling them pictures. It's at the Freer Gallery in Washington.

James_McNeill_Whistler_-_La_Princesse_du.title: The Princess from the Land of Porcelain

source.canonical_title: File:James McNeill Whistler - La Princesse du pays de la porcelaine - Google Art Project edit2.jpg
source.credit: This file was derived from: James McNeill Whistler - La Princesse du pays de la porcelaine - Google Art Project.jpg :

title.fr: La Princesse du pays de la porcelaine

James_McNeill_Whistler_-_La_Princesse_du.story: A British shipping magnate named Frederick Leyland bought this painting in 1864 and hung it in his London dining room. Whistler, who'd painted his model Christina Spartali in a kimono against Japanese screens, then redecorated the entire room around it in peacock blue and gold while Leyland was away, sending a famously outrageous bill. Leyland refused to pay in full. The painting and the whole feud-stained room are now installed at the Freer Gallery in Washington.

James_McNeill_Whistler_-_The_Artist_in_H.title: The Artist in His Studio

source.canonical_title: File:James McNeill Whistler - The Artist in His Studio - 1912.141 - Art Institute of Chicago.jpg

James_McNeill_Whistler_-_The_Artist_in_H.story: A tiny oil sketch, barely bigger than a sheet of paper, showing Whistler himself standing at an easel with two models, one of them Joanna Hiffernan, in a crowded London studio. He intended a much larger painting from it and never finished one. The date is around 1865, just as Whistler was soaking up Japanese prints and turning away from realism. The sketch is at the Art Institute of Chicago.

James_McNeill_Whistler_-_The_Thames_in_I.story: Painted during the brutal London freeze of winter 1860, when the Thames clogged with ice floes and shipping ground to a halt. Whistler had just arrived from Paris and was living in rough Wapping; he set up on the riverbank and worked fast, in the cold, catching the moored hulls and cracked grey water. The brushwork is shockingly loose for a 26-year-old. Signed 'Whistler 1860.' It's at the Freer Gallery in Washington.

James_McNeill_Whistler_-_Valparaiso_Harb.title: Valparaiso Harbor

source.canonical_title: File:James McNeill Whistler - Valparaiso Harbor - Google Art Project.jpg
source.credit: SAHIU1kIf-Bfhw at Google Cultural Institute maximum zoom level

James_McNeill_Whistler_-_Valparaiso_Harb.story: In 1866 Whistler did the oddest thing of his career: he sailed to Chile to help the Chileans in their war with Spain. He never fought, but he sat in Valparaiso harbor and painted ships at dusk. This is one of them, the masts thin as needles against a pink-grey sky, the water gone violet. These Chilean nocturnes were the direct ancestors of his famous Thames nocturnes back in London. It's at the Freer Gallery in Washington.

James_McNeill_Whistler_-_Variations_in_P.title: Variations in Pink and Grey: Chelsea

source.canonical_title: File:James McNeill Whistler - Variations in Pink and Grey- Chelsea - Google Art Project.jpg

James_McNeill_Whistler_-_Variations_in_P.story: Whistler lived on Cheyne Walk in Chelsea and painted the view from his windows obsessively in the early 1870s. This one is daylight, not nocturne, the Thames flat and milky, barges at anchor, a smokestack going. The colour scheme is exactly what the title says, pink and grey, with a single dab of Whistler's butterfly signature at the lower edge. Painted in 1871, it's held by the Freer Gallery in Washington.

Jan_Brueghel_I_&_Peter_Paul_Rubens_-_Hea.title: Hearing
Jan_Brueghel_I_&_Peter_Paul_Rubens_-_Hea.artist: Jan Brueghel the Elder / Peter Paul Rubens

source.canonical_title: File:Jan Brueghel I & Peter Paul Rubens - Hearing (Museo del Prado).jpg

Jan_Brueghel_I_&_Peter_Paul_Rubens_-_Hea.story: Hearing is the second Sense in the 1617 collaboration. Brueghel filled the room with every instrument he could think of: lutes, virginals, a harpsichord, brass horns, a table of sheet music, songbirds in a cage, a stag belling in the garden beyond. Rubens painted Venus reclining with Cupid while an orchestra of putti strikes up behind them. Look closely: there's a clock, a cannon, even a barking dog. The Count Palatine gave the series to Cardinal-Infante Ferdinand in 1634, and it's hung at the Prado since 1819.

Jan_Brueghel_I_&_Peter_Paul_Rubens_-_Sig.title: Allegory of sight
Jan_Brueghel_I_&_Peter_Paul_Rubens_-_Sig.artist: Jan Brueghel the Elder / Peter Paul Rubens

source.canonical_title: File:Jan Brueghel I & Peter Paul Rubens - Sight (Museo del Prado).jpg

Jan_Brueghel_I_&_Peter_Paul_Rubens_-_Sig.story: The year on the file is wrong; this is 1617, not 1585. Brueghel was still a teenager then, and Rubens unborn. Sight is the first of a five-part collaboration: Brueghel painted the setting (a collector's cabinet crammed with telescopes, globes, tapestries, and roughly eighty paintings), Rubens added the nude Venus and the winged putto holding up a picture of Christ healing a blind man. The series was a gift from the Count Palatine to the Cardinal-Infante in 1634, later Philip IV's. It's been at the Prado since the museum opened in 1819.

Jan_Brueghel_I_&_Peter_Paul_Rubens_-_Sme.title: Smell
Jan_Brueghel_I_&_Peter_Paul_Rubens_-_Sme.artist: Jan Brueghel the Elder / Peter Paul Rubens
Jan_Brueghel_I_&_Peter_Paul_Rubens_-_Sme.description: Allegory of the sense of smell

source.canonical_title: File:Jan Brueghel I & Peter Paul Rubens - Smell (Museo del Prado).jpg

Jan_Brueghel_I_&_Peter_Paul_Rubens_-_Sme.story: Brueghel was known as 'Velvet' for good reason, and Smell is him showing off: a garden stuffed with named, botanically correct flowers, civet cats, a musk deer, a still of perfume on a low table. Rubens dropped in a Venus sniffing a bouquet while putti mix scents at her feet. Each plant is small enough to press your nose to. The picture was painted in Antwerp in 1617, travelled to Spain in 1634 as a royal gift, and has hung at the Prado since 1819.

Jan_Brueghel_de_Oude_en_Peter_Paul_Ruben.title: The Garden of Eden with the Fall of Man
Jan_Brueghel_de_Oude_en_Peter_Paul_Ruben.artist: Peter Paul Rubens / Jan Brueghel the Elder

source.canonical_title: File:Jan Brueghel de Oude en Peter Paul Rubens - Het aards paradijs met de zondeval van Adam en Eva.jpg
source.credit: Geheugen van Nederland : Home : Info : Pic

title.pt: O jardim do Éden e a queda do homem
title.es: El Jardín del Edén con la caída del hombre
title.de: Der Garten Eden mit dem Sündenfall
title.ja: 人間の堕落のあるエデンの園
title.pt-br: O Jardim do Éden e a Queda do Homem
title.nl: Het hof van Eden met de zondeval

Jan_Brueghel_de_Oude_en_Peter_Paul_Ruben.story: Brueghel packed Eden with a zoological catalogue — parrots, horses, a lion, monkeys, leopards, peacocks, more than thirty species in a single lush clearing — while Rubens slipped in Adam and Eve at the far right, mid-transgression. The fruit is already in Eve's hand. It's a painting about a world still perfect everywhere except the one spot you're looking at. Hangs in the Mauritshuis in The Hague, and remains the best example of how these two Antwerp masters divided the labour.

Jan_Cossiers_-_Narciso.jpg.title: Narcissus

source.canonical_title: File:Jan Cossiers - Narciso.jpg
source.credit: Details of painting at the Prado Museum site Narciso at the Prado

Jan_Cossiers_-_Narciso.jpg.story: A muscular young Narcissus in a red drape crouches at the water's edge, one hand reaching down, his face tilted toward his own reflection just breaking into the pool below. Dark tree trunk to the left, open Flemish landscape to the right, flesh lit warm against all of it. Cossiers had worked in Rome and Paris before joining the Rubens orbit in Antwerp, and you can feel the Italian south in the modelling — less porcelain than most northern mythologies, more weight in the limbs. He painted mythological subjects throughout the 1640s and 50s for private clients and for Philip IV's hunting lodge outside Madrid.

Jan_Vermeer_-_The_Art_of_Painting_-_Goog.title: The Art of Painting" Alternative title(s): The Allegory of Painting Painter in his Studio

source.canonical_title: File:Jan Vermeer - The Art of Painting - Google Art Project.jpg

Jan_Vermeer_-_The_Art_of_Painting_-_Goog.story: Vermeer never sold this one. He kept it in the house on Delft's Oude Langendijk until he died in debt in 1675, and his widow Catharina tried to shield it from creditors by transferring it to her mother — the bailiff overruled her. The map on the back wall is a real published map of the Seventeen Provinces, drawn before the northern and southern Netherlands split. The model wearing the laurel and holding the trumpet is Clio, muse of history. The painter, seen from behind in a slashed doublet, has just laid down his first strokes: the laurel wreath, in blue.

Jan_Vermeer_van_Delft_-_Brieflezend_meis.story: A young woman stands at a cracked-open window, absorbed in a letter, her face reflected faintly in the pane. For 300 years the wall behind her was a flat cream expanse, until a 2017-2021 restoration at Dresden peeled back layers of overpaint and revealed a huge Cupid hanging there, brandishing his bow. Someone, not Vermeer, had painted him out. Seeing him back changes everything: this is a love letter. Painted roughly 1657 to 1659, now at the Gemäldegalerie in Dresden.

Jan_Vermeer_van_Delft_-_The_Glass_of_Win.title: The Wine Glass

source.canonical_title: File:Jan Vermeer van Delft - The Glass of Wine - Google Art Project.jpg

title.de: Herr und Dame beim Wein / Das Glas Wein

Jan_Vermeer_van_Delft_-_The_Glass_of_Win.story: A gentleman in a black cloak hovers while a woman tips back her wineglass, the whole cup hiding her face. On the open window, a stained-glass roundel shows Temperance holding a bridle, which is Vermeer's way of whispering 'slow down' to anyone reading the scene. Courtship or seduction? He won't say. The light pools on her satin dress like melted pewter. Painted around 1660, now in the Gemäldegalerie in Berlin.

Jan_van_der_Hoecke_(Antwerp_1611_-_Antwe.title: The Battle of Nördlingen, 1634
Jan_van_der_Hoecke_(Antwerp_1611_-_Antwe.artist: Jan van den Hoecke / Jacob Jordaens / Peter Paul Rubens

source.canonical_title: File:Jan van der Hoecke (Antwerp 1611 - Antwerp or Brussels 1651) - The Battle of Nördlingen, 1634 - RCIN 400100 - Royal Collection.jpg

Jan_van_der_Hoecke_(Antwerp_1611_-_Antwe.story: The single biggest engagement of the Thirty Years War. On 2 September 1634 the Cardinal-Infante Ferdinand and his cousin the King of Hungary crushed the Swedes at Nördlingen. For Ferdinand's triumphal entry into Antwerp the following spring, Rubens designed a sequence of commemorative canvases and handed the sketches out. Jan van den Hoecke, then a studio assistant, executed this one in late 1634; Jordaens was called in to retouch it in 1636 after van den Hoecke had left for Italy. It now hangs in the Royal Collection.

Japanese_Anemones_-_Henri_Fantin-Latour_.title: Japanese Anemones

source.canonical_title: File:Japanese Anemones - Henri Fantin-Latour - ABDAG002274.jpg
source.credit: Aberdeen City Council (Archives, Gallery and Museums Collection)

Japanese_Anemones_-_Henri_Fantin-Latour_.story: A pale vase, a dark ground, a handful of Japanese anemones leaning out at every angle — Fantin-Latour barely bothered with a setting because he didn't need one. He knew each flower had its own texture, and anemones wanted thin, almost translucent petals around those bright yellow stamens. English collectors couldn't get enough of these intimate bouquets; nearly all his flower pieces crossed the Channel in his lifetime. This small 1884 canvas, only 58 by 38 centimetres, now lives at Aberdeen Art Gallery.

Jean-Auguste-Dominique_INGRES_-_Tu_Marce.story: Virgil reads the Aeneid aloud and has just reached the line about young Marcellus, Augustus's dead nephew. Octavia, the boy's mother, has fainted into the emperor's arms. Livia sits rigid, holding the red cloak that slipped from her sister-in-law's lap. Ingres stages it like a bas-relief - Greek-key floor, oil lamp, blue curtain framing the scene - and gives every surface that cool porcelain finish he drilled into generations of pupils. Painted in Rome in 1811 and reworked afterward; the composition haunted him for decades.

Jean-Auguste-Dominique_Ingres_-_Comtesse.title: Portrait of Comtesse d'Haussonville

source.canonical_title: File:Jean-Auguste-Dominique Ingres - Comtesse d'Haussonville - Google Art Project.jpg

Jean-Auguste-Dominique_Ingres_-_Comtesse.story: Louise de Broglie, granddaughter of Madame de Staël and a working writer herself, stood for this portrait on and off for three years. Ingres did roughly eighty preparatory drawings, abandoned an earlier oil, and was interrupted when she got pregnant with her third child. She's in a blue silk dress, finger resting against her cheek, caught mid-thought; behind her, a mirror returns the nape of her neck and a finger that, strictly speaking, shouldn't be visible from that angle. The Frick bought it in 1927 for $125,000.

Jean-Auguste-Dominique_Ingres_-_La_Baign.title: The Large Bather

Jean-Auguste-Dominique_Ingres_-_La_Baign.story: An envoi from Rome, sent home to prove Ingres was earning his Prix de Rome stipend. You see her from behind, her pale back turned, a white turban twisted on her head, a slim foot stepping off the rumpled white sheet. A green curtain hangs heavy at the left; at the right, a dark basin trickles water into a pool you can just hear. No face, no story, only calm geometry and that long, famously impossible spine. It picked up its nickname decades later, from the collector Valpinçon.

Jean-Auguste-Dominique_Ingres_-_Reclinin.title: Reclining Venus
Jean-Auguste-Dominique_Ingres_-_Reclinin.description: Ingres was deeply inspired by ancient Greek and Roman art as well by Italian painting of the High Renaissance. Although he spent much of his career in Rome, he resided in Florence from 1820 to 1824, where he painted this copy of Titian's "Venus of Urbino" (1538), from the collection at the Pitti Palace. "The Venus of Urbino" had inspired generations of artists. Ingres's version is the same size as the original. He intended it to serve as a model for his close friend, the sculptor Lorenzo Bartolini (1777-1850), who was creating a sculpture based on the same subject.

Jean-Auguste-Dominique_Ingres_-_Reclinin.story: Ingres was in his Florence years, 1820 to 1824, when he copied Titian's Venus of Urbino full-size from the Pitti Palace. Not a student exercise: he made it for his friend the sculptor Lorenzo Bartolini, who was planning a marble of the same pose and wanted a working reference. The point was to feel Titian's warmth through his own cold, flawless line - and for once, to let himself lose. The canvas ended up with Henry Walters in Baltimore, where it still lives.

Jean-Leon_Gerome_-_Egyptian_Recruits_Cro.story: Gérôme had just come back from his first trip up the Nile with the sculptor Bartholdi. In Asyut they watched Arnaut soldiers round up a corvée of fellaheen and march them into the army, roped together. That's what this is. A sandstorm bruises the horizon; the conscripts trudge in a dun-colored line, guarded by mounted Arnauts; one figure stumbles. No glory, no battle, just forced labor under a yellow sky. Gérôme showed it at the Salon of 1857 and it made his name.

Jean-Leon_Gerome_Pollice_Verso.jpg.story: A murmillo plants his foot on a fallen retiarius and looks up at the stands; the Vestal Virgins stab their thumbs downward, meaning kill. Gérôme studied real gladiator armour excavated at Pompeii to get the kit right. In 1994, the producers of Gladiator showed Ridley Scott a reproduction before he'd even read the script. Scott said later: 'That image spoke to me of the Roman Empire in all its glory and wickedness.' Phoenix Art Museum bought the painting in 1968, and it has been the jewel of the collection ever since.

Jean-Léon_Gerôme,_The_Grief_of_the_Pas.description: Jean-Léon Gerôme, The Grief of the Pasha, 1882, Joslyn Art Museum, Omaha

source.canonical_title: File:Jean-Léon Gerôme, The Grief of the Pasha, 1882, Joslyn Art Museum, Omaha.jpg

Jean-Léon_Gerôme,_The_Grief_of_the_Pas.story: A dead tiger on a blue carpet, heaped with pink roses. Two green candles burn in the cold afternoon light of an Alhambra-style courtyard, and the pasha sits slumped against a column in his red robe and turban, brass coffee pot beside him. Gerome painted the Moorish stonework with his usual finicky accuracy - every carved stalactite, every band of Kufic inscription. The grief is theatrical and a little absurd; that's the point. By 1882 this kind of Orientalist set-piece was Gerome's brand, the sort of picture the Impressionists were busy making unfashionable.

Jean-Léon_Gérome_-_Le_bain_(1880-85).j.title: The Bath

source.canonical_title: File:Jean-Léon Gérome - Le bain (1880-85).jpg

Jean-Léon_Gérome_-_Le_bain_(1880-85).j.story: In a marble-clad hammam, a pale nude sits at the rim of a fountain while a Black attendant pours water over her shoulder. The hammam was Gérôme's favourite alibi — a tiled box that let him paint academic nudes under the pretext of ethnography. Every stripe of inlay, every brass ewer, every curl of steam is calibrated. What looks like observation is almost entirely studio work, Paris models against Cairo fittings. A picture that has aged into its own critique.

Jean-Léon_Gérôme,_Phryne_revealed_bef.title: Phryne before the Areopagus.
Jean-Léon_Gérôme,_Phryne_revealed_bef.description: A depiction of Phryne , a famous hetaera ( courtesan ) of Ancient Greece , being disrobed before the Areopagus . Phryne was on trial for profaning the Eleusinian Mysteries , and is said to have been disrobed by Hypereides , who was defending her, when it appeared the verdict would be unfavourable. The sight of her nude body apparently so moved the judges that they acquitted her. Some authorities claim that this story is a later invention.

source.canonical_title: File:Jean-Léon Gérôme, Phryne revealed before the Areopagus (1861) - 01 (cropped).jpg

Jean-Léon_Gérôme,_Phryne_revealed_bef.story: Phryne, Athens' most famous courtesan, stood trial for impiety, and when the verdict looked grim her lawyer Hypereides allegedly yanked off her robe. The judges, the story goes, acquitted her on the spot. Gérôme stages the moment as pure theatre: Phryne twists away, one arm thrown across her eyes, while a bench of bearded elders recoils in a comic wave of shock. It's cheerfully lurid, and Gérôme knows it. Scholars now suspect the disrobing was a later embellishment anyway, which only makes the painting's wink more pointed.

Jean-Léon_Gérôme,_Pygmalion_and_Galat.title: Pygmalion and Galatea

source.canonical_title: File:Jean-Léon Gérôme, Pygmalion and Galatea, ca. 1890.jpg

title.ja: ピュグマリオンとガラテア

Jean-Léon_Gérôme,_Pygmalion_and_Galat.story: Gérôme was obsessed enough with the Ovid story that he attacked it in paint, marble, and polychrome tinted sculpture, all roughly at once. This is the canvas version at the Met: Pygmalion lunges up on tiptoe to kiss his ivory girl just as Venus's spark runs down her body, flesh tones blooming from the hips upward while her feet are still stone. A winged Cupid plinks an arrow in from the right. Look past the lovers and you spot a theatrical mask grinning on the wall and Gérôme's own painted shields — the studio as enchanted cabinet.

Jean-Léon_Gérôme,_The_Story_of_Anacre.title: Jean-Léon Gérôme, The Story of Anacreon 1--Cupid at the Door in a Rainstorm, c 1899
Jean-Léon_Gérôme,_The_Story_of_Anacre.description: Jean-Léon Gérôme, The Story of Anacreon 1: Cupid at the Door in a Rainstorm, c. 1899

source.canonical_title: File:Jean-Léon Gérôme, The Story of Anacreon 1--Cupid at the Door in a Rainstorm, c 1899.jpg

Jean-Léon_Gérôme,_The_Story_of_Anacre.story: First panel of a four-part set Gérôme showed at the Salon in 1899, illustrating the third ode of the Greek lyric poet Anacreon. It's pouring rain; a tiny wet Cupid knocks at the poet's door in the middle of the night, begging to come in. The grey-haired Anacreon, candle in hand, hesitates inside. Gérôme is seventy-five and working the classical vein one more time — soft-edged, stage-lit, almost vignette-like, a long way from his gladiatorial thunderclaps.

Jean-Léon_Gérôme,_The_Story_of_Anacre.title: Jean-Léon Gérôme, The Story of Anacreon 2--Young Love's Shivering Limbs the Embers Warm, c 1899
Jean-Léon_Gérôme,_The_Story_of_Anacre.description: Jean-Léon Gérôme, The Story of Anacreon 2-: Young Love's Shivering Limbs the Embers Warm, c. 1899

source.canonical_title: File:Jean-Léon Gérôme, The Story of Anacreon 2--Young Love's Shivering Limbs the Embers Warm, c 1899.jpg

Jean-Léon_Gérôme,_The_Story_of_Anacre.story: Panel two of the Anacreon set. The old poet has taken pity: Cupid is inside now, crouched by the hearth while Anacreon towels warmth back into the boy's shivering limbs. The title lifts a line of English verse rendering Anacreon's ode. Gérôme stages the whole thing as a small, lamp-lit interior — firelight on skin, a wet bow propped against the stones. A softer register than most of his career, dating from around 1899, sold as a set at Sotheby's in 2021.

Jean-Léon_Gérôme,_The_Story_of_Anacre.title: Jean-Léon Gérôme, The Story of Anacreon 3--Cupid Runs out the Door, c1899
Jean-Léon_Gérôme,_The_Story_of_Anacre.description: Jean-Léon Gérôme, The Story of Anacreon 3: Cupid Runs out the Door, c. 1899

source.canonical_title: File:Jean-Léon Gérôme, The Story of Anacreon 3--Cupid Runs out the Door, c1899.jpg

Jean-Léon_Gérôme,_The_Story_of_Anacre.story: The payoff of the story. Warmed and dried, Cupid tests his bow on his host — the arrow goes straight into Anacreon's chest — then scampers laughing out the door, wings flashing, never to return. Gérôme catches the boy mid-scarper, the poet reeling in the doorway. The moral of the ode is flat and funny: never let Love in out of the rain. Third of four, c. 1899.

Jean-Léon_Gérôme,_The_Story_of_Anacre.title: Jean-Léon Gérôme, The Story of Anacreon 4--The Poet Dreams of Cupid by the Fire, c 1899
Jean-Léon_Gérôme,_The_Story_of_Anacre.description: Jean-Léon Gérôme, The Story of Anacreon 4: The Poet Dreams of Cupid by the Fire, c. 1899

source.canonical_title: File:Jean-Léon Gérôme, The Story of Anacreon 4--The Poet Dreams of Cupid by the Fire, c 1899.jpg

Jean-Léon_Gérôme,_The_Story_of_Anacre.story: The closing panel is the quietest: Anacreon alone, slumped in his chair by the dying fire, dreaming of the god who shot him and vanished. Gérôme gives the whole set a proper narrative arc — knock, welcome, betrayal, regret. It reads almost like four illustrations for a book that was never made. Painted around 1899, five years before his death; the four panels were shown together at the Salon.

Jean-Léon_Gérôme--La_Danse_pyrrhique-.title: The Pyrrhic Dance
Jean-Léon_Gérôme--La_Danse_pyrrhique-.description: Jean-Léon Gérôme, La Danse Pyrrhique, c. 1890, private collection. Signed J.L. GEROME lower right, oil on canvas, 66 by 92cm. (26 by 36in.). Auctioned at Sotheby's 2020.

source.canonical_title: File:Jean-Léon Gérôme--La Danse pyrrhique--sothebys--2020.jpg

Jean-Léon_Gérôme--La_Danse_pyrrhique-.story: A war dance performed for the Ptolemies: bronze-helmeted men stamp and clash swords in unison before the pylons of a temple of Isis, while a seated flute-and-drum band keeps time on the steps. Gérôme had visited Egypt repeatedly and reconstructed the costumes and architecture with his usual forensic appetite — Homer mentions Achilles dancing the pyrrhic at Patroclus's funeral, and Gérôme wanted you to feel the martial pulse of it. Auctioned at Sotheby's in 2020 out of a private collection; still in private hands.

Jean-Léon_Gérôme_-_At_Prayer_(1858)_(.title: Jean-Léon Gérôme - At Prayer (1858) (Sotheby's) l21104-bwnbv-01a
Jean-Léon_Gérôme_-_At_Prayer_(1858)_(.description: A painting of a Muslim man praying, by Jean-Léon Gérôme.

source.canonical_title: File:Jean-Léon Gérôme - At Prayer (1858) (Sotheby's) l21104-bwnbv-01a.jpg

Jean-Léon_Gérôme_-_At_Prayer_(1858)_(.story: One of Gérôme's earliest Orientalist pictures, painted two years after his first trip to Egypt when the sketches were still fresh. A robed, turbaned man stands before the minbar of Qaytbay in Cairo's Northern Cemetery - slippers set aside, yataghan still tucked in his sash - and raises both hands for the Takbir that opens Muslim prayer. Seeing him head-on rather than from the side is the trick of the picture: it collapses the distance between worshipper and viewer. The BBC's Fake or Fortune team reauthenticated the panel in 2021.

Jean-Léon_Gérôme_-_Bashi-Bazouk_-_201.title: Bashi-Bazouk

source.canonical_title: File:Jean-Léon Gérôme - Bashi-Bazouk - 2014.435.1 - Metropolitan Museum of Art.jpg

Jean-Léon_Gérôme_-_Bashi-Bazouk_-_201.story: Gérôme had just come back from a twelve-week trip to the Near East in 1868 when he dressed a dark-skinned model in his Paris studio in a silk tunic and a jewelled turban from his own costume trunk. Bashi-bazouks were Ottoman irregular troops, poorly paid and feared across the empire for looting. The Turkish word, Gérôme noted, means something close to 'headless.' Still, this man looks nothing like a marauder; he looks like a portrait sitter wearing extraordinary clothes. The Met received it from Mrs. Charles Wrightsman in 2008.

Jean-Léon_Gérôme_-_Diogenes_-_Walters.title: Diogenes
Jean-Léon_Gérôme_-_Diogenes_-_Walters.description: The Greek philosopher Diogenes (404-323 BC) is seated in his abode, the earthenware tub, in the Metroon, Athens, lighting the lamp in daylight with which he was to search for an honest man. His companions were dogs that also served as emblems of his " Cynic " (Greek: "kynikos," dog-like) philosophy, which emphasized an austere existence. Three years after this painting was first exhibited, Gerome was appointed a professor of painting at the Ecole des Beaux-Arts where he would instruct many students, both French and foreign.

source.canonical_title: File:Jean-Léon Gérôme - Diogenes - Walters 37131.jpg

Jean-Léon_Gérôme_-_Diogenes_-_Walters.story: The philosopher sits inside his famous clay tub in the Metroon at Athens, striking a lamp in broad daylight to begin his hunt for an honest man. Four dogs lounge around him, more family than prop: the Cynics took their name from the Greek for dog-like, and Diogenes wore it proudly. Gérôme paints the scene with dry, sun-scoured realism, marble worn smooth, bronze tarnished, a stray bone. Three years after showing this painting he was made professor at the École des Beaux-Arts, where generations of students filed past his easel.

Jean-Léon_Gérôme_-_El_rey_Candaules.j.title: King Candaules

source.canonical_title: File:Jean-Léon Gérôme - El rey Candaules.jpg
source.credit: Museo de Arte de Ponce online – click the right arrow by the bottom series of images several (currently 6) times, then its image, to see details about this painting.

Jean-Léon_Gérôme_-_El_rey_Candaules.j.story: Herodotus: King Candaules of Lydia is so besotted with his wife's beauty that he hides his bodyguard Gyges behind the bedroom door to watch her undress, just to show her off. She catches Gyges on the way out and gives him a choice the next morning - die, or kill Candaules and take both throne and queen. Gérôme shows the moment the trap is still invisible: the queen lifting her robe, Gyges half-concealed at right, Candaules lounging in bed. Painted for the 1859 Salon, part of the neo-Greek revival he led. Now at the Museo de Arte de Ponce.

Jean-Léon_Gérôme_-_Evening_Prayer,_Ca.title: Jean-Léon Gérôme - Evening Prayer, Cairo (1865)
Jean-Léon_Gérôme_-_Evening_Prayer,_Ca.description: Oil painting on panel Dimensions: 49.5 by 81cm., 19½ by 31¾in. In the 1860s Gérôme began a series of paintings depicting Muslim men at prayer. These would become a signature theme of the artist's, and among his most popular Orientalist works. Evening Prayer holds a special place within this important group: a same-size, 'perfected' version of one of Gérôme's most evocative compositions exhibited at the Paris Salon in 1865 (Hamburg, Hamburger Kunsthalle, fig. 1), it is the culmination of his developing thoughts on, and ambitions for, this subject. Gérôme's path to Orientalism began in 1856, when he travelled to Egypt for the first time. In Cairo, he accumulated a virtual library of souvenirs, costumes, and local crafts, as well as photographs, sketches, and drawings, which served as inspiration for his studio works. Subsequent trips to the region made during the 1860s and 1870s expanded his repertoire of subjects, confirming his talents as an ethnographer and his reputation as a privileged witness to all aspects of Middle Eastern life. In the present work, Gérôme depicts the daily maghrib, or evening prayer, performed on the housetops of Cairo. In the background, the distinctive skyline of the city is visible, with the Mosque of Muhammad Ali and the Medrasa of Sultan Hasan helping to identify the setting as the Qasaba, near the Bayn al-Qasrayn. Gérôme's choice of subject may have been influenced by his friend and fellow Orientalist Alexandre Bida (1813-95): Bida apparently showed the artist his ink drawing of Prayer on the Housetops (fig. 2, Walters Art Gallery), to which Gérôme responded, 'I have done nothing to equal this.' Gérôme's figures are executed with comparable documentary care: the men face east, towards Mecca, as the crescent moon and direction of the waning light suggest. They demonstrate each of the ritual postures associated with the prayer, from the initial standing qiyam to the last prostrate sajda. The motivation for this encyclopaedic view was likely a favourite reference of Gérôme's: Edward William Lane's An Account of the Manners and Customs of the Modern Egyptians, first published in London in 1836, also described these poses, in pictures and in text. Despite these glosses of realism, Gérôme's image is far from true. A minaret from the Madrasa of the Amir Sarghitmish (1356), placed prominently on the left, is in actual fact miles from this scene, and the rooftop wind scoops are likewise curiously placed (to catch the prevailing winds that sweep through Cairo, they should be facing north). Several of the men, moreover, inspire a strong sense of déjà vu. They reappear in other compositions by Gérôme, in various contexts and dress. The kneeling figure on the right, for example, forehead to the ground, reappears in the same golden yellow robes in Prayer in the Mosque (Ackerman, no. 510) of 1875. The imam, or leader of the prayer on the far left, makes another appearance in Gérôme's The Muezzin of 1866 (Joslyn Art Museum), and its many variations. Rather than thoughtless oversights, however, these manipulations and distortions were deliberate choices by the artist, made for aesthetic or effect or even out of commercial considerations. In a letter to the dealer Knoedler, the artist explained: 'Prayer in the Mosque had been reserved by Monsieur Simon and I remember that he made me put a figure facing the spectator, by saying that since all the others were seen from the back or in profile, it would not sell. I did as he wanted because his reasons were commercially sound.' Such artistic liberty did not diminish the overall popularity of Gérôme's works, nor jeopardise their worth. On the contrary, at least three painted versions of the present subject are known, and numerous reproductions and copies were made during the course of the artist's career - a testament to its success. The original painting in the Hamburger Kunsthalle, exhibited at the Paris Salon in 1865, shares many of the same features with the present picture, including its formidable size. It is the differences, however, that are the most important here: in the present work, the absence of background figures and the substitution of a striking man in red - a favourite model of the artist's - serve to focus all attention on the devotions of the group, and the poetry of prayer. The third confirmed version is a small oil sketch in a private collection. In the nineteenth century, making versions of a favourite or highly coveted subject was the standard practice of any artists, and held a specific societal value. Those without the resources to purchase a popular Salon painting could, by these means, enjoy similar works in their own homes, particularly through the production of a reduction, or smaller version, of the piece. For those who wished for a grander addition to their well-hung walls, a répétition was the answer to their needs. This was understood to be a later version of a painting, of roughly the same size. Owing to a few compositional differences - a requisite of this type - the répétition was considered to be an original and costly work of art. As Patricia Mainardi explains: 'The correct term for an artist's later version of his own theme ... was...répétition, the same word used in performance for a rehearsal. In performance, we never assume that opening night is qualitatively better than later presentations - first presentations are, in fact, usually weaker than subsequent ones, which gain in depth from greater experience and familiarity with the material.' ('The Nineteenth-Century Art Trade: Copies, Variations, Replicas', The Van Gogh Museum Journal, 2000, pp. 63-4). Evening Prayer, then, the last of the three painted versions of this subject to be made, may be interpreted as Gérôme's most valuable and profound rendition of this beloved theme. The artist himself articulated this notion in a letter to the Belgian art dealer Ernest Gambart: 'The alterations that I have made from the original picture [The Duel after the Masquerade, Walters Art Museum] have singularly improved this composition, especially in its general aspect...and I regret not to have thought of it at first when I executed the original.' The techniques that Gérôme employs throughout this composition exhibit the trademarks of his style, as does the distinctive signature located along a background ledge. Written in capital letters, and devoid of accents and embellishment, it suggests that this work was intended as a finished and marketable version, rather than as a study or a personal gift. The application of the paint around the head of the imam is particularly noteworthy, as it offers a glimpse into the artist's working method. Here, Gérôme simultaneously applies fresh paint to both the figure and the ground, allowing him to balance the painting's overall tones and avoid the hard-edged outlines of others' academic style. The consequent appearance of this painted passage and across the surface of the picture as a whole, as a seamless, luminous sheet of glass, became identified closely with the artist, and with nineteenth-century Orientalism as well. The photographic quality of these works has long encouraged their interpretation as 'factual' - for better or for worse (for more on this subject, see Emily Weeks, 'A Veil of Truth: The Art and Artistry of Jean-Léon Gérôme', Private Journey Magazine, January 2011) The appearance of Evening Prayer by 1870 in two prominent private collections in England and, fifteen years later, on the East Coast of America, was in keeping with the history of many of Gérôme's best-known works. In 1859, Gérôme signed a contract with the French publisher and art dealer Adolphe Goupil. Goupil's calculated marketing of Gérôme's works, through both the sale of originals and affordable, mass-produced reproductions, guaranteed their widespread distribution, and the growth of his international success. The industrial and commercial booms of the nineteenth century also had a critical role to play. They generated a new group of art purchasers and patrons in these countries, who were eager to prove the sophistication of their nouveau riche tastes. Scenes of Middle eastern prayer offered a broad and somewhat ironic appeal: in addition to reflecting - despite their foreign guise - the familiar moral principles that these new collectors were anxious to uphold, they could also offer hope and comfort at a time of rapid change. As the corruptive influences of capitalism were beginning to be recognised and the complexities of modern life were starting to take their toll, the idea of a pure and unquestioned faith was doubtless reassuring. Gérôme's Evening Prayer, then, a window on to a distant and exotic world, may also, in this context, be read as the final solemn sermon to one closer than it seems.

Jean-Léon_Gérôme_-_Evening_Prayer,_Ca.story: Evening in Cairo, the maghrib prayer, performed on a rooftop with the Mosque of Muhammad Ali and the Madrasa of Sultan Hasan silhouetted behind. Gérôme gives us every canonical posture, standing, bowing, prostrate, like a diagram pulled straight from Edward Lane's handbook of Egyptian customs. A minaret on the left is actually miles away in reality, and the wind scoops face the wrong direction; he moved things around for the composition. This is the third and most refined version of a subject he painted repeatedly, each round a little more concentrated, a little more devotional.

Jean-Léon_Gérôme_-_Le_charmeur_de_ser.title: The Snake Charmer

source.canonical_title: File:Jean-Léon Gérôme - Le charmeur de serpents.jpg
source.credit: 1. Unknown source Unknown source 2. ArtDaily.org 3. Bridgeman Art Library : Object 339940 4./5. Clark Art Institute, Williamstown

Jean-Léon_Gérôme_-_Le_charmeur_de_ser.story: A naked boy wound in a python stands before a row of turbaned men on a tiled bench, one of them an armed guard leaning on his rifle. Behind them, a wall of cracked Iznik tile catches the light. For most of the 20th century the painting was a market-stall fantasy; in 1978 Edward Said put it on the cover of Orientalism and made it Exhibit A — the Western viewer invited to leer at the spectacle while the Arab crowd watches something else, something we can't quite see. The Clark Art Institute has it.

Jean-Léon_Gérôme_-_Moorish_bath.jpg.title: Moorish Bath
Jean-Léon_Gérôme_-_Moorish_bath.jpg.description: A naked woman with an assistant washing in a Turkish bath

source.canonical_title: File:Jean-Léon Gérôme - Moorish bath.jpg

Jean-Léon_Gérôme_-_Moorish_bath.jpg.story: A nude woman sits on the tiled edge of a hammam pool while a darker-skinned attendant pours water over her shoulder. Gérôme returned to the bath scene again and again, building it from his collection of tiles, copper basins and brass-inlaid doors hauled back from Cairo and Istanbul. The architecture is rendered with almost tiresome precision; the nude is softened into marble. It's the classic Orientalist fantasy, an imagined private space no European man could have entered, painted to flatter exactly that fiction. Seen now, it's as much a study in how European painters manufactured intimacy as a bathing scene.

Jean-Léon_Gérôme_-_On_the_Desert_-_Wa.title: On the Desert
Jean-Léon_Gérôme_-_On_the_Desert_-_Wa.description: Gerome was a frequent traveler first visiting the East in 1854 and returning in 1867, 1869, 1875, and 1881. Some of his "Orientalist" paintings are of documentary interest whereas others are highly romanticized. This small panel, commissioned by William T. Walters, depicts two hounds being walked by a Nubian in a barren and windy desert. The trim shapes of the dogs suggest that they are "Pharaoh Hounds," a breed descended from the hunting dogs of ancient Egypt.
