Jean-Léon_Gérôme_-_On_the_Desert_-_Wa.story: Two slender hounds, almost certainly Pharaoh Hounds descended from ancient Egyptian hunting dogs, stride across a windblown stretch of sand led by a Nubian handler. The wind pulls at robes and tails; everything is sun and grit. Gérôme painted this small panel for the Baltimore collector William T. Walters, who had a taste for his Orientalist work. It's an intimate commission, less theatrical than the big Salon pieces, and all the better for it. The dogs, trim and alert, are the real protagonists, and their long ancestry is part of the quiet joke.

Jean-Léon_Gérôme_-_Pool_in_a_Harem.jp.title: Pool in a Harem.

source.canonical_title: File:Jean-Léon Gérôme - Pool in a Harem.jpg

Jean-Léon_Gérôme_-_Pool_in_a_Harem.jp.story: Inside a tiled courtyard heavy with Iznik blues and greens, a nude bather lounges at the edge of a pool while an attendant holds a long-stemmed pipe. Gérôme built the architecture from his own sketches of Istanbul and Cairo, stitching real tilework and real fountains into an entirely invented scene — the harem was famously off-limits to Western men. This is the formula that made him rich: pin-sharp detail wrapped around a voyeuristic fiction, sold to Paris and New York as documentary truth. The Hermitage owns it.

Jean-Léon_Gérôme_-_Prayer_in_the_Dese.title: Jean-Léon Gérôme - Prayer in the Desert (1864)
Jean-Léon_Gérôme_-_Prayer_in_the_Dese.description: Oil painting on panel. Dimensions: 33 by 54.5cm., 13 by 21½in. Taking leave from the caravan visible in the background, an Arnaut has laid his cape on the floor and, positioning himself facing towards Mecca, is now fully absorbed in a moment of prayer in the vastness of the north African desert. Arnauts, or bashi-bazouks, were irregulars in the Ottoman army and hailed from Albania and the Balkans. The strain on the Ottoman feudal system caused by the Empire's wide expanse required heavier reliance on irregular soldiers. They were armed and maintained by the government, but did not receive pay and did not wear uniforms or distinctive badges. Because not formally trained, they could not serve in major military operations, but were useful for other tasks such as reconnaissance and outpost duty. Throughout his travels in the 1860s and 1870s, Gérôme made hundreds of sketches and studies and amassed an impressive collection of photographs and local goods, which were later used toward the meticulously detailed, highly polished oil paintings executed at his Paris studio, including the present work. Painted in 1864, in the year the artist was appointed by Emperor Napoleon III to head one of the three official ateliers of the École des Beaux-Arts, Prayer in the Desert was possibly the result of Gérôme’s second trip to the Orient just a few years earlier, in 1862. The present work appears to be a réduction of a larger work of the same title currently in private hands. The production of réductions, smaller versions after the ‘official’ Salon paintings, was a common practice in the nineteenth century, to satisfy the wishes of collectors who did not have the means to buy at the annual Salon. Also made to serve as prototypes for engravers to copy in the production of commercial prints after original paintings, these were often given over to the studio, with the resulting work being only partially by the artist’s hand. However, after recent thorough examination, the present work has been identified and fully re-instated as an autograph painting by Gérôme.

source.canonical_title: File:Jean-Léon Gérôme - Prayer in the Desert (1864).jpg

Jean-Léon_Gérôme_-_Prayer_in_the_Dese.story: A lone Arnaut, one of the Ottoman Empire's unpaid Balkan irregulars, has dismounted from his caravan, spread his cape toward Mecca, and folded into prayer. Behind him, the others wait as tiny specks in a buff-coloured emptiness. Gérôme painted this in 1864, the year Napoleon III installed him at the head of an atelier at the École des Beaux-Arts. It's a small panel, a reduction of a larger Salon canvas, but painted entirely by his own hand: thumbprint-precise detail, enormous sky, one man quietly outlasting the desert.

Jean-Léon_Gérôme_-_Rider_and_his_Stee.title: Jean-Léon Gérôme - Rider and his Steed in the Desert (1872)
Jean-Léon_Gérôme_-_Rider_and_his_Stee.description: Oil painting on canvas Dimensions: 60 by 101cm., 23¾ by 39½in. Painted in 1872, this evocative work captures the moment on a hot afternoon in the implacable brightness of the desert sun, as a horseman comforts his exhausted steed against the backdrop of a range of barren hills. With great mastery and a director's eye for narrative, Gérôme evokes the utter stillness and loneliness of the desert air. The heat is made almost palpable to the viewer through the bright sun on the rider's brilliant white headdress and dishdasha, and the sun reflecting off the horse's shiny coat. Gérôme had seen such landscapes during his first trip to Egypt with the sculptor and photographer Frederic Auguste Bartholdi in 1856, and again in 1868, notably accompanied by his brother-in-law and photographer Albert Goupil and fellow painters Paul Lenoir, Léon Bonnat, and Willem de Famars Testas. He was therefore familiar with this harsh, wild world, and the way in which its inhabitants braved it with impassive dignity. The glossy coat of the steed and the crisp white linens of the figure seem clean and fresh despite their adverse situation. Gérôme’s controlled brush lends the man and his horse the ancient calm and panache of great viziers straight out of The Arabian Nights, much as in related works such as Arabs Crossing the Desert (1870, Najd Collection). The conception of the painting was based on sketches Gérôme had made of the desert, but more importantly, on the photographs first taken by Bartholdi and later by Goupil on the expeditions he made with them. Both the panoramic backdrop and the precise style in which it is executed make Rider and his Steed in the Desert a fascinating example of the link between photography and Gérôme’s own painterly vision, based on precision draftsmanship and clear composition. The aesthetics of photography, a process that produced a unique image on metal, had many similarities to academic painting, and Gérôme used the new invention as justification for his obsessive drive for verisimilitude. 'Photography is a vocabulary that can guide artists in their translation of nature, an album in which they can find fresh ideas and new inspiration,' wrote the photographer Antoine Claudet. In this respect, Gérôme’s work also has to be deciphered in the context of contemporary rationalist desires to organise and categorise knowledge, with the founding of the French archaeological institutes in Athens, Rome, and Cairo, and with the birth of the new field of ethnology. Yet Gérôme skilfully played on his reputation for accuracy. While his travels to Egypt and his use of photography lent his Oriental visions the impact of eyewitness statements, Rider and his Steed in the Desert bore the seal of the artist's nostalgic imagination, perpetuating the notion of the North African desert as a theatrical, cruel, immutable, timeless place at a point when Egypt was, in fact, a fast-changing country and its society was undergoing modernisation from the top down. From 1850, French ships sailed from Marseille to Alexandria via Malta in seven days. From the 1870s, journeys became faster, and soon Alexandria had a rail connection to Cairo. Only three years before painting the present work, Gérôme had been sent to Egypt as part of the French delegation for the inauguration of the Suez Canal, turning Egypt into an international shipping thoroughfare. As Linda Nochlin observed, Gérôme’s paintings underlined 'a strategy of realist mystification', at a time when the Orient was fast becoming more accessible. 'Time stands still in Gérôme’s painting... [He] suggests that this Oriental world is a world without change.' The theme of the rider comforting his mount had been developed by a number of French Romantic painters in the first quarter of the 19th century, notably by Théodore Géricault. The Ecole des Beaux-Arts in Paris owns a drawing featuring a similar composition, evidently a design for the frontispiece of a book never completed. Another version of this frontispiece was sold in the Hans E. Buhler sale at Christie's, London, on 15 November 1985. A drawing in the Bonnat museum in Bayonne has the scene transported to nineteenth-century France in Currassier auprès de son cheval blessé. Gérôme was a good friend of Bonnat, and may have come across the theme through Bonnat's enthusiasm for collecting Géricault drawings. Or again, perhaps the subject was suggested to Gérôme by a similar composition painted by Rosa Bonheur in 1852 (Sudeley House, Liverpool).

source.canonical_title: File:Jean-Léon Gérôme - Rider and his Steed in the Desert (1872).jpg

Jean-Léon_Gérôme_-_Rider_and_his_Stee.story: A lone horseman pauses on a sunbaked afternoon, one hand steadying his exhausted horse against a wall of bare hills. Gérôme built the scene from sketches and photographs gathered on his Egyptian trips with Bartholdi and Albert Goupil — the glassy coat of the animal, the blinding white of the dishdasha, all rendered with his trademark forensic polish. The theme of rider comforting mount came out of French Romanticism (Géricault, Bonheur), but Gérôme strips away the drama. What's left is heat, silence, and a staged timelessness — the desert as the West wanted it, right as steamships and railways were dragging Egypt somewhere else.

Jean-Léon_Gérôme_-_Riders_Crossing_Th.title: Jean-Léon Gérôme - Riders Crossing The Desert (1870) HQ
Jean-Léon_Gérôme_-_Riders_Crossing_Th.description: Dimensions: 41cm x 56cm., 16 by 22in. This intensely evocative work captures a moment on a hot day in the implacable brightness of the Egyptian sun, as a group of riders, seemingly undeterred by the adverse conditions, stoically traverses the vastness of the desert against the backdrop of a range of barren hills. With great mastery and a director's eye for narrative, Gérôme evokes the utter stillness and loneliness of the desert air. The heat is made palpable to the viewer through the bright sun on the riders’ brightly coloured robes. Gérôme first travelled into the Egyptian desert in 1856, together with the sculptor and photographer Frederic Auguste Bartholdi as well as fellow painters Léon Charles Bailly and Narcisse Berchère. He returned in 1868 with his brother-in-law Albert Goupil, pupil Paul Lenoir, painters Willem de Farmas Testas and Léon Bonnat, and the writer Edmond About. Their expedition took them into the Sinai desert, offering privileged insights into the harsh world so masterfully captured in the present work. The frieze-like composition of the painting stresses the riders’ determined progress, while the contrast between the pin-sharp precision of the foreground group and the distant travellers on foot and camel suggest a caravan stretching far into the distance. These various elements create an impression of space and movement which arguably no other Orientalist artist could have conveyed in a canvas of this size. The painting was based on sketches Gérôme had made of the desert and, more importantly, on the photographs first taken by Bartholdi and later by Goupil on the expeditions he made with them. Both the panoramic backdrop and the precise style in which it is executed make Riders Crossing the Desert a fascinating example of the link between photography and Gérôme’s own painterly vision, which was based on precision draftsmanship and clear composition. The aesthetics of photography, a process that produced a unique image on metal, had many similarities to academic painting, and Gérôme used the new invention as justification for his obsessive drive for verisimilitude. 'Photography is a vocabulary that can guide artists in their translation of nature, an album in which they can find fresh ideas and new inspiration,' wrote the photographer Antoine Claudet. In this respect, Gérôme’s work also has to be deciphered in the context of contemporary rationalist desires to organise and categorise knowledge, with the founding of the French archaeological institutes in Athens, Rome, and Cairo, and with the birth of the new field of ethnology. Yet Gérôme skilfully played on his reputation for accuracy. While his travels to Egypt and his use of photography lent his Orientalist visions the impact of eyewitness statements, Riders Crossing the Desert bore the seal of the artist's nostalgic imagination, perpetuating the notion of the North African desert as a theatrical, cruel, immutable, timeless place at a point when Egypt was, in fact, a fast-changing country undergoing modernisation from the top down. From 1850, French ships sailed from Marseille to Alexandria via Malta in seven days. From the 1870s, journeys became faster, and soon Alexandria had a rail connection to Cairo. Only a year before painting the present work, Gérôme had been sent to Egypt as part of the French delegation for the inauguration of the Suez Canal, which transformed Egypt into an international shipping thoroughfare. As Linda Nochlin observed, Gérôme’s paintings underlined 'a strategy of realist mystification', at a time when the Orient was fast becoming more accessible. She writes: 'Time stands still in Gérôme’s painting... [He] suggests that this Oriental world is a world without change.'

Jean-Léon_Gérôme_-_Riders_Crossing_Th.story: A line of riders moves across a blinding stretch of Egyptian desert, sharp and close in the foreground, then dissolving into tiny figures at the base of barren hills. You can almost feel the heat off the bright robes. Gérôme built the composition from sketches made on his 1868 expedition into the Sinai, supplemented by photographs taken by his companions. The frieze-like arrangement and the pin-sharp detail are deliberately photographic. As Linda Nochlin noted, this is Egypt frozen as timeless spectacle, painted just as railways and the new Suez Canal were rapidly dragging the country into the modern age.

Jean-Léon_Gérôme_-_The_Death_of_Caesa.title: The Death of Caesar
Jean-Léon_Gérôme_-_The_Death_of_Caesa.description: Julius Caesar was assassinated in Rome on the Ides of March (March 15), 44 BC. Characteristically, Gérôme has depicted not the incident itself, but its immediate aftermath. The illusion of reality that Gérôme imparted to his paintings with his smooth, polished technique led one critic to comment, "If photography had existed in Caesar's day, one could believe that the picture was painted from a photograph taken on the spot at the very moment of the catastrophe."

Jean-Léon_Gérôme_-_The_Death_of_Caesa.story: Gérôme sidesteps the stabbing itself. Caesar is already a crumpled heap at the base of Pompey's statue, and the conspirators are halfway out the door, daggers raised, shouting for Rome. That emptiness in the middle of the composition is the whole point, the hush after the blow. A contemporary critic joked that if photography had existed in 44 BC, you'd swear this canvas was shot at the scene. Gérôme loved that kind of praise. His smooth, almost enamel finish turns a political murder into a frozen newsreel, theatrical and queasily matter-of-fact at once.

Jean-Léon_Gérôme_-_The_Duel_After_the.title: The Duel After the Masquerade
Jean-Léon_Gérôme_-_The_Duel_After_the.description: In this painting, showing the outcome of a duel after a costume ball, Gérôme replicates, with slight variations, a composition he had executed for the Duc d'Aumale in 1857. It is dawn on a wintry day in the Bois de Boulogne, Paris, and Pierrot succumbs in the arms of the Duc de Guise. A Venetian doge examines Pierrot's wound while Domino clasps his head in despair. To the right, the victorious American Indian departs, accompanied by Harlequin.

Jean-Léon_Gérôme_-_The_Duel_After_the.story: Dawn in the Bois de Boulogne, a wintry Tuesday morning. Pierrot is dying in the arms of the Duc de Guise, his white costume turning red; a Venetian doge kneels with a handkerchief trying to stem the wound; Domino cradles his head. At right the victor, absurdly got up as an American Indian, walks off with Harlequin toward the carriage. Gérôme had painted the original in 1857 for the Duc d'Aumale; this slightly varied replica was bought by William Walters in New York in 1859 for $2,500. Paris could not stop talking about it.

Jean-Léon_Gérôme_-_The_Harem_in_the_K.title: Jean-Léon Gérôme - The Harem in the Kiosk (1870) (Sotheby's) 099l1905-b9ddk
Jean-Léon_Gérôme_-_The_Harem_in_the_K.description: A painting of a harem guard overlooking the water, by Jean-Léon Gérôme.

source.canonical_title: File:Jean-Léon Gérôme - The Harem in the Kiosk (1870) (Sotheby's) 099l1905-b9ddk.jpg

Jean-Léon_Gérôme_-_The_Harem_in_the_K.story: A Black eunuch guard leans on the balustrade of a waterside kiosk, pipe in hand, watching over veiled women in the shadows behind him. The Bosphorus glitters below. Gérôme loved this type of half-public, half-secret architecture: it let him stage the supposedly forbidden world of the harem as a stretch of tilework, fretted woodwork and glinting water, entirely visible. The guard is the painting's real subject, posed between two worlds he cannot enter. As so often with Gérôme, the documentary detail is meticulous and the premise is pure European fantasy.

Jean-Léon_Gérôme_-_The_Slave_Market_-.title: The Slave Market

source.canonical_title: File:Jean-Léon Gérôme - The Slave Market - Google Art Project.jpg
source.credit: CQHyY347a4a2Vw at Google Cultural Institute , zoom level maximum

Jean-Léon_Gérôme_-_The_Slave_Market_-.story: A naked woman stands exposed in a sunlit courtyard while a turbaned buyer reaches into her mouth to check her teeth. Gérôme travelled extensively in Egypt and Turkey, but the Clark Art Institute, which has owned the painting since 1955, notes he almost certainly never saw a slave market; the scene is assembled from sketches and imagination. The painting was exploited in 2019 by Germany's far-right AfD in anti-Muslim posters, and the Clark publicly condemned the use. Dated around 1866.

Jean-Léon_Gérôme_-_The_Tulip_Folly_-_.title: The Tulip Folly
Jean-Léon_Gérôme_-_The_Tulip_Folly_-_.description: Gérôme illustrates an incident during the "tulipomania", or the craze for tulips, that swept the Netherlands and much of Europe during the 17th century. The tulip, originally imported from Turkey in the 16th century, became an increasingly valuable commodity. By 1636/7, tulipomania peaked, and, when the market crashed, speculators were left with as little as 5 percent of their original investments. In this scene, a nobleman guards an exceptional bloom as soldiers trample flowerbeds in a vain attempt to stabilize the tulip market by limiting the supply.

Jean-Léon_Gérôme_-_The_Tulip_Folly_-_.story: Haarlem, 1637: the tulip bubble has burst and the Dutch authorities have sent soldiers into the fields to trample bulbs and force prices back up. In the foreground a nobleman stands guard over a single prize bloom with drawn sword while troops flatten the rows behind him. Gérôme treats it as absurdist comedy — the world's first futures crash, reduced to men stomping on flowers. The Walters in Baltimore has it. A 19th-century parable about speculation that reads, today, like it could have been painted last Tuesday.

Jean-Léon_Gérôme_-_Tiger_on_the_Watch.title: Tiger on the Watch

source.canonical_title: File:Jean-Léon Gérôme - Tiger on the Watch - Google Art Project.jpg
source.credit: SAFVOlZNHeEt6A at Google Cultural Institute maximum zoom level

Jean-Léon_Gérôme_-_Tiger_on_the_Watch.story: A tiger crouches on a bare ridge above a far-off desert caravan, its body tensed, its head turned just enough to meet the viewer's eye. Gérôme was in his sixties by 1888, and animal paintings were an increasingly obsessive late-career subject: he went to the Paris menageries to sketch big cats from life. The painting measures about 63 by 90 cm and hangs in the Museum of Fine Arts, Houston, a bequest from George M. Dickson through the Houston Art League.

Jean-Léon_Gérôme_-_Young_Greeks_in_th.title: Young Greeks in the Mosque
Jean-Léon_Gérôme_-_Young_Greeks_in_th.description: Greek Muslims in the Mosque, portrayed by Jean-Léon Gérôme (oil on panel, 1865)

source.canonical_title: File:Jean-Léon Gérôme - Young Greeks in the Mosque - 62.85 - Minneapolis Institute of Arts.jpg

Jean-Léon_Gérôme_-_Young_Greeks_in_th.story: Inside a cool, tile-lined mosque, a cluster of young Greek Muslims kneels at prayer, their bright sashes and red caps catching the light off the carpets. Gérôme worked the panel in oil, building up his usual lacquer-smooth surface so the patterned tilework reads almost photographically. The picture sits in his long, career-spanning investigation of Islamic devotion, subjects that sold briskly to European collectors hungry for a whiff of the exotic. What's striking now is how quiet it is: no drama, no gladiators, just a handful of boys concentrating in a room built for stillness.

Jean-Léon_Gérôme_011.jpg.title: Dance of the Almeh

source.canonical_title: File:Jean-Léon Gérôme 011.jpg

Jean-Léon_Gérôme_011.jpg.story: An almeh, a professional Egyptian singer and dancer, performs in a smoke-hazed café for a row of seated Ottoman soldiers and musicians. Gérôme turns the scene into a study of watching: the dancer's stance, the slouched intensity of the men, the long pipes, the coffee cups. Everything is painted with his usual obsessive finish, ornament by ornament. Ethnographers have pointed out that he cheerfully rearranged costumes, architecture and props to suit his compositions. The result feels documentary but works more like staged tableau, a French fantasy dressed in carefully collected Cairo souvenirs.

Jean-Léon_Gérôme_015_Carpets.jpg.title: The Carpet Merchant / Carpet Merchant in Cairo

source.canonical_title: File:Jean-Léon Gérôme 015 Carpets.jpg
source.credit: Minneapolis Institute of Arts via artsconnected.org

Jean-Léon_Gérôme_015_Carpets.jpg.story: A Cairene souk, cool and deep in shadow, with a gigantic red carpet unrolled down a wall and a knot of buyers haggling at its foot. Sunlight slants in from above and catches the pile. Gérôme based the scene on sketches from his Egyptian trips and on photographs by friends like Albert Goupil; the architecture is real Cairo, the merchants plausibly so. The painting's now at the Minneapolis Institute of Art and remains one of his most reproduced — a picture of commerce that became, ironically, a blue-chip commodity itself.

Jean-Léon_Gérôme_Consummatum_est.jpg.title: Jerusalem
Jean-Léon_Gérôme_Consummatum_est.jpg.description: «Consummatum est», h/t, 63.5 x 98 cm, Musée d’Orsay, Paris

source.canonical_title: File:Jean-Léon Gérôme Consummatum est.jpg

title.ja: すべてこと終われり(Consummatum est）

Jean-Léon_Gérôme_Consummatum_est.jpg.story: The title, Consummatum est, comes from Christ's last words on the cross, and Gérôme gives them a startling treatment. Instead of Golgotha's hilltop and the crowd, we look down on Jerusalem from above: three long shadows of crucifixes stretch across the dusty foreground, the crosses themselves cropped out of frame entirely. The city glows beyond. It's almost cinematic, a reverse shot where the subject is implied by absence. The painting now hangs in the Musée d'Orsay, and it remains one of Gérôme's boldest compositional gambits, religious narrative reduced to three dark stripes on the ground.

Jean-Paul_Flandrin_-_Odalisque_with_Slav.title: Odalisque with Slave
Jean-Paul_Flandrin_-_Odalisque_with_Slav.description: An odalisque (female member of a harem) reclines exposed in the harem listening to a servant's lute music. This painting was commissioned by King Wilhelm I of Württemberg and was executed by Ingres with the assistance of his pupil Paul Flandrin. A version of this subject painted three years earlier shows the odalisque in an enclosed room rather than with the garden vista in the background ( Fogg Art Museum , Cambridge, Massachusetts). This exotic composition, which was inspired by a passage from Lady Mary Wortley Montagu's Turkish Letters (1763), may have been conceived by Ingres in response to his rival Eugène Delacroix 's success as a painter of Near Eastern subjects.

Jean-Paul_Flandrin_-_Odalisque_with_Slav.story: Commissioned by King Wilhelm I of Württemberg, this is Ingres's second version of a subject he had painted three years earlier for Charles Marcotte. The nude odalisque sprawls on rumpled silks, a musician strums at her feet, a eunuch guards the doorway. The big change here is the garden vista behind them, added by Ingres's pupil Paul Flandrin and modelled on the park at Dampierre. The harem opens onto French countryside. Ingres was sixty-two, still elbowing Delacroix for the Orientalist crown.

Jean-leon_gerome_arnaut_fumant.jpg.title: Arnaut fumant

source.canonical_title: File:Jean-leon gerome arnaut fumant.jpg

Jean-leon_gerome_arnaut_fumant.jpg.story: An Arnaut, one of the Ottoman empire's Albanian irregulars, leans against a wall and draws on a long-stemmed chibouk. The fur-trimmed cap, the embroidered vest, the carpet under his slippers, all of it Gérôme painted from props and costumes he'd hauled back from his travels and kept in his studio. These mercenaries were famous across the empire for ferocity and flamboyance, but here the soldier is doing nothing more dangerous than enjoying his tobacco. Oil on panel, roughly the size of a sheet of typing paper, painted in 1865.

Jean_Auguste_Dominique_Ingres,_La_Grande.title: Grande Odalisque
Jean_Auguste_Dominique_Ingres,_La_Grande.date_created: 1810 Romanticism (second half of 18 th century date QS:P,+1750-00-00T00:00:00Z/7,P4241,Q40719707 –first half of 19 th century date QS:P,+1850-00-00T00:00:00Z/7,P4241,Q40719687 )

Jean_Auguste_Dominique_Ingres,_La_Grande.story: Caroline Murat, Napoleon's sister and Queen of Naples, commissioned this for her private apartments. She barely got to enjoy it. Napoleon fell the next year, the Murat throne collapsed, and Ingres was never paid. His odalisque stretches across blue silk like a slow exhale, a jeweled fan in her hand, a hookah and peacock feathers piled at her feet. Critics counted her vertebrae and complained she had three too many. She reached the Louvre in 1899.

Jean_Auguste_Dominique_Ingres_-_The_Spri.title: The Spring.

source.canonical_title: File:Jean Auguste Dominique Ingres - The Spring - Google Art Project 2.jpg
source.credit: Google Art Project: Home – pic Maximum resolution.

Jean_Auguste_Dominique_Ingres_-_The_Spri.story: Ingres began this nude in Florence in 1820 and didn't sign it until 1856, when he was in his seventies. A young woman stands in a rocky niche, tipping a jug against her shoulder so a thin stream of water falls into the pool at her feet. Ivy hangs beside her; a single lily lifts from the grass. Her body is cool, symmetrical, almost Greek, and the water ribbon is the only thing that moves. The painting entered the Louvre in 1878.

Jean_Leon_Gerome_Selling_Slaves_in_Rome..title: A Roman Slave Market
Jean_Leon_Gerome_Selling_Slaves_in_Rome..description: Gérôme painted six slave-market scenes set in either ancient Rome or 19th-century Istanbul. The subject provided him with an opportunity to depict facial expressions and to undertake figurative studies of sensual beauty. He painted another view of the same event-- Slave Market in Rome (St. Petersburg, Hermitage Museum)--in which the viewer looks over the heads of the spectators towards the slave.

source.canonical_title: File:Jean Leon Gerome Selling Slaves in Rome.jpg

Jean_Leon_Gerome_Selling_Slaves_in_Rome..story: A young woman stands stripped on an auction block while Roman bidders lift their hands. Gérôme painted six slave-market scenes across his career, some set in ancient Rome, some in contemporary Istanbul, all pretexts for academic nudes and studies of faces in a crowd. This one, from 1884, is a pair to another canvas in the Hermitage in St Petersburg, where the viewpoint is reversed and you look over the buyers' heads instead of past them. Here Gérôme puts you at eye level with the auctioneer.

source.canonical_title: File:Jean auguste dominique ingres princesse albert de broglieFXD.jpg

Jean_auguste_dominique_ingres_princesse_.story: Pauline de Galard de Brassac de Béarn, married into the de Broglie family, posed for Ingres when he was 71. She stands in a blue satin gown with lace trim, one hand resting on a gilded chair, chignon perfectly pinned, a dark shawl slipped down behind her elbows. Every thread of the moiré catches light. She died of tuberculosis in 1860, only nine years after the portrait was finished, and her husband kept the painting veiled on the wall. The Met acquired it in 1975.

Jerusalem_Artichoke_Flowers_E10330.jpg.title: Jerusalem Artichoke Flowers

source.canonical_title: File:Jerusalem Artichoke Flowers E10330.jpg
source.credit: National Gallery of Art, Washington, D. C., online collection

Jerusalem_Artichoke_Flowers_E10330.jpg.story: Canary-yellow blooms with pumpkin-orange centres, stacked nearly a metre high on the canvas, backed by vertical streaks of salmon, turquoise and denim blue. Monet painted it in 1880 and sold it that November. The bouquet passed through Georges de Bellio and a string of later owners before the American collector Chester Dale bought it in 1929 and left it to the National Gallery of Art in Washington in 1963.

Jeune_Orpheline_au_cimetière_-_Eugène_.story: She sits alone among the graves, lips parted, eyes pulled upward toward something the viewer can't see. The sky behind her is bruised; her shawl has slipped off one bare shoulder. Delacroix painted her in 1824 as a study for the enormous Massacre at Chios, a warm-up sketch of grief that somehow outlived its purpose. Even so, he showed her that same year at the Salon Carré. After his death the canvas drifted through private hands until Étienne Moreau-Nélaton bought it and gave it to the Louvre in 1906.

Jheronimus_Bosch_-_De_hooiwagen_(c.1516,.title: The Hay Wagon

source.canonical_title: File:Jheronimus Bosch - De hooiwagen (c.1516, Prado).jpg

Jheronimus_Bosch_-_De_hooiwagen_(c.1516,.story: A giant haywagon rumbles across a landscape while nuns shovel the stuff into sacks, lovers canoodle on top, and a mob below kills each other for a handful. Demons pull the cart toward hell; Christ watches from a cloud, unnoticed. The image illustrates a Flemish proverb that the world is a haystack and everyone grabs what they can. Dendrochronology dates the Prado panels to around 1516, after Bosch's death in 1516, so the Madrid version is now read as a high-quality workshop copy of the El Escorial original.

Jheronimus_Bosch_011.jpg.title: The Ship of Fools
Jheronimus_Bosch_011.jpg.description: Fragment of the left wing of a triptych; see File:Jheronimus Bosch 003.jpg for the second fragment of the left wing of this triptych, File:Jheronimus Bosch 050.jpg for the right wing, and File:Jheronimus Bosch 112.jpg for the exterior.

source.canonical_title: File:Jheronimus Bosch 011.jpg

Jheronimus_Bosch_011.jpg.story: A boatload of clerics, peasants and a hanging fool drifting nowhere, too drunk to row. A nun plays lute while a monk howls along, a cherry dangles on a string waiting for a snapping jaw, pancakes sizzle in a pan on deck. Bosch painted the 'Ship of Fools' around 1500, borrowing from Sebastian Brant's bestselling satire of 1494. The panel is actually a fragment, the top of a triptych wing that was sawn up centuries ago; its bottom piece is at Yale, labelled 'Allegory of Gluttony.' Camille Benoit gave this piece to the Louvre in 1918.

Jheronimus_Bosch_050.jpg.story: A dying man props himself up in bed while Death shoulders through the door with an arrow. An angel tugs his gaze toward a crucifix in the window; a demon leans from the canopy offering a last sack of gold. Below, the miser's past self still gleefully stuffs coins into a strongbox guarded by more imps. Bosch paints the whole crisis on a narrow vertical panel barely 93 cm tall, turning a deathbed into a courtroom. It's the right wing of a dismembered altarpiece; the National Gallery of Art in Washington has owned it since 1952.

Joachim_Patinir,_St_Christopher_Bearing_.title: St Christopher Bearing the Christ Child

Joachim_Patinir,_St_Christopher_Bearing_.story: The giant ferryman wades across a river that barely notices him. Christopher leans on his tree-trunk staff with the Christ child on his shoulder, but Patinir's real subject is what unfolds behind them: blue mountains stacking into the distance, a hermit's hut, villages pricking the middle ground, the whole world seen from a viewpoint no human ever occupies. This small panel at the Rockox House in Antwerp is the world landscape in miniature. The saint is almost an excuse.

Joachim_Patinir_-_Rest_during_the_Flight.title: Rest during the Flight to Egypt
Joachim_Patinir_-_Rest_during_the_Flight.description: Rest on the flight into Egypt

source.canonical_title: File:Joachim Patinir - Rest during the Flight to Egypt, Museo del Prado.jpg

title.es: Descanso en la huida a Egipto
title.el: Η ανάπαυση κατά τη φυγή στην Αίγυπτο (Πατινίρ, Πράδο)

Joachim_Patinir_-_Rest_during_the_Flight.story: Mary sits on a grassy knoll with the Christ Child on her lap, nursing a moment of quiet. Joseph fusses with provisions. Look past them, though, and Patinir packs the middle distance with farms, walled towns, rolling forests, and off to the right, the Massacre of the Innocents playing out like a news ticker. The Holy Family's calm foreground and the horror they fled both live in one panoramic eye-shot. Painted between 1518 and 1520, hanging in the Prado.

Joachim_Patinir_-_St_Jerome_in_the_Deser.title: St Jerome in the Desert

source.canonical_title: File:Joachim Patinir - St Jerome in the Desert - WGA17100.jpg
source.credit: 1. Web Gallery of Art : Image Info about artwork wga QS:P11807,"p/patenier/s_jerome" 2. GalleriX

Joachim_Patinir_-_St_Jerome_in_the_Deser.story: Patinir gives Saint Jerome a whole world to be small in. The hermit kneels by a cave in the lower left, beating his chest with a stone, the lion snoozing nearby — but your eye slides right past him into miles of blue-green valleys, cliffs like rotten molars, tiny villages, a glassy river looping toward the horizon. This is the Louvre panel, c. 1515, and one of the founding documents of landscape as a subject in its own right. Patinir notably skips the cardinal's red hat; his Jerome is stripped-down, penitent, lost in geography.

Joachim_Patinir_010.jpg.title: Landscape with the Destruction of Sodom and Gomorrah

source.canonical_title: File:Joachim Patinir 010.jpg

title.nl: Landschap met de ondergang van Sodom en Gomorra

Joachim_Patinir_010.jpg.story: Patinir puts the apocalypse in the background. Up close, Lot and his daughters scramble down a path in the foreground, led by two angels; in the middle distance, Lot's wife has already stopped to look back and is crystallising into her pillar of salt. Beyond them Sodom and Gomorrah burn under a bruised red sky, fire pouring from the heavens. The disaster is real but scaled down to the world's panorama — exactly Patinir's move, making sin and salvation small inside geography. Now at Museum Boijmans Van Beuningen in Rotterdam.

Johann_Heinrich_Füssli_011.jpg.title: Thor's Battle with the Midgard Serpent

source.canonical_title: File:Johann Heinrich Füssli 011.jpg
source.credit: The Yorck Project (2002) 10.000 Meisterwerke der Malerei (DVD-ROM), distributed by DIRECTMEDIA Publishing GmbH. ISBN : 3936122202 .

Johann_Heinrich_Füssli_011.jpg.story: Thor leans so far over the gunwale his ox-head bait drags the water, and up from the deep rises Jörmungandr, the world-girdling serpent. The giant Hymir cowers astern; Odin watches from a bank of cloud. Fuseli, an enthusiast of the French Revolution, half-admitted that the god thrashing the monster had contemporary overtones. He submitted the canvas as his diploma work and was elected to the Royal Academy on the strength of it in 1790. It still hangs in the RA's collection in Burlington House.
Johann_Heinrich_Füssli_011.jpg.year_note: Thor Battering the Midgard Serpent is Fuseli's Royal Academy diploma work, accepted on his election in 1790, not 1788.

Johann_Heinrich_Füssli_054.jpg.title: Odysseus in front of Scylla and Charybdis ( See also separate articles: Scylla and Charybdis ) .

source.canonical_title: File:Johann Heinrich Füssli 054.jpg
source.credit: The Yorck Project (2002) 10.000 Meisterwerke der Malerei (DVD-ROM), distributed by DIRECTMEDIA Publishing GmbH. ISBN : 3936122202 .

title.fr: Ulysse face à Charybde et Scylla .

Johann_Heinrich_Füssli_054.jpg.story: Odysseus clings to the mast while Scylla's six necks arc down over his deck and Charybdis boils up from the left — a double disaster squeezed into one compressed, tilted composition. Fuseli loved a mythic bottleneck, and he paints this one with the stage lighting of a nightmare rather than the geography of the Strait of Messina. The canvas, often dated 1794 to 1796, belongs to the Aargauer Kunsthaus in Aarau and is one of several Homeric subjects Fuseli tackled in the mid-1790s.

Johann_Heinrich_Füssli_059.jpg.title: Riders Attacked by a Giant Serpent

source.canonical_title: File:Johann Heinrich Füssli 059.jpg
source.credit: The Yorck Project (2002) 10.000 Meisterwerke der Malerei (DVD-ROM), distributed by DIRECTMEDIA Publishing GmbH. ISBN : 3936122202 .

Johann_Heinrich_Füssli_059.jpg.story: A horseman has been dragged from the saddle and a giant serpent is wound round his legs, crushing upward. The horse bolts; the rider's face tilts into full shadow. Fuseli drew this around 1800 and almost certainly meant Siegfried of the Nibelungenlied — the medieval German epic was one of his obsessions in the London years, alongside Milton and Shakespeare. The pen-and-ink sheet ended up in the Frick Collection via Charles Ryskamp's 2010 bequest; other versions of the motif, in watercolour and oil, surface across the Fuseli catalogue.

Johann_Heinrich_Füssli_064.jpg.title: Thetis beweint den toten Achilleus

source.canonical_title: File:Johann Heinrich Füssli 064.jpg
source.credit: The Yorck Project (2002) 10.000 Meisterwerke der Malerei (DVD-ROM), distributed by DIRECTMEDIA Publishing GmbH. ISBN : 3936122202 .

Johann_Heinrich_Füssli_064.jpg.story: Achilles is dead at last, felled by Paris's arrow, sprawled hugely across his own shield in the foreground. His mother Thetis bursts from the rocks at the right, arms flung wide, and far off his spirit rides the airborne shield toward the afterlife. Fuseli wrote three Greek inscriptions on the sheet — one from the Odyssey: 'thou in the whirl of dust didst lie, mighty in thy mightiness.' The 1780 drawing is brush and brown wash over graphite, a signature piece of his London years, now at the Art Institute of Chicago.

Johannes_(Jan)_Vermeer_-_Christ_in_the_H.title: Christ in the House of Martha and Mary
Johannes_(Jan)_Vermeer_-_Christ_in_the_H.description: Jesus at the home of Martha and Mary

source.canonical_title: File:Johannes (Jan) Vermeer - Christ in the House of Martha and Mary - Google Art Project.jpg

title.it: Cristo in casa di Marta e Maria
title.fr: Le Christ dans la maison de Marthe et Marie
title.bs: Krist u Martinoj i Marijinoj kući
title.mk: Христос во домот на Марта и Марија
title.eo: Kristo en la Domo de Marta kaj Maria
title.ru: Христос в доме Марфы и Марии
title.es: Cristo en casa de Marta y María
title.pt: Cristo na Casa de Marta e Maria
title.mt: Kristu fid-Dar ta' Marta u Marija
title.fa: مسیح در خانه مرثا و مریم (فرمیر)
title.ml: ക്രൈസ്റ്റ് ഇൻ ദി ഹൗസ് ഓഫ് മാർത്ത ആന്റ് മറിയ
title.ja: マリアとマルタの家のキリスト
title.uk: Христос в домі Марфи і Марії
title.sv: Kristus i Martas och Marias hus
title.pl: Chrystus w domu Marii i Marty
title.nl: Christus in het huis van Martha en Maria
title.th: พระเยซูในบ้านมาร์ธาและแมรี
title.avk: Krist koe mona ke Marta is Maria (trutca ke Vermeer)
title.br: Krist e ti Marta ha Mari
title.ar: المسيح في منزل مارتا و مريم
title.ary: لمسيح ف دار مارطا و مريم

Johannes_(Jan)_Vermeer_-_Christ_in_the_H.story: This is the biggest painting Vermeer ever made, and one of the first we know he made, before he found his quiet rooms and window light. Martha plunks a basket of bread on the table and complains that Mary isn't helping. Christ, hand raised, tells her Mary has chosen the better part. The figures are almost life-size, the drapery heavy with Italian influence. Painted around 1655, now at the Scottish National Gallery in Edinburgh.

Johannes_Vermeer_-_Gezicht_op_huizen_in_.title: View of Houses in Delft, known as 'The little Street'

source.canonical_title: File:Johannes Vermeer - Gezicht op huizen in Delft, bekend als 'Het straatje' - Google Art Project.jpg

title.nl: Gezicht op huizen in Delft, bekend als 'Het straatje'

Johannes_Vermeer_-_Gezicht_op_huizen_in_.story: No story, no saints, just a stretch of Delft brick on an ordinary afternoon. A woman sews in a doorway; two children crouch on the tiles; another figure washes something in a back passage. The mortar is wet-looking, the shutters faded, every crack in the facade painted with the patience of someone in love with his hometown. It's one of only two surviving outdoor views Vermeer ever made. Painted around 1658, now at the Rijksmuseum in Amsterdam.

Johannes_Vermeer_-_Het_melkmeisje_-_Goog.title: The Milkmaid

source.canonical_title: File:Johannes Vermeer - Het melkmeisje - Google Art Project.jpg
source.credit: Google Arts & Culture — AHrw. Z3. Av6. Zhjg 9. AHrw. Z3. Av6. Zhjg

Johannes_Vermeer_-_Het_melkmeisje_-_Goog.story: A thick-armed kitchen maid tips a pitcher and a ribbon of milk falls into an earthenware bowl. That's it; that's the whole event. But Vermeer renders the crusty loaves, the nail holes in the plaster and the blue apron with such weight that the moment feels monumental. She isn't posing, she isn't thinking about us. Recent Rijksmuseum research found he'd originally included a fire basket and a jug on the wall, then painted them out to strip the scene bare. Painted around 1658 to 1659.

Johannes_Vermeer_-_The_Astronomer_-_1668.title: The Astronomer

source.canonical_title: File:Johannes Vermeer - The Astronomer - 1668.jpg

Johannes_Vermeer_-_The_Astronomer_-_1668.story: A scholar in a long blue robe reaches out to a celestial globe, fingers just grazing it. The globe is a real one, a Jodocus Hondius model; the book on the table is an identifiable 1621 edition of Adriaan Metius on astronomy. On the wall behind him hangs a painting of Moses being found in the bulrushes, as if to say even science needs a bit of inspiration. It's one of only two Vermeers dated by the artist himself: 1668.

Johannes_Vermeer_-_The_Geographer_-_Goog.title: The Geographer

source.canonical_title: File:Johannes Vermeer - The Geographer - Google Art Project.jpg

Johannes_Vermeer_-_The_Geographer_-_Goog.story: Same room, same robe, probably same model as The Astronomer, but now he's leaning over a chart with dividers in hand, caught mid-thought, staring out the window. A terrestrial globe sits on top of the cupboard (its celestial twin showed up in the companion picture). He looks alive in a way Vermeer's figures rarely do, as if he's about to say something. Signed and dated 1668 or 1669, now at the Städel in Frankfurt.

Johannes_Vermeer_-_The_lacemaker_(c.1669.title: The lacemaker .

source.canonical_title: File:Johannes Vermeer - The lacemaker (c.1669-1671).jpg

Johannes_Vermeer_-_The_lacemaker_(c.1669.story: Lean close. You almost have to: this is the smallest painting Vermeer ever made, roughly the size of a sheet of writing paper. A young woman bends over her pillow, pins glinting, bobbins in motion, her face calm and her fingers precise. The red threads in the foreground seem to spill off the canvas in a blur of paint, while the lace itself is rendered with almost microscope-sharp attention. Picasso and Dali both considered it a touchstone. It measures just 24.5 by 21 centimetres, and has hung in the Louvre since 1870.

John_Atkinson_Grimshaw_-_Boar_Lane,_Leed.title: John Atkinson Grimshaw - Boar Lane, Leeds

source.canonical_title: File:John Atkinson Grimshaw - Boar Lane, Leeds.jpg

John_Atkinson_Grimshaw_-_Boar_Lane,_Leed.story: Wet cobbles, gaslight pooling on black pavement, the spire of Holy Trinity rising into a murky sky. Grimshaw knew this street - he was born in Leeds and worked its foggy evenings into a whole career. The shop signs (TAYLOR, TOBACCO) glow from the pavement like embers; tiny figures with umbrellas thread between cabs. It's a city picture, but quiet, almost devotional. The tonal narrowness - all ambers and sooty browns - is what Whistler noticed with some annoyance when he realised this provincial painter had beaten him to the nocturne.

John_Constable_(1776-1837)_-_Maria_Bickn.title: Maria Bicknell, Mrs John Constable

source.canonical_title: File:John Constable (1776-1837) - Maria Bicknell, Mrs John Constable - N02655 - National Gallery.jpg

John_Constable_(1776-1837)_-_Maria_Bickn.story: Constable painted his fiancee Maria Bicknell in July 1816, after a seven-year engagement her family had done its best to smother. Her grandfather called the struggling landscape painter unworthy of her. She sat for him in a high-waisted white dress, her hair pinned up, looking faintly tired and utterly herself. They married that October, partly on the strength of his sale of Wivenhoe Park. Maria bore him seven children and died of tuberculosis in 1828, leaving Constable in mourning dress for the rest of his life.

John_Constable_-_Flatford_Mill.jpg.title: Flatford Mill ('Scene on a Navigable River')

source.canonical_title: File:John Constable - Flatford Mill.jpg

John_Constable_-_Flatford_Mill.jpg.story: This is the view Constable grew up with: his father's mill on the Stour, barges nosing through the lock, a boy on horseback pausing to unhitch a tow rope. He painted most of it outdoors in the summer of 1816, the first of the huge six-foot canvases that would make his name. Look closely and the sky is restless, not quite finished, scrubbed and overpainted. When he showed it at the Royal Academy in 1817 as 'Scene on a Navigable River', nobody bought it. It stayed with him for the rest of his life.

John_Constable_-_Harwich-_The_Low_Lighth.title: Harwich: The Low Lighthouse and Beacon Hill

source.canonical_title: File:John Constable - Harwich- The Low Lighthouse and Beacon Hill - Google Art Project.jpg
source.credit: yAGr9d4fNHBv5A at Google Cultural Institute maximum zoom level

John_Constable_-_Harwich-_The_Low_Lighth.story: A small, brisk painting: slate-green sea, a lighthouse like a stub of chalk, two distant sailing vessels leaning into the wind, and the whole sky in motion. Constable had first sketched Harwich around 1815, and returned to the subject in oils a few years later. No literary subject, no narrative, just weather happening on the Essex coast. He pulled the low horizon down to a third of the canvas to let the clouds do the work. The Tate in London acquired it in 1986.

John_Constable_-_Salisbury_Cathedral_fro.title: Salisbury Cathedral from the Bishop's Grounds

source.canonical_title: File:John Constable - Salisbury Cathedral from the Bishop's Grounds.jpg
source.credit: The Yorck Project (2002) 10.000 Meisterwerke der Malerei (DVD-ROM), distributed by DIRECTMEDIA Publishing GmbH. ISBN : 3936122202 .

title.de: Die Kathedrale von Salisbury vom Garten des Bischofs aus gesehen

John_Constable_-_Salisbury_Cathedral_fro.story: The cathedral framed by two enormous trees that arch overhead like a Gothic portal of their own, a little joke about architecture imitating nature. In the foreground, Bishop Fisher himself strolls with his wife, pointing up at the spire with his stick. Fisher had commissioned the picture in 1823 and then complained about the stormy sky, so Constable eventually painted him a second, sunnier version. Both men were close friends of the artist; the bishop's nephew, John Fisher, was the painter's closest confidant. The original hangs in the V&A.

John_Constable_-_Stonehenge_-_Google_Art.title: Stonehenge

source.canonical_title: File:John Constable - Stonehenge - Google Art Project.jpg
source.credit: QwG39cxEne2qGQ at Google Cultural Institute maximum zoom level

John_Constable_-_Stonehenge_-_Google_Art.story: A watercolour, not an oil, and late: Constable was nearly sixty, widowed, and working mostly in his studio. The stones squat under a cracked, bruised sky with a double rainbow and a hare bolting through the grass. He had visited the site only once, back in 1820, and kept the memory like a pressed flower. When he exhibited it in 1836 he added a caption about the 'mysterious monument' standing 'on a bare and boundless heath'. It is in the Victoria and Albert Museum.

John_Constable_-_Wivenhoe_Park,_Essex_-_.title: Wivenhoe Park, Essex

source.canonical_title: File:John Constable - Wivenhoe Park, Essex - Google Art Project.jpg
source.credit: vAG0ovJU1U65Rw at Google Cultural Institute maximum zoom level

John_Constable_-_Wivenhoe_Park,_Essex_-_.story: General Rebow, an old friend of Constable's father, commissioned this sunlit view of his Essex estate in August 1816, and the commission kept growing. First the patron's seven-year-old daughter had to be squeezed in, driving her donkey cart on the left. Then the deer house on the right. Constable simply sewed extra strips of canvas onto both sides to fit everything in. The fee paid for his wedding: three months after finishing it, he finally married Maria Bicknell. It hangs today in the National Gallery of Art in Washington.

John_Everett_Millais_-_Blow_Blow_Thou_Wi.title: Blow Blow Thou Winter Wind

source.canonical_title: File:John Everett Millais - Blow Blow Thou Winter Wind - Google Art Project.jpg
source.credit: KAFjkUpsnAJxZQ at Google Cultural Institute maximum zoom level

John_Everett_Millais_-_Blow_Blow_Thou_Wi.story: A young mother hunched on a rock in the snow, shawl dragged up over her head, feeding a baby. At her feet a dog hesitates, torn between her and the man walking away. The title is Shakespeare, from As You Like It, but Millais said he actually saw the scene near Perth. One of his last big pictures, painted in 1892, four years before his death, and a late return to the social-theme work of his Pre-Raphaelite youth. It now hangs at the Auckland Art Gallery.

John_Everett_Millais_-_Chill_October.jpe.title: Chill October

source.canonical_title: File:John Everett Millais - Chill October.JPG

John_Everett_Millais_-_Chill_October.jpe.story: A Scottish backwater in autumn. Pale water, rushes blown sideways, willows on an island, a flock of birds scribbling across the sky. Millais painted it outdoors near Perth in 1870, from a platform he had built in the reeds - the weather was apparently miserable. After twenty years of tight Pre-Raphaelite detail he had loosened his brush and turned to landscape, and this is the first big one. No figures, no story, just chilly river air. He said later he wanted to paint what he felt, not what he saw; the result is both.

John_Everett_Millais_-_Christmas_Eve.jpg.title: Christmas Eve

source.canonical_title: File:John Everett Millais - Christmas Eve.jpg
source.credit: Christie's , LotFinder: entry 5631469 (sale 5969, lot 23, London, King Street, 13 December 2012)

John_Everett_Millais_-_Christmas_Eve.jpg.story: Snow on the lawns of Murthly Castle in Perthshire, the oaks sheltering bare patches beneath them, the last daylight glowing off the windows while the family inside gets on with the festive roast. Millais painted it from a wooden hut pitched in the grounds during a brutal Highland winter, his seventh annual stay at nearby Birnham Hall. It's his first full snow landscape. He added the last touches on Christmas Eve itself, 1887, with rooks drifting across a sky he'd studied in separate sketches now at the Royal Academy.

John_Everett_Millais_-_Glen_Birnam.jpeg.title: Glen Birnam

source.canonical_title: File:John Everett Millais - Glen Birnam.JPG

John_Everett_Millais_-_Glen_Birnam.jpeg.story: A lone figure in a dark cloak walks a snowy lane between bare birches, a basket on her arm. The sky behind the wooded hill is the colour of weak tea. Millais painted Glen Birnam in Perthshire - the same country that gave Macbeth his moving forest - and by 1890 he was the most lucrative painter in Britain, cranking out landscapes between portrait commissions. The picture is subdued, almost drab, and all the better for it. You can feel the cold in your feet just from the paint.

John_Everett_Millais_-_Mariana_-_Google_.title: Mariana

source.canonical_title: File:John Everett Millais - Mariana - Google Art Project.jpg
source.credit: Google Arts & Culture — 6wGvnPEiyH8RFA Also available at http://www.tate-images.com/results.asp?image=T07553&wwwflag=3&imagepos=41 .

John_Everett_Millais_-_Mariana_-_Google_.story: Tennyson's abandoned bride, stretching her stiff back after hours at the embroidery table: 'I am aweary, aweary, I would that I were dead.' Millais was twenty-one when he painted her in 1850-51, stained-glass light pouring over her deep blue velvet dress, autumn leaves blowing across the floorboards. The stained glass is copied from the chapel of Merton College, Oxford. She looks less heartbroken than seething. Millais exhibited it at the Royal Academy in 1851; the Tate bought it in 1999 for over four million pounds.

John_Everett_Millais_-_Ophelia_-_Google_.title: Ophelia
John_Everett_Millais_-_Ophelia_-_Google_.description: Depicted people: w:Ophelia and Elizabeth Siddal (sitter)

source.canonical_title: File:John Everett Millais - Ophelia - Google Art Project.jpg

John_Everett_Millais_-_Ophelia_-_Google_.story: Elizabeth Siddal lay in a bathtub of water in Millais's London studio through the winter of 1851-52, kept just warm by oil lamps beneath. One day the lamps went out; she caught a bad chill and her father sent Millais the doctor's bill. Meanwhile Millais had spent the previous summer by the Hogsmill River in Surrey, painting every willow and forget-me-not on the bank for months at a stretch. The flowers double as grave-symbols. Dante Gabriel Rossetti later married Siddal. The Tate has owned the picture since 1894.

John_Everett_Millais_The_Black_Brunswick.title: The Black Brunswicker

source.canonical_title: File:John Everett Millais The Black Brunswicker.jpg

title.ja: ブラック・ブランズウィッカー

John_Everett_Millais_The_Black_Brunswick.story: Black broadcloth against pearl satin: a Brunswicker officer yanks the door open, his sweetheart leans her whole body against it to keep him from Quatre Bras. The setting is the Duchess of Richmond's ball, 15 June 1815. Millais's models never met. Charles Dickens's auburn-haired daughter Kate posed clutching a wooden lay-figure; the soldier, a real trooper who died of consumption soon after, embraced another dummy. Three months of work, and Gambart paid a thousand guineas, the most Millais had ever earned for a canvas.

John_Frederick_Lewis_-_A_Frank_Encampmen.title: A Frank Encampment in the Desert of Mount Sinai. 1842 - The Convent of St. Catherine in the Distance
John_Frederick_Lewis_-_A_Frank_Encampmen.description: The camp of Frederick Stewart, Viscount Castlereagh, later fourth Marquess of Londonderry (1805-1872).

source.canonical_title: File:John Frederick Lewis - A Frank Encampment in the Desert of Mount Sinai. 1842 - The Convent of St. Catherine in the Distance - Google Art Project.jpg
source.credit: DgFnh3a4-_8sAw at Google Cultural Institute maximum zoom level

John_Frederick_Lewis_-_A_Frank_Encampmen.story: The "Frank" is Viscount Castlereagh, who paused five days at Sinai in May 1842 en route to Damascus and paid Lewis to paint his camp. He lounges in native dress with a hookah, tea service, newspapers, and a bottle of Harvey's Sherry; opposite him the sheik Hussein of Gebel Tor stands bolt upright, the guide who'll take him across the desert. Lewis finished the watercolour in 1856 and exhibited it at the Society of Painters in Water-Colours; Ruskin singled it out for his highest praise that year.

John_Frederick_Lewis_-_A_Lady_Receiving_.title: A Lady Receiving Visitors (The Reception)

source.canonical_title: File:John Frederick Lewis - A Lady Receiving Visitors (The Reception) - Google Art Project.jpg
source.credit: 3gFFY2gmy4bgYg at Google Cultural Institute maximum zoom level

John_Frederick_Lewis_-_A_Lady_Receiving_.story: The mandarah, a first-floor reception room in an Egyptian house, rendered with the obsessive clarity Lewis brought back from his decade in Cairo. The decoration is from his own Cairo house; a pet gazelle wanders in, as it does in several of his pictures. Here's the quiet joke: women weren't actually allowed into the mandarah, which was men's space. Lewis paints them lounging there anyway, a sly rebuttal to British commentators lecturing Egypt about secluded women while drawing-room rules kept their own wives boxed in.

John_Frederick_Lewis_-_Highland_Hospital.title: Highland Hospitality

source.canonical_title: File:John Frederick Lewis - Highland Hospitality - Google Art Project.jpg
source.credit: vwF_I_gCRIKQcw at Google Cultural Institute maximum zoom level

John_Frederick_Lewis_-_Highland_Hospital.story: Two hunters in tartan trews slump by a peat fire with their dogs after a day on the hill; a girl spins wool, a boy sprawls on the floor, an old woman watches the cauldron. Lewis was twenty-eight and still the English watercolourist par excellence, years before Cairo turned him into "Oriental" Lewis. He worked the paper with watercolour, gouache, gum, and graphite, scratching out to catch the sheen of brass and wet dog. Now at the Yale Center for British Art.

John_Frederick_Lewis_-_On_the_Banks_of_t.title: On the Banks of the Nile, Upper Egypt

source.canonical_title: File:John Frederick Lewis - On the Banks of the Nile, Upper Egypt - Google Art Project.jpg
source.credit: nQGSS6UcbBlXUQ at Google Cultural Institute maximum zoom level

John_Frederick_Lewis_-_On_the_Banks_of_t.story: Springtime on the Nile: a Bedouin in kufiyeh sits with his saluki hound in the shadow of a towering camel, while in the distance fellah women pick their way through orange and white wildflowers toward the river. Lewis was seventy-two and painting from memory, twenty-five years out of Cairo. 1875 had just seen the Khedive Isma'il Pasha go bankrupt and sell his Suez Canal shares to Britain, which may be why Lewis chose this year to stage so tender and un-imperial an evocation of Egyptian life.

John_Frederick_Lewis_-_Roman_Pilgrims_-_.title: Roman Pilgrims

source.canonical_title: File:John Frederick Lewis - Roman Pilgrims - Google Art Project.jpg
source.credit: YQEyub_NfGMHxg at Google Cultural Institute maximum zoom level

John_Frederick_Lewis_-_Roman_Pilgrims_-_.story: A family of pilgrims kneels in a shadowy sanctuary, a peacock strutting near them, frescoes and tapestries piling detail on detail. Lewis had just come back from a decade in Cairo and was dazzling London with watercolours so minute one critic called this one "the ne plus ultra of finish in watercolour art." The sheet is actually watercolour, gouache, gum and graphite on thick cream paper mounted to board, built up stroke by tiny stroke into something that glows like enamel. Yale Center for British Art.

John_Frederick_Lewis_-_“And_the_Prayer_o.title: “And the Prayer of Faith Shall Save the Sick”

source.canonical_title: File:John Frederick Lewis - “And the Prayer of Faith Shall Save the Sick” - Google Art Project.jpg
source.credit: 1gEp7ztczN5A8w at Google Cultural Institute maximum zoom level

John_Frederick_Lewis_-_“And_the_Prayer_o.story: A woman lies sick in a Cairo courtyard while her family prays; the reclining figure is modelled on Lewis's wife Marianne, and the cross-legged reader is a quiet self-portrait. On the wall, a relief of the Egyptian goddess Hathor; above it, Arabic script from the Qur'an: "We have embraced the faith, so forgive us." Lewis gave the picture a biblical title from James 5:15 when it went to the Royal Academy. A Victorian viewer was meant to notice that a Muslim household at prayer looked a great deal like their own.

John_Frederick_Lewis_004.jpg.title: The Coffee Bearer

source.canonical_title: File:John Frederick Lewis 004.jpg
source.credit: The Yorck Project (2002) 10.000 Meisterwerke der Malerei (DVD-ROM), distributed by DIRECTMEDIA Publishing GmbH. ISBN : 3936122202 .
source.permission: http://mail.wikipedia.org/pipermail/wikide-l/2005-April/012195.html

John_Frederick_Lewis_004.jpg.story: A servant woman framed in a pointed Cairene archway, silver tray of coffee cups balanced in both hands, a glimpse of sunlit garden wall behind her. Lewis painted it in 1857, years after his return from Egypt, working up finished pictures from the mountain of sketches he had brought home. The head-scarf, the embroidered waistcoat, the long pink sash wrapped over a white skirt - every fold is accounted for. She meets your eye with something between amusement and suspicion. It's a small picture that took months; Lewis worked the way miniaturists work.

John_Henry_Newman_by_Sir_John_Everett_Mi.title: John Newman
John_Henry_Newman_by_Sir_John_Everett_Mi.description: John Henry Newman , by Sir John Everett Millais, 1st Bt (died 1896)

John_Henry_Newman_by_Sir_John_Everett_Mi.story: The 15th Duke of Norfolk wrote to Cardinal Newman in April 1881 asking him to sit; Norfolk and a group of friends were footing the bill as a gift to the nation. Newman, nearly eighty, gave Millais seven one-hour sittings at Norfolk House that summer, in his scarlet cardinal's robes. Lady Millais played the violin through each one, which Newman loved. Agnew's paid Millais £800 including copyright and issued a mezzotint in 1884. The correct title is John Henry Newman, not just John Newman.

John_Liston_Byam_Shaw_Boer_War.jpg.title: John Liston Byam Shaw Boer War

source.canonical_title: File:John Liston Byam Shaw Boer War.jpg

John_Liston_Byam_Shaw_Boer_War.jpg.pd_status_reason: year 2008 is >= 1931; US 95-year copyright term not yet expired

John_Liston_Byam_Shaw_The_Woman_The_Man_.title: The Woman, the Man and the Serpent
John_Liston_Byam_Shaw_The_Woman_The_Man_.description: Eve, Adam, and the serpent in the Garden of Eden

source.canonical_title: File:John Liston Byam Shaw The Woman The Man the Serpent.jpg

John_Liston_Byam_Shaw_The_Woman_The_Man_.story: Eve stands out in front, eyes closed, skin lit like porcelain against a riot of scarlet blooms. Adam crouches behind her, one hand raised to his forehead. The serpent coils down the right edge in diamond-patterned scales, head resting near her hip; a peacock and a parrot peer through the foliage. Byam Shaw was forty when he painted this, still faithful to the Pre-Raphaelite recipe of hot colour and botanical precision long after Burne-Jones and Rossetti were gone. It's Eden as overripe hothouse - beautiful, stifling, already doomed.

John_Singer_Sargent,_Synagogue,_1919.jpg.title: John Singer Sargent, Synagogue, 1919
John_Singer_Sargent,_Synagogue,_1919.jpg.description: John Singer Sargent, Synagogue, 1919, Boston Public Library (part of the "Triumph of Religion" cycle at the Central Library in Copley Square)

source.canonical_title: File:John Singer Sargent, Synagogue, 1919.jpg

John_Singer_Sargent,_Synagogue,_1919.jpg.story: Part of Sargent's vast Triumph of Religion cycle for the Boston Public Library, installed in 1919 and immediately controversial. Synagogue personifies Judaism as a blindfolded woman with a broken staff and crown, slumped in defeat, paired across the corridor with a triumphant Church. Boston's Jewish community protested; a Massachusetts law was even proposed to have it removed. Sargent was shaken, abandoned the cycle, and its intended final panel, a Sermon on the Mount, was never painted.

John_Singer_Sargent_-_An_Out-of-Doors_St.title: An Out-of-Doors Study
John_Singer_Sargent_-_An_Out-of-Doors_St.description: Depicted people: Paul César Helleu and his wife Alice

source.canonical_title: File:John Singer Sargent - An Out-of-Doors Study - Google Art Project.jpg
source.credit: 7wHaMBbXrHQstQ at Google Cultural Institute maximum zoom level

John_Singer_Sargent_-_An_Out-of-Doors_St.story: The etcher Paul Helleu lies in the grass painting, while his bride Alice props herself on one elbow beside him and watches. Sargent caught them on a summer visit at Fladbury on the Avon in 1889; the couple had married only the year before. A copper canoe glints behind them, and the whole thing hums with wet paint and Impressionist light. It belongs to the Brooklyn Museum.

John_Singer_Sargent_-_Atlas_and_the_Hesp.title: Atlas and the Hesperides

source.canonical_title: File:John Singer Sargent - Atlas and the Hesperides, 1922-1925.jpg

John_Singer_Sargent_-_Atlas_and_the_Hesp.story: The MFA Boston commissioned Sargent in 1921 for $40,000 to decorate the ceiling over the Huntington Avenue stairway, and he gave them Atlas crouching on the world, three golden daughters coiled around him like sleeping cats. It's a tondo, meant to be read from below, with necks and arms wheeling around the central hunched titan. He worked on it until his death in 1925, and it was installed that same year.

John_Singer_Sargent_-_Cancale.jpg.title: Setting Out to Fish

source.canonical_title: File:John Singer Sargent - Cancale.jpg
source.credit: National Gallery of Art, Washington, D. C., online collection

John_Singer_Sargent_-_Cancale.jpg.story: Barefoot women and kids from the Breton fishing village of Cancale step across a low-tide beach, lighthouse and quay behind them, hunting shallow pools for the evening's supper. Sargent, twenty-two, had spent the summer of 1877 there sketching individual figures on the sand; he assembled the final canvas in his Paris studio for the 1878 Salon, tightening every stroke for the conservative jury. He sold it before the Salon even closed, only the second sale of his career. A smaller sister version, Fishing for Oysters at Cancale, is in Boston.

John_Singer_Sargent_-_Carnation,_Lily,_L.story: Two little girls light Japanese paper lanterns among tall lilies at dusk. Sargent could only paint it for about ten minutes each evening, when the light hit right, so he worked through the summers of 1885 and 1886 in a Cotswold garden at Broadway, repainting the flowers as they bloomed and died. The title comes from a popular song of the day. It was a huge hit at the Royal Academy in 1887 and bought on the spot for the Tate.

John_Singer_Sargent_-_Repose.jpg.story: Also called Nonchaloir. Sargent's niece Rose-Marie Ormond is sprawled on a loveseat under a cashmere shawl, deep in an afternoon doze. By 1911 Sargent had sworn off the grand society portrait and was painting family and friends in soft, near-abstract puddles of fabric. The shawl is the real subject, really: ivory, pearl, silver. It hangs in the National Gallery of Art in Washington, a bequest from Sargent's friend Curt Freer.

John_Singer_Sargent_-_The_Chess_Game.jpg.title: The Chess Game

source.canonical_title: File:John Singer Sargent - The Chess Game.jpg

John_Singer_Sargent_-_The_Chess_Game.jpg.story: Two women bend over a tiny travel chess set in a tent pitched in the Italian Alps, probably the Simplon. Sargent spent his summers after about 1900 hiking with friends and painting watercolors and oils of them lounging in shawls, picnicking, napping in canoes. This one is from 1907 and the players are his niece Rose-Marie Ormond and her cousin Reine. Rose-Marie would be killed eleven years later when a German shell hit Saint-Gervais church in Paris.

John_Singer_Sargent_-_Venetian_Onion_Sel.title: Venetian Onion Seller

source.canonical_title: File:John Singer Sargent - Venetian Onion Seller.jpg

John_Singer_Sargent_-_Venetian_Onion_Sel.story: A girl balances a thick rope of onions on her hip in a hushed Venetian interior, her face half-lost in the gloom. Sargent made it during his Venice sojourns around 1880 to 1882, part of a series of genre pieces set in dim palazzo rooms rather than on the sunny canals tourists expected. No pretty gondoliers, no glitter. Just working girls, doorways, stone floors, and that peculiar greenish indoor light. It now hangs at the Museo Thyssen-Bornemisza in Madrid.

Joseon-Kang_Huian-Gosagwansudo.jpg.title: Joseon-Kang Huian-Gosagwansudo
Joseon-Kang_Huian-Gosagwansudo.jpg.description: “Gosagwansudo” (A seonbi (scholar) overlooking water from the high hill)

source.canonical_title: File:Joseon-Kang Huian-Gosagwansudo.jpg

Joseon-Kang_Huian-Gosagwansudo.jpg.story: A small scholar props his chin on his fist and stares down at the water, tucked under a dark cliff with vines trailing overhead. The whole composition is maybe four confident passages of ink - the rock, the leaves, the figure, the wash of paper left as sky - and almost everything is negative space. Kang Hui-an passed the gwageo in 1441 and served at court under Sejong, painting in the gaps around his official duties. This tiny leaf is the anchor of early Joseon literati painting: not a landscape with a figure in it, but a mind with a landscape arranged around it.

Joseph_Mallord_William_Turner,_A_Coast_S.title: A Coast Scene with Fishermen Hauling a Boat Ashore

Joseph_Mallord_William_Turner,_English_-.story: On the night of 16 October 1834 the old Palace of Westminster went up in flames — an overstoked furnace full of tally sticks. Turner was in the crowd on the Thames, sketching in watercolour from a hired boat. This version, looking upstream from Westminster Bridge, was his first finished response, shown at the British Institution in February 1835. Reflections of fire smear all the way across the river. The Philadelphia Museum of Art acquired it in 1928.
