Joseph_Mallord_William_Turner_(1775-1851.title: A Ship Aground, Yarmouth; Sample Study

source.canonical_title: File:Joseph Mallord William Turner (1775-1851) - A Ship Aground, Yarmouth, Sample Study - N02065 - National Gallery.jpg

Joseph_Mallord_William_Turner_(1775-1851.story: A 'sample study' was the rough Turner showed to a potential client before committing paint to a full commission. This one pitches a grounded ship against a gunmetal Yarmouth sky, a tidy demonstration of what he could do with disaster and weather if someone would only write a cheque. It stayed in the studio. The Turner Bequest of 1856 scooped it up and it now sits in Tate's collection as N02065.

Joseph_Mallord_William_Turner_(1775-1851.title: Buttermere Lake, with Part of Cromackwater, Cumberland, a Shower

source.canonical_title: File:Joseph Mallord William Turner (1775-1851) - Buttermere Lake, with Part of Cromackwater, Cumberland, a Shower - N00460 - National Gallery.jpg

Joseph_Mallord_William_Turner_(1775-1851.story: A rainbow cuts across a bruised Cumbrian sky while the shower still drags over the fells. Turner sketched the Lake District on his 1797 tour and worked this one up for the Academy in 1798, pairing it in the catalogue with lines from Thomson's 'Seasons'. The boat on the water is a speck; the weather is the subject. Part of the Turner Bequest, it hangs at Tate Britain as N00460.

Joseph_Mallord_William_Turner_(1775-1851.title: Calais Sands at Low Water: Poissards Collecting Bait

source.canonical_title: File:Joseph Mallord William Turner (1775-1851) - Calais Sands at Low Water, Poissards Collecting Bait - 0114-1901 - Bury Art Museum.jpg

title.de: Strand von Calais bei Ebbe, Poissards sammeln Fischköder

Joseph_Mallord_William_Turner_(1775-1851.story: Fort Rouge sticks up on the left, the Calais jetty to its right, and a row of fisherwomen — poissardes — stoop across the wet sand digging lugworms for tomorrow's lines. But the real subject is the sunset, which takes over about half the canvas and turns every pool on the beach into a sheet of molten brass. The Morning Chronicle of 1830 got it exactly right: 'literally nothing in labour but extraordinary in art.' Bury Art Museum bought it in 1897 to mark Queen Victoria's Diamond Jubilee.

Joseph_Mallord_William_Turner_(1775-1851.title: Cassiobury Park: Reaping

source.canonical_title: File:Joseph Mallord William Turner (1775-1851) - Cassiobury Park, Reaping - N04663 - National Gallery.jpg

Joseph_Mallord_William_Turner_(1775-1851.story: An unfinished harvest scene for the 5th Earl of Essex, who'd invited Turner to his Hertfordshire estate near Watford in 1807. Reapers bend over the wheat, the mansion floats pale in the middle distance. Turner started it that year, kept tinkering, and eventually set it aside. It's thinly painted enough that you can see the underdrawing tracking through the gold.

Joseph_Mallord_William_Turner_(1775-1851.title: First Sketch for ‘The Battle of Trafalgar’

source.canonical_title: File:Joseph Mallord William Turner (1775-1851) - First Sketch for 'The Battle of Trafalgar' - N05480 - National Gallery.jpg

Joseph_Mallord_William_Turner_(1775-1851.story: A thought on canvas, not a finished statement. Turner was wrestling with a royal commission from George IV, the only one he ever received, and needed to work out how to cram the fall of the Victory's masts, the smoke, and Nelson's death into a single hieratic image. The final oil hangs at the National Maritime Museum and the king hated it. This first sketch survived the Turner Bequest of 1856 and now belongs to Tate.

Joseph_Mallord_William_Turner_(1775-1851.title: Fishing Boats Bringing a Disabled Ship into Port Ruysdael

source.canonical_title: File:Joseph Mallord William Turner (1775-1851) - Fishing Boats Bringing a Disabled Ship into Port Ruysdael - N00536 - National Gallery.jpg

title.nl: Vissersboten brengen een toegetakeld schip naar de haven van Ruysdael

Joseph_Mallord_William_Turner_(1775-1851.story: There is no Port Ruysdael. Turner invented the harbour as a tip of the hat to Jacob van Ruisdael, the seventeenth-century Dutch marine painter whose work had knocked him sideways on his first Louvre visit in 1802. He used the name more than once. Here, in 1844, fishing boats tow a wounded ship into a port that exists only on canvas. It came to the nation in the Turner Bequest of 1856.

Joseph_Mallord_William_Turner_(1775-1851.title: Grenoble Seen from the River Drac with Mont Blanc in the Distance

source.canonical_title: File:Joseph Mallord William Turner (1775-1851) - Grenoble Seen from the River Drac with Mont Blanc in the Distance - N02988 - National Gallery.jpg

Joseph_Mallord_William_Turner_(1775-1851.story: One small liberty: Mont Blanc isn't actually visible from Grenoble. Turner put it in anyway, pulling Alpine drama toward the viewer from a sketch made on his 1802 continental tour, the first trip abroad possible after the Peace of Amiens cracked the door open. The Drac winds through a pale, dusty valley; the town sits low and warm; the mountain floats impossibly at the back. Tate N02988.

Joseph_Mallord_William_Turner_(1775-1851.title: Head of a Person Asleep

source.canonical_title: File:Joseph Mallord William Turner (1775-1851) - Head of a Person Asleep - N05494 - National Gallery.jpg

Joseph_Mallord_William_Turner_(1775-1851.story: Less than a foot across, painted in oil on canvas around 1835, and nothing like the thunderous Royal Academy pieces Turner was showing the same year. A face tilted back on a pillow, eyes closed, breathing. He never exhibited it, never named it, possibly never meant anyone to see it. It turned up in his studio after his death and went to the nation with the 1856 Bequest, catalogued by the Tate as N05494.

Joseph_Mallord_William_Turner_(1775-1851.title: Hill Town on the Edge of the Campagna

source.canonical_title: File:Joseph Mallord William Turner (1775-1851) - Hill Town on the Edge of the Campagna - N05526 - National Gallery.jpg

Joseph_Mallord_William_Turner_(1775-1851.story: Turner reached Rome in October 1828 on his second Italian trip, and spent the next few months painting on canvas rolls and muslin-covered millboards shipped out from London. This is one of those rapid tonal studies: a hill town blurring into the Campagna's hazy sunlight, the whole thing barely more than a breath of colour. He never finished it. It stayed rolled up with the rest of his Roman output, travelled back to England with him in January 1829, and entered the Turner Bequest of 1856 still effectively a private note to himself.

Joseph_Mallord_William_Turner_(1775-1851.title: Petworth House from the Lake: Dewy Morning

source.canonical_title: File:Joseph Mallord William Turner (1775-1851) - Petworth, Sussex, the Seat of the Earl of Egremont, Dewy Morning - T03880 - Tate.jpg

Joseph_Mallord_William_Turner_(1775-1851.story: Petworth House across its own lake, seen through the gilded damp of a Sussex morning, fishermen already at work on the Upper Pond. Commissioned by George Wyndham, 3rd Earl of Egremont, and shown at the Royal Academy in 1810, this was the painting that started Turner's long love affair with the house, where he would later be given his own studio. It still hangs at Petworth today, on long-term loan from Tate to the National Trust.

Joseph_Mallord_William_Turner_(1775-1851.title: Petworth Park: Tillington Church in the Distance

source.canonical_title: File:Joseph Mallord William Turner (1775-1851) - Petworth Park, Tillington Church in the Distance - N00559 - National Gallery.jpg

Joseph_Mallord_William_Turner_(1775-1851.story: Turner painted this long, low panel around 1828 for the Carved Room at Petworth, the Sussex house of his friend and patron the 3rd Earl of Egremont. It was designed to slot into the panelling below Grinling Gibbons' carvings, which is why the canvas stretches nearly five feet wide and only two feet tall. The sun is setting over Egremont's park, Tillington's church spire pricks the far horizon, and a handful of deer graze the gold. Egremont died in 1837; the painting came to the nation with the 1856 Turner Bequest.

Joseph_Mallord_William_Turner_(1775-1851.title: Rocky Coast

source.canonical_title: File:Joseph Mallord William Turner (1775-1851) - Rocky Coast - N05499 - National Gallery.jpg

Joseph_Mallord_William_Turner_(1775-1851.story: Unfinished and all the better for it. You can practically feel Turner's palette knife dragging the cold tonal ground across the canvas, scrubbing cliff out of fog, fog out of sea. There are no figures, barely any incident. It came to the nation in 1856 as part of the enormous Turner Bequest of roughly 300 oils and 30,000 works on paper, and it's now held by Tate, catalogued N05499.

Joseph_Mallord_William_Turner_(1775-1851.title: Shipping by a Breakwater

source.canonical_title: File:Joseph Mallord William Turner (1775-1851) - Shipping by a Breakwater - N00469 - National Gallery.jpg

Joseph_Mallord_William_Turner_(1775-1851.story: Heavy sky, choppy grey-green water, a huddle of small craft riding under the lee of a stone mole. Turner is still in his twenties here and learning from the Dutch masters he'd studied in London collections - de Vlieger, van de Velde - but already pushing the weather harder than they did. The paint goes on thin and nervous in the clouds, thick where a wave catches light. It's N00469 in the Turner Bequest.

Joseph_Mallord_William_Turner_(1775-1851.title: Shipping off East Cowes Headland

source.canonical_title: File:Joseph Mallord William Turner (1775-1851) - Shipping off East Cowes Headland - N01999 - National Gallery.jpg

Joseph_Mallord_William_Turner_(1775-1851.story: Turner spent the summer of 1827 on the Isle of Wight as a guest of the architect John Nash, who'd asked him for paintings of the Cowes regatta. While there he knocked out roughly seventy drawings and eight oil sketches in rapid fire, this working oil among them. You can see him rehearsing how sails catch wind and how hulls carve water. It entered Tate via the Turner Bequest of 1856.

Joseph_Mallord_William_Turner_(1775-1851.title: Sketch for ‘East Cowes Castle, the Regatta Beating to Windward’ No. 1

source.canonical_title: File:Joseph Mallord William Turner (1775-1851) - Sketch for 'East Cowes Castle, the Regatta Beating to Windward' No. 1 - N01995 - National Gallery.jpg

Joseph_Mallord_William_Turner_(1775-1851.story: Nash had commissioned two paintings of his castle and the yacht race running past it, so Turner tore through oil sketches on the spot, working out how to balance Nash's towers against the scatter of sails. This is one of the rougher rehearsals, paint smeared thin, horizon still moving. The finished canvas went up at the Royal Academy in 1828. The sketch stayed with Turner until his 1856 bequest and now hangs at Tate.

Joseph_Mallord_William_Turner_(1775-1851.title: Sketch for ‘East Cowes Castle, the Regatta Beating to Windward’ No. 2

source.canonical_title: File:Joseph Mallord William Turner (1775-1851) - Sketch for 'East Cowes Castle, the Regatta Beating to Windward' No. 2 - N01994 - National Gallery.jpg

Joseph_Mallord_William_Turner_(1775-1851.story: The second study for Nash's Cowes commission, painted in the summer of 1827 on the Isle of Wight. Here Turner's pushed the viewpoint lower and the yachts closer, so you're almost on the water with them, heeling into a grey blast. He made around eight of these oil trials before committing to the Royal Academy canvas of 1828. This one entered Tate through the Turner Bequest as N01994.

Joseph_Mallord_William_Turner_(1775-1851.title: Sun Setting over a Lake

source.canonical_title: File:Joseph Mallord William Turner (1775-1851) - Sun Setting over a Lake - N04665 - National Gallery.jpg

title.fr: Coucher de soleil sur un lac

Joseph_Mallord_William_Turner_(1775-1851.story: This one never made it to a frame in Turner's lifetime. One of a run of square canvases he painted privately in the 1840s and left unfinished, it's mostly sky - reds, yellows, oranges smeared across water. Those white passages at the right might be Alpine snow, possibly the mountains around Lake Lucerne, where he loved to go late in life. It entered the Turner Bequest in 1856.

Joseph_Mallord_William_Turner_(1775-1851.title: Sunset on the River

source.canonical_title: File:Joseph Mallord William Turner (1775-1851) - Sunset on the River - N02311 - National Gallery.jpg

Joseph_Mallord_William_Turner_(1775-1851.story: Painted on a scrap of mahogany veneer no bigger than a sheet of notepaper. In 1805 Turner rented Syon Ferry House at Isleworth and spent the summer drifting the Thames in a small boat with a box of oils, painting straight from the motif. This is one of those sketches - molten orange light, water gone to liquid gold, everything else dissolving. It sat unseen for decades; it came to the nation in the Turner Bequest of 1856.

Joseph_Mallord_William_Turner_(1775-1851.title: Teignmouth Harbour, Devon

source.canonical_title: File:Joseph Mallord William Turner (1775-1851) - Teignmouth - T03882 - Tate.jpg

Joseph_Mallord_William_Turner_(1775-1851.story: A Devon harbour, a working ship under construction on the slips, soft west-country light doing the rest. Turner toured the West Country in summer 1811 and worked this up from those sketches the following year. The 3rd Earl of Egremont bought it, probably from Turner's own gallery in 1812, and hung it at Petworth. It's still there, on loan from Tate, quietly glowing in a room full of grander Turners.

Joseph_Mallord_William_Turner_(1775-1851.title: The Battle of Trafalgar, as Seen from the Mizen Starboard Shrouds of the Victory

source.canonical_title: File:Joseph Mallord William Turner (1775-1851) - The Battle of Trafalgar, as Seen from the Mizen Starboard Shrouds of the Victory - N00480 - National Gallery.jpg

Joseph_Mallord_William_Turner_(1775-1851.story: Turner went aboard the Victory at Sheerness in December 1805, six weeks after Trafalgar, sketching the bloodstained deck while the ship was still fouled with battle damage. The finished picture compresses the whole day into one chaotic instant: Nelson collapsing left of centre, the French marksman's smoking musket visible up in the Redoutable's rigging. Turner worked on it off and on until 1808. A separate keyed diagram names each figure, essentially a program for viewers at his gallery.

Joseph_Mallord_William_Turner_(1775-1851.title: The Confluence of the Thames and Medway

source.canonical_title: File:Joseph Mallord William Turner (1775-1851) - The Confluence of the Thames and the Medway - T03874 - Tate.jpg

Joseph_Mallord_William_Turner_(1775-1851.story: Turner loved the estuary where the Thames meets the Medway, the muddy, choppy place where London's river finally surrenders to the sea. Barges lean, sails snap, and the whole working river seems to shoulder its way past you. He showed this one in his own gallery in 1808 rather than at the Royal Academy, part of a deliberate run of maritime pictures aimed at rivals like the Dutch masters he'd been studying in English collections. It's oil on canvas, 910 by 1220 millimetres, and lives at Tate.

Joseph_Mallord_William_Turner_(1775-1851.title: The Field of Waterloo

source.canonical_title: File:Joseph Mallord William Turner (1775-1851) - The Field of Waterloo - NG500 - Tate.jpg

Joseph_Mallord_William_Turner_(1775-1851.story: No trumpets, no charging cavalry. Turner went to the battlefield in 1817 and came back with this: a lantern held over a heap of the dead, women searching by its light, the sky churning with smoke and flare. When he showed it at the Royal Academy in 1818 he pinned a stanza from Byron's Childe Harold to the catalogue entry, the one that calls the field a place 'rider and horse,-friend, foe,-in one red burial blent.'

Joseph_Mallord_William_Turner_(1775-1851.title: The Garreteer’s Petition

source.canonical_title: File:Joseph Mallord William Turner (1775-1851) - The Garreteer's Petition - N00482 - National Gallery.jpg

Joseph_Mallord_William_Turner_(1775-1851.story: A poet scratches away in a freezing attic, candle guttering, a print of Mount Parnassus pinned above him as a joke the Muses haven't read. Turner painted this in 1809, part of a running rivalry with the young genre star David Wilkie, and sent it to the Royal Academy's summer show. It's a parody of the starving-artist cliche, with a wink: Turner himself had just built a private gallery to bypass exactly this kind of patronage. Now at Tate, via the Turner Bequest of 1856.

Joseph_Mallord_William_Turner_(1775-1851.title: The Pass of Saint Gotthard, Switzerland

source.canonical_title: File:Joseph Mallord William Turner (1775-1851) - The Pass of Saint Gotthard, Switzerland - 1935P198 - Birmingham Museums Trust.jpg

Joseph_Mallord_William_Turner_(1775-1851.story: Sheer rock crowds in on a thread of path; a tiny mule train inches across a bridge over nothing. Turner made the St Gotthard crossing in August 1802 and the experience haunted his work for decades. This oil, worked up from sketches around 1803-4, compresses the terror of the gorge into vertical cliff and empty air. It's been at Birmingham Museums since 1935.

Joseph_Mallord_William_Turner_(1775-1851.title: The Thames near Windsor

source.canonical_title: File:Joseph Mallord William Turner (1775-1851) - The Thames near Windsor - T03871 - Tate.jpg

Joseph_Mallord_William_Turner_(1775-1851.story: Thin, fast, and on mahogany veneer rather than canvas. Turner was painting the Thames from a rowing boat in these months, working wet oil straight onto panels small enough to balance on his knees. Cows stand in the shallows, the water barely registers the breeze, and Windsor Castle hangs in the far distance as a pale silhouette. It stayed in the studio unfinished and came to Tate from a private collection in 1984.

Joseph_Mallord_William_Turner_(1775-1851.title: Tree Tops and Sky, Guildford Castle(?), Evening

source.canonical_title: File:Joseph Mallord William Turner (1775-1851) - Tree Tops and Sky, Guildford Castle(^), Evening - N02309 - National Gallery.jpg

Joseph_Mallord_William_Turner_(1775-1851.story: Almost nothing but sky and a fringe of leaves, painted on the spot as the light went. The question mark in the title is the cataloguer's: nobody's sure if the smudge in the middle distance really is Guildford Castle. Turner was travelling around Surrey in 1807 with a small paintbox, training his eye on cloud structure the way a musician runs scales. It never left his studio.

Joseph_Mallord_William_Turner_(1775-1851.title: Venice Quay, Ducal Palace

source.canonical_title: File:Joseph Mallord William Turner (1775-1851) - Venice Quay, Ducal Palace - N00540 - National Gallery.jpg

Joseph_Mallord_William_Turner_(1775-1851.story: An oblique glance down the Riva degli Schiavoni, Venice's main waterfront: Doge's Palace and the Campanile of San Marco on the left, the dome and tower of San Zaccaria answering on the right, everything else melting into lagoon light. Turner exhibited it in 1844, by which point Venice had become less a city to him than a set of dissolving verticals. It entered the Turner Bequest in 1856.

Joseph_Mallord_William_Turner_(1775-1851.title: View of Orvieto, Painted in Rome

source.canonical_title: File:Joseph Mallord William Turner (1775-1851) - View of Orvieto, Painted in Rome - N00511 - National Gallery.jpg

Joseph_Mallord_William_Turner_(1775-1851.story: Turner had passed through Orvieto in the autumn of 1828 on his way south, then painted this view from memory in his Roman studio near the Piazza Mignanelli. He hung it there for a public showing that December alongside two other new pictures, and the Roman critics were not kind. He shipped it home, reworked the canvas in 1830, and sent it to the Royal Academy's Summer Exhibition. The cliff-top town hovers in Umbrian haze; a peasant woman washes linen in the foreground stream.

Joseph_Mallord_William_Turner_(1775-1851.title: Waves Breaking against the Wind

source.canonical_title: File:Joseph Mallord William Turner (1775-1851) - Waves Breaking against the Wind - N02881 - National Gallery.jpg

Joseph_Mallord_William_Turner_(1775-1851.story: A private canvas, not a public statement - Turner working out on his own easel what saltwater actually does when a gale rolls in off Margate. He painted it around 1840 as a kind of cousin to Waves Breaking on a Lee Shore, and the ideas fed directly into Rockets and Blue Lights the same year. Sadly the red lake he used fades badly in light; the pink sunset only survives on the right strip that sat under the frame rebate.

Joseph_Mallord_William_Turner_(1775-1851.title: Weir and Cattle

source.canonical_title: File:Joseph Mallord William Turner (1775-1851) - Weir and Cattle - N02705 - National Gallery.jpg

Joseph_Mallord_William_Turner_(1775-1851.story: A small, hushed thing. Cattle stand in the shallows below a low weir, the water going over in a pale stripe. Turner was living at Isleworth and painting outdoors a lot in these months, experimenting with how fast he could set down a scene in oil. No exhibition, no patron, just practice. It came to Tate in the Turner Bequest of 1856 along with hundreds of other unfinished studies nobody had seen.

Joseph_Mallord_William_Turner_(1775-1851.title: Willows beside a Stream

source.canonical_title: File:Joseph Mallord William Turner (1775-1851) - Willows beside a Stream - N02706 - National Gallery.jpg

Joseph_Mallord_William_Turner_(1775-1851.story: Another Thames-side oil sketch from the 1805 Isleworth summer: no grand subject, just willows leaning over slow water and a soft inland light. Turner worked these small panels fast, outdoors, a full generation before the phrase plein air caught on. You can see him pushing green against green, finding structure in a wall of foliage. Part of the Turner Bequest, Tate N02706.

Joseph_Mallord_William_Turner_(1775-1851.title: Windsor Castle from the Thames

source.canonical_title: File:Joseph Mallord William Turner (1775-1851) - Windsor Castle from the Thames - T03870 - Tate.jpg

Joseph_Mallord_William_Turner_(1775-1851.story: The castle sits small and hazy on its hill; the river does most of the work, carrying a pale sky and a few boats down to the foreground. Painted around 1805 during Turner's Thames campaign, it's one of several views he made of Windsor that summer from the water. He showed it in his own gallery at Harley Street rather than the Academy. Tate T03870, on long loan to Petworth.

Joseph_Mallord_William_Turner_(1775–1851.title: The Tenth Plague of Egypt

source.canonical_title: File:Joseph Mallord William Turner (1775–1851) - The Tenth Plague of Egypt - N00470 - National Gallery.jpg

Joseph_Mallord_William_Turner_(1775–1851.story: The killing of the firstborn, with Turner treating the Bible story as a chance to stage Poussin-sized architecture under a sky the colour of old bronze. Exhibited at the Academy in 1802, it shows his ambition boiling over into 'historical landscape' - the grand genre that was supposed to be beyond a young watercolourist from Covent Garden. Tiny figures mourn at the steps of vast, empty temples. He later made a mezzotint of it for his Liber Studiorum.

Joseph_Mallord_William_Turner_(British_-.title: Modern Rome - Campo Vaccino

source.canonical_title: File:Joseph Mallord William Turner (British - Modern Rome-Campo Vaccino - Google Art Project.jpg
source.credit: 9wG1GfGh9530qg at Google Cultural Institute maximum zoom level

Joseph_Mallord_William_Turner_(British_-.story: Ten years after his last trip to Rome, Turner painted the Forum the way you remember a city you loved. Baroque domes and ancient ruins dissolve in opalescent light, a moon rising left while the sun sets behind the Capitoline on the right - that shared-sky conceit lifted from a Byron line he pinned to the catalogue. Exhibited 1839 as the modern pendant to Ancient Rome; Agrippina. It now lives at the J. Paul Getty Museum.

Joseph_Mallord_William_Turner_(British_-.title: Van Tromp, Going About to Please His Masters

source.canonical_title: File:Joseph Mallord William Turner (British - Van Tromp, Going About to Please His Masters - Google Art Project.jpg
source.credit: OwF7vTnPbV9UwQ at Google Cultural Institute maximum zoom level

Joseph_Mallord_William_Turner_(British_-.story: Turner returned to the Dutch admiral Maarten Tromp four times across his career, and this 1844 canvas is the late, loosest of the series. The ship heels so far into the swell you can almost feel the spray; the full subtitle Turner gave it, 'Ships a Sea Getting a Good Wetting,' tells you exactly what he was after. Forms dissolve into weather. The critics complained, as they often did, that you couldn't tell a rope from a ray of sun. It now hangs at the Getty in Los Angeles.

Joseph_Mallord_William_Turner_-_Ancient_.title: Ancient Rome; Agrippina Landing with the Ashes of Germanicus

Joseph_Mallord_William_Turner_-_Ancient_.story: Tacitus tells the story: Agrippina the Elder steps ashore at Brundisium carrying the urn of her poisoned husband Germanicus, and a nation goes into mourning. Turner gilds the scene so completely that grief almost dissolves in sunlight. The painting went up at the Royal Academy in 1839 as half of a pair - its companion, Modern Rome-Campo Vaccino, hung alongside - and both carried the same Byron epigraph about moon and sun sharing the sky.

Joseph_Mallord_William_Turner_-_Caligula.story: Caligula, Suetonius tells us, built a floating bridge of boats across the Gulf of Baiae just to ride a chariot over the sea and mock a prophecy. Turner gives the story a vast golden morning, ruins crumbling on the left, the pontoon fading into haze on the right. He hung it at the Royal Academy of 1831 next to Constable's Salisbury Cathedral, with Constable doing the hanging. The Times called it 'one of the most beautiful and magnificent landscapes that ever mind conceived or pencil drew.'

Joseph_Mallord_William_Turner_-_Campo_Sa.story: Turner's Venice is never quite Venice - it's Venice as a fever of light. Campo Santo (1842) looks across the lagoon toward the cemetery island of San Michele, the walled burial ground Napoleon had decreed in 1807 because Venice could no longer bury its dead inside the city. Turner gives it white walls, a glassy sea and a sky that barely bothers to separate itself from the water. The painting now hangs at the Toledo Museum of Art in Ohio.

Joseph_Mallord_William_Turner_-_Clare_Ha.title: Clare Hall and King’s College Chapel, Cambridge, from the Banks of the River Cam

source.canonical_title: File:Joseph Mallord William Turner - Clare Hall and King’s College Chapel, Cambridge, from the Banks of the River Cam - Google Art Project.jpg
source.credit: jAEdez5qz_FbpQ at Google Cultural Institute maximum zoom level

Joseph_Mallord_William_Turner_-_Clare_Ha.story: King's College Chapel's pinnacles spike the skyline across the Cam; Clare sits low beside it, punts and willows in front. Turner was eighteen, on a tour of Cambridgeshire in 1793, still earning his living by topographical watercolours for engravers and antiquarians. The eye already stretches toward the dissolving distance he'd spend the next fifty years chasing. The sheet belongs to the Indianapolis Museum of Art.

Joseph_Mallord_William_Turner_-_Cliveden.title: Cliveden on Thames

source.canonical_title: File:Joseph Mallord William Turner - Cliveden on Thames - Google Art Project.jpg
source.credit: Google Arts & Culture — AAF7MnUg-TIdUQ Tate Images ( http://www.tate-images.com/results.asp?image=N01180&wwwflag=3&imagepos=1 )

Joseph_Mallord_William_Turner_-_Cliveden.story: The wooded bluff at Cliveden, where the Thames swings hard south below the Astor estate-to-be, painted from a boat in summer light. Turner had been floating up and down this stretch of river between 1805 and 1807, filling the Thames from Reading to Walton sketchbook. The picture's unfinished, with the foliage still blocked in as masses of olive and slate, but the reflections in the water are done to within an inch of being right.

Joseph_Mallord_William_Turner_-_Death_on.title: Death on a pale horse

source.canonical_title: File:Joseph Mallord William Turner - Death on a pale horse - Google Art Project.jpg
source.credit: Google Arts & Culture — VAEyZU0R3M3O5Q Tate images ( http://www.tate-images.com/results.asp?image=N05504&wwwflag=3&imagepos=1 )

Joseph_Mallord_William_Turner_-_Death_on.story: A bony rider, a bony horse, a storm-smear of brown and bruise. The canvas was never finished and Turner never exhibited it; scholars have argued for two centuries over whether it really illustrates Revelation 6 or something darker and more personal. It may have been painted around the time his father died in 1829. The Tate acquired it through the Turner Bequest of 1856 and now dates it roughly 1825 to 1830.

Joseph_Mallord_William_Turner_-_Dort_or_.title: Dort or Dordrecht: The Dort Packet-Boat from Rotterdam Becalmed

source.canonical_title: File:Joseph Mallord William Turner - Dort or Dordrecht- The Dort Packet-Boat from Rotterdam Becalmed - Google Art Project.jpg
source.credit: 4AFo7BatGeF12Q at Google Cultural Institute maximum zoom level

Joseph_Mallord_William_Turner_-_Dort_or_.story: High-res scan of Turner's 1818 showpiece, exhibited at the Royal Academy that spring. The packet-boat Swan drifts windless on the Meuse outside Dordrecht, rowboats pulling up alongside to pass bread and beer aboard. Turner is openly courting Aelbert Cuyp here, borrowing that buttery Dutch light and pouring too much of it on. One contemporary critic thought it the finest thing in the show. It now lives at the Yale Center for British Art.

Joseph_Mallord_William_Turner_-_Fall_of_.title: Fall of the Rhine at Schaffhausen

source.canonical_title: File:Joseph Mallord William Turner - Fall of the Rhine at Schaffhausen - 13.2723 - Museum of Fine Arts.jpg

Joseph_Mallord_William_Turner_-_Fall_of_.story: Turner stood at the Rhine Falls in 1802 and came back obsessed. Exhibited in 1806, this canvas catches the thunder by flattening white paint with a palette knife so the water looks as solid as the rocks. In the foreground, a mother snatches her child away from fighting carthorses - a small human panic dwarfed by geology. The Museum of Fine Arts in Boston bought it in 1913 and it's been theirs ever since.
Joseph_Mallord_William_Turner_-_Fall_of_.year_note: Exhibited at the Royal Academy in 1806, not 1805. Based on 1802 sketches.

Joseph_Mallord_William_Turner_-_Fisherma.title: Fisherman's Cottage, Dover

source.canonical_title: File:Joseph Mallord William Turner - Fisherman's Cottage, Dover - Google Art Project.jpg
source.credit: IAEH0C4fbQn60w at Google Cultural Institute maximum zoom level

Joseph_Mallord_William_Turner_-_Fisherma.story: A squat cottage under Dover's chalk cliffs, a couple of beached boats, one fisherman hunched over his gear. Turner is fifteen or sixteen, back from a sketching tour of the south coast, and he's already more interested in the weather above the roofline than in the roof. Watercolour with graphite and grey wash on a sheet barely 13 by 20 cm. The drawing sits in the Yale Center for British Art in New Haven.

Joseph_Mallord_William_Turner_-_Fisherme.title: Fishermen at Sea

source.canonical_title: File:Joseph Mallord William Turner - Fishermen at Sea - Google Art Project.jpg
source.credit: Google Arts & Culture — UwG73jK8wqshlw Tate Images ( http://www.tate-images.com/results.asp?image=T01585&wwwflag=3&imagepos=2 )

Joseph_Mallord_William_Turner_-_Fisherme.story: A single lantern on a pitching boat, a cold moon behind scudding cloud, and the Needles off the Isle of Wight looming dark to one side. This was Turner's first oil shown at the Royal Academy, exhibited in 1796 when he was 21. Critics noticed instantly: the handling of moonlight on water was unlike anything around it. You can almost feel the swell under the hull. The painting stayed with the man who bought it until it came to the Tate in 1972.

Joseph_Mallord_William_Turner_-_Fishing_.story: Blythe Sands lie off Sheerness, facing Canvey Island, and Turner painted them with the tide coming back in: flat light, wading figures, a sky doing most of the work. Shown in his gallery in 1809, it was one he couldn't bear to part with. He reportedly refused to sell it to Sir George Beaumont and offered it instead to Sir John Leicester. Later, in his chaotic Queen Anne Street house, the canvas is said to have ended up pressed into service as a cat flap.

Joseph_Mallord_William_Turner_-_Keelmen_.title: Keelmen Heaving in Coals by Moonlight

source.canonical_title: File:Joseph Mallord William Turner - Keelmen Heaving in Coals by Moonlight - Google Art Project.jpg
source.credit: 5AHnYBRd8dD08g at Google Cultural Institute maximum zoom level

Joseph_Mallord_William_Turner_-_Keelmen_.story: On the Tyne at night: flat-bottomed keels pull up alongside tall colliers, and men shovel coal from one to the other by torchlight, bound for London's hearths. A moon breaks through the cloud in a great silver arch, turning the smoke pearly. Turner had sketched the scene at South Shields in 1823 and held it in reserve for over a decade before painting this for the Royal Academy of 1835. It's at the National Gallery of Art in Washington now, and travelled back to Tate Britain for the Turner and Constable show in 2025.

Joseph_Mallord_William_Turner_-_Linlithg.title: Linlithgow Palace

source.canonical_title: File:Joseph Mallord William Turner - Linlithgow Palace - Google Art Project.jpg
source.credit: SQGDHWt5XOVyOQ at Google Cultural Institute maximum zoom level

Joseph_Mallord_William_Turner_-_Linlithg.story: Turner had toured Scotland in 1801 and was still mining the sketchbooks five years later. Linlithgow, where Mary Queen of Scots was born in 1542, sits dead-centre in blue haze, framed by classical clumps of trees that could be straight out of Claude. The watercolour finally went on show at Turner's own gallery in 1810. He worked the same view up again decades later as a moonlit vignette.

source.canonical_title: File:Joseph Mallord William Turner - London from Greenwich Park - Google Art Project.jpg

Joseph_Mallord_William_Turner_-_London_f.story: From the top of Greenwich Hill, the Queen's House and Hospital in the middle distance and St Paul's floating far off through the haze. Turner exhibited this in 1809 with his own verses pinned to the frame, calling the city below a 'world of care' under a 'murky veil' of smoke. Read as a celebration today, it was meant at the time as half-warning, half-lament. Oil on canvas, 90.2 by 120 centimetres, and on display at Tate Britain.

Joseph_Mallord_William_Turner_-_Newark_A.title: Newark Abbey

source.canonical_title: File:Joseph Mallord William Turner - Newark Abbey - Google Art Project.jpg
source.credit: NwGAR5f7wgk8Pw at Google Cultural Institute maximum zoom level

Joseph_Mallord_William_Turner_-_Newark_A.story: Ruins of a 12th-century Augustinian priory on the River Wey in Surrey, wrecked during Henry VIII's dissolution and left to the ivy. Turner first sketched it from a boat. This oil, around 1806, is all warm brown water and crumbling walls; you can almost hear the wood-pigeons. He liked the spot enough to paint a second, nearly identical version the following year.

Joseph_Mallord_William_Turner_-_Norham_C.title: Norham Castle, Sunrise

source.canonical_title: File:Joseph Mallord William Turner - Norham Castle, Sunrise - WGA23182.jpg

Joseph_Mallord_William_Turner_-_Norham_C.story: Turner sketched Norham Castle on the River Tweed again and again from 1797 onward; this late version, left in his studio at his death in 1851, barely bothers with the castle. A blue smudge of ruin, a pale gold wash of sun, a cow drinking. That's it. The painting was probably made around 1845 and wasn't exhibited in his lifetime. It now lives at Tate Britain, part of the Turner Bequest of nearly 300 oils.

Joseph_Mallord_William_Turner_-_Raby_Cas.title: Raby Castle, the Seat of the Earl of Darlington
Joseph_Mallord_William_Turner_-_Raby_Cas.description: Before he painted Romantic subjects drawn from classical, biblical, literary, and contemporary sources, Turner specialized in topographical views. This work, commissioned by the third earl of Darlington, is one of Turner's most successful "house portraits." It is also one of the first works in which he fully exploits the dramatic potential of the sky. The earl, an avid sportsman who reportedly hunted six days a week, may have influenced Turner's rendering of the scene. When the painting was first exhibited at the Royal Academy in 1818, it included a mounted huntsman in the foreground. Turner subsequently painted over this figure after his work had been denounced as a "detestable fox-hunting scene." Raby Castle, a ca. 1380 structure, is located in County Durham, England.

Joseph_Mallord_William_Turner_-_Raby_Cas.story: A 14th-century castle in County Durham, painted for the 3rd Earl of Darlington, who hunted six days a week and wanted his seat shown off with proper theatre in the sky. Turner obliged, piling up one of the first truly dramatic heavens of his career. When it went up at the Royal Academy in 1818 a mounted huntsman galloped in the foreground, until critics denounced the whole thing as a 'detestable fox-hunting scene' and Turner painted the rider out. It now lives at the Walters Art Museum in Baltimore.

Joseph_Mallord_William_Turner_-_Sheernes.title: Sheerness as seen from the Nore

source.canonical_title: File:Joseph Mallord William Turner - Sheerness as seen from the Nore - 2005.31 - Museum of Fine Arts.jpg

Joseph_Mallord_William_Turner_-_Sheernes.story: Sheerness, one of the Royal Navy's four big Thames dockyards, seen from the Nore anchorage at first light. The rising sun flattens the guardship into a black silhouette, and small boats pitch in a nervy, glittering swell. Turner showed this in his own gallery in 1808, the year he was turning maritime painting into a kind of weather report. It's now one of the early masterpieces in the Museum of Fine Arts, Houston, oil on canvas at 104.4 by 149.5 centimetres.

Joseph_Mallord_William_Turner_-_Shipping.title: Shipping at the Mouth of the Thames

source.canonical_title: File:Joseph Mallord William Turner - Shipping at the Mouth of the Thames - Google Art Project.jpg
source.credit: Google Arts & Culture — qgGcWeWQCxwJMQ Tate Images ( http://www.tate-images.com/results.asp?image=N02702&wwwflag=3&imagepos=1 )

Joseph_Mallord_William_Turner_-_Shipping.story: Painted at the estuary where the Thames finally gives up being a river, with cargo brigs heeling in a stiff breeze and a rowboat taking a pounding in the foreground. The brown-green swell and the low bruised sky are straight out of the Dutch seascapes Turner was studying, Willem van de Velde the Younger especially. He showed it at his own Harley Street gallery rather than the Royal Academy, part of a run of sea pieces from 1806.

Joseph_Mallord_William_Turner_-_Snow_Sto.title: Snow Storm: Steam-Boat off a Harbour's Mouth

source.canonical_title: File:Joseph Mallord William Turner - Snow Storm - Steam-Boat off a Harbour's Mouth - WGA23178.jpg
source.credit: Web Gallery of Art : Image Info about artwork wga QS:P11807,"t/turner/2/2040turn"

Joseph_Mallord_William_Turner_-_Snow_Sto.story: Turner claimed he had the sailors of the Ariel lash him to the mast for four hours off Harwich so he could watch the storm properly - the full exhibition title insists on it. Scholars have been sceptical for decades. One critic at the 1842 Academy dismissed it as "soapsuds and whitewash." Ruskin fired back that it was "one of the very grandest statements of sea-motion, mist and light, that has ever been put on canvas." The Ariel itself was a Dover packet, built 1821-22.

Joseph_Mallord_William_Turner_-_The_Angl.title: The Angler

source.canonical_title: File:Joseph Mallord William Turner - The Angler - Google Art Project.jpg
source.credit: HAHWiWo1pknk2Q at Google Cultural Institute maximum zoom level

Joseph_Mallord_William_Turner_-_The_Angl.story: One man, one rod, one crumbling stone bridge, a river running under heavy afternoon trees. Turner was nineteen in 1794, exhibiting eight watercolours at the Royal Academy that year and being noticed for the first time by critics who called his work original and masterly. He sold the little fishing scene for the kind of fee that let him live without his father's barber shop. The sheet is in the Tate.

Joseph_Mallord_William_Turner_-_The_Burn.title: The Burning of the Houses of Parliament, 16 October 1834

source.canonical_title: File:Joseph Mallord William Turner - The Burning of the Houses of Lords and Commons, 16 October 1834 - 1942.647 - Cleveland Museum of Art.jpg

Joseph_Mallord_William_Turner_-_The_Burn.story: Turner's second take on the same fire, painted within months of the first and shown at the Royal Academy's Summer Exhibition of 1835. This time he moved his viewpoint downriver to the southeast bank, so Westminster Bridge runs across the foreground and the flames erupt behind it in a pale hot tower. Witnesses that October night reported the Thames itself seemed to burn. Cleveland Museum of Art bought the canvas in 1942.

Joseph_Mallord_William_Turner_-_The_Fish.title: The Fish Market at Hastings Beach

source.canonical_title: File:Joseph Mallord William Turner - The Fish Market at Hastings Beach - Google Art Project.jpg
source.credit: rQED3TH4yBQtgg at Google Cultural Institute maximum zoom level

Joseph_Mallord_William_Turner_-_The_Fish.story: Wet wind off the Channel, a squall just receding, shafts of sun lighting up distant sails and the catch being hawked on the shingle at Hastings. Turner painted this in 1810 for the eccentric Sussex politician John 'Mad Jack' Fuller and showed it in his own gallery rather than at the Academy. The debt to 17th-century Dutch beach scenes is deliberate, part of his campaign to out-Cuyp the Dutch. It now hangs at the Nelson-Atkins Museum of Art in Kansas City.

Joseph_Mallord_William_Turner_-_The_Harb.title: The Harbor of Dieppe

Joseph_Mallord_William_Turner_-_The_Harb.story: Critics muttered that no northern French harbour ever blazed like this. Turner had sketched Dieppe in 1821 and gave it a Mediterranean sun anyway, firing the water and rigging with a yellow so intense that visitors to the 1825 Royal Academy accused him of painting Italy by mistake. He stuck to his guns. The full title reads Harbour of Dieppe: Changement de Domicile, and Henry Clay Frick bought it in 1914; it still hangs at the Frick.

Joseph_Mallord_William_Turner_-_The_Ship.title: The Shipwreck

Joseph_Mallord_William_Turner_-_The_Ship.story: All white crests and black water, with an overloaded lifeboat pitching under a mast that's about to come down. Turner painted it after the East Indiaman Earl of Abergavenny went down off Weymouth in February 1805, though he never named the ship. Sir John Leicester snapped it up, then traded it back two years later because a relative had drowned and he couldn't stand looking at it. The canvas is huge, nearly eight feet wide, and it was the first Turner reproduced as a print.

Joseph_Mallord_William_Turner_-_The_Sun_.title: The Sun of Venice Going to Sea

source.canonical_title: File:Joseph Mallord William Turner - The Sun of Venice Going to Sea - Google Art Project.jpg
source.credit: Google Arts & Culture — dwEYd5yKW43wWQ Tate Images ( http://www.tate-images.com/results.asp?image=N00535&wwwflag=3&imagepos=5 )

Joseph_Mallord_William_Turner_-_The_Sun_.story: The boat's name - Sol di Venezia - is painted right onto its sail as it glides out of the lagoon at dawn. Turner gave the 1843 Academy catalogue a poem to match, warning that a "demon in grim repose" was waiting for the little fishing vessel offshore. Beauty with a knife behind its back - classic late Turner. The picture came to the nation in the Turner Bequest of 1856 and is now at Tate Britain.

Joseph_Mallord_William_Turner_-_The_Temp.title: The Temple of Jupiter Panellenius Restored

source.canonical_title: File:Joseph Mallord William Turner - The Temple of Jupiter Panellenius Restored, 1816.jpg

Joseph_Mallord_William_Turner_-_The_Temp.story: The ruined temple on Aegina, which Turner knew only from his friend Henry Gally Knight's sketches, rebuilt in paint and set at dawn with a wedding procession winding past it. At the 1816 Royal Academy he hung it beside a companion picture showing the same temple in ruins at sunset: a then-and-now pairing, optimism next to decline. A critic said the pair looked 'like two guineas fresh from the mint; yellow, shining, gorgeous and sterling.' The restored version is now untraced in public collections.

Joseph_Mallord_William_Turner_-_The_Vict.title: The Victory Returning from Trafalgar, in Three Positions

source.canonical_title: File:Joseph Mallord William Turner - The Victory Returning from Trafalgar, in Three Positions - Google Art Project.jpg
source.credit: PgH780ODwlK-ng at Google Cultural Institute maximum zoom level

Joseph_Mallord_William_Turner_-_The_Vict.story: Three views of the same ship on one canvas, bow-on, broadside, and stern, like a ship-portraitist's trade card. The Victory had carried Nelson's body home in a cask of brandy after Trafalgar, but Turner cheats the geography: the chalk stacks of the Needles off the Isle of Wight don't match the actual homeward route. It's a salute, not a logbook. Now at the Yale Center for British Art.

Joseph_Mallord_William_Turner_-_Tummel_B.title: Tummel Bridge, Perthshire

source.canonical_title: File:Joseph Mallord William Turner - Tummel Bridge, Perthshire - Google Art Project.jpg
source.credit: GQHBAgj90T1exA at Google Cultural Institute maximum zoom level

Joseph_Mallord_William_Turner_-_Tummel_B.story: Pale afternoon light on a Highland stone bridge, with the Tummel running shallow underneath and figures picking along the bank. Turner had toured Scotland in 1801 and worked up this oil on panel around 1802-3, one of a small group of intimate, on-the-spot-feeling Scottish pieces. It's not a roar or a sunset - just the quiet specific Perthshire gold of a late summer day. Now at the Yale Center for British Art in the Paul Mellon Collection.

Joseph_Mallord_William_Turner_-_Undine_G.title: Undine Giving the Ring to Massaniello, Fisherman of Naples

source.canonical_title: File:Joseph Mallord William Turner - Undine Giving the Ring to Massaniello, Fisherman of Naples - WGA23184.jpg
source.credit: Web Gallery of Art : Image Info about artwork wga QS:P11807,"t/turner/2/208turne"

Joseph_Mallord_William_Turner_-_Undine_G.story: A water nymph and a Neapolitan revolutionary: Turner mashed up a German fairy tale and the 1647 Naples uprising and hoped nobody would ask questions. Shown at the Royal Academy in 1846 as a pair with 'The Angel Standing in the Sun,' the painting is pure late-Turner swirl, all coral pinks and seawater greens with figures half-dissolved in light. Ruskin called the late works wilful; the Academy hung it anyway. It's in the Tate collection.

Joseph_Mallord_William_Turner_024.jpg.title: Calais Pier

source.canonical_title: File:Joseph Mallord William Turner 024.jpg

Joseph_Mallord_William_Turner_024.jpg.story: October 1802, Turner and a boatload of travellers trying to land at Calais pier in a gale. He nearly drowned getting ashore - and promptly started painting it. The finished canvas, exhibited 1803 as 'Calais Pier, with French Poissards preparing for Sea: an English Packet arriving', is all wind-torn spray and arguing figures on the jetty. It set the template for every shipwreck he'd paint after. Now hangs in the National Gallery, London.

Joseph_Wright_-_An_Iron_Forge_-_Google_A.title: An Iron Forge

source.canonical_title: File:Joseph Wright - An Iron Forge - Google Art Project.jpg
source.credit: 8QFaV4btMWcjBA at Google Cultural Institute , zoom level maximum

Joseph_Wright_-_An_Iron_Forge_-_Google_A.story: Step into the forge and the white-hot iron bar does the lighting for you. Wright stages the scene like a nativity: a baby on its mother's hip, a grandfather slumped on a bench, a smith pausing mid-swing, all washed in the glow of a glowing billet under a tilt-hammer. He'd spent years painting candlelit experiments, but here the marvel is mechanical, a water-powered hammer pounding in a rural workshop. No saints, no kings, just a family business lit by their own trade. He exhibited it at the Society of Artists in 1772.

Joseph_Wright_of_Derby_(1734-1797)_-_A_M.title: A Moonlight with a Lighthouse, Coast of Tuscany

source.canonical_title: File:Joseph Wright of Derby (1734-1797) - A Moonlight with a Lighthouse, Coast of Tuscany - N05882 - National Gallery.jpg

title.zh: 月光下的灯塔，托斯卡纳海岸

Joseph_Wright_of_Derby_(1734-1797)_-_A_M.story: Wright never actually saw this coast by moonlight. He'd been to Italy in the 1770s and kept mining the sketchbooks for years afterward, mixing what he remembered with what he wanted. A lighthouse burns orange on a headland, the moon does its silver trick on the water, and a little fishing boat noses in below. It's less a document than a mood. The National Gallery in London acquired it in 1947.

Joseph_Wright_of_Derby_-_Dovedale_by_Moo.title: Dovedale by Moonlight

source.canonical_title: File:Joseph Wright of Derby - Dovedale by Moonlight - Google Art Project.jpg
source.credit: OwHAUYcn31UU7g at Google Cultural Institute maximum zoom level

Joseph_Wright_of_Derby_-_Dovedale_by_Moo.story: Wright loved a single light source, and the moon is a gift: one cool disc doing all the work. He's in Dovedale, the Derbyshire limestone gorge he painted again and again, the river catching the sky in a silver skid between black cliffs. A tiny fire pricks the bank, human and warm against all that cold stone. He made it in 1785 as a pendant to a sunlit daytime view of the same valley, so a collector could hang noon and midnight side by side.

Joseph_Wright_of_Derby_The_Alchemist.jpg.title: The Alchemist Discovering Phosphorus or The Alchemist in Search of the Philosophers Stone
Joseph_Wright_of_Derby_The_Alchemist.jpg.description: Full title: The Alchymist, In Search of the Philosopher’s Stone, Discovers Phosphorus, and prays for the successful Conclusion of his operation, as was the custom of the Ancient Chymical Astrologers, by Joseph Wright of Derby , now in Derby Museum and Art Gallery , Derby , U.K.

source.canonical_title: File:Joseph Wright of Derby The Alchemist.jpg

Joseph_Wright_of_Derby_The_Alchemist.jpg.story: A bearded alchemist kneels in a vaulted cellar, hands flung open, watching his retort glow ghost-white with newly isolated phosphorus. Two young assistants hunch over books in the far corner, their candle a small warm dot against the cold chemical light. Wright loved moments when a single light source did the dramatic work, and here the flask is the light source, as if knowledge itself were radiating from the glass. The title is a wink: the old adept was hunting the philosopher's stone and stumbled on a real element instead. Painted in 1771, reworked ten years later.

Judit_decapitando_a_Holofernes,_por_Arte.title: Judith Beheading Holofernes
Judit_decapitando_a_Holofernes,_por_Arte.description: Two women pin down a man on a bed. With one hand, Judith holds his head; with the other, she slices his throat with a long sword. The intensity of the scene is highlighted by the dripping blood soaking the white bed sheets and the man's eyes wide open — conscious, but helpless. Artemisia is more a champion of strong women rather than a woman obsessed with violence and revenge.

source.canonical_title: File:Judit decapitando a Holofernes, por Artemisia Gentileschi.jpg

Judit_decapitando_a_Holofernes,_por_Arte.story: The earlier of Artemisia's two great 'Judiths,' painted around 1612-1613 and now at the Museo di Capodimonte in Naples; the better-known Uffizi version followed about a decade later. Judith and her maid Abra pin the drunken Assyrian general to the bed; Judith, sleeves rolled up, braces one hand against his head while the other drives a long sword through his throat. Blood soaks the white sheets in thick ropes. She was around twenty when she painted it, roughly a year after her rape trial against Agostino Tassi.

Judith_and_her_maid_Abra_with_the_Head_o.title: Judith and her maid Abra with the Head of Holofernes

source.canonical_title: File:Judith and her maid Abra with the Head of Holofernes by Artemisia Gentileschi ca. 1645-1650.jpg

title.it: Giuditta e la fantesca Abra con la testa di Oloferne

title.fr: Judith et sa servante Abra avec la tête d'Holopherne
title.ca: Judith i la seva criada Abra amb el cap d'Holofernes

Judith_and_her_maid_Abra_with_the_Head_o.story: Abra stoops to drop Holofernes' severed head into a sack while Judith, sword still shouldered, cocks her head at a sound outside the tent. Artemisia returned to this pairing in at least eight canvases across her career; the Cannes version, over two metres tall, dates to the early 1640s. It hangs in the Musée de la Castre on the old Le Suquet hill above the harbour.

Jüdische_Hochzeit_in_Marokko-1024.jpg.story: Delacroix attended a Jewish wedding in Tangier in 1832 and took copious notes; seven years later he turned them into this painting, which the heir to the French throne snapped up the moment it hit the Salon. A dancer twists in the foreground, musicians sit against the wall, guests crowd the balcony. The architecture is observed, not imagined — one of the more ethnographically careful Orientalist pictures of its decade. Louvre.

KIYONOBU-Yamanaka-Ichikawa-1714.jpg.title: KIYONOBU-Yamanaka-Ichikawa-1714

source.canonical_title: File:KIYONOBU-Yamanaka-Ichikawa-1714.jpg

KIYONOBU-Yamanaka-Ichikawa-1714.jpg.story: Kiyonobu I made his living painting kabuki billboards for the Edo theaters, and this hand-colored 1714 print carries that big-signboard energy onto paper. Yamanaka Heikuro, sword over his shoulder, looms above a squat, bright-orange Ichikawa Danjuro II in fighting stance - cheeks blown out, limbs splayed in full aragoto bluster. The style got nicknamed hyotan-ashi mimizu-gaki, 'gourd-legs and earthworm-lines,' for exactly this: swollen calves, wriggling contours. Early ukiyo-e before the medium got refined - loud, graphic, unembarrassed.

Kagesue,_Takatsuna_and_Shigetada_crossin.story: The Battle of the Uji River, 1184 — one of the set-piece episodes of the Genpei War, endlessly replayed in ukiyo-e. Kagesue and Takatsuna are racing to be first across the flooded river; Shigetada is the one who waded in on foot and hauled a fallen comrade out by the scruff. Kuniyoshi gives the whole thing as churning water, rearing horses, and soaked lacquer armour. By 1849 he had been drawing samurai for two decades, and prints like this were why Edo men were suddenly tattooing Genpei heroes down their backs.

Kaigetsudo_Ando_-_Standing_Portrait_of_a.story: A Yoshiwara courtesan stands alone on a blank field of paper, hip cocked, head tilted, one hand disappearing into a sleeve stacked with chrysanthemums and tiny red shibori. Kaigetsudo Ando ran a small Edo workshop making exactly this: single-figure hanging scrolls of famous beauties, affordable souvenirs of the pleasure quarter. The bold silhouette and patterned layering would shape the first generation of ukiyo-e printmakers. Around 1714 Ando was caught up in the Ejima-Ikushima scandal at Edo Castle and exiled to Izu, which effectively ended the studio. Scrolls like this one are what's left of it.

Kajikazawa_in_Kai_province.jpg.story: A fisherman plants himself on a rock in the middle of the Fuji River's white water, lines trailing downstream, a small boy beside him clutching the basket. His stooped body, the angle of his lines, the jutting rock — every shape echoes the cone of Fuji on the horizon. In the earliest impressions, the whole thing is printed entirely in imported Prussian blue: an aizuri-e, flooded with a single cold color.

Kalisz_Rubens.jpg.title: Descent from the Cross .

source.canonical_title: File:Kalisz Rubens.jpg

Kalisz_Rubens.jpg.story: A limp, luminous Christ slides down a white winding sheet into the arms of mourners. This is the Kalisz version, a smaller workshop variant of the towering altarpiece Rubens finished for Antwerp Cathedral in 1614. It hangs in the Jesuit collegiate church in Kalisz, Poland, a gift that eventually tied a provincial town to one of the Baroque's most copied compositions. The diagonal of the body does all the work, shoulder to heel.

Kanae_Yamamoto_(1915)_Cow.jpg.title: Kanae Yamamoto (1915) Cow
Kanae_Yamamoto_(1915)_Cow.jpg.description: Woodblock print by Japanese artist Kanae Yamamoto

source.canonical_title: File:Kanae Yamamoto (1915) Cow.jpg

Kanae_Yamamoto_(1915)_Cow.jpg.story: A black-and-white cow grazes on a tuft of grass at the edge of a bay, red-sailed fishing boats tacking behind it. Yamamoto cuts the whole scene from a handful of flat colour blocks, the water pale blue, the headland pink, the grass scribbled rather than drawn. He had launched sosaku-hanga a decade earlier by insisting one artist should design, carve and print a block themselves, and this small 1915 piece shows why that mattered: every decision feels personal, slightly rough, nothing handed off to a publisher's craftsmen. It is humble subject matter treated with real affection.

Kanae_Yamamoto_(1926)_Tokko_Sanroku_Shū.title: Kanae Yamamoto (1926) Tokko Sanroku Shūi
Kanae_Yamamoto_(1926)_Tokko_Sanroku_Shū.description: Oil painting by Japanese artist Kanae Yamamoto

source.canonical_title: File:Kanae Yamamoto (1926) Tokko Sanroku Shūi.jpg

Kanae_Yamamoto_(1926)_Tokko_Sanroku_Shū.story: Sharp volcanic ridges rake the horizon, a stubbled field runs in furrows toward fat golden haystacks, and the whole thing vibrates with late-afternoon orange. By 1926 Yamamoto had mostly set aside printmaking to run his peasant-art school in rural Nagano, and this oil is the view that surrounded him - the foothills of Mount Tokko with the harvest stacked for winter. The brushwork is blunt and unfussy, closer to the carved plank of a woodblock than to European plein-air, and the colour is pushed past local truth into something frankly joyful. A painter settling into his chosen landscape.

Kannon_Riding_a_Dragon_by_Harada_Naojiro.story: Harada studied in Munich under Gabriel von Max and came back to Meiji Tokyo with a European oil technique and no patience for separating subjects by culture. In 1890 he painted a Buddhist bodhisattva in full academic realism: Kannon in flowing white robes, haloed, standing weightless on the neck of a green dragon that rears out of cloud and orange fire. Japanese critics lost their minds. It became one of the defining arguments about what 'modern Japanese painting' was even supposed to be. Harada died nine years later, aged thirty-six.

Kano_Hideyori_-_Maple_Viewers_-_Google_A.title: 観楓図屏風
Kano_Hideyori_-_Maple_Viewers_-_Google_A.artist: Kano Hideyori (1501 - 1700) Details on Google Art Project

Kano_Hideyori_-_Maple_Viewers_-_Google_A.story: A folding screen full of autumn picnickers, painted in the mid-1500s when Kyoto's Takao hills blazed red every November. People spread mats by the Kiyotaki river, pour sake, dance, fuss with a baby, eat. Kano Hideyori signs it with a stamp at the far left, and for Japanese painting this is a small revolution: commoners at leisure, treated as worthy subjects in their own right. It's now a designated National Treasure at the Tokyo National Museum.

Kanō_Sansetsu_-_Frolicking_Birds_in_Plu.title: Frolicking Birds in Plum and Willow Trees

source.canonical_title: File:Kanō Sansetsu - Frolicking Birds in Plum and Willow Trees.jpg

Kanō_Sansetsu_-_Frolicking_Birds_in_Plu.story: Four sliding panels, gold leaf floor to ceiling, one gnarled plum branch writhing across the whole span like calligraphy that forgot to stop. Willow drips in from the left, a pair of pheasants eye each other from a snowy bank on the right, and pink blossoms sit against the gold with real insolence. Sansetsu inherited the Kyoto branch of the Kanō school from Sanraku after the main line decamped to the shogun's new capital, and he kept the Momoyama taste for scale and swagger going into the quieter Edo years. This is that holdout aesthetic at full voice.

Karl_Friedrich_Schinkel_-_Der_Morgen_-_G.story: Schinkel was Berlin's great architect, but in 1813, with Napoleonic armies crawling across Europe, he kept turning to paint. Morning: a valley stretches out in that first pale hour, every leaf and roof pin-sharp, a tiny Gothic town tucked into the hills. It reads as hope with a blueprint attached. The painting hangs in the Alte Nationalgalerie in Berlin.

source.canonical_title: File:Karl Friedrich Schinkel - Gotische Kirche auf einem Felsen am Meer - Google Art Project.jpg

Karl_Friedrich_Schinkel_-_Gotische_Kirch.story: Another Schinkel cathedral that couldn't exist, planted on a sea cliff this time, spires catching a theatrical late sun while a storm rolls off to the side. Pilgrims climb the rock in a thin line. He made it in 1815, the year Napoleon finally fell, and it belongs to the same dream-Germany his stage sets kept building. The painting is in the Alte Nationalgalerie, Berlin.

Karl_Friedrich_Schinkel_-_Schloß_am_Stro.story: A neoclassical palace on a riverbank, its portico catching the last warm light, swans on the water, a woman in white descending the steps. It's Schinkel drawing the building he'd build if he could: symmetrical, serene, perched exactly where landscape meets civilization. He painted it in 1820, by which time his day job as Prussia's state architect meant he mostly designed places like this for real.

Karl_Friedrich_Schinkel_-_The_Gate_in_th.title: Gate in the Rocks
Karl_Friedrich_Schinkel_-_The_Gate_in_th.description: Pendant zum " Blick auf eine italienische Landschaft "

source.canonical_title: File:Karl Friedrich Schinkel - The Gate in the Rocks - WGA20999.jpg
source.credit: Web Gallery of Art : Image Info about artwork wga QS:P11807,"/s/schinkel/gaterock"

Karl_Friedrich_Schinkel_-_The_Gate_in_th.story: Travelers crest a narrow pass and a whole Alpine valley drops away below them, threaded by a river, dotted with little towns. Schinkel painted it in 1818 as the pendant to a sunny Italian landscape, and you can feel him staging the reveal like a theater curtain rising, which makes sense since he designed sets for The Magic Flute. The pair now hangs in the Alte Nationalgalerie.

Karl_Friedrich_Schinkel_Allegorie_auf_Be.title: Karl Friedrich Schinkel Allegorie auf Beuth, den Pegasus reitend, 1837

source.canonical_title: File:Karl Friedrich Schinkel Allegorie auf Beuth, den Pegasus reitend, 1837.tif

title.de: Allegorie auf Beuth, den Pegasus reitend

Karl_Friedrich_Schinkel_Allegorie_auf_Be.story: A gift from one old friend to another: Schinkel made this watercolor in 1837 for Peter Beuth, the Prussian civil servant who spent his life trying to drag the country into industrial modernity. Beuth rides Pegasus above a smoking factory town, blowing soap bubbles as he goes. Schinkel had toured England's mills in 1826 and come back rattled. The bubbles are tender and skeptical at once. It lives in Berlin's Kupferstichkabinett.

Karl_Friedrich_Schinkel_Gotischer_Dom_am.title: Gothic Cathedral by the Water

source.canonical_title: File:Karl Friedrich Schinkel Gotischer Dom am Wasser.tif

Karl_Friedrich_Schinkel_Gotischer_Dom_am.story: A colossal Gothic cathedral rises from a harbor town, bigger than any cathedral anyone ever built, with pinnacles climbing into a sunset sky. Schinkel painted this in 1813 as Prussia fought to throw off Napoleon, and the fantasy cathedral stands in for a German future that existed mostly in his head. The original was destroyed in 1931; what survives is a careful copy his student Wilhelm Ahlborn made in 1823.

Karl_Joseph_Stieler_-_Porträt_von_Kathar.title: Katerina Rosa Botsaris
Karl_Joseph_Stieler_-_Porträt_von_Kathar.description: Katharina Botzaris, born 1820 in Janira, Greece

source.canonical_title: File:Karl Joseph Stieler - Porträt von Katharina Botzaris, 1841.jpg

Karl_Joseph_Stieler_-_Porträt_von_Kathar.story: Katharina Botsari arrived in Munich in 1841 as lady-in-waiting to Queen Amalia of Greece. Her father Markos Botsaris had died a hero of the Greek War of Independence; she grew up in the new Athenian court. Ludwig I, a committed philhellene, helped her down from the carriage, noticed the face, and commissioned Stieler on the spot. The portrait keeps her in Greek costume, gold-embroidered, direct. A damask rose bred in 1856 was later named Rosa Botsaris for her. She was twenty-one.

Karolina_Lizius.jpg.title: Karolina Lizius

source.canonical_title: File:Karolina Lizius.jpg

Karolina_Lizius.jpg.story: Painted in 1841 and almost immediately awkward. Ludwig I thought the public had not taken to the canvas when it was shown; Leo von Klenze reported the king saying it had pleased no one. The tradition is that Ludwig then quietly gave the portrait to Karolina herself. She later married a legation counsellor and raised a son widely rumoured to be the king's. The Gallery of Beauties version at Nymphenburg is the tactful one. The gossip it sits on is the interesting part.

Katsushika_Hokusai,_Goten-yama_hill,_Shi.title: Katsushika Hokusai, Goten-yama hill, Shinagawa on the Tōkaidō, ca. 1832
Katsushika_Hokusai,_Goten-yama_hill,_Shi.description: 東海道品川御殿山の不二 ( Tōkaidō Shinagawa Goten'yama no Fuji , Goten-yama hill, Shinagawa on the Tōkaidō)

Katsushika_Hokusai,_Goten-yama_hill,_Shi.story: Cherry trees lean out over the bluff at Goten-yama, their blossoms crowding the top of the frame while tiny picnickers cluster below and travellers on the Tokaido road thread past thatched teahouses. Way back across Edo Bay, Mount Fuji sits small and blue, almost an afterthought - the whole point of the Thirty-six Views series was to catch the mountain from every ordinary angle people actually saw it. This is the spring version: the famous peak reduced to a blue triangle behind a wall of pink, which is really what hanami in Edo felt like anyway.

Katsushika_Hokusai,_published_by_Nishimu.story: A yellow canary drops through a tangle of heavy pink peonies, wings slightly open, against a wall of saturated Prussian blue. Hokusai turns each bloom a different direction, showing them from above, below, in profile, the way a botanist might. The inscription is a line from the Song-dynasty scholar Wang Shipeng: the many-leaved Yangzhou peony reigns over every other fragrance at spring's height. Published by Nishimuraya Yohachi around 1834, it's from the untitled kacho-e set collectors call Small Flowers.

title.ja: 相州大山ろうべんの滝

Katsushika_Hokusai_(1760-1849),_De_Roben.story: The falls at Oyama were no scenic stop. Pilgrims climbing to the mountain's shrines had to strip, stand beneath the cascade, and let the cold water hammer them clean. Hokusai catches them mid-ritual: some braced under the torrent, others dressing, a few cradling wooden swords meant as offerings higher up the slope. Prussian blue deepens the plunge pool. It's part of A Tour of Waterfalls in Various Provinces, the first ukiyo-e series ever devoted entirely to falling water, published around 1833.
Katsushika_Hokusai_(1760-1849),_De_Roben.year_note: Series A Tour of Waterfalls in Various Provinces dated c. 1833; source metadata had filename year 1835 but painting date 1833 is correct.

title.ja: 諸国瀧廻り 和州吉野義経馬洗滝
title.fr: Chute d'eau à Yoshino où Yoshitsune a lavé son cheval.
title.pl: Wodospad w Yoshino, gdzie Yoshitsune mył swego konia

Katsushika_Hokusai_(1760-1849),_In_de_Pa.story: Hokusai is in his seventies, still obsessed with how water actually moves. The full title is The Waterfall Where Yoshitsune Washed His Horse at Yoshino in Yamato Province, part of his series A Tour of Waterfalls in Various Provinces, around 1832. Legend says the warrior Minamoto no Yoshitsune bathed his horse here; Hokusai puts two ordinary stablehands at the job instead, while the falls above them curl into a stylized design that looks almost woven.

Katsushika_Hokusai_(1760-1849),_Kirifuri.story: The water doesn't fall so much as braid, splitting into pale ropes that coil down the rock like tentacles. Three travellers stare up from the base; two more peer down from a ledge, so small you almost miss them. That's the trick: the pilgrims exist to make the cascade enormous. Kirifuri, on Mount Kurokami in Shimotsuke, is still ranked among Japan's hundred most beautiful waterfalls. This print is part of Hokusai's A Tour of Waterfalls in Various Provinces, published around 1832-33.

Katsushika_Hokusai_(1760-1849),_Ono_wate.story: One of Hokusai's eight waterfall prints from A Tour of Waterfalls in Various Provinces, around 1832. The Ono Falls tumbles beside a post road through the Kiso mountains, travelers pausing on a bridge to watch. He draws the water as ribbons of pale blue, carved into the page like wood grain, which is almost literally true since these are woodblocks. He was in his seventies and convinced he was only now starting to understand drawing.

title.ja: 木曽路ノ奥阿弥陀ケ滝
title.de: Der Wasserfall von Amida hinter der Kiso-Straße (aus der Serie: Wasserfälle in den Provinzen)

Katsushika_Hokusai_(1760-1849),_Veld_in_.story: Despite the Dutch label, this is the Amida Falls in the Far Reaches of the Kisokaidō, from Hokusai's waterfalls series around 1832. Travelers picnic at the base of a cliff while above them the water pours out of a perfect dark circle the shape of a Buddha's head, which is how the falls got their name. Hokusai gives the top half a flat graphic strangeness and the bottom half a thundering descent. It's one of his weirdest, best prints.

Kawase_Ebisu-11.jpg.title: Kawase Ebisu-11
Kawase_Ebisu-11.jpg.description: Kawase Hasui (1883-1957): Port of Ebisu on Sado Island (Sado Ebisu minato), from the series Souvenirs of Travel II (Tabi miyage dai nishû) 旅みやげ第二集 佐渡夷港. Vertical ôban; 26.5 x 39.1 cm (10 7/16 x 15 3/8 in.)

source.canonical_title: File:Kawase Ebisu-11.jpg

Kawase_Ebisu-11.jpg.story: Ebisu is a small fishing port on Sado, the island off the Niigata coast that Hasui kept coming back to. He designed this sheet in December 1921 for the second Souvenirs of Travel series, and turned it into a snow scene — a row of low houses along the harbour, the dark sea, flakes falling and dissolving as they hit the water. Snow printed with real variation across the surface was Hasui's new party trick in 1920–21, and it's on full display here. A seldom-seen pre-earthquake impression from an unshowy coastal town.

Kawase_Tenno-ji-27.jpg.story: Shitenno-ji in Osaka is one of Japan's oldest Buddhist temples, founded in 593 by Prince Shotoku. Hasui shows it from the quiet north side on a snowy night: a single figure under a parasol, the main hall and five-storied pagoda dissolving into falling snow behind her. From Souvenirs of Travel III, dated 1927. A particularly fine impression sold at Sotheby's in 2024 for over $100,000, the highest auction result ever recorded for a Hasui print.

Kawase_Zôjôji.jpg.title: Kawase Zôjôji
Kawase_Zôjôji.jpg.description: Kawase Hasui woodcut Shiba Zôjôji from series "20 views of Tokyo"

source.canonical_title: File:Kawase Zôjôji.jpg

Kawase_Zôjôji.jpg.story: Hasui's most famous design, and for good reason. A lone figure, half-swallowed by a red umbrella, trudges through thick snow toward the massive Sangedatsumon gate of Zojoji Temple in Shiba. The 1622 gate still stands today, the oldest wooden building in Tokyo. Published by Watanabe Shozaburo in 1925, the print became the emblem of shin-hanga, and when Hasui was named a Living National Treasure in 1956, the government documented the entire production of a commemorative reissue to preserve the collaboration of designer, carver, and printer.

source.canonical_title: File:Kenkō Shōkei - Shōshō Hakkei - Enji Banshō.png

Kenkō_Shōkei_-_Shōshō_Hakkei_-_Enji_.story: One leaf from Shōkei's take on the Eight Views of Xiaoxiang, a Chinese poetic cycle Japanese ink painters returned to obsessively. A gnarled pine leans off a cliff, a temple roof catches the last light on the ridge, and a lone traveller crosses a plank bridge toward home. The far shore dissolves into mist and the paper's own tone. Shōkei was a Zen secretary at Kenchō-ji in Kamakura who went to Kyoto to study Southern Song models under the shogun's painter Geiami, and carried that vocabulary back east. The red seal near the cliff-face is his.

Khnopff,_Listening_to_Schumann.jpg.title: Khnopff, Listening to Schumann

source.canonical_title: File:Khnopff, Listening to Schumann.jpg

Khnopff,_Listening_to_Schumann.jpg.story: A woman sits by a dark fireplace with one hand pressed over her eyes, shoulders turned in, black dress pooling across a red Turkish carpet. On the far left, at the edge of the frame, just the cuff and knee of the pianist are visible. Khnopff cuts the performer out entirely and lets the music live in the listener, in the shuttered face, the gilt mirror, the cold candle. Painted in 1883, the year he helped found Les XX, it is already the mature Khnopff: interiority as subject, silence carrying the weight.

Kitagawa_Utamaro_-_Hairdresser_(Kamiyui).story: One woman's hands are deep in another woman's hair, combing and shaping while the client holds perfectly still. Utamaro's Twelve Types of Women's Handicraft went through the working life of Edo women one craft at a time, cotton ginning, weaving, sewing, embroidery, painting. Hairdressing got its own sheet. The series was published by Wakasaya Yoichi around 1798-99 as vertical oban prints, and this one puts the viewer close enough to feel the tug at the scalp.
Kitagawa_Utamaro_-_Hairdresser_(Kamiyui).year_note: Series dated c. 1798-99, published by Wakasaya Yoichi; source's 1797 is slightly early.

Kitagawa_Utamaro_-_Takashima_Ohisa_Using.story: Ohisa worked the counter at a teahouse her family ran near the Asakusa temple, and Edo treated her like a pop star. Utamaro catches her checking the back of her hair in a hand mirror held up to a larger one, the kind of glance anyone who's ever dressed up already recognises. It's the night of the Asakusa marketing festival, so the coiffure has to be right. The print dates to around 1795, when Ohisa was one of the most drawn women in Japan.

Kiyonaga_bathhouse_women-2.jpg.title: Kiyonaga bathhouse women-2
Kiyonaga_bathhouse_women-2.jpg.artist: Torii Kiyonaga, 1752–1815 derivative work: Torsodog ( talk )
Kiyonaga_bathhouse_women-2.jpg.description: Onna yu (Bathhouse women) 1 print : woodcut, color.

source.canonical_title: File:Kiyonaga bathhouse women-2.jpg

Kiyonaga_bathhouse_women-2.jpg.story: An onna-yu, the women's side of an Edo bathhouse. Kiyonaga gives us the full social texture: attendants in loose kimono on the right, bathers crouching with wooden buckets at center, a toddler being washed, someone drying off under a paper parasol used here as a bath umbrella, a glimpse through the lattice to the men's side. Around 1780 he was the commanding figure in bijin-ga and you can see why - tall figures drawn with calm, unfussy line, color held to a handful of soft notes, the crowd arranged without ever feeling posed.

Konrad_Witz_004.jpg.title: Saint Christopher

source.canonical_title: File:Konrad Witz 004.jpg
source.credit: The Yorck Project (2002) 10.000 Meisterwerke der Malerei (DVD-ROM), distributed by DIRECTMEDIA Publishing GmbH. ISBN : 3936122202 .

Konrad_Witz_004.jpg.story: Christopher wades across in a soaking red cloak, staff planted in the current, the Christ Child light as a bird on his shoulder. Witz, working in Basel around 1435, cares less about the miracle than the water itself: you can see the riverbed shelving under the saint's knees, fish-sized ripples around his thighs, a village reflected on the far bank with a monk and two tiny boats going about their afternoon. This is the painter who a decade later would put the real Lake Geneva into an altarpiece, and the instinct is already here: sacred story, real weather.

KorinsScreen.webp.title: KorinsScreen
KorinsScreen.webp.description: This is the screen from Ogata Kōrin's Waves at Matsushima, a painting from 1658 to 1716

source.canonical_title: File:KorinsScreen.webp
source.credit: Ogata Kōrin's Waves at Matsushima, public domain from the Smithsonian Museum of Asian Art

KorinsScreen.webp.story: Waves at Matsushima, a six-panel folding screen in ink, colour and gold leaf. Kōrin takes the famous pine-clad islands off Sendai and flattens them into pattern: hills as lobes of green and copper, waves as endless ribbed curls silvered over a gold sea. There is no horizon to speak of, no weather, no people; the whole thing hums along at the same decorative pitch. Kōrin was copying, loosely, a Tawaraya Sōtatsu composition a century older, and in copying it he defined what came to be called Rinpa.

Kunisada_futamigaura.jpg.title: Futamigaura
Kunisada_futamigaura.jpg.description: Sunrise at Futamigaura by Utagawa Kunisada (1786 - 1865)

source.canonical_title: File:Kunisada futamigaura.jpg

Kunisada_futamigaura.jpg.story: Kunisada rarely worked landscape, and this 1832 view of Futamigaura feels like the pupil of portraitists stretching into something new. The Meoto Iwa — the 'Wedded Rocks' linked by a shimenawa rope — sit centre as tiny worshippers kneel on the shore. What's striking is the sky: black night still hanging at the crown, a prismatic sunrise breaking in hard diagonal rays, a flock of birds thrown across them. It's less Hokusai's patient geometry than a sudden splash of theatre lighting on a sacred site.

Kuniyoshi_Utagawa,_The_arhat_Handaka.jpg.title: hanging scroll, painting
Kuniyoshi_Utagawa,_The_arhat_Handaka.jpg.description: Painting, hanging scroll. Arhat Handaka Sonja: wearing monastic robe with shaven head and large earrings; poking with finger little dragon emanating from begging bowl in middle of rain cloud. Ink and slight colour on paper. Signed and sealed.

source.canonical_title: File:Kuniyoshi Utagawa, The arhat Handaka.jpg
source.permission: © The Trustees of the British Museum, released as CC BY-NC-SA 4.0

Kuniyoshi_Utagawa,_The_arhat_Handaka.jpg.story: A hanging-scroll painting rather than a print — Kuniyoshi in more sober mode, ink on paper with a touch of colour. Handaka is one of the sixteen arhats, disciples of the Buddha, and his usual trick is coaxing a dragon out of his begging bowl. Here the little dragon rises on a curl of rain cloud while the monk, shaven-headed and heavy-eared, pokes at it with one finger like a man testing a flame. Signed and sealed. The looseness of the brush is miles from the tight linework of his warrior prints, and shows Kuniyoshi could drop the bravado when he wanted.

Kuroda-seiki-kohan00-6-1b.jpeg.title: Lakeside

source.canonical_title: File:Kuroda-seiki-kohan00-6-1b.jpeg
source.permission: The author died in 1924, so this work is in the public domain in its country of origin and other countries and areas where the copyright term is the author's life plus 100 years or fewer .
