Kuroda-seiki-kohan00-6-1b.jpeg.story: A woman in a pale blue striped summer kimono sits at the edge of a lake at Hakone, uchiwa fan loose in her hand, looking out at hills the colour of steamed rice. Kuroda had just returned from a decade in France, where he trained with Raphaël Collin and painted outdoors at Grez-sur-Loing, and you can feel that schooling in the cool grey-green palette and soft frontal light. But the subject is unmistakably Japanese: his wife Teruko, the fan, the hot-spring stillness. This picture became one of the founding images of yōga, Japanese Western-style painting.

L'Embarquement_pour_Cythère,_by_Antoine_.title: Pilgrimage to Cythera , so-called The Embarkation for Cythera

source.canonical_title: File:L'Embarquement pour Cythère, by Antoine Watteau, from C2RMF retouched.jpg
source.credit: Retouched from File:L'Embarquement pour Cythere, by Antoine Watteau, from C2RMF.jpg , originally C2RMF: Galerie de tableaux en très haute définition : image page

L'Embarquement_pour_Cythère,_by_Antoine_.story: Elegant couples in silk gather on a wooded hillside to embark — or are they disembarking? — for Cythera, Venus's island of love. Cupids hover in a pink swarm over the water; a garlanded statue of the goddess presides from the right; a barge waits below. Every figure is in mid-turn, mid-gesture, mid-thought, as if the whole company were caught deciding whether to go. Watteau submitted this in 1717 as his reception piece for the Académie, which had to invent a brand-new category — the fête galante — to classify it. He was already coughing badly; within four years he was dead at 36.

L'Enlèvement,_par_Paul_Cézanne,_FWN_59.title: The Abduction

source.canonical_title: File:L'Enlèvement, par Paul Cézanne, FWN 590.jpg

L'Enlèvement,_par_Paul_Cézanne,_FWN_59.story: Painted when Cézanne was twenty-eight, still raw and still under Delacroix's spell, in his friend Émile Zola's Paris house - Zola owned it for years afterward. A massive dark-skinned male carries off a limp pale nude while distant bathers watch. Most scholars read it as Pluto abducting Proserpine from Ovid, though the figures could equally be Hercules rescuing Alcestis. The eroticism and violence are typical of Cézanne's work in these late 1860s years, long before the patient Provençal geometries took over. In 1935 Keynes bought it for £3,500 and left it to King's College, Cambridge.

L'Enlèvement_des_Sabines_–_Nicolas_Pouss.story: Painted 1637-38, on commission from Cardinal Omodei in Rome. Romulus stands on a plinth at left, cloak raised — the signal. His soldiers seize the Sabine women mid-banquet; mothers claw, old men crumple, a child howls. Poussin worked the whole scene out first with little wax figures on a stage-like box, shifting them under candlelight until the bodies locked together. Louis XIV absorbed it into the royal collection in 1685. The Louvre has it under inventory 7290.

L'Ermitage_par_Paul_Berthon_2.jpg.title: The Hermitage

source.canonical_title: File:L'Ermitage par Paul Berthon 2.jpg

L'Ermitage_par_Paul_Berthon_2.jpg.story: An Art Nouveau cover for the Parisian literary review L'Ermitage, printed in the soft, tapestry-like palette Berthon preferred to Mucha's glossy pastels. A red-haired woman in profile leans among enormous lilies, a pearl drop swinging from her headband, a single white star overhead. Everything is flattened into decorative zones — the mossy grille of the background, the striped border up top, the heavy lettering along the bottom. Berthon was Grasset's pupil, and the lithograph shows the master's love of ornament applied to a magazine that needed to look serious.

L'ultimo_bacio_di_Giulietta_e_Romeo.jpg.story: Dawn is breaking over Verona and Romeo has one foot on the balcony rope-ladder, mouth pressed to Juliet's for the last time they'll meet alive. Hayez painted the moment in 1823, when the Veronese lovers were a new Italian fixation, fed by the recent translations of Shakespeare. Juliet's satin slips off the bed; the dog sleeps through it. The painting belongs to the Villa Carlotta on Lake Como.

LE_PORT_DE_ZAANDAM.png.title: LE PORT DE ZAANDAM

source.canonical_title: File:LE PORT DE ZAANDAM.PNG

LE_PORT_DE_ZAANDAM.png.story: Fleeing the Franco-Prussian War and the Commune, Monet spent four months of 1871 holed up in the Dutch town of Zaandam, eight kilometres north of Amsterdam. From the balcony of his room at the Hôtel de Beurs he turned out some two dozen views of the port — this one among them. The sky goes down in broad impasto streaks of orange and yellow; the reflections are thick daubs, water reduced to mosaic. It is a quiet picture painted by a man in political exile, and one of the first where Monet trusts paint itself to do the talking.

La_Bohémienne_endormie.jpg.story: A lion leans over a sleeping Bedouin on a moonlit sand flat, sniffing her striped robe but not — quite — pouncing. Her mandolin lies beside her, a water jar at her feet, and the whole thing floats in that airless clarity Rousseau could conjure without ever leaving Paris. He offered it to his hometown of Laval for 1,800 francs in 1898; the mayor turned it down. It vanished into private hands for decades and resurfaced in 1923; since 1939 it has lived at MoMA in New York.

La_Fornarina_by_Raffaello.jpg.description: Portrait of a Young Woman (La Fornarina, Raphael's mistress) (1518-1519). Oil on wood, 85 × 60 cm (33 × 24 in). Galleria Nazionale d'Arte Antica, Rome

La_Fornarina_by_Raffaello.jpg.story: A photograph of Raphael's painting on the wall of the Galleria Nazionale d'Arte Antica in Rome, gilt frame and all. The sitter, by tradition Margherita Luti, a baker's daughter from Trastevere and Raphael's lover, holds a sheer veil across her body with studied casualness. Look at her left arm: a blue ribbon bears the inscription RAPHAEL VRBINAS, as if she were a work he signed. The picture was on his easel, unfinished, when he died in 1520. The wide pristine frame and the slight glare are Livioandronico2013's photograph; the painting inside is Raphael's.

La_Liberté_guidant_le_peuple_-_Eugène_.story: Gunpowder smoke, a top hat beside a workman's blouse, and a barefoot woman stepping over the dead with a tricolor raised high. Delacroix painted the July Revolution of 1830 the same autumn the paving stones were still being relaid, telling his brother, "If I haven't fought for my country, at least I'll paint for her." The French state bought it, then hid it, wary of its power to incite. The Louvre finished a full restoration in 2024 that lifted decades of yellowed varnish from Liberty's sky.

La_Seine_à_Lavacourt.jpeg.title: The Seine at Lavacourt

source.canonical_title: File:La Seine à Lavacourt.JPG

La_Seine_à_Lavacourt.jpeg.story: Monet had just moved his family from Argenteuil to Vétheuil, a medieval village forty miles down the Seine from Paris, and their rented house looked straight across the water at the hamlet of Lavacourt. Broke, recently widowed by Camille's death that September, he painted the opposite bank obsessively through 1879 — the flat river, the low roofs, the poplar-lined slope. The calm here is deceptive: within months the Seine would freeze solid, then crack open in the great thaw he raced outside to capture.

La_Seine_à_Vétheuil_(Monet).jpg.title: The Seine at Vétheuil

source.canonical_title: File:La Seine à Vétheuil (Monet).jpg
source.credit: Collection Olivier Senn, Taken on 15 May 2019

La_Seine_à_Vétheuil_(Monet).jpg.story: Painted from Monet's studio boat in 1879, the summer after he moved his family from Paris to the village of Vétheuil to cut expenses. He used a tight palette — greys, greens, a little mauve — and stood the canvas tall so sky and water could share equal weight, the sky in soft round dabs, the river in long drawn-out strokes. Dr Georges de Bellio, the Romanian physician who kept Monet afloat through these years, bought it straight from the studio. It's now in the Musée des Beaux-Arts in Rouen, on loan from the Louvre.

La_Visión_de_San_Huberto_por_Jan_Brueghe.title: The Vision of St Hubert
La_Visión_de_San_Huberto_por_Jan_Brueghe.artist: Jan Brueghel the Elder / Peter Paul Rubens

title.nl: Het visioen van de heilige Hubertus
title.ja: 聖フベルトゥスの幻視

La_Visión_de_San_Huberto_por_Jan_Brueghe.story: A friendship painting. Jan Brueghel the Elder laid out the forest, the hounds and the miraculous stag with the crucifix lodged between its antlers; Rubens dropped in the kneeling figure of Hubert, reusing the horse from his own 1603 portrait of the Duke of Lerma. The legend: a young nobleman hunting on Good Friday is stopped cold by the vision and converts on the spot. Finished around 1617-20 in Antwerp, the panel passed to the Marqués de Leganés, who gave it to Philip IV in 1655. Now in the Prado.

La_Yole_-_The_Skiff_-_Renoir.jpg.title: The Skiff

source.canonical_title: File:La Yole - The Skiff - Renoir.jpg

La_Yole_-_The_Skiff_-_Renoir.jpg.story: Two rowers in a startling orange skiff slice across a river so blue it almost hums. Renoir painted it at Chatou on the Seine in 1875, loading the boat with pure chrome orange straight from the tube and setting it against cobalt water, a collision the critics of the day found vulgar. Willows nod on the far bank, a little steam train puffs past a pale bridge, and a sail leans into the breeze. It hangs now in London's National Gallery, bought from Samuel Courtauld's collection in 1982.

La_debacle_-_Monet_w562.jpg.title: The Break-up of the Ice

source.canonical_title: File:La debacle - Monet w562.jpg

La_debacle_-_Monet_w562.jpg.story: The winter of 1879-80 was one of the coldest in European memory. When the Seine finally thawed near Vétheuil, great slabs of ice cracked loose and careened downriver, battering bridges as they went. Monet painted it again and again, maybe twenty canvases in all. Here the floes drift in mauves and pale blues, horizontal shards laid against the vertical shimmer of reflected trees. It's the same motif Monet would chase for the rest of his life, light shifting by the hour. This is one of the earliest runs.

La_famille_Lafitte_(détail).jpg.title: The Laffite Family

source.canonical_title: File:La famille Lafitte (détail).jpg

La_famille_Lafitte_(détail).jpg.story: A cropped detail of one of Rigaud's rare group portraits, showing the Parisian banker Pierre Laffite with his wife and children in the stiff half-light of his Right Bank apartment. Rigaud, newly famous but not yet Louis XIV's painter, kept his usual state-portrait apparatus, the velvet drape, the column, the cascade of lace, but scaled it down for a private client. The full canvas was signed and dated 1694 and hung in the Laffite family home for more than two centuries before entering a French regional museum.

La_grande_piscine_de_brousse.jpg.title: The Great Pool at Bursa

source.canonical_title: File:La grande piscine de brousse.jpg
source.credit: Gérôme, La grande piscine de brousse , leo.jeje , 2011-04-12 11:30

La_grande_piscine_de_brousse.jpg.story: Women drift around an octagonal hot pool under the dome of Yeni Kaplica, the 'New Baths' built in Bursa in 1552. Gérôme had first visited Turkey in 1875, and ten years later he sat down to turn his sketches of the caldarium into the grandest of all his hammam paintings. The bathers themselves were posed and painted back in his Paris studio; the building is drawn from life, the bodies are studio work. Exhibited at the Salon of 1885.

La_route_de_Vétheuil,_effet_de_neige_by_.title: The Road to Vétheuil, Snow Effect

source.canonical_title: File:La route de Vétheuil, effet de neige by Claude Monet.jpg

La_route_de_Vétheuil,_effet_de_neige_by_.story: Another of Monet's effets de neige from the savage winter of 1878–79. The road climbs away from the viewer between snowbanks; a small figure pushes along it under a flat pearl sky. The whites aren't white — they're lilac, pale blue, the faintest pink — mixed on the canvas so snow looks like it's still falling. The painting is now in the Museum of Fine Arts, St. Petersburg, Florida.

Lac_d'Annecy,_par_Paul_Cézanne.jpg.title: Annecy Lake

source.canonical_title: File:Lac d'Annecy, par Paul Cézanne.jpg
source.credit: The Yorck Project (2002) 10.000 Meisterwerke der Malerei (DVD-ROM), distributed by DIRECTMEDIA Publishing GmbH. ISBN : 3936122202 .

Lac_d'Annecy,_par_Paul_Cézanne.jpg.story: Cézanne painted this in 1896 on a summer trip to the Haute-Savoie, grumbling in letters that the view was too conventionally pretty - 'a little like we've been taught to see it in the albums of young lady travellers.' He made only one picture there, and it is this one. The Château de Duingt squats in the middle distance; trees, water and mountain get flattened into interlocking planes of blue, green and ochre. The prettiness loses, the architecture wins. Samuel Courtauld gave it to his institute in 1932.

Landscape_with_Pan_and_Syrinx_by_Sir_Pet.title: River landscape with Pan and Syrinx (Metamorphoses 1:689-713)
Landscape_with_Pan_and_Syrinx_by_Sir_Pet.artist: Jan Brueghel the Younger / Peter Paul Rubens

source.canonical_title: File:Landscape with Pan and Syrinx by Sir Peter Paul Rubens Jan Breughel the Younger.jpg

Landscape_with_Pan_and_Syrinx_by_Sir_Pet.story: Jan Brueghel the Younger's daybook for 1626 records: "Made another piece of Pan and Syrinx, Sig. Rubens did the figures, priced at 120." This is almost certainly it. Ovid tells how the nymph Syrinx, pledged to Diana's chastity, ran from Pan to the river Ladon and begged to be changed into reeds - which Pan then cut and bound into the first panpipe. Rubens paints the grab; Brueghel surrounds it with densely observed foliage and water. Desire gets frustrated and turns into music, just offstage.

Landscape_with_the_Good_Samaritan_-_Remb.title: Landscape with the Good Samaritan

source.canonical_title: File:Landscape with the Good Samaritan - Rembrandt.jpg

title.ja: 善きサマリア人のいる風景

Landscape_with_the_Good_Samaritan_-_Remb.story: One of only about a dozen surviving landscape paintings by Rembrandt, and the parable almost hides inside it. At the left, far from the cracked ruined tower that dominates the sky, a tiny Samaritan is helping the beaten traveller toward an inn; you can miss them entirely on a first look. Storm light, silver-black clouds and a lone rider crossing a bridge do most of the talking. It's dated 1638 and lives at the Princes Czartoryski Museum in Kraków, one of only three Rembrandts in Polish collections.

Landschaft_mit_Kühen_und_Entenjägern_-_G.story: Cows graze at a river's edge; in the middle ground, hunters creep up on ducks. Women milk and pour into copper cans for market. Late Rubens, around 1635, painting his own neighbourhood as a working farm rather than a backdrop for gods. It's in Berlin's Gemäldegalerie.

Landschaft_mit_Turm_-_Gemäldegalerie_Ber.story: Warm evening sun across a wide Brabant landscape, a defensive tower perched on a low hill, a little bridge leading up to it. Rubens painted it near the end of his life, inspired by the countryside around Het Steen, the manor he'd bought in 1635. Berlin's Gemäldegalerie, inv. 776D.

Las_Meninas,_by_Diego_Velázquez,_from_Pr.title: The Maids of Honour

source.canonical_title: File:Las Meninas, by Diego Velázquez, from Prado in Google Earth.jpg
source.credit: The Prado in Google Earth: Home - 7 th level of zoom, JPEG compression quality: Photoshop 8.

Las_Meninas,_by_Diego_Velázquez,_from_Pr.story: The little princess Margarita stands center, stiff in her silver dress, while a maid offers her water and a dwarf kicks the dog. Velázquez paints himself at a huge canvas on the left, looking out at us, or at the king and queen whose reflection floats in the mirror at the back. Nobody has agreed since 1656 on who is watching whom. The painting is 3.18 meters tall and hasn't left the Prado since 1819, except to shelter from the Civil War.

Laurits_Tuxen_-_The_North_Sea_in_stormy_.title: Vesterhavet i storm. Efter solnedgang. Højen

source.canonical_title: File:Laurits Tuxen - The North Sea in stormy weather. After sunset. Højen - Google Art Project.jpg
source.credit: ygHVVTXFanFoYw at Google Cultural Institute , zoom level maximum

Laurits_Tuxen_-_The_North_Sea_in_stormy_.story: No beach, no boats, no people, just water and a sky that's still burning after the sun has gone. Tuxen lived in Skagen, on the northern tip of Denmark, and he planted himself at Højen on the west coast to watch the North Sea throw itself around. The blues and greens of the waves bite against the orange afterglow in the upper half. At 176 by 234 centimetres, it's one of the largest paintings he ever made, finished in 1909.

Le_Bain_Turc,_by_Jean_Auguste_Dominique_.title: The Turkish bath

source.canonical_title: File:Le Bain Turc, by Jean Auguste Dominique Ingres, from C2RMFFXD.jpg
source.credit: This file was derived from: Le Bain Turc, by Jean Auguste Dominique Ingres, from C2RMF.jpg :

Le_Bain_Turc,_by_Jean_Auguste_Dominique_.story: Ingres was 82, inscribed his age on the frame, and cut the canvas from a rectangle into a circle so you feel like you're looking through a peephole. Inside the round: a heap of nude bathers in a dim vaulted hall, a lute player at center with her back arched, steam, coffee cups, a small pool. The central figure is lifted straight from his own Valpinçon Bather of 1808, now turned away from the viewer more than fifty years later. The Louvre acquired it in 1911.

Le_Chapeau_de_Paille_by_Peter_Paul_Ruben.title: Portrait of Susanna Lunden

source.canonical_title: File:Le Chapeau de Paille by Peter Paul Rubens.jpg

title.ja: シュザンヌ・フールマンの肖像

Le_Chapeau_de_Paille_by_Peter_Paul_Ruben.story: The hat isn't straw. An 1823 engraver slapped the name "Le Chapeau de Paille" on it and the mistake stuck — it's actually a wide-brimmed felt beaver, high fashion in the Netherlands of the 1620s. Susanna Fourment was probably newly married to Arnold Lunden when Rubens painted her around 1622-25; she wears a ring and looks about 23. Rubens later married her younger sister Helena. The sidelong glance, the shadow under the brim, the blush — this is probably the painting Gainsborough stood in front of decades later and swore he'd figure out how Rubens lit a face from two directions at once. It hangs in London's National Gallery.

Le_Concert_champêtre,_by_Titian,_from_C.title: Pastoral Concert
Le_Concert_champêtre,_by_Titian,_from_C.artist: Giorgione and/or his disciple Titian (who probably finished the painting after Giorgione's death in 1510).

source.canonical_title: File:Le Concert champêtre, by Titian, from C2RMF retouchedFXD.jpg
source.credit: This file was derived from: Le Concert champêtre, by Titian, from C2RMF retouched.jpg :

Le_Concert_champêtre,_by_Titian,_from_C.story: Two clothed young men ignore two nude women in a golden Venetian meadow while a shepherd watches his flock in the middle distance. One woman tips water from a glass pitcher into a marble wellhead; the other turns, recorder in hand, toward the lute player. The nudes are understood to be invisible muses rather than real company, which is the trick that lets the picture be both lewd and lofty at once. Attribution has ping-ponged between Giorgione and the young Titian for four centuries. Manet borrowed the whole idea for Déjeuner sur l'herbe.

Le_Débarquement_de_la_reine_à_Marseille,.story: Marie de' Medici steps onto French soil at Marseille on 3 November 1600, and Rubens makes sure nobody forgets it. France, in a blue fleur-de-lis cloak, welcomes her with open arms. Fame trumpets overhead. Below, three writhing Nereids and a bearded Triton heave themselves out of the water, as if the sea itself were delivering her. Rubens painted it between 1622 and 1625 for the queen's Luxembourg Palace cycle. Today it hangs in the Louvre's Galerie Médicis, one of 24 panels telling her life as mythology.

Le_Pont_d`_Argenteuil_-_Claude_Monet.jpg.title: The Bridge at Argenteuil

source.canonical_title: File:Le Pont d` Argenteuil - Claude Monet.jpg

title.es: Le Pont d`Argenteuil (El Puente de Argenteuil)

Le_Pont_d`_Argenteuil_-_Claude_Monet.jpg.story: Sailboats crowd the foreground, masts jabbing up into the sky, while the road bridge's stone piers cut hard verticals into the Seine. Monet painted the bridge at Argenteuil seven times in 1874 alone, the year of the first Impressionist exhibition. The water is smooth in front, choppier with reflections further out, and the orange roofs behind play against the blue water in textbook complementary pairs. The canvas hangs in the Musee d'Orsay.

Le_bassin_aux_nymphéas_-_Claude_Monet.jp.title: The Water Lily Pond

Le_bassin_aux_nymphéas_-_Claude_Monet.jp.story: One of four monumental 1919 canvases Monet painted of the same corner of his pond in sequence, each one a little more dissolved than the last. The willow on the bank has vanished; only its reflection remains, a green curtain falling into blue water. Monet was seventy-eight, nearly blind in one eye, and had just refused to let a visiting Duke of Windsor interrupt his afternoon work. This canvas measures about 1 by 2 metres.

Le_havre_muma_monet_fecamp.jpeg.title: Fécamp, seaside

source.canonical_title: File:Le havre muma monet fecamp.JPG

Le_havre_muma_monet_fecamp.jpeg.story: In 1881 Monet returned to the Norman coast of his childhood, staying briefly at Fécamp to paint its chalk cliffs and windswept shore. The wind-torn sea and eroded rock kicked off a decade of coastal work — Pourville, Varengeville, Étretat — but this canvas was the opening shot. Le Havre's MuMa bought it in 1994, the first Monet the municipal museum had been able to afford; even then, a provincial purchase like this was already at the edge of what a public collection could reach.

Lebrun,_Self-portrait.jpg.title: Self-portrait

source.canonical_title: File:Lebrun, Self-portrait.jpg
source.credit: Art Renewal Center old image: from [1]

Lebrun,_Self-portrait.jpg.story: The Uffizi self-portrait, painted in 1790 after Vigée Le Brun fled Paris and stopped in Florence on her way to Rome. Giuseppe Bencivenni Pelli, director of the Uffizi, invited her to join the gallery's famous collection of artists' self-portraits — she was particularly moved by Angelica Kauffmann's nearby — and accepted immediately. She shows herself at the easel, palette in one hand, brush poised in the other, sketching Marie Antoinette in white chalk on the canvas before her. A loyalty oath to the queen she had painted thirty times, made in exile.

Leda_and_the_Swan_by_Jean-Leon_Gerome.jp.title: Leda and the Swan

source.canonical_title: File:Leda and the Swan by Jean-Leon Gerome.jpg

Leda_and_the_Swan_by_Jean-Leon_Gerome.jp.story: The old Greek story goes that Zeus, smitten with Leda, ditched the thunderbolts for feathers and waddled up as a swan. Gérôme gives you the encounter in polished academic marble-skin, the bird all purposeful neck and outstretched wing, Leda reclining with a studied sort of calm. No thrashing, no melodrama, just the moment hanging there. Typical of his late mythologies, which pull classical subjects into an almost photographic stillness. Painted in 1895.

Leda_and_the_Swan_by_Peter_Paul_Rubens_-.story: Leda reclines across a dark bed, one leg folded, the swan's neck pressed along her cheek in an embrace that's somehow both tender and unsettling. Rubens painted the subject twice in quick succession, around 1598 to 1602, working from a lost Michelangelo composition he'd studied from copies. The pose is almost sculptural — a woman turned inside a diagonal of wings and bedsheets. From that union, in the myth, came two sets of twins, including Helen, whose face would launch the ships.

Leda_et_le_cygne_par_Paolo_Veronese_1.jp.title: Leda and the Swan

source.canonical_title: File:Leda et le cygne par Paolo Veronese 1.jpg

Leda_et_le_cygne_par_Paolo_Veronese_1.jp.story: A late, intimate Veronese of a subject Renaissance painters could not leave alone: Zeus, in swan form, pressing against the Spartan queen Leda. From this union, depending which version you believe, came Helen of Troy. Gone is the architectural theatre of the feast pictures; the scale is small, the palette warm gold and rose against the swan's white. The painting entered Cardinal Joseph Fesch's enormous collection - Napoleon's uncle was an omnivorous buyer - and still hangs in the Palais Fesch in Ajaccio, Corsica, one of the odder final addresses for a Venetian nude.

Leighton-Alain_Chartier-1903.jpg.title: Alain Chartier Alternative title: Margaret of Scotland, Dauphine of France, one day discovered Alain Chartier, the poet, asleep. In the prescence of her attendants, she stopped and kissed his lips, saying, "Parce qu'elles avaient dit de si belles choses."

source.canonical_title: File:Leighton-Alain Chartier-1903.jpg

Leighton-Alain_Chartier-1903.jpg.story: The story goes that Margaret of Scotland, passing through a French court around 1428, found the poet Alain Chartier asleep in a chair and kissed him on the mouth. Her scandalized ladies asked how she could kiss so ugly a man. "I did not kiss the man," she said, "but the mouth that has uttered so many beautiful things." Leighton stages the kiss itself: Margaret bent low, the attendants in frozen disbelief, Chartier still oblivious. Exhibited 1903.

Leighton-God_Speed!.jpg.title: God Speed

source.canonical_title: File:Leighton-God Speed!.jpg

Leighton-God_Speed!.jpg.story: A knight in polished plate leans from his saddle; his lady, halfway up a turret step, ties a red sash to his arm. Her maids watch with the careful blankness of people who have seen this scene end both ways. Leighton painted it in 1900, at the high tide of Victorian chivalric nostalgia, and it became one of his most reproduced images. The little dog at the bottom of the stairs is the giveaway that he never took himself too seriously.

Leighton-Stitching_the_Standard.jpg.title: Stitching the Standard

source.canonical_title: File:Leighton-Stitching the Standard.jpg

Leighton-Stitching_the_Standard.jpg.story: A young woman on a castle battlement puts the last stitches into a banner, a black eagle on gold, while her gaze drifts out over the valley to wherever the war actually is. Leighton painted it in 1911, three years before the whole medieval-revival daydream would collide with the Somme. In hindsight the picture feels less innocent than it meant to. Oil on canvas.

Leighton-The_King_and_the_Beggar-maid.jp.title: The King and the Beggar-maid

source.canonical_title: File:Leighton-The King and the Beggar-maid.jpg

Leighton-The_King_and_the_Beggar-maid.jp.story: Tennyson's poem told the old legend in miniature: King Cophetua, bored of princesses, falls for a barefoot beggar girl and crowns her on the spot. Leighton paints the crowning itself. She stands pale and still in her rags while the king's courtiers pretend very hard not to gossip. The throne room is done up in jewel tones and gold leaf, as if the painting itself can't quite believe what's happening. 1898.

Leo_Tolstoy02.jpg.story: Tolstoy at his writing desk in the vaulted room under the eaves at Yasnaya Polyana, quill in hand, the monkish work cell the novelist had chosen in his late ascetic phase. Repin was by then a regular visitor — the two men had met in 1880 and Repin would paint, draw and sculpt Tolstoy dozens of times over the following decades, from plowing the fields barefoot to reading in the forest. This one belongs to a group he made during stays in 1891, and remains the standard image of Tolstoy-at-work. State Tretyakov Gallery, Moscow.

source.canonical_title: File:Les Oceanides Les Naiades de la mer.jpg

Les_Oceanides_Les_Naiades_de_la_mer.jpg.story: Doré, the empire's most in-demand illustrator, wanted to be taken seriously as a painter — so he reached for mythology at mural scale. The sea nymphs drift up through cold green water, and if you follow their gaze to the cliff behind, Prometheus is chained there, liver-bound. It first hung in the Paris salon of Adèle Cassin, a society hostess whose guest lists ran to statesmen and generals, before going to auction at Galerie Georges Petit in 1912.

Les_Soleils,_jardin_du_petit_Gennevillie.story: Caillebotte had bought a house across the Seine from Argenteuil in 1881, and by the mid-1880s he was, in Monet's phrase, a painter-gardener. This tall vertical canvas from around 1885 packs a dense wall of sunflowers along the bottom and presses the house and outbuildings up behind them, flattened in a way that feels borrowed from Japanese prints. The Musee d'Orsay acquired it in 2022 through a tax-payment arrangement. Sunflowers were ornamental novelties at the time; Caillebotte and Monet grew them competitively.

Levé_de_lune_sur_le_Mont_Nanping.jpg.title: Rising moon on the mount Nanping
Levé_de_lune_sur_le_Mont_Nanping.jpg.description: Levé de lune sur le Mont Nanping contemplé par Cao Cao

source.canonical_title: File:Levé de lune sur le Mont Nanping.jpg

Levé_de_lune_sur_le_Mont_Nanping.jpg.story: Another plate from 'One Hundred Aspects of the Moon': the Chinese warlord Cao Cao watches the moon rise over Mount Nanping on the eve of the Battle of Red Cliffs in 208 CE. According to the 'Romance of the Three Kingdoms,' he composed a poem that night and then killed a general who criticized it. Yoshitoshi shows him alone in armor, staring out from a high terrace — no violence, just the pause before disaster. The whole series trades ukiyo-e's usual brothels and actors for this kind of literary, moonlit stillness.

source.canonical_title: File:Lille PdBA monet la debacle.JPG

title.de: Schneeschmelze in Vétheuil, Blick auf Lavacourt
title.fr: La Débâcle à Vétheuil, avec vue sur Lavacourt

Lille_PdBA_monet_la_debacle.jpeg.story: The winter of 1879-80 was one of the coldest on record. The Seine froze to a shelf of ice outside Monet's Vétheuil window, and when it finally gave in early January he raced outdoors in the cold to paint the break-up — the débâcle — as huge floes ground downstream in the weak sun. He produced seventeen canvases of the thaw. This one, now at the Palais des Beaux-Arts in Lille, looks across to Lavacourt on the far bank with pale ice drifting past like wreckage.

Lille_Pdba_rubens_marie_madeleine.jpeg.title: S. Mary Magdalene in Extasy

source.canonical_title: File:Lille Pdba rubens marie madeleine.JPG

Lille_Pdba_rubens_marie_madeleine.jpeg.story: Magdalene thrown back in a swoon of divine love, tears on her cheeks, hair tumbling, an angel gripping her shoulder. Rubens paints her in the standard penitent kit — loose robe, skull, crucifix — but cranks the ecstasy dial to full Baroque. The flesh is heavy, flushed, almost feverish; the upward gaze deliberately teeters on the edge between religious rapture and something earthier. It hangs today at the Palais des Beaux-Arts in Lille, one of several Magdalenes Rubens produced for Counter-Reformation patrons hungry for emotional saints.

Lion_tentant_de_saisir_un_papillon.jpg.title: Lion tentant de saisir un papillon
Lion_tentant_de_saisir_un_papillon.jpg.description: Lion tentant de saisir un papillon , par Jean-Léon Gérôme

source.canonical_title: File:Lion tentant de saisir un papillon.jpg

Lion_tentant_de_saisir_un_papillon.jpg.story: A shaggy lion swipes at a flitting butterfly, and the whole thing is a joke you have to be in on. Gérôme adopted the lion as his personal emblem (his middle name was Léon); Whistler signed his canvases with a tiny butterfly. Paint this, and you have the grouchy French academic snapping at the mischievous American aesthete who kept needling him. The brushwork of the mane is loving; the butterfly, untouchable. Painted in 1889, it now lives at the Carnegie Museum of Art in Pittsburgh.

Little_Red_Riding_Hood_(136547615).jpg.story: From Doré's 1862 illustrations for Perrault's Contes, reprinted everywhere after. The girl and the wolf meet on the path; she looks up wide-eyed and the wolf watches her with the patience of something that already knows how this ends. Doré keeps the forest shadowed and the child lit like a candle — it's the contrast that does the work. Perrault's version ends badly, and Doré never lets you forget it.

title.fr: Londres, le Parlement. Trouée de soleil dans le brouillard

London,_the_Houses_of_Parliament,_Sunlig.story: The French title is Trouée de soleil dans le brouillard — literally, a gap of sunlight in the fog — and that's exactly what Monet painted. A hot yellow wound rips through the murk and lights the Thames in a narrow shaft; the Palace of Westminster stays drowned in violet. Finished and dated 1904, shown at Durand-Ruel that May alongside thirty-six other Thames views. The canvas now hangs in the Musée d'Orsay, where it catches afternoon light almost as dramatically as the scene it depicts.

Los_horrores_de_la_guerra.jpg.story: Mars stomps forward in armor while Venus tries to drag him back; a woman in black, Europa, throws her arms up in grief. A book, a lute, and a mother with a baby go under his boots. Rubens sent this to Ferdinando II de' Medici in 1638 with a letter explaining every figure (rare for him). He was 60, exhausted by a war that had ground on for decades. The painting now hangs at the Palazzo Pitti in Florence.

source.canonical_title: File:Lot and his daughters, by Peter Paul Rubens.jpg

Lot_and_his_daughters,_by_Peter_Paul_Rub.story: Sodom burns offstage while the daughters pour wine into their fleeing father's cup, the plan already in their eyes. Rubens gives Lot the slack face of a man three drinks in and the daughters the calm hands of cooks on a deadline. The painting vanished from public view for more than a century, then surfaced at Christie's in July 2016 and sold for 44.8 million pounds, a house record. It later went on loan to the Met, reunited with its original pendant, Venus and Adonis.

Lot_en_zijn_dochters_Rijksmuseum_SK-A-48.title: Lot and his Daughters
Lot_en_zijn_dochters_Rijksmuseum_SK-A-48.description: Lot and his daughters. Sitting under a tree Lot's daughters are seducing their father. All three figures are depicted naked and sitting or laying on the ground. The daughter on the left is holding a wine jar. Lot is holding a wine-drinking cup in his right hand. Bottom left stands a small table with cheeses and bread. A little dog is sitting by it. In the background on the right Sodom and Gomorra are burning. In front of the fire Lot's wife, who was turned into a pillar of salt, is standing. Behind the tree a fox looks on.

source.canonical_title: File:Lot en zijn dochters Rijksmuseum SK-A-4866.jpeg
source.permission: Public domain

Lot_en_zijn_dochters_Rijksmuseum_SK-A-48.story: A picnic after the apocalypse. Behind the tree Sodom burns orange, Lot's wife is already a pillar of salt, and in the foreground the surviving three share wine and cheese on a blanket. Goltzius, painting in 1616, plays the biblical scandal for all its awkwardness: two daughters, afraid the world's ended for real, get their father drunk to keep the family line going. The contrast between Lot's weathered skin and his daughters' pale ones is almost cruelly precise. A fox watches from the bushes. The Rijksmuseum acquired it in 1988.

Louis-Francois_Bertin.jpg.story: Bertin ran the Journal des débats and was the loudest voice of the liberal-constitutional press under the July Monarchy. Ingres, who hated portrait commissions, struggled for months and reportedly broke down crying because he couldn't find the man's pose. He spotted it by accident: Bertin at an outdoor café, hands planted square on his knees, leaning forward as if about to argue. That's the pose. Rumpled black coat, silvering hair, the grip of a man who owns the conversation. He sat in 1832, aged 66; he lived until 1841.

Louis_XIV_of_France.jpg.story: Louis XIV was sixty-three and wanted a portrait for his grandson in Spain; instead, he kept this one and sent Philip V a copy. The king plants one red-heeled shoe forward, hip cocked, ermine cloak cascading off the shoulder, and lets Rigaud's brush do the propaganda. Every inch advertises absolute monarchy — the gold fleurs-de-lis, the coronation sword Joyeuse, the columns of a temple to kingship. It has hung in the Louvre since 1793, and the ballet-dancer stance has been copied, parodied and memed ever since. Rigaud was paid 40,000 livres.

Louise_Jane_Jopling_(née_Goode,_later_Ro.story: A painter painting a painter. Louise Jopling sat five days in Millais's Palace Gate studio in 1879, a gift from one artist to a friend, commissioned by her husband Joseph. One day she forgot to hold her "tranquil" pose and the look that slipped out she later called her "defiant" face, and that's the one Millais kept. Jopling moved in the same circles as Whistler, who saw the finished canvas at the Grosvenor Gallery in 1880 and pronounced it "superb."

Low_Tide_at_Pourville,_by_Claude_Monet,_.title: Low Tide at Pourville, near Dieppe, 1882
Low_Tide_at_Pourville,_by_Claude_Monet,_.description: This is one of several views Monet painted of the cliffs and sand flats of Pourville, a small fishing village on the Normandy coast of France. The title indicates a momentary stage in the continuous cycle of nature, just as the quick, spontaneous application of paint reflects Monet's efforts to capture shifting effects of light, weather, and tide. The paint layers under the beach indicate that this part of the composition originally depicted water, as would have been appropriate for a depiction of high rather than low tide. Similar changes were made in the clouds during the painting process.

source.canonical_title: File:Low Tide at Pourville, by Claude Monet, Cleveland Museum of Art, 1947.196.jpg

Low_Tide_at_Pourville,_by_Claude_Monet,_.story: Tide out, sand flats exposed, a rim of cliff curving off into blue. Monet started this canvas at high tide in 1882 and then changed his mind — X-ray-like examination shows paint layers where water used to be, clouds rearranged on the fly. The picture is a record of weather-chasing in real time. Quick, wet, improvised. It's been at the Cleveland Museum of Art since 1947, catalogue 1947.196.

Luca_Signorelli_-_Portrait_of_an_Old_Man.title: Portrait of a Man

source.canonical_title: File:Luca Signorelli - Portrait of an Old Man - Gemäldegalerie Berlin.jpg

title.ja: 男の肖像 (シニョレッリ)
title.pt: Retrato de um homem mais velho

Luca_Signorelli_-_Portrait_of_an_Old_Man.story: A man in his sixties, thin-lipped and watchful, in a scarlet berretta and heavy black-and-red robes. Behind him Signorelli builds two little theatres: on the left a group in classical dress seems to be staging a debate or judgement; on the right, nude wrestlers grapple among Roman ruins. Those muscled, near-sculptural bodies are the painter's signature, the same anatomy lesson he would soon unleash across the Orvieto Last Judgment. The sitter's identity is lost, but he paid for something unusual: to be portrayed with the painter's own obsession playing out in miniature behind him.

Lucas_Cranach_-_Der_Jungbrunnen_(Gemäld.title: The fountain of youth

source.canonical_title: File:Lucas Cranach - Der Jungbrunnen (Gemäldegalerie Berlin).jpg

Lucas_Cranach_-_Der_Jungbrunnen_(Gemäld.story: One of Cranach's great late jokes. Old women are carted in from the left — wheelbarrowed, dragged, hobbling — lowered into a rectangular pool, and emerge on the right as fresh young nudes, led off to feast and flirt in a pavilion. Only women need the bath; the implication is that the men are fine as they are. The landscape divides neatly: barren rocks on the crones' side, soft green meadows on the beauties'. Painted the year Luther died, when the artist himself was over seventy, it reads as a wry, slightly rueful meditation on age, desire, and the limits of what paint can promise.

Lucas_Cranach_d.Ä._-_Herkules_und_Atlas.title: Hercules Relieving Atlas of the Globe

source.canonical_title: File:Lucas Cranach d.Ä. - Herkules und Atlas (National Gallery of Art).jpg
source.credit: National Gallery of Art, Washington, D. C., online collection

title.de: Herkules nimmt Atlas die Last der Weltenkugel

Lucas_Cranach_d.Ä._-_Herkules_und_Atlas.story: Atlas has been holding up the sky for eternity and his shoulders have had enough. Hercules, mid-labour, takes over the load while Atlas fetches the golden apples of the Hesperides. Cranach pins the two men in a narrow vertical panel, letting the weight of the celestial globe compress everything downward. A Latin inscription at top-left, SYDEREVM FESSO GESTAT ATLANTE POLVM, notes that a weary Atlas carries the starry pole. The painting dates to around 1537.
Lucas_Cranach_d.Ä._-_Herkules_und_Atlas.year_note: Workshop dating places the composition after 1537; source's 1530 is early.

Lucas_Cranach_d.Ä._-_Simson_bezwingt_de.title: Samson battling with the lion

source.canonical_title: File:Lucas Cranach d.Ä. - Simson bezwingt den Löwen.jpg
source.credit: 1. Web Gallery of Art : Image Info about artwork wga QS:P11807,"s-e.html?/html/c/cranach/lucas_e/06/3samson" 2. nevsepic.com.ua

title.de: Simson im Kampf mit dem Löwen

Lucas_Cranach_d.Ä._-_Simson_bezwingt_de.story: The Old Testament strongman Samson, en route to a wedding, tears a lion apart with his bare hands — later he'll go back and find bees nesting in the carcass, which becomes the riddle that ends his marriage. Cranach gives the episode to us small and close-up: bulging thighs, a startled beast, Samson's face weirdly placid for a man mid-kill. The winged serpent signature sits in the lower left. The panel lives at the Klassik Stiftung Weimar; a smaller private-collection version exists too. Pure Cranach workshop energy — violent myth, dollhouse scale.

Lucas_Cranach_d._Ä._(Werkst.)_-_Moses_un.title: Moses and the Pillar of Cloud
Lucas_Cranach_d._Ä._(Werkst.)_-_Moses_un.artist: Workshop of Lucas Cranach the Elder

source.canonical_title: File:Lucas Cranach d. Ä. (Werkst.) - Moses und die Wolkensäule (nach 1530).jpg
source.credit: 1. M.S. Rau, New Orleans 2. Stockholms Auktionsverk, Stockholm, 7 December 2021, Lot 345 via auctionet

Lucas_Cranach_d._Ä._(Werkst.)_-_Moses_un.story: A small Old Testament panel from Cranach's Wittenberg workshop: Moses in a blue robe gestures toward a tall pillar of cloud rising over the sea at the left, while on the right the Israelites, shown as a tight knot of armored soldiers and a red-clad captain, wait for the signal to march. The pillar guided them by day through the wilderness. It's the kind of small didactic picture the shop turned out steadily for Reformation patrons, Luther's circle having a particular taste for Exodus imagery. Painted some time after 1530 - likely by an assistant working from Cranach the Elder's designs.

Lucas_Cranach_d._Ä._-_Judith_Victorious_.title: Judith with the head of Holofernes

source.canonical_title: File:Lucas Cranach d. Ä. - Judith Victorious - WGA05720.jpg
source.credit: Web Gallery of Art : Image Info about artwork wga QS:P11807,"c/cranach/lucas_e/06/2judith2"

title.es: Judit con la cabeza de Holofernes
title.fr: Judith avec la tête de Holopherne
title.nl: Judith met het hoofd van Holofernes
title.pt: Judite com a cabeça de Holofernes
title.it: Giuditta con la testa di Oloferne
title.de: Judith mit dem Haupt des Holofernes

Lucas_Cranach_d._Ä._-_Judith_Victorious_.story: Judith in a feathered hat and velvet dress, one hand resting casually on a sword, the other on the severed head of Holofernes as if it were a prop on a table. Cranach and his workshop painted at least thirteen of these — all around 1530, all close variants, all cool and courtly rather than gory. The timing lines up with the founding of the Schmalkaldic League: the widow who walked into the enemy's tent and came out with his head became a Protestant symbol of resistance to Charles V. This version is in Vienna.

Lucas_Cranach_d._Ä._044FXD.jpg.title: Portrait of the Elector John Frederic the Magnanimous of Saxony (1503-1554)

source.canonical_title: File:Lucas Cranach d. Ä. 044FXD.jpg
source.credit: This file was derived from: Lucas Cranach d. Ä. 044.jpg :

title.fr: Portrait de l'Électeur de Saxe Jean-Frédéric de Saxe dit le Magnanime
title.de: Porträt des Kurfürsten Johann Friedrich des Großmütigen von Sachsen (1503-1554)
title.da: Portræt af kurfyrst Johan Frederik den Højmodige af Sachsen (1503-1554)

Lucas_Cranach_d._Ä._044FXD.jpg.story: John Frederick the Magnanimous — Cranach's friend, patron and Elector of Saxony — painted here in 1531, the year before he formally inherited the title. Once he did, he promptly commissioned Cranach's workshop to turn out around 120 near-identical electoral portraits to distribute across Saxon courts and allies. The face in all of them was traced from a single master drawing; only the costume and setting really varied. Green ground, half-length, steady gaze, fur collar. A piece of early propaganda from the man who would lead the Protestant Schmalkaldic League into war and, eventually, into defeat.

Lucas_Cranach_d.Ä._-_Adam_und_Eva_(Court.title: Adam and Eve

source.canonical_title: File:Lucas Cranach d.Ä. - Adam und Eva (Courtauld Institute of Art).jpg

Lucas_Cranach_d.Ä._-_Adam_und_Eva_(Court.story: A second 1526 Courtauld Adam and Eve — one of many close variants Cranach and his Wittenberg workshop spun out once they landed on a working formula. Black ground, slim pale bodies, the tree down the centre, the serpent peering from the leaves, Eve passing over the fruit. The same composition recurs in Schwerin, Chicago, the Norton Simon, and private collections on both sides of the Atlantic. Each is slightly different; none is a copy. Cranach had turned Original Sin into a product line, and somehow that didn't hurt the pictures.

Lucas_Cranach_d.Ä._-_Amor_beklagt_sich_b.title: Cupid Complaining to Venus

source.canonical_title: File:Lucas Cranach d.Ä. - Amor beklagt sich bei Venus (National Gallery, London).jpg

title.it: Cupido con un favo di miele
title.ja: ヴィーナスに訴えるキューピッド
title.fr: Vénus avec Cupidon le voleur de miel
title.nl: Venus en Cupido de honing dief
title.es: Venus y Cupido ladrón de miel

Lucas_Cranach_d.Ä._-_Amor_beklagt_sich_b.story: Cupid has stolen a honeycomb and the bees are furious. He runs back to his mother, finger in the air, whining, while Venus stands beside a tree wearing nothing but a jewelled choker and a ridiculous red velvet hat stacked with ostrich feathers. The Latin verse overhead is from the Greek poet Theocritus: pleasure, briefly snatched, comes mixed with pain. Moral served, punchline intact. Cranach painted this version around 1526-27; it's now in the National Gallery, London.

Lucas_Cranach_d.Ä._-_Caritas_(Koninklijk.title: Caritas

source.canonical_title: File:Lucas Cranach d.Ä. - Caritas (Koninklijk Museum v. Schone Kunsten Antwerpen).jpg

Lucas_Cranach_d.Ä._-_Caritas_(Koninklijk.story: Charity in Cranach's hands is a mother besieged: one child at the breast, another tugging at her knee, a third clinging to her shoulder. She stands nude against the usual black ground, serene amid the small riot. The painter turned out Caritas panels repeatedly in the 1530s for Saxon patrons who wanted domestic virtue dressed in Renaissance skin. The children are plump and wriggly, faintly comic. It is a subject that ought to feel pious, and in any other studio probably would, but Cranach's cool linear style pushes it toward something gentler and stranger — tenderness without sentimentality.

Lucas_Cranach_d.Ä._-_Das_Goldene_Zeitalt.title: The Golden Age

source.canonical_title: File:Lucas Cranach d.Ä. - Das Goldene Zeitalter (Nasjonalgalleriet, Oslo).jpg
source.credit: 1. Unknown source Unknown source 2. Nasjonalgalleriet, Presse, aktuelle Utstillinger i Oslo

Lucas_Cranach_d.Ä._-_Das_Goldene_Zeitalt.story: Six naked couples dance, bathe, eat and lounge in a walled paradise — Cranach's riff on the classical Golden Age, the pre-civilisation idyll Hesiod sketched in Works and Days: humans lived carefree, peaceful, godlike. The painter hangs gold chains on the figures like flimsy signifiers of the title and fills the garden with animals and flowering trees. The nudes are stretched thin in his mannered Wittenberg way, bodies more emblem than anatomy. A very similar version hangs in Munich; this one is in Oslo, quietly one of his most beguiling secular pictures.

Lucas_Cranach_d.Ä._-_Das_Martyrium_der_H.title: The Martyrdom of Saint Barbara

source.canonical_title: File:Lucas Cranach d.Ä. - Das Martyrium der Heiligen Barbara.jpg
source.credit: This file was donated to Wikimedia Commons as part of a project by the Metropolitan Museum of Art . See the Image and Data Resources Open Access Policy

title.ja: 聖バルバラの殉教 (クラナッハ)
title.nl: Het martelaarschap van de H. Barbara

Lucas_Cranach_d.Ä._-_Das_Martyrium_der_H.story: Saint Barbara, locked in a tower and eventually beheaded by her own pagan father for refusing to renounce Christianity, kneels here in a gown of cloth-of-gold and turns her face up toward Dioscorus as he lifts the sword. Cranach crushes the figures into a frieze across the foreground, cloudless sky above, the horror treated almost as a courtly event. The coat-of-arms in the picture traces it to the Rem family, wealthy Augsburg merchants. The panel is substantial — over a metre and a half tall — and now hangs at the Met.

Lucas_Cranach_d.Ä._-_Hofjagd_bei_Schloss.title: Hunting near Hartenfels Castle

source.canonical_title: File:Lucas Cranach d.Ä. - Hofjagd bei Schloss Hartenfels.jpg
source.credit: 1./2. The AMICA Library 3. Unknown source Unknown source 4. The Cleveland Museum of Art

Lucas_Cranach_d.Ä._-_Hofjagd_bei_Schloss.story: A stag hunt at full tilt around the moat of Schloss Hartenfels in Torgau, the Elector's residence. Dogs leap, boar crash through the undergrowth, crossbowmen take aim from the bank, and the water churns with trapped deer. Cranach paints the scene from a high vantage so the castle towers frame the slaughter like a stage set. These court-hunt panels were status pieces, recording specific events attended by specific princes — you can pick out the Elector himself among the archers. The mood is festive and slightly horrifying, and the surface reads almost like a tapestry, every twig and antler crisply accounted for.

Lucas_Cranach_d.Ä._-_Klage_unter_dem_Kre.title: Christ on the cross with Mary and John

source.canonical_title: File:Lucas Cranach d.Ä. - Klage unter dem Kreuz, 1503 (Alte Pinakothek).jpg

title.ja: キリストの磔刑 (クラナッハ、ミュンヘン)

Lucas_Cranach_d.Ä._-_Klage_unter_dem_Kre.story: An early Cranach, painted before he moved to Wittenberg, and already a jolt. He spins the Crucifixion ninety degrees: Christ's cross shoved to the right edge, the two thieves at left, Mary and John wedged into the middle looking up. Behind them a Danube landscape opens out — mountains, a lake, a moated castle — lending the scene a strange northern chill. Down at the bottom edge, on a scrap of trompe-l'oeil paper, Cranach paints the date 1503, a small signature flourish on what is arguably the picture that announced him.

Lucas_Cranach_d.Ä._-_Porträt_eines_sächs.title: A Prince of Saxony

source.canonical_title: File:Lucas Cranach d.Ä. - Porträt eines sächsischen Prinzen.jpg
source.credit: National Gallery of Art, Washington, D. C., online collection

Lucas_Cranach_d.Ä._-_Porträt_eines_sächs.story: A small, crisply observed likeness of an unnamed Saxon prince, painted on limewood in oil and tempera. Cranach spent his Wittenberg years producing dozens of these compact court portraits — green or blue-black backgrounds, sharp profile-plus-three-quarter angles, a stare that doesn't entirely commit to the viewer. This one, from 1517, is in the National Gallery of Art in Washington. The sitter's identity has slipped through the record, but he was almost certainly a child of the Ernestine line Cranach served for decades.

Lucas_Cranach_the_Elder_-_Adam_und_Eva_i.title: Adam and Eve in paradise (The Fall)

source.canonical_title: File:Lucas Cranach the Elder - Adam und Eva im Paradies (Sündenfall) - Google Art Project.jpg

Lucas_Cranach_the_Elder_-_Adam_und_Eva_i.story: Cranach painted this scene dozens of times, at least fifty by the end, and this 1533 version sticks to the formula: two slender, almost identical bodies, the serpent coiled in the apple tree, a stag and a lion browsing in uneasy peace, and Eve holding the fruit like she already knows the ending. Cranach's signature, a tiny winged serpent, sits on the trunk with the date. He was court painter in Wittenberg, close friend of Martin Luther, and running one of the most productive workshops in Europe.

Ludwig_Deutsch_-_The_Inspection_-_1883.j.title: The Inspection

source.canonical_title: File:Ludwig Deutsch - The Inspection - 1883.jpg

Ludwig_Deutsch_-_The_Inspection_-_1883.j.story: An early Deutsch, from before his first Egyptian trip, when he was still staging Orientalist scenes largely from studio props and imagination. A figure in elaborate robes examines an object — a weapon, a document — under concentrated light. The surfaces are already doing the heavy lifting: brass, silk, inlaid wood, each rendered with the enamelled precision that would become his trademark. The theatre is complete but slightly airless, the way Paris-studio Orientalism often is. Two years later he would finally reach Cairo, and the tiles and lamps in his paintings would stop being quoted and start being copied from life.

source.canonical_title: File:Ludwig Deutsch - The Nubian Palace Guard.jpg

Ludwig_Deutsch_-_The_Sahleb_Vendor_Cairo.title: The Sahleb Vendor, Cairo

source.canonical_title: File:Ludwig Deutsch - The Sahleb Vendor Cairo, 1886.jpg

Ludwig_Deutsch_-_The_Sahleb_Vendor_Cairo.story: Sahleb is a thick, sweet winter drink made from orchid-root flour, sold hot on Cairo streets at dawn. Deutsch paints the vendor as a monumental figure, his brass urn gleaming, customers waiting in the cool blue shadow of a stone wall. Painted the year after his first trip to Egypt, when everything he was seeing on the street was suddenly material. The tilework behind the vendor, the patinated metal, the rough weave of the robes — all rendered with that slightly unreal sharpness that makes Deutsch's pictures feel less like paintings than preserved specimens. A humble trade, monumentalised.

Ludwig_Deutsch_-_The_Smoker,_1903.jpg.title: The Smoker

source.canonical_title: File:Ludwig Deutsch - The Smoker, 1903.jpg

Ludwig_Deutsch_-_The_Smoker,_1903.jpg.story: A man seated against a tiled wall, drawing on a long pipe, wreathed in the small private cloud that is the whole point of the picture. By 1903 Deutsch had been making paintings like this for nearly twenty years, and the formula was perfected — shallow space, one or two figures, surfaces polished to the point of trompe-l'oeil. The Orientalist market was starting to fade by then, outflanked by photography and a shifting taste in Paris, but Deutsch kept refining. The smoke here is the soft note against all that hard tile and metal, a small painterly indulgence in a picture otherwise built like a jeweller's showcase.

Luisa_Maria_Amelia_Teresa_di_Borbone-Due.title: Maria Luisa di Borbone, Princess of the Two Sicilies

source.canonical_title: File:Luisa Maria Amelia Teresa di Borbone-Due Sicilie V2.jpg

Luisa_Maria_Amelia_Teresa_di_Borbone-Due.story: Painted in Naples in 1790 while Vigée Le Brun was working her way across the courts of Europe as a Revolution exile. Queen Maria Carolina, Marie Antoinette's sister, commissioned portraits of her children, and this one caught seventeen-year-old Maria Luisa just before her August wedding to her cousin Ferdinand, Grand Duke of Tuscany. Signed 'a Naples 1790'. It's a pre-marital document as much as a likeness — half dynastic announcement, half farewell — and still hangs at the Museo di Capodimonte.

Löwenjagd_Peter_Paul_Rubens.jpg.title: Lion Hunt (Oil Sketch); Reverse: Marriage by Proxy (Sketch for the Medici Cycle)
Löwenjagd_Peter_Paul_Rubens.jpg.description: La chasse au lion. Esquisse à l'huile. Alte Pinakothek, Munich

source.canonical_title: File:Löwenjagd Peter Paul Rubens.jpg

MANET_-_Música_en_las_Tullerías_(Nationa.title: Music in the Tuileries.
MANET_-_Música_en_las_Tullerías_(Nationa.description: This painting of the Tuileries Gardens in Paris was Manet's first major work depicting modern city life. The band is playing and a fashionable crowd has gathered to listen. The picture includes portraits of Manet's friends and family. These include Manet himself as well as: Baudelaire - poet (1821 - 1867); Théophile Gautier - poet and novelist (1811 - 1872); Ignace Fantin-Latour - flower-painter (1836 - 1904); Jacques Offenbach (1819 - 1880) - composer; Eugène - the artist's brother (1833 - 1892).

source.canonical_title: File:MANET - Música en las Tullerías (National Gallery, Londres, 1862).jpg

MANET_-_Música_en_las_Tullerías_(Nationa.story: Twice a week the Tuileries Gardens filled up for a concert, and one afternoon Manet showed up with a sketchbook and painted his whole address book into the crowd. Baudelaire leans against a tree. Offenbach is in there. Gautier, Fantin-Latour, Manet's brother Eugène, and Manet himself all appear, the painter cut off by the left edge as if he wandered into his own picture. No central subject, no story, just modern Paris looking at itself. Critics hated it in 1862; it's now called the first true painting of modern life.

MB-Mon-14_Monet_Strada-Romana-in-Bordigh.title: Strada Romana in Bordighera

source.canonical_title: File:MB-Mon-14 Monet Strada-Romana-in-Bordighera.jpg
source.credit: Own work MuseumBarberini Taken on 19 April 2022

MB-Mon-14_Monet_Strada-Romana-in-Bordigh.story: The Strada Romana is the old Roman road threading through Bordighera — narrow, walled, shadowed by orange trees and cypresses. Monet painted it during his three-month 1884 stay, when he cranked out nearly forty Riviera canvases at a fevered clip. Here the road dips between garden walls, a patch of sunlit stucco burning at the end. He wrote Alice he was working 'like a man possessed' and still couldn't keep up with the light.

Ma_Yuan_-_Dancing_and_Singing-_Peasants_.story: Classic Ma Yuan: the mountains shoved against one edge, cliff faces dropping into mist, a long diagonal of pines, and down in the corner a string of peasants dancing their way home along a path. He was nicknamed One-Corner Ma for exactly this kind of composition, where most of the silk is empty and the eye does the rest. Painted at the Southern Song court around 1200, it is also a piece of quiet politics: the emperor likes to see that the peasants are happy. The inscription at upper right is a later imperial hand joining the consensus.

Macke,_August_-_Promenade_-_Google_Art_P.title: Promenade

source.canonical_title: File:Macke, August - Promenade - Google Art Project.jpg
source.credit: nwGW-7U9Uhbm9Q at Google Cultural Institute , zoom level maximum

Macke,_August_-_Promenade_-_Google_Art_P.story: Oil on cardboard, painted in 1913 just after August Macke moved to Hilterfingen on Lake Thun: a man in a summer hat and a woman in a red dress walk along a bridge, faces left blank, the world around them chopped into saturated fields of colour. Macke had just absorbed Robert Delaunay's orphic canvases in Paris and you can see him testing what happens when you give everyday Swiss bourgeoisie the stained-glass treatment. The painting is in the Lenbachhaus in Munich. A year later Macke was dead in Champagne, killed at twenty-seven in the opening weeks of the war.

Macke_-_Seiltänzerin_(1913).jpg.title: The Tightrope Walker

source.canonical_title: File:Macke - Seiltänzerin (1913).jpg

Macke_-_Seiltänzerin_(1913).jpg.story: A tiny tightrope walker in a black leotard crosses a taut diagonal against a wall of lemon, emerald and mustard blocks. In the foreground, hatted spectators are reduced to plum and black silhouettes; a fragment of pink-and-yellow striped circus tent hangs overhead. The whole thing is stitched from flat coloured facets that feel lifted from Delaunay, whom Macke had visited in Paris the year before. Painted in 1913, a year before he was killed at 27 in the first weeks of the war in Champagne.

Madame_Monet_au_canapé_Monet_1871.jpg.story: Camille Doncieux, Monet's first wife, sunk into a sofa with a book. Painted around 1871, shortly after the London-and-Holland exile of the Franco-Prussian War. She's only 23 or 24 here; she'd die at 32 in 1879. The touch is unusually tender for Monet, who rarely painted interiors. Oil on canvas, 48.2 by 74.5 cm, Musee d'Orsay, Paris.

Madame_X_(Madame_Pierre_Gautreau),_John_.story: Virginie Amelie Avegno Gautreau was Louisiana-born, Paris-married, and famous for powdering her skin a pale lavender. Sargent chased her for months before she sat. When he finally showed the portrait at the Salon of 1884 under the alias 'Portrait de Mme ***,' the one jeweled strap slipping off her right shoulder read as a nightgown falling open - the crowd jeered, her mother begged him to withdraw it, and Sargent painted the strap back up onto her shoulder after the exhibition closed. He kept the canvas in his studio for over thirty years. 'I suppose it is the best thing I have done,' he finally wrote when the Met bought it in 1916.

Madeleine_undressing_–_Eve_of_St_Agnes,_.title: Eve of St Agnes

source.canonical_title: File:Madeleine undressing – Eve of St Agnes, John Everett Millais.jpg

title.fr: Madeleine se déshabillant – Vigile de la Saint Agnès

Madeleine_undressing_–_Eve_of_St_Agnes,_.story: Madeline undressing in winter moonlight, straight out of Keats's stanza XXVI, the chill silvering down across her shift like light through stained glass. Millais worked the scene on the spot at Knole in Kent, chasing an effect critics praised for its "silvery-green tones." It caused a fuss at the Royal Academy in 1863, but the fuss won him his full Academician's seat, shared with that year's other Millais hit, My First Sermon. No candle, no visible saint, just cold light and a girl paused mid-gesture.

Madonna-and-child-Gentileschi.jpg.title: Virgin with the Child

source.canonical_title: File:Madonna-and-child-Gentileschi.jpg

Madonna-and-child-Gentileschi.jpg.story: Painted around 1613, a year after the trial of Agostino Tassi and Artemisia's move from Rome, now at the Galleria Spada. The Virgin sits on a plain wooden chair in a deep pink dress, eyelids heavy, head tilted as if she's nearly dozing off; the Child, wide awake, turns and presses his left hand against her cheek. It is an unusually tired, domestic Madonna - the weight of early motherhood written into her half-closed eyes. A near-identical composition exists at the Pitti; scholars now regard the Spada picture as the stronger autograph version.

Male_Nude_-_Edgar_Degas.jpg.title: Male Nude
Male_Nude_-_Edgar_Degas.jpg.description: Male Nude Artist: Edgar Degas (French, Paris 1834–1917 Paris) Date: 1856 Medium: Oil on canvas Dimensions: 13 3/4 x 24 1/4 in. (34.9 x 61.6 cm) Classification: Paintings Credit Line: Gift of Philip and Catherine Korsant, 2007 This unfinished picture dates to Degas’s early years as an art student in Paris. Rather than using a fresh canvas, he painted the nude on top of another figure study, which is partially visible underneath. The toes and foot of the earlier figure—possibly the same model—may be seen in the lower left corner, just below the male nude’s head, while his bearded face appears in the area of the reclining nude’s foot.

Marc,_Franz_-_The_Tiger_-_Google_Art_Pro.story: A tiger coiled out of crystal shards. Marc painted it in March 1912, at the height of his Blaue Reiter years, breaking the animal into cubic facets of yellow, green, and violet so it reads less like a beast than a geological event. The stare is what holds you - two hard yellow eyes fixed through the geometry. It hangs at the Lenbachhaus in Munich; Marc would be dead at Verdun four years later.

Maria_Cristina_by_Élisabeth_Vigée.jpg.story: Another Naples commission from Queen Maria Carolina, painted around 1790 while Vigée Le Brun was in residence and turning out portraits of the royal children. Maria Christina, about eleven, stands in a garden in a white dotted dress with a red sash, one hand reaching toward a rose on its bush. The formula — child, flower, soft Neapolitan light — is one the artist used often, but it suits this sitter: she would later marry into the Savoy line and become Queen of Sardinia. Still at Capodimonte.

Maria_de_Tassis,_by_Anthony_van_Dyck.jpg.story: Painted in Antwerp around 1629-1630, between Van Dyck's Italian years and his move to London, now in the Princely Collections in Vaduz-Vienna. Maria was eighteen or so, from the Antwerp branch of the Bergamo-born de Tassis family who had built Europe's first postal network and held the hereditary title of Imperial Postmaster. She stands in a silver-grey satin gown, a huge ostrich-feather fan in her right hand, a wide Flemish lace collar framing the small, cautious smile. The fan's texture shows Van Dyck's Titian-soaked handling. She died in 1638, not yet thirty.

Maria_omringd_door_heiligen_-_Rubens.jpg.title: Virgin with Child and saints
Maria_omringd_door_heiligen_-_Rubens.jpg.description: Maria omringd door heiligen , schilderij in de grafkapel van Peter Paul Rubens (Sint Jacobskerk te Antwerpen)

source.canonical_title: File:Maria omringd door heiligen - Rubens.jpg

title.pt: A Virgem e o Menino com Santos

Maria_omringd_door_heiligen_-_Rubens.jpg.story: Rubens painted this altarpiece for his own funeral chapel at Sint-Jacobskerk in Antwerp, where he'd be buried two years later. The Virgin sits enthroned surrounded by saints, and the figures are his family in disguise: his first wife Isabella as Mary Magdalene, Helene Fourment as Martha, his father as Saint Jerome. A final family portrait dressed up as a holy conversation. The panel has never left the chapel it was made for.

Marie_Buloz_Pailleron_A28390.jpg.title: Marie Buloz Pailleron (Madame Édouard Pailleron)

source.canonical_title: File:Marie Buloz Pailleron A28390.jpg

Marie_Buloz_Pailleron_A28390.jpg.story: Sargent was 23 and still building his name in Paris when he painted Marie Buloz Pailleron at her family's country house in the Ain. She was the wife of the playwright Édouard Pailleron and daughter of the publisher of the Revue des Deux Mondes, and the sittings reportedly dragged on miserably outdoors in variable light. The result is pure early Sargent: a dark dress against a tangle of green, a direct gaze, the hands loose and alive. It was shown at the Salon of 1880.

Market_Scene_on_a_Quay_-_Frans_Snyders_a.title: Market Scene on a Quay - Frans Snyders and Workshop - Google Cultural Institute
Market_Scene_on_a_Quay_-_Frans_Snyders_a.description: Market Scene on a Quay . circa 1635-1640. Frans Snyders and Workshop. Oil on canvas. 79 5/16 x 135 in. (201.5 x 342.9 cm). North Carolina Museum of Art via Google Cultural Institute.

source.canonical_title: File:Market Scene on a Quay - Frans Snyders and Workshop - Google Cultural Institute.jpg

Market_Scene_on_a_Quay_-_Frans_Snyders_a.story: Over eleven feet of quayside commerce. Crates of fish, slabs of meat, towers of fruit, and arguing vendors sprawl across a canvas wide enough to swallow a wall. Snyders ran one of Antwerp's busiest workshops, and you can feel the assembly line: the boar carcass, the lobsters, the sweating cheeses, each painted by a specialist hand. Painted circa 1635-1640, it now hangs at the North Carolina Museum of Art at 201.5 by 342.9 cm.

MarktJaffaGustavBauernfeind1887.jpg.title: Market at Jaffa
MarktJaffaGustavBauernfeind1887.jpg.description: Gustav Bauernfeind: Market at Jaffa , 1877 painting

source.canonical_title: File:MarktJaffaGustavBauernfeind1887.jpg

MarktJaffaGustavBauernfeind1887.jpg.story: A busy morning on the Jaffa waterfront: camels, porters, a blue-tiled minaret, merchants haggling in striped robes under the Mediterranean glare. Bauernfeind was trained as an architect in Stuttgart, and you can feel it in the drafted precision of every arch and tile. He made repeat trips to Palestine through the 1870s and 80s before settling in Jerusalem for good. A later version of this subject fetched over four million pounds at Sotheby's and made him, posthumously, Germany's most expensive Orientalist.

source.canonical_title: File:Martin Schongauer - Christ Bearing His Cross - Google Art Project.jpg
source.credit: HQGtPypGGry5Rw at Google Cultural Institute , zoom level maximum

Martin_Schongauer_-_Christ_Bearing_His_C.story: Not a painting but an engraving, and when Schongauer cut it around 1475 the copperplate was the largest anyone had ever attempted. Look at the crush: soldiers, mourners, horses, a dog underfoot, Simon of Cyrene reaching for the crossbeam, Christ turning to Veronica. Schongauer leaned on a lost Jan van Eyck composition for the bones of the scene but filled it with his own wiry, nervous line. Durer studied impressions of it obsessively as a teenager. Over a hundred figures fit on a single sheet roughly 28 by 43 centimeters.

Martin_Schongauer_-_Nativity_-_WGA21041..story: A Nativity squeezed into the ruin of a stone shed, ox and ass peering over the manger, Joseph hovering with his candle. Schongauer works in engraving's small scale the way other artists work in altarpieces — every fold of drapery, every brick, every wisp of straw is given its own line. The Virgin kneels in adoration, hands pressed together, while the Child radiates small rays onto the straw. It is intimate and slightly stiff, in the best late-Gothic way, and the technical control is astonishing: you can read the weight of each garment and the age of each stone from the hatching alone.

Martin_Schongauer_-_The_Holy_Family_-_Go.title: The Holy Family

source.canonical_title: File:Martin Schongauer - The Holy Family - Google Art Project.jpg
source.credit: JgEImTKh_ZlKTA at Google Cultural Institute maximum zoom level

Martin_Schongauer_-_The_Holy_Family_-_Go.story: A tiny oil panel, only 17 by 26 centimeters, barely bigger than a postcard. Mary sits on a tuft of grass nursing the Christ child while Joseph hovers with a walking staff, the whole scene backed by a loose Rhenish landscape. Schongauer spent his life cutting copperplates, and the brushwork here is close to his burin: tight contours, miniaturist patience, flesh modeled with Netherlandish glazes borrowed from van Eyck and Rogier. Only a handful of paintings by him survive. The Kunsthistorisches in Vienna picked this one up in 1865.

Mary_Cassatt_-_The_Child's_Bath_-_Google.title: The Child’s Bath

source.canonical_title: File:Mary Cassatt - The Child's Bath - Google Art Project.jpg

Mary_Cassatt_-_The_Child's_Bath_-_Google.story: Seen from above, which almost no Western painter did before Cassatt studied Japanese woodblock prints in Paris in 1890. A woman in a striped dress washes a small girl's feet in a painted basin; the child's plump leg dangles, a hand rests on the mother's knee. The tilted floor, the cropped pitcher, the flattened pattern on pattern on pattern — all pure ukiyo-e, rerouted through Impressionist color. Cassatt finished the picture in 1893. It's been at the Art Institute of Chicago since 1910.

Mary_Cassatt_-_The_Tea_-_MFA_Boston_42.1.title: Five O'Clock Tea

source.canonical_title: File:Mary Cassatt - The Tea - MFA Boston 42.178.jpg

Mary_Cassatt_-_The_Tea_-_MFA_Boston_42.1.story: Two women in a Philadelphia drawing room, one a guest still in her bonnet, the other Cassatt's sister Lydia, silent behind a silver tea service that catches every lamp in the room. Cassatt painted it in Paris in 1880 from memory of her family's American parlors. The striped wallpaper and flowered mantel crowd the sitters into the lower half of the canvas; the teapot, not the faces, is the picture's true portrait. Degas praised it. The MFA Boston has held the canvas since 1942.

Mary_Stevenson_Cassatt,_American_-_Woman.title: Woman with a Pearl Necklace in a Loge
Mary_Stevenson_Cassatt,_American_-_Woman.artist: Mary Stevenson Cassatt, American, 1844 - 1926 (1844 - 1926) – Artist/Maker (American) Born in Alleghney City, Pennsylvania, United States. Died in Le Mesnil-Théribus, France. Details on Google Art Project

Mary_Stevenson_Cassatt,_American_-_Woman.story: Lydia Cassatt again, this time perched in a red plush box at the Paris Opera, gaslight bouncing off her pearls and pinking her cheeks. Behind her, a vast mirror flattens the rest of the auditorium into a blur of other boxes and other women watching. Mary Cassatt submitted it to the fourth Impressionist exhibition in 1879, her debut with the group; Degas had pushed her to join. Critics singled it out. The Philadelphia Museum of Art acquired it in 1978.

Masked_Ball_at_the_Opera_(1873)_Edouard_.title: Masked Ball at the Opera

source.canonical_title: File:Masked Ball at the Opera (1873) Edouard Manet (National Gallery of Art, Washington D.C.).jpg

Masked_Ball_at_the_Opera_(1873)_Edouard_.story: Twenty-three black top hats jostle in a narrow frieze while five masked women work the crowd and a showgirl's legs dangle from the balcony above, cut off at the thigh. Manet sketched the scene at the old opera house on rue Le Peletier during a Lenten masked ball in spring 1873; the building burned down later that year. He finished the canvas in his studio. The 1874 Salon rejected it as too naturalist. It now hangs at the National Gallery of Art in Washington.

Matsue,_Izumo_(5765901488).jpg.title: Matsue, Izumo (5765901488)

Matsue,_Izumo_(5765901488).jpg.story: Matsue by crescent moon, from Souvenirs of Travel III (1924). Matsue sits on a lagoon in Izumo, the old province thick with shrine mythology, and Hasui gives it the dreamy treatment the place invites: dark water, silhouetted roofs, that sliver of moon doing the light work. He is a night painter at heart, and Matsue — with its castle and its fishing lights — was made for him.

Matteo_Ripa001_-_Morning_Glow_on_the_Wes.title: Matteo Ripa001 - Morning Glow on the Western Ridge
Matteo_Ripa001_-_Morning_Glow_on_the_Wes.description: Copper plate print from "Imperial Production of Illustrated Poetry on the Summer Mountain Retreat" (御製避暑山莊詩圖). The image is a view of the Chengde Mountain Resort built by Emperor Kangxi near Chengde. Width 28 cm, Height 45 cm. Located in the National Palace Museum, Taipei.

source.canonical_title: File:Matteo Ripa001 - Morning Glow on the Western Ridge.jpg
source.credit: Scan from "New Visions at the Ch'ing Court"

Matteo_Ripa001_-_Morning_Glow_on_the_Wes.story: An Italian missionary, asked by the Kangxi emperor to engrave views of the imperial retreat at Chengde, made the first copperplate prints ever produced in China. This one shows dawn breaking over a lake, sun-rays stabbing from the left, a pavilion on stilts at the water's edge. The horizontals in the sky are pure European etching grammar; the pine clumps and folded hills are pure Chinese landscape. Ripa was learning both languages at once, and the seams show. He took the technique home in 1723, and Naples soon had the first school of Chinese studies in Europe.

Max_Schmitt_in_a_Single_Scull.jpg.title: The Champion Single Sculls (Max Schmitt in a Single Scull)

source.canonical_title: File:Max Schmitt in a Single Scull.jpg
source.permission: For background information, see the explanations on Non-U.S. copyrights . Note: This tag should not be used for sound recordings.

Max_Schmitt_in_a_Single_Scull.jpg.story: Eakins painted his old schoolmate Max Schmitt on the Schuylkill in October 1871, just after Schmitt won the Philadelphia single-sculls championship. A second sculler in the middle distance, glancing out at us from his own boat, is Eakins himself. This was his first major rowing picture and you can feel the care: the reflections worked out with near-architectural precision, the Girard Avenue Bridge diagrammed stroke by stroke, the low autumn light catching one side of the yellow hull. Sport painting treated as seriously as a history picture.

MedusaRubens.jpg.title: Head of Medusa

source.canonical_title: File:MedusaRubens.jpg
source.credit: 1. Moravská Galerie v Brně 2. schwerin-news.de 3. Web umenia, on-line katalóg

MedusaRubens.jpg.story: Severed and still twitching, Medusa's head lies flung across a rock, the eyes rolled, the mouth open, and a whole writhing riot of snakes spilling from her skull onto the stone. Lizards and a scorpion scuttle in for good measure. The snakes, art historians now agree, were not Rubens at all — they're by his frequent collaborator Frans Snyders, the great painter of animals and still life. Dated around 1617 to 1618, it lives at the Kunsthistorisches Museum in Vienna, where viewers still flinch at the scorpion before they flinch at the head.

Mehmet_Alí,_pachá_de_Egipto,_por_David_W.title: His Highness Muhemed Ali, Pacha of Egypt
Mehmet_Alí,_pachá_de_Egipto,_por_David_W.description: This is a portrait of the Albanian Khedive (ruler) of Egypt, Muhammad Ali (1769–1849). He was a commander in the Ottoman army and had seized power after a civil war. Muhammad Ali oversaw dramatic reforms of Egyptian military, economy and culture. He commissioned this work from Wilkie. Here, he presents himself in traditional Islamic dress but sitting in a European chair and wearing a fez rather than the traditional turban. Wilkie met Muhammad Ali in Egypt on his return journey from travels in the Middle East. This was Wilkie’s last painting, he fell ill and died on his journey back to Britain.

Mehmet_Alí,_pachá_de_Egipto,_por_David_W.story: Wilkie painted this in Alexandria in the spring of 1841, waiting for a ship home from his Holy Land travels. Muhammad Ali, the Albanian-born ruler who had remade Egypt's army and economy, commissioned the portrait himself and posed in traditional robes but on a European chair, with a fez in place of a turban — a careful self-image of modernising power. Wilkie never finished the voyage back. He fell ill and was buried at sea off Gibraltar. This was his last painting; it now hangs at Tate Britain.

Menter_by_Repin.jpg.story: Sophie Menter was Liszt's favourite pupil, the first woman professor at the St Petersburg Conservatory, and a virtuoso famous across Europe for a thunderous left hand. Repin caught her in 1887, in Petersburg, during her ten-year stint teaching there. She sits very upright, a faint smile, hair severely pinned — nothing of the stage about her in repose. Repin's brush loosens around the lace at her throat, tightens on the alert, amused eyes. Menter would later co-write a Hungarian rhapsody with Tchaikovsky. The portrait remained in private Russian collections for decades.

Menzel_Adolph_Frederick_the_Great_at_Lis.story: December 1757. Frederick the Great has just routed an Austrian army at Leuthen and ridden ahead to Lissa castle, only to walk straight into a stairwell full of enemy officers who'd been billeted there. The line Menzel hangs the picture on — Bonsoir, messieurs, j'espere qu'on me fait place — comes from the anecdote: the king nods, the Austrians freeze. Menzel stages it at the moment of recognition, candlelight catching the gold braid, everyone a half-second behind. He'd spent twenty years by then drawing Frederick; this is one of his last full history paintings before he let modern Berlin take over.

Menzels_Schwester_Emilie_im_Schlaf_(ca._.title: Menzel's sister Emilie, sleeping

source.canonical_title: File:Menzels Schwester Emilie im Schlaf (ca. 1848) Adolf Friedrich Erdmann von Menzel (Hamburger Kunsthalle).jpg
