Menzels_Schwester_Emilie_im_Schlaf_(ca._.story: Menzel's sister Emilie shared his Berlin flat for most of his working life, and he drew and painted her constantly — washing, reading, dozing in a chair. Here she's simply asleep, head tipped onto her shoulder, in oil on paper laid down on canvas, barely two feet across. No symbolism, no story: just the weight of a head on a cushion, the slack of an exhausted face. It reads like a sketch someone forgot to finish, which is exactly why it survives as one of the most intimate things he ever made. Hamburger Kunsthalle, catalogued HK-1267.

Michelangelo_Caravaggio_020.jpg.story: This is the Hermitage Lute Player, the more polished of the two versions, on a bare marble tabletop instead of a carpet. A violin and bow lie ready on one side, a cluster of flowers and split fruit on the other; the madrigal on the open book is by Jacques Arcadelt, a love song. The boy's lips are parted mid-phrase. Del Monte commissioned it, hung it in his palazzo, and later Vincenzo Giustiniani — who owned the other version — apparently liked it enough to want one of his own.

Michelangelo_libyan.jpg.story: A red-chalk study for the Libyan Sibyl on the Sistine ceiling, around 1511. Michelangelo worked out the twisting pose from a male studio model, then painted the figure as a woman high above the altar. You can see him testing the torso over and over, the great diagonal of the shoulders, the foreshortened toe, close-ups of the left hand and the profile head. The paper is worn and foxed; his initials are scrawled along the bottom. Drawings like this are where the ceiling was actually invented. Metropolitan Museum of Art, New York.

Mikhail_Nesterov_001.jpg.title: Vision of Youth Bartholomew
Mikhail_Nesterov_001.jpg.description: one of a series of works depicting the acts of the Venerable St Sergius of Radonezh (c.1321-91), baptised Bartholomew or Varfolomei, shown here encountering a monk who helps him learn to read by sharing a piece of holy bread

source.canonical_title: File:Mikhail Nesterov 001.jpg

Mikhail_Nesterov_001.jpg.story: A pale boy in a peasant tunic stares up at a black-robed monk who has materialised by a tree in an autumn meadow. This is the young Bartholomew, future Saint Sergius of Radonezh, receiving the gift of literacy in the form of a piece of blessed bread. The landscape — thin birches, ripening rowan, a distant wooden church — is Nesterov's invention of a specifically Russian sacred countryside, and it became a template for a generation. The boy's huge, earnest eyes and the monk's shadowy stillness gave the picture its icon-like charge. Shown in 1890, it launched Russian Symbolism almost single-handedly.

Mikhail_Nesterov_009.jpeg.title: The Hermit

source.canonical_title: File:Mikhail Nesterov 009.jpeg

Mikhail_Nesterov_009.jpeg.story: An old man in black monastic robes walks alone along the edge of a still northern lake, a cat-like creature trotting at his feet. This was Nesterov's breakthrough subject — the Russian pustynnik, the forest hermit — and the painting that announced him to Moscow at twenty-six. The landscape does most of the work: bare birches, cold pale water, a sky going the colour of tin. The figure is small and tired, absorbed in his own quiet. Nesterov was looking for something specifically Russian and specifically spiritual, and he found it here, in a mood halfway between melancholy and peace. Tretyakov bought it off the easel.

Millais,_John_Everett_(Sir)_-_Pizarro_Se.title: Pizarro Seizing the Inca of Peru
Millais,_John_Everett_(Sir)_-_Pizarro_Se.artist: Millais, John Everett (Sir) (1829 - 1896) – artist Details on Google Art Project

source.canonical_title: File:Millais, John Everett (Sir) - Pizarro Seizing the Inca of Peru - Google Art Project.jpg
source.credit: ZgEnAhLJz5AJNA at Google Cultural Institute maximum zoom level

Millais,_John_Everett_(Sir)_-_Pizarro_Se.story: Millais was sixteen when he finished this in 1846 — still at the Royal Academy Schools, three years shy of founding the Pre-Raphaelite Brotherhood. The subject is 1532, the moment Francisco Pizarro hauls Atahualpa off his throne at Cajamarca. The teenager piled on everything a Victorian audience wanted: plumed helmets, terrified virgins, a toppled idol, a priest brandishing a crucifix. The drawing is confident; the politics are pure empire. It now hangs at the V&A in London.

Millais_-_Das_Tal_der_Stille.jpg.title: The Vale of Rest

source.canonical_title: File:Millais - Das Tal der Stille.jpg

Millais_-_Das_Tal_der_Stille.jpg.story: Two nuns in a twilight burial ground: one heaves a shovel of earth, the other sits ringed with funeral wreaths, a rosary hung with a tiny skull draped at her waist. She stares straight at you, unblinking. Millais said the idea came on his honeymoon with Effie in 1855, and he started it in her family's Perth garden. The subtitle, "Where the weary find repose," he lifted from a Mendelssohn part-song his brother was humming around the house. It ended up his own favourite of everything he painted.

Millais_-_Überfahrt_nach_Nordwest.jpg.title: The North-West Passage

source.canonical_title: File:Millais - Überfahrt nach Nordwest.jpg

Millais_-_Überfahrt_nach_Nordwest.jpg.story: An old sailor sits jaw-set in an eighteenth-century armchair, a Union Jack bunched behind him, his daughter reading aloud from a logbook at his knee. The subtitle Millais exhibited with it, "It might be done, and England should do it," was the patriotic rallying cry the old man seems to growl at you. The model is Edward John Trelawny, Shelley's old friend; Effie Millais coaxed him into sitting by agreeing to attend the Turkish bath he was promoting. Henry Tate bought it in 1888 for £4,930.

Millais_Order_of_Release.jpg.title: The Order of Release 1746

source.canonical_title: File:Millais Order of Release.jpg
source.credit: Transferred from en.wikipedia to Commons by Mattis . Original uploader was Paul Barlow

title.th: คำสั่งปล่อย

Millais_Order_of_Release.jpg.story: A Jacobite rebel, just freed from an English prison after the 1745 rising, falls into the arms of his Highland wife. She has his release papers crumpled in her hand; a collie presses against his knee and a sleeping child slumps on her shoulder. The model for the wife was Effie Ruskin, still married to the critic John Ruskin when she sat. By the time Millais showed the picture at the Royal Academy in 1853, they were in love; a year later her marriage was annulled and she married Millais. Tate Britain.

Moitessier_(Ingres,_1851)_NGA.jpg.title: Portrait of Madame Moitessier

source.canonical_title: File:Moitessier (Ingres, 1851) NGA.jpg
source.credit: National Gallery of Art, Washington, D. C., online collection

Moitessier_(Ingres,_1851)_NGA.jpg.story: This is the standing Moitessier, the one Ingres knocked out in a few months in 1851 after dragging his feet for years on the seated version. Inès Moitessier poses against violet damask in a black Chantilly lace gown, a red shawl folded over her arm, a small bouquet of violets at her waist. She looks straight at you, calm, rich, entirely aware of the effect. Ingres called her beauty junonienne, Juno-like. She's at the National Gallery in Washington.

Monet,_Claude,_Houses_of_Parliament,_Sea.title: The Houes of Parliament, Seagulls
Monet,_Claude,_Houses_of_Parliament,_Sea.description: Escaping the Franco-Prussian War , Monet moved to London in the fall of 1870 and stayed until the summer of 1871. Fascinated by the fog, he attempted to capture an atmosphere suffused with moisture, dissolving the distinctions between sky, buildings, and water. During three trips to London between 1899 and 1901, Monet painted many such views. He continued to paint these scenes from photographs when he returned home, eventually producing around one hundred works in all. His favorite sites were on the Thames River: Charing Cross Bridge, Waterloo Bridge, and the Houses of Parliament. -Gallery label from the Princeton University Art Museum

Monet,_Claude,_Houses_of_Parliament,_Sea.story: Gulls wheel across a pearl-gray sky; the Palace of Westminster looms as a single bruised silhouette. Monet first saw London as a refugee from the Franco-Prussian War in 1870 and fell for its fogs; he came back three times between 1899 and 1901 to paint them properly. This canvas, dated 1903, was finished from photographs and memory at Giverny — he wasn't embarrassed about using the camera, just about admitting it. The Princeton University Art Museum now owns it, part of the haul William Church Osborn gathered in the early twentieth century.

Monet,_Claude_-_Hut_in_Trouville,_Low_Ti.title: The Hut in Trouville, Low Tide

source.canonical_title: File:Monet, Claude - Hut in Trouville, Low Tide, the (1881).jpg

Monet,_Claude_-_Hut_in_Trouville,_Low_Ti.story: A customs hut on the Trouville shore at low tide, the sand stretching out in wet blondes and the sea a thin blue line beyond. Monet only managed a short trip to Trouville in late August 1881; he wrote to Durand-Ruel on September 13 complaining that bad weather had driven him home almost empty-handed. This one escaped. The real subject isn't the hut at all, it's the water glazing the sand, the horizon so faint you could miss it. Now at the Thyssen-Bornemisza in Madrid.

Monet,_Pond-at-Montgeron.jpg.story: Ernest Hoschedé, a department-store financier, commissioned four big decorative canvases for the round salon of his Montgeron château. This is one of them: a lily-dabbed pond with the barely-there silhouette of a woman holding a fishing rod in the middle distance. That woman is almost certainly Alice Hoschedé, Ernest's wife, who a few years later, after Ernest's bankruptcy, would move in with the Monets and eventually become Monet's second wife. The canvas is huge, nearly two metres across, and now hangs at the Hermitage in Saint Petersburg.
Monet,_Pond-at-Montgeron.jpg.year_note: Commissioned by Ernest Hoschedé as one of four decorative panels for his Montgeron château; consistently dated 1876 by the Hermitage and catalogue raisonné.

Monet-Barque-Marmottan.jpg.title: The Boat

source.canonical_title: File:Monet-Barque-Marmottan.jpg

Monet-Barque-Marmottan.jpg.story: A moored boat, empty, half-swallowed by the reeds. Monet painted this on the Epte near Giverny during a summer when he was obsessed with boats and the strange optics of water plants. No figures, no drama — just the hull sitting in a tangle of green, the water surface doing that Monet trick where you can't tell reflection from riverbed. The canvas lives at the Musée Marmottan Monet in Paris, part of the hoard Michel Monet bequeathed in 1966.

Monet-Mer_agitée_à_Etretat-MBA-Lyon.jpg.title: Agitated Sea at Etretat

source.canonical_title: File:Monet-Mer agitée à Etretat-MBA-Lyon.jpg

Monet-Mer_agitée_à_Etretat-MBA-Lyon.jpg.story: Painted on the pebble beach at Étretat in 1883, this one's all weather. Two fishing boats lie hauled up on the shingle while the Channel slams itself to foam behind them. Monet liked a rough sea — it gave him the broken surfaces he could chase with a loaded brush. The canvas has hung at the Musée des Beaux-Arts de Lyon since 1901, a gift that helped seed the museum's strong Impressionist holdings.

Monet-Poly-Marmottan.jpg.title: Portrait of Poly (Hippolyte Guillaume, Lobster Fisherman of Belle-Île-en-Mer)

source.canonical_title: File:Monet-Poly-Marmottan.jpg

Monet-Poly-Marmottan.jpg.story: A weatherbeaten Breton fisherman stares out from under a battered hat, red scarf blazing at his throat. Poly — real name Hippolyte Guillaume — was a lobsterman on Belle-Île who lugged Monet's gear to the cliffs and posed for him in the autumn of 1886. Monet liked the portrait enough to keep it; it's now at the Musée Marmottan Monet in Paris.

Monet-Water-lily-pond-Chichu-museum.tif.title: Water-Lily pond

source.canonical_title: File:Monet-Water-lily-pond-Chichu-museum.tif

Monet-Water-lily-pond-Chichu-museum.tif.story: A late Giverny pond painting, made around 1920 when Monet was seventy-nine and the lilies had become almost a private language. It now lives in the Chichu Art Museum on Naoshima island in Japan, a building designed by Tadao Ando so that three Monet water lily canvases hang together in a single gallery lit entirely by daylight filtered through the ceiling. You enter in stockinged feet.

Monet_-_Boat_Lying_at_Low_Tide,_1881.jpg.title: Monet - Boat Lying at Low Tide, 1881

source.canonical_title: File:Monet - Boat Lying at Low Tide, 1881.jpg

Monet_-_Boat_Lying_at_Low_Tide,_1881.jpg.story: A fishing boat canted over on wet sand at Fécamp, waiting for the tide to come back and lift it. Monet spent spring 1881 working the Normandy harbor, painting boats the way he'd later paint haystacks, same object, different light. The hull is a dark wedge against the pale tidal flat; a few gulls, a pink-gray sky. The Art Institute of Chicago holds a closely related composition as catalogue 18 of his Fécamp campaign.

Monet_-_Camille_Monet_and_a_Child_in_the.description: Camille Monet and a Child in the Artist's Garden in Argenteuil

source.canonical_title: File:Monet - Cliffs near Dieppe, 1882.jpg

Monet_-_Cliffs_near_Dieppe,_1882.jpg.story: The chalk headlands between Dieppe and Pourville, painted in 1882 during Monet's second and longer Normandy stint that year. He'd tramp out from Père Paul's hotel in Pourville with canvases strapped to his back, sometimes working as many as eight at once depending on where the sun landed. The cliffs here go pale green-white under a mild sky, the sea cold even in summer. One site, countless weathers — and a body of work that essentially invented the idea of a painting series.

Monet_-_Das_Nachtessen,_1868-69.jpg.title: The Dinner

source.canonical_title: File:Monet - Das Nachtessen, 1868-69.jpg

Monet_-_Das_Nachtessen,_1868-69.jpg.story: A rare interior by Monet, painted in the winter of 1868-69 while he was living in Étretat and nearly penniless: his partner Camille at the table with their toddler Jean, lamplight pooling on white linen, two guests arriving late in their hats. You can practically hear the soup spoons. Monet was so broke that year he'd tried to drown himself in the Seine, by his own later account. The canvas is in the Foundation E.G. Bührle Collection in Zurich, acquired by Emil Bührle in 1944.

Monet_-_Die_Zaan_bei_Zaandam.jpg.title: The Zaan at Zaandam

source.canonical_title: File:Monet - Die Zaan bei Zaandam.jpg

Monet_-_Die_Zaan_bei_Zaandam.jpg.story: The river Zaan, one of some twenty small canvases Monet brought home from his four-month detour through Holland in 1871. He was drifting back to France after wartime exile in London, landed in Zaandam near Amsterdam in May, and found the low Dutch light, the windmills and the water endlessly paintable. Quick, loose, on-the-spot work; you can feel him using the trip as a palette cleanser between wars.

source.canonical_title: File:Monet - Frühling in Giverny.jpg

Monet_-_Frühling_in_Giverny.jpg.story: Spring at Giverny — fruit trees in blossom, the grass acid-bright, the whole field vibrating. Monet planted his famous garden only in 1890 after finally buying the Giverny house he'd been renting since 1883, and this is the moment just before that transformation: a working orchard, still somebody else's land. He'd bought the property that November for 22,000 francs.

Monet wrote to the Louvre in April 1867 asking for permission to paint "views of Paris from the windows" of the palace; the authorization came through on the 27th. He painted three canvases from that perch. This one, an unusual vertical, belongs to the Allen Memorial Art Museum at Oberlin.

Monet_-_Grainstacks,_White_Frost_Effect_.story: Two grainstacks in a field outside Giverny, furred with morning frost, the sun just burning through. This is one of the precursors to Monet's famous Haystacks series — painted in the winter of 1888–89, two years before he properly launched the sequence of twenty-five. The stacks belonged to a neighbor farmer and stood just behind Monet's house. The picture is held at the Hill-Stead Museum in Farmington, Connecticut, in a room arranged exactly as its collector Theodate Pope left it in 1946.

Monet_-_Impression,_Sunrise.jpg.story: The painting that gave a movement its name. Monet did it from his hotel window at Le Havre, fast and thin, orange sun smeared over a misty harbour and a tiny rowboat for scale. When he showed it at the 1874 independent exhibition, a critic sneered that it was barely an "impression" of a sunrise, and the label stuck. Infrared analysis and tide tables suggest he actually painted it in November 1872, at 7:35 a.m. It was stolen from the Musee Marmottan in 1985 and recovered five years later.

Monet_-_In_der_Barke.jpg.story: Three young women in straw hats, rods in hand, drift on the Epte in a flat-bottomed Norwegian skiff. The sitters are the Hoschedé daughters — Germaine, Suzanne, and Blanche — Monet's soon-to-be stepdaughters. What makes the picture sing is the water: a thick, acid-green weave of brushstrokes that tips the whole composition forward like a stage set. Monet worked on it through 1887 at Giverny. The painting entered the Louvre in 1947 and now hangs at the Musée d'Orsay.

Monet_-_Nenúfares.jpg.story: By 1904 Monet had stopped including the Japanese bridge in his water-lily paintings — the pond itself was subject enough. The viewpoint tilts downward, sky disappears, and the canvas becomes a floating disc of violet water and lily clusters. He'd dug the pond in 1893, expanded it twice since, and now spent mornings adjusting plantings and afternoons painting them. This is from the first full Nymphéas series, forty-eight canvases shown at Durand-Ruel in May 1909 under the title Les Nymphéas, série de paysages d'eau.

Monet_-_Red_Boats,_Argenteuil,_1875.jpg.title: Red Boats, Argenteuil

source.canonical_title: File:Monet - Red Boats, Argenteuil, 1875.jpg

Monet_-_Red_Boats,_Argenteuil,_1875.jpg.story: Two red rowboats anchor the composition like punctuation marks on the bright Seine. Monet worked this basin at Argenteuil repeatedly, usually from his floating studio, but the low vantage here suggests he set up on the shore. He quietly edited out the factory smokestacks you'd actually have seen, and x-rays later revealed he even painted over a sixth paddling duck. The canvas came to the Fogg Museum at Harvard in 1951 through the Maurice Wertheim bequest.

Monet_-_Small_Country_Farm_at_Bordighera.description: Small Country Farm at Bordighera (Un coin de ferme à Bordighera)

Monet_-_Small_Country_Farm_at_Bordighera.story: Not every Bordighera canvas was palm trees and blue sea. Monet also hunted down the quieter corners — a peasant farmhouse tucked under olives, its plaster warm against the cool grey-greens of the grove. Painted in 1884, this 'coin de ferme' reads almost like a Normandy subject wearing a Ligurian costume. The brushwork is dense, the shadow under the trees woven from a dozen colours. He told Durand-Ruel the southern trees were the hardest thing he'd ever painted.

source.canonical_title: File:Monet - The Church at Varengeville, 1882.jpg

title.de: Die Kirche in Varengeville im Gegenlicht

Monet_-_The_Church_at_Varengeville,_1882.story: The sailors' church at Varengeville, seen across the ravine that cuts the cliff in two. The building is medieval — parts of it go back to the twelfth century — and Monet painted it seven times in 1882, morning, noon, evening. By this stage he was finishing canvases back in the studio rather than purely en plein air, a quiet break from orthodox Impressionism. The church is still standing in 2026, though rising seas are slowly claiming its cliff.

Monet worked fast during his two-week trip near Sassenheim in spring 1886 — the bulbs are only in bloom for a couple of weeks a year. Monet_-_Wildenstein_1996,_1497.png.story: By 1897 Monet barely needed to leave his garden - Giverny was the motif. This clump of chrysanthemums, painted close up and almost filling the frame, is practically abstract: a hot orange and crimson mat with nothing behind it, no horizon, no ground. You can feel him working his way toward the huge lily pictures still twenty years off. Signed and dated '97, catalogued as W.1497 in Wildenstein's 1996 raisonne.

Monet_-_Wildenstein_1996,_1661.jpg.story: By 1907 Monet had been painting his lily pond for a decade and had stopped including the banks. No horizon, no ground - just water, sky reflected in water, and the flat pink pads. He was sixty-seven, his eyesight already troubling him, and he'd destroy canvases he wasn't satisfied with by kicking them. This one survived. It catalogued as Wildenstein 1661 and belongs to the Musee Marmottan Monet in Paris, which holds the largest Monet collection in the world thanks to a bequest from his son Michel.
Monet_-_Wildenstein_1996,_1661.jpg.year_note: The source year '1661' is the Wildenstein catalogue number. W.1661 falls in Monet's 1907 water-lily group.

Monet_-_Wildenstein_1996,_1823.jpg.title: Monet - Wildenstein 1996, 1823

source.canonical_title: File:Monet - Wildenstein 1996, 1823.jpg

Monet_-_Wildenstein_1996,_1823.jpg.story: Water lilies with irises spiking up through the reflections — a Giverny motif Monet worked hard in the war years. He was in his seventies, half-blind from cataracts, and still carrying easels down to the pond at dawn. The purple stabs of iris break the horizontal drift of the pads and the mirrored sky, a vertical he liked when he felt a canvas needed an anchor. It is catalogued in Daniel Wildenstein's 1996 raisonné at number 1823, part of the long last reckoning with his garden.

Monet_-_dahlias.jpg.title: Monet - dahlias

source.canonical_title: File:Monet - dahlias.jpg

Monet_-_dahlias.jpg.story: Painted in 1873 while Monet was renting the pink house at Argenteuil, this is his own back garden: tall dahlias blazing red and pink against a wooden fence, the steep roofs of suburban villas pushing up behind. He was thirty-three, newly flush from a run of sales, and would plant and paint this garden obsessively for the next three years until the rent caught up with him. Dahlias were a relatively new flower in France at the time, prized for their outrageous colour in the Paris flower market.
Monet_-_dahlias.jpg.year_note: Source year 1926 is Monet's death year; the dahlias canvas dates to 1873, painted in the Argenteuil garden.

Monet_-_ice-floes-on-the-seine-at-bougiv.title: Ice Floes at Bougival

source.canonical_title: File:Monet - ice-floes-on-the-seine-at-bougival-1868.jpg

Monet_-_ice-floes-on-the-seine-at-bougiv.story: The winter of 1867-68 on the Seine at Bougival, just west of Paris, where the river broke up into grey-green slabs of ice drifting past people hauling buckets up the bank. A local newspaper reported Monet out there working in three jumpers, a foot-warmer, and fingerless gloves, the paint threatening to freeze on his palette. Camille had just given birth to their son Jean and Monet had no money; the picture carries that bitten-cold, anxious clarity. It hangs in the Louvre as part of the Hélène and Victor Lyon bequest.

Monet_-_the-bridge-at-bougival.jpg.title: The Bridge at Bougival

source.canonical_title: File:Monet - the-bridge-at-bougival.jpg

Monet_-_the-bridge-at-bougival.jpg.story: 1869 was the Bougival year. Monet had just moved into a cottage at Saint-Michel with Camille Doncieux and their son Jean, and the road bridge just across the Seine, built in 1858 to link the left bank to the Ile de Croissy, became his subject. He planted himself at an unconventional angle, right at the foot of the span, and tucked Camille and Jean into the scene near the pier. Plein-air work was taking over. The painting now lives at the Currier Museum of Art in Manchester, New Hampshire.

Monet_-_yellow-irises-1917.jpg.title: Monet - yellow-irises-1917

source.canonical_title: File:Monet - yellow-irises-1917.jpg

Monet_-_yellow-irises-1917.jpg.story: By about 1917 Monet's cataracts were turning reds muddy and blues electric, and he painted yellow irises like a man who had decided to shout back. Thick buttery strokes, unapologetic greens, the flowers shoving right up against the picture plane. Irises lined the paths and pond banks at Giverny; he made roughly twenty canvases of them between 1914 and 1917. Many were found in his studio after his death in 1926, damaged by shell fragments during the Second World War.

Monet_1401.jpg.title: Monet 1401
Monet_1401.jpg.description: Claude Monet, The Fjord near Christiania, W.1401

source.canonical_title: File:Monet 1401.jpg

Monet_1401.jpg.story: Monet turned 55 in Norway. In early 1895 he went to visit his stepson Jacques Hoschede in Sandviken, outside Christiania (today's Oslo), and ended up staying two months, painting in snowshoes. The fjord paintings are all about that strange pale northern light bouncing off frozen water - no shadows, no warmth, just lilac and rose on white. He wrote home that Mount Kolsaas reminded him of Fuji. Twenty-nine canvases came back with him. This one is W.1401.
Monet_1401.jpg.year_note: The source year '1401' is the Wildenstein catalogue number. The Fjord near Christiania was painted in 1895 during Monet's trip to Norway.

Monet_Extérieur_de_la_gare_Saint-Lazare,.title: Exterior of the Gare Saint-Lazare, Sunlight Effect

source.canonical_title: File:Monet Extérieur de la gare Saint-Lazare, effet de soleil.jpg

Monet_Extérieur_de_la_gare_Saint-Lazare,.story: Monet rented a room near the Gare Saint-Lazare in early 1877 and got permission to set up his easel on the platforms. This canvas steps back outside, where sun cuts down between the iron sheds and the smoke of an arriving train blurs into the Paris haze. Gustave Caillebotte, Monet's friend and fellow painter, bought it in 1878. When Caillebotte died in 1894 it passed to the French state with the rest of his bequest, and it's been at the Musée d'Orsay since the museum opened in 1986.

Monet_Houses_of_Parliament,_Sunset.jpg.title: Houses of Parliament, sunset

source.canonical_title: File:Monet Houses of Parliament, Sunset.jpg
source.credit: Unknown Unknown (image is in the public domain; see below)

Monet_Houses_of_Parliament,_Sunset.jpg.story: Monet painted the Houses of Parliament from a terrace at St Thomas' Hospital, directly across the Thames, working only in late afternoon when the sun dropped behind the towers. He began the first Parliament canvas on 13 February 1900 and returned the following two winters. Here the building is pure silhouette — a cathedral of smog cut against molten orange water. He carried these canvases back to Giverny unfinished and wrestled with them for years; this one is dated 1902, though he wouldn't show the series publicly until May 1904.

Monet_Lavacourt.jpg.title: The Seine at Lavacourt

source.canonical_title: File:Monet Lavacourt.jpg
source.credit: 1. Unknown source Unknown source 2. Dallas Museum of Arts

Monet_Lavacourt.jpg.story: This is the olive branch. After years of Salon rejection, Monet painted a calm, rule-abiding view across the Seine, central triangle of trees mirrored in still water, nothing to frighten a juror. It worked: the Salon of 1880 accepted it. His impressionist friends accused him of selling out, and the painting got hung too high to be seen properly anyway. Monet never submitted to the Salon again. In 1938 the Dallas Museum of Art bought it, their first serious European painting.

Monet_Luncheon.jpg.title: The Luncheon

source.canonical_title: File:Monet Luncheon.jpg

Monet_Luncheon.jpg.story: A laid table in the garden at Argenteuil, the remains of a summer lunch: a half-drunk glass of wine, a cut pear, a straw hat hung on a branch. No people in sight, just the aftermath, as if the diners have wandered off mid-conversation. Monet submitted it to the 1876 Impressionist exhibition as a "decorative panel," and it is enormous, over two metres tall. The shaded corner feels personal; this is his own garden, his own family's leftovers. The painting hangs at the Musee d'Orsay.

Monet_Meadow-with-Poplars-Homepage.jpg.title: Meadow with Poplars

source.canonical_title: File:Monet Meadow-with-Poplars-Homepage.jpg

Monet_Meadow-with-Poplars-Homepage.jpg.story: A meadow near Argenteuil, a row of poplars, and two small grainstacks in the middle distance: all the motifs Monet would obsess over twenty years later in his famous series, already here in miniature. Red and green, purple and yellow flick across the foreground in bright impasto, pushing the grasses toward you while the background thins into hazy, fluid strokes. Painted about 1875, it entered the Museum of Fine Arts, Boston in 1923 as a bequest from David P. Kimball.

Monet_Pointe_de_la_Hève.jpg.title: The Pointe de la Hève, Sainte-Adresse
Monet_Pointe_de_la_Hève.jpg.description: Pointe de la Hève à Sainte-Adresse, olio su tela, 41x74 cm, National Gallery, London

source.canonical_title: File:Monet Pointe de la Hève.jpg

title.it: La Pointe de la Hève, Sainte-Adresse
title.pt: La Pointe de la Hève, Sainte-Adresse
title.pt-br: La Pointe de la Hève, Sainte-Adresse
title.fr: La Pointe de la Hève, Sainte-Adresse

Monet_Pointe_de_la_Hève.jpg.story: Monet painted this in the last week of May 1864, having travelled to the Normandy coast with his friend Frederic Bazille. It's a sketch made on the spot - you can see the rowing boat pulled up on the shingle - and he used it to work up a larger studio version that got him into the Paris Salon of 1865. That bigger picture swapped the boat for a cart and horses, to make clear this was a working beach. The smaller, fresher one is the one in the National Gallery in London.

Monet_The_Thames_at_Westminster_1871_Wes.title: The Thames below Westminster
Monet_The_Thames_at_Westminster_1871_Wes.description: El cuadro llamado The Thames at Westminster fue pintado por Monet durante su estancia en Londres en 1872

source.canonical_title: File:Monet The Thames at Westminster 1871 Westminster.jpg

Monet_The_Thames_at_Westminster_1871_Wes.story: Monet reached London in September 1870, fleeing the war, and stayed till May 1871. He made only five cityscapes in all those months. This one looks south across the Thames to a just-finished Houses of Parliament, a Victoria Embankment still new on the right, and St Thomas' Hospital on the left, about to open that summer. He's exaggerated the towers, turning Westminster into something fairytale, and he's let the fog do most of the architectural detail for him. Oil on canvas, 43 by 73 cm, National Gallery, London.

Monet_Veduta_di_Rouelles.jpg.title: View At Rouelles, Le Havre

source.canonical_title: File:Monet Veduta di Rouelles.jpg

Monet_Veduta_di_Rouelles.jpg.story: Monet was eighteen when he painted this, and it's thought to be his earliest surviving canvas. Eugene Boudin had just taken him out of Le Havre for a proper painting excursion to the little valley of Rouelles, and this quiet stretch of stream and pasture is the result. No waterlilies yet, no haystacks, no fog - just a serious teenager copying what he saw, and doing it well enough that he'd later let the picture stay in circulation. It's dated 1858.

Monet_View_of_Bordighiera_31db607334.jpg.title: View of Bordighera

source.canonical_title: File:Monet View of Bordighiera 31db607334.jpg

Monet_View_of_Bordighiera_31db607334.jpg.story: From a hill above Bordighera, Monet looked down over the town, the Alps, and the curve of the sea — and panicked. The composition kept multiplying. He painted several versions in 1884, each shifting the palms, the villas, the distant peaks. This view pushes the town into the middle distance, swallowed by feathery trees. He wrote Alice the scene was 'absolutely fairy-like' and that he'd never sell a single one because nobody would believe the colours were real.

Monet_W108.jpg.title: Monet W108

source.canonical_title: File:Monet W108.jpg

Monet_W108.jpg.story: Monet's infant son Jean, born out of wedlock in August 1867, asleep in his cot with a small doll tucked under one arm. Daniel Wildenstein dated the canvas to early 1868; more recent scholarship has pushed it as late as 1869, when the child was nearly two. Either way, it's a private, unsaleable picture — the kind Monet made for himself and Camille during their most precarious years. Catalogued as Wildenstein 108.

source.canonical_title: File:Monet Zaandam 1871 Musee d'Orsay.jpg
source.permission: You may select the license of your choice.

Monet_barques_w_137.jpg.title: Boote

source.canonical_title: File:Monet barques w 137.jpg
source.permission: public domain

Monet_barques_w_137.jpg.story: Rowing boats at rest, from the summer Monet and Renoir worked shoulder to shoulder at La Grenouillere, the little resort on the Seine near Bougival. 1869. Monet was piling up quick oil sketches of water, boats and bathers, feeling his way toward a big Salon painting he wanted to submit the following year. He never finished that grand canvas; what survived were these fast, fresh studies where the brushwork itself became the point. Catalogued as Wildenstein 137.

Monet_grainstacks-at-giverny-sunset_W121.title: Haystacks at Giverny, Sunset

source.canonical_title: File:Monet grainstacks-at-giverny-sunset W1213.jpg

Monet_grainstacks-at-giverny-sunset_W121.story: Two stacks of wheat at Giverny, catching the last red of a winter sunset. Monet painted this around 1888–89, before the proper Haystacks series began in 1890, but the obsession is already visible — the same motif, the same low viewpoint, the fascination with how a single shape changes under different light. The thatched stacks were a local storage method: wheat sheaves piled and weatherproofed with straw, meant to last until the spring threshing.

Monet_trouville.jpg.title: The boardwalk on the beach at Trouville

source.canonical_title: File:Monet trouville.jpg

Monet_trouville.jpg.story: Trouville boardwalk, same 1870 summer honeymoon, painted fast on the spot. Monet loved the fluttering tricolors lining the promenade, and you can almost hear them cracking in the sea breeze. Parasols, stove-pipe hats, the glitter of the Channel. Within weeks the Franco-Prussian War would send Monet fleeing to England, and this easy seaside world would be gone. An oil study, about 48 by 73 cm.

Monet_w0145.jpg.title: Monet w0145
Monet_w0145.jpg.description: Claude Monet, Snow at Sunset, W.145

source.canonical_title: File:Monet w0145.jpg

Monet_w1001.jpg.title: Monet w1001

source.canonical_title: File:Monet w1001.jpg

Monet_w1001.jpg.story: Almost certainly the departmental road climbing the left bank of the Seine toward Notre-Dame-de-la-Mer, with the houses of Port-Villez visible on the left. 65 by 81 cm, signed 85. The collector Georges Viau owned it, then Mrs Gustavia A. Senff of New York from 1916, before it surfaced at a Sotheby Parke Bernet sale in 1974 and went to a Swiss private buyer.

Monet_w1003.jpg.title: Monet w1003

source.canonical_title: File:Monet w1003.jpg

Monet_w1003.jpg.story: The houses of Port-Villez on the right, dominated by the Gibet hill, are half-masked by the trees of a little island in the foreground. 65 by 92 cm, signed 85. Durand-Ruel probably bought it that December. It then passed through the Desfosses collection, sold at the Hotel Desfosses in 1899, and eventually to Herbert and Elizabeth Wechsler in the United States around 1965.

source.canonical_title: File:Monet w1010.jpg

Monet_w1016.jpg.title: Monet w1016

source.canonical_title: File:Monet w1016.jpg

Monet_w1016.jpg.story: The cliffs at Etretat were Monet's obsession in the 1880s, and this canvas catches them at the hour he loved best: sunset, when the Falaise d'Aval glows like a lit coal and the sea goes flat and lilac. He worked through winter storms here, rigging shelters against the spray, sometimes cursing the tide for shifting faster than his paint could dry. The arch itself has been carved by the sea for millennia, but Monet wanted the fifteen minutes of a particular evening. This one is now at the Pola Museum of Art in Hakone, Japan.

source.canonical_title: File:Monet w1018.jpg

Monet_w1032.jpg.title: Monet w1032
Monet_w1032.jpg.description: Claude Monet, Sailboats of the Rock Needle, W.1032

source.canonical_title: File:Monet w1032.jpg

Monet_w1035.jpg.title: Monet w1035

source.canonical_title: File:Monet w1035.jpg

Monet_w1035.jpg.story: Another of the Etretat canvases, zeroing in on the Manneporte and the Falaise d'Aval, the arch-and-needle silhouette that stopped Monet cold every time he rounded the beach. He painted roughly fifty views of these cliffs between 1883 and 1886, sometimes lowering himself down the rocks on ropes to reach a ledge no one else would bother with. The chalk face changes colour almost by the minute in sea light. This canvas now lives in a private collection, one of many from the campaign that never entered a museum.

Monet_w1042.jpg.title: Monet w1042

source.canonical_title: File:Monet w1042.jpg

Monet_w1042.jpg.story: The Falaise d'Aval again, that great hooked cliff with the needle of rock beyond. Monet went back to Etretat winter after winter through the mid-1880s because the low sun did things to the chalk that he couldn't invent in the studio. Guy de Maupassant, summering in the same village, watched him lug five or six canvases onto the shingle at once, switching between them as the light shifted. This version is held by the Kreeger Museum in Washington, D.C., tucked into a Philip Johnson-designed house.

Monet_w1048.jpg.title: Monet w1048
Monet_w1048.jpg.description: Claude Monet, Cliff and Porte d'Amont in Rough Weather, W.1048

source.canonical_title: File:Monet w1048.jpg

Monet_w1050.jpg.title: Monet w1050

source.canonical_title: File:Monet w1050.jpg

Monet_w1050.jpg.story: Monet catches the Needle framed through the Porte d'Aval at Etretat, but only at the few hours of low tide when the sea retreats from the arch's feet. He had just months before been racing the light on the Riviera; now, back on the Normandy chalk, the palette cools to grey-greens and foam. Bernheim-Jeune and Durand-Ruel bought it jointly from Monet in May 1920, decades after its 1885-86 making.

Monet_w1054.jpg.title: Monet w1054

source.canonical_title: File:Monet w1054.jpg

Monet_w1054.jpg.story: January 1886, and Monet is out in the snow at Falaise, writing to Alice about the cold. This 66 by 81 cm canvas shows the village from the south, the val de Falaise climbing the slope to the left of the buildings. Faure bought it direct in 1886, then Durand-Ruel in 1893, and eventually Edward G. Robinson the actor owned it in Los Angeles. It went through Sotheby's in 1973.

Monet_w1056.jpg.title: Monet w1056

source.canonical_title: File:Monet w1056.jpg

Monet_w1056.jpg.story: Painted in the main street of Limetz, near the western edge of the village, with the hills of Port-Villez glimpsed at the far end through the snow. One of the winter 1886 canvases Monet squeezed in between the Etretat trips. It passed through Bernheim-Jeune and Durand-Ruel, then Cassirer in 1900, then sat with Parisian collectors until Rene Drouet gave it to the University of California, San Diego in 1972.

Monet_w1061.jpg.title: Monet w1061
Monet_w1061.jpg.description: Claude Monet, Panorama of Vernon, W.1061

source.canonical_title: File:Monet w1061.jpg

Monet_w1065.jpg.title: Monet w1065

source.canonical_title: File:Monet w1065.jpg

Monet_w1065.jpg.story: Before Monet's famous gardens existed, the plot at Giverny was mostly orchard, and here Suzanne Hoschede, his favorite model, stands among the spring blossom. Signed Claude Monet 86, shown at Georges Petit's fifth international exhibition that summer, where Feneon singled Monet out in La Vogue. Durand-Ruel probably bought it off Monet in January 1887. It later went through the dealer Stephen Hahn to a Swiss private collection around 1973.
Monet_w1065.jpg.year_note: Wildenstein catalogue no. 1065, with Suzanne Hoschede

Monet_w1075.jpg.title: Monet w1075

source.canonical_title: File:Monet w1075.jpg

Monet_w1075.jpg.story: A sketch, not a finished painting: 1.02 by 0.75 m, no signature. Out boating at the ile aux Orties where he kept his skiffs, Monet saw his stepdaughters Germaine and Suzanne Hoschede, their mother Alice, and his son Michel silhouetted against the sky on a raised bank. He blocked in the group left to right in one go, a first pass for the larger plein-air figure studies (W1076, W1077) that followed. It surfaced at the Bonnard sale in Paris in 1954.
Monet_w1075.jpg.year_note: Wildenstein catalogue no. 1075, preparatory oil sketch

Monet_w1089.jpg.title: Monet w1089

source.canonical_title: File:Monet w1089.jpg

Monet_w1089.jpg.story: Signed Claude Monet 87 but actually begun on Belle-Ile in autumn 1886, during the two-month campaign where Monet produced around 39 canvases of the Atlantic cliffs. He finished and dated several back at Giverny the following year. Durand-Ruel bought it from him in November 1887; it drifted through Wiesbaden, then reemerged at a 1975 Johannesburg Sotheby's sale.

Monet_w109.jpg.title: Monet w109

source.canonical_title: File:Monet w109.jpg

Monet_w109.jpg.story: An early Le Havre canvas from the young Monet, painted where the Seine meets the Channel. He grew up in this port — his father ran a ship-chandler's shop in nearby Sainte-Adresse — and the jetty, the lighthouse, and the grey working water were his first real subjects. Long before the water lilies, before Impressionism had a name, he was already drawn to the way weather sat on a harbor. Catalogued as W.109 in Wildenstein's raisonné, among the Havre pictures of his twenties.

Monet_w1120.jpg.title: Monet w1120

source.canonical_title: File:Monet w1120.jpg

Monet_w1120.jpg.story: On the bad-weather days when the Belle-Ile coast was off-limits, Monet set up at a window in Kervilahouen and painted inland. A 60 by 60 cm square: to the left a windmill on the Donnant road, in the middle the hamlet of Cosquet, all of it smeared by rain. His son Michel inherited it and gave it in 1927 to the Societe des Amis de Gustave Geffroy, the critic who'd been Monet's Belle-Ile companion. It hangs today in the Musee des Beaux-Arts in Morlaix.
Monet_w1120.jpg.year_note: Wildenstein catalogue no. 1120, Musee des Beaux-Arts Morlaix

Monet_w1121.jpg.title: Monet w1121
Monet_w1121.jpg.description: Claude Monet, Rain in Belle-Ile, W.1121

source.canonical_title: File:Monet w1121.jpg

Monet_w1135.jpg.title: Poplars in the Sun

source.canonical_title: File:Monet w1135.jpg

title.fr: Sous les peupliers, effet de soleil

Monet_w1135.jpg.story: Suzanne Hoschede again, carrying the green parasol from last year's big outdoor decorations, in the flowering meadows of Les Essarts between the two branches of the Epte. Dappled sun, not the later Poplars series. The baritone Jean-Baptiste Faure owned it first; Durand-Ruel and Cassirer passed it on in 1906, and Stuttgart's Gemaldegalerie acquired it that same year, where it still hangs.
Monet_w1135.jpg.year_note: Wildenstein catalogue no. 1135. Original batch title 'Poplars in the Sun' conflates this with the 1891 NMWA Tokyo canvas (W1305); this W1135 is the 1887 Stuttgart canvas with Suzanne Hoschede

Monet_w1138.jpg.title: Monet w1138
Monet_w1138.jpg.description: Claude Monet, Field of Irises at Giverny, W.1138

source.canonical_title: File:Monet w1138.jpg

Monet_w1155.jpg.title: Monet w1155

source.canonical_title: File:Monet w1155.jpg

Monet_w1155.jpg.story: A double line of poplars in the plaine des Ajoux south of Giverny, a first run at a motif Monet would return to and serialize in 1891. Signed Claude Monet 87. Durand-Ruel bought it from him in 1890, and it passed to Robert Treat Paine of Boston in 1911, who kept it in the family for decades.
Monet_w1155.jpg.year_note: Wildenstein catalogue no. 1155, precursor to the 1891 Poplars series

Monet_w1179.jpg.title: Monet w1179

source.canonical_title: File:Monet w1179.jpg

Monet_w1179.jpg.story: Monet spent four months in Antibes in 1888, and came back with thirty-odd canvases and a complaint that the place was so beautiful it felt "impossible" to paint. The Alpes-Maritimes rise across the bay in a pale, sugared blue; the Mediterranean light was harsher than Normandy's and forced him toward pinks and turquoises he'd never used before. He wrote to Alice Hoschede that he was "fencing" with the sun. This canvas is in a private collection.

Monet_w1200.jpg.title: Monet w1200
Monet_w1200.jpg.description: Claude Monet, Meadow at Giverny Morning Effect, W.1200

source.canonical_title: File:Monet w1200.jpg

Monet_w1200.jpg.story: By 1888 Monet had been at Giverny five years and was walking the same meadows over and over, tracking how a single field changed with the hour. This canvas catches one of them at morning: pale light flooding the grass, a rhythm of thin trees, everything in that cool green-and-lavender key he loved before sunlight hardens. No drama, no figures - just the minute when dew is still on the ground. Catalogued as Wildenstein number 1200 in the 1996 raisonne.
Monet_w1200.jpg.year_note: The source year '1200' is the Wildenstein catalogue number, not a date. W.1200 corresponds to c.1888.

Monet_w1245.jpg.title: Monet w1245
Monet_w1245.jpg.description: Claude Monet, Effect of Spring at Giverny, W.1245

source.canonical_title: File:Monet w1245.jpg

Monet_w1245.jpg.story: Spring 1890, Monet's seventh year at Giverny and the year he started buying the house he'd been renting. The field by his door is in full explosion - young poplars, powdery pink blossom, grass the saturated green that only lasts a week or two. He's about to launch the Grainstacks series in the same fields a few months later; you can already feel him noticing how the same spot reads completely differently at a different hour. Catalogue number W.1245.
Monet_w1245.jpg.year_note: The source year '1245' is the Wildenstein catalogue number. Effect of Spring at Giverny was painted in 1890.

Monet_w1296.jpg.title: Monet w1296

source.canonical_title: File:Monet w1296.jpg

Monet_w1296.jpg.story: From the Poplars series, painted in the summer and autumn of 1891 along a bend of the Epte near Giverny. When the local commune voted to fell the trees for timber halfway through his campaign, Monet actually paid a wood merchant to leave them standing until he was finished. He worked from a flat-bottomed studio boat, chasing the ribbon of trees as they zigzagged downstream. This canvas is now at the Museum of Fine Arts, Boston.

Monet_w1336.jpg.title: Monet w1336
Monet_w1336.jpg.description: Claude Monet, Floating Ice near Bennecourt, W.1336

source.canonical_title: File:Monet w1336.jpg

Monet_w1336.jpg.story: January 1893, bitter cold, the Seine freezing up near Bennecourt - the same bend where Monet had painted Camille in a white dress twenty-five years earlier. This time no figures. Just ice floes shouldering each other downstream, bare poplars, a sky the colour of pewter. He did a whole small run of these icefloe pictures that winter, working fast before the thaw. Wildenstein catalogue number 1336.
Monet_w1336.jpg.year_note: The source year '1336' is the Wildenstein catalogue number. Floating Ice near Bennecourt was painted in 1893.

Monet_w1370.jpg.title: Monet w1370

source.canonical_title: File:Monet w1370.jpg

Monet_w1370.jpg.story: A quiet stretch of the Seine at Port-Villez, across the river from Vernon, painted in 1894. Monet would row down from Giverny in his studio-boat to work on these long horizontal landscapes, all of them tuned to mist and flat early-morning light. The 65 × 100 cm canvas is now at the Musée des Beaux-Arts in Rouen.

Monet_w148.jpg.title: Monet w148

source.canonical_title: File:Monet w148.jpg

Monet_w148.jpg.story: Route à Louveciennes, neige fondante, soleil couchant — the road to Louveciennes, melting snow, sunset. Winter of 1869–70. Monet was living at Bougival, broke, and went out with Pissarro onto the same avenue to paint the same storm. You can almost date it to January 1870 from Pissarro's three matching views. A tree-lined road, wet patches breaking through the white, the low sun catching what's left of the snow. Forty-three by sixty-five centimeters, oil on canvas, now at the Musée des Beaux-Arts in Rouen.

Monet_w1524.jpg.title: Monet w1524
Monet_w1524.jpg.description: Claude Monet, Charing Cross Bridge, W.1524

source.canonical_title: File:Monet w1524.jpg

Monet_w1524.jpg.story: Monet hauled himself to London three winters running, 1899 through 1901, and rented a room at the Savoy with a view over the Thames. From the balcony he worked Charing Cross Bridge in the morning, then turned the easel to Waterloo in the afternoon, chasing the fog. Back in Giverny he kept reworking the canvases for years - this one probably began in 1900 or 1901 and was only signed around 1903. He was after the coal smoke, really: that orange-pink filter London got from a million chimneys. W.1524.
Monet_w1524.jpg.year_note: The source year '1524' is the Wildenstein catalogue number. Charing Cross Bridge canvases were begun on site in London (1899-1901) and generally signed/dated in Giverny around 1902-1903.

Monet_w1558.jpg.title: Monet w1558
Monet_w1558.jpg.description: Claude Monet, Waterloo Bridge Overcast, W.1558

source.canonical_title: File:Monet w1558.jpg

Monet_w1558.jpg.story: Waterloo Bridge, looking downstream from the Savoy, with the Lambeth factory chimneys smoking on the far bank - Monet loved those chimneys, he told Clemenceau the smoke was what made London worth painting. "Overcast" means the sun never really arrives; the whole picture settles into a wet lilac haze with the bridge's arches just barely drawn. Begun on one of his London trips between 1900 and 1901, finished in the studio at Giverny and dated around 1903. Catalogue number W.1558.
Monet_w1558.jpg.year_note: The source year '1558' is the Wildenstein catalogue number. Waterloo Bridge, Overcast was painted from the Savoy on trips 1900-1901 and finished around 1903.

Monet_w1563.jpg.title: Monet w1563

source.canonical_title: File:Monet w1563.jpg

Monet_w1563.jpg.story: One of roughly forty-one Waterloo Bridge canvases Monet produced between 1899 and 1904, most of them begun from a fifth-floor window at the Savoy Hotel. London's coal smoke gave him exactly the atmosphere he wanted: a bridge that dissolved into mauve, violet, sulphur-yellow depending on the hour. He'd work on several canvases at once, swapping them as the fog shifted, then ship the whole batch back to Giverny to finish. This version is in a private collection.

Monet_w159.jpg.title: Camille sitting on the beach at Trouville

source.canonical_title: File:Monet w159.jpg

title.fr: Camille assise sur la plage à Trouville

Monet_w159.jpg.story: Summer of 1870. Monet, just married to Camille, took her and their three-year-old son Jean to Trouville for a working honeymoon. This small canvas — 38 by 46 centimeters — shows Camille cropped like a snapshot, cut by the frame. Grains of beach sand are stuck into the paint: proof he set the easel up right there on the sand. Weeks later France declared war on Prussia and Monet fled to London to dodge the draft. The picture is at the Yale University Art Gallery, from the Whitney collection.
Monet_w159.jpg.year_note: Metadata year 1840 is Monet's birth year. W.159 dates to summer 1870, Yale University Art Gallery.

Monet_w1636.jpg.title: Monet w1636

source.canonical_title: File:Monet w1636.jpg

Monet_w1636.jpg.story: The Seine at Vetheuil, painted from the balcony of a small rented house in Lavacourt during the summer of 1901. Monet did fifteen canvases of this view, all the same strip of river and the same small church on the far bank, differing only in light and weather. He'd moved away from Vetheuil more than twenty years earlier; coming back was a way of testing what the serial method could do with a motif he'd already painted dozens of times as a younger man.

source.canonical_title: File:Monet w1656.jpg

Monet_w1668.jpg.title: Monet w1668

source.canonical_title: File:Monet w1668.jpg

Monet_w1668.jpg.story: A late pond picture from the stretch between 1916 and 1919 when Monet was working almost entirely on the Grandes Décorations and had stopped bothering with sky or bank. Lily pads float as soft ovals on a vertical curtain of water, their pink and white blooms almost afterthoughts against the deep blue-green. The W-number in the filename refers to its entry in Daniel Wildenstein's catalogue raisonné, the standard reference that tracks all 2,050-odd surviving Monets.

Monet_w1675.jpg.title: Monet w1675

source.canonical_title: File:Monet w1675.jpg

Monet_w1675.jpg.story: Late Monet, with the motif almost swallowed by reflection. By the time he worked canvases in the W.1670s range of the Wildenstein catalogue, his eyesight was failing from cataracts and the pond at Giverny had become less a subject than an excuse to mix color. No horizon, no shore, no clear up or down. Just water, sky, and the thick pads of nymphéas pushed across the surface with a loaded brush. He insisted the garden was his most beautiful masterpiece, and he kept returning to it until the year he died, in 1926.

Monet_w1695.jpg.title: Monet w1695

source.canonical_title: File:Monet w1695.jpg

Monet_w1695.jpg.story: Catalogue number W.1695 in Daniel Wildenstein's raisonné, this is one of the Water Lily canvases Monet painted at Giverny in his late seventies. The attribution to 'Clause Monet' on Wikimedia is a transcription slip — it is Claude. By this stage the pond had become his entire subject: the banks are gone, the horizon is gone, and what remains is a floating field of lilies and reflected sky, painted with eyes so clouded by cataracts that he worked largely by colour memory.

Monet_w1708.jpg.title: Water Lilies

source.canonical_title: File:Monet w1708.jpg

Monet_w1708.jpg.story: A long horizontal band of pond, painted in 1907, the lily pads floating in loose constellations. W1708 is the Wildenstein catalog number — a bookkeeping tag that lets curators pin down which Nymphéas is which, since Monet gave most of them the same title. He planned a grand unified installation of these panels for years; it wouldn't arrive until the Orangerie opened in 1927, months after his death in December 1926.

Monet_w1725.jpg.title: Monet w1725

source.canonical_title: File:Monet w1725.jpg

Monet_w1725.jpg.story: Another Nymphéas, catalogued as W.1725. By this late stretch of the series Monet had stopped pretending there was a pond in any ordinary sense — the canvas is all reflection, with pads floating where they feel like floating. He worked from a wheeled easel in his studio garden, and from canvases propped around the walls of the huge new atelier built specifically for these late pictures. One man, one small water garden, and a decade of staring at it.

Monet_w1726.jpg.title: Monet w1726

source.canonical_title: File:Monet w1726.jpg

Monet_w1726.jpg.story: One canvas in the enormous late water-lily harvest. By the 1900s Monet had turned his Giverny pond into a private motif factory, painting the same few square meters of water in every hour of light. The pads sit, the reflections drift, and the eye never quite finds a place to rest. He told a visitor the pond took him a long time to understand before he could paint it, and then all at once he saw it. This one belongs to that patient, obsessive looking, and lives in a private collection.

Monet_w1781.jpg.title: Monet w1781

source.canonical_title: File:Monet w1781.jpg

Monet_w1781.jpg.story: Bassin aux nymphéas, les rosiers — the water-lily pond with the rose bushes. By the 1910s Monet had two gardens going at Giverny: the Clos Normand with its cottage flowers, and the separate water garden reached by a tunnel under the road, fed from the little Ru stream. The roses climbed the trellises behind the pond, and he occasionally let them push into a canvas instead of painting the water straight-on. W.1781 in the catalogue, part of the series that fed his final Orangerie rooms.

Monet_w1786.jpg.title: Monet w1786

source.canonical_title: File:Monet w1786.jpg

Monet_w1786.jpg.story: A Nymphéas of the late teens, Wildenstein 1786. Monet was in his late seventies, cataracts clouding the color he saw, working on the huge decorative panels he had promised the French state to mark the end of the war. The small canvases from this moment often read like rehearsals for the big ones — a square of water, a cluster of pads, color pushed harder than life because he could no longer see subtle things. He gifted the Grandes Décorations to the nation the day after the Armistice.

Monet_w182.jpg.title: Monet w182

source.canonical_title: File:Monet w182.jpg

Monet_w182.jpg.story: Holland, summer 1871. Exiled by the Franco-Prussian War, Monet detoured from London to Zaandam on Daubigny's tip and stayed five months. He painted twenty-odd canvases of windmills, canals, and the flat lit horizon of the Voorzaan. The mills were working industry, not picturesque ruins — sawing timber, grinding spices, pressing oil — and he painted them as machines against sky. W.182 is one of the Zaandam group, the trip that reset his eye just before he settled into Argenteuil.
Monet_w182.jpg.year_note: Metadata year 1840 is Monet's birth year. W.182 belongs to the Zaandam group painted summer 1871.

Monet_w1883.jpg.title: The Water-Lily Pond

source.canonical_title: File:Monet w1883.jpg

Monet_w1883.jpg.story: Oil on canvas, 131 by 201 centimeters, painted in 1919. Monet was seventy-nine. He had drained and re-stocked the lily pond, had cataract surgery looming, and was already deep into the room-sized panels for the state. This Water-Lily Pond is one of a handful of two-meter canvases in which he let the motif go wide and almost abstract — pads and reflections, no shore, no sky except the sky caught in the water. It's at the Museum Folkwang in Essen (inv. G 343).
Monet_w1883.jpg.year_note: Metadata year 1840 is Monet's birth year. W.1883 is dated 1919, Museum Folkwang, Essen.

Monet_w1884.jpg.title: Monet w1884

source.canonical_title: File:Monet w1884.jpg

Monet_w1884.jpg.story: Le Bassin aux nymphéas, W.1884 — a late Water-Lily Pond from around 1918, part of the yellow-and-green group Monet was painting as the Great War ended. He had dedicated the huge panels-in-progress to France the day after the Armistice, and the small canvases of this period often tested colors he then scaled up. No sky, no bank, just surface: lily pads floating through a warm green-gold haze. The picture lives in the Hasso Plattner Collection.

Monet_w1897.jpg.title: Monet w1897
Monet_w1897.jpg.description: Claude Monet, The Water Lily Pond, W.1897

source.canonical_title: File:Monet w1897.jpg

Monet_w1897.jpg.story: The water lily pond at Giverny, painted around 1897 — before the famous decorative cycles, when Monet was still working out what the motif even was. He'd diverted a branch of the Epte to feed the pond in 1893 and fought the local council for permission to plant exotic water lilies, which farmers feared would poison their livestock. He won. He would paint this pond for the next thirty years.

Monet_w1900.jpg.title: Monet w1900
Monet_w1900.jpg.description: Claude Monet, The Water Lily Pond, W.1900

source.canonical_title: File:Monet w1900.jpg

Monet_w1900.jpg.story: Catalogued as Wildenstein 1900, this is another of Monet's water-lily-pond views — Japanese footbridge arching over a churn of pink and green reflections. By 1900 he'd added wisteria to the bridge rails and widened the pond again. The serial approach was the radical part: the same motif, same framing, again and again, only the weather changing. He exhibited a clutch of these bridge paintings at Durand-Ruel in Paris in late 1900, and they sold almost instantly — enough to fund yet another expansion of the water garden.

Monet_w197.jpg.title: Monet w197

source.canonical_title: File:Monet w197.jpg

Monet_w197.jpg.story: A Seine-at-Argenteuil canvas, Wildenstein 197. Monet moved to Argenteuil in December 1871 after Holland, rented a house with the help of his dealer Durand-Ruel, and built himself a little floating studio to work from the water. For the next several years the bassin, its sailboats, and the industrial bridges across the river were his daily subject — the stretch of painting that made Impressionism a thing with a name. This one stayed in private hands.

source.canonical_title: File:Monet w1976.jpg

Monet_w199.jpg.title: Monet w199

source.canonical_title: File:Monet w199.jpg

Monet_w199.jpg.story: An orchard in bloom, the grass still winter-pale, petals catching the light like thrown confetti. This is springtime at Argenteuil, painted in Monet's first full year in the town, when the garden behind his rented house was essentially his outdoor studio. He worked the blossoms in quick daubs, letting the canvas show through as shadow. The figures are barely indicated, more mood than people. It's a small canvas with an outsized sense of air moving through it. The painting is held by the Portland Museum of Art in Maine.

Monet_w222.jpg.title: Monet w222

source.canonical_title: File:Monet w222.jpg

Monet_w222.jpg.story: A strolling couple in a straw hat and a dark dress, a child in tow — Monet painting his own patch of Argenteuil in 1872, the year he'd moved his family into a rented house along the Seine. He was 32 and broke, dodging creditors, but the garden paths and tree-lined promenades of this river suburb gave him subject after subject. Quick, broken strokes for the leaves; a softer wash for the sky. The picture has stayed in private hands.

source.canonical_title: File:Monet w224.jpg

Monet_w24.jpg.title: Monet w24
Monet_w24.jpg.description: Claude Monet, Road by Saint-Simeon Farm, W.24

source.canonical_title: File:Monet w24.jpg

Monet_w265.jpg.title: Monet w265

source.canonical_title: File:Monet w265.jpg

Monet_w265.jpg.story: Sainte-Adresse, 1873 — the Norman coast just north of Le Havre, where Monet's father and aunt had a villa and where he kept returning to paint the Channel. A regatta scene: small sails tipping across choppy water, the kind of brisk day that turns the sea silver-green. He'd already painted the same shore in 1867 with his family parked on the terrace; six years later he'd dropped the figures and gone straight for weather. Private collection.

source.canonical_title: File:Monet w288 the sheltered path.jpg

Monet_w327.jpg.title: Monet w327

source.canonical_title: File:Monet w327.jpg

Monet_w327.jpg.story: A low sun burning through sea haze, a schooner crossing the light — Monet in roughly 1875, painting the coast in a looser, more atmospheric register than his Argenteuil river scenes. He stacks thin horizontal bands of orange and violet across the water, letting the sun do most of the work. No drama, no staffage. The Philadelphia Museum of Art bought it for their Impressionist holdings, where it hangs today as Marine View with a Sunset.

Monet_w357.jpg.title: Monet w357

source.canonical_title: File:Monet w357.jpg

Monet_w357.jpg.story: Argenteuil under snow, winter 1875 — the Boulevard Saint-Denis vanishing into a grey-white smear of sky and track. Monet painted at least eighteen snow scenes that winter, often standing outside in it, gloves off, layering cold whites over warmer underpaint so the picture seems to shiver. A train steams through the background. The canvas hangs at the Musée d'Art et d'Histoire in Geneva.

Monet_w368.jpg.title: Monet w368

source.canonical_title: File:Monet w368.jpg

Monet_w368.jpg.story: Red Boats, Argenteuil, 1875 — three gaudy pleasure craft moored along the Seine, their hulls doubled in the water as wobbling vertical strokes. Argenteuil was a weekend sailing town for Parisians, and Monet lived the life: he kept his own studio boat here, paddled up and down the river, and painted the marina over and over. The red is almost violent against the greens. Private collection.

Monet_w386.jpg.title: Monet w386

source.canonical_title: File:Monet w386.jpg

Monet_w386.jpg.story: Argenteuil, summer 1875 — Camille and little Jean half-lost among roses and gladioli in the garden of Monet's second rented house. He was painting his family as motif, not portrait: the figures dissolve into the flowerbeds, foliage stitched together in short, dry strokes. The baritone Jean-Baptiste Faure bought it straight from Monet, one of the first serious collectors to back him, and hung onto it for over thirty years before Durand-Ruel took it in 1907.

Monet_w392.jpg.title: The Studio Boat, on the Seine

source.canonical_title: File:Monet w392.jpg

Monet_w392.jpg.story: Monet had a boat built so he could paint the Seine from the middle of it. This 1874 canvas shows that floating studio moored at Argenteuil, its little plank cabin big enough, he said, for just an easel. From here he could chase light on water from angles no shoreline painter could reach. The small painting, 50 by 64 cm, is in the Kroller-Muller Museum in Otterlo, the Netherlands.

Monet_w397.jpg.title: Monet w397

source.canonical_title: File:Monet w397.jpg

Monet_w397.jpg.story: Argenteuil, 1876 — a quiet stretch of bank where trees lean out over still water and the reflections run almost the full height of the canvas. Monet had been living here four years and knew every willow along the Seine. The picture has stayed in private hands.

Monet_w419.jpg.title: Monet w419

source.canonical_title: File:Monet w419.jpg

Monet_w419.jpg.story: One of four big decorative panels the department-store tycoon Ernest Hoschedé commissioned for the salon of his chateau at Montgeron in 1876 — the same Hoschedé who'd go bankrupt within two years, sending his wife Alice and their six children into a shared household with the Monets. The pond itself: green water, a slip of far bank, everything loosened into patches of color. Over six feet wide. The Hermitage in St Petersburg now owns it.

source.canonical_title: File:Monet w421.jpg

Monet_w429.jpg.title: Evening at Argenteuil

source.canonical_title: File:Monet w429.jpg

Monet_w429.jpg.story: Argenteuil, 1876 — the Seine going pink and orange under a late sky, the far bank just a ragged horizontal smudge. Monet painted the river here dozens of times; this one strips it down to color and reflection, water doing nearly all the work. The picture remains in private hands.

Monet_w433.jpg.title: Hunting

source.canonical_title: File:Monet w433.jpg

Monet_w433.jpg.story: Not the usual Monet. In summer 1876 the collector Ernest Hoschede invited him to the Chateau de Rottembourg and commissioned four giant decorative canvases for the salon rotunda. This one, 173 by 140 cm, drops a group of hunters onto a forest path in the Senart woods, with Hoschede himself tucked among them. Hoschede went bankrupt months later and the paintings never reached the salon. La Chasse now hangs in the Musee de la Chasse et de la Nature in Paris.

Monet_w472.jpg.title: Bouquet de glaïeuls, lis et marguerites

source.canonical_title: File:Monet w472.jpg

title.de: Bouquet de glaïeuls, lis et marguerites
title.es: Bouquet de glaïeuls, lis et marguerites
title.fr: Bouquet de glaïeuls, lis et marguerites
title.nl: Bouquet de glaïeuls, lis et marguerites

Monet_w472.jpg.story: Vétheuil, 1878 — Monet had just fled Argenteuil for this smaller, cheaper village on the Seine, Camille was dying, money was gone, and he painted flowers. Gladioli, lilies, daisies crammed into a vase, handled with thick, bright, almost impatient strokes. The American railroad baron Collis P. Huntington picked it up at a New York auction in 1892; it stayed in private collections and was sold again at Sotheby's in 2018.

Monet_w502.jpg.title: Monet w502

source.canonical_title: File:Monet w502.jpg

Monet_w502.jpg.story: The road running out of Vétheuil toward La Roche-Guyon, 1878 — a dirt track, a scatter of houses, trees going coppery. Monet had just moved here from Argenteuil, broke and with a sick wife, and he painted the road home over and over through the changing seasons. Private collection.

source.canonical_title: File:Monet w526.jpg

Monet_w579_springtime_in_vetheuil.jpg.title: Monet w579 springtime in vetheuil

source.canonical_title: File:Monet w579 springtime in vetheuil.jpg

Monet_w579_springtime_in_vetheuil.jpg.story: A single tree erupts in pale blossom against a washed-out sky, and behind it the village of Vétheuil rises in soft dabs, a church spire breaking through. Monet was living here with a crowded household, the Hoschedés sharing the rent and Alice running the kitchen. Spring 1880 was a relief after the brutal thaw that had flooded his studio boat. You can feel the release in the brushwork, loose, quick, almost giddy. Catalogued as Wildenstein 579.

Monet_w58.jpg.title: Monet w58

source.canonical_title: File:Monet w58.jpg

Monet_w58.jpg.story: Fontainebleau, 1865 — Monet at 25, not yet the Monet of haystacks and lily ponds, painting the forest in a register closer to Courbet and the Barbizon painters he was trying to outgrow. A cart track runs into shadow under heavy trees; the brushwork is still tight, the palette dark-green and brown. The picture sits in the Sammlung Rau für UNICEF, now on long-term loan at the Arp Museum in Rolandseck.

Monet_w593(1).jpg.title: Poppy Field

source.canonical_title: File:Monet w593(1).jpg

Monet_w593(1).jpg.story: A field of red dots bursting across a green slope, treated with the same brushy indifference as the grass itself. Monet had painted poppy fields before, famously at Argenteuil in 1873, but the Vétheuil versions feel looser, less composed. No stroller with a parasol here, just the field. He was forty, widowed a year, broke, and working fast. The canvas is all surface, no fuss about distance. Wildenstein gave it number 593.

Monet_w601.jpg.title: Monet w601

source.canonical_title: File:Monet w601.jpg

Monet_w601.jpg.story: Vétheuil, 1880 — the Seine running low past the village, poplars along the far bank, sky taking up half the canvas. Monet had been in the village two years by then and was painting his way out of the worst stretch of his life: Camille had died the previous autumn. The picture has stayed in private hands.

Monet_w611.jpg.title: Monet w611

source.canonical_title: File:Monet w611.jpg

Monet_w611.jpg.story: Willows along the Seine, their drooping branches dissolving into reflection until water and trees become one green shimmer. Monet painted scores of riverbank studies in these Vétheuil years, each one a chance to watch what light does to leaves. This is Wildenstein 611, summer 1880. The horizon sits low, the eye drops into the water, and the whole thing hums in greens ticked with yellow. No narrative, no figures, just a patch of river he could walk to in ten minutes.

Monet_w646_jetty_at_fecamp_in_rough_weat.title: Monet w646 jetty at fecamp in rough weather
Monet_w646_jetty_at_fecamp_in_rough_weat.description: Jetty at Fecamp in rough weather

source.canonical_title: File:Monet w646 jetty at fecamp in rough weather.jpg

Monet_w646_jetty_at_fecamp_in_rough_weat.story: Monet went to the Normandy coast in spring 1881, rented a room in Fécamp, and painted the sea when the weather turned ugly. Here the jetty juts into a churning gray-green, spray breaking over the stone, the horizon lost in weather. He worked fast, sometimes finishing a canvas in a session before the light shifted again. This one is Wildenstein 646. It's the start of a decade where Monet would chase storms up and down the Channel coast, from Pourville to Belle-Île.

Monet_w647.jpg.title: At Fécamp, Seascape

source.canonical_title: File:Monet w647.jpg

Monet_w647.jpg.story: Sea piece at Fécamp. Monet climbed the cliffs above the Norman fishing town in 1881 and painted the Channel from the top, no foreground, no figures, just water and weather stacked to the horizon. The chalk headlands fall away at the edges; the sea does all the work. It's the same instinct that would drive him to Étretat the next year and eventually to the Creuse. Wildenstein catalogued it as number 647.

source.canonical_title: File:Monet w648.jpg

Monet_w649.jpg.title: Monet w649

source.canonical_title: File:Monet w649.jpg

Monet_w649.jpg.story: Fécamp, on the Normandy coast, spring 1881 — Monet had come up to stay near his brother Léon and spent a few weeks climbing the cliffs at Grainval with his easel. Chalk face dropping into the Channel, scrub clinging to the ledges, the water a hard green. Short, rapid strokes, the kind of thing he could set down while the light held. The painting passed through private collections.

Monet_w651_morning_by_the_sea.jpg.title: Monet w651 morning by the sea

source.canonical_title: File:Monet w651 morning by the sea.jpg

Monet_w651_morning_by_the_sea.jpg.story: Early light, a rocky shore, the water still half-asleep. Monet worked this seascape in 1881, during the final summer he and the Hoschedé household spent at Vétheuil before moving downstream to Poissy. The brush moves fast — pastel sky, a smudge of cliff on the horizon, waves built up in short wet strokes. You can almost hear the hiss of foam against stone. It's a study in how little paint it takes to make cold morning air. Listed as W651 in Daniel Wildenstein's catalogue raisonné.

Monet_w653.jpg.title: Monet w653

source.canonical_title: File:Monet w653.jpg

Monet_w653.jpg.story: Another of the Grainval cliff studies, 1881 — Monet scrambling around the chalk headlands south of Fécamp to catch the coast from a different angle. The foreground vegetation is done in quick dabs, the sea in broad horizontal sweeps. He'd come back to Normandy repeatedly over the next few years; these 1881 canvases are where the habit began.

Monet_w658.jpg.title: Monet w658

source.canonical_title: File:Monet w658.jpg

Monet_w658.jpg.story: March 1881. Monet had written to Durand-Ruel: "I'm leaving tomorrow for Fécamp where I'm going to do some seascapes." He stayed a month, knocking out roughly twenty canvases in the salt wind off the Côte d'Albâtre. This is one of them. Chalk cliffs, working boats, and a sky that shifts while you're still mixing paint. Monet was forty, newly widowed, broke, and Camille's death two years earlier had hollowed him out. The sea gave him something to fight. He finished many of these pieces back in the studio, but they were begun on the sand, in a hurry, with the tide closing in.
Monet_w658.jpg.year_note: Source listed 1840 (Monet's birth year). Fécamp seascape from Monet's March 1881 campaign.

Monet_w662.jpg.title: Monet w662

source.canonical_title: File:Monet w662.jpg

Monet_w662.jpg.story: A small seascape out of Monet's Normandy campaign. He was working in bursts along the Alabaster Coast, sometimes starting a canvas, abandoning it to the light, and beginning another twenty paces down the beach. This one stays with the water itself, horizon high, and builds the sea out of short, dragging strokes loaded wet into wet. Pigment is gritty where the wind kicked sand into it, a hazard Monet complained about in letters home. The painting passed through the Simonow collection and now sits in a private holding, catalogued W662 in Wildenstein.
Monet_w662.jpg.year_note: Source listed 1840 (Monet's birth year). Wildenstein 662, seascape c. 1881 (formerly Simonow collection).

Monet_w663.jpg.title: Monet w663

source.canonical_title: File:Monet w663.jpg

Monet_w663.jpg.story: Rough Sea, 1881, now at the National Gallery of Canada in Ottawa. Monet painted it on the beach at Fécamp or Les Petites-Dalles - he was shuttling between both that spring, staying part of the time with his brother Léon, a chemist who had a villa up the coast. Notice how little land there is: a sliver of cliff, a strip of sand, the rest churn. He was testing how much sky and water a canvas could hold before it tipped into abstraction. The answer, apparently, was: quite a lot.
Monet_w663.jpg.year_note: Source listed 1840 (Monet's birth year). 'Rough Sea,' National Gallery of Canada, 1881.

Monet_w664.jpg.title: Monet w664

source.canonical_title: File:Monet w664.jpg

Monet_w664.jpg.story: The cliffs at Les Petites-Dalles, painted in September 1880 on Monet's first trip to the little Norman resort where brother Léon had a summer house. He came for two weeks and ended up returning every year through 1886. The chalk face here catches hard morning light; the shadow at its foot is a cold violet, not black. Monet had just broken publicly with the Salon that spring and was painting to sell, to survive. Camille had died the previous September. The cliffs weren't a retreat - they were work.
Monet_w664.jpg.year_note: Source listed 1840 (Monet's birth year). Cliffs of Les Petites-Dalles, September 1880.

Monet_w668.jpg.title: Monet w668

source.canonical_title: File:Monet w668.jpg

Monet_w668.jpg.story: The Seine at Vétheuil at sunset. Monet had moved to the village on the Seine in 1878 with his wife Camille, the children, and the Hoschedé family - a chaotic blended household that only got messier when Camille died there in 1879. He painted the river obsessively: the same reach, different hours. Here the water holds more colour than the sky. He worked from his studio-boat, a modified fishing skiff moored at the bank, which let him sit low on the water and watch the reflections break up as barges went past.
Monet_w668.jpg.year_note: Source listed 1840 (Monet's birth year). Seine at Vétheuil (sunset), 1880.

Monet_w678_lane_in_ile_st_martin.jpg.title: Monet w678 lane in ile st martin

source.canonical_title: File:Monet w678 lane in ile st martin.jpg

Monet_w678_lane_in_ile_st_martin.jpg.story: A sunken cart track on the Île Saint-Martin, the low island in the Seine just opposite Vétheuil. Monet crossed here constantly in 1881 — it was walking distance from the house he shared with Alice Hoschedé and their combined brood of eight children. The lane is barely a lane: grass crowding the ruts, orchard trees leaning in, everything keyed to the same warm late-summer green. No grand view, no drama. Just the path you take when you're not going anywhere in particular. Catalogued as W678.

Monet_w679.jpg.title: Monet w679

source.canonical_title: File:Monet w679.jpg

Monet_w679.jpg.story: Vétheuil, 1880. The village sits on a horseshoe bend of the Seine about sixty kilometres northwest of Paris, and Monet painted it from every angle - across the water, from the hillside, in snow, in flood. He'd arrived in 1878 nearly destitute, sharing rent with Ernest Hoschedé, a bankrupt department-store owner whose wife Alice would eventually become Monet's second wife. By 1880 the arrangement was strange and permanent. The brushwork here is quick and comma-like; the church tower anchors the composition, as it does in dozens of other canvases from these years.
Monet_w679.jpg.year_note: Source listed 1840 (Monet's birth year). Vétheuil, c. 1880.

Monet_w683.jpg.title: Monet w683

source.canonical_title: File:Monet w683.jpg

Monet_w683.jpg.story: The garden at Vétheuil, summer 1881. Monet painted four closely related canvases of this same view: a path shaded by towering sunflowers, blue-and-white delft pots flanking the steps, a small child (probably his son Michel, or one of the Hoschedé boys) halfway up. He'd planted the garden himself, digging in soil that wasn't really his - he was renting. The sunflowers are almost at eye level. You can practically smell the dust in the gravel. Within two years Monet would leave Vétheuil for Giverny and start again from scratch.
Monet_w683.jpg.year_note: Source listed 1840 (Monet's birth year). Jardin à Vétheuil (Artist's Garden at Vétheuil), summer 1881.

Monet_w684.jpg.title: Monet w684

source.canonical_title: File:Monet w684.jpg

Monet_w684.jpg.story: Another of the 1881 Vétheuil garden studies - same sunflower-lined steps, same blue pots, different light.
