Monet worked in series long before the haystacks made it famous; at Vétheuil he already understood that painting the same thing twice wasn't repetition, it was how you caught time. The children on the steps are small, almost decorative. What he cared about was the yellow of the flower heads against the cool green behind them, a complementary clash that makes the whole canvas vibrate. The National Gallery of Art version of this motif is the best-known; this is one of its close siblings.
Monet_w684.jpg.year_note: Source listed 1840 (Monet's birth year). One of four Vétheuil garden canvases, 1881.

Monet_w691.jpg.title: Monet w691

source.canonical_title: File:Monet w691.jpg

Monet_w691.jpg.story: Vétheuil, Monet's garden again, but broader now - the flowers spilling toward the Seine instead of climbing the steps. He was at the end of his time in the village. The rent was unpaid, Durand-Ruel had started buying again after a long drought, and Alice Hoschedé was increasingly running the household. Note the warm pinks and oranges worked dry into the foliage; Monet liked to load a loaded brush and drag it, leaving a ridge of pigment you can see in raking light. In 1883 he'd move the whole tribe to Giverny.
Monet_w691.jpg.year_note: Source listed 1840 (Monet's birth year). Vétheuil garden, 1881.

Monet_w694.jpg.title: Monet w694

source.canonical_title: File:Monet w694.jpg

Monet_w694.jpg.story: Gladioli in a vase, 1881, an oil on canvas now at the Pola Museum of Art in Hakone, Japan. The canvas is tall and narrow - only 41 centimetres wide but nearly a metre high - to match the upright spike of the flowers themselves. Monet rarely painted still life compared to his friend Renoir, but when he did he went at it the same way he went at the river: quick, wet, loaded. These gladioli almost certainly came out of the Vétheuil garden, the same one feeding his sunflower paintings that summer. Cut, vased, and in the studio before they wilted.
Monet_w694.jpg.year_note: Source listed 1840 (Monet's birth year). 'Gladioli' still life, 1881, Pola Museum of Art.

Monet_w700_near_vetheuil.jpg.title: Monet w700 near vetheuil

source.canonical_title: File:Monet w700 near vetheuil.jpg

Monet_w700_near_vetheuil.jpg.story: Monet's last months at Vétheuil, painted from the fields above town before the family packed up for Poissy in December 1881. The hillside tips away toward the Seine, wheat and scrub catching a hazy light. He was forty-one, broke, and about to lose this view for good — the move downriver was driven by money and schools, not love of scenery. Maybe that's why the canvas feels so unhurried. Wildenstein number 700, from the final Vétheuil summer.

Monet_w706.jpg.title: Monet w706

source.canonical_title: File:Monet w706.jpg

Monet_w706.jpg.story: A seascape on the Normandy coast, 1882. After three difficult years at Vétheuil, Monet went back to the Channel that winter: Dieppe first, then Pourville in February, then Varengeville. He travelled cheaply, stayed in modest hotels, and painted in the cold. This canvas belongs to that campaign. The paint is dry and scratchy in the sky, wet and rolling in the water; you can see where the brush skipped over the tooth of the canvas and left little islands of unpainted ground. The cliffs of the Alabaster Coast were his subject, but really the weather was.
Monet_w706.jpg.year_note: Source listed 1840 (Monet's birth year). Normandy seascape from 1882 campaign.

Monet_w712_low_tide_at_pourville.jpg.title: Monet w712 low tide at pourville

source.canonical_title: File:Monet w712 low tide at pourville.jpg

Monet_w712_low_tide_at_pourville.jpg.story: Another low-tide day at Pourville, 1882. Wet sand takes the sky's reflection; a few tiny figures wander out where water used to be. Monet catalogued this one as W712 — part of a tight cluster of Pourville beach scenes from that summer, when he was running between motifs trying to keep up with the weather. The brushwork is quick and dry, the palette scrubbed: chalk, sand, pale blue. A painter in a hurry, doing some of his best work.

Monet_w717.jpg.title: Monet w717

source.canonical_title: File:Monet w717.jpg

Monet_w717.jpg.story: Pourville, 1882. Monet arrived in February after a short stop in Dieppe and stayed through April in the small fishing village west of the port. He later wrote that he sometimes worked on as many as eight canvases in a single day, carrying them up and down the cliff path as the light shifted. The sea here is that particular Channel green-grey, and the cliffs drop sheer to the beach. A tiny figure or two gives you the scale. Alice and the children joined him for part of the stay; the letters from Pourville are some of the most practical and least anguished Monet ever wrote.

Monet_w724.jpg.title: Monet w724

source.canonical_title: File:Monet w724.jpg

Monet_w724.jpg.story: Normandy coast, 1882. Part of the long winter-into-spring campaign Monet mounted that year along the Channel - Dieppe, Pourville, Varengeville - chasing weather. He had just come off a period of serious money trouble; Durand-Ruel's restarted buying was the only reason the trip was possible. You can see him thinking about Japanese prints here in the cropping, the way a cliff or a slope runs off the edge of the canvas instead of sitting politely inside it. He'd been collecting ukiyo-e since the 1870s, and by this point they were rearranging how he framed a view.
Monet_w724.jpg.year_note: Source listed 1840 (Monet's birth year). Normandy coast, 1882.

Monet_w726_the_church_at_varengeville_su.title: The Church of Varengeville, Sunset

source.canonical_title: File:Monet w726 the church at varengeville sunset.jpg

title.de: Die Kirche von Varengeville, untergehende Sonne

Monet_w726_the_church_at_varengeville_su.story: Sunset behind the Varengeville church — the stone dissolving into backlight, foreground foliage lit up like a struck match. Monet painted four sunset versions of this motif in 1882; this one, W726, was bought by the Barber Institute of Fine Arts in Birmingham, England, in 1938. It's the moment the building stops being architecture and becomes a silhouette, the cliff and the gorse suddenly more solid than the church itself. He finished the canvas back in the studio.

Monet_w736.jpg.title: Monet w736

source.canonical_title: File:Monet w736.jpg

Monet_w736.jpg.story: Another Normandy coast canvas from 1882. Monet was forty-one, finally starting to sell well enough to stop panicking about the rent, and painting the cliffs with a new confidence - long horizontal strokes in the sea, shorter upright ones in the chalk face, the whole thing built in maybe two or three sittings before he'd declare it blocked-in and move to the next. He kept several going at once on the beach. The salt air wasn't kind to the canvases; some of these works arrived back in Paris already slightly warped, and Durand-Ruel's framer had to nurse them flat.
Monet_w736.jpg.year_note: Source listed 1840 (Monet's birth year). Normandy coast, 1882.

Monet_w752.jpg.title: Monet w752

source.canonical_title: File:Monet w752.jpg

Monet_w752.jpg.story: A late canvas from the 1882 Normandy campaign. By April, Monet was heading home from Pourville with dozens of marines and cliff studies rolled and crated. It had been a turning-point trip: the sea paintings sold, Durand-Ruel kept buying, and within a year Monet would be able to move the household to Giverny and stop renting. You can feel some of that confidence in the brushwork - fewer hesitations, bigger shapes. The Côte d'Albâtre gave Monet the same subject Courbet and Daubigny had painted before him, but he came back with weather instead of scenery.
Monet_w752.jpg.year_note: Source listed 1840 (Monet's birth year). Late 1882 Normandy campaign.

Monet_w753.jpg.title: Monet w753

source.canonical_title: File:Monet w753.jpg

Monet_w753.jpg.story: February 1882, and Monet has fled a sour Paris winter for the Normandy coast. He settles in Pourville, a fishing village west of Dieppe, and spends two months hauling his easel up cliff paths and down to the shingle. This canvas, catalogued as Wildenstein 753, belongs to that burst of roughly thirty-six works he brought back — sky, cliff face, a slice of Channel water, all painted quickly before the light turned. Durand-Ruel bought the lot. No sitters, no story: just chalk cliffs and salt air.
Monet_w753.jpg.year_note: Source year 1840 was Monet's birth-year placeholder. Wildenstein 753 belongs to the 1882 Normandy/Pourville campaign (Wildenstein Vol. II covers 1882–1886, nos. 706–1122).

Monet_w757.jpg.title: Monet w757

source.canonical_title: File:Monet w757.jpg

Monet_w757.jpg.story: Monet rented a holiday house in Pourville after his 1882 Impressionist exhibition paid off, and for weeks he clambered along these clifftops with canvases strapped to his back. Here he paints directly into the sun: the cliff edge glows, wildflowers nod in the meadow grass, and sailboats drift on a sea that dissolves into the sky. The backlighting was the point — coast and water made to read as a single luminous thing. It's 60 by 73 cm, signed 1882, and hangs today at the Staatsgalerie Stuttgart.
Monet_w757.jpg.year_note: Source year 1840 was a placeholder. Staatsgalerie Stuttgart confirms 'Rand der Steilküste bei Pourville', 1882, inv. 60×73 cm.

Monet_w759.jpg.title: Monet w759

source.canonical_title: File:Monet w759.jpg

Monet_w759.jpg.story: Signed "Claude Monet 82" in the lower left, this is Dieppe seen from the cliffs — not the picturesque harbour but the raw geology behind it. Monet had tried Dieppe proper and found it too urban, too full of promenaders. So he walked out to where the chalk broke off into the Channel and worked there instead. The paint is scrubby, the horizon high, the sea a cold green-grey. It measures 65 by 81 cm and sits now in the Kunsthaus Zürich, accession 2252.
Monet_w759.jpg.year_note: Source year 1840 was a placeholder. Canvas is signed and dated 'Claude Monet 82', Kunsthaus Zürich accession 2252.

Monet_w764.jpg.title: Monet w764

source.canonical_title: File:Monet w764.jpg

Monet_w764.jpg.story: Another of the Normandy coast canvases Monet produced during his feverish 1882 campaign along the chalk cliffs between Dieppe and Pourville. He was painting fast — dozens of canvases in weeks — trying to fix the light before the Channel weather changed it. Look for the loose, hurried brushwork and a horizon that refuses to sit still. Catalogued as Wildenstein 764.
Monet_w764.jpg.year_note: Source year 1840 was a placeholder. Wildenstein 764 falls in the 1882 Pourville/Normandy campaign.

Monet_w767.jpg.title: Monet w767

source.canonical_title: File:Monet w767.jpg

Monet_w767.jpg.story: Low tide at Pourville exposes the jagged black rocks that the sea spends half its day hiding. Monet planted himself on the shore in 1882 and painted them bare — foam breaking white against the foreground teeth, the water beyond flecked grey. The angular shoreline pushes hard against smoother waves, the kind of collision Monet was beginning to hunt for. Emily Sibley Watson later gave the canvas to the Memorial Art Gallery in Rochester, where it hangs at 64 by 79 cm.
Monet_w767.jpg.year_note: Source year 1840 was a placeholder. Memorial Art Gallery, Rochester (inv. 39.22) dates 'The Rocks at Pourville, Low Tide' to 1882.

Monet_w772.jpg.title: Monet w772

source.canonical_title: File:Monet w772.jpg

Monet_w772.jpg.story: A patch of Channel water off Étretat, no cliffs in frame, no famous arch — just sea, sky, and a sliver of shore. Monet painted it in 1882, between the Pourville campaign and his later Étretat obsession with the Manneporte. It's a study in restraint: 55 by 74 cm of grey-green swell under a pearled sky. The Philadelphia Museum of Art holds it now, part of their substantial Monet collection.
Monet_w772.jpg.year_note: Source year 1840 was a placeholder. Dated 1882, Philadelphia Museum of Art collection (Marine near Étretat).

Monet_w776.jpg.title: Monet w776

source.canonical_title: File:Monet w776.jpg

Monet_w776.jpg.story: This belongs to a run of roughly sixteen canvases Monet painted looking west from the Pourville cliffs toward the setting sun — Wildenstein numbers 776 through 791, more or less. He'd often climb down the steep Moutiers Gorge trail to reach his vantage. The evening light here is the whole point: sea and sky pinked and bronzed, the cliff edge going dark. It stayed in private hands after leaving his studio.
Monet_w776.jpg.year_note: Source year 1840 was a placeholder. Part of the Wildenstein 776–791 Pourville cliff/sunset series, all painted Feb–April 1882.

Monet_w778a.jpg.title: Monet w778a

source.canonical_title: File:Monet w778a.jpg

Monet_w778a.jpg.story: Pointe de l'Ailly at low tide, 1882. Monet walked out along the headland west of Pourville when the sea had pulled back far enough to leave puddles of Channel water glinting in the foreground. The composition is unusually horizontal — 60 by 100 cm — with the horizon slung right across the middle, so the eye moves between tide pools and distant cliff like a slow sweep. The canvas belongs now to the Kerry Stokes Collection in Perth, Australia.
Monet_w778a.jpg.year_note: Source year 1840 was a placeholder. 'Pointe de l'Ailly, marée basse', 1882, 60×100 cm, Kerry Stokes Collection.

Monet_w787.jpg.title: Monet w787

source.canonical_title: File:Monet w787.jpg

Monet_w787.jpg.story: Another of Monet's westward-facing Pourville cliff views from 1882, part of the Wildenstein 776–791 cluster painted from vantage points he reached via the Moutiers Gorge. The cliff mass fills the left, the Channel opens beyond, and the brushwork is fast — he was working against the light more than the weather. Monet returned home to Poissy in mid-April with almost forty canvases; this one went with him.
Monet_w787.jpg.year_note: Source year 1840 was a placeholder. Part of the W776–791 Pourville westward-sunset cluster, 1882.

Monet_w807.jpg.title: Monet w807

source.canonical_title: File:Monet w807.jpg

Monet_w807.jpg.story: The Normandy cliffs again, 1882 — Monet hauling his easel up another chalk bluff between Dieppe and Pourville while the light moved faster than he could. The Pourville and Varengeville campaigns that spring produced a small mountain of work, most of which Durand-Ruel promptly bought to keep his painter afloat through the French economic slump. This one, Wildenstein 807, keeps the same fast, scrubby handling of sea and stone.
Monet_w807.jpg.year_note: Source year 1840 was a placeholder. Wildenstein 807 falls within the 1882 Normandy campaign (Vol. II covers 1882–1886).

Monet_w81.jpg.title: Monet w81

source.canonical_title: File:Monet w81.jpg

Monet_w81.jpg.story: January 1867, and Monet is twenty-six and broke. Camille is pregnant, his family in Le Havre is furious, and a heavy snowfall has blanketed the road past the Ferme Saint-Siméon near Honfleur — the farm where Boudin and Jongkind had taught him to paint outdoors. He goes out anyway with his easel. The result is one of his earliest snow scenes, bare trees black against the white lane, part of his first real serial experiment: he'd paint this same road at least ten times between 1864 and 1867.
Monet_w81.jpg.year_note: Source year 1840 was Monet's birth-year placeholder. Wildenstein 81 is the Saint-Siméon farm winter scene, painted January 1867 during a heavy snowfall near Honfleur.

Monet_w812_vase_of_chrysantemums.png.title: Monet w812 vase of chrysantemums

source.canonical_title: File:Monet w812 vase of chrysantemums.png

Monet_w812_vase_of_chrysantemums.png.story: Monet was a gardener first, painter second — he'd say so himself. Between 1878 and 1883 he turned out roughly twenty floral still lifes, and this shaggy tumble of chrysanthemums belongs to that run. The petals don't so much sit in the vase as erupt from it, mop-headed and slightly unkempt. Forget botanical precision: he's after the way light snags on a curled edge. Wildenstein catalogued it as W812, dating it around 1882.

Monet_w816.jpg.title: Monet w816

source.canonical_title: File:Monet w816.jpg

Monet_w816.jpg.story: Catalogued by Wildenstein as W816, this Monet still life sits in the cluster of flower pieces he produced around 1882, when his Poissy studio was doubling as a greenhouse-in-reverse — cut blooms hauled indoors, painted fast before they drooped. Monet later grumbled that flower painting was harder than landscape because the subject wilted on you. The brushwork here is loose and hungry, chasing petals before the light shifted on the windowsill.

Monet_w822.jpg.title: Hollowed Cliff near Étretat

source.canonical_title: File:Monet w822.jpg

Monet_w822.jpg.story: Wildenstein W822, painted at Étretat around 1884: the Porte d'Aval arch hollowed out against a bruised sky, the cliff a slab of weathered chalk. Monet kept returning to these three arches — Manneporte, Aval, Amont — in all weathers, convinced each hour repainted them. He worked from a skiff when the tide allowed, from the beach when it didn't. Here the rock goes ochre and violet, the sea a skin of agitated green.

Monet_w835.jpg.title: Monet w835

source.canonical_title: File:Monet w835.jpg

Monet_w835.jpg.story: Port-Villez sits on the Seine just across from Giverny, and in 1883 — the year Monet moved into the pink house that would anchor the rest of his life — he rowed across and painted the bend of the river from a boat moored in the current. The bluff rises on the far bank, dawn pink just catching the top of it. He'd return to this exact stretch of water again and again over the next decade; this canvas is among the earliest of those looks.
Monet_w835.jpg.year_note: Source year 1840 was a placeholder. Wildenstein 835 is from the early Port-Villez group, dated 1883.

Monet_w844.jpg.title: Monet w844

source.canonical_title: File:Monet w844.jpg

Monet_w844.jpg.story: The collégiale Notre-Dame at Vernon, seen from the Seine — the medieval church that rises above the town just downstream of Monet's new home at Giverny. He painted it three times in 1883, the year he moved in, mostly from a boat. A decade later he'd return to the same motif and turn out a full serial meditation on mist and architecture (Wildenstein 1386–1391). This is the first look, more straightforward, less dissolved.
Monet_w844.jpg.year_note: Source year 1840 was a placeholder. One of three views of the collégiale Notre-Dame de Vernon Monet painted in 1883; the later Vernon series is W1386–1391 (1894).

Monet_w849.jpg.title: Monet w849
Monet_w849.jpg.description: Claude Monet, Poppies in a Vase, W.849

source.canonical_title: File:Monet w849.jpg

Monet_w867.jpg.title: Monet w867

source.canonical_title: File:Monet w867.jpg

Monet_w867.jpg.story: "Maison du jardinier" — the gardener's house, tucked somewhere in the cliff-backed landscape Monet worked during his Étretat campaigns of the mid-1880s. He'd rented rooms in the village every winter between 1883 and 1886, usually in the off-season when the resort emptied out and the light on the chalk turned hard and cold. Most of those canvases fixate on the three great rock arches; this one looks inland instead, to a quieter building with a roof and a garden.
Monet_w867.jpg.year_note: Source year 1840 was a placeholder. Wildenstein 867 'Maison du jardinier' belongs to the 1883 Étretat campaign (Vol. II, 1882–1886).

Monet_w868.jpg.title: Monet w868

source.canonical_title: File:Monet w868.jpg

Monet_w868.jpg.story: Early 1884, and Monet has traded the Channel for the Italian Riviera. He's in Bordighera, just across the French border, painting the Moreno gardens and dazzled by olive trees he'd never seen in full Mediterranean light. This is a study — "Étude d'oliviers," 73 by 60 cm — one of the tighter, quieter pieces from a trip that would produce about fifty canvases and nearly break him ("this blue, this pink" he complained in letters, "I can't manage it"). It stayed in private hands.
Monet_w868.jpg.year_note: Source year 1840 was a placeholder. 'Étude d'oliviers', 73×60 cm, painted during Monet's first quarter 1884 trip to Bordighera, not 1883.

Monet_w871.jpg.title: Monet w871
Monet_w871.jpg.description: Claude Monet, Study of Olive Trees in Bordighera, W.871

source.canonical_title: File:Monet w871.jpg

Monet_w875.jpg.title: Monet w875
Monet_w875.jpg.description: Claude Monet, Palm Trees Bordighera, W.875

source.canonical_title: File:Monet w875.jpg

Monet_w885.jpg.title: Monet w885

source.canonical_title: File:Monet w885.jpg

Monet_w885.jpg.story: Perched above the Nervia, Monet pins down Dolceacqua from the south: the Doria towers stepping up on the right, the little bell tower of Sant'Antonio tucked lower to the left. He had come to Bordighera in early 1884 to chase light he'd only glimpsed from Menton with Renoir. A 65 by 81 cm canvas, it stayed with his son Michel at Giverny for decades before drifting into private hands around 1972.
Monet_w885.jpg.year_note: Wildenstein catalogue no. 885, painted in Bordighera 1884

Monet_w891a.jpg.title: Monet w891a

source.canonical_title: File:Monet w891a.jpg

Monet_w891a.jpg.story: An unsigned, half-finished portrait of a bearded, beret-wearing Monet slouched with a cigarette, arms on his thighs, a Cap Martin landscape hanging behind him. Long paraded as a Monet self-portrait, then reattributed by Wildenstein to Sargent in 1979, then re-upgraded to Monet in 1996 after Wildenstein himself had bought it. Joachim Pissarro argues it's Charles Giron's, based on an 1885 diary entry describing an hour-long sitting at Giverny. In 2020 the Musee Marmottan downgraded it.
Monet_w891a.jpg.year_note: Wildenstein 891a; attribution contested, possibly by Charles Giron, not Monet

Monet_w891b.jpg.title: Monet w891b

source.canonical_title: File:Monet w891b.jpg

Monet_w891b.jpg.story: A big studio canvas, 1.39 by 1.80 m, worked up at Giverny from the smaller Corniche de Monaco study (W890) Monet had brought home. The path hugs Cap Martin with the Tete de Chien looming over Monte-Carlo and the rock of Monaco in the distance. Durand-Ruel bought it off him in May 1885; it later appeared as a backdrop in John Singer Sargent's portrait of Monet before passing through Chicago and into private American hands.
Monet_w891b.jpg.year_note: Wildenstein catalogue no. 891, large studio canvas after W890

Monet_w892.jpg.title: Monet w892

source.canonical_title: File:Monet w892.jpg

Monet_w892.jpg.story: Painted from the lower corniche road near Roquebrune, looking down on Monte-Carlo with the Tete de Chien as backdrop. 65 by 81 cm, signed but not dated. Part of the haul Monet brought back from his 1884 Riviera campaign, when he complained to Alice that the blue and pink of the Mediterranean were impossible and that nobody would believe him. The canvas passed through Potter Palmer of Chicago and Wildenstein before landing with the Somlo collection in New York.

Monet_w904.jpg.title: Monet w904
Monet_w904.jpg.description: Claude Monet, Cliffs at Les Petites-Dalles, W.904

source.canonical_title: File:Monet w904.jpg

File:Monet w928.jpg

Monet_w948.jpg.title: Monet w948

source.canonical_title: File:Monet w948.jpg

Monet_w948.jpg.story: A still life of flowers, probably rhododendrons, set against a dark ground so the blooms read almost like specimens under glass. Monet painted perhaps twenty floral still lifes between 1878 and 1883, partly because they sold faster than his landscapes when he was short on rent. He liked the discipline of the genre: no weather to chase, no tide coming in, just the problem of how a white petal turns green in shadow. This canvas is in a private collection.

Monet_w961.jpg.title: Monet w961

source.canonical_title: File:Monet w961.jpg

Monet_w961.jpg.story: A winter scene, the kind of motif Monet kept returning to after his move to Giverny: bare trees, a flat sky, snow that isn't really white. He once told a visitor that snow was the hardest thing of all to paint because every painter before him had got it wrong and made it the colour of paper. He preferred lilacs, blues, pale ochres. This canvas is held in a private collection.

Monet_w962.jpg.title: Monet w962

source.canonical_title: File:Monet w962.jpg

Monet_w962.jpg.story: The Seine near Port-Villez in winter, a stretch of river a short walk downstream from Giverny where Monet often took his easel when the garden was dead and snow sat on the banks. He painted this corner in most seasons from the mid-1880s onward, renting a boat to reach the motifs he wanted. The trees here are stripped bare; the water runs a cold grey-green. This canvas is in a private collection.

Monet_w965.jpg.title: Coming into Giverny in the Snow

source.canonical_title: File:Monet w965.jpg

Monet_w965.jpg.story: The path into Giverny disappears under a quiet layer of snow, poplars standing like pencil strokes against the flat winter light. This is Wildenstein 965, one of a small group Monet painted soon after renting the pink house in April 1883. The snow reads almost lavender where it meets the shadows — a trick he'd keep using his whole life.

Monet_w977.jpg.title: House at Falaise in the Fog

source.canonical_title: File:Monet w977.jpg

Monet_w977.jpg.story: Fog eats the middle distance. A tile roof pokes through, then a suggestion of chimney, and the cliff behind is barely a rumor. Monet made this during the same hard winter he spent tramping the Normandy coast around Étretat and Falaise, and the canvas is catalogued as Wildenstein 977.

Monet_w982.jpg.title: Monet w982
Monet_w982.jpg.description: Claude Monet, Trees by the River Springtime in Giverny, W.982

source.canonical_title: File:Monet w982.jpg

Monet_w986.jpg.title: Monet w986
Monet_w986.jpg.description: Claude Monet, Spring in Giverny Morning Effect, W.986

source.canonical_title: File:Monet w986.jpg
File:Monet w996.jpg

Monet_w_106.jpg.title: Monet w 106

source.canonical_title: File:Monet w 106.jpg

Monet_w_106.jpg.story: A quiet river scene from 1868, one of the unnamed early landscapes catalogued simply as Wildenstein 106 in Daniel Wildenstein's four-volume raisonné of Monet's work. Painted during the same broke, itinerant stretch that produced The Magpie and the Frankfurt Luncheon, when Monet was shuttling between Le Havre, Étretat, and Bennecourt with Camille and baby Jean in tow. The dated inscription places it to August 1868.

Monet_w_208.jpg.title: Monet w 208

source.canonical_title: File:Monet w 208.jpg

Monet_w_208.jpg.story: Rouen in 1872, and Monet is watching the Seine do its working-harbour business: ships riding at anchor, quays busy, a pale cathedral-town sky. He had come up from Argenteuil to visit his brother Leon, who lived in the area, and he used the trip to knock out a handful of river views. The brushwork is breezy, almost offhand, sails and masts struck in as quick verticals against the horizontal drift of water. Decades later he would return to paint Rouen's cathedral thirty times over. This 1872 Seine scene is catalogued as Wildenstein 208.

Monet_w_235.jpg.title: Monet w 235

source.canonical_title: File:Monet w 235.jpg

Monet_w_235.jpg.story: The Seine at Argenteuil, painted the year Monet settled there with Camille and their young son Jean. You can tell he's still getting the lay of the water: the reflections are sharper than in his later canvases, the boats more carefully drawn, the sky given room to breathe. Argenteuil was a sailing town, a factory town, and a weekend town all at once, and Monet's eye moved between those registers without fuss. The brushwork is quick but the composition is classical. The painting is listed in the Wildenstein catalogue as number 235.

Monet_w_272_Apple_Trees_in_Bloom.jpg.title: Monet w 272 Apple Trees in Bloom

source.canonical_title: File:Monet w 272 Apple Trees in Bloom.jpg

Monet_w_272_Apple_Trees_in_Bloom.jpg.story: Spring had barely caught its breath when Monet set up in this orchard. The trunks lean like old gossips; the blossom is laid on in short, crowded strokes that almost itch to fall. Painted at Argenteuil, the Paris suburb where he and Camille rented a riverside house and where he cranked out roughly 170 canvases between 1871 and 1878. The catalogue number is Wildenstein 272.

Monet_w_290_autumn_effect_in_argenteuil..title: Monet w 290 autumn effect in argenteuil
Monet_w_290_autumn_effect_in_argenteuil..description: Monet w 290 autumn effect in argenteuil

source.canonical_title: File:Monet w 290 autumn effect in argenteuil.jpg

Monet_w_338.jpg.title: Monet w 338

source.canonical_title: File:Monet w 338.jpg

Monet_w_338.jpg.story: Catalogued as Wildenstein 338 in the standard reference on Monet compiled by Daniel Wildenstein, this canvas belongs to the 1874 run at Argenteuil, when Monet was painting the Seine and its boats almost daily from his floating studio. The Wildenstein catalogue raisonné eventually accounted for some 2,050 paintings across four volumes, published from 1974 onward.

Monet_w_42.jpg.title: Monet w 42

source.canonical_title: File:Monet w 42.jpg

Monet_w_42.jpg.story: An early portrait from around 1864-65, when Monet was in his mid-twenties and still supporting himself partly through figure commissions. The Wildenstein catalogue lists a handful of portraits from these years - of friends, family, and the occasional paying sitter - before he gave the genre up almost entirely for landscape. The sober palette and tight handling are a world away from the Giverny canvases, which is partly the point: you can see him looking hard at Courbet, at Manet, at what a serious young painter was supposed to do.

source.canonical_title: File:Monet w 763 the path.jpg

Moreno_Garden_Bordighera_1884_-_The_Nort.title: Moreno Garden Bordighera 1884 - The Norton Museum Miami Florida
Moreno_Garden_Bordighera_1884_-_The_Nort.description: Painting by Claude Monet visiting Bordighera 1884

source.canonical_title: File:Moreno Garden Bordighera 1884 - The Norton Museum Miami Florida.jpg

Moreno_Garden_Bordighera_1884_-_The_Nort.story: Monet arrived in Bordighera in January 1884 and immediately begged his way into the Moreno estate — reportedly the finest garden on the Riviera, a jungle of palms, olives, and citrus. He wrote to Alice that the colours were so intense he feared nobody would believe them. This canvas is pure Mediterranean delirium, greens shot through with pink and gold. It now hangs at the Norton Museum of Art in West Palm Beach, Florida.
Moreno_Garden_Bordighera_1884_-_The_Nort.year_note: Metadata year was 1883; painting is dated 1884 (Monet arrived in Bordighera January 1884). Norton Museum is in West Palm Beach, Florida, not Miami — filename is misleading.

Morning_Mist_in_Taj_Mahal,_no._5,_Hirosh.title: Morning Mist in Taj Mahal, no. 5
Morning_Mist_in_Taj_Mahal,_no._5,_Hirosh.description: Morning Mist in Taj Mahal, no. 5, Hiroshi yoshida

source.canonical_title: File:Morning Mist in Taj Mahal, no. 5, Hiroshi yoshida.jpg

Mortlake_Terrace_A11264.jpg.title: Mortlake Terrace

source.canonical_title: File:Mortlake Terrace A11264.jpg

Mortlake_Terrace_A11264.jpg.story: Turner painted the terrace at The Limes, William Moffatt's Thames-side house near Kew, looking straight into the setting sun. Here's the legend: Edwin Landseer dropped by the Academy varnishing day, thought the scene needed a dark accent, cut a little dog out of black paper and stuck it on the parapet. Turner came back from lunch and left it there. The paper dog is still on the canvas, which hangs at the National Gallery of Art in Washington.

Mother_of_Pearl_and_Silver_The_Andalusia.title: Mother of Pearl and Silver: The Andalusian

source.canonical_title: File:Mother of Pearl and Silver The Andalusian.jpg

Mother_of_Pearl_and_Silver_The_Andalusia.story: The model is Ethel Birnie Philip, Whistler's sister-in-law and secretary, got up in a Spanish-inflected grey silk gown with a gauzy bolero on top. Whistler fiddled with the canvas from 1888 until 1900, which is why the National Gallery of Art dates it across that whole stretch. One historian said it isn't a portrait of a person but a portrait of a dress. It went to the Exposition Universelle in Paris the year he finally let it go.

Mr._Carlyle_delivering_the_address_on_hi.title: Mr. Carlyle delivering the address on his installation as Lord Rector of Edinburgh University, April 2, 1866
Mr._Carlyle_delivering_the_address_on_hi.description: Engraving Carlyle giving his Edinburgh speech from the Illustrated London News, 1881

source.canonical_title: File:Mr. Carlyle delivering the address on his installation as Lord Rector of Edinburgh University, April 2, 1866.jpg

Mr._Carlyle_delivering_the_address_on_hi.story: A wood engraving from the Illustrated London News commemorating Thomas Carlyle's rectorial address at Edinburgh, where the aging Scottish sage stands with one arm raised before a bench of formally robed academics. Carlyle had been elected rector by the students and spoke without notes for over an hour on the duties of books and learning. The speech was a triumph; within a fortnight his wife Jane died while he was away, and he never really recovered. The print was reissued in 1881, the year of Carlyle's own death, which is probably when this impression was pulled.

Mu-ch'i_001.jpg.title: Eight Views of Xiao-Xiang, Detail: Evening Glow over a Fishing Village

source.canonical_title: File:Mu-ch'i 001.jpg
source.credit: The Yorck Project (2002) 10.000 Meisterwerke der Malerei (DVD-ROM), distributed by DIRECTMEDIA Publishing GmbH. ISBN : 3936122202 .

Mu-ch'i_001.jpg.story: Detail from one of the Eight Views of Xiao and Xiang, attributed to the Chan monk Muqi and now cut up between collections in Japan. Mountains dissolve into wet haze behind a fishing village; the foreground trees are done in a few soaked brush-loads; three tiny boats float on nothing. Chinese critics of the Ming dynasty thought Muqi too rough, too unscholarly, and let his work drift to Kyoto. Tea masters there treated these scrolls as sacred objects. Most of his surviving oeuvre is still in Japan.

title.de: Apotheose. Das Slawentum für die Menschheit

Mucha_Apoteoza.jpg.story: The final canvas of the Slav Epic, unveiled in 1926 as the twenty-painting cycle's summation — egg tempera and oil, a wall-sized 480 by 405 centimetres. Mucha organised the composition by colour rather than setting: blue for ancient myth, red for the medieval flourishing, black for occupation, gold for the 1918 liberation that let Czechoslovakia exist. A giant Slav stands at the centre holding wreaths of freedom and unity; a faint Christ blesses the nations behind him. The rainbow arcing over the whole thing is peace. National Gallery Prague.

Mucha_seasons_1897_spring.jpg.title: Mucha seasons 1897 spring

source.canonical_title: File:Mucha seasons 1897 spring.jpg

Mucha_seasons_1897_spring.jpg.story: This is Spring from Mucha's second Seasons set, the 1897 follow-up to his runaway 1896 hit. Champenois wanted more of the same and Mucha obliged, but reworked the figures into taller, narrower panels. Spring stands barefoot in blossom, fingers threading a lyre strung with her own hair while songbirds gather at her feet — the music practically drawn as a stave of curves around her head. Printed as a colour lithograph and sold cheaply, it was exactly the sort of secular icon a Parisian could tack to a wall next to the calendar.

Munch_-_Self-Portrait_with_Palette,_1926.title: Self-Portrait with Palette

source.canonical_title: File:Munch - Self-Portrait with Palette, 1926, Lot 114.jpg

Munch_-_Self-Portrait_with_Palette,_1926.story: Munch at Ekely, sixty-two, holding his palette and brushes like a man on duty. He sold the canvas the year he painted it to the Kunsthalle in Mannheim, a rare case of a living Munch going straight to a museum. Seven years later the Nazis seized it during the Degenerate Art purge; it came back to market and eventually to the Olsen collection in Norway, passing through Sotheby's in 2021. The face is frank, a little wary. The palette is the only thing between him and the viewer.

Murillo_Descanso_en_la_huida_a_Egipto.jp.title: Rest on the Flight into Egypt
Murillo_Descanso_en_la_huida_a_Egipto.jp.description: Descanso en la huida a Egipto pintura al óleo de Bartolomé Esteban Murillo, se conserva en el museo del Hermitage en San Petersburgo 180 x 136 cm

source.canonical_title: File:Murillo Descanso en la huida a Egipto.jpg

title.es: Descanso en la huida a Egipto
title.fr: Le repos pendant la fuite en Égypte
title.ja: エジプト逃避途上の休息 (ムリーリョ)
title.th: พระเยซูหนี ไปอียิปต์
title.ru: Отдых святого семейства на пути в Египет
title.it: Riposo durante la fuga in Egitto

Murillo_Descanso_en_la_huida_a_Egipto.jp.story: The donkey drowses, the gourds are full, and Jesus has finally fallen asleep on his mother's lap while two small cherubs fuss above. Murillo paints the very end of a long day on the road to Egypt, all warm browns and the cooled blue of a Castilian dusk. Measuring 136 by 180 centimetres, it entered the Hermitage in 1768 with the Parisian Gaignat collection and has hung in Room 239 since the 1840s.

Musizierender_Einsiedler_vor_seiner_Fels.title: Musizierender Einsiedler vor seiner Felsenklause

source.canonical_title: File:Musizierender Einsiedler vor seiner Felsenklause (Carl Spitzweg).jpg

Musizierender_Einsiedler_vor_seiner_Fels.story: A grey-bearded hermit sits on a rock outside his grotto playing a violin to nobody in particular, his few chickens scratching at his feet. Spitzweg returned to the hermit type again and again, half-mocking the Romantic ideal and half-envying it. A related version, The Hermit in Front of His Retreat, became in 1900 the very first painting acquired by the Städel Museum in Frankfurt.

NDL-DC_1302763-Tsukioka_Yoshitoshi-芳年武者无.story: From 'Yoshitoshi musha burui' — 'Yoshitoshi's Incomparable Warriors,' his 1883 series of single-sheet prints pitting famous fighters of Japanese history against each other. This one sets the young Minamoto no Ushiwakamaru — the future hero Yoshitsune — against the bandit chief Kumasaka Chohan in their legendary midnight duel. Ushiwakamaru, still a boy, killed the far larger brigand with supernatural speed. Yoshitoshi handles the clash as a blur of drapery and blade, the mature warrior looming, the child balletic. The series caught him in his prime before the quieter 'Moon' work took over.

NDL-DC_2586549-03_Kawase_Hasui_S02_crd.j.description: Morning on the Daikon Wharf (Daikon-gashi no asa), from the series Twenty Views of Tōkyō (Tōkyō nijūkei)

NDL-DC_2586549-03_Kawase_Hasui_S02_crd.j.story: Daikon-gashi — Radish Wharf — was a riverside market along a Tokyo canal, named for the crates of daikon once unloaded there. Hasui sets the scene at early morning: pale water, long shadows, the small bustle of a working waterfront waking up. Part of Twenty Views of Tokyo, dated 1927. Like most of the series, it pairs a documentary interest in specific Tokyo places with a compositional calm that owes as much to Hiroshige as to any Western source.

NDL-DC_2586549-04_Kawase_Hasui_S03_crd.j.title: Kiyomizu-dō Temple in Ueno
NDL-DC_2586549-04_Kawase_Hasui_S03_crd.j.description: Kiyomizu-dō Temple in Ueno (Ueno Kiyomizu-dō), from the series Twenty Views of Tōkyō (Tōkyō nijūkei)

NDL-DC_2586549-04_Kawase_Hasui_S03_crd.j.story: The Kiyomizu-dō in Ueno is a modest vermilion hall modeled after its famous Kyoto namesake, with a stage jutting out over the slope. Hasui returned to it repeatedly — most famously in the snow — but here it's part of his Twenty Views of Tōkyō, one of a run of prints surveying a capital still rebuilding after 1923. His Ueno leans on atmosphere over monument: the architecture half-veiled by trees, the palette keyed to a single time of day. Watanabe Shōzaburō published the set; it helped establish Hasui as shin-hanga's premier Tokyo chronicler.

NDL-DC_2586549-10_Kawase_Hasui_S04_crd.j.title: Shinobazu Pond in Rain
NDL-DC_2586549-10_Kawase_Hasui_S04_crd.j.description: Shinobazu Pond in Rain (Shinobazu no ike no ame), from the series Twenty Views of Tōkyō (Tōkyō nijūkei)

NDL-DC_2586549-10_Kawase_Hasui_S04_crd.j.story: Shinobazu Pond, in the middle of Ueno, has the small Benten temple set on its islet. Hasui paints it all in rain — umbrellas dotted along the bank, the temple softened by grey, reflections broken by the surface. Rain is his signature subject; the bokashi gradients and streaked lines of downpour are the kind of thing a shin-hanga team of carver and printer could execute beautifully from his watercolor studies. From Twenty Views of Tōkyō, 1929, published by Watanabe Shōzaburō, vertical ōban — now held at institutions including the Art Institute of Chicago and the Edo-Tokyo Museum.

NDL-DC_2586549-13_Kawase_Hasui_T15_crd.j.title: Kōjaku cavern at Oga Peninsula
NDL-DC_2586549-13_Kawase_Hasui_T15_crd.j.description: Kōjaku cavern at Oga Peninsula (Oga Hantō, Kōjaku no Iwaya), from the series Souvenirs of Travel III (Tabi miyage dai sanshū)

NDL-DC_2586549-13_Kawase_Hasui_T15_crd.j.story: Kojaku no Iwaya — Peacock Cave — can only be entered from the water, so Hasui must have hired a boat to reach this vantage inside it. The 1926 print flexes the shin-hanga printer's toolkit: deep bokashi gradations in the cave walls, glossy wavelets on the water, a bright slice of sea framed by darkness. Part of Souvenirs of Travel III, published by Watanabe Shozaburo. The Oga Peninsula is now a quasi-national park.

NDL-DC_2586549-14_Kawase_Hasui_S02_crd.j.title: Karasu Marsh, Akita
NDL-DC_2586549-14_Kawase_Hasui_S02_crd.j.description: Karasu Marsh, Akita (Akita Karasunuma), from the series Souvenirs of Travel III (Tabi miyage dai sanshū)

NDL-DC_2586549-14_Kawase_Hasui_S02_crd.j.story: A rare warm-weather print in an artist better known for snow and rain. Karasu Marsh, somewhere in rural Akita, on a still summer afternoon: a tall pine in the foreground, dried grasses paling against green distant hills, and the whole scene doubled in the flat mirror of the lake. Part of Souvenirs of Travel III (1927), published by Watanabe Shozaburo. Hasui had traveled through northern Honshu the previous year and brought back enough material for several prints.

NDL-DC_2586549-15_Kawase_Hasui_S02_crd.j.title: Hachirōgata Lagoon, Akita
NDL-DC_2586549-15_Kawase_Hasui_S02_crd.j.description: Hachirōgata Lagoon, Akita (Akita Hachirōgata), from the series Souvenirs of Travel III (Tabi miyage dai sanshū)

NDL-DC_2586549-15_Kawase_Hasui_S02_crd.j.story: Hachirogata was, in 1927, Japan's second-largest lake — a vast brackish lagoon in Akita, long since mostly drained for farmland in the postwar years. Hasui caught it while it was still water: an unseen moon throwing shadows across a wooden building, three stars pricking through between branches, the reeds and shoreline dissolving into early-evening blue. It belongs to Souvenirs of Travel III, the series he built from sketches made on a 102-day swing through the Hokuriku, San'in and San'yō regions. The print now doubles as a quiet record of a landscape that no longer exists.

NDL-DC_2586549-18_Kawase_Hasui_S03_crd.j.title: Starlit Night at Miyajima
NDL-DC_2586549-18_Kawase_Hasui_S03_crd.j.description: Starlit Night at Miyajima (Hoshizukiyo [Miyajima]), from the series Souvenirs of Travel III (Tabi miyage dai sanshū)

NDL-DC_2586549-18_Kawase_Hasui_S03_crd.j.story: The great torii of Itsukushima rises out of calm water, flanked by silhouetted trees and distant mountains, with a scattering of stars and a warm lantern throwing the only non-blue note in the image. Hasui restricts his palette almost entirely to graded indigo, which is where the print does its work — the color has to carry the hush. It's a vertical ōban from 1928, signed Hasui and sealed Kawase, part of Souvenirs of Travel III and published by Watanabe Shōzaburō. Few shin-hanga night scenes are better known.

NDL-DC_2586549-19_Kawase_Hasui_S03_crd.j.description: Hōrai Rock, Kiso River (Kisogawa Hōraiiwa), from the series Souvenirs of Travel III (Tabi miyage dai sanshū)

NDL-DC_2586549-19_Kawase_Hasui_S03_crd.j.story: Hōrai Rock is a craggy outcrop in the Kiso River, on the border of Gifu and Aichi, named after the mythical island of immortals. Hasui renders it in full daylight — an unusual choice for him — with green water curling past the stone and pines picking up highlights. The print belongs to Souvenirs of Travel III, drawn from sketches made during his long 1923–24 trip through western Japan. It is one of a few images in the set where Hasui works in clear, dry weather rather than his signature mist and rain.

NDL-DC_2586549-20_Kawase_Hasui_S03_crd.j.description: Kamezaki in Owari Province (Bishū Kamezaki), from the series Souvenirs of Travel III (Tabi miyage dai sanshū)

NDL-DC_2586549-20_Kawase_Hasui_S03_crd.j.story: Kamezaki is a fishing district on the Chita Peninsula south of Nagoya, in what used to be called Owari Province. Hasui shows it at night: a path curling away, moonlight on low tiled roofs, the whole composition quieter and smaller-scaled than his coastal set-pieces. Like the other Souvenirs of Travel III prints, it comes out of the sketches he accumulated during the 102-day 1923–24 trek — the longest sketching journey of his life. Published by Watanabe Shōzaburō in 1928, vertical ōban, signed Hasui with the Kawase seal.

NDL-DC_2586549-22_Kawase_Hasui_S03_crd.j.description: Nishi Park, Fukuoka (Fukuoka Nishi kōen), from the series Souvenirs of Travel III (Tabi miyage dai sanshū)

NDL-DC_2586549-22_Kawase_Hasui_S03_crd.j.story: Nishi Park sits on a hill at the north edge of Fukuoka city, overlooking Hakata Bay. Hasui frames the view through a stand of pines near the shore, the trunks doing most of the compositional work while the water and islands fall away behind. It's the kind of half-landscape, half-travel-poster image shin-hanga did well — specific enough to feel like a place, generalized enough to be any pine-and-bay evening in western Japan. Part of Souvenirs of Travel III, 1928, published by Watanabe; first editions carry the early Watanabe A seal.

NDL-DC_2586549-23_Kawase_Hasui_S03_crd.j.description: Dawn at Beppu (Beppu no asa), from the series Souvenirs of Travel III (Tabi miyage dai sanshū)

NDL-DC_2586549-23_Kawase_Hasui_S03_crd.j.story: Beppu, on the Kyushu coast, is an onsen town built on top of steaming hot springs. Hasui gives it at dawn: soft rose and grey in the sky, thin steam rising, the mountain bulk behind half-resolved out of haze. He would return to Beppu in the same series with an evening counterpart, Beppu no yū — the two function almost as a diptych of the same resort across the day. Souvenirs of Travel III, 1928, published by Watanabe Shōzaburō; the design exists in various impressions now scattered across the Toledo Museum and other collections.

NDL-DC_2586549-25_Kawase_Hasui_S04_crd.j.title: Takinogawa River
NDL-DC_2586549-25_Kawase_Hasui_S04_crd.j.description: Takinogawa River (Takinogawa), from the series Twenty Views of Tōkyō (Tōkyō nijūkei)

NDL-DC_2586549-25_Kawase_Hasui_S04_crd.j.story: The Takinogawa runs through the Ōji district in northern Tokyo, an area Hiroshige had already canonized in One Hundred Famous Views of Edo. Hasui takes it up again in Twenty Views of Tōkyō — the same subject, same publisher lineage (Watanabe Shōzaburō), seventy years later and in shin-hanga's softer, more atmospheric register. The series as a whole is his inventory of a city rebuilding after the 1923 earthquake: not the new concrete Tokyo but its surviving pockets of river, temple and old neighborhood.

NDL-DC_2586549-26_Kawase_Hasui_S04_crd.j.title: Evening in Beppu
NDL-DC_2586549-26_Kawase_Hasui_S04_crd.j.description: Evening in Beppu (Beppu no yū), from the series Souvenirs of Travel III (Tabi miyage dai sanshū)

NDL-DC_2586549-26_Kawase_Hasui_S04_crd.j.story: Evening companion to Dawn at Beppu: a wintry stretch of the waterside promenade, two bare trees wedged into a stone wall, a row of timber inns glowing yellow at the base of the mountain behind. Hasui keeps the palette almost entirely to greys and blues so the lit windows can do the work of warmth. Souvenirs of Travel III, 1929, vertical ōban, 38.2 × 26 cm, published by Watanabe Shōzaburō, signed Hasui with the Kawase seal. The two Beppu prints together read as one place seen across a single day.

NDL-DC_2586549-31_Kawase_Hasui_S05_crd.j.description: Moon at Magome (Magome no tsuki), from the series Twenty Views of Tōkyō (Tōkyō nijūkei)

NDL-DC_2586549-31_Kawase_Hasui_S05_crd.j.story: A full moon climbs behind tall pines, silvering a cluster of roofs below. Magome — now part of Ōta Ward — was still semi-rural in 1930, and this is probably Hasui's most famous night view; he actually built himself a house there the same year the print came out, so the view is partly domestic. Twenty Views of Tōkyō, vertical ōban, 39.5 × 26.4 cm, published by Watanabe Shōzaburō. Among collectors it's treated as one of the defining Hasui blue-moonlight images and one of shin-hanga's best-known landscapes.

NDL-DC_2586550-07_Kawase_Hasui_S05_crd.j.story: Ōmori beach, on the bay south of central Tokyo, was still a working shoreline in 1930 — canals, creeks, fishing skiffs, lights strung across the water. Hasui paints it at night, and the whole print runs on blues: the carver and printer built up the depth with dozens of impressions, each laying down another subtle gradient. It's the kind of technical showpiece Watanabe Shōzaburō's workshop could execute and shin-hanga collectors prized. From Twenty Views of Tōkyō; impressions are now in the Art Institute of Chicago, the Smithsonian, and the Tokyo Fuji Art Museum.

Nacimiento_de_San_Juan_Bautista_(Artemis.story: The newborn Baptist is lowered into a basin by a kneeling woman while Zechariah, still mute, scratches the name 'John' on a tablet at the right edge. The scene is domestic, almost crowded, at nearly two by three metres. It was painted around 1635 for the Buen Retiro palace in Madrid and hangs today in the Museo del Prado.

Nakahara_in_the_Sagami_province.jpg.story: A plank bridge over a shallow river in Sagami, and on it the whole cross-section of a day. A woman with a baby on her back, two pilgrims, a farmer angling to sell seeds, a fisherman hunting in the shallows. Rattles strung on rope scare birds off the fields. The thatched rooftops echo Fuji's shape in miniature. It's one of Hokusai's quieter prints — no wave, no storm, just people getting somewhere.

Narcissus-Caravaggio_(1594-96)_edited.jp.story: A boy in a brocaded doublet leans over a pool, and his arm in the dark water closes a perfect circle around him. Nothing else — no landscape, no Echo, no flowers. Just the loop. The attribution was only made in 1916, when Roberto Longhi pulled the canvas out of obscurity and gave it to Caravaggio; some scholars still argue. It hangs at Palazzo Barberini in Rome now, and the date is usually given as around 1597 to 1599.

Natoire_-_Adam_et_Eve_chassés_du_Paradis.title: The Rebuke of Adam and Eve

source.canonical_title: File:Natoire - Adam et Eve chassés du Paradis terrestre.jpg

Natoire_-_Adam_et_Eve_chassés_du_Paradis.story: The moment between the bite and the angel. Natoire painted this small, meticulous panel on copper in 1740 as a homage to his old teacher François Le Moyne, pairing it with a Le Moyne piece on the fall itself. God the Father looms from a cloud, pointing; Eve clutches the fatal fruit; Adam covers himself in embarrassment more than shame. It is a Rococo Genesis — the bodies long and silvery, the rebuke almost decorous. The painting now lives at the Metropolitan Museum of Art in New York.

Neapolitan_woman_(1894)_by_Ilya_Repin_-_.title: Portrait of a Neapolitan woman

source.canonical_title: File:Neapolitan woman (1894) by Ilya Repin - Неаполитанка.jpg

Neapolitan_woman_(1894)_by_Ilya_Repin_-_.story: Repin spent the spring of 1894 in Italy, and this is one of the heads he brought back — a young Neapolitan woman in a pale blouse, painted quickly, more study than finished portrait. It's looser than his Russian commissions: the background is barely blocked in, the brush tracking the turn of the cheek and collarbone rather than building anything up. These Italian studies were partly a holiday from the heavy Peredvizhniki subjects (he'd just finished the huge They Did Not Expect Him and was working on Cossacks) and partly a way of keeping his hand limber on something unfamiliar.

NesterovMV_NaRusi206x483GTG.jpg.title: In Russia. Soul of the people.

source.canonical_title: File:NesterovMV NaRusi206x483GTG.jpg

title.de: In Russland. Die Seele des Volkes.

NesterovMV_NaRusi206x483GTG.jpg.story: Nesterov worked on this nearly five-metre-wide canvas from 1905 through 1916, first calling it 'Christians,' then giving it its final, freighted title. A procession streams along the Volga: peasants, pilgrims, a boy leading the way, and among the crowd Dostoevsky, Tolstoy, and the philosopher Vladimir Solovyov, walking shoulder to shoulder with ordinary Russia. Begun after the 1905 revolution and finished in the thick of the First World War, it is Nesterov trying to fix the idea of a national soul on canvas before history buried it. The painting now hangs in the Tretyakov Gallery.

Nesterov_Florensky_Bulgakov.jpg.title: Philosophers
Nesterov_Florensky_Bulgakov.jpg.description: This is a portrait of Russian philosophers Pavel Florensky and Sergei Bulgakov .

source.canonical_title: File:Nesterov Florensky Bulgakov.jpg

Nesterov_Florensky_Bulgakov.jpg.story: Painted in the summer of 1917, months before the October Revolution, this double portrait shows the priest-mathematician Pavel Florensky in a white cassock listening to the theologian Sergei Bulgakov, wrapped in a dark coat, at Sergiev Posad. Nesterov said he worked without sketches, 'done in one stroke,' and valued the picture more as philosophy than painting. Within a generation Florensky would be shot in Stalin's camps and Bulgakov exiled to Paris; the quiet northern landscape behind them reads now like a final pause before catastrophe. In the Tretyakov Gallery.

Newton-WilliamBlake.jpg.title: Newton
Newton-WilliamBlake.jpg.description: William Blake 's Newton (1795), colour print with pen & ink and watercolour. Blake's picture of Newton as a divine geometer was one of a series he created while living in Lambeth in the late 1790s . Blake's printing appears to have been a form of self-developed monoprint which he then finished with additions in pen and ink coupled with watercolour washes.

Newton-WilliamBlake.jpg.story: Blake made this image around 1795 at his Lambeth house, pulling it with a small group of 'large colour prints' in a monoprint process he seems to have invented, then finishing each by hand in ink and watercolour. Newton crouches naked at the bottom of the sea, compasses in hand, drawing geometry on a scroll while the universe blooms in mossy rock behind him. For Blake, Newton was not a hero but a warning: reason bent double, staring at its own diagram.

NiccoloPaganini.jpeg.title: The Violinist Niccolò Paganini

source.canonical_title: File:NiccoloPaganini.jpeg
source.credit: Web Gallery of Art : Image Info about artwork wga QS:P11807,"i/ingres/08ingres"

NiccoloPaganini.jpeg.story: Ingres met Paganini in Rome around April 1819, very likely at a recital for the Austrian ambassador. The two musicians hit it off. Ingres was a serious amateur violinist himself, and that same year he played second violin in Beethoven quartets directed by Paganini. The drawing shows the virtuoso in a neat tailcoat, violin tucked under his arm, bow loose in the right hand. The pencil stops at the waist; everything lives in the alert, narrow face. He signed and dated the sheet right there in Rome.

Nichiren_bezweert_de_golven_bij_Kakuda_t.story: A small boat pitches between green breakers. Nichiren, in a red robe with prayer beads, chants the sutra — and the characters namu myō hō renge kyō surface in the foam itself. The year is 1271: the Buddhist reformer is being shipped to exile on Sado Island, and legend says he quieted the storm at Kakuda with his voice. Kuniyoshi cut the scene for his series A Concise Illustrated Biography of the Priest Nichiren, published around 1835 — six centuries after the fact, but painted like last night's nightmare.

Nicolas_Poussin,_French_-_The_Birth_of_V.story: Tritons blowing conches, nereids tumbling in spray, cupids overhead with a torch — but scholars now suspect the central figure on the cockleshell isn't Venus at all. She may be Galatea, the sea nymph with her own dolphin chariot. Poussin painted it in Rome around 1635 or 1636, when mythology let him show off every trick he'd learned from Titian. The canvas belonged to Catherine the Great; the Soviets sold it in 1930 and it landed at the Philadelphia Museum of Art, where a Hermitage inventory number is still scratched into one corner.

Nicolas_Poussin_(French_-_Landscape_with.title: Landscape with a Calm

source.canonical_title: File:Nicolas Poussin (French - Landscape with a Calm - Google Art Project.jpg
source.credit: xgGrcOwaU1-r9Q at Google Cultural Institute maximum zoom level

Nicolas_Poussin_(French_-_Landscape_with.story: Poussin was in his late fifties, done with narrative heroics, wanting weather. A walled town, a glassy pond, a shepherd calming spooked goats, everything doubled in reflection — the air so still you can almost hear the water lap. He painted it in 1650-51 for the Paris merchant Jean Pointel as half of a pair; the companion piece, Landscape with a Storm, is in Rouen and rages with black cloud. Buy the calm, get the tempest. The Getty acquired this panel in 1997.

Nicolas_Poussin_-_Le_massacre_des_Innoce.title: Massacre of the Innocents
Nicolas_Poussin_-_Le_massacre_des_Innoce.date_created: Entre 1625-1626 (selon Jacques Thuillier) et 1628-1629 (selon Anthony Blunt)

source.canonical_title: File:Nicolas Poussin - Le massacre des Innocents - Google Art Project.jpg

Nicolas_Poussin_-_Le_massacre_des_Innoce.story: Poussin strips the Gospel horror down to three figures: a soldier with one boot planted on a child's chest, a sword raised; the mother's open mouth; a second woman fleeing with a dead infant. That scream haunted Picasso and was the direct model for Francis Bacon's screaming popes. The palette is almost austere — red, blue, the pale stone of a Roman temple — and the whole composition pivots on two crossed diagonals. Painted around 1628 for Vincenzo Giustiniani in Rome. Now at the Musee Conde, Chantilly.

Nicolas_Poussin_-_Stormy_Landscape_with_.title: Stormy Landscape with Pyramus and Thisbe

source.canonical_title: File:Nicolas Poussin - Stormy Landscape with Pyramus and Thisbe - WGA18334.jpg
source.credit: Web Gallery of Art : Image Info about artwork wga QS:P11807,"p/poussin/4/38landsc"

Nicolas_Poussin_-_Stormy_Landscape_with_.story: Ovid's doomed lovers get the full Poussin weather system. Lightning rips across a slate sky, wind bends the trees sideways, figures scatter around a lake as a lion attacks a horse in the middle ground. At far right, tiny, Thisbe flings her arms up over the body of Pyramus. Poussin painted this in Rome in 1651 for the Lyon silk merchant Jean Pointel, and spent a long letter defending the storm as a scientific study of air and light rather than theatre. It reads as both.

Nicolas_Poussin_-_The_Sacrament_of_Ordin.title: The Sacrament of Ordination (Christ presenting the Keys to Saint Peter)

Nicolas_Poussin_-_The_Sacrament_of_Ordin.story: Part of Poussin's first Seven Sacraments, painted in Rome around 1636 for Cassiano dal Pozzo — the antiquary who fed him ancient coins and reliefs to copy. Christ hands the keys to a kneeling Peter while the other apostles lean in, arranged like a frieze on a sarcophagus. No theatrics, no swirling drapery; every gesture weighed. The full series left Italy in 1785 when the 4th Duke of Rutland bought it for Belvoir Castle. The Kimbell in Fort Worth paid a reported 24 million dollars for this one canvas in 2011.

Night_Bivouac_of_Great_Army.jpg.story: Late in the 1812 cycle, the Grande Armee sleeps — or dies — in the snow on the road back from Moscow. Figures huddle under greatcoats that are no longer quite enough; the horses have lain down; a few still fires burn thinly in the dark. Vereshchagin refuses the epic register. There is no Napoleon here, no banners, just a frozen crust of men reduced to lumps under a Russian winter. He had read the memoirs carefully and walked the route himself. State Historical Museum, Moscow.
