Nihon_fūkei_senshū,_Abuto_no_Kannon_by.title: Nihon fūkei senshū, Abuto no Kannon by Kawase Hasui
Nihon_fūkei_senshū,_Abuto_no_Kannon_by.description: Kannon Temple at Abuto (Abuto no Kannon), from the series Selected Views of Japan (Nihon fūkei senshū), woodblock print

source.canonical_title: File:Nihon fūkei senshū, Abuto no Kannon by Kawase Hasui.jpg

Nihon_fūkei_senshū,_Abuto_no_Kannon_by.story: Abuto Kannon — properly Bandai-ji's Kannon-dō — sits on a rocky promontory on the Seto Inland Sea in what is now Hiroshima Prefecture, its red hall perched over the water on wooden piers. Sailors prayed there for safe passage and for children. Hasui drew it for Selected Views of Japan in 1922, the year he turned the looser travel sketches into a more organized national series. Published by Watanabe Shōzaburō, carved and printed with the full shin-hanga division of labor that Hasui relied on throughout his career.

Nihon_fūkei_senshū,_Amakusa_Goryō_by_.title: Nihon fūkei senshū, Amakusa Goryō by Kawase Hasui
Nihon_fūkei_senshū,_Amakusa_Goryō_by_.description: Goryō in Amakusa, from the series Selected Views of Japan (Nihon fūkei senshū), woodblock print

source.canonical_title: File:Nihon fūkei senshū, Amakusa Goryō by Kawase Hasui.jpg

Nihon_fūkei_senshū,_Amakusa_Goryō_by_.story: Goryō is a village on Amakusa, the island chain off Kyushu's west coast that was home to Japan's hidden Christian communities for three centuries after the Shimabara rebellion. Hasui didn't advertise that history in his prints, but he did keep going back to Amakusa for the light: pines, tiled roofs, the particular way the Ariake Sea handles haze. This 1922 sheet from Selected Views of Japan is one of several from that trip, produced for Watanabe Shōzaburō in the full shin-hanga workshop system of carvers and printers.

Nihon_fūkei_senshū,_Amakusa_yori_mitar.title: Nihon fūkei senshū, Amakusa yori mitaru Onsengadake by Kawase Hasui
Nihon_fūkei_senshū,_Amakusa_yori_mitar.description: Onsengadake Seen from Amakusa (Amakusa yori mitaru Onsengadake), from the series Selected Views of Japan (Nihon fūkei senshū), woodblock print

source.canonical_title: File:Nihon fūkei senshū, Amakusa yori mitaru Onsengadake by Kawase Hasui.jpg

Nihon_fūkei_senshū,_Amakusa_yori_mitar.story: Unzen — here called by its older name Onsengadake, 'hot-spring peak' — is the volcano that looms over Shimabara Bay. Hasui painted it from across the water on Amakusa, which is the classic long view: the mountain floats above its own steam and the haze of the Ariake Sea. The print is from Selected Views of Japan, the 1922 series Hasui made after extended travel through Kyushu. Unzen would erupt catastrophically again in 1991, but in 1922 it was simply the backdrop shin-hanga travelers knew from the ferry.

Nihon_fūkei_senshū,_Beppu_no_asa_by_Ka.title: Nihon fūkei senshū, Beppu no asa by Kawase Hasui
Nihon_fūkei_senshū,_Beppu_no_asa_by_Ka.description: Morning at Beppu (Beppu no asa), from the series Selected Views of Japan (Nihon fūkei senshū), woodblock print

source.canonical_title: File:Nihon fūkei senshū, Beppu no asa by Kawase Hasui.jpg

Nihon_fūkei_senshū,_Beppu_no_asa_by_Ka.story: Beppu, on Kyushu's east coast, is the hot-spring town where steam rises straight out of the ground in dozens of places at once. 'Morning at Beppu' catches that hour when the vents are most visible against cold air. Hasui included it in Selected Views of Japan (1922), a series he built out of a long Kyushu trip the previous year. Shin-hanga publishers like Watanabe Shōzaburō were betting that Western collectors would buy this kind of quiet, weather-specific landscape — and by 1922 they were, in considerable numbers.

Nihon_fūkei_senshū,_Bingo_no_Iwafune_b.title: Nihon fūkei senshū, Bingo no Iwafune by Kawase Hasui
Nihon_fūkei_senshū,_Bingo_no_Iwafune_b.description: Iwafune in Bingo Province , from the series Selected Views of Japan (Nihon fūkei senshū), woodblock print

source.canonical_title: File:Nihon fūkei senshū, Bingo no Iwafune by Kawase Hasui.jpg

Nihon_fūkei_senshū,_Bingo_no_Iwafune_b.story: Iwafune — literally "stone boat" — is a rock formation on the Inland Sea coast of old Bingo province, now part of Hiroshima prefecture. Hasui included it in the 1923 installment of his Selected Views of Japan series for Watanabe Shōzaburō, drawn to the low, flat shape of the offshore stone and the way coastal mist collapsed distance. The series was effectively cut short that September, when the Kantō earthquake destroyed Watanabe's workshop. The original blocks burned, along with 188 of Hasui's travel sketchbooks — the raw material for work like this.

Nihon_fūkei_senshū,_Bungo_Kakize_by_Ka.title: Nihon fūkei senshū, Bungo Kakize by Kawase Hasui
Nihon_fūkei_senshū,_Bungo_Kakize_by_Ka.description: Cherry Trees at Kakize, Bungo Province , from the series Selected Views of Japan (Nihon fūkei senshū), woodblock print

source.canonical_title: File:Nihon fūkei senshū, Bungo Kakize by Kawase Hasui.jpg

Nihon_fūkei_senshū,_Bungo_Kakize_by_Ka.story: Cherry trees at Kakize, in the old Bungo province of eastern Kyushu — now Ōita prefecture. Hasui drew the scene in early 1923 for the continuing Selected Views of Japan series he was producing with publisher Watanabe Shōzaburō. The timing gives the print a particular poignancy: that September, the Great Kantō earthquake leveled Watanabe's Tokyo workshop, destroying the original blocks for most of the series along with 188 of Hasui's sketchbooks. Blossom scenes were something of a departure for him; he was better known for rain, snow, and dusk.

Nihon_fūkei_senshū,_Chikuzen_Hakozaki_.title: Nihon fūkei senshū, Chikuzen Hakozaki by Kawase Hasui
Nihon_fūkei_senshū,_Chikuzen_Hakozaki_.description: Hakozaki in Chikuzen Province, from the series Selected Views of Japan (Nihon fūkei senshū), woodblock print

source.canonical_title: File:Nihon fūkei senshū, Chikuzen Hakozaki by Kawase Hasui.jpg

Nihon_fūkei_senshū,_Chikuzen_Hakozaki_.story: Hakozaki, in old Chikuzen Province on the bay outside modern Fukuoka, is where the Mongol invasion fleets of 1274 and 1281 were broken up by the storms later called kamikaze. The shrine commemorating that deliverance still stands. Hasui drew the area for Selected Views of Japan in 1922 without staging the history — just the pines and the shore. Published by Watanabe Shōzaburō, who kept pushing Hasui to collect the whole country this way, province by province, weather by weather, through the 1920s.

Nihon_fūkei_senshū,_Chōmonkyō_Kayaga.title: Nihon fūkei senshū, Chōmonkyō Kayagafuchi by Kawase Hasui
Nihon_fūkei_senshū,_Chōmonkyō_Kayaga.description: Kayagafuchi Rapids in Chōmonkyō Gorge, from the series Selected Views of Japan (Nihon fūkei senshū), woodblock print

source.canonical_title: File:Nihon fūkei senshū, Chōmonkyō Kayagafuchi by Kawase Hasui.jpg

Nihon_fūkei_senshū,_Chōmonkyō_Kayaga.story: Chōmonkyō is a narrow gorge on the Abu River in Yamaguchi Prefecture — old Suō and Nagato country — with a run of named rapids and pools. Kayagafuchi is one of the pools. Hasui brought it into Selected Views of Japan in 1922, one of the more deliberately hidden subjects in a series that was already pushing away from famous places. The shin-hanga draw of a print like this was partly the carving: the water, worked across several blocks, is doing most of the compositional work.

Nihon_fūkei_senshū,_Higo_Tochinoki_ons.title: Nihon fūkei senshū, Higo Tochinoki onsen by Kawase Hasui
Nihon_fūkei_senshū,_Higo_Tochinoki_ons.description: Tochinoki Hot Springs in Higo Province (Higo Tochinoki onsen), from the series Selected Views of Japan (Nihon fūkei senshū), woodblock print

source.canonical_title: File:Nihon fūkei senshū, Higo Tochinoki onsen by Kawase Hasui.jpg

Nihon_fūkei_senshū,_Higo_Tochinoki_ons.story: Tochinoki is a small mountain hot spring in old Higo Province — today the Kumamoto interior, up in the hills between Aso and the Amakusa coast. The bath itself is older than the road to it. Hasui drew it for Selected Views of Japan in 1922, the Kyushu-heavy series he put together after a long trip south. Watanabe Shōzaburō's workshop printed it with the damp, green palette the shin-hanga carvers had worked out for wet stone and cedar bark.

Nihon_fūkei_senshū,_Hizen_Kabeshima_by.title: Nihon fūkei senshū, Hizen Kabeshima by Kawase Hasui
Nihon_fūkei_senshū,_Hizen_Kabeshima_by.description: Kabeshima in Hizen Province , from the series Selected Views of Japan (Nihon fūkei senshū), woodblock print

source.canonical_title: File:Nihon fūkei senshū, Hizen Kabeshima by Kawase Hasui.jpg

Nihon_fūkei_senshū,_Hizen_Kabeshima_by.story: Kabeshima is a small island off the old Hizen coast in what is now Saga Prefecture, known locally for its seabird colonies and the black-tailed gulls that still nest there. Hasui caught it for Selected Views of Japan in 1922 — one of several Hizen subjects in a series that kept drifting toward the quieter corners of the country rather than the famous ones. A Watanabe Shōzaburō woodblock print in the full shin-hanga manner, carved and printed by the workshop's regular team.

Nihon_fūkei_senshū,_Hizen_Kanahama_by_.title: Nihon fūkei senshū, Hizen Kanahama by Kawase Hasui
Nihon_fūkei_senshū,_Hizen_Kanahama_by_.description: Kanahama in Hizen Province, from the series Selected Views of Japan (Nihon fūkei senshū), woodblock print

source.canonical_title: File:Nihon fūkei senshū, Hizen Kanahama by Kawase Hasui.jpg

Nihon_fūkei_senshū,_Hizen_Kanahama_by_.story: Kanahama is a coastal stretch in the old Hizen province — now split between Saga and Nagasaki prefectures on Kyushu. Hasui drew it in 1923 for Selected Views of Japan, the travel series Watanabe Shōzaburō was publishing from Tokyo. Shin-hanga landscapes were often accused of prettifying a modernizing country, but Hasui's Kyushu coast prints tend to emphasize working shorelines rather than scenic ones. The 1923 Kantō earthquake would destroy Watanabe's workshop later that year, along with most of this series' original blocks, making pre-earthquake impressions the primary surviving record.

Nihon_fūkei_senshū,_Hizen_Kyōdomari_b.title: Nihon fūkei senshū, Hizen Kyōdomari by Kawase Hasui
Nihon_fūkei_senshū,_Hizen_Kyōdomari_b.description: Kyōdomari in Hizen Province , from the series Selected Views of Japan (Nihon fūkei senshū), woodblock print

source.canonical_title: File:Nihon fūkei senshū, Hizen Kyōdomari by Kawase Hasui.jpg

Nihon_fūkei_senshū,_Hizen_Kyōdomari_b.story: Kyōdomari is a fishing hamlet on the old Hizen coast — present-day Saga Prefecture, on the Genkai Sea side — the kind of place a sketchbook traveler reaches by boat and leaves the same way. Hasui drew it in 1922 for Selected Views of Japan, which he was assembling province by province for Watanabe Shōzaburō. The appeal of the series, for collectors then and since, is exactly this: a minor harbor given the same seriousness of printing craft that ukiyo-e had once reserved for Edo celebrities.

Nihon_fūkei_senshū,_Izumo_Mihogaseki_n.title: Nihon fūkei senshū, Izumo Mihogaseki no asa by Kawase Hasui
Nihon_fūkei_senshū,_Izumo_Mihogaseki_n.description: Dawn at Mihogaseki in Izumo Province (Izumo Mihogaseki no asa), from the series Selected Views of Japan (Nihon fūkei senshū), woodblock print

source.canonical_title: File:Nihon fūkei senshū, Izumo Mihogaseki no asa by Kawase Hasui.jpg

Nihon_fūkei_senshū,_Izumo_Mihogaseki_n.story: Dawn over a fishing harbor on the Shimane coast. Hasui visited Mihogaseki during his travels through Izumo Province and caught the moment when pink-gold light begins to define rooftops, mooring poles, and the still water of the inlet. Part of the Selected Views of Japan series published by Watanabe in 1925, it pairs the quiet composure of ukiyo-e with a Western painter's eye for atmosphere — fog, temperature, the hush before a working day begins.

Nihon_fūkei_senshū,_Izumo_Yasugi_Kiyom.title: Nihon fūkei senshū, Izumo Yasugi Kiyomizu by Kawase Hasui
Nihon_fūkei_senshū,_Izumo_Yasugi_Kiyom.description: Yasugi Kiyomizu Temple, Izumo Province(Izumo, Yasugi Kiyomizu), from the series Selected Views of Japan (Nihon fūkei senshū), woodblock print

source.canonical_title: File:Nihon fūkei senshū, Izumo Yasugi Kiyomizu by Kawase Hasui.jpg

Nihon_fūkei_senshū,_Izumo_Yasugi_Kiyom.story: Yasugi Kiyomizu, a hillside temple in eastern Shimane, in the middle of a snowfall. A small red pagoda rises out of snow-heavy pines and stone walls while fine flakes drift across a dark sky. Hasui went through Izumo in the mid-1920s and made several prints from the trip; this one, from 1926's Selected Views of Japan series, keeps the palette mostly grey and white so the vermillion architecture can do the work.

Nihon_fūkei_senshū,_Kagoshima_Kōtsuki.title: Nihon fūkei senshū, Kagoshima Kōtsuki-gawa by Kawase Hasui
Nihon_fūkei_senshū,_Kagoshima_Kōtsuki.description: Kōtsuki River in Kagoshima (Kagoshima Kōtsuki-gawa), from the series Selected Views of Japan (Nihon fūkei senshū), woodblock print

source.canonical_title: File:Nihon fūkei senshū, Kagoshima Kōtsuki-gawa by Kawase Hasui.jpg

Nihon_fūkei_senshū,_Kagoshima_Kōtsuki.story: The Kōtsuki runs through central Kagoshima, the castle town at the southern tip of Kyushu where Sakurajima smokes across the bay. Hasui drew the river for Selected Views of Japan in 1922, on the long Kyushu tour that fed much of that series. Shin-hanga subjects like this — a city river, not a volcano or shrine — were part of how the movement updated ukiyo-e: keeping the carved-block technique of the Edo masters while turning the attention toward ordinary working water in modern provincial towns.

Nihon_fūkei_senshū,_Kagoshima_Sakurash.title: Nihon fūkei senshū, Kagoshima Sakurashima by Kawase Hasui (cropped)
Nihon_fūkei_senshū,_Kagoshima_Sakurash.description: Sakurajima , Kagoshima, from the series Selected Views of Japan (Nihon fūkei senshū), woodblock print

source.canonical_title: File:Nihon fūkei senshū, Kagoshima Sakurashima by Kawase Hasui (cropped).jpg

Nihon_fūkei_senshū,_Kagoshima_Sakurash.story: Sakurajima rises across the bay from Kagoshima, a smoldering volcano that had erupted violently just eight years before Hasui drew it, hurling lava far enough to fuse the island to the mainland. The print dates to 1922, from his ambitious Selected Views of Japan series for publisher Watanabe Shōzaburō. Much of Hasui's work from this moment is poignant in hindsight: a year later the Great Kantō earthquake leveled Watanabe's Tokyo workshop, incinerating the original blocks and 188 sketchbooks. Early impressions like this one survived the fire and now carry the weight of what was lost.

Nihon_fūkei_senshū,_Kasuga-machi,_Kuma.title: Nihon fūkei senshū, Kasuga-machi, Kumamoto by Kawase Hasui
Nihon_fūkei_senshū,_Kasuga-machi,_Kuma.description: Kasuga-machi , Kumamoto, from the series Selected Views of Japan (Nihon fūkei senshū), woodblock print

source.canonical_title: File:Nihon fūkei senshū, Kasuga-machi, Kumamoto by Kawase Hasui.jpg

Nihon_fūkei_senshū,_Kasuga-machi,_Kuma.story: A quiet street in Kasuga-machi, a Kumamoto neighborhood Hasui passed through on one of the sketching tours that fed his 1922 series Selected Views of Japan. Rather than hunt for monuments, he drew what the castle town looked like at working scale, with ordinary buildings, ordinary light, ordinary weather. The series was published by Watanabe Shōzaburō at the peak of the shin-hanga revival. A year later the 1923 Kantō earthquake destroyed Watanabe's workshop and the original blocks for most of these prints, leaving surviving first-run impressions as the full record of what Hasui had seen.

Nihon_fūkei_senshū,_Kiso_no_Nezame_by_.title: Nihon fūkei senshū, Kiso no Nezame by Kawase Hasui
Nihon_fūkei_senshū,_Kiso_no_Nezame_by_.description: Nezame on the Kiso River(Kiso no Nezame), from the series Selected Views of Japan (Nihon fūkei senshū), woodblock print

source.canonical_title: File:Nihon fūkei senshū, Kiso no Nezame by Kawase Hasui.jpg

Nihon_fūkei_senshū,_Kiso_no_Nezame_by_.story: Nezame-no-toko is a famous stretch of the Kiso River in Nagano — pale granite worn by the current into blocky, almost architectural shapes. Hasui visited in 1925 and kept the composition lean: bleached rock, green-blue water, a sliver of pine-covered slope. The print sits inside his Selected Views of Japan series and shows how far shin-hanga had pushed woodblock technique, with flat color areas doing the work a painter would normally reach for oil to achieve.

Nihon_fūkei_senshū,_Kiso_no_Suhara_by_.title: Nihon fūkei senshū, Kiso no Suhara by Kawase Hasui
Nihon_fūkei_senshū,_Kiso_no_Suhara_by_.description: Suhara , Kiso(Kiso no Suhara), from the series Selected Views of Japan (Nihon fūkei senshū), woodblock print

source.canonical_title: File:Nihon fūkei senshū, Kiso no Suhara by Kawase Hasui.jpg

Nihon_fūkei_senshū,_Kiso_no_Suhara_by_.story: Night rain in the Kiso mountains. Suhara is a small post-town on the old Nakasendo road, and Hasui conjures a miserable, soaking evening — dark trees, a path, almost nothing visible. The rain itself is a technical marvel: the printer hand-worked the streaks with a baren rather than cutting them into a block, so the downpour varies across the sheet, thicker and thinner as if actually falling. One of the most atmospheric prints in the 1925 Selected Views series.

Nihon_fūkei_senshū,_Kumamoto-jō_Miyuk.title: Nihon fūkei senshū, Kumamoto-jō Miyukibashi by Kawase Hasui
Nihon_fūkei_senshū,_Kumamoto-jō_Miyuk.description: Miyuki Bridge at Kumamoto Castle , from the series Selected Views of Japan (Nihon fūkei senshū), woodblock print

source.canonical_title: File:Nihon fūkei senshū, Kumamoto-jō Miyukibashi by Kawase Hasui.jpg

Nihon_fūkei_senshū,_Kumamoto-jō_Miyuk.story: Miyuki Bridge crosses the Tsuboigawa river near Kumamoto Castle, one of the stock views of the town. Hasui drew it in 1923 for the Selected Views of Japan series he was making with publisher Watanabe Shōzaburō. Later that year the castle's neighborhood would be far from the disaster zone, but Hasui and Watanabe would not escape it: the September Kantō earthquake destroyed the Tokyo workshop along with the original blocks for most of this series and 188 of Hasui's travel sketchbooks, the reference material for quiet scenes exactly like this one.

Nihon_fūkei_senshū,_Kumamoto_Ezu-ko_by.title: Nihon fūkei senshū, Kumamoto Ezu-ko by Kawase Hasui
Nihon_fūkei_senshū,_Kumamoto_Ezu-ko_by.description: Lake Ezu in Kumamoto , from the series Selected Views of Japan (Nihon fūkei senshū), woodblock print

source.canonical_title: File:Nihon fūkei senshū, Kumamoto Ezu-ko by Kawase Hasui.jpg

Nihon_fūkei_senshū,_Kumamoto_Ezu-ko_by.story: Lake Ezu sits on the eastern edge of Kumamoto, a shallow spring-fed pond famous locally for lotus flowers and for the underground water that still supplies the city. Hasui drew it in 1923 for Selected Views of Japan, the travel series he was making with publisher Watanabe Shōzaburō. In September of the same year the Great Kantō earthquake destroyed Watanabe's Tokyo workshop along with the original blocks for most of the series, which is why quiet-water scenes like this one are usually encountered only in early impressions.

Nihon_fūkei_senshū,_Kyōto_Daigoku-den.title: Nihon fūkei senshū, Kyōto Daigoku-den by Kawase Hasui
Nihon_fūkei_senshū,_Kyōto_Daigoku-den.description: Main Hall at Heian-jingū Shrine , Kyōto, from the series Selected Views of Japan (Nihon fūkei senshū), woodblock print

source.canonical_title: File:Nihon fūkei senshū, Kyōto Daigoku-den by Kawase Hasui.jpg

Nihon_fūkei_senshū,_Kyōto_Daigoku-den.story: The outsized roofs here belong to Heian Jingū, a Kyoto shrine built in 1895 to celebrate the city's 1,100th anniversary, its main hall a scaled-down replica of the ancient Daigokuden audience chamber. In 1922 it was barely a generation old, and Hasui draws it with the same deliberate calm he gave genuinely old places. The print belongs to his Selected Views of Japan series for Watanabe Shōzaburō, most of which was orphaned when the 1923 Kantō earthquake destroyed the workshop, the blocks, and Hasui's travel sketchbooks in a single afternoon.

Nihon_fūkei_senshū,_Kyōto_Kamogawa_no.title: Nihon fūkei senshū, Kyōto Kamogawa no yūgure by Kawase Hasui
Nihon_fūkei_senshū,_Kyōto_Kamogawa_no.description: Evening at the Kamo River in Kyōto, from the series Selected Views of Japan (Nihon fūkei senshū), woodblock print

source.canonical_title: File:Nihon fūkei senshū, Kyōto Kamogawa no yūgure by Kawase Hasui.jpg

Nihon_fūkei_senshū,_Kyōto_Kamogawa_no.story: Dusk on the Kamo River, that long Kyoto ribbon where the city goes to cool off on summer evenings. Hasui strips the scene to essentials: flat water, a darkening bank, the last warmth leaking out of the sky. It is 1923, the opening salvo of his Selected Views of Japan series, and he is already doing the thing that will make him famous — catching a specific minute, the one just before lamps come on, when even a familiar river turns strange.

Nihon_fūkei_senshū,_Kyōto_Nonomiya_by.title: Nihon fūkei senshū, Kyōto Nonomiya by Kawase Hasui
Nihon_fūkei_senshū,_Kyōto_Nonomiya_by.description: Nonomiya Shrine in Kyōto, from the series Selected Views of Japan (Nihon fūkei senshū), woodblock print

source.canonical_title: File:Nihon fūkei senshū, Kyōto Nonomiya by Kawase Hasui.jpg

Nihon_fūkei_senshū,_Kyōto_Nonomiya_by.story: Nonomiya, the little shrine in Kyoto's Arashiyama bamboo grove where imperial princesses once purified themselves before being sent to serve at Ise. Hasui is drawn to its black torii and the green hush around it. He gives you the shrine as pilgrims actually find it: half-hidden, quiet, with the bamboo doing most of the talking. From Selected Views of Japan, 1923 — early Hasui, already in command of mood.

Nihon_fūkei_senshū,_Nagasaki_Kanaya-ma.title: Nihon fūkei senshū, Nagasaki Kanaya-machi by Kawase Hasui
Nihon_fūkei_senshū,_Nagasaki_Kanaya-ma.description: Kanaya-machi in Nagasaki , from the series Selected Views of Japan (Nihon fūkei senshū), woodblock print

source.canonical_title: File:Nihon fūkei senshū, Nagasaki Kanaya-machi by Kawase Hasui.jpg

Nihon_fūkei_senshū,_Nagasaki_Kanaya-ma.story: A street in Nagasaki's Kanaya-machi quarter, 1923. Nagasaki had spent centuries as Japan's one crack open to foreign trade, and some of that oddness still clings to its hill lanes. Hasui is less interested in the exotic than in the ordinary texture: tiled roofs stacked up a slope, the particular grey of the light. It is travel reportage by someone who walks a lot and waits for the right weather.

Nihon_fūkei_senshū,_Nagasaki_Sōfuku-j.title: Nihon fūkei senshū, Nagasaki Sōfuku-ji by Kawase Hasui
Nihon_fūkei_senshū,_Nagasaki_Sōfuku-j.description: Sōfuku-ji in Nagasaki , from the series Selected Views of Japan (Nihon fūkei senshū), woodblock print

source.canonical_title: File:Nihon fūkei senshū, Nagasaki Sōfuku-ji by Kawase Hasui.jpg

Nihon_fūkei_senshū,_Nagasaki_Sōfuku-j.story: Sōfukuji is the anomaly of Nagasaki, a Ming-dynasty Chinese temple built in 1629 by Fujian merchants who needed a place to bury their dead during Japan's closed-country centuries. Its scarlet gates and upturned eaves are unlike anything else in Kyushu. Hasui included it in Selected Views of Japan, the 1922 series he was still finishing for publisher Watanabe Shōzaburō when the 1923 Kantō earthquake burned the workshop to the ground, taking the blocks and his sketchbooks with it. The series was never fully reissued.

Nihon_fūkei_senshū,_Okayama-jō_by_Kaw.title: Nihon fūkei senshū, Okayama-jō by Kawase Hasui
Nihon_fūkei_senshū,_Okayama-jō_by_Kaw.description: Okayama Castle (Okayama-jō), from the series Selected Views of Japan (Nihon fūkei senshū), woodblock print

source.canonical_title: File:Nihon fūkei senshū, Okayama-jō by Kawase Hasui.jpg

Nihon_fūkei_senshū,_Okayama-jō_by_Kaw.story: Okayama Castle earned the nickname "Crow Castle" for its black-lacquered walls — a deliberate contrast to the white-plaster keeps elsewhere in Japan. Hasui drew it in 1922 for Watanabe Shōzaburō's Selected Views of Japan, treating the fortress as landscape rather than monument, grounded by moat and morning light. The building he saw here was destroyed by American firebombs in 1945; the current keep is a 1966 concrete reconstruction. The print also survived a disaster: the 1923 Kantō earthquake that consumed Watanabe's workshop, most of the series' original blocks, and Hasui's working sketchbooks.

Nihon_fūkei_senshū,_Onomichi_Senkō-ji.title: Nihon fūkei senshū, Onomichi Senkō-ji no saka by Kawase Hasui
Nihon_fūkei_senshū,_Onomichi_Senkō-ji.description: Slope of Senkō-ji Temple in Onomichi (Onomichi Senkō-ji no saka), from the series Selected Views of Japan (Nihon fūkei senshū), woodblock print

source.canonical_title: File:Nihon fūkei senshū, Onomichi Senkō-ji no saka by Kawase Hasui.jpg

Nihon_fūkei_senshū,_Onomichi_Senkō-ji.story: Onomichi is a port town in Hiroshima prefecture built into a hillside, and the climb to Senkōji temple threads between old houses on stone steps barely wide enough for two people. Hasui walked it in the early 1920s and gave the slope to the Selected Views of Japan series his publisher Watanabe Shōzaburō was building around his travels. The print dates from 1922. Copies with genuine pre-earthquake provenance are scarce, because the 1923 Kantō quake destroyed Watanabe's workshop along with most of the series' original blocks.

Nihon_fūkei_senshū,_Ōsumi_Anraku_onse.title: Nihon fūkei senshū, Ōsumi Anraku onsen by Kawase Hasui
Nihon_fūkei_senshū,_Ōsumi_Anraku_onse.description: Anraku Hot Springs, Ōsumi , from the series Selected Views of Japan (Nihon fūkei senshū), woodblock print

source.canonical_title: File:Nihon fūkei senshū, Ōsumi Anraku onsen by Kawase Hasui.jpg

Nihon_fūkei_senshū,_Ōsumi_Anraku_onse.story: Anraku hot springs, tucked into the Osumi peninsula at the southern tip of Kyushu — about as far from the Tokyo publishing scene as a Japanese printmaker could get in 1923. Hasui went anyway. The draw of an onsen print is always the same: steam, wood, bodies folded into the landscape. He catches the bathhouse in its setting without sentimentalising it. A postcard from the country's quiet edge.

Nihon_fūkei_senshū,_Shimabara-kō_Mayu.title: Nihon fūkei senshū, Shimabara-kō Mayuyama by Kawase Hasui
Nihon_fūkei_senshū,_Shimabara-kō_Mayu.description: Mayuyama and the Port of Shimabara (Shimabara-kō Mayuyama), from the series Selected Views of Japan (Nihon fūkei senshū), woodblock print

source.canonical_title: File:Nihon fūkei senshū, Shimabara-kō Mayuyama by Kawase Hasui.jpg

Nihon_fūkei_senshū,_Shimabara-kō_Mayu.story: Mayuyama is a lava dome looming over the port of Shimabara in Nagasaki prefecture, famously unstable — an eruption in 1792 had collapsed half of it into the sea, triggering a tsunami that killed roughly fifteen thousand people. When Hasui drew the quiet harbor below it in 1922 for Selected Views of Japan, the mountain had been dormant for more than a century. A year later, on the mainland, the Kantō earthquake destroyed Watanabe Shōzaburō's workshop and the blocks for most of this series, ending the project almost before it was finished.

Nihon_fūkei_senshū,_Shimabara_Tsukumoj.title: Nihon fūkei senshū, Shimabara Tsukumojima by Kawase Hasui
Nihon_fūkei_senshū,_Shimabara_Tsukumoj.description: Tsukumojima in Shimabara , from the series Selected Views of Japan (Nihon fūkei senshū), woodblock print

source.canonical_title: File:Nihon fūkei senshū, Shimabara Tsukumojima by Kawase Hasui.jpg

Nihon_fūkei_senshū,_Shimabara_Tsukumoj.story: Tsukumojima — literally "Ninety-Nine Islands" — is the scatter of small rocky outcrops off the Shimabara peninsula in Nagasaki, debris from the 1792 collapse of Mount Mayuyama. Hasui drew them in 1922 as part of Selected Views of Japan, the travel series Watanabe Shōzaburō was building around his sketching tours. A year later the Kantō earthquake destroyed Watanabe's Tokyo workshop along with the original blocks for most prints in this series and 188 of Hasui's sketchbooks, which is why pre-1923 impressions carry unusual weight.

Nihon_fūkei_senshū,_Yuki_no_Kinkaku-ji.title: Nihon fūkei senshū, Yuki no Kinkaku-ji by Kawase Hasui
Nihon_fūkei_senshū,_Yuki_no_Kinkaku-ji.description: Kinkaku-ji in Snow (Yuki no Kinkaku-ji), from the series Selected Views of Japan (Nihon fūkei senshū), woodblock print

source.canonical_title: File:Nihon fūkei senshū, Yuki no Kinkaku-ji by Kawase Hasui.jpg

Nihon_fūkei_senshū,_Yuki_no_Kinkaku-ji.story: The Golden Pavilion under snow — Kyoto's Kinkakuji, reflected in its pond, gold leaf muted against white. Hasui handled snow like a printer rather than a painter, leaving the paper bare so the fibers read as drift. The print belongs to Selected Views of Japan, the 1922 series that made his early reputation with publisher Watanabe Shōzaburō. It is also, by accident, a document of a building that no longer exists: the original pavilion burned to the ground in 1950 when a disturbed novice monk set fire to it. The current Kinkakuji is a 1955 reconstruction.

Nikko_kaido_hasui_kawase.jpg.title: Nikkō Kaidō

source.canonical_title: File:Nikko kaido hasui kawase.jpg

Nikko_kaido_hasui_kawase.jpg.story: The Nikkō Kaidō was the old pilgrimage and shogunal road running north from Edo to Nikkō, and its defining feature is the avenue of cryptomeria — towering cedars planted in the 17th century that still line parts of the route. Hasui drops a single traveler into that corridor of trunks, small against the scale of the trees, the road vanishing into green shade. There's no spectacle, just path and forest. Published by Watanabe in 1930, vertical ōban around 40 × 26 cm, hand-printed from the original blocks and still reissued from them in later editions.

Nikolay_II_of_Russia_by_I.Repin_(1896,_G.story: Nicholas II had been on the throne less than two years when Repin painted this. The young tsar stands in a dark military frock-coat, hand resting on a table, the room behind him barely indicated — formal but oddly tentative, which was the man. Repin was by then Russia's unofficial imperial-grade portraitist (he'd done the huge Ceremonial Sitting of the State Council a few years later), and the Nicholas he gives here is the one contemporaries described: polite, quiet, a little lost in his own inheritance. The canvas is in the State Historical Museum, Moscow.

source.canonical_title: File:Nitta Yoshisada - Tsuchiya Koitsu.jpg

Nitta_Yoshisada_-_Tsuchiya_Koitsu.jpg.story: A medieval death scene turned into a 1900 commercial chromolithograph. The 14th-century general Nitta Yoshisada, pinned against a pine on his rearing white horse, takes arrow after arrow - the air is literally a hatching of feathered shafts. The picture commemorates Oyamada Takaie, the retainer who (so the Taiheiki says) rode out wearing Yoshisada's armor to draw the volleys away from his lord. Koitsu was still in his long apprenticeship to Kiyochika here, and the bright aniline palette and smoke-heavy distance show the Meiji print industry importing European lithographic effects wholesale.

Nocturne_by_James_Abbott_McNeil,_1870-18.title: Nocturne

source.canonical_title: File:Nocturne by James Abbott McNeil, 1870-1877.jpg
source.permission: PD-art

Nocturne_by_James_Abbott_McNeil,_1870-18.story: Whistler liked the word nocturne so much he used it for dozens of paintings, each one a night on the Thames reduced to two or three tones. He'd stand at Chelsea looking across to Battersea, then go home and paint from memory, because memory edits better than the eye. This one is a smudged chord of blue and grey, signed with his butterfly monogram. He worked on Nocturnes throughout the 1870s; the Tate owns several.

Northeaster_by_Winslow_Homer_1895.jpg.title: Northeaster

source.canonical_title: File:Northeaster by Winslow Homer 1895.jpg
source.credit: Metropolitan Museum of Art, online collection (The Met object ID 20011487)

Northeaster_by_Winslow_Homer_1895.jpg.story: A wave exploding against ledge rock, nothing else. Homer first painted two oilskinned fishermen in the foreground, then, years later, painted them out, you can still see their ghost in raking light. What's left is pure weather. He finished the revision in 1901 and sent it to the Metropolitan Museum of Art, which bought it the same year for $800.

Nuremberg_chronicles_-_Dance_of_Death_(C.title: Nuremberg chronicles - Dance of Death (CCLXIIIIv)
Nuremberg_chronicles_-_Dance_of_Death_(C.description: Illustrations from the Nuremberg Chronicle, by Hartmann Schedel (1440-1514)

source.canonical_title: File:Nuremberg chronicles - Dance of Death (CCLXIIIIv).jpg

Nuremberg_chronicles_-_Dance_of_Death_(C.story: Four skeletons caper out of an open grave while a fifth crawls back in, exhausted. This is the Totentanz woodcut from Schedel's 1493 Nuremberg Chronicle, designed in Wolgemut's workshop, where the teenaged Dürer was finishing his apprenticeship. Plague had run through Nuremberg repeatedly that century, and the image belongs to a whole genre meant to remind rich merchants that the reaper dances with bishops too. The cut is coarse, the bones anatomically wrong, the energy unbeatable.

Nympheas_71293_3.jpg.story: A 1915 pond study from the years Monet spent circling one subject until it dissolved. No sky, no bank, no framing trees, just the water lilies and what lies beneath them: reflected clouds, sunken stems, small green rafts holding still. He had recently built a vast new studio at Giverny specifically to accommodate the mural-scale canvases he was beginning to imagine. By this point he'd painted the same pond more than two hundred times.

O_Soldado_Esquecido.jpg.story: A Russian soldier lies alone in a dry landscape; two eagles have found him first. No comrades, no grave detail, no flag — just the body and the birds and a vast empty distance. Vereshchagin called it "Eagles (The Forgotten Soldier)," and at almost three by four and a half metres it is one of his largest Balkan canvases. It still hangs in the museum named after him in Mykolaiv. The painting is an argument: this is what a soldier actually looks like after the dispatches have been filed and the speeches have been given.

Ochanomizu_(5758871675).jpg.title: Ochanomizu (5758871675)
Ochanomizu_(5758871675).jpg.description: Display Title: Ochanomizu Translation(s): Ochanomizu Series Title: Twenty Views of Tokyo Suite Name: Tokyo nijukkei Creation Date: 1926 Publisher: Watanabe Shozaburo Credit Line: Gift of Alice Klauber Label Copy: "This arist was famous for his depictions of different varieties of snow. Here, wet cotton-like balls of snow blanket the rooftops of Tokyo. It adds a dimension of silence to the sense of isolation in the city." Collection: The San Diego Museum of Art

source.canonical_title: File:Ochanomizu (5758871675).jpg

Ochanomizu_(5758871675).jpg.story: A blizzard over the Kanda River. From the bridge at Ochanomizu, Hasui watched a boat stall in the wind, snow piling on rooftops along the opposite bank and yellow window-lights burning through the squall. The carver and printer rendered the flakes as slanted ovals ranging from bright white to soft grey — a virtuoso piece of technique. Part of Twenty Views of Tokyo (1926) and good enough that it was chosen as the cover of Hasui's catalogue raisonné decades later.

Oeillets_et_clématite_dans_un_vase_de_cr.story: By 1882 Manet was dying. Locomotor ataxia made standing agony, so friends brought him cut flowers and he painted them small, close, and quickly from a chair. Here white carnations and a sprig of purple clematis lean out of a faceted crystal vase, the petals built from a few confident slashes of lead white. He made about twenty of these late flower pictures in the last months of his life. This one is at the Musée d'Orsay.

Ono_Shindon_in_the_Suraga_province.jpg.story: Early morning in the new paddies at Ono, mist still hanging over the water. Farmers drive five oxen along the dike, each animal loaded down with bundles of reeds so huge they look like walking haystacks. Two women carry smaller bundles. Waterfowl skim the surface. 'Shinden' meant newly reclaimed land — Edo-era shoguns kept pushing the frontier of rice cultivation outward to feed a swelling population.

P.1948.SC_.276-scaled-aspect-ratio-16-9-.story: 'Antibes, vue du Massif de l'Estérel' — the medieval town seen across the bay, with the red Estérel peaks floating in the distance. Monet painted this during his 1888 Riviera campaign, standing on the Cap d'Antibes side, letting a single windblown pine frame the view. He wrote to Alice that the atmosphere was 'swimming in blue and pink' and that he was drowning trying to catch it. The canvas, W1192, is at the Courtauld Gallery in London.

source.canonical_title: File:Paisaje con san Jerónimo, Joachim Patinir, Museo del Prado.jpg

title.ja: 聖ヒエロニムスのいる風景 (パティニール)
title.nl: Landschap met de boetvaardige H. Hieronymus

Paisaje_con_san_Jerónimo,_Joachim_Patini.story: Saint Jerome has tucked himself into a leaning wooden hut against the rocks, pulling a thorn from a lion's paw. But Patinir really cares about everything else: jagged Namur-style outcrops, winding rivers, tiny villages, a horizon line hoisted sky-high so landscape becomes the subject. Jerome is almost a pretext. This is the moment European painting starts treating nature itself as worth a canvas, and Patinir is the reason we have the word 'landscape' at all. Painted around 1516 to 1517, now at the Prado.

Pallas_Athena_by_Rembrandt_Museu_Caloust.title: Pallas Athena

source.canonical_title: File:Pallas Athena by Rembrandt Museu Calouste Gulbenkian 1488.jpg

Pallas_Athena_by_Rembrandt_Museu_Caloust.story: The goddess stands in black armour and a Macedonian helmet trimmed with red feathers and a small owl, her aegis emblazoned with Medusa's head. The brushwork is dense and the lighting Rembrandt's, but since 1991 scholars have hedged — the Netherlands Institute for Art History now lists it as Rembrandt and workshop. Catherine the Great once owned it; Calouste Gulbenkian bought it from the Soviet Antikvariat in Paris in 1930.

Pallasetlecentaure.jpg.title: Pallas and the Centaur

source.canonical_title: File:Pallasetlecentaure.jpg

Pallasetlecentaure.jpg.story: She has him by the hair. The centaur — half-man, half-beast, all brute appetite — winces as Pallas twists a fistful of his locks, her halberd cocked, her gown embroidered with interlocked diamond rings. Those rings are the Medici impresa, a family badge; this was almost certainly commissioned for Lorenzo di Pierfrancesco de' Medici's townhouse around 1482. Reason disciplining lust, civilization taming wildness — that's the standard read. The painting hung for centuries in the Uffizi's storerooms unrecognized, then resurfaced in 1895 when an inventory finally matched it to Vasari's description.

Pan_syrinx_Rubens.jpg.title: Pan and Syrinx
Pan_syrinx_Rubens.jpg.artist: Peter Paul Rubens / Jan Brueghel the Elder
Pan_syrinx_Rubens.jpg.description: Pan and Syrinx" Polish: Pan i Syrinx Pan and Syrinx

source.canonical_title: File:Pan syrinx Rubens.jpg

description.pl: Pan i Syrinx" German: Pan und Syrinx Pan and Syrinx

Pan_syrinx_Rubens.jpg.story: Ovid's chase rendered by the two best hands in Antwerp: Rubens painted Pan lunging through the reeds, lust on his face, while Brueghel did the riverbank — every blade of grass, every duck and dragonfly, the water glinting realistically cold. Syrinx is already half-becoming the reeds that will save her, her body pale and panicked against Pan's ruddy flesh. A small panel, now in Kassel, where the collaboration compresses an entire myth into a single breathless moment.

Paolo_Uccello_Heiliger_Georg_und_der_Dra.title: Hl. Georg im Kampf mit dem Drachen

source.canonical_title: File:Paolo Uccello Heiliger Georg und der Drachen 1 470.jpg

Paolo_Uccello_Heiliger_Georg_und_der_Dra.story: A late, small Uccello from around 1470, and one of the strangest takes on the George legend. The dragon is a neat green pinwheel with bat-wing eyespots; the princess holds him on a leather leash as if walking a poodle. George's lance drives through the beast into a cave mouth painted like theatre canvas. Above, a perfectly round storm cloud spirals outward — a vortex that looks lifted from a twentieth-century cartoon. Half icon, half fairy-tale illustration, with Uccello's usual ruled ground plane under everything.

Paolo_Veronese,_The_Conversion_of_Mary_M.title: The Conversion of Mary Magdalene

source.canonical_title: File:Paolo Veronese, The Conversion of Mary Magdalene.jpg

Paolo_Veronese,_The_Conversion_of_Mary_M.story: One of Veronese's earliest surviving paintings, made around age eighteen before he left Verona for Venice. Martha has dragged her sister to hear Christ preach; Mary, still in a fashionably low-cut Cinquecento gown, crumples to her knees as the jewels slip from her throat. The light slanting in from the right suggests the panel was hung on the side wall of a chapel. Already the Veronese signature is there: the thick dabs of gold and pearls against bare skin, the refusal to let a moral scene be anything less than sumptuous. National Gallery, London.

Paolo_Veronese_-_Juno_Showering_Gifts_on.title: Juno Showering Gifts on Venetia

source.canonical_title: File:Paolo Veronese - Juno Showering Gifts on Venetia - WGA24937.jpg
source.credit: Web Gallery of Art : Image Info about artwork wga QS:P11807,"/v/veronese/08/dieci/3dieci"

Paolo_Veronese_-_Juno_Showering_Gifts_on.story: A ceiling canvas for the Hall of the Council of Ten in the Doge's Palace, seen from sharply below. Juno leans out of the clouds and dumps an armful of wealth onto the personification of Venice: crowns, gold coins, a peace wreath, and the doge's horned cap itself. The allegory is unsubtle - Venice deserves both power and peace - but the foreshortening is the point. Veronese makes the goddess's arm and Venice's upturned face lunge out of a dark-blue sky with the sculptural weight he would spend the rest of his career perfecting.

Paolo_Veronese_-_The_Family_of_Darius_be.story: 330 BC, the morning after Issus. Darius III's mother kneels before Hephaestion, mistaking the taller friend for the conqueror; Alexander, in silver, gently corrects her. Veronese costumed the whole Persian court as Venetian nobility — brocade, pearls, a dwarf, a monkey — and set them against an imaginary palace loggia. The Pisani family commissioned it around 1565 and kept it for nearly three centuries. The National Gallery in London bought it in 1857 for 13,650 pounds, then a record for the institution.

Parmigianino_-_Madonna_and_Child_with_An.title: Madonna and Child with Angels , known as the Madonna with the Long Neck

source.canonical_title: File:Parmigianino - Madonna and Child with Angels, known as the Madonna with the Long Neck.jpg

Parmigianino_-_Madonna_and_Child_with_An.story: Parmigianino's most famous impossibility, left unfinished at his death in 1540. The Virgin's neck stretches like a swan's, her fingers taper past anatomy, the sleeping Christ slides across her lap in a boneless arc. A crowd of angels presses in from the left carrying an urn; on the right, a single white column goes nowhere, and a shrunken prophet unrolls a scroll at the base of a staircase that makes no architectural sense. Mannerism as deliberate strangeness — elegance pushed until it tips into the uncanny.

Parmigianino_004.jpg.title: Madonna mit dem langen Hals, Detail: Kopf der Madonna

source.canonical_title: File:Parmigianino 004.jpg
source.credit: The Yorck Project (2002) 10.000 Meisterwerke der Malerei (DVD-ROM), distributed by DIRECTMEDIA Publishing GmbH. ISBN : 3936122202 .

Parmigianino_004.jpg.story: A close detail of the Madonna's head and shoulders from Parmigianino's Madonna of the Long Neck. Pulled in tight, you see what the full panel only hints at: the tiny pursed smile, the pearl fillet laced into curls of reddish-gold hair, the impossibly long fingers splayed across the breast. The neck itself runs almost uninterrupted from jaw to collarbone. Isolated from the crowd of angels and the trick architecture, the face reads less as sacred subject than as a Mannerist exercise in how far refinement can be pushed.

Parting_Spring_by_Kawai_Gyokudo_(Nationa.story: The left panel of a two-screen painting from 1916, now an Important Cultural Property. Gyokudo had spent the previous two summers sketching on the Nagatoro gorge in Saitama, drifting down the river on waterwheel boats, and the whole work builds from those trips. Here cherry petals scatter onto the water, the gorge opens, spring is visibly leaving. The challenge he set himself was painting the blur of the waterwheel's spin against the fixed pattern of the current. You can feel him solving it.

Parting_Spring_by_Kawai_Gyokudo_(Nationa.story: The right panel of Gyokudo's 1916 Parting Spring, held at the National Museum of Modern Art in Tokyo and designated an Important Cultural Property. Three waterwheel boats are moored at the gorge, petals coming down around them. Gyokudo had boated the Nagatoro himself in 1915 and 1916, and the painting is not an invented scene but a remembered one, scaled up to screen size. The genius of the pair is rhythmic: water that keeps moving, blossoms that keep falling, a spring that will not quite stay.

PatenierChristopher.jpg.story: A giant Saint Christopher wades a river with the Christ Child on his shoulder, the infant's small weight bearing down on the ferryman's staff until it bends. Patinir unfurls his trademark world behind them: cliffs, villages, a winding estuary, all seen from high up. The panel is at El Escorial outside Madrid, painted late in Patinir's short career around 1520–24. One of only a handful of signed works that survive — he died in 1524, leaving Antwerp's landscape painters to carry on the formula he had basically invented.

Paul_Cézanne,_1892-95,_Les_joueurs_de_c.title: The Card Players

source.canonical_title: File:Paul Cézanne, 1892-95, Les joueurs de carte (The Card Players), 60 x 73 cm, oil on canvas, Courtauld Institute of Art, London.jpg

Paul_Cézanne,_1892-95,_Les_joueurs_de_c.story: The Courtauld's version is the tightest of Cézanne's five Card Players, painted in the mid-1890s at Jas de Bouffan using local Provençal labourers as models. Everything extraneous has been stripped away: no onlookers, no tavern clutter, just two men bent over their hands across a wedge of tablecloth. The bottle stood up between them acts as a structural axis. Cézanne spent years working through this motif and this canvas is where the composition lands. Another version sold in 2011 for something over two hundred million dollars, then a record.

Paul_Cézanne_-_Montagne_Saint-victoire_.title: Montagne Saint-Victoire

source.canonical_title: File:Paul Cézanne - Montagne Saint-victoire - Google Art Project.jpg
source.credit: FgH8RRkGP4EUfg at Google Cultural Institute maximum zoom level

Paul_Cézanne_-_Montagne_Saint-victoire_.story: Cezanne painted this limestone ridge outside Aix-en-Provence more than sixty times. In this version, around 1890, a stone pine splits the foreground like a curtain; the valley beyond is built from small tilted planes of green, ochre and blue, each brushstroke laid down like a tile. No atmosphere, no softening — the mountain looks chipped out of the sky. His father had died in 1886 and left him the family estate at Jas de Bouffan; he finally had time to do nothing but this. Forty years later Picasso called him 'the father of us all.'

Paul_Gauguin_001.jpg.story: Before the islands, before the yellow Christs, there was Suzanne, hunched over her sewing in a bare Paris room. Gauguin was still a stockbroker when he painted her in 1880, moonlighting as an artist on weekends. The light is cool, the pose unidealized, the body slack with real fatigue. Critic Joris-Karl Huysmans singled the painting out at the 1881 Impressionist exhibition as the first convincing nude by a modern artist since Rembrandt. The canvas now hangs at the Ny Carlsberg Glyptotek in Copenhagen.

Paul_Gauguin_085.jpg.story: Autumn 1888, the famous Arles experiment. Gauguin has just moved into the Yellow House with Van Gogh, and on afternoons the two of them walk out to Les Alyscamps, the old Roman burial alley lined with poplars. Gauguin's version goes full Cloisonnist: flat russet leaves, a blue river of path, figures drifting in dark shawls. Vincent painted the same trees on the same days in his own scalding palette. Nine weeks later, Gauguin was on a train back to Paris and Vincent's ear was in a bandage.

Paul_Gauguin_087.jpg.story: Women in long skirts reach into the mango branches while a goat watches. Gauguin painted Among the Mangoes during those same five sweltering months on Martinique in 1887, working outdoors with Laval on a hillside above Saint-Pierre. Vincent van Gogh saw it in Paris, loved it, and talked his brother Theo into buying it. It hung in Theo's apartment and then passed down through the family to the museum Vincent never lived to see: today it's one of the anchor Gauguins at the Van Gogh Museum.

Paul_Gauguin_113.jpg.title: Day of the God

source.canonical_title: File:Paul Gauguin 113.jpg
source.credit: 1. The Yorck Project (2002) 10.000 Meisterwerke der Malerei (DVD-ROM), distributed by DIRECTMEDIA Publishing GmbH. ISBN : 3936122202 . 2. Google Art Project works from the Art Institute of Chicago

Paul_Gauguin_113.jpg.story: Mahana no atua — Day of the God. A Polynesian deity looms on the shore while bathers curl like fetuses in pools of pure color at her feet. Gauguin painted it in Paris in 1894, between his two Tahiti trips, working from memory and imagination rather than any specific ritual he'd witnessed. The foreground water is almost abstract — violet, ochre, pink puddles butted against each other with no modeling. It entered the Art Institute of Chicago in 1926 as part of the Helen Birch Bartlett Memorial Collection.

Paul_de_Vos_-_Bull_subdued_by_dogs.jpg.title: Bull subdued by dogs

source.canonical_title: File:Paul de Vos - Bull subdued by dogs.jpg

Paul_de_Vos_-_Bull_subdued_by_dogs.jpg.story: A heaving, furious tangle of teeth and hide. Part of the vast hunting series Rubens designed for Philip IV's hunting lodge, the Torre de la Parada, outside Madrid - de Vos was one of the specialists brought in to execute the animal subjects. Bullfight and hound-pack were stock entertainments of seventeenth-century Europe and painters like de Vos pitched them at the baroque energy level of a battle piece, all diagonal thrust and flying spittle. Now in the Prado alongside dozens of its companion canvases from the same royal commission.

Paul_de_Vos_-_Cats_Fighting_in_a_Larder..title: Cats Fighting in a Larder

source.canonical_title: File:Paul de Vos - Cats Fighting in a Larder.jpg

Paul_de_Vos_-_Cats_Fighting_in_a_Larder..story: The humans are out; the animals have taken over the pantry. A tabby and a ginger claw at each other over a hanging carcass while birds scatter and a basket of fish spills onto the floor. These proverbial chaos scenes were a Flemish specialty - a moral wink about what happens when responsibility is abandoned - and de Vos, Snyders's brother-in-law, made them with a warmer, looser touch than his more famous relative. The picture first shows up in Isabel Farnese's inventory in 1746 and has hung in the Prado since.

Paul_de_Vos_-_Still_Life_with_Servant_-_.title: Still Life with Servant
Paul_de_Vos_-_Still_Life_with_Servant_-_.artist: Paul de Vos / Possibly Cornelis de Vos

source.canonical_title: File:Paul de Vos - Still Life with Servant - Google Art Project.jpg
source.credit: 8gF_WAOn6cnSwg at Google Cultural Institute maximum zoom level

Paul_de_Vos_-_Still_Life_with_Servant_-_.story: A kitchen table piled past the point of sense: a boar's head, fish, game birds, oysters, a heaped bronze pan with two live chicks flapping on its rim. At the left a servant stands blank-faced; at the right a cat and a dog tear at the same scrap. Paul de Vos trained with his brother-in-law Frans Snyders in Antwerp and built a whole career out of this kind of prosperous Flemish chaos. He died in Antwerp on 30 June 1678. The picture now belongs to the Fundacion Banco Santander collection.

Pedro_Pablo_Rubens_-_Susana_y_los_viejos.title: Susana y los viejos
Pedro_Pablo_Rubens_-_Susana_y_los_viejos.description: El lienzo, que está inspirado en un pasaje del Antiguo Testamento , muestra a la joven judía Susana huyendo de las proposiciones deshonestas de dos ancianos judíos que la amenazaron con denunciarla si no accedía a sus deseos, aunque la falsedad de ambos fue descubierta por el joven Daniel y ambos fueron ejecutados por su crimen.

source.canonical_title: File:Pedro Pablo Rubens - Susana y los viejos - Google Art Project.jpg
source.credit: PAFsIkDw-5vK7Q at Google Cultural Institute , zoom level maximum

Pedro_Pablo_Rubens_-_Susana_y_los_viejos.story: Two old men crouch in the bushes behind Susanna, watching her bathe — and she turns, mid-gesture, catching them before you do. In the apocryphal Book of Daniel the pair threaten to accuse her of adultery unless she submits; she refuses, they lie, and the young Daniel unmasks them at her trial. Rubens kept returning to the subject; this version, oil on panel roughly 198 by 218 centimetres, dates to about 1609 to 1610 and hangs at the Real Academia de Bellas Artes de San Fernando in Madrid.

PeinturesMuséeFabre150_Natoire_Vulcain17.title: Venus asks Vulcan for Weapons for his Son Aeneas
PeinturesMuséeFabre150_Natoire_Vulcain17.description: Morceau de réception à l' Académie Royale de Peinture et de Sculpture , le 31 décembre 1734.

source.canonical_title: File:PeinturesMuséeFabre150 Natoire Vulcain1734.jpg

title.fr: Vénus demande à Vulcain des armes pour son fils Énée

PeinturesMuséeFabre150_Natoire_Vulcain17.story: The ticket of admission to the Académie Royale. Natoire delivered this canvas on 31 December 1734 — his morceau de réception — and on the same day was voted in as a full history painter. Venus, pearly and coaxing, leans on Vulcan in his sooty forge to ask for arms for her son Aeneas; Cupid hovers nearby to translate the request into a language the limping smith-god best understands. All the Rococo equipment is here: warm flesh, crumpled drapery, Olympian stagecraft. The picture still hangs in the Musée Fabre in Montpellier.

Peter_Paul_Rubens,_,_Kunsthistorisches_M.title: The Four Continents

source.canonical_title: File:Peter Paul Rubens, , Kunsthistorisches Museum Wien, Gemäldegalerie - Die vier Flüsse des Paradieses - GG 526 - Kunsthistorisches Museum.jpg

Peter_Paul_Rubens,_,_Kunsthistorisches_M.story: Four river gods lounge with four continents personified as women, plus a tiger, a crocodile and a cluster of chubby putti. The German title, Die vier Flusse des Paradieses, calls them the rivers of Paradise; most catalogues know it as The Four Continents. Rubens stacks skin tones against each other like a flesh palette, pale Europe next to dark Africa, and keeps everyone tangled in one lazy, heavy pile. It has been in Vienna's Kunsthistorisches Museum since the imperial collection absorbed it.

Peter_Paul_Rubens,_Flemish_(active_Italy.title: Prometheus Bound

source.canonical_title: File:Peter Paul Rubens, Flemish (active Italy, Antwerp, and England) - Prometheus Bound - Google Art Project.jpg

title.ja: 繋がれたプロメテウス
title.nl: De bestraffing van Prometheus door de adelaar van Zeus

Peter_Paul_Rubens,_Flemish_(active_Italy.story: Rubens painted the writhing Titan; Snyders painted the eagle ripping out his liver. The division of labor was industrial and unapologetic, and the result is one of Rubens's most violent canvases, with Prometheus plunging head-first out of the frame as his punishment begins anew each dawn. Begun around 1611 and completed by 1618, it now hangs at the Philadelphia Museum of Art.

Peter_Paul_Rubens,_Kunsthistorisches_Mus.title: Lamentation of Christ by Mary and John

source.canonical_title: File:Peter Paul Rubens, Kunsthistorisches Museum Wien, Gemäldegalerie - Beweinung Christi durch Maria und Johannes - GG 529 - Kunsthistorisches Museum.jpg

title.de: Beweinung Christi durch Maria und Johannes

Peter_Paul_Rubens,_Kunsthistorisches_Mus.story: Three figures, one shroud, no sky. Rubens strips the Lamentation down to Mary cradling her son's head and John reaching across the body, foreheads nearly touching above the wound. The oak panel is small for him, barely a metre wide, and the intimacy is the point: a picture for private prayer, not a chapel wall. Dated about 1614-15, it sits in Vienna's Kunsthistorisches Museum as inventory GG 529, hung with his more theatrical altarpieces to remind you he could whisper too.

Peter_Paul_Rubens,_Kunsthistorisches_Mus.title: Landscape with Philemon and Baucis

source.canonical_title: File:Peter Paul Rubens, Kunsthistorisches Museum Wien, Gemäldegalerie - Gewitterlandschaft mit Jupiter, Merkur, Philemon und Baucis - GG 690 - Kunsthistorisches Museum.jpg

title.ja: ピレモンとバウキスのいる風景
title.nl: Stormachtig landschap met Philemon en Baucis

Peter_Paul_Rubens,_Kunsthistorisches_Mus.story: A flash flood tears trees off their roots, a bridge collapses, bodies spin downriver. Up on the hill the old couple who'd offered Jupiter and Mercury a bowl of soup watch, untouched, their hut turning into a temple. Recent restoration showed Rubens started out painting just the storm and only later added the myth, tucking Philemon and Baucis in late. Kunsthistorisches Museum, Vienna; begun around 1620 and worked on for years.

Peter_Paul_Rubens,_Kunsthistorisches_Mus.title: Theodosius and Saint Ambrose
Peter_Paul_Rubens,_Kunsthistorisches_Mus.artist: Anthony van Dyck / Peter Paul Rubens

source.canonical_title: File:Peter Paul Rubens, Kunsthistorisches Museum Wien, Gemäldegalerie - Hl. Ambrosius und Kaiser Theodosius - GG 524 - Kunsthistorisches Museum.jpg

title.ja: 皇帝テオドシウスと聖アンブロシウス

Peter_Paul_Rubens,_Kunsthistorisches_Mus.story: A workshop collaboration from around 1615-1616 in Antwerp, when the teenage Van Dyck was Rubens's most trusted assistant. Rubens designed the composition; Van Dyck executed most of the painting. Bishop Ambrose of Milan stands in the cathedral doorway, arm raised, blocking Emperor Theodosius from entering as penance for the massacre at Thessalonica. The emperor's armour, the nervous horses and the clergy behind Ambrose are all painted with the young van Dyck's thinner, more anxious touch. It hangs at the Kunsthistorisches Museum in Vienna; Van Dyck later made his own larger version, now in London.

Peter_Paul_Rubens,_The_Death_of_Adonis,_.title: The Death of Adonis (with Venus, Cupid, and the Three Graces)

source.canonical_title: File:Peter Paul Rubens, The Death of Adonis, ca. 1614. The Israel Museum, Jerusalem.jpg

Peter_Paul_Rubens,_The_Death_of_Adonis,_.story: The boar has done its work. Adonis lies gored, the wound on his thigh painted with the same dark red Rubens used for the drapery, and Venus bends over him while Cupid wipes his eyes and the Three Graces arrange themselves into a Renaissance frieze of grief. It's Ovid by way of Titian, staged for maximum pathos. Saul Steinberg gave the canvas to the Israel Museum in 2000, the first time Israeli audiences could see Rubens working at full mythological throttle.

Peter_Paul_Rubens-Der_Heilige_Hieronymus.title: Saint Jerome in his study

source.canonical_title: File:Peter Paul Rubens-Der Heilige Hieronymus.jpg

title.nl: De Heilige Hiëronymus in zijn studie

Peter_Paul_Rubens-Der_Heilige_Hieronymus.story: An old man stripped to the waist, beard tangled, cardinal's red cloak slipping off the shoulder, a skull on the book and a lion padding somewhere in the dark. Rubens's Saint Jerome is copied closely from a Titian he'd studied in Italy, then inflated into full Flemish muscle. The picture dates to around 1615, shortly after his return to Antwerp, and hangs in the Gemäldegalerie Alte Meister in Dresden — where the lion, faintly visible in the gloom, almost looks embarrassed to be there.

Peter_Paul_Rubens_(1577-1640)_(after)_-_.title: Hercules and the Nemean Lion

source.canonical_title: File:Peter Paul Rubens (1577-1640) (after) - Hercules and the Nemean Lion - WM.1608-1948 - Apsley House.jpg

Peter_Paul_Rubens_(1577-1640)_(after)_-_.story: Hercules, all ropes of muscle, crushes the Nemean lion in a bear hug — first of the twelve labors, and the beast whose invulnerable pelt he'll wear for the rest of his career. This is a copy after Rubens, now at Apsley House, the Duke of Wellington's London home. Wellington came by a lot of his Spanish-school pictures the hard way: he captured Joseph Bonaparte's baggage train at Vitoria in 1813, rolled up with looted canvases, and tried to hand them back. Ferdinand VII told him to keep them.

Peter_Paul_Rubens_(1577-1640)_(after)_-_.title: Man in a Ruff

source.canonical_title: File:Peter Paul Rubens (1577-1640) (after) - Man in a Ruff - R.1990-58.23 - Colchester and Ipswich Museums Service.jpg

Peter_Paul_Rubens_(1577-1640)_(after)_-_.story: A stout, bearded man in a cartwheel ruff stares out of a dark ground — the kind of starched linen collar that required its own wire frame and the attention of a servant. This is a copy after a Rubens portrait type, held by Colchester and Ipswich Museums. Rubens was brilliant at ruffs: he painted the linen with loose flicks of lead white over gray, letting the weave suggest itself rather than counting threads. Even a later hand following him had to reckon with that trick.

Peter_Paul_Rubens_(1577-1640)_(copy_afte.title: Madonna and Child

source.canonical_title: File:Peter Paul Rubens (1577-1640) (copy after) - Madonna and Child - PCF48 - Lady Margaret Hall.jpg

Peter_Paul_Rubens_(1577-1640)_(copy_afte.story: A warm, fleshy Madonna cradling a plump Christ child — the domestic Rubens, softer than the battle scenes and altarpieces that paid the bills. This version hangs at Lady Margaret Hall, one of the Oxford colleges, and is catalogued as a copy after Rubens rather than from his own hand. Rubens painted his second wife Helena Fourment and their children into more than one Madonna in the 1630s; the type became workshop currency that copyists chased for the next two centuries.

Peter_Paul_Rubens_(1577-1640)_(school_of.title: The Lamentation

source.canonical_title: File:Peter Paul Rubens (1577-1640) (school of) - The Lamentation - 1.OP.0049 - Durham University.jpg

Peter_Paul_Rubens_(1577-1640)_(school_of.story: Christ's body across Mary's lap, Magdalene at the feet, John bent forward — the grief choreography Rubens returned to again and again. This Lamentation at Durham University is school-of Rubens, painted by someone trained in his Antwerp workshop rather than the master himself. Rubens ran one of the largest studios in Europe; pupils prepared panels, blocked in compositions, and specialized in drapery or flowers while he handled the faces. A good school piece like this one is the next best thing.

Peter_Paul_Rubens_(1577-1640)_-_Christ_G.title: Christ Giving the Keys to St. Peter

source.canonical_title: File:Peter Paul Rubens (1577-1640) - Christ Giving the Keys of Heaven to Saint Peter - B.116 - Gemäldegalerie.jpg

title.de: Christus übergibt dem Heiligen Petrus die Himmelsschlüssel
title.nl: Christus overhandigt de sleutels aan Petrus

Peter_Paul_Rubens_(1577-1640)_-_Christ_G.story: Two gold keys change hands and the Church is founded. Rubens paints the moment as a private transaction between kneeling fisherman and upright Christ, the other apostles pressed in like witnesses at a signing. The panel was commissioned for the Kapellekerk in Brussels to mark the tomb of Pieter Bruegel the Elder, a quiet nod from one Flemish master to another. Sold off by the church in 1765, it changed hands repeatedly before landing in Berlin's Gemäldegalerie, where it still hangs.

Peter_Paul_Rubens_(1577-1640)_-_Diana_an.title: Diana and two nymphs surprised by satyrs while bathing

source.canonical_title: File:Peter Paul Rubens (1577-1640) - Diana and two nymphs surprised by satyrs while bathing - 762C - Gemäldegalerie.jpg

title.es: Diana y ninfas en el baño sorprendidas por sátiros
title.de: Diana mit zwei Nymphen von Satyrn beim Bade überrascht

Peter_Paul_Rubens_(1577-1640)_-_Diana_an.story: Chastity bumps into appetite. Diana and her nymphs, cooling off, suddenly have goat-legged company; every face in the picture is caught in a different phase of surprise. The Berlin picture is an earlier Rubens than its catalogue year suggests, about 1616, when he was still digesting Italy and painting bodies as polished marble come to life. Gemäldegalerie, inv. 762C.

Peter_Paul_Rubens_(1577-1640)_-_Diana_hu.title: Diana on the stag hunt
Peter_Paul_Rubens_(1577-1640)_-_Diana_hu.artist: Jan Wildens / Frans Snyders / Peter Paul Rubens

source.canonical_title: File:Peter Paul Rubens (1577-1640) - Diana hunting deer - 774 - Gemäldegalerie.jpg

title.nl: Diana en haar gevolg tijdens de hertenjacht

Peter_Paul_Rubens_(1577-1640)_-_Diana_hu.story: A Rubens workshop production of the kind Antwerp turned out at court speed. Rubens lays in Diana and her nymphs mid-pursuit; Jan Wildens is traditionally credited with the long, airy landscape behind them; Frans Snyders, the city's great animal painter, handles the hounds and the straining stag. Later scholars have been skeptical of the triple attribution, but the division of labour is real enough in principle: one shop, three specialists, one picture. It hangs in the Gemäldegalerie in Berlin, inventory number 774.

Peter_Paul_Rubens_(1577-1640)_-_Head_Stu.title: Head Study of a Bearded Man

source.canonical_title: File:Peter Paul Rubens (1577-1640) - Head Study of a Bearded Man - PD.13-1980 - Fitzwilliam Museum.jpg

Peter_Paul_Rubens_(1577-1640)_-_Head_Stu.story: A bearded man, eyes cast down, the jaw caught in a warm raking light, the whole head painted on a panel no bigger than a dinner plate. Rubens kept shelves of these oil sketches as raw material for saints, prophets and bystanders. This one entered the Fitzwilliam Museum in Cambridge in 1980, accession PD.13-1980. You can still see the underdrawing through the thinned brown paint in the beard.

Peter_Paul_Rubens_(1577-1640)_-_Neptune_.title: Neptune and Amphitrite

source.canonical_title: File:Peter Paul Rubens (1577-1640) - Neptune and Amphitrite - 776A - Gemäldegalerie.jpg

Peter_Paul_Rubens_(1577-1640)_-_Neptune_.story: You're looking at a ghost. Rubens's Neptune and Amphitrite, inventory 776A of the Kaiser-Friedrich-Museum, was stashed for safekeeping in the Friedrichshain flak tower in Berlin during the war. In May 1945 the tower burned, and ten Rubenses went up with it, this canvas among them. What remains is photographs: the sea god twisting toward his nereid bride, tritons blowing horns, horses rearing out of surf. The painting dated to about 1615, roughly two metres across, and only the black-and-white record survives.

Peter_Paul_Rubens_(1577-1640)_-_Portrait.title: Portrait of an Old Man

source.canonical_title: File:Peter Paul Rubens (1577-1640) - Portrait of an elderly man - 776F - Gemäldegalerie.jpg

Peter_Paul_Rubens_(1577-1640)_-_Portrait.story: An old man in near-profile, white beard combed, gaze withdrawn — no grand rhetoric, no saintly attributes, just a face Rubens wanted to paint around 1622-25. The coat of arms at upper left was added later and linked him to Jan van Ghindertalen, a Brussels magistrate, though the identification stays tentative. The panel is small, about 65 by 50 centimetres, and the handling is intimate in a way the vast allegories never are. It hangs in Berlin's Gemäldegalerie as inventory 776F.

Peter_Paul_Rubens_(1577-1640)_-_Teresa_o.title: Saint Teresa of Avila's vision of the dove

source.canonical_title: File:Peter Paul Rubens (1577-1640) - Teresa of Avila's Vision of the Dove - PD.43-1999 - Fitzwilliam Museum.jpg

title.es: Aparición del Espíritu Santo a santa Teresa de Jesús
title.nl: Het visioen van de Heilige Theresa van Avila

Peter_Paul_Rubens_(1577-1640)_-_Teresa_o.story: On the eve of Pentecost 1569, Teresa of Avila wrote, the Holy Spirit came to her as a dove with wings like mother-of-pearl. Rubens paints her in the brown Carmelite habit, hands flung open, face tipped up at the bird hovering just above her head. It's one of three versions he made of the subject. The Fitzwilliam in Cambridge got this one in 1999, allocated by the UK government after it was accepted in lieu of inheritance tax. The panel is about a metre tall.

Peter_Paul_Rubens_(1577-1640)_-_The_Bacc.title: Drunken Silenus
Peter_Paul_Rubens_(1577-1640)_-_The_Bacc.artist: Anthony van Dyck / Peter Paul Rubens

source.canonical_title: File:Peter Paul Rubens (1577-1640) - The Bacchanal - 776B - Gemäldegalerie.jpg

Peter_Paul_Rubens_(1577-1640)_-_The_Bacc.story: A bacchanal of the Drunken Silenus type, inventoried as no. 776B in the Berlin Gemäldegalerie. Silenus, Bacchus's fat old tutor, tips sideways through the wood, held up by a crush of satyrs, women and children; a child tugs at his cloak while grapes are pushed at his mouth. The whole weight of the composition seems to sag with him. The Berlin canvas is one of several Rubens bacchanals from the later 1610s, related in design to the more famous 'Drunken Silenus' now in Munich's Alte Pinakothek.

Peter_Paul_Rubens_(Flemish)_-_The_Return.title: The Return from War: Mars Disarmed by Venus
Peter_Paul_Rubens_(Flemish)_-_The_Return.artist: Peter Paul Rubens / Jan Brueghel the Elder

source.canonical_title: File:Peter Paul Rubens (Flemish) - The Return from War- Mars Disarmed by Venus - Google Art Project.jpg
source.credit: JwGEkfavTuicrA at Google Cultural Institute maximum zoom level

Peter_Paul_Rubens_(Flemish)_-_The_Return.story: Mars just got home and Venus is already unbuckling his armor. Cupids tug at his breastplate and pile weapons on the floor; doves settle where helmets used to be. Rubens painted the figures, Jan Brueghel the Elder handled the still life — every olive branch, dove feather, and rose petal is his. The two friends collaborated on panels like this around 1610-1612, trading brushes across Antwerp. The panel is at the Getty. Count the cupids: there are seven.

Peter_Paul_Rubens_(Kopie_nach)_-_Ecce_ho.title: Ecce homo

source.canonical_title: File:Peter Paul Rubens (Kopie nach) - Ecce homo - 1922 - Bavarian State Painting Collections.jpg

Peter_Paul_Rubens_(Kopie_nach)_-_Ecce_ho.story: Pilate's line: behold the man. Christ stands crowned with thorns, a reed for a scepter, the rope still around his wrists — the moment before the crowd shouts for crucifixion. Rubens painted the subject several times with his signature bruised, mortal flesh and spotlight staging. This copy is held by the Bavarian State Painting Collections in Munich under inventory 1922, the number to look for rather than any date. The original type circulated widely in northern Europe in engraved form.

Peter_Paul_Rubens_(Schule)_-_Der_lachend.title: The Laughing Philosopher (Democritus)

source.canonical_title: File:Peter Paul Rubens (Schule) - Der lachende Philosoph (Demokrit) - 7043 - Bavarian State Painting Collections.jpg

Peter_Paul_Rubens_(Schule)_-_Der_lachend.story: Democritus, the laughing philosopher of Abdera, is grinning at you. He's the ancient who reportedly could not stop laughing at the absurdity of human behavior — paired, in the old tradition, with the weeping Heraclitus. Rubens painted a famous pair of the two in 1603 during his time at the Spanish court in Valladolid, now in the Prado. This Munich canvas (inventory 7043) is a workshop or school-of version that descends from that pairing, and it keeps the open mouth and tilted head that make Democritus immediately readable.

Peter_Paul_Rubens_-_Adam_and_Eve,_after_.title: Adam and Eve

source.canonical_title: File:Peter Paul Rubens - Adam and Eve, after Titian, between 1628 and 1629.jpg
source.credit: 1. The Yorck Project (2002) 10.000 Meisterwerke der Malerei (DVD-ROM), distributed by DIRECTMEDIA Publishing GmbH. ISBN : 3936122202 . , [1] 2. Museo del Prado, Madrid

Peter_Paul_Rubens_-_Adam_and_Eve,_after_.story: During Rubens's 1628-29 diplomatic mission to Madrid he spent months in the royal collection copying Titian — his idol — sometimes nine hours a day. This Adam and Eve follows Titian's 1550 composition but with Rubens fingerprints all over it: Adam's torso bulked up on the Belvedere Torso he'd drawn in Rome, a parrot added as a symbol of Redemption, the palette cranked brighter. Both versions now hang in the Prado, often shown together so you can watch one master speak back to another across eighty years.

Peter_Paul_Rubens_-_Adoration_of_the_She.title: The Adoration of the Shepherds

source.canonical_title: File:Peter Paul Rubens - Adoration of the Shepherds (Saint Paul's, Antwerp).jpeg

Peter_Paul_Rubens_-_Adoration_of_the_She.story: Shepherds shove in from the dark, faces lit only by the child. One old man cups his weathered hand against the glare as if the baby were a candle. Rubens had just returned from eight years in Italy, and you can see Caravaggio in the bruised shadows, Correggio in the radiating light. The altarpiece still hangs where he put it: the Lady Chapel of Saint Paul's Church in Antwerp, finished in 1609.

Peter_Paul_Rubens_-_Anatomical_study_of_.title: Anatomical study

source.canonical_title: File:Peter Paul Rubens - Anatomical study of a man.jpg

Peter_Paul_Rubens_-_Anatomical_study_of_.story: Not one figure but several: forearms rotated into two positions, torsos peeled back, a skull angle or two, all crammed onto a single sheet in confident pen strokes. These are Rubens's working notes, made during his Italian years — roughly 1600 to 1610, with most scholars leaning earlier in that span — studying how muscle attaches, how weight shifts, how to build a body from the inside out. Sheets from the series are scattered across the Getty, the Met, the Art Institute of Chicago, and others.

Peter_Paul_Rubens_-_Cain_slaying_Abel_(C.title: Cain slaying his brother Abel (Genesis 4:2-12)

source.canonical_title: File:Peter Paul Rubens - Cain slaying Abel (Courtauld Institute).jpg
source.credit: The Courtauld Institute of Art, London

Peter_Paul_Rubens_-_Cain_slaying_Abel_(C.story: Genesis 4 in sixty seconds: Cain's knee on his brother's chest, the raised bone poised, Abel's hand already going slack. Rubens paints it as grappling, not murder — the two bodies locked in the same torque, as if they couldn't be separated if they tried. Painted in oil on oak around 1608 to 1609, just after Rubens's return from eight years in Italy. Samuel Courtauld's bequest eventually brought it to The Courtauld in London, where it still hangs under inventory number P.1978.PG.353.

Peter_Paul_Rubens_-_Crucifixion_of_Saint.title: The Crucifixion of Saint Peter
Peter_Paul_Rubens_-_Crucifixion_of_Saint.description: Peter Paul Rubens (1577-1640): Die Kreuzigung Petri, 1638, Sankt Peter Köln

source.canonical_title: File:Peter Paul Rubens - Crucifixion of Saint Peter.jpg

Peter_Paul_Rubens_-_Crucifixion_of_Saint.story: Peter, crucified upside down at his own request (he didn't feel worthy of dying like Christ), strains against the ropes while torturers heave the cross upright. Rubens painted this for Sankt Peter in Cologne, the church where he'd been baptized in 1577. He finished it just before his death in 1640 and never saw it installed. The altarpiece is still there, in the same Cologne church, visible to anyone who walks in.

Peter_Paul_Rubens_-_Das_Kind_mit_dem_Vog.title: A child with bird
Peter_Paul_Rubens_-_Das_Kind_mit_dem_Vog.description: Obgleich er selber weniger begeistert in diesem Genre arbeitete, genoss Rubens auch als Porträtist große Anerkennung, wo er Dutzende von Aufträgen erhielt. Mit Ausnahme des Porträts seiner zwei Söhne … (weiterlesen)

source.canonical_title: File:Peter Paul Rubens - Das Kind mit dem Vogel (Gemäldegalerie Berlin).jpg
source.credit: Objekt in der Onlinesammlung der Staatlichen Museen zu Berlin: 870518 Fotograf: Christoph Schmidt

title.nl: Portret van een jongetje met een vogeltje, mogelijk Albert Rubens, zoon van de kunstenaar, 1616-1625

Peter_Paul_Rubens_-_Das_Kind_mit_dem_Vog.story: A small boy in profile, coral necklace at his throat, a finch tethered to his finger by a short string. Rubens rarely painted children posed; here he catches one mid-flap, the bird about to bolt. The coral was believed to ward off illness, the finch stood for a soul under instruction, but the picture's real subject is a child who can't sit still. Possibly his son Albert, born 1614. The small oak panel is in Berlin's Gemäldegalerie, about 50 centimetres tall.

Peter_Paul_Rubens_-_Descent_from_the_Cro.title: Descent from the Cross (outside right)

source.canonical_title: File:Peter Paul Rubens - Descent from the Cross (outside right) - WGA20217.jpg
source.credit: Web Gallery of Art : Image Info about artwork wga QS:P11807,"r/rubens/11religi/07desce5"

Peter_Paul_Rubens_-_Descent_from_the_Cro.story: This is the outside of the right wing: when the great triptych in Antwerp Cathedral is closed, you see the Visitation on one side and this, the Presentation in the Temple, on the other. Simeon cradles the infant Christ while Anna the prophetess raises a hand. Rubens finished the whole altarpiece for the Arquebusiers' guild between 1612 and 1614. It's still there.

title.es: Diana y sus ninfas sorprendidas por sátiros
title.hu: Dianát és nimfáit meglepik a szatírok (Rubens-kép)
title.de: Diana und die Nymphen, von Faunen überrascht
title.nl: Diana en nimfen aangevallen door saters

Peter_Paul_Rubens_-_Diana_and_her_Nymphs.story: A hunt turns into an ambush. Diana's nymphs, flush from the chase with hares and a dead roebuck at their feet, look up to find leering satyrs crashing the party. Rubens didn't paint it alone — Frans Snyders handled the game, Jan Wildens laid in the landscape, and Rubens delivered the glowing flesh and charged glances. It's from his final, most sensual decade, painted 1638-1640 for his own collection. The picture was still hanging in his Antwerp studio when he died.

Peter_Paul_Rubens_-_Diana_cazadora,_1617.title: Diana returning from the Hunt

source.canonical_title: File:Peter Paul Rubens - Diana cazadora, 1617-1620.jpg

Peter_Paul_Rubens_-_Diana_cazadora,_1617.story: Diana strides back from the hunt with her nymphs, bare-armed, a dead hare slung over a spear, dogs panting at the edges of the frame. Rubens paints the goddess as a Flemish athlete, broad-shouldered and sun-warmed, not the icy marble of antiquity. The canvas is usually dated 1617 to 1620 and is part of a cycle of hunt and mythology pictures the studio turned out for aristocratic walls across Europe.
