Peter_Paul_Rubens_-_Dying_Seneca.jpg.story: The Stoic philosopher, ordered by Nero to kill himself, bleeds out in a basin of water while a scribe copies his last words and a doctor reads his pulse. Rubens based the figure on an antique marble he'd sketched in Rome, believing it was a portrait of Seneca. It wasn't, but the mistake gave him a gaunt, heroic model. Munich's Alte Pinakothek, around 1612-15.

Peter_Paul_Rubens_-_Evening_Landscape_wi.title: Avondlandschap met boerenkar

source.canonical_title: File:Peter Paul Rubens - Evening Landscape with Timber Wagon - Google Art Project.jpg
source.credit: cgFcDUneAqR5KQ at Google Cultural Institute maximum zoom level

Peter_Paul_Rubens_-_Evening_Landscape_wi.story: Painted in Rubens' last decade, when he'd bought a country estate and kept pointing his brush at the flat Brabant horizon. A team hauls a timber wagon through low gold light; trees lean, cattle drift, the day closes down. No mythology, no kings, just weather. It's now in Rotterdam's Museum Boijmans Van Beuningen.

Peter_Paul_Rubens_-_Four_Studies_of_a_He.title: Four Studies of a Head of a Moor

source.canonical_title: File:Peter Paul Rubens - Four Studies of a Head of a Moor - Google Art Project.jpg
source.credit: LgE6l73zlShsKQ at Google Cultural Institute maximum zoom level

Peter_Paul_Rubens_-_Four_Studies_of_a_He.story: Same man, four angles, no narrative — just looking. Rubens painted this unidentified African sitter from life and kept the sheet as studio ammunition, pulling from it for years whenever a painting needed a Balthasar in an Adoration or a groom in a mythology. The turned profile, the three-quarter gaze, the upturned head — each catches different light on the same cheekbones. The canvas now lives at the Royal Museums of Fine Arts of Belgium in Brussels. Rubens reused the head at least three times in finished works.

Peter_Paul_Rubens_-_Heilige_Familie_met_.title: Yhe holy Family with the parrot

source.canonical_title: File:Peter Paul Rubens - Heilige Familie met de papegaai - KMSK.A.0312 - Rubenshuis.jpg

title.de: Die Heilige Familie mit einem Papagei

Peter_Paul_Rubens_-_Heilige_Familie_met_.story: Rubens started with Mary and the child, then, two decades later, reopened the panel and added Joseph, a landscape, and a green parrot on a branch. The parrot was a standard symbol of Mary's purity and a favourite household pet of the Antwerp rich, prized for mimicking speech. He donated the finished picture to the Guild of Saint Luke in 1633 as a painter's calling card. KMSKA in Antwerp restored it over two years, 2012 to 2014, and now shares custody with the Rubenshuis next door.

Peter_Paul_Rubens_-_Hercules_Strangling_.title: Hercules Strangling the Nemean Lion
Peter_Paul_Rubens_-_Hercules_Strangling_.description: Heracles and the Nemean Lion Nemean lion

source.canonical_title: File:Peter Paul Rubens - Hercules Strangling the Nemean Lion - 2000.199 - Busch–Reisinger Museum.jpg

Peter_Paul_Rubens_-_Hercules_Strangling_.story: No sword, no club, no trick — just bare hands around a throat. The Nemean lion's hide couldn't be pierced by any weapon, so Hercules had to choke it out. Rubens renders the struggle as one muscular coil, man and beast locked so tightly you can't separate their limbs. The fingers dig in; the lion's jaws strain open in silent roar. It's a late oil sketch, about 1639, now at Harvard's Busch-Reisinger Museum. Hercules would later skin the lion using its own claws.

Peter_Paul_Rubens_-_Hercules_as_Heroic_V.title: Hercules as Heroic Virtue Overcoming Discord

source.canonical_title: File:Peter Paul Rubens - Hercules as Heroic Virtue Overcoming Discord (cropped).jpg

title.de: Herkules als heroische Tugend überwindet die Zwietracht

Peter_Paul_Rubens_-_Hercules_as_Heroic_V.story: Hercules swings his club down on a snake-haired woman sprawled beneath his feet, Discord herself. A putto floats in with a victor's wreath. This is one of four corner ovals Rubens designed around 1632 for the ceiling of the Banqueting House at Whitehall, a glorification of Charles I's peace, virtue, and Stuart kingship. It's the only surviving Baroque ceiling cycle installed in its original location in Britain; sixteen years after it went up, Charles walked beneath it to his execution outside.

Peter_Paul_Rubens_-_Isabella_Brant_as_Gl.title: Isabella Brant as Glycera

source.canonical_title: File:Peter Paul Rubens - Isabella Brant as Glycera - 38.1616 - Museum of Fine Arts.jpg

Peter_Paul_Rubens_-_Isabella_Brant_as_Gl.story: Rubens dresses his first wife Isabella Brant as Glycera, the Greek flower-seller Pliny said could outdo the painter Pausias with a garland. She holds a basket of blossoms, her cheeks flushed, the collar of her dress cutting a crisp edge against her skin. It is a love letter dressed as a classical conceit. The panel has been in Boston's Museum of Fine Arts since 1938, accession number 38.1616.

Peter_Paul_Rubens_-_Judith_with_the_Head.title: Judith with the Head of Holofernes

source.canonical_title: File:Peter Paul Rubens - Judith with the Head of Holofernes.jpg

Peter_Paul_Rubens_-_Judith_with_the_Head.story: Judith grips a fistful of the general's hair, his head still dripping, her maid's face half in shadow behind her. Rubens gives her a jewelled brocade and a cool, almost bored expression, as if beheading a tyrant were a civic chore. The Deuterocanonical heroine was a favorite after the Council of Trent, and Rubens returned to her several times. His version leans on Caravaggio's without the clinical horror, trading it for Flemish weight and warmth.

Peter_Paul_Rubens_-_Junger_Mann_mit_schw.title: Young man with a black hat
Peter_Paul_Rubens_-_Junger_Mann_mit_schw.artist: Peter Paul Rubens / After Willem Key

source.canonical_title: File:Peter Paul Rubens - Junger Mann mit schwarzem Barett.JPG

Peter_Paul_Rubens_-_Junger_Mann_mit_schw.story: One of Rubens's study-copies after an earlier Flemish master, in this case Willem Key, painted around 1620. A young man in a soft black beret and dark coat glances sideways; a pleated white shirt ruffles at the throat and a gold ring catches light on the raised hand. Rubens copies the format of a sober mid-century Antwerp portrait but can't resist warming the flesh and loosening the brushwork — the cheeks pink up, the eyes moisten. A Baroque painter keeping his hand in by rereading the generation before him.

Peter_Paul_Rubens_-_Juno_and_Argus_-_WGA.title: Juno and Argus

source.canonical_title: File:Peter Paul Rubens - Juno and Argus - WGA20280.jpg
source.credit: Web Gallery of Art : Image Info about artwork wga QS:P11807,"r/rubens/21mythol/08mythol"

Peter_Paul_Rubens_-_Juno_and_Argus_-_WGA.story: Juno kneels in her peacock chariot and plucks eyes from the severed head of her hundred-eyed watchman, setting them into her bird's tail. Io, transformed into a white heifer, lurks at the left, the cause of all this trouble. Rubens paints the gore cheerfully; this is mythology, not tragedy. The canvas hangs in the Wallraf-Richartz-Museum in Cologne, painted around 1611.

Peter_Paul_Rubens_-_Lamentation_(Christ_.title: Lamentation (Christ on the Straw)

source.canonical_title: File:Peter Paul Rubens - Lamentation (Christ on the Straw).jpg

Peter_Paul_Rubens_-_Lamentation_(Christ_.story: A body laid on yellow straw, knees bent, the skin gone grey-blue in the chill. This little triptych was commissioned by Jan Michielsen, an Antwerp merchant, for his own tomb in the cathedral, and Rubens pitched the mood accordingly: no crowd, no drama, just the Virgin, John and the Magdalene gathered close over the corpse. The straw is the trick. You can almost smell it, dry and a bit musty, cutting against the pallor of the flesh. It's the painting's nickname now. It's dated to 1617 and hangs in the Royal Museum of Fine Arts, Antwerp.

Peter_Paul_Rubens_-_Lamentation_of_Chris.title: The lamentation of Christ

source.canonical_title: File:Peter Paul Rubens - Lamentation of Christ (Liechtenstein Museum).jpg

Peter_Paul_Rubens_-_Lamentation_of_Chris.story: Christ is laid on a stone slab, pale as marble, while Mary leans in and John cradles the head. Mary Magdalene kisses the nailed feet. Rubens paints the body as sculpture, lit from above like a morgue. This small panel, around 1612, was bought by Prince Johann Adam I of Liechtenstein and still belongs to the princely collections in Vienna.

Peter_Paul_Rubens_-_Landscape_with_a_Rai.title: Landscape with a Rainbow

source.canonical_title: File:Peter Paul Rubens - Landscape with a Rainbow - WGA20411.jpg
source.credit: https://wallacelive.wallacecollection.org:443/eMP/eMuseumPlus?service=ExternalInterface&module=collection&objectId=64938&viewType=detailView Web Gallery of Art : Image Info about artwork wga QS:P11807,"r/rubens/5landsca/16landsc"
source.permission: Copyright expired, PD-Art

Peter_Paul_Rubens_-_Landscape_with_a_Rai.story: The morning-after-storm picture, around 1636, the arc of light curving across Rubens' own Brabant estate at Het Steen. Haymakers straighten up, cattle head home, a wagon creaks forward, and a rainbow settles over everything like a blessing on working ground. The painting stayed in Rubens' house until his death in 1640; today it's in London's Wallace Collection.

Peter_Paul_Rubens_-_Landscape_with_the_R.title: Landscape with the Ruins of Mount Palatine in Rome

source.canonical_title: File:Peter Paul Rubens - Landscape with the Ruins of Mount Palatine in Rome.JPG

Peter_Paul_Rubens_-_Landscape_with_the_R.story: An oil on panel, roughly a metre tall, painted around 1608 - at the tail end of Rubens's eight years in Italy or just after his return to Antwerp. Broken arches of the imperial palaces on the Palatine crumble over the Roman Campagna, with tiny figures dwarfed beneath. Rubens is working a genre the Flemish and the Italians both loved: ancient grandeur run to ruin, vegetation eating back the stones. It is one of the relatively small number of pure landscapes from his hand, and it hangs in the Louvre.

Peter_Paul_Rubens_-_Last_Supper_-_WGA202.story: A dog gnaws a bone under the table. Above it, Christ lifts the bread; eleven apostles lean in; Judas twists outward in a blue robe, cheek muscles tight, eyes unable to land anywhere. The dog and the traitor share a frame on purpose, an old symbol of appetite and betrayal. Painted around 1631 as an altarpiece for a Mechelen church, commissioned by Catherine Lescuyer to honour her late father. It's now at the Pinacoteca di Brera in Milan.

Peter_Paul_Rubens_-_Lot_and_his_daughter.title: Lot and his daughters in a rock grotto
Peter_Paul_Rubens_-_Lot_and_his_daughter.description: Bildtext Staatliche Museen Schwerin: "Peter Paul Rubens. Siegen 1577 - 1640 Antwerpen. Lot und seine Töchter, um 1610. Leinwand." "Das Gemälde gehört zu Rubens' frühen Werken nach seiner Rückkehr aus Italien. Der Bildraum wird ganz von den Figuren im Bildvordergrund beherrscht. Die Szene zeigt den Moment, in dem die Töchter Lots ihren Vater betrunken machen, um sich von ihm schwängern zu lassen (Gen. 18, 30-38). Rubens entschied sich, den Vater keineswegs als Opfer weiblicher Verführungskünste darzustelnne. Vielmehr schildert er ihn als zwar bärtigen, aber kräftigen Mann, der hier aktiv nach der jungen Frau strebt."

source.canonical_title: File:Peter Paul Rubens - Lot and his daughters in a rock grotto (Schwerin).jpg
source.credit: 1. akbrzeski.de 2. Staatliches Museum Schwerin 3. Google Art Project works from the Staatliches Museum Schwerin

title.nl: Lots dochters maken hun vader dronken (Genesis 19:33-34)
title.pl: Lot i jego córki w skalnej grocie

Peter_Paul_Rubens_-_Lot_and_his_daughter.story: The Genesis story gets a Flemish rewrite. Rubens refuses to play Lot as the drunken victim of his scheming daughters; here the bearded father lunges for the younger woman with clear appetite while the elder tips more wine. A discarded shoe, a tilted jug, the cave mouth black behind them. Painted around 1613-14, just after his Italian years. It hangs in the Staatliches Museum Schwerin.

Peter_Paul_Rubens_-_Mariae_Himmelfahrt_-.title: Mariae Himmelfahrt

source.canonical_title: File:Peter Paul Rubens - Mariae Himmelfahrt - 1303 - Bavarian State Painting Collections.jpg

Peter_Paul_Rubens_-_Mariae_Himmelfahrt_-.story: The Virgin rockets upward on a cloud of wind-whipped drapery while apostles below crane their necks and reach into empty air. Rubens painted the Assumption over and over, from small panels to the enormous high altar at Antwerp Cathedral. This Munich version, inventory 1303 in the Bavarian State Painting Collections, is tighter and more intimate, all the drama packed into a vertical shaft of gold.

Peter_Paul_Rubens_-_Mercury_and_Argos,_1.title: Mercury and Argus (Ovid, Metamorphoses, I, 668-721)

source.canonical_title: File:Peter Paul Rubens - Mercury and Argos, 1636-1638.jpg

Peter_Paul_Rubens_-_Mercury_and_Argos,_1.story: Juno gave the hundred-eyed giant Argus one job: guard the white heifer (who is really the nymph Io). Mercury, sent by Jupiter to free her, plays a pipe until every eye finally closes, then draws his sword. Rubens paints the sleep and the sword in the same breath. It was made around 1636-38 for the Torre de la Parada, Philip IV's hunting lodge outside Madrid, part of a giant Ovid cycle. Prado, Madrid.

Peter_Paul_Rubens_-_Moses_and_the_Brazen.title: Anyone who is bitten by a snake is cured by looking at the brazen serpent raised by Moses (Numbers 21:6-9)

source.canonical_title: File:Peter Paul Rubens - Moses and the Brazen Serpent.jpg

title.nl: Al wie gebeten is door een slang en opziet naar de door Mozes opgerichte Koperen Slang wordt genezen (Numeri 21:6-9), ca. 1609-1610

Peter_Paul_Rubens_-_Moses_and_the_Brazen.story: The Israelites writhe under snake-bite. A mother tears a serpent from her baby's leg; another figure arches backward, already poisoned. Moses, calm in the upper right, points to the bronze serpent on its pole: look up and live. Rubens stacks bodies in a diagonal pile straight out of Michelangelo. The canvas is in the National Gallery, London, dated around 1609-10.

source.canonical_title: File:Peter Paul Rubens - Nicolas Rubens, the artist's son - 1954.299 - Art Institute of Chicago.jpg

Peter_Paul_Rubens_-_Old_Woman_with_a_Bas.title: Old Woman with a Basket of Coal

source.canonical_title: File:Peter Paul Rubens - Old Woman with a Basket of Coal - Google Art Project.jpg

title.nl: Oude vrouw zich de handen warmend boven een vuurtest

Peter_Paul_Rubens_-_Old_Woman_with_a_Bas.story: A hunched woman cups her hand around a glowing coal, and her face leaps out of the dark. This is Rubens doing Caravaggio — a nocturne where the only light source is the ember itself, reddening her knuckles and the creased skin of her cheek. Look at the hand: three colors of flesh in the span of a finger. The picture sits in Dresden's Gemäldegalerie and is dated around 1618, not 1650. Rubens was testing what a single point of fire could do.

Peter_Paul_Rubens_-_Perseus_and_Andromed.story: Perseus has just slain the sea-monster and lands beside the chained princess, still holding the gorgon-shielded Pegasus by the bridle. Putti do most of the heavy lifting — one hauls Medusa's head, another fumbles at Andromeda's manacles. The armour gleams; her skin glows pink against her own dark hair. Rubens painted it around 1620-22, one of several takes he made on the myth. Count Heinrich von Brühl owned it before Catherine the Great bought his collection in 1769, which is how it ended up at the Hermitage in St Petersburg.

Peter_Paul_Rubens_-_Peter_Finds_the_Coin.title: Peter Finds the Coin in the Mouth of the Fish

source.canonical_title: File:Peter Paul Rubens - Peter Finds the Coin in the Mouth of the Fish.jpg

Peter_Paul_Rubens_-_Peter_Finds_the_Coin.story: A three-metre vertical panel of Peter kneeling at the lakeshore, prying open a fish to fish out the coin that pays the temple tax (Matthew 17). Rubens gives him sunburned arms and a working fisherman's crouch, Christ pointing behind him. It was painted around 1618-19 for the Church of Our Lady across the Dijle in Mechelen, where it still hangs. If you've only seen the JPEG, you haven't seen it: in person it's over ten feet tall.

Peter_Paul_Rubens_-_Portrait_of_Kaspar_S.story: A scholar at his desk — pen in hand, dog at his hip, the corner of a book peeking out — and the whole thing catches a flash of personal friendship. Kaspar Scioppius, or Caspar Schoppe, was a German polymath and bruising controversialist whom Rubens knew well in Italy. The portrait is generally dated to around 1606, during Rubens's Roman years, and measures 116 by 88 centimetres. It hangs in the Galleria Palatina of the Palazzo Pitti in Florence.

Peter_Paul_Rubens_-_Portrait_of_Marchese.title: Portrait of Marchese Ambrogio Spinola
Peter_Paul_Rubens_-_Portrait_of_Marchese.description: Depicted person: Ambrogio Spinola, 1st Marquis of the Balbases – Italian general (1569–1630)

source.canonical_title: File:Peter Paul Rubens - Portrait of Marchese Ambrogio Spinola (NG Prague).jpg
source.credit: Národní galerie v Praze - online collection

Peter_Paul_Rubens_-_Portrait_of_Marchese.story: Ambrogio Spinola was the Genoese banker's son who became Spain's best general — the man who took Breda in 1625, the siege Velázquez would later paint. Rubens knew him well and portrayed him several times; this one, roughly 1627, catches him in black armour with the sash of the Golden Fleece, face lean and wary. Spinola was a friend of Rubens as well as a patron, and the two discussed diplomacy as seriously as art. He died in 1630 muttering about his lost honour after being sidelined by Madrid. The portrait is considered the finest of the set and hangs at the National Gallery in Prague.

Peter_Paul_Rubens_-_Portrait_of_a_Young_.title: Portrait of Clara Serena Rubens, the Artist's Daughter

source.canonical_title: File:Peter Paul Rubens - Portrait of a Young Girl - WGA20359.jpg
source.credit: Web Gallery of Art : Image Info about artwork wga QS:P11807,"/r/rubens/41portra/10portra"

title.ja: クララ・セレーナ・ルーベンスの肖像
title.de: Ein Kinderkopf (Porträt der Clara Serena Rubens)

Peter_Paul_Rubens_-_Portrait_of_a_Young_.story: Clara Serena Rubens looks straight at her father with a faint, uncertain smile, hair pinned back, cheeks full of the pink only an oil painter who loves his child can mix. She was about five. She would die at twelve, in 1623, and Rubens never painted another portrait this tender. The little panel now lives in the Liechtenstein princely collections in Vienna.

Peter_Paul_Rubens_-_Saint_Francis_-_1983.title: Saint Francis

source.canonical_title: File:Peter Paul Rubens - Saint Francis - 1983.372 - Art Institute of Chicago.jpg

Peter_Paul_Rubens_-_Saint_Francis_-_1983.story: Francis kneels in brown robes, hands crossed over a skull, eyes turned up toward a light you can feel but not see. Rubens paints the saint as a workman of prayer, not a mystic floating off the ground. The small panel, bought by the Art Institute of Chicago in 1983, is one of several variations Rubens and his shop produced for Counter-Reformation patrons hungry for Franciscan devotion. The skull catches the sharpest highlight in the picture.

Peter_Paul_Rubens_-_Self-Portrait_(Kunst.title: Selfportrait

source.canonical_title: File:Peter Paul Rubens - Self-Portrait (Kunsthistorisches Museum).jpg

Peter_Paul_Rubens_-_Self-Portrait_(Kunst.story: Rubens at about 60, in a wide black hat and dark cloak, a dress sword at his hip. The gouty right hand rests on the pommel: by 1638 the arthritis was bad enough that he was dictating his brushwork to assistants some days. He painted this for himself, not a commission, dressed as the gentleman-diplomat he'd worked his whole life to become. The portrait hangs at the Kunsthistorisches Museum in Vienna.

Peter_Paul_Rubens_-_Silenus,_1636-1638.j.title: Silenus

source.canonical_title: File:Peter Paul Rubens - Silenus, 1636-1638.jpg

Peter_Paul_Rubens_-_Silenus,_1636-1638.j.story: Silenus staggers through the canvas, a tubby, wine-soaked old satyr propped up by a tipsy retinue. He's the tutor of Bacchus, and Rubens clearly relishes painting drunk flesh: pink, pliant, hilariously undignified. This sketch belongs to the Torre de la Parada cycle, a hunting lodge outside Madrid for Philip IV, where Rubens and his workshop pumped out more than 60 mythological panels between 1636 and 1638. Silenus here is less god than village drunk with hooves, and that's the point.

Peter_Paul_Rubens_-_Sleeping_Silenus.jpg.title: Bacchic scene with the dream of Silenus (?)

source.canonical_title: File:Peter Paul Rubens - Sleeping Silenus.jpg

Peter_Paul_Rubens_-_Sleeping_Silenus.jpg.story: Around 1611 the young Rubens, newly back in Antwerp from Italy, painted a sprawling Bacchic scene — Silenus, drunken tutor of Bacchus, slumped asleep as satyrs and nymphs riot around him. He didn't do it alone. Specialists were brought in for the props: David Rijckaert II painted the glassware, metalwork and porcelain, and a third hand added the heaped grapes. The picture now hangs at the Academy of Fine Arts in Vienna, a reminder that a 'Rubens' in this period was often a workshop collaboration, each man painting what he painted best.

Peter_Paul_Rubens_-_The_Birth_of_the_Mil.title: The creation of the milky way (Ovid, Metamorphoses, I, 168-171)
Peter_Paul_Rubens_-_The_Birth_of_the_Mil.description: The Birth of the Milky Way

source.canonical_title: File:Peter Paul Rubens - The Birth of the Milky Way, 1636-1637.jpg

title.eo: La naskiĝo de la Lakta Vojo
title.nl: The Origin of the Milky Way
title.es: El nacimiento de la Vía Láctea
title.de: The Origin of the Milky Way

Peter_Paul_Rubens_-_The_Birth_of_the_Mil.story: Juno's breast sprays across the night sky, milk scattering into stars. Baby Hercules, pressed to her by a nervous Jupiter, has latched on too hard, and the goddess pulls away mid-feed. Rubens paints the spilt milk as pale arcs of light, peacocks fanning below. The scene comes from Ovid's Metamorphoses, and the panel was made for Philip IV's Torre de la Parada hunting lodge near Madrid. It now hangs at the Prado, one of the tenderest cosmologies ever painted.

Peter_Paul_Rubens_-_The_Brazen_Serpent.j.title: The Brazen Serpent
Peter_Paul_Rubens_-_The_Brazen_Serpent.j.description: Its shows a scene from the Old Testament (Numbers 21: 6-9)

source.canonical_title: File:Peter Paul Rubens - The Brazen Serpent.jpg

Peter_Paul_Rubens_-_The_Brazen_Serpent.j.story: The Israelites, gnawed by a plague of venomous snakes (Numbers 21), must simply look up at a bronze serpent on a pole and they'll live. Bodies twist and writhe; Moses gestures; Eleazar holds the pole. Dead centre, a woman in black stares the cure down, calm while everyone around her thrashes. She's probably Helena Fourment, Rubens' second wife, slipped into yet another of his late biblical scenes. National Gallery, London.

Peter_Paul_Rubens_-_The_Deposition_(Gall.title: The Deposition

source.canonical_title: File:Peter Paul Rubens - The Deposition (Galleria Borghese.jpg

Peter_Paul_Rubens_-_The_Deposition_(Gall.story: The body of Christ slumps green-white against a shroud, hauled down by mourners whose hands sink into his flesh. Rubens painted this during his first stay in Rome, around 1601 to 1602, while still soaking up Caravaggio and the Carracci. For centuries the picture was given to Van Dyck; only in 1916 did the art historian Rudolf Oldenbourg return it to Rubens. It hangs in the Galleria Borghese in Rome, next to works by the very Italians the young Fleming had come south to study.

Peter_Paul_Rubens_-_The_Elevation_of_the.title: The raising of the cross (Matthew 27: 31-37)
Peter_Paul_Rubens_-_The_Elevation_of_the.description: crucifixion of Jesus Raising of the Cross

source.canonical_title: File:Peter Paul Rubens - The Elevation of the Cross.JPG

Peter_Paul_Rubens_-_The_Elevation_of_the.story: Rubens came home from Italy in 1610 and promptly blew Antwerp's doors off with this triptych for St. Walburga's church — now in the city's cathedral. The central panel is pure muscular strain: nine executioners heaving the cross upright at a wrenching diagonal, Christ's body taut and luminous against a stormy sky. Every back arches, every rope bites. It's Rubens translating Caravaggio's drama and Michelangelo's anatomy into something faster and more violent, the painting that announced Flemish Baroque had arrived.

Peter_Paul_Rubens_-_The_Entombment_-_93..title: The Entombment

source.canonical_title: File:Peter Paul Rubens - The Entombment - 93.PA.9 - J. Paul Getty Museum.jpg

Peter_Paul_Rubens_-_The_Entombment_-_93..story: Four mourners lower Christ into the tomb; Mary reaches for his hand, Joseph of Arimathea takes the weight at the shoulders. Rubens borrowed the diagonal composition straight from Caravaggio's Entombment, which he'd seen in Rome. The dead body is blue-white, heavy, all muscle gone slack. The Getty bought the panel in 1993; it was painted around 1612.

Peter_Paul_Rubens_-_The_Fall_of_Phaeton_.title: The Fall of Phaeton

source.canonical_title: File:Peter Paul Rubens - The Fall of Phaeton (National Gallery of Art).jpg
source.credit: nga.gov National Gallery of Art, Washington D.C.

Peter_Paul_Rubens_-_The_Fall_of_Phaeton_.story: The sun-chariot shatters mid-sky. Horses rear, the zodiac cracks, and Phaeton — the boy who begged his father Apollo to let him drive — is flung from the reins while Jupiter's thunderbolt lights the whole wreck. X-rays show Rubens kept coming back to this picture, begun around 1604 or 1605 and reworked a few years later, fiddling with the horses, shifting the composition. Oil on canvas, 98.4 by 131.2 centimetres, and it hangs today in the National Gallery of Art in Washington.

Peter_Paul_Rubens_-_The_Feast_of_Venus_-.title: The Feast of Venus

source.canonical_title: File:Peter Paul Rubens - The Feast of Venus - Google Art Project.jpg
source.credit: XgGjucvfTejNUg at Google Cultural Institute maximum zoom level

Peter_Paul_Rubens_-_The_Feast_of_Venus_-.story: A storm of cupids boils around a marble statue of Venus while nymphs and satyrs lock arms in a circle dance. It's the Veneralia, the Roman festival where women washed the goddess's image and asked for love. Rubens painted this around 1636-1637 after studying Titian's lost Worship of Venus, and it's an explicit homage: the same winged swarm, the same thick, rosy flesh. The canvas now lives at the Kunsthistorisches Museum in Vienna.

Peter_Paul_Rubens_-_The_Hermit_and_the_S.title: The Hermit and the Sleeping Angelica

Peter_Paul_Rubens_-_The_Hermit_and_the_S.story: A small oak panel, barely 43 by 65 centimetres, illustrating a sleazy moment from Ariosto's Orlando Furioso — the hermit has drugged Angelica asleep on a shore so he can leer at her unhindered. Rubens paints her loose and luminous, the old man a cowled shadow beside her. The discomfort is the point. Dated around 1626-28, it's in Vienna's Kunsthistorisches Museum as GG 692.

Peter_Paul_Rubens_-_The_Judgement_of_Par.title: The Judgment of Paris

source.canonical_title: File:Peter Paul Rubens - The Judgement of Paris, c.1606 (Museo del Prado).jpg

Peter_Paul_Rubens_-_The_Judgement_of_Par.story: Paris, seated on a bank, weighs the apple while three goddesses pose in front of him — Juno with her peacock, Minerva with her armour, Venus already smiling like she knows. This is Rubens young, around 1606 to 1608, still mixing Italian idealism with a cooler palette than he'd later use. Three decades later he returned to the subject for Philip IV's hunting lodge near Madrid; the two Prado Paris paintings now hang within the same museum, one pale and compact, the other warm and grand.

Peter_Paul_Rubens_-_The_Raising_of_the_C.title: The Raising of the Cross

source.canonical_title: File:Peter Paul Rubens - The Raising of the Cross (1638).jpeg

Peter_Paul_Rubens_-_The_Raising_of_the_C.story: Muscular men strain to heave the cross upright, Christ's body twisted against the beam. This version from around 1638 is a small late reworking of the massive triptych Rubens made in 1610-1611 for Antwerp's Sint-Walburgakerk (now in the cathedral). The young Rubens had just come back from Italy, bursting with Caravaggio and Michelangelo. Thirty years later he came back to the subject, softer, sadder, the same diagonal thrust but without the swagger.

Peter_Paul_Rubens_-_The_Rape_of_Europe,_.title: The Rape of Europe

source.canonical_title: File:Peter Paul Rubens - The Rape of Europe, 1636.jpg

Peter_Paul_Rubens_-_The_Rape_of_Europe,_.story: Jupiter has swapped thunderbolts for a white bull's hide, and Europa, fooled by how gentle he seems, is already being carried out to sea. Her scarf flies like a warning flag. This is Rubens's copy after Titian's famous version, painted for Philip IV around 1628-1629 on a trip to Madrid, not 1636. Titian's original was in the Spanish royal collection, and Rubens copied everything he could get near. His version still hangs in the Prado.

Peter_Paul_Rubens_-_The_Virgin_and_Child.title: The Virgin and Child in a Garland of Flowers
Peter_Paul_Rubens_-_The_Virgin_and_Child.artist: Peter Paul Rubens / Jan Brueghel the Elder

source.canonical_title: File:Peter Paul Rubens - The Virgin and Child in a Garland of Flowers - WGA20240.jpg
source.credit: Web Gallery of Art : Image Info about artwork wga QS:P11807,"r/rubens/13religi/51religi"

Peter_Paul_Rubens_-_The_Virgin_and_Child.story: A Counter-Reformation device: Rubens paints a tender Madonna and Child in the centre, and Brueghel wreathes them in a thick, perfumed ring of cut flowers — roses, tulips, peonies, irises — each bloom a sermon on the Virgin's purity and transience. The garland format was hugely popular in early-seventeenth-century Antwerp as a response to Protestant iconoclasm, insisting that images could still be devotional. Two putti hover above, crowning the ensemble. Now in the Alte Pinakothek, Munich.

Peter_Paul_Rubens_-_The_miracles_of_St._.title: The miracles of St. Francis Xavier

source.canonical_title: File:Peter Paul Rubens - The miracles of St. Francis Xavier - Google Art Project.jpg
source.credit: mAG-VIH-g-_RNA at Google Cultural Institute maximum zoom level

Peter_Paul_Rubens_-_The_miracles_of_St._.story: Xavier lifts a hand and the dead start climbing out of their shrouds while a pagan idol topples off its column in the background. Rubens painted this monster of an altarpiece, more than five metres tall, for the new Jesuit church in Antwerp (now St. Charles Borromeo), paired with a matching scene for Ignatius of Loyola. When fire gutted the church in 1718 both altarpieces survived; Empress Maria Theresa scooped them up in the 1770s. Done in 1617-18, it's now in Vienna's Kunsthistorisches Museum.

Peter_Paul_Rubens_-_The_toilet_of_Venus..title: The Toilet of Venus

source.canonical_title: File:Peter Paul Rubens - The toilet of Venus.jpg
source.credit: 1. The Yorck Project (2002) 10.000 Meisterwerke der Malerei (DVD-ROM), distributed by DIRECTMEDIA Publishing GmbH. ISBN : 3936122202 .

Peter_Paul_Rubens_-_The_toilet_of_Venus..story: A companion to the Liechtenstein version: Venus at her dressing table, cupid with the mirror, pearls and combs scattered, an attendant dressing her hair. Rubens painted the Toilet of Venus more than once because patrons kept asking for it, the Titian formula translated into Flemish flesh and Flemish light. The setup is ancient, a reckoning with the self through glass, but Rubens domesticates it: there's a cushion, a small dog, a morning feel. The goddess is caught looking, which is the whole game.

Peter_Paul_Rubens_-_Two_Satyrs_-_WGA2030.title: Two Satyrs

source.canonical_title: File:Peter Paul Rubens - Two Satyrs - WGA20303.jpg
source.credit: Web Gallery of Art : Image Info about artwork wga QS:P11807,"r/rubens/22mythol/32mythol"

Peter_Paul_Rubens_-_Two_Satyrs_-_WGA2030.story: Two bleary half-men crowd the frame, the one in front cradling a bunch of grapes and grinning straight at you like he's about to offer a drink you shouldn't accept. X-rays show Rubens originally painted just the single foreground satyr on a smaller panel, then nailed on extra planks to the left and bottom and squeezed the second one in. The composition got rowdier as it grew. Painted 1618-19, Alte Pinakothek, Munich.

Peter_Paul_Rubens_-_Venus_and_Adonis_-_W.title: Venus and Adonis

source.canonical_title: File:Peter Paul Rubens - Venus and Adonis - WGA20288.jpg
source.credit: Web Gallery of Art : Image Info about artwork wga QS:P11807,"r/rubens/21mythol/16mythol" http://hermitagemuseum.org/wps/portal/hermitage/digital-collection/01.+paintings/48132?lng=en

Peter_Paul_Rubens_-_Venus_and_Adonis_-_W.story: Adonis wants to go hunting. Venus, pressed against him, and Cupid, clutching his leg, both know what's waiting in the underbrush. Rubens paints the goodbye with two knowing faces and one determined one, the dogs already pulling on their leashes. This is the earliest of his Venus and Adonis treatments, painted soon after he got back from Italy with Titian and Cambiaso in his head. It belonged to Elector Johann Wilhelm of the Palatinate and stayed put when his collection moved; it's now at the Museum Kunstpalast in Düsseldorf.

Peter_Paul_Rubens_-_View_of_Het_Steen_Ca.title: A View of Het Steen in the Early Morning

source.canonical_title: File:Peter Paul Rubens - View of Het Steen Castle in the Early Morning.jpg

title.ro: Vedere asupra castelului Het Steen dimineața devreme

Peter_Paul_Rubens_-_View_of_Het_Steen_Ca.story: Rubens bought Het Steen, a moated castle south of Antwerp, in 1635, and this is his own estate at dawn: low sun raking across stubble fields, a hunter creeping toward partridges, his wagon rolling out with produce. No mythology, no saints, just his land. He painted it for himself, not a patron. The oak panel is enormous, pieced together as he kept adding sky and horizon. It's now at the National Gallery in London.

Peter_Paul_Rubens_-_Warrior_-_79.15_-_De.title: Warrior

source.canonical_title: File:Peter Paul Rubens - Warrior - 79.15 - Detroit Institute of Arts.jpg

Peter_Paul_Rubens_-_Warrior_-_79.15_-_De.story: A bust-length soldier in burnished steel, gorget catching one strip of light, expression unreadable. Rubens painted these heads as reference pieces, stock characters filed away for the battle scenes and hunts he turned out by the dozen. This one surfaced at Christie's in London in June 1956, where it went for 180 guineas. The dealer Julius Weitzner held it through the late 1970s and gave it to the Detroit Institute of Arts in 1979, accession 79.15. The armour is the portrait; whoever sat for it is long forgotten.

Peter_Paul_Rubens_-_Woman_with_a_Mirror_.title: Woman with a Mirror

source.canonical_title: File:Peter Paul Rubens - Woman with a Mirror - WGA20336.jpg
source.credit: Web Gallery of Art : Image Info about artwork wga QS:P11807,"r/rubens/30allego/08allego"

Peter_Paul_Rubens_-_Woman_with_a_Mirror_.story: A woman settles at her dressing table and a servant raises the glass. The mirror doesn't show us her face — only a sliver of cheek and the gleam of an earring — because the point isn't vanity, it's the soft weight of a shoulder, the coil of braided hair being arranged. Rubens painted it around 1640, the last year of his life, when he kept returning to intimate interiors over grand mythologies. The second figure, hands busy with the mirror, watches her mistress rather than the reflection.

Peter_Paul_Rubens_013.jpg.story: Bathsheba has just finished bathing. A maid combs her hair; a little dog nudges her foot; a messenger hands her a sealed letter from King David, who is already watching her from a balcony on the upper left. Everything in the next chapter, adultery, a murdered husband, a dead baby, a future king named Solomon, is implied in the unopened letter. Painted around 1635, acquired by Dresden's Gemäldegalerie Alte Meister in 1749, where it still hangs.

Peter_Paul_Rubens_018.jpg.title: English: The Feast of Herod

source.canonical_title: File:Peter Paul Rubens 018.jpg

Peter_Paul_Rubens_018.jpg.story: Herodias leans in with the knife, poised to stab the tongue of John the Baptist. Her daughter Salome has just delivered the head on a silver dish, and the guests recoil mid-feast — a toppled goblet, a dog under the table, a blast of red drapery behind. Rubens painted this late, not as a young man; it's a work of his last decade, dated roughly 1635 to 1638, probably for the Flemish merchant Gaspar Roomer in Naples. The National Galleries of Scotland bought it in 1958, and it has stayed in Edinburgh ever since.

Peter_Paul_Rubens_019.jpg.title: The Little Fur (Portrait of Hélène Fourment)

source.canonical_title: File:Peter Paul Rubens 019.jpg
source.credit: The Yorck Project (2002) 10.000 Meisterwerke der Malerei (DVD-ROM), distributed by DIRECTMEDIA Publishing GmbH. ISBN : 3936122202 .

Peter_Paul_Rubens_019.jpg.story: Helene Fourment, Rubens's second wife, steps out of a bath wrapped in nothing but a dark fur. Het Pelsken means the little fur. She was 22, he was near the end; they'd married in 1630 when she was 16. This is a private painting, kept in his bedroom, referenced in his will as a bequest to her alone. The pose quotes Titian's Venus, but Helene's feet are pink from the cold. It hangs at the Kunsthistorisches Museum in Vienna.

Peter_Paul_Rubens_072.jpg.title: Landscape with the Tower of Castle "Steen"

source.canonical_title: File:Peter Paul Rubens 072.jpg
source.credit: The Yorck Project (2002) 10.000 Meisterwerke der Malerei (DVD-ROM), distributed by DIRECTMEDIA Publishing GmbH. ISBN : 3936122202 .

title.de: Landschaft mit dem Turm des Schlosses Steen

Peter_Paul_Rubens_072.jpg.story: A wide golden view across his own estate: Het Steen's tower rises on the left, a hay wagon crawls through the middle distance, and the whole thing spreads under a dramatic Flemish sky. Rubens painted this in his last years after retiring to the countryside in 1635. He kept enlarging the panel as he worked, adding strips of oak to make room for more sky. It's at the National Gallery in London, paired with the early-morning view.

Peter_Paul_Rubens_115.jpg.title: The Judgment of Paris

source.canonical_title: File:Peter Paul Rubens 115.jpg

Peter_Paul_Rubens_115.jpg.story: Paris holds out the golden apple toward Venus, who's already undressing; Juno sulks in her peacock robe; Athena keeps a hand on her shield. The shepherd has no idea he's about to start the Trojan War. Rubens painted several Judgments of Paris, but this late version from around 1636-1638 is the loosest and most sensual. Mercury, above, delivered the apple and stays to watch. The painting hangs at the Prado in Madrid.

Peter_Paul_Rubens_123.jpg.story: A ten-year-old prince in a stiff ruff and gold-thread doublet — all seriousness, all Mantua. This is Vincenzo II Gonzaga, painted around 1604 to 1605, while Rubens was on the Duke of Mantua's payroll as court artist. It isn't really a standalone portrait: it was cut out of a much larger altarpiece, The Gonzaga Family in Adoration of the Holy Trinity, after the big canvas was dismembered, probably in the Napoleonic era. The boy in the ruff would later become the 7th and final Duke of Mantua, dying childless in 1627.

Peter_Paul_Rubens_137.jpg.title: The Death of Decius Mus in Battle

source.canonical_title: File:Peter Paul Rubens 137.jpg

Peter_Paul_Rubens_137.jpg.story: Decius Mus, the Roman consul, has vowed his life to the underworld gods in exchange for victory, so he charges straight into the enemy line and gets speared off his horse. Rubens paints the moment of impact, bodies and hooves exploding outward. This is one of a six-panel cycle Rubens produced between November 1616 and May 1618 as cartoons for Genoese tapestries; the paintings were eventually acquired by Prince Johann Adam of Liechtenstein in 1693 and still live in the Liechtenstein Princely Collections.

Peter_Paul_Rubens_148.jpg.story: Elisabeth of France, known in Spain as Isabel de Borbón, was Louis XIII's sister and Philip IV's queen. Rubens painted her in Madrid during his 1628-29 mission, one of many court portraits his aunt Isabel Clara Eugenia wanted for her palace in Brussels. She's in the standard uniform of Habsburg queenship — huge lace ruff, hair piled with pearls, a heavy necklace terminating in a pendant jewel. Isabel died in 1644 at age 41; two years later Philip lost his heir too, and the dynasty started its long unravelling.

Peter_Paul_Rubens_166.jpg.title: Saint Teresa of Avila's Vision

source.canonical_title: File:Peter Paul Rubens 166.jpg

title.nl: Het visioen van de Heilige Theresa van Avila

Peter_Paul_Rubens_166.jpg.story: Teresa kneels, mouth parted, as a smiling angel lifts a golden spear toward her heart. Rubens paints her vision in warm, buttery light, the sort of moment she described in her autobiography as so sweet she wanted the pain to last forever. Commissioned for the Discalced Carmelites in Brussels, the altarpiece came just a few years after Teresa's beatification in 1614. Bernini would carve his famous marble version four decades later, but Rubens got there first.

Peter_Paul_Rubens_206.jpg.title: Portrait of a man, possibly Peter van Hecke (1591–1645)
Peter_Paul_Rubens_206.jpg.artist: Anthony van Dyck / Peter Paul Rubens

source.canonical_title: File:Peter Paul Rubens 206.jpg

title.nl: Portret van een man, mogelijk Peter van Hecke (1591-1645)

Peter_Paul_Rubens_206.jpg.story: A late portrait from around 1630, now at the Mauritshuis in The Hague. The sitter is almost certainly Peter van Hecke, an Antwerp silk and tapestry dealer, painted as a companion piece to a portrait of his wife Clara Fourment. Clara was the elder sister of Hélène Fourment, Rubens's own young second wife, which made this family as much as patronage. Van Hecke stands in glossy black with a broad lace collar, one hand resting easily on his hip, the other clasping a glove. A preparatory black-chalk drawing for the head survives at the British Museum.

Peter_Paul_Rubens_The_Three_Crosses.jpg.title: The Three Crosses . [ 1 ] Alternative title(s): Christ on the cross flanked by the two murderers . [ 2 ]

source.canonical_title: File:Peter Paul Rubens The Three Crosses.jpg
source.credit: Web Gallery of Art : Image Info about artwork wga QS:P11807,"r/rubens/12religi/45religi"

Peter_Paul_Rubens_The_Three_Crosses.jpg.story: Three tall crosses against a bruised sky, Christ in the middle, the two thieves writhing either side. It's a small panel, and Rubens apparently never meant it to feel as vertiginous as it does; later hands set it into a larger panel, which stretched the sky and exaggerated the height of those crosses. The effect is now part of the painting's identity. Dated around 1620, it's in Rotterdam's Museum Boijmans Van Beuningen.

Philipp_Otto_Runge,_Head_of_a_Dog_(1805-.title: Philipp Otto Runge, Head of a Dog (1805-06), chalk & lead
Philipp_Otto_Runge,_Head_of_a_Dog_(1805-.description: Philipp Otto Runge, Head of a Dog (1805-06), chalk & lead, 29.5 x 35.9 cm., Hamburger Kunsthalle

source.canonical_title: File:Philipp Otto Runge, Head of a Dog (1805-06), chalk & lead.jpg

Philipp_Otto_Runge,_Head_of_a_Dog_(1805-.story: A small, unnervingly alive drawing: Runge's dog stares past the viewer with the soft, unfocused attention of an animal hearing something in the next room. Done in black chalk with touches of lead, it's a study rather than a finished piece, but the fur has weight and the eye is wet. Runge was as obsessed with direct observation as he was with cosmic allegory, and this drawing sits on the observation side of that ledger. In the Hamburger Kunsthalle.

Philipp_Otto_Runge,_Sophia_Sieveking_on_.title: Philipp Otto Runge, Sophia Sieveking on Her Deathbed (1810), black & white chalk
Philipp_Otto_Runge,_Sophia_Sieveking_on_.description: Philipp Otto Runge, Sophia Sieveking on Her Deathbed (1810), black & white chalk, 43.5 x 51.2 cm., Hamburger Kunsthalle

source.canonical_title: File:Philipp Otto Runge, Sophia Sieveking on Her Deathbed (1810), black & white chalk.jpg

Philipp_Otto_Runge,_Sophia_Sieveking_on_.story: Sophia Sieveking, a young woman from the Hamburg patrician family Runge had married into, died in early 1810. Runge, himself already consumptive and with only months to live, sat at her bedside with chalk in hand. What he drew is not quite a portrait and not quite a mourning picture: her profile in sharp black line, the pillow and shroud brushed in with white on toned paper, everything else left to breathe. He would be dead before the year was out. The sheet sits in the Hamburger Kunsthalle beside his great unfinished 'Morning' canvases, a small intimate counterweight to the cosmic Romantic programme.

Philipp_Otto_Runge,_Study_for_The_Great_.title: Philipp Otto Runge, Study for The Great Morning (1809), chalk & pencil
Philipp_Otto_Runge,_Study_for_The_Great_.description: Philipp Otto Runge, Study for The Great Morning (1809), chalk & pencil, 40.6 x 53.4 cm., Hamburger Kunsthalle

source.canonical_title: File:Philipp Otto Runge, Study for The Great Morning (1809), chalk & pencil.jpg

Philipp_Otto_Runge,_Study_for_The_Great_.story: A working drawing for Runge's most ambitious painting, the large version of Morning from his planned Times of Day cycle. The sheet shows him thinking through the central figure of Aurora and the attendant children with their lilies — bodies rendered in soft chalk, proportions still being tested. Runge believed the cycle would unite landscape, figure, allegory and colour theory into a total work. He died the next year with the project unfinished. The study is in the Hamburger Kunsthalle.

Philipp_Otto_Runge_-_Der_Maler_und_Schri.title: The painter and writer Friedrich August von Klinkowström

source.canonical_title: File:Philipp Otto Runge - Der Maler und Schriftsteller Friedrich August von Klinkowström - 2840 - Österreichische Galerie Belvedere.jpg

title.de: Der Maler und Schriftsteller Friedrich August von Klinkowström
title.ru: Художник и писатель Фридрих Август фон Клинковстрём
title.nl: De schilder en schrijver Friedrich August von Klinkowström
title.fr: Le peintre et écrivain Friedrich August von Klinkowström
title.bar: Der Maler und Schriftsteller Friedrich August von Klinkowström

Philipp_Otto_Runge_-_Der_Maler_und_Schri.story: Runge painting a close friend: Klinkowström, painter and writer, caught in a quiet, frontal pose with the kind of unblinking intensity Runge reserved for people he loved. The palette is sober — dark coat, pale face, plain ground — and the brushwork is tighter than in his allegorical work. Klinkowström later became a Catholic convert and a key figure in Vienna's Romantic circle, which is how the portrait ended up at the Belvedere.

Philipp_Otto_Runge_-_Die_Hülsenbeckschen.title: The Hülsenbeck Children

source.canonical_title: File:Philipp Otto Runge - Die Hülsenbeckschen Kinder.jpg
source.credit: The Yorck Project (2002) 10.000 Meisterwerke der Malerei (DVD-ROM), distributed by DIRECTMEDIA Publishing GmbH. ISBN : 3936122202 .

title.ja: ヒュルゼンベック家の子供たち

Philipp_Otto_Runge_-_Die_Hülsenbeckschen.story: Three children of Runge's Hamburg neighbours, painted larger than life in their parents' garden. The baby sits in a wagon gnawing a sunflower leaf; the older two grip the handle with unsettling seriousness, as if about to pull each other into the future. Everything is oversized — the sunflowers tower, the cabbage leaves are huge, the Hamburg skyline is tiny — because Runge is painting the world from a child's point of view. One of the great Romantic images of childhood, now in the Hamburger Kunsthalle.

Philipp_Otto_Runge_-_Pedro_sobre_el_mar..title: Peter on the sea

source.canonical_title: File:Philipp Otto Runge - Pedro sobre el mar.jpg

Philipp_Otto_Runge_-_Pedro_sobre_el_mar..story: Peter stepping out of the boat onto the stormy Sea of Galilee, faith wavering, Christ reaching to catch him. Runge treats the Gospel episode with uncharacteristic restraint — no allegorical flowers, no symbolic children, just the two figures on black water under a broken sky. It's one of his late biblical works, painted as his health was failing, and the mood is closer to Friedrich's austerity than to Runge's usual ornamental style.

Philipp_Otto_Runge_-_The_Great_Morning_(.title: The Great Morning

source.canonical_title: File:Philipp Otto Runge - The Great Morning (detail) - WGA20518.jpg
source.credit: Web Gallery of Art : Image Info about artwork wga QS:P11807,"r/runge/2morning"

Philipp_Otto_Runge_-_The_Great_Morning_(.story: Detail of The Great Morning, the second and more ambitious version of Runge's meditation on dawn. Aurora rises out of light; below her, small naked children tumble among lilies, each pose a diagram of something — the soul waking, the day beginning, the colour spectrum emerging from darkness. Runge cut the canvas into pieces himself, unsatisfied; the Hamburger Kunsthalle painstakingly reassembled the fragments. What survives is incomplete but luminous, the clearest glimpse of the cosmic cycle he didn't live to finish.

Pierre-Auguste_Renoir,_1880,_Portrait_of.title: Portrait of Mademoiselle Irène Cahen d'Anvers ( Little Irene )

source.canonical_title: File:Pierre-Auguste Renoir, 1880, Portrait of Mademoiselle Irène Cahen d'Anvers, Sammlung E.G. Bührle.jpg

Pierre-Auguste_Renoir,_1880,_Portrait_of.story: Eight-year-old Irene, daughter of a Paris banker, sits very still while her copper hair tumbles down a pale-blue dress. Renoir finished the portrait in 1880 and her father grumbled about the price and hung it in a servants' corridor. The Nazis looted it from the Cahen d'Anvers family in 1940; Hermann Goering took it for himself. After the war it ended up in the Buhrle collection in Zurich, where it still hangs, despite ongoing restitution disputes.

Pierre-Auguste_Renoir,_French_-_The_Larg.title: The Great Bathers

source.canonical_title: File:Pierre-Auguste Renoir, French - The Large Bathers - Google Art Project.jpg
source.credit: 2wE1mqTuUoBmtA at Google Cultural Institute maximum zoom level

Pierre-Auguste_Renoir,_French_-_The_Larg.story: After a trip to Italy Renoir got obsessed with Raphael and Ingres, and spent three years on this: nude women laughing by a riverbank, every outline pin-sharp. Friends were scandalized by the change of style, calling it his 'dry' or 'sour' period. He made dozens of preparatory drawings, unusual for him. The two figures sprawled on the grass are based on his sister-in-law Suzanne Valadon and the model Aline Charigot. Mrs. Carroll S. Tyson gave it to the Philadelphia Museum of Art in 1963.

Pierre-Auguste_Renoir_-_By_the_Water.jpg.title: By the Water or Near the Lake

source.canonical_title: File:Pierre-Auguste Renoir - By the Water.jpg
source.permission: Public domain for life of author plus 106 years (as 106 years since December 1919).

Pierre-Auguste_Renoir_-_By_the_Water.jpg.story: A young woman leans on a rustic wooden railing at the water's edge, straw hat tilted, cheeks pink from the breeze. Renoir painted the scene around 1880, probably at Chatou where he was spending long afternoons with boaters and models. The water behind her is a froth of turquoise and violet strokes, less a river than a mood. The Art Institute of Chicago owns the painting, part of the Mr. and Mrs. Martin A. Ryerson Collection bequeathed in 1933.

Pierre-Auguste_Renoir_-_Children_on_the_.title: Children on the Seashore, Guernsey

source.canonical_title: File:Pierre-Auguste Renoir - Children on the Seashore, Guernsey (Enfants au bord de la mer à Guernesey) - BF10 - Barnes Foundation.jpg

Pierre-Auguste_Renoir_-_Children_on_the_.story: Renoir spent September 1883 on Guernsey and wrote his dealer that the place was 'simply beautiful' and the bathers swam among the rocks 'like figures in a Watteau.' Three small children crouch in the shallows here, digging, the sea behind them a rumple of blue-green, granite cliffs glinting pink. The handling is loose and quick, pure holiday. Dr. Albert Barnes bought it in 1927 for his foundation outside Philadelphia, where it remains as BF10.

Pierre-Auguste_Renoir_-_Frédéric_Bazille.title: Pierre-Auguste Renoir - Frédéric Bazille
Pierre-Auguste_Renoir_-_Frédéric_Bazille.description: Frédéric Bazille at his Easel (1867). Oil on canvas, 105 × 73.5 cm (41 × 28.9 in). Musée Fabre, Montpellier, France

source.canonical_title: File:Pierre-Auguste Renoir - Frédéric Bazille.jpg

Pierre-Auguste_Renoir_-_Luncheon_of_the_.title: Luncheon of the Boating Party

source.canonical_title: File:Pierre-Auguste Renoir - Luncheon of the Boating Party - Google Art Project.jpg
source.credit: mgHsTKDNJVzPAg at Google Cultural Institute maximum zoom level

Pierre-Auguste_Renoir_-_Luncheon_of_the_.story: Fourteen friends on the terrace of the Maison Fournaise at Chatou, wine glasses half full, oysters demolished, the awning snapping overhead. Renoir packed it with people he loved: the seamstress Aline Charigot (his future wife) cooing at a tiny dog, the actress Ellen Andree drinking, his pals Gustave Caillebotte and Baron Raoul Barbier lounging in straw boaters. He started it in summer 1880 and fussed over it for months. Duncan Phillips bought it in 1923 for his museum in Washington for $125,000.

Pierre-Auguste_Renoir_-_Spring_Bouquet_-.title: Spring Bouquet

source.canonical_title: File:Pierre-Auguste Renoir - Spring Bouquet - 1943.277 - Fogg Museum.jpg

Pierre-Auguste_Renoir_-_Spring_Bouquet_-.story: A fat jug of peonies, daisies, and greenery, painted in 1866 when Renoir was 25 and broke. The flowers tumble out every direction; the background is dark, almost Courbet-dark, and the petals catch light the way cream catches sun. It's a young painter showing off what porcelain training taught him — every blossom has the polish of enameled china. The canvas entered Harvard's Fogg Art Museum via the bequest of collector Grenville L. Winthrop in 1943.

Pierre-Auguste_Renoir_096.jpg.title: Portrait of Jeanne Samary

source.canonical_title: File:Pierre-Auguste Renoir 096.jpg
source.credit: The Yorck Project (2002) 10.000 Meisterwerke der Malerei (DVD-ROM), distributed by DIRECTMEDIA Publishing GmbH. ISBN : 3936122202 .

Pierre-Auguste_Renoir_096.jpg.story: Jeanne Samary was a star of the Comedie-Francaise and, for a year or so, half in love with Renoir, who painted her at least a dozen times. Here she is in 1877, chin propped on one hand, red-gold hair catching the studio light, the whole background a blur of pink and green like a pastel smeared by a thumb. The critic Georges Riviere called her skin 'lit from within.' The canvas is in the Pushkin Museum in Moscow.

Pierre-Cécile_Puvis_de_Chavannes_003.jp.title: The Dream

source.canonical_title: File:Pierre-Cécile Puvis de Chavannes 003.jpg
source.credit: The Yorck Project (2002) 10.000 Meisterwerke der Malerei (DVD-ROM), distributed by DIRECTMEDIA Publishing GmbH. ISBN : 3936122202 .

Pierre-Cécile_Puvis_de_Chavannes_003.jp.story: A poor traveler sleeps against a scrubby hillock under a crescent moon, his little bundle beside him. Three winged figures glide in from the sky carrying what the tradition calls Love, Glory and Fortune — one scatters coins, another lifts a laurel. The palette is Puvis at his most muted: dusty mauves, bone-white drapery, a brown plain that could be anywhere. The drama is deliberately undercooked, almost faded, as if the dream is already slipping. It was this quality of hushed, flattened allegory that Gauguin and the young Picasso kept coming back to when they wanted to learn how to say less.

Pierre-Cécile_Puvis_de_Chavannes_007.jp.title: Hope

source.canonical_title: File:Pierre-Cécile Puvis de Chavannes 007.jpg
source.credit: The Yorck Project (2002) 10.000 Meisterwerke der Malerei (DVD-ROM), distributed by DIRECTMEDIA Publishing GmbH. ISBN : 3936122202 .

Pierre-Cécile_Puvis_de_Chavannes_007.jp.story: Painted in 1872, the year after the Franco-Prussian War and the Commune, this is Hope as a barefoot girl on rubble. She sits in a white empire-waist shift on broken masonry, holding out a small green sprig; behind her, a scarred field with what look like fresh crosses and the pale silhouettes of ruined buildings. Puvis drains the palette to chalky pastels — his signature — and flattens the space so it reads almost like a fresco. The gesture is modest to the point of being almost embarrassed, which is precisely what makes it work as an allegory of a bruised country.

Pierre_Auguste_Renoir_-_The_Piazza_San_M.title: The Piazza San Marco, Venice

source.canonical_title: File:Pierre Auguste Renoir - The Piazza San Marco, Venice - Google Art Project.jpg
source.credit: -QFkcq_EZt-41Q at Google Cultural Institute , zoom level maximum

Pierre_Auguste_Renoir_-_The_Piazza_San_M.story: Renoir worked fast in Venice — the domes of San Marco go down in quick unmixed strokes, pigeons are suggested more than drawn, the crowd is a shimmer of hats. He stopped in the city in late October 1881 during his Italian tour and this small canvas came out of that stay. It's almost a snapshot: bright midday light, the basilica's silhouette broken up by heat. Now at the Minneapolis Institute of Art. The trip convinced him he needed to study Raphael next.

Pierre_Puvis_de_Chavannes_-_The_Poor_Fis.title: The poor fisherman

source.canonical_title: File:Pierre Puvis de Chavannes - The Poor Fisherman - Google Art Project.jpg
source.credit: qwEqQiy4PXmwKw at Google Cultural Institute maximum zoom level

Pierre_Puvis_de_Chavannes_-_The_Poor_Fis.story: A man stands in a flat-bottomed boat with his net slack, his wife and child on the bank behind him, and nothing between them but dry grass and bleached water. Puvis painted it in 1881 and critics hated it — too stark, too pale, too depressing. But Seurat studied it, Gauguin loved it, Picasso copied it. The flattened space and thin, chalky paint feel closer to mural than easel. It's at the Musée d'Orsay. Van Gogh called it one of the strangest pictures he'd ever seen.

Pieter_Bruegel_d._Ä._066.jpg.title: The Fight Between Carnival and Lent

source.canonical_title: File:Pieter Bruegel d. Ä. 066.jpg

title.fr: Le Combat de Carnaval et Carême
title.ca: La batalla entre Carnestoltes i Quaresma
title.pt: O Combate entre o Carnaval e a Quaresma
title.ja: 謝肉祭と四旬節の喧嘩
title.vi: Trận chiến giữa Hội hè và Chay tịnh
title.nl: De strijd tussen Vasten en Vastenavond
title.hu: A karnevál és a böjt csatája

Pieter_Bruegel_d._Ä._066.jpg.story: A town square turned ideological battlefield. On the left, Carnival rides a fat beer barrel, wearing a meat pie as a helmet and jousting with a pig on a spit. On the right, scrawny Lent perches on a church cart armed with a baker's peel and two herrings. Around them nearly two hundred figures eat, beg, mourn, gamble, and drag the dead, the whole square split between tavern and church. Bruegel signs and dates the panel 1559, the year he settled into the dense, morally busy compositions that would make his name. Infrared shows he overpainted the grimmest scenes, probably at a patron's request. It hangs in Vienna's Kunsthistorisches Museum.

Pieter_Bruegel_der_Ältere_-_Landschaft_.title: Landscape with the flight into Egypt
Pieter_Bruegel_der_Ältere_-_Landschaft_.description: « Бегство в Египет » ( нид. De vlucht naar Egypte ). 1563. Дерево, масло. 37,1 × 55,6 см. Институт искусства Курто , Лондон ( Великобритания )

source.canonical_title: File:Pieter Bruegel der Ältere - Landschaft mit der Flucht nach Ägypten.jpg

title.de: Landschaft mit der Flucht nach Ägypten

Pieter_Bruegel_der_Ältere_-_Landschaft_.story: A tiny Mary and Joseph thread through a vast alpine valley, dwarfed by cliffs and distant estuary. Bruegel had crossed the Alps as a young man and never got the view out of his head. On the right, a pagan idol tips off its dead tree as the Holy Family passes, a quiet sign that the old gods are done. Cardinal Granvelle owned it; Rubens owned it after him; then it vanished for centuries before Count Seilern bought it cheap at Christie's in 1939 and eventually gave it to the Courtauld. Panel, just 37 by 56 centimetres, and still the best Bruegel in Britain.

Pieter_Bruegel_the_Elder_-_Landscape_wit.title: Landscape with the Fall of Icarus

source.canonical_title: File:Pieter Bruegel the Elder - Landscape with the Fall of Icarus - Brussels, Royal Museums of Fine Arts of Belgium - Google Arts & Culture.jpg

title.es: Paisaje con la caída de Ícaro
title.eo: Pejzaĝo kun la Falo de Ikaro

title.de: Landschaft mit dem Sturz des Ikarus
title.pt: Paisagem com a Queda de Ícaro
title.ja: イカロスの墜落のある風景

Pieter_Bruegel_the_Elder_-_Landscape_wit.story: The most famous Bruegel that probably isn't one. The ploughman turns his back, the shepherd stares at the sky, the fisherman tends his line, and in the lower right a pair of legs vanishes into the harbour — Icarus, unnoticed. Technical examinations in 1996 found the canvas itself dates from around 1600, three decades after Bruegel's death, so the Brussels picture is now usually read as a very good early copy of a lost original of about 1558. Auden wrote his famous poem about suffering happening while someone else is eating in front of this exact copy.

Pieter_Bruegel_the_Elder_-_Massacre_of_t.title: Massacre of the Innocents
Pieter_Bruegel_the_Elder_-_Massacre_of_t.description: « Избиение младенцев » ( нид. De kindermoord te Bethlehem ). ок. 1565-1567. Дерево, масло. 109,2 × 158,1 см. Королевская коллекция , Виндзорский замок ( Великобритания )

source.canonical_title: File:Pieter Bruegel the Elder - Massacre of the Innocents - Google Art Project.jpg
source.credit: qgGZ6pq1mTaabw at Google Cultural Institute maximum zoom level

Pieter_Bruegel_the_Elder_-_Massacre_of_t.story: Soldiers on horseback have ridden into a snowbound Flemish village to do Herod's dirty work, except this version in Windsor has been tampered with. Rudolf II's agents had the slaughtered babies painted over as calves, geese and bundles so the scene reads as livestock theft, not child-murder. Look closely and you can still see the ghost of an infant under a goose. Peasants plead in doorways, a woman clutches what's now a swaddled pot. Bruegel finished it around 1565-67; the censorship came later. The Royal Collection still holds the altered original.

Pieter_Bruegel_the_Elder_-_The_Parable_o.title: The Parable of the Blind Leading the Blind

Pieter_Bruegel_the_Elder_-_The_Parable_o.story: Six blind men in a staggered line, roped together by staffs and shoulders, and the front one's already in the ditch. The second is going over. You can read the whole disaster in the tilt of their heads. Bruegel painted the faces with such clinical accuracy that modern ophthalmologists have diagnosed specific conditions in each, from leucoma to atrophy of the eyeball. It's his illustration of Matthew 15:14, painted in 1568 in tempera on linen, which is why it looks so matte. The church spire in the background belongs to Sint-Anna in Dilbeek. Naples has it.

Pieter_Bruegel_the_Elder_-_The_Tower_of_.title: The building of the tower of Babel (Genesis 11:3-5)
Pieter_Bruegel_the_Elder_-_The_Tower_of_.description: Bruegel painted three versions of the Tower of Babel . This "Little" version (60 cm × 74.5 cm) is kept in the Museum Boijmans Van Beuningen in Rotterdam, the second "Great" version, in the Kunsthistorisches Museum in Vienna (see Category:The Tower of Babel by Pieter Bruegel the Elder ), while the location of the third version (a miniature on ivory) is unknown.

source.canonical_title: File:Pieter Bruegel the Elder - The Tower of Babel (Rotterdam) - Google Art Project - edited.jpg
source.credit: Levels adjusted from File:Pieter_Bruegel_the_Elder_-_The_Tower_of_Babel_(Vienna)_-_Google_Art_Project.jpg , originally from Google Art Project.

Pieter_Bruegel_the_Elder_-_The_Tower_of_.story: The smaller of Bruegel's two surviving Babels, and the bleaker one. No king at the foot of the tower here, no tiny workers scurrying up the ramps with dignity. Just an immense brick-and-stone mountain already cracking, clouds circling the upper tiers, and the sense that the whole thing is quietly doomed. Bruegel probably based the architecture on Rome's Colosseum, which he'd sketched during his trip south in the 1550s. This panel is about 60 by 75 cm, painted around 1568, and lives at Museum Boijmans Van Beuningen in Rotterdam.

Pieter_Bruegel_the_Elder_-_The_Tower_of_.title: The Tower of Babel

source.canonical_title: File:Pieter Bruegel the Elder - The Tower of Babel (Vienna) - Google Art Project - edited.jpg
source.credit: Levels adjusted from File:Pieter_Bruegel_the_Elder_-_The_Tower_of_Babel_(Vienna)_-_Google_Art_Project.jpg , originally from Google Art Project.

Pieter_Bruegel_the_Elder_-_The_Tower_of_.story: Bruegel's tower rears up like a Roman Colosseum mid-construction, clouds snagging on the upper tiers, the whole thing listing slightly and already cracking. King Nimrod stands in the foreground with stonecutters bowing before him. Painted around 1563 after Bruegel's trip over the Alps to Rome, it is the larger and grander of the two surviving Babel paintings, about 114 by 155 centimeters. It has hung in the Kunsthistorisches Museum in Vienna since Emperor Rudolf II's collection.

Polder_Landscape_with_Herd_of_Cows_-_Pet.story: A herd shuffles across flat Flemish polder, and in the distance a church spire pricks the horizon. Rubens painted this in the last years of his life, after country life at Het Steen softened him into a landscapist. The cows are specific, dairy breeds he'd have seen every morning, and the light is the washed, silver kind that follows rain. The panel hangs at the Gemaldegalerie in Berlin.

Pont-Neuf_(1872)_-_Pierre-Auguste_Renoir.title: Pont-Neuf

source.canonical_title: File:Pont-Neuf (1872) - Pierre-Auguste Renoir (National Gallery of Art, Washington D.C.).jpg

Pont-Neuf_(1872)_-_Pierre-Auguste_Renoir.story: Renoir's brother Edmond paced the Pont-Neuf stopping strangers to ask directions while Auguste, stationed at a café window above, painted the frozen gestures. The trick bought him time to catch pedestrians, carriages, and the bright flags of a spring morning in 1872, Paris still rebuilding after the Commune. The scale is small; the mood is giddy with sunshine. It's at the National Gallery of Art in Washington. The painting sold for 300 francs the year it was made.

Pont_Argenteuil_Monet_1.jpg.title: Pont Argenteuil Monet 1

source.canonical_title: File:Pont Argenteuil Monet 1.jpg

Pont_Argenteuil_Monet_1.jpg.story: The Argenteuil road bridge again, Monet's favourite 1874 motif. Pleasure yachts bob in the foreground, the new iron-and-stone span strides across behind them. The bridge had been rebuilt after the Prussians wrecked it in the war of 1870, and painting it whole again was quietly political. Monet painted this bridge seven times that single year.

Pope-peter_pprubens.jpg.story: Peter in papal vestments, clutching the enormous gold keys to heaven as if weighing them. His face is a worker's face, not a saint's, lined and squinting. The pallium hangs heavy across his shoulders. Part of an apostle series Rubens painted around 1610-12 for the Duke of Lerma, now scattered across museums. This one lives in the Prado, Madrid.

Pope_Julius_II.jpg.title: Portrait of Pope Julius II

source.canonical_title: File:Pope Julius II.jpg

title.ja: 教皇ユリウス2世の肖像

Pope_Julius_II.jpg.story: Julius II, the warrior pope who hired Michelangelo for the Sistine ceiling and Raphael for the Stanze, sits with his head slightly bowed, rings heavy on his fingers, beard grown out in mourning for the lost city of Bologna. It was so unnervingly lifelike that Vasari wrote people trembled in its presence, as if the pope himself were there. Raphael painted it around 1511-12. For centuries a studio copy at the Uffizi was thought to be the original, until cleaning in the 1970s confirmed that the version in London's National Gallery is the one that came off Raphael's brush.

Portrait_Of_The_Artists_Brother_by_Élisa.title: The Artist's Brother

source.canonical_title: File:Portrait Of The Artists Brother by Élisabeth Vigée-Lebrun.jpg

Portrait_Of_The_Artists_Brother_by_Élisa.story: Vigée Le Brun was eighteen when she painted her fifteen-year-old brother Étienne, a future man of letters caught mid-turn with a book in one hand and a quill in the other. You can feel the affection — the half-smile, the slight spontaneity of the pose — and also the young painter testing what she'd absorbed from Greuze and from Joseph Vernet, who had told her to trust nature over schools. It's among her finest early works, made before the Marie Antoinette commissions remade her life. Now at the Saint Louis Art Museum.

Portrait_d'Edmond_Aman-Jean_par_Georges_.title: Portrait d'Edmond Aman-Jean par Georges Seurat
Portrait_d'Edmond_Aman-Jean_par_Georges_.description: Georges Seurat's study of his friend the artist Aman-Jean (1860–1936) '

source.canonical_title: File:Portrait d'Edmond Aman-Jean par Georges Seurat.jpg

Portrait_d'Edmond_Aman-Jean_par_Georges_.story: A friend, drawn not painted - conte crayon on rough Michallet paper, which is why the face emerges from a fog of velvety blacks. Aman-Jean (1860-1936) was a fellow student at the Beaux-Arts; Seurat shows him at the easel in three-quarter view, cheekbone catching the light. When this drawing was exhibited at the 1883 Salon it was Seurat's debut there, and critics singled it out.

Portrait_de_l'artiste_avec_un_ami,_by_Ra.title: Self-portrait with a friend

source.canonical_title: File:Portrait de l'artiste avec un ami, by Raffaello Sanzio, from C2RMF retouched.jpg
source.credit: Retouched from File:Portrait de l'artiste avec un ami, by Raffaello Sanzio, from C2RMF retouched.jpg , originally C2RMF: Galerie de tableaux en très haute définition : image page

Portrait_de_l'artiste_avec_un_ami,_by_Ra.story: Raphael, standing at the back, rests his hand on the shoulder of a seated friend who twists round and points directly at us. It's an unusually tender double portrait, almost conspiratorial. Who the friend is has never been settled: proposals include the fencing master Pontormo, Raphael's assistant Giulio Romano, or more romantically the painter's lover. The picture is dated around 1519-20, right at the end of Raphael's short life. He died that Good Friday 1520 at thirty-seven. The Louvre acquired it from the collection of Louis XIV.

Portrait_of_George_Villiers,_1st_Duke_of.title: George Villiers (1592–1628), 1st Duke of Buckingham
Portrait_of_George_Villiers,_1st_Duke_of.description: Thought to be a later copy of a lost painting by Rubens, the work had hung on public display in the dinning room of Pollok House. A technique called dendrochronology, used to examine the tree rings of the wood, dated the panel to be from the 1620s and further technical analysis revealed the panel on which the portrait was painted had been prepared in the same way as was custom in Rubens’ studio. Ben van Beneden, director of the Rubenshuis in Antwerp, authenticated the painting of George Villiers, the 1st Duke of Buckingham, confirming it to be by the Flemish artist. After centuries of dirt and overpainting was cleaned off by restorer Simon Gillespie the piece revealed many of Ruben’s trademark techniques. ( Extracted from [1] ).

source.canonical_title: File:Portrait of George Villiers, 1st Duke of Buckingham (by Peter Paul Rubens).jpg

title.es: Retrato de George Villiers, primer Duque de Buckingham
title.de: Porträt von George Villiers, 1. Herzog von Buckingham
title.he: הדיוקן האבוד של ג'ורג' וילירס, הדוכס הראשון מבקינגהאם

Portrait_of_George_Villiers,_1st_Duke_of.story: For a century everyone assumed this glossy young duke hanging in the dining room at Pollok House was a decent copy. Then in 2017 Bendor Grosvenor took a closer look, and conservator Simon Gillespie spent two months lifting off dirt and overpaint. Tree-ring dating put the panel in the 1620s; pentimenti showed a mind at work, not a copier; Ben van Beneden at the Rubenshuis signed off on it. Rubens sketched Villiers from life in Paris in 1625, the year James I died. That's the face on this panel.

Portrait_of_Peder_Severin_Krøyer_by_Laur.title: Portrait of Painter Peder Severin Kröyer
Portrait_of_Peder_Severin_Krøyer_by_Laur.description: Portrait of the Danish painter Peder Severin Krøyer (1851-1909) by Laurits Tuxen, 1904. Hungarian National Museum Inv.Nr 191 B. Acquired in 1907.

source.canonical_title: File:Portrait of Peder Severin Krøyer by Laurits Tuxen.jpg

Portrait_of_Peder_Severin_Krøyer_by_Laur.story: Two Skagen painters, old classmates from the Royal Danish Academy. Tuxen sets Krøyer on the beach in his trademark white suit, paintbox slung on a shoulder, smock folded over his arm, sedge rustling at his feet and the North Sea behind — as if caught walking home after a day's work. It was painted in 1904, when Krøyer's eyesight and mental health were already failing; he would die five years later. The portrait is now in Budapest, acquired by the Hungarian museum in 1907.

Portrait_of_Princess_Karoline_of_Liechte.story: Painted in Vienna for the Liechtenstein palace on the Herrengasse, one of two grand canvases Vigée Le Brun produced for the family. Princess Karoline, wife of Alois I, trails cloud and rainbow as Iris, messenger of the gods. According to the painter's memoirs she originally showed the princess barefoot — perfectly in character — but once hung, the family was scandalised, and Prince Alois had a pair of shoes added. Still in the Princely Collections today.

source.canonical_title: File:Portret van Etienne-Lucien Martin - s0125V1962 - Van Gogh Museum.jpg

Portret_van_Etienne-Lucien_Martin_-_s012.story: A bearded man in a dark jacket, painted fast, scraped thin — Etienne-Lucien Martin, manager of the restaurant Le Chalet on avenue de Clichy. Van Gogh ate there, sometimes paying in pictures, and in late 1887 he organised an exhibition on its walls of his Montmartre friends — Bernard, Anquetin, Toulouse-Lautrec. This portrait probably dates from that moment of bartered goodwill. It's oil on cardboard, 33 by 23 cm, now at the Van Gogh Museum.

Pozzi,_Samuel_-_Par_Sargent.jpg.title: Dr. Pozzi at Home
Pozzi,_Samuel_-_Par_Sargent.jpg.description: Samuel Pozzi chez lui Portrait par John Singer Sargent (1856-1925)

source.canonical_title: File:Pozzi, Samuel - Par Sargent.jpg

title.fr: Un portrait, dit aussi Le Docteur Pozzi dans son intérieur
title.es: Doctor Samuel Jean Pozzi en casa

Pozzi,_Samuel_-_Par_Sargent.jpg.story: Samuel Pozzi, the brilliant Parisian gynecologist and serial seducer, posed for Sargent in a floor-length scarlet dressing gown, fingering its cord like a cardinal in mufti. Sargent was 25; Pozzi was 35 and already the most glamorous doctor in Paris. The red is the painting: curtain, robe, rug, all burning. Julian Barnes built an entire book around this man. It was painted in 1881 and now hangs at the Hammer Museum in Los Angeles.

Prado_-_Los_Desastres_de_la_Guerra_-_No..title: The Disasters of War, No. 4: The Women Give Courage
Prado_-_Los_Desastres_de_la_Guerra_-_No..description: Los desastres de la guerra , plate No. 4, (1st edition, Madrid: Real Academia de Bellas Artes de San Fernando, 1863)

source.canonical_title: File:Prado - Los Desastres de la Guerra - No. 04 - Las mugeres dan valor.jpg

Prado_-_Los_Desastres_de_la_Guerra_-_No..story: A woman drives a pike into a French soldier while another clutches a baby and still finds a hand for a rock. Goya titles the plate "Las mugeres dan valor" — "The women give courage." He etched the Disasters of War between 1810 and 1820, working from things he'd seen during the Peninsular War and the famine that followed. The plates were considered too hot to publish in his lifetime. The Real Academia de Bellas Artes de San Fernando finally brought out the first edition in Madrid in 1863, thirty-five years after his death.

Prado_-_Los_Desastres_de_la_Guerra_-_No..title: The Disasters of War, No. 46: This Is Bad
Prado_-_Los_Desastres_de_la_Guerra_-_No..description: Los desastres de la guerra , plate No. 46, (1st edition, Madrid: Real Academia de Bellas Artes de San Fernando, 1863)

source.canonical_title: File:Prado - Los Desastres de la Guerra - No. 46 - Esto es malo.jpg

Prado_-_Los_Desastres_de_la_Guerra_-_No..story: A friar lies bleeding on the ground while a fat monk turns away. Goya's caption is short: "Esto es malo" — "This is bad." Plate 46 of the Disasters of War, etched during or just after the Peninsular War, published only in 1863 by the Real Academia in Madrid. Goya saved his sharpest scorn for the Church when it failed the people it was supposed to comfort. The composition is almost empty — a corpse, a coward, a smear of aquatint for shadow — and that's the whole point.

Prado_-_Los_Desastres_de_la_Guerra_-_No..title: The Disasters of War, No. 47: This Is How It Happened
Prado_-_Los_Desastres_de_la_Guerra_-_No..description: Los desastres de la guerra , plate No. 47, (1st edition, Madrid: Real Academia de Bellas Artes de San Fernando, 1863)

source.canonical_title: File:Prado - Los Desastres de la Guerra - No. 47 - Así sucedió.jpg

Prado_-_Los_Desastres_de_la_Guerra_-_No..story: French soldiers strip a church. One drags an altar cloth, another hauls off a silver reliquary, a third steps over a dying priest without slowing down. Goya's three-word caption underneath: "Así sucedió" — "This is how it happened." No allegory, no muses, just looted property and a body on the flagstones. Plate 47 of the Disasters of War, etched in the decade after 1810 and held back from print until the Real Academia finally published the set in 1863.

Prayer_in_the_Mosque.jpg.title: Prayer in the Mosque Alternative title(s): The mosque of Borurssa

source.canonical_title: File:Prayer in the Mosque.jpg

Prayer_in_the_Mosque.jpg.story: Rows of men bow toward Mecca under the arches of the Mosque of 'Amr in Cairo, one of the oldest in the Islamic world, founded in the seventh century. Gérôme painted it in 1871, three years after his 1868 visit to Egypt, but the mosque had fallen into disuse by then; he never witnessed a service there. The whole interior is a composite, assembled from his sketches and photographs. The light falls in long diagonal bands across the stone floor. Held by the Metropolitan Museum of Art.

Print,_The_Flight_into_Egypt,_1470–75_(C.title: Print, The Flight into Egypt, 1470–75
Print,_The_Flight_into_Egypt,_1470–75_(C.description: The Virgin, seated on a donkey, with the Christ Child on her lap, passes under a date palm, from which the fruit is being shaken by angels, and caught by Joseph.

source.canonical_title: File:Print, The Flight into Egypt, 1470–75 (CH 18428015).jpg

Print,_The_Flight_into_Egypt,_1470–75_(C.story: The Holy Family rests under a date palm on the road to Egypt. Mary sits sidesaddle on the donkey with the Christ Child; Joseph reaches up for the fruit, helped by small angels bending the branches. Schongauer packs the scene with that Colmar tenderness — the donkey's sleepy eye, the folds of Joseph's cloak, the palm fronds etched line by patient line. Early northern engraving at its most accomplished, made when the medium was still new enough that craftsmen were figuring out what a burin could do. Dürer owned Schongauer prints and studied them obsessively, and you can see here exactly why.
