Procesión_de_Pascua_en_la_región_de_Kurs.story: A dust cloud rolls out of the canvas ahead of the procession — landowners in finery, priests sweating under robes, a crippled boy lurching forward with his crutch while a mounted official shoves the peasants back. Repin spent years travelling to Kursk watching these Easter processions, refusing to idealise anyone. The sun is brutal, the gold icons flash, and the social hierarchy of Russia in 1883 is laid out in a single moving column. Critics attacked it from left and right. Pavel Tretyakov bought it anyway, and it still hangs in his gallery in Moscow.

Promenade_sur_la_falaise_de_Sainte-Adres.title: Promenade sur la falaise de Sainte-Adresse
Promenade_sur_la_falaise_de_Sainte-Adres.description: Exhibit in the Matsuoka Museum of Art - 5 Chome-12-6 Shirokanedai, Minato, Tokyo 108-0071, Japan.

source.canonical_title: File:Promenade sur la falaise de Sainte-Adresse, by Claude Monet, 1867, oil on canvas - Matsuoka Museum of Art - Tokyo, Japan - DSC07396.JPG

Promenade_sur_la_falaise_de_Sainte-Adres.story: Summer 1867 on the Normandy coast, painted from the clifftop at Sainte-Adresse where Monet was staying with his aunt. He was twenty-six, broke, and had just had his second Salon submission rejected. The canvas still has the crisp edges and diagonal promenade of a Boudin or a Jongkind — Impressionism proper is a year or two off — but the light on the Channel is already doing its work. The painting ended up far from home: it now hangs in the Matsuoka Museum of Art in Tokyo.

Purfleet_and_the_Essex_Shore_as_seen_fro.title: Purfleet and the Essex Shore as seen from Long Reach

source.canonical_title: File:Purfleet and the Essex Shore as seen from Long Reach.jpg

Purfleet_and_the_Essex_Shore_as_seen_fro.story: Fishermen wrestle boats in the chop of Long Reach, that wide stretch of the Thames below London where the river starts tasting of the sea. Turner signed and dated it 1808 and sold it straight out of his own gallery that year to the 5th Earl of Essex, who hung it at Cassiobury Park. It stayed in private hands for two centuries. In July 2021 Sotheby's put it under the hammer with an estimate of four to six million pounds.

Pythagoras_advocating_vegetarianism_(161.title: Pythagoras advocating vegetarianism

source.canonical_title: File:Pythagoras advocating vegetarianism (1618-20); Peter Paul Rubens.jpg

Pythagoras_advocating_vegetarianism_(161.story: Another version of the Pythagoras subject — or a later copy after the Prado canvas. The philosopher makes his case against meat to a group of listeners, flanked by Snyders's signature pile of produce: peaches, pomegranates, artichokes, quinces, the whole summer market rendered with tactile precision. Rubens's nudes and draped figures frame the composition, but your eye keeps sliding back to the fruit. A philosophical argument staged as a grocery advertisement — arguably the point.

Qian_Xuan_-_Early_Autumn.jpg.title: Early Autumn

source.canonical_title: File:Qian Xuan - Early Autumn.jpg

Qian_Xuan_-_Early_Autumn.jpg.story: Low to the ground: frogs on lotus pads, grasshoppers picking through tall grass, a bright red dragonfly and a translucent one floating above the reeds, a fat black beetle. Qian Xuan paints insects and amphibians at their own eye-level, with the silk bare around them, so the scroll reads like a long slow pan through wet undergrowth at the tail end of summer. The colophons and collector's seals crowding the margins are their own history. For a painter who spent his life refusing to serve the Yuan dynasty, the politics of this kind of attention — small creatures, quiet ground — is its own statement.

Quai_du_Louvre_1867,_by_Claude_Monet.jpg.title: Quai du Louvre

source.canonical_title: File:Quai du Louvre 1867, by Claude Monet.jpg

Quai_du_Louvre_1867,_by_Claude_Monet.jpg.story: Top-hatted figures strolling the quay, carriages rattling past, the Pont Neuf visible in the distance and the spire of Sainte-Chapelle needling up behind it. Painted in spring 1867 from a colonnade window at the Louvre, where Monet had been granted special access. It's the broadest of his three Paris views from that perch. The canvas is about 65 by 92 cm and lives at the Kunstmuseum Den Haag.

Raffaello_Sanzio_-_Ritratto_di_Bindo_Alt.story: A twenty-something Florentine banker turns his head over his shoulder and looks straight out at you with the kind of confidence money early buys. The blonde hair falls in a careful wave, the green sleeve catches the light. For ages people thought this was Raphael's own self-portrait, partly because of that pose. It's actually Bindo Altoviti, one of Rome's richest and best-connected patrons, painted around 1515. The picture stayed in the Altoviti family for almost three hundred years. Andrew Mellon bought it in 1938, and it's now in the National Gallery of Art in Washington.

Raimondi_Lucretia's_suicide.jpg.title: Raimondi Lucretia's suicide

source.canonical_title: File:Raimondi Lucretia's suicide.jpg

Raimondi_Lucretia's_suicide.jpg.story: Raimondi's engraving after a lost drawing by Raphael: Lucretia, raped by the king's son, kills herself on the threshold of her own house rather than let Rome excuse the crime. She stands between two marble columns, robe sliding off one shoulder, dagger already into her side, with a vague Italian landscape opening behind her. The print was a bestseller. Raimondi's line is the reason: he turned Raphael's chalk into something reproducible, sellable, shippable to Antwerp and Paris. This is roughly how northern Europe learned what the Italian High Renaissance looked like, one small sheet at a time.

Raphael_-_Fire_in_the_Borgo.jpg.title: Fire in the Borgo.

source.canonical_title: File:Raphael - Fire in the Borgo.jpg

Raphael_-_Fire_in_the_Borgo.jpg.story: Rome, 847, and the Borgo district near the old St Peter's is burning. Pope Leo IV appears in the loggia at the back and makes the sign of the cross, and the flames go out. In the foreground Raphael gives us pure classical drama: a muscular young man carrying his aged father on his back like Aeneas fleeing Troy, women rushing water jugs, a boy lowering himself by the wrist from a wall. Raphael designed the fresco around 1514 for what became the Stanza dell'Incendio, but his workshop, especially Giulio Romano, did much of the execution.

Raphael_-_The_Miraculous_Draft_of_Fishes.title: The Miraculous Draft of Fishes

source.canonical_title: File:Raphael - The Miraculous Draft of Fishes - Google Art Project.jpg
source.credit: ywH0tF2CcmYUxA at Google Cultural Institute maximum zoom level

Raphael_-_The_Miraculous_Draft_of_Fishes.story: Peter is on his knees in the boat, realizing who's sitting across from him. The nets are splitting with fish, the second boat is low in the water, and three cranes pose inexplicably on the shore. This is one of ten cartoons Raphael was commissioned in 1515 by Leo X to design as full-size templates for tapestries to hang in the Sistine Chapel on feast days. Painted in glue distemper on paper, they were shipped to Brussels for weaving. Seven survive and have been on loan from the Royal Collection to the V&A in London since 1865.

Raphael_-_Young_Man_Carrying_an_Old_Man_.title: Young Man Carrying an Old Man on His Back

source.canonical_title: File:Raphael - Young Man Carrying an Old Man on His Back, c. 1514 - Google Art Project.jpg

Raphael_-_Young_Man_Carrying_an_Old_Man_.story: A red-chalk study for the Aeneas-and-Anchises figure at the left of the Fire in the Borgo fresco. The younger man strains under the weight, his thigh taut, the older man's arm slack over his shoulder. Raphael has worked the anatomy hard, rubbing and cross-hatching the muscles until they almost move. Sheets like this were how the big Vatican commissions got built: the master drew, the workshop enlarged and painted. It's dated around 1514 and lives in the Albertina in Vienna, one of the largest and most unruly drawings collections anywhere.

Red_Fuji_southern_wind_clear_morning.jpg.story: Late summer, early morning, a warm south wind: the conditions that briefly turn Fuji's snowless flank red at dawn. Hokusai strips the image to three elements — red mountain, ribbed clouds, Prussian blue sky — and lets the triangle do everything. The Japanese title, Gaifu kaisei, just means 'fair wind, fine weather'. The print's red, a pigment called bengara, required nerve-wracking block alignment to keep from smearing across the sky.

Remaining_Snow_at_Inokashira.jpg.title: Remaining Snow at Inokashira ( Inokashira no zansetsu), from the series Twelve Subjects of Tokyo

source.canonical_title: File:Remaining Snow at Inokashira.jpg

Remaining_Snow_at_Inokashira.jpg.story: Inokashira Park in early spring, the snow not quite gone. Hasui lays out the scene in long horizontal bands — trailing cloud on a pale violet sky, placid blue pond, ochre reeds starting to yellow, white patches clinging under the cedars. Nothing in it is loud. From the 1920 Twelve Scenes of Tokyo, pulled before the 1923 earthquake destroyed Watanabe's original blocks, which makes the early impressions unusually scarce. A good example of what shin-hanga is actually for: weather and season rendered patiently enough that you feel both.

Rembrandt,_Portrait_of_Saskia_van_Uylenb.title: Portrait of Saskia van Uylenburgh (1612-1642)

source.canonical_title: File:Rembrandt, Portrait of Saskia van Uylenburgh (1612–1642), circa 1633–1634, Gemäldegalerie Alte Meister, Kassel.jpg

Rembrandt,_Portrait_of_Saskia_van_Uylenb.story: His new wife, caught in a feathered hat the size of a small umbrella. Saskia was the orphaned daughter of a Frisian mayor and the cousin of Rembrandt's art dealer, which is how they met. They married in 1634; he painted and drew her constantly until tuberculosis took her in 1642. Here the brim throws her face into a soft half-light, a pearl earring glints, and she looks a little amused, as if he's taking too long. The panel hangs today in Kassel's Gemäldegalerie Alte Meister.

Rembrandt-Belsazar.jpg.title: Belshazzar's Feast
Rembrandt-Belsazar.jpg.description: According to Daniel 5:1-31, King Belshazzar of Babylon takes sacred golden and silver vessels from the Jewish Temple in Jerusalem by his predecessor Nebuchadnezzar. Using these holy items, the King and his court praise 'the gods of gold and silver, bronze, iron, wood, and stone'. Immediately, the disembodied fingers of a human hand appear and write on the wall of the royal palace the words "MENE", "MENE", "TEKEL", "UPHARSIN"

source.canonical_title: File:Rembrandt-Belsazar.jpg

Rembrandt-Belsazar.jpg.story: Babylon's king has been drinking from the looted Temple vessels when a glowing hand writes on the wall in Hebrew: mene, mene, tekel, upharsin. Numbered, numbered, weighed, divided. Belshazzar jerks so hard the gold cup flies and red wine sheets across a woman's sleeve. His eyes bulge, chains of office swing, a musician freezes mid-note. Rembrandt probably got the Hebrew, written top-to-bottom rather than right-to-left, from his Amsterdam neighbour the rabbi and scholar Menasseh ben Israel. That same night, Daniel says, Belshazzar died.

Rembrandt_-_Susanna_and_the_Elders_-_WGA.title: Susanna and the Elders

source.canonical_title: File:Rembrandt - Susanna and the Elders - WGA19104.jpg
source.credit: Web Gallery of Art : Image Info about artwork wga QS:P11807,"r/rembran/painting/biblic1/suzanna"

Rembrandt_-_Susanna_and_the_Elders_-_WGA.story: Two old judges have caught Susanna at her bath and are bargaining with her body. Rembrandt drops the seduction and shows the grab: one elder yanks her mantle while she twists away, flesh and cloth wrenched in opposite directions. He started the mahogany panel around 1635 and only signed it in 1647, more than a decade of second-guessing. In 2015 conservators at Berlin's Gemäldegalerie discovered that Sir Joshua Reynolds, who owned the picture in the 1780s, had repainted large stretches of it and dissolved others with solvents before selling it on.

Rembrandt_-_The_Abduction_of_Europa_-_Go.title: The abduction of Europa

source.canonical_title: File:Rembrandt - The Abduction of Europa - Google Art Project.jpg
source.credit: JwHVmnI-bQWnRw at Google Cultural Institute zoom level scaled down maximum

Rembrandt_-_The_Abduction_of_Europa_-_Go.story: Zeus has already turned himself into a white bull and waded out from shore. Europa, still clutching flowers, twists back toward her friends on the bank, one of whom has thrown up her hands in the universal shape of wait, no, come back. A coachman gapes. A tiny coach hovers on the hill. It's a myth, sure, but Rembrandt stages it like a Dutch harbor scene on a bad afternoon, with massed trees, a choppy sky and a distant city smudged in brown. Painted in 1632, it's his only surviving seascape on panel.

Rembrandt_-_The_Abduction_of_Ganymede_-_.title: Rape of Ganymede , detail.

source.canonical_title: File:Rembrandt - The Abduction of Ganymede - Google Art Project - cropped.jpg
source.credit: Cropped from File:Rembrandt - The Abduction of Ganymede - Google Art Project.jpg , originally from Google Art Project.

Rembrandt_-_The_Abduction_of_Ganymede_-_.story: Classical myth says Zeus, smitten by a beautiful Trojan prince, turned into an eagle and bore him up to be cupbearer to the gods. Rembrandt's Ganymede is a howling toddler in a nightshirt, peeing himself in sheer terror as talons puncture his arm. The boy clutches a cherry, a Dutch symbol of paradise he is leaving behind. It's a shocking, almost satirical reading of a myth usually painted as erotic idyll, and critics have argued for centuries about whether it was commissioned as a memorial to a dead child. Signed and dated 1635.

Rembrandt_-_The_Anatomy_Lesson_of_Dr_Nic.story: The corpse is a petty thief named Aris Kindt, hanged that morning in January 1632 for robbery. Dr Tulp, gloved and calm, has peeled back the left forearm to show the flexor muscles, tugging a tendon with forceps so the dead hand seems to curl on its own. Seven surgeons lean in, each paid to be included, their heads staggered like notes on a staff. Rembrandt was twenty-five, newly arrived in Amsterdam, and this civic commission made him. The open book at the feet is Vesalius, the anatomist's bible.

Rembrandt_-_The_windmill_-_Google_Art_Pr.title: The Windmill

source.canonical_title: File:Rembrandt - The windmill - Google Art Project.jpg

Rembrandt_-_The_windmill_-_Google_Art_Pr.story: Not a painting: a small etching, about six by eight inches, of a very specific mill. It was called the Little Stink Mill, owned by the Amsterdam leatherworkers' guild, and it softened hides by grinding cod-liver oil into them. You can smell the place just reading that. Rembrandt probably traced the sails and the shaggy thatched cottage on site, then finished the plate at home, brushing acid across the sky to rough up the clouds. Dated 1641, it's one of his most quietly observed prints.

Rembrandt_-_Zelfportret_-_Google_Art_Pro.story: By 1658 Rembrandt had buried a wife and three children, lost his house, and filed for bankruptcy; he was fifty-two. So he painted himself on a throne. A heavy velvet beret stands in for a crown, a painter's maulstick for a sceptre, and the coat is a warm wall of red and gold that dares the viewer to pity him. The Frick Collection canvas is over four feet tall, the largest of his more than forty self-portraits, and the most frontal. The signature and date sit low on the left: Rembrandt f 1658.

Rembrandt_Christ_in_the_Storm_on_the_Lak.story: Fourteen men, counting Christ, clinging to one small boat as the sail splits and a wave climbs over the bow. One disciple vomits over the side; another wrestles a rope; a third, staring straight out at you in a blue cap, is Rembrandt himself. Christ, stern-lit at the back, hasn't stood up yet. It's the only seascape Rembrandt ever painted, and on 18 March 1990 two men dressed as Boston police walked out of the Isabella Stewart Gardner Museum carrying it. It has never been recovered.

Rembrandt_Christus_aan_het_volk_getoond..title: Christ presented to the people: the oblong plate

source.canonical_title: File:Rembrandt Christus aan het volk getoond.jpg

Rembrandt_Christus_aan_het_volk_getoond..story: Pilate presents Christ to a crowd of stone: magistrates, merchants, a hooded thief, all pressed against the front of the stage like a bas-relief. Rembrandt worked this plate in drypoint around 1655 and could not leave it alone. Eight states survive. By the fourth, he had shaved an inch off the top, lopping the architrave, so the whole composition fit a single sheet. In the later states the crowd below vanishes entirely, replaced by two dark arches and a surfacing figure, as if the judgement had gone underground. Nearly eighteen inches wide, it is among his largest prints.

Rembrandt_Girl_in_a_Picture_Frame.jpg.title: The Girl in a Picture Frame (The Jewish Bride).

source.canonical_title: File:Rembrandt Girl in a Picture Frame.jpg

Rembrandt_Girl_in_a_Picture_Frame.jpg.story: She's leaning out of the frame, fingers hooked over the gilt edge as if she might actually step into your room. The red-feathered hat is tilted back, a chain glints at her neck, and her expression sits somewhere between curious and about to laugh. It isn't a portrait of anyone in particular, it's a tronie, a study done for sale, and Rembrandt was using the painted frame itself as a trompe-l'oeil gag. Dated 1641, it's now at the Royal Castle in Warsaw, where locals call it the Warsaw Mona Lisa.

Rembrandt_Harmensz._van_Rijn_(Dutch_-_St.title: St. Bartholomew

source.canonical_title: File:Rembrandt Harmensz. van Rijn (Dutch - St. Bartholomew) - Google Art Project.jpg
source.credit: EQETBP79d47TVQ at Google Cultural Institute maximum zoom level

Rembrandt_Harmensz._van_Rijn_(Dutch_-_St.story: Bartholomew was flayed alive, and Rembrandt lets you notice the knife before the man. It rests in his right hand, blade angled down, almost bashful. The face above it is thick with paint, lumpy impasto on the forehead and nose, while the body dissolves into thinly brushed shadow. He looks less like a martyr than like someone thinking through the sentence that will kill him. Painted in 1661, the canvas measures 86.7 by 75.6 centimetres and hangs at the J. Paul Getty Museum in Los Angeles.

Rembrandt_Harmensz._van_Rijn_-_Portret_v.title: Portrait of a couple as figures from the Old Testament, known as ‘The Jewish bride’ .

source.canonical_title: File:Rembrandt Harmensz. van Rijn - Portret van een paar als oudtestamentische figuren, genaamd 'Het Joodse bruidje' - Google Art Project.jpg

title.nl: Portret van een paar als Oud-Testamentische figuren, genaamd ‘Het Joodse bruidje’ .

Rembrandt_Harmensz._van_Rijn_-_Portret_v.story: A man rests his hand on a woman's breast with a tenderness that stops the painting cold. The sleeve of his coat is built up in gold so thick Rembrandt scratched through it with the butt end of the brush to carve the embroidery. A 19th-century Amsterdam collector decided the couple were a Jewish father and daughter, and the nickname stuck; scholars now think they are Isaac and Rebecca, caught in the moment Abimelech glimpses them through a window. Rijksmuseum dating puts the canvas around 1665-1669, making it one of Rembrandt's last great paintings.

Rembrandt_Harmensz._van_Rijn_049.jpg.title: The evangelist Matthew and the angel

source.canonical_title: File:Rembrandt Harmensz. van Rijn 049.jpg
source.credit: The Yorck Project (2002) 10.000 Meisterwerke der Malerei (DVD-ROM), distributed by DIRECTMEDIA Publishing GmbH. ISBN : 3936122202 .

Rembrandt_Harmensz._van_Rijn_049.jpg.story: An old evangelist pauses over his page while a boyish angel leans in from behind, lips near his ear. Matthew's beard is a cloud of loaded brushwork; the angel barely emerges from the gloom, a sliver of forehead, a hand at the shoulder. The intimacy is startling, less divine messenger than a son reminding a father of a word. One of a series Rembrandt painted in 1661, oil on canvas, 96 by 81 centimetres. It entered the French royal collection under Louis XVI and now hangs in the Louvre.

Rembrandt_The_Artist_in_his_studio.jpg.title: The Artist in his Studio

source.canonical_title: File:Rembrandt The Artist in his studio.jpg

Rembrandt_The_Artist_in_his_studio.jpg.story: A tiny figure in a smock and oversized hat stands across the room from a massive wooden easel that dwarfs him. We only see the back of the panel. All the drama is in the standoff: painter versus unseen painting, tools on the wall, light pouring in from the left onto the cracked plaster. Rembrandt was about twenty when he made this in Leiden around 1628, and already turning the studio itself into a subject. The panel is barely 25 by 31 cm. It was bought by the Museum of Fine Arts in Boston in 1938.

Rembrandt_Winterlandschap_1646.jpg.title: Winter Landscape

source.canonical_title: File:Rembrandt Winterlandschap 1646.jpg

Rembrandt_Winterlandschap_1646.jpg.story: Barely the size of a sheet of paper, this is Rembrandt's only known winter landscape. A pale sweep of ice, a horizon of leafless trees and leaning barns, bundled figures slipping across the cold. The brushwork is so loose it looks like a sketch, but nobody worked outdoors in a Dutch January, so he made it from memory in the studio. The sky lifts from blue-green to pearl without a shadow anywhere, which is unusual for him. The panel, in oil, measures just 16 by 22 centimetres and hangs at the Gemäldegalerie in Kassel.

Rembrandt_van_Rijn_-_Borststuk_van_een_o.title: Bust of an old man with a fur cap

source.canonical_title: File:Rembrandt van Rijn - Borststuk van een oude man met bontmuts (1630).jpg

title.fr: Buste d'un vieil homme avec un chapeau en fourrure
title.de: Büste eines alten Mannes mit Peltzmütze

title.nl: Borststuk van een oude man met bontmuts

Rembrandt_van_Rijn_-_Borststuk_van_een_o.story: Not a portrait, a performance. This anonymous old man, draped in fur and lit like a stage actor, is what the Dutch called a tronie: a head study done for the market, dealer-ready. Rembrandt, only twenty-four, hires a weathered face and lets every wrinkle do the work. The beard glows, the cap eats the light, and the eyes settle into a dim hollow you have to lean in for. He signed the panel with his Leiden monogram RHL and dated it 1630, the year before he moved to Amsterdam and stopped bothering with the initials.

Rembrandt_van_Rijn_-_Self-Portrait_-_Goo.title: Self-portrait

source.canonical_title: File:Rembrandt van Rijn - Self-Portrait - Google Art Project.jpg
source.credit: -gHQe8vbiHn2xw at Google Cultural Institute maximum zoom level

Rembrandt_van_Rijn_-_Self-Portrait_-_Goo.story: A year after the throne-sized Frick portrait, Rembrandt scaled back. Same beret, same turned-up collar, but now he sits wrapped in a loose fur cloak with his hands clasped in his lap, looking faintly exhausted. The light picks out forehead, nose, and knuckles and lets the rest go soft. Andrew Mellon bought it in the 1930s and it has hung at the National Gallery of Art in Washington since 1937. Oil on canvas, 84.5 by 66 centimetres, signed and dated 1659.

Rembrandt_van_Rijn_-_The_Mill_-_Google_A.title: The Mill

source.canonical_title: File:Rembrandt van Rijn - The Mill - Google Art Project.jpg
source.credit: agGDXrJtBtu64Q at Google Cultural Institute maximum zoom level

Rembrandt_van_Rijn_-_The_Mill_-_Google_A.story: A lone windmill perches on a promontory, its vanes catching the last bruised light before a storm rolls in. Rembrandt pushed the mill high against steel-gray clouds and a thin topaz sky, muting the land into rust and brown so the eye climbs straight to those sails. For centuries the picture was treated as a poetic farewell, almost a self-portrait in landscape form. A 1977-79 cleaning stripped yellowed varnish and, to everyone's surprise, brought the sails back bright against the weather. The National Gallery of Art now dates it 1645/1648.

Rembrandt_van_Rijn_-_Zelfportret.jpg.title: Rembrandt van Rijn - Zelfportret

source.canonical_title: File:Rembrandt van Rijn - Zelfportret.jpg

Rembrandt_van_Rijn_-_Zelfportret.jpg.story: One of the earliest of the roughly eighty self-portraits Rembrandt left behind, painted in Leiden around 1628 when he was twenty-two. He backlights himself so harshly that his whole face disappears into shadow under the mop of frizzy hair, and then scratches through the wet paint with the pointed end of his brush to dig individual strands of light back out. It's technique showing off, but also a young painter figuring out that the interesting thing about a face might be what you can't see. The panel is in the Rijksmuseum, Amsterdam.

Renoir,_Pierre-Auguste_-_Dance_at_Le_Mou.story: Sunday afternoon at an open-air Montmartre dance hall, and Renoir has caught it all shimmering: couples swaying, glasses catching light, a little girl leaning on a bench. He dragged his canvas up the hill to the Moulin each day and paid his friends to pose, including the painter Franc-Lamy and the writer Georges Riviere in straw boaters around the table. The signature pink-and-lilac dapples of sunlight through leaves ripple across every jacket. It hangs at the Musee d'Orsay in Paris.

Renoir_-_Jeune_fille_se_peignant_(La_Toi.title: Young Girl Combing Her Hair, 1894

source.canonical_title: File:Renoir - Jeune fille se peignant (La Toilette), 1894.jpg

Renoir_-_Jeune_fille_se_peignant_(La_Toi.story: A girl in a rose-pink shift lifts a tortoiseshell comb through her hair, elbows raised, the whole canvas pulled into warm flesh tones and russet. By 1894 Renoir's arthritis was settling in and his late style was softening into this cottony glow. The sitter is likely Gabrielle Renard, the family's young housekeeper and his favorite model for the last twenty-five years of his life. The painting is in the collection of the Fondation Bemberg in Toulouse.

Renoirgarden.jpg.title: Renoirgarden
Renoirgarden.jpg.description: Woman with a Parasol in a Garden, Painting by Renoir

source.canonical_title: File:Renoirgarden.jpg

Renoirgarden.jpg.story: A woman in white drifts through a riot of green, her parasol tipped against the sun while a child crouches in the grass beside her. Renoir loved painting his friend Monet's garden at Argenteuil and often set up his easel beside him, brush dabbing the same dappled light. The pigment is laid on in soft, broken touches so the figures almost dissolve into the foliage. It belongs to the National Gallery of Art in Washington, a gift of Sam A. Lewisohn in 1951.

Repin_studying_exam.jpg.title: Preparation for the exam

source.canonical_title: File:Repin studying exam.jpg

Repin_studying_exam.jpg.story: Repin was twenty and broke, newly arrived at the St Petersburg Academy from provincial Chuguev, when he painted this. A young man hunches over his books by lamplight, the kind of late-night cramming Repin himself was living through. The brushwork is tight, the mood domestic — no Volga haulers yet, no tsars. It is one of the earliest surviving paintings by the artist who would become the giant of Russian realism, done the same year, 1864, that he finally passed the exams to enter the Academy.

Repin_turf_bench.jpg.title: turf bench
Repin_turf_bench.jpg.description: Изображены Вера Алексеевна Репина (1855–1918), жена художника; дочери Вера (1872–1948) и Надя (1874–1931); Алексей Иванович и Евгения Дмитриевна Шевцовы, родители жены художника; Алексей Алексеевич и Мария Павловна Шевцовы, его шурин с женой.

source.canonical_title: File:Repin turf bench.jpg

Repin_turf_bench.jpg.story: A summer afternoon at the family dacha: Repin's wife Vera, their daughters Vera and Nadya, and her parents and brother all packed onto a turf bench in the garden. No narrative, no drama — just the heavy quiet of a Russian July. Repin, fresh from five years studying abroad, was experimenting with plein-air and pared-back composition, painting the people he actually lived with. The loose brushwork and offhand grouping feel closer to the French Impressionists he had just seen in Paris than to the thunderous canvases he would soon be making. Dated 1876.

Reply_of_the_Zaporozhian_Cossacks_(sketc.title: The Reply of the Zaporozhian Cossacks to Sultan of Turkey.

source.canonical_title: File:Reply of the Zaporozhian Cossacks (sketch, 1880-90, GTG).JPG

Retrato_de_Juan_Pareja,_by_Diego_Velázqu.title: Juan de Pareja (ca. 1608–1670)

source.canonical_title: File:Retrato de Juan Pareja, by Diego Velázquez.jpg

Retrato_de_Juan_Pareja,_by_Diego_Velázqu.story: Velázquez brought his enslaved assistant Juan de Pareja to Rome and painted him in 1650 as a warm-up before tackling the pope. The canvas caused a sensation at the Pantheon that spring, critics saying the other portraits looked like paintings while this one looked like a man. Within a year Velázquez granted Pareja his freedom. Pareja went on to paint his own canvases. The Met bought the portrait in 1971 for a record 5.5 million dollars.

title.eo: Portreto de Papo Inocento la Deka
title.ja: インノケンティウス10世の肖像

Retrato_del_Papa_Inocencio_X._Roma,_by_D.story: The pope took one look and muttered that it was troppo vero, too truthful. Velázquez caught Innocent X mid-glare, jowls heavy, eyes suspicious, the reds of his cape and chair vibrating against each other like a warning. Painted in Rome in 1650, it's still in the Doria Pamphilj palace where the family has kept it since. Francis Bacon spent the 1950s trying to scream his way out of it.

Reverend_Robert_Walker_(1755_-_1808)_Ska.title: The Skating Minister

source.canonical_title: File:Reverend Robert Walker (1755 - 1808) Skating on Duddingston Loch.jpg
source.credit: National Gallery of Scotland, Edinburgh, online collection

Reverend_Robert_Walker_(1755_-_1808)_Ska.story: A Church of Scotland minister in black coat and top hat, arms crossed, leaning into a glide across Duddingston Loch with the Pentland Hills dissolving behind him into brown weather. There is something faintly absurd about the dignity of it — the stark silhouette, the rigidly vertical posture, the tiny leather skate strapped under his shoe — and that is precisely why the painting became a Scottish icon two centuries later. Raeburn worked fast and loose; up close the face is almost a sketch. Long attributed to him with confidence, though a few scholars still argue about the hand. Either way, it is the coolest portrait the Enlightenment produced.

Réception_du_Grand_Condé_à_Versailles.title: Reception of the Grand Condé at Versailles

source.canonical_title: File:Réception du Grand Condé à Versailles (Jean-Léon Gérôme, 1878).png

title.fr: Réception du Grand Condé par Louis XIV (Versailles, 1674)
title.it: Ricevimento del Grand Condé a Versailles

Réception_du_Grand_Condé_à_Versailles.story: 1674: Louis XIV descends the grand staircase at Versailles to greet the Great Condé, his cousin and general, returning from the Dutch wars a limping old man. Gérôme stages it as pure court theatre — Sun King framed by the marble arch, the prince bowing, a whole hierarchy hanging on the gesture. It's a strange choice for the 1870s, a Third Republic painter lingering on Bourbon ritual, but Gérôme loved this kind of historical dress-up. Every buckle and sash gets its moment. The figures feel less painted than installed.

Robert_Delaunay,_1912,_La_Ville_de_Paris.title: The City of Paris

source.canonical_title: File:Robert Delaunay, 1912, La Ville de Paris, oil on canvas, 267 × 406 cm, Musée National d'Art Moderne.jpg

Robert_Delaunay,_1912,_La_Ville_de_Paris.story: Four metres wide, finished just in time for the 1912 Salon des Indépendants, where it caused the expected scandal. Delaunay split the vast canvas into three zones: a view of Paris with the Seine on the left, the Eiffel Tower on the right, and between them, unexpectedly, three mask-faced nudes lifted straight out of Picasso's recent 'Demoiselles d'Avignon'. Classical Graces meet modern skyline meet primitivist faces, all stitched together by faceted plane. Apollinaire loved it. It went on to the Armory Show in New York the following year and now hangs at the Centre Pompidou as one of the foundation documents of Orphism.

Robert_Delaunay,_Der_Eiffelturm,_1910.jp.title: The Eiffel Tower

source.canonical_title: File:Robert Delaunay, Der Eiffelturm, 1910.jpg

Robert_Delaunay,_Der_Eiffelturm,_1910.jp.story: Delaunay painted his first Eiffel Tower to celebrate his engagement to Sonia Terk, and for the next few years he could hardly leave the thing alone. This early version from 1909-10 is where he later said his 'destructive period' began: the iron lattice starts to fracture, buildings crowd in from the sides, clouds tilt at impossible angles. He is not depicting the tower so much as dismantling and reassembling it on the canvas. Over the following decade he would make at least thirty pictures of it, each more fragmented than the last, until the monument dissolved into nothing but colour.

Robert_Delaunay_-_Eiffel_Tower_(Hirschho.title: The Eiffel Tower and the Champ de Mars Gardens

source.canonical_title: File:Robert Delaunay - Eiffel Tower (Hirschhorn II).jpg
source.credit: Hirshhorn Museum and Sculpture Garden Collection

Robert_Delaunay_-_Eiffel_Tower_(Hirschho.story: After a decade spent chasing abstraction, colour discs and 'Simultaneous Windows', Delaunay came back to Paris in 1921 and promptly back to the tower. By the early 1920s the destructive period is over; the structure stands upright again, legible as architecture, anchored in a Champ de Mars planted with actual trees and pedestrians. The fractured Cubist facets have softened into broad panels of flat colour, the kind of pattern-making that Sonia was simultaneously taking into textiles. It is a calmer, almost touristic tower, painted by a man who had already taken the monument apart and could now afford to put it back together.

Robert_Delaunay_-_Eiffel_Tower_-_1911_-_.title: Eiffel Tower

source.canonical_title: File:Robert Delaunay - Eiffel Tower - 1911 - Solomon R. Guggenheim Museum.jpg

Robert_Delaunay_-_Eiffel_Tower_-_1911_-_.story: Over two metres tall, dated 1911 by Delaunay though begun the year before. The tower shears sideways as if hit by an invisible wind, buildings crumpling around its base, the whole composition on the edge of collapse. Delaunay called this his destructive period and meant it literally: he wanted to break the monument apart and leave the pieces visible. The canvas went to Solomon Guggenheim early and has anchored the museum's Delaunay holdings since. Look closely and the tower is less engineered than geological, a red iron cliff face being quarried by the painter in real time.

Robert_Delaunay_L'homme_à_la_tulipe_(Po.title: The Man with a Tulip (Portrait of Jean Metzinger)

source.canonical_title: File:Robert Delaunay L'homme à la tulipe (Portrait de Jean Metzinger) 1906.jpg

Robert_Delaunay_L'homme_à_la_tulipe_(Po.story: Delaunay at twenty-one painting Jean Metzinger, who was painting him back the same year: the two young artists had just met and exchanged portraits in a pact of mutual encouragement. This one is pure Neo-Impressionist mosaic, stroke after stroke of unmixed colour, with Metzinger dapper in a boater and buttonhole tulip. Cubism and Orphism are still six years off. What you see is a painter testing how far a pointillist dot can be pushed before it stops reading as skin or fabric. The pair would soon drift apart aesthetically; Metzinger went analytical, Delaunay went chromatic, and this friendly early portrait marks the fork in the road.

Rocks_at_Mouthier_by_Gustave_Courbet.jpg.title: Rocks at Mouthier by Gustave Courbet
Rocks_at_Mouthier_by_Gustave_Courbet.jpg.description: Rocks at Mouthier by Gustave Courbet , on display in The Phillips Collection

source.canonical_title: File:Rocks at Mouthier by Gustave Courbet.jpg

Rocks_at_Mouthier_by_Gustave_Courbet.jpg.story: Courbet didn't render these cliffs with a brush so much as quarry them out with a palette knife, smearing and scraping until the paint itself feels like stone. The outcrop is Hautepierre, looming over Mouthier-Haute-Pierre near his native Ornans — the same rocks that appear on the easel inside his manifesto-painting The Painter's Studio. Duncan Phillips snapped this one up early in his collecting life. It's hung at The Phillips Collection in Washington since 1925.

Rogier_van_der_Weyden,_Netherlandish_(ac.title: Christ on the cross with Mary and Saint John the Evangelist

source.canonical_title: File:Rogier van der Weyden, Netherlandish (active Tournai and Brussels) - The Crucifixion, with the Virgin and Saint John the Evangelist Mourning - Google Art Project.jpg

title.ja: キリストの磔刑の二連祭壇画 (ファン・デル・ウェイデン)
title.pl: Ukrzyżowanie z Marią i św. Janem pod krzyżem
title.ca: Díptic de la Crucifixió (Van der Weyden)

Rogier_van_der_Weyden,_Netherlandish_(ac.story: Two panels, two figures each, stitched together by grief. On the left Mary collapses into John's arms, her face crumpling behind her wimple; on the right the dead Christ hangs against a blood-red cloth pinned to a flat stone wall. Rogier strips away the usual Jerusalem panorama so nothing competes with the weight of the bodies. A human skull at the foot of the cross marks Golgotha, the place of the skull. Dated around 1460, the diptych now hangs at the Philadelphia Museum of Art, a close cousin of his Crucifixion at the Escorial.

Rogier_van_der_Weyden_(1399_-_1464)_-_Po.title: Portrait of a Young woman with a Winged Bonnet

source.canonical_title: File:Rogier van der Weyden (1399 - 1464) - Portrait of a Young Woman with a White Headdress - 545D - Gemäldegalerie.jpg

title.de: Bildnis einer jungen Frau mit Flügelhaube
title.ca: Dona amb un tocat de gasa
title.ja: 若い女性の肖像 (ファン・デル・ウェイデン)
title.sv: Porträtt av en ung kvinna med huvudduk

Rogier_van_der_Weyden_(1399_-_1464)_-_Po.story: A half-length on oak, roughly 49 by 33 centimetres, painted around 1440. The sitter wears the Flügelhaube, the starched winged bonnet that marked a married woman, with a grey wool gown and a few slender rings on crossed fingers. The background is plain black. Everything is in the face: lowered eyelids, tight mouth, the slightest forward lean as if she is about to say something and has thought better of it. The identification has long been speculative, a tradition holds this may be Elisabeth Goffaert, the painter's wife, though nothing confirms it. Berlin's Gemäldegalerie acquired it in 1908.

Rogier_van_der_Weyden_-_Triptych-_The_Cr.title: Rogier van der Weyden - Triptych- The Crucifixion - Google Art Project

Rogier_van_der_Weyden_-_Virgin_and_Child.story: Mary sits hooded in a long red robe against a plain black void, and on her lap the Christ Child is rumpling the pages of a book, one fist crushing the parchment, more toddler than Saviour. Rogier gives the figures a polished, almost sculpted edge, as if a polychrome carving had been lifted from its niche. The hood and the book seem to foreshadow mourning and scripture to come. Painted in oil on oak around 1435-1438, the panel passed to collector Pedro Fernández-Durán, who donated it to the Prado in 1930.

Romaine_Lacaux,_by_Pierre-Auguste_Renoir.title: Romaine Lacaux
Romaine_Lacaux,_by_Pierre-Auguste_Renoir.description: This painting may be Renoir's earliest signed canvas. Its sensitive display of color and light communicates an ideal of delicate, youthful beauty. The luminous tones of the background drapery and of the child's white blouse result from the artist's careful observation of reflected light and color on translucent materials. The delicate nuances of color, particularly in the young girl's face, reveal Renoir's previous training as a decorator of porcelain. He painted this portrait, commissioned by the vacationing Lacaux family, during his stay at an artist's colony in the village of Barbizon, near Paris.

source.canonical_title: File:Romaine Lacaux, by Pierre-Auguste Renoir, Cleveland Museum of Art, 1942.1065.jpg

Romaine_Lacaux,_by_Pierre-Auguste_Renoir.story: A seven-year-old girl sits bolt upright in a white dress and looks straight at you. Renoir was 23, still finding his way out of porcelain painting — which is exactly what the luminous flesh and whisper-fine white fabric betray. This is likely the earliest canvas he signed. The Lacaux family commissioned it while on summer vacation near Barbizon in 1864. Every translucent layer of blouse and bow is a former china painter remembering how glaze catches light. Now at the Cleveland Museum of Art.

Roman_Charity_-_Pieter_Pauwel_Reubens.jp.title: Roman Charity

source.canonical_title: File:Roman Charity - Pieter Pauwel Reubens.jpg
source.credit: Originally from en.wikipedia ; description page is/was here . 2006-03-28 (original upload date)

Roman_Charity_-_Pieter_Pauwel_Reubens.jp.story: An old man condemned to starve in prison; his daughter Pero, slipping in on visiting day, offers the only food she has. Rubens lifts the subject straight from Valerius Maximus and stages it like a Caravaggio: one candle of pale flesh, the rest darkness, Cimon's hands manacled, Pero's eyes cutting sideways toward the door. It's tender and transgressive at once, and the viewer is placed exactly where a jailer would stand. The Hermitage bought the panel in Brussels in 1768; it has hung in Saint Petersburg ever since.

Rome,_From_Mount_Aventine.jpg.story: Painted from drawings Turner made on the Aventine in 1828, this is the Eternal City filtered through seven years of memory and a lot of atmospheric glaze. The Morning Post in May 1836 called it "beyond praise." History vindicated the reviewer: at Sotheby's London on 3 December 2014 it hammered down for £30.3 million including premium, a world auction record for Turner and for any pre-20th-century British painter.

Roses_-_Vincent_van_Gogh.JPG.story: One of four big flower still lifes Vincent painted in his last week at the Saint-Rémy asylum, in May 1890, as "a sort of farewell" before leaving for the north. He wanted calm: pink and white roses piled in a simple green vase on a green table. The pink has since faded — those roses were originally rose-pink, not the near-white we see now, because the red pigment was fugitive. It hangs at the National Gallery of Art in Washington.

Rubens,_Peter_Paul_-_Massacre_of_the_Inn.title: The Massacre of the Innocents

source.canonical_title: File:Rubens, Peter Paul - Massacre of the Innocents - Art Gallery of Ontario.jpg

title.th: การประหารทารกผู้วิมล

Rubens,_Peter_Paul_-_Massacre_of_the_Inn.story: Herod's soldiers wrench babies from mothers; a woman claws at a helmet, a dead infant sprawls on Roman cobblestones. Lost for centuries and catalogued as by a follower, it reemerged at Sotheby's in 2002 and sold for 49.5 million pounds to Kenneth Thomson, then a world record for an Old Master. He gave it to the Art Gallery of Ontario, where it hangs today.

Rubens,_Peter_Paul_-_The_Three_Graces.jp.title: The Three Graces

source.canonical_title: File:Rubens, Peter Paul - The Three Graces.jpg

title.ja: 三美神 (ルーベンス、プラド美術館)

Rubens,_Peter_Paul_-_The_Three_Graces.jp.story: Three goddesses share a soft, circular embrace while a garland of roses links their shoulders, a cupid spills a cornucopia overhead, and two deer idle nearby. The blonde on the left is widely read as Helena Fourment, Rubens' second wife, whom he married in December 1630 when he was 53 and she was 16. He never sold it; it stayed in his studio until he died in 1640, then Philip IV bought it for the Spanish royal collection. It hangs in the Prado.

Rubens,_de_vereniging_van_aarde_en_water.title: Union of Earth and Water (Antwerp and the Scheldt)

source.canonical_title: File:Rubens, de vereniging van aarde en water Gallerix.jpg
source.credit: Рубенс, Питер Пауль - Союз Земли и Воды (Антверпен и Шельда) (1618). Часть 14, высокое разрешение • описание картины, скачать репродукцию • Gallerix.ru

title.sl: Zveza Zemlje in vode (Antwerpen in Šelda)
title.fr: L'Union de la Terre et de l'Eau
title.nl: Neptunus en Ceres: het verbond tussen water en aarde
title.eo: La Unuiĝo de Tero kaj Akvo

Rubens,_de_vereniging_van_aarde_en_water.story: A river god and a water nymph clasp hands while a triton blows his conch and an eagle hovers above: Rubens is staging an allegory of Antwerp cut off from the sea. The Scheldt had been closed to shipping since 1585, strangling the city, and this painting is a plea for reunion. Rubens handled the flesh, Snyders likely the eagle and dolphins. The pair worked constantly together through the 1610s, Snyders providing animals for Rubens's Prometheus Bound and hunt scenes, Rubens returning the favour with figures.

Rubens-Feast_of_Simon_the_Pharisee.jpg.title: Christ at Simon the Pharisee

source.canonical_title: File:Rubens-Feast of Simon the Pharisee.jpg
source.credit: Web Gallery of Art : Image Info about artwork wga QS:P11807,"r/rubens/12religi/39religi"

Rubens-Feast_of_Simon_the_Pharisee.jpg.story: Simon's dinner party, and a woman has crashed it. She's down on the floor wiping Christ's feet with her hair while the tablecloth frames her like a second spotlight. Rubens lets Simon bluster in his beard at the far end; Christ's hand reaches across and down to her, the one diagonal holding the painting together. Tradition calls her Mary Magdalene. Painted around 1618-20, the canvas hangs in the Hermitage in St. Petersburg.

Rubens-Landscape.with.Rainbow1632-1635.j.title: Landscape with a Rainbow

source.canonical_title: File:Rubens-Landscape.with.Rainbow1632-1635.jpg

title.ja: 虹のある風景 (エルミタージュ美術館)
title.nl: Landschap met rustende en musicerende landlieden; in de lucht een regenboog

Rubens-Landscape.with.Rainbow1632-1635.j.story: A huge arc of rain-wash bends across the Flemish countryside near Rubens' manor Het Steen, which he'd bought in 1635. Haymakers load a wagon, cattle amble down a track, milkmaids joke with a farmhand. Long evening shadows say the work is nearly done. Rubens kept this painting and its morning-light partner until he died, and scholars think he hung the pair together at Het Steen itself. The Rainbow Landscape now lives in London's Wallace Collection.

Rubens_-_Der_gefesselte_Prometheus,_um_1.title: Prometheus bound

source.canonical_title: File:Rubens - Der gefesselte Prometheus, um 1613, Landesmuseum Oldenburg 923340078c.jpg

Rubens_-_Der_gefesselte_Prometheus,_um_1.story: Chained to his rock, Prometheus kicks and twists while the eagle digs a beak into his liver — Rubens painting pain as choreography. The work dates to around 1613 or 1614, shortly after his return from Italy. Its story since is almost as brutal as its subject: seized from the Jewish dealer Jacques Goudstikker's circle under Nazi persecution, earmarked for Hitler's planned Führermuseum in Linz, damaged in a salt-mine store during the war, and only restituted to the rightful heirs in 2009. It now hangs in the Landesmuseum Kunst und Kultur in Oldenburg.

Rubens_-_Mars_et_Rhea_Silvia.jpg.title: Mars and Rhea Silvia

source.canonical_title: File:Rubens - Mars et Rhea Silvia.jpg

title.ja: マルスとレア・シルウィア

Rubens_-_Mars_et_Rhea_Silvia.jpg.story: Mars has just shoved aside the Vestal's veil and is leaning in; a putto is already tugging at Rhea Silvia's sleeve like he knows what's coming. What's coming is Romulus and Remus and eventually Rome itself. Rubens paints her resigned rather than resisting, still holding her sacred flame-keeper's gaze on the viewer. The composition is tight and warm, all flesh and red velvet. Painted around 1616-17 for Vincenzo Gonzaga in Mantua, it now hangs in the Liechtenstein Princely Collections in Vienna.

Rubens_-_Portrait_of_a_woman_with_braide.title: Portrait of a woman with braided blond hair

source.canonical_title: File:Rubens - Portrait of a woman with braided blond hair.jpg

title.de: Bildnis einer Frau mit geflochtenem blonden Haar

Rubens_-_Portrait_of_a_woman_with_braide.story: No one knows who she is. Pale skin, a fat blonde plait coiled around her head, a dark bodice that makes the hair glow. Rubens paints her without any of his usual props - no pearls, no parrot, no mythological excuse - just the face and that braid. The sitter has been tentatively linked to Susanna Fourment and to one of the Brant sisters, but nothing sticks. Painted around 1618-20.

Rubens_-_RKDimages,_276003.jpg.title: Christ between the two malefactors, the 'coup de lance'

source.canonical_title: File:Rubens - RKDimages, 276003.jpg

title.nl: Hoofd van Christus (aan het kruis tussen de twee moordenaars, van de 'De lanssteek')

Rubens_-_RKDimages,_276003.jpg.story: The soldier Longinus drives his lance into Christ's side and blood streams down the cross. Mary swoons. The thieves twist on their crosses, one still alive and howling. Rubens painted this huge altarpiece, called the Coup de Lance, in 1620 for the Recollects in Antwerp, not 1610. It now hangs in the Royal Museum of Fine Arts Antwerp, over fourteen feet tall.
Rubens_-_RKDimages,_276003.jpg.year_note: The Coup de Lance altarpiece for the Recollects, Antwerp, is documented as 1620, not 1610.

Rubens_-_RKDimages,_276589.jpg.title: Study of the head of a young man turned to the left

source.canonical_title: File:Rubens - RKDimages, 276589.jpg

title.sl: Študija glave mladeniča, obrnjene v levo, 1611–1612
title.nl: Studie van het hoofd van een jongeman naar links gedraaid

Rubens_-_RKDimages,_276589.jpg.story: A working drawing, not a commission. Rubens catches a young man mid-turn, head cocked left, light grazing one cheek, and files the sheet away in his tronie cabinet for reuse. Heads like this one surface again and again in later altarpieces and mythologies, recycled wherever a bystander was needed. The cataloguing number on the file, RKDimages 276589, points to the Dutch archive that keeps tabs on these studies. What survives is a habit: he drew people the way other painters drew grapes, for the pantry.

Rubens_Medusa.jpeg.title: Head of Medusa

source.canonical_title: File:Rubens Medusa.jpeg
source.credit: 1. Kunsthistorisches Museum Wien, Bilddatenbank . 2. Unknown source Unknown source 3. GalleriX

Rubens_Medusa.jpeg.story: Severed head, still glaring, blood pooling into a snake-nest that's already hatching: Rubens handed the reptiles over to his friend Frans Snyders, the animal specialist, and Snyders gave him a squirming knot of European grass snakes plus two vipers slipped in on the right. For centuries it was kept behind a curtain because viewers reportedly fainted. Dated around 1617-18, it's now on open display in Vienna's Kunsthistorisches Museum.

Rubens_Painting_Adam_Eve.jpg.title: Adam and Eve .

source.canonical_title: File:Rubens Painting Adam Eve.jpg

Rubens_Painting_Adam_Eve.jpg.story: A young Rubens, still in Antwerp and not yet Rubens-famous, borrows the pose straight from a Marcantonio Raimondi print after Raphael — then loosens the limbs and warms the skin until the borrowed figures feel like his own. Eve leans in, the serpent coils down from a branch, and the apple changes hands with almost domestic calm. The landscape behind them sits flat and still, a giveaway that this was painted before Italy taught him how to move air. It hangs today in the Rubenshuis in Antwerp, dated roughly 1598 to 1600.

Rubens_Pieter_Paul_Coronation_Of_Marie_D.title: The Coronation of Marie de' Medici in Saint-Denis
Rubens_Pieter_Paul_Coronation_Of_Marie_D.description: Coronation Of Marie De Medici To Strengthen Authority Regent

source.canonical_title: File:Rubens Pieter Paul Coronation Of Marie De Medici To Strengthen Authority Regent louvre.jpg

title.fr: Couronnement de Marie de Médicis le 13 mai 1610
title.de: Gemäldezyklus für Maria de' Medici, Königin von Frankreich, Szene: Krönung Maria de' Medicis in St. Denis in Paris
title.nl: De kroning van Maria de' Medici te Saint Denis, 13 maart 1610

Rubens_Pieter_Paul_Coronation_Of_Marie_D.story: 13 May 1610 at Saint-Denis. Marie de' Medici kneels as the Cardinal de Joyeuse sets the crown on her head — Henry IV watches from a gallery at upper right. What the painting doesn't say: the next day, Henry was stabbed to death by Ravaillac in a Paris traffic jam, and Marie became regent of France. Rubens crammed around a hundred identifiable figures into the canvas, more portraiture than most artists manage in a decade. Painted 1622-25 for the Luxembourg Palace, it now hangs in the Louvre's Galerie Médicis.

Rubens_and_Snyders-Philopoemen.jpg.title: The Recognition of Philopoemen

source.canonical_title: File:Rubens and Snyders-Philopoemen.jpg
source.credit: Philopoemen Recognized . Museo del Prado. Retrieved on 23 October 2013 .

Rubens_and_Snyders-Philopoemen.jpg.story: A collaboration from the early Antwerp years: Rubens handled the figures, Snyders heaped the kitchen with the day's catch. The Greek general Philopoemen, travelling incognito to a supper, has been mistaken for a servant and sent to chop firewood — the host's wife, on the right, realizes her mistake too late. The real star is Snyders's foreground: a swan, a deer, a boar's head, heaps of vegetables and game, spilling toward the viewer with appetite. A Plutarch anecdote as an excuse for a still life.

Rubens_apostel_andreas_grt.jpg.title: St. Andrew

source.canonical_title: File:Rubens apostel andreas grt.jpg

Rubens_apostel_andreas_grt.jpg.story: Andrew leans on the X-shaped cross he was martyred on, face upturned, beard catching the light. Rubens painted twelve apostles around 1610-12, each holding the instrument of his death, for the Duke of Lerma's chapel in Valladolid. The set ended up in the Prado. Andrew's cross became the saltire on Scotland's flag because legend sent his bones there.

Rubens_apostel_paulus_grt.jpg.title: St. Paul

source.canonical_title: File:Rubens apostel paulus grt.jpg

Rubens_apostel_paulus_grt.jpg.story: Paul grips the sword that beheaded him, the book of his epistles tucked against his chest. Rubens gives him a balding forehead and the alert, argumentative eyes of a man who wrote more of the New Testament than anyone else. From the apostle series commissioned around 1610 by the Duke of Lerma, now in the Prado, Madrid.

Rubens_apostel_simon.jpg.title: St. Simon
Rubens_apostel_simon.jpg.description: from Rubens famous Twelve Apostles series

source.canonical_title: File:Rubens apostel simon.jpg

Rubens_apostel_simon.jpg.story: Simon the Zealot leans on the saw that supposedly cut him in half in Persia. Rubens paints him grizzled, knotted hands, the blade dulled. One of twelve apostles made for the Duke of Lerma around 1610-12, and among the earliest commissions Rubens took after coming home from Italy. The whole set is in the Prado.

Rubens_peace-war.jpg.title: Minerva protects Pax from Mars (Peace and War)

source.canonical_title: File:Rubens peace-war.jpg

title.es: Minerva protege a Pax de Marte
title.it: Minerva protegge la Pace da Marte
title.hu: Minerva megvédi Paxot Marstől, avagy Béke és Háború.

Rubens_peace-war.jpg.story: Rubens painted this in London in 1629-30 while he was there as Philip IV's envoy, trying to talk Charles I into peace with Spain. Minerva shoves Mars back into the shadows; Pax squeezes milk from her breast toward a hungry child; a satyr offers fruit. The kids are real — they're the children of Rubens's host, the art dealer Balthasar Gerbier. The painting worked. A treaty was signed in November 1630, Rubens was knighted before he left, and the canvas stayed in England. It now hangs in the National Gallery, London.

Rubens_saturn.jpg.title: Saturn (Ovid, Fasti, IV, 197-200)
Rubens_saturn.jpg.description: Saturn, Jupiter's father, devours one of his sons .

source.canonical_title: File:Rubens saturn.jpg

title.ja: 我が子を食らうサトゥルヌス

Rubens_saturn.jpg.story: Saturn, pale and wolfish, tears into his own infant while Jupiter (not yet born strong enough to stop him) hangs in the future. The baby's mouth is open in a small, thin scream. Ovid's Fasti gives the story, but Rubens adds a detail from Cicero: the planet Saturn, three bright dots, hangs above the god's head. Painted around 1636-1638 for Philip IV's Torre de la Parada, it now hangs in the Prado. The ribs are what stay with you.

Rudolf_Ernst_After_Prayers.jpg.title: Rudolf Ernst After Prayers

source.canonical_title: File:Rudolf Ernst After Prayers.jpg

Rudolf_Ernst_After_Prayers.jpg.pd_status_reason: year 1932 is >= 1931; US 95-year copyright term not yet expired

Sailing_Boats,_Afternoon,_Hiroshi_Yoshid.title: Sailing Boats, Afternoon

source.canonical_title: File:Sailing Boats, Afternoon, Hiroshi Yoshida.jpg

Sailing_Boats,_Afternoon,_Hiroshi_Yoshid.story: Afternoon light flattens the Inland Sea to a hard blue plate, the sails above it almost bleached. This is one impression from Yoshida's famous 1926 experiment: six prints pulled from the same set of blocks, differing only in the inks chosen to evoke a time of day. Afternoon needed the hottest palette, a thin cadmium warmth over cobalt. Yoshida often boasted that the Sailing Boats set was proof a single drawing could hold a dozen kinds of weather, and the block register here still lines up to within a fraction of a millimetre.

Sailing_Boats,_Evening,_Hiroshi_Yoshida..title: Sailing Boats, Evening

source.canonical_title: File:Sailing Boats, Evening, Hiroshi Yoshida.jpg

Sailing_Boats,_Evening,_Hiroshi_Yoshida..story: The same two boats, the same rigging, but now the horizon bruises into orange and the sails pick up a russet warmth from the setting sun. Evening is the fourth state in Yoshida's 1926 Sailing Boats set, cut from one shared keyblock and pulled with a different colour scheme for each hour. He claimed it was the version that sold best in the United States, where buyers recognised the motif from Turner and Whistler. The signature at upper-left, a small jizuri seal, confirms this sheet was self-published in his Tokyo workshop.

Sailing_Boats,_Mist,_Hiroshi_Yoshida.jpg.title: Sailing Boats, Mist

source.canonical_title: File:Sailing Boats, Mist, Hiroshi Yoshida.jpg

Sailing_Boats,_Mist,_Hiroshi_Yoshida.jpg.story: Mist erases most of the rigging and leaves only the faintest grey sails drifting above a pearl-white sea. Yoshida pulled this variant from the same 1926 Sailing Boats blocks as Morning and Night, but asked his printer to wipe the colour block almost dry, so the pigment barely clings to the paper. The result is the quietest print in his career, and arguably the most technically difficult; a single heavy wipe and the whole image collapses into white.

Sailing_Boats,_Morning,_Hiroshi_Yoshida..title: Sailing Boats, Morning

source.canonical_title: File:Sailing Boats, Morning, Hiroshi Yoshida.jpg

Sailing_Boats,_Morning,_Hiroshi_Yoshida..story: Morning opens the 1926 Sailing Boats cycle in a thin blue-pink wash, the two hulls still half in shadow and the sails catching the first pale glow. Yoshida carved the set after a trip through the Seto Inland Sea in his small plein-air boat; the rigging is accurate enough that historians have identified the craft as a local cargo sabani. This impression carries his jizuri seal in the margin, the mark he added from 1925 onward to distinguish prints supervised in his own studio from the commercial Watanabe editions.

Sailing_Boats,_Night,_Hiroshi_Yoshida.jp.title: Sailing Boats, Night

source.canonical_title: File:Sailing Boats, Night, Hiroshi Yoshida.jpg

Sailing_Boats,_Night,_Hiroshi_Yoshida.jp.story: Night plunges the same two boats into an indigo so dense it swallows the rigging, with only a bar of silver where the moon touches the sail. Yoshida's printer used an unusually thick oiled pigment for this variant of the 1926 set, built up over more than two dozen passes to get the black to sit without bleeding. It is the scarcest of the six Sailing Boats impressions, because the heavy inks wore the blocks down faster than the daylight versions.

San_Jerónimo_leyendo_(Murillo).jpg.description: San Jerónimo de Estridón , uno de los Padres de la Iglesia, aparece en el interior de una gruta, con el torso desnudo y profundamente concentrado en la oración y la penitencia, al tiempo que sostiene un crucifijo con su mano izquierda.

San_Jerónimo_leyendo_(Murillo).jpg.story: Jerome is stripped to the waist in his rocky hollow, a book open across his knee, fingers still laced around the crucifix he has just set down. Murillo's brush lingers on sunburnt shoulders and a tangled grey beard rather than on theology; the penitent looks less like a Doctor of the Church than a lean old hermit caught mid-breath. The canvas came to the Prado from Isabella Farnese's collection at La Granja.

title.fr: Niccolo Mauruzi da Tolentino à la tête de ses troupes
title.de: Niccolò Mauruzi da Tolentino in der Schlacht von San Romano
title.nl: Niccolo Maruzi da Tolentino, in de verpletterende slag van San Romano

San_Romano_Battle_(Paolo_Uccello,_London.story: The London panel of Uccello's three-part Battle of San Romano, and the most often reproduced. Niccolò da Tolentino rides the white charger at centre, red-and-gold hat bigger than his head. Lances point in rigid converging rows, broken shafts on the pink ground line up along an invisible grid, and a fallen soldier's body is foreshortened into a neat rectangle — Vasari's perspective-obsessed painter hiding a geometry lesson inside a cavalry charge. Hunts unfold up the hillside behind, oblivious, as if the battle were a tournament.

Sandro_Botticelli_(Alessandro_Filipepi)_.title: The Virgin and Child

source.canonical_title: File:Sandro Botticelli (Alessandro Filipepi) - The Virgin and Child - 1943.105 - Fogg Museum.jpg

Sandro_Botticelli_(Alessandro_Filipepi)_.story: A tondo — a round panel, popular in Florentine bedrooms as a kind of domestic icon. Mary tilts her head toward the child, who clutches at her veil with both small hands. Botticelli painted dozens of these Madonnas in the 1480s and 90s, usually with heavy workshop assistance; attribution debates still bubble around them. This one came to the Fogg Museum at Harvard as part of the Paul J. Sachs bequest in 1943, hence the accession number 1943.105. The gold ground was added, or at least heavily restored, in the nineteenth century.

Sandro_Botticelli_-_Idealized_Portrait_o.title: Idealised Portrait of a Lady (Portrait of Simonetta Vespucci as Nymph)

source.canonical_title: File:Sandro Botticelli - Idealized Portrait of a Lady (Portrait of Simonetta Vespucci as Nymph) - Google Art Project.jpg

title.fr: Portrait ideale d'une jeune femme (Simonetta Vespucci?)
title.nl: Ideaalportret van een jonge vrouw (Simonetta Vespucci?)
title.de: Weibliches Idealbildnis (Bildnis der Simonetta Vespucci als Nymphe)
title.ml: പോർട്രയിറ്റ് ഓഫ് എ യങ് വുമൺ (ബോട്ടിസെല്ലി, ഫ്രാങ്ക്ഫർട്ട്)
title.it: Ritratto ideale d'una donna giovane (Simonetta Vespucci?)

Sandro_Botticelli_-_Idealized_Portrait_o.story: Larger than life, a young woman in profile wears a cameo of Apollo and Marsyas at her throat and a braid threaded with pearls that could not possibly hold itself up in real life. Nothing about her is a likeness in the strict sense; the props are myth. The art historian Aby Warburg first argued the features belonged to Simonetta Vespucci, Giuliano de' Medici's beloved, dead of tuberculosis at twenty-two. Painted around 1480 in mixed technique on poplar, the panel has been at the Städel Museum in Frankfurt since 1880.

Sandro_Botticelli_-_La_nascita_di_Venere.title: The Birth of Venus
Sandro_Botticelli_-_La_nascita_di_Venere.description: Depicts the goddess Venus, having emerged from the sea as a fully grown woman, arriving at the sea-shore. The seashell she stands on was a symbol in classical antiquity for a woman's vulva. Thought to be based in part on the Venus de' Medici , an ancient Greek marble sculpture of Aphrodite.

source.canonical_title: File:Sandro Botticelli - La nascita di Venere - Google Art Project - edited.jpg
source.credit: Adjusted levels from File:Sandro Botticelli - La nascita di Venere - Google Art Project.jpg , originally from Google Art Project. Compression Photoshop level 9.

title.vi: Sự ra đời của thần Vệ Nữ
title.th: กำเนิดวีนัส

Sandro_Botticelli_-_La_nascita_di_Venere.story: She arrives on a scallop shell, blown to shore by Zephyrus and Chloris while an attendant rushes up with a flowered cloak. Her pose — hand at breast, other hand drawing hair across her hip — is lifted directly from the Venus Pudica type, a Greek sculptural cliché Botticelli knew through the Medici's own marble copies. The canvas is enormous, nearly six by nine feet, and painted on cheap linen rather than expensive wood panel, probably for a villa at Castello owned by Lorenzo di Pierfrancesco de' Medici. The surface was coated with egg yolk to mimic fresco.

Sandro_Botticelli_-_Lamentation_over_the.story: Savonarola's Florence had started to show. Mary cradles her dead son's head against hers, eyes closed, while Mary Magdalene presses her cheek to his feet — a mourning pose borrowed from earlier Flemish pietàs. Botticelli fills the tight vertical composition almost entirely with bodies, no landscape, no sky; the black mouth of the tomb swallows the background. Painted around 1490-95 for the church of San Paolino in Florence, the panel is now in Munich's Alte Pinakothek. The saints flanking the central group — Jerome, Paul, and Peter — are the identifying trio.

Sandro_Botticelli_-_Madonna_with_Saints_.title: Madonna Bardi
Sandro_Botticelli_-_Madonna_with_Saints_.description: Maria auf dem Thron bereitet sich vor dem Jesuskind die Brust zu geben. Sie ist umgeben von den heiligen Johannes der Täufer , links, und Johannes dem Evangelisten , rechts, mit seinen traditionellen Attributen Buch und Feder.

source.canonical_title: File:Sandro Botticelli - Madonna with Saints - Google Art Project.jpg

title.de: Thronende Maria mit dem Kind und den beiden Johannes

Sandro_Botticelli_-_Madonna_with_Saints_.story: Mary loosens her bodice to nurse. The two Johns flank her throne — Baptist on the left in his camelhair rag, Evangelist on the right with book and quill — while Botticelli piles the foreground with painted still-life: glass vases of lilies and roses tucked into niches behind them, cucumbers and figs at their feet. Every detail carries Marian symbolism; the cucumber, oddly, stood for resurrection. The altarpiece was commissioned by Giovanni d'Agnolo Bardi for his family chapel in Santo Spirito, Florence, and finished in 1485. It's now in Berlin's Gemäldegalerie.

Sandro_Botticelli_-_Retour_de_Judith_1.j.title: The Return of Judith to Bethulia

source.canonical_title: File:Sandro Botticelli - Retour de Judith 1.JPG
source.credit: Botticelli : de Laurent le Magnifique à Savonarole : catalogue de l'exposition à Paris, Musée du Luxembourg, du 1er octobre 2003 au 22 février 2004 et à Florence, Palazzo Strozzi, du 10 mars au 11 juillet 2004. Milan : Skira editore, Paris : Musée du Luxembourg, 2003. ISBN 9788884915641

title.ja: ユディトのベツリアへの帰還
title.fr: Le Retour de Judith à Béthulie
title.nl: The Return of Judith to Bethulia

Sandro_Botticelli_-_Retour_de_Judith_1.j.story: One of Botticelli's earliest surviving panels, painted when he was barely past twenty. Judith has just beheaded the Assyrian general Holofernes in his tent to save her besieged city; she walks home across the dawn landscape with a sprig of olive in one hand and the sword still in the other, while her maid follows carrying the head wrapped in cloth. The violence is entirely offstage. What you get instead is that uncanny Botticelli lightness, wind catching drapery, the stride almost a dance. The Uffizi pairs it with its bloodier companion panel showing the discovery of the body.

Sandro_Botticelli_015.jpg.title: Beweinung Christi

source.canonical_title: File:Sandro Botticelli 015.jpg
source.credit: The Yorck Project (2002) 10.000 Meisterwerke der Malerei (DVD-ROM), distributed by DIRECTMEDIA Publishing GmbH. ISBN : 3936122202 .

Sandro_Botticelli_015.jpg.story: Another Lamentation, this one tighter, more vertical, more claustrophobic. Christ's body sags across the Virgin's lap, his arm dangling, his head lolling back toward the viewer. Botticelli stacks the mourners in an almost Gothic compression — John clutches Mary from behind while the Magdalene collapses at Christ's feet. This version was painted for the Panciatichi chapel in the Florentine church of Santa Maria Maggiore around 1495, during Botticelli's late religious phase under Savonarola's shadow. It now hangs in the Poldi Pezzoli Museum in Milan, having been acquired in the 19th century.

Sandro_Botticelli_050.jpg.title: Hl.Augustinus

source.canonical_title: File:Sandro Botticelli 050.jpg
source.credit: The Yorck Project (2002) 10.000 Meisterwerke der Malerei (DVD-ROM), distributed by DIRECTMEDIA Publishing GmbH. ISBN : 3936122202 .

Sandro_Botticelli_050.jpg.story: Augustine stops mid-sentence. Quill poised, astrolabe at his elbow, books stacked like he'd been ransacking them for answers — the saint is caught in the middle of thought, not lost in prayer. Botticelli painted this fresco for the Ognissanti church in Florence in 1480, as a companion to Ghirlandaio's St. Jerome on the opposite wall. The two artists were effectively competing in plain sight. The clock above Augustine's head reads just past noon. According to legend, it marks the very hour Jerome died in Bethlehem — the saints acknowledging each other across the nave.

Sandro_Botticelli_La_calumnia_de_Apeles..title: Calumny of Apelles
Sandro_Botticelli_La_calumnia_de_Apeles..description: Botticelli made this painting on the description of a painting by Apelles, a Greek painter of the Hellenistic period. Apelles' works have not survived, but Lucian recorded details of one in his On Calumny : “On the right of it sits Midas with very large ears, extending his hand to Slander while she is still at some distance from him. Near him, on one side, stand two women—Ignorance and Suspicion. On the other side, Slander is coming up, a woman beautiful beyond measure, but full of malignant passion and excitement, evincing as she does fury and wrath by carrying in her left hand a blazing torch and with the other dragging by the hair a young man who stretches out his hands to heaven and calls the gods to witness his innocence. She is conducted by a pale ugly man who has piercing eye and looks as if he had wasted away in long illness; he represents envy. There are two women in attendance to Slander, one is Fraud and the other Conspiracy. They are followed by a woman dressed in deep mourning, with black clothes all in tatters—she is Repentance. At all events, she is turning back with tears in her eyes and casting a stealthy glance, full of shame, at Truth , who is slowly approaching.”

source.canonical_title: File:Sandro Botticelli La calumnia de Apeles.jpg
source.credit: The Yorck Project (2002) 10.000 Meisterwerke der Malerei (DVD-ROM), distributed by DIRECTMEDIA Publishing GmbH. ISBN : 3936122202 .

Sandro_Botticelli_La_calumnia_de_Apeles..story: A lost painting, reconstructed. Apelles' original — his revenge on a rival who'd slandered him to Ptolemy — survived only as a description in Lucian. Botticelli read the text (likely in the Latin translation circulating in Florence in the 1490s) and rebuilt the scene beat for beat: King Midas with ass's ears on the throne, Ignorance and Suspicion whispering, Slander dragging an innocent youth by the hair, naked Truth pointing to heaven at the left. The marble hall behind them is crusted with reliefs of classical myths. It was painted around 1494-95 and now hangs in the Uffizi.

Sansón_matando_al_león_-_Pedro_Pablo_Rub.title: Samson Slaying the Lion

source.canonical_title: File:Sansón matando al león - Pedro Pablo Rubens.jpg

Sansón_matando_al_león_-_Pedro_Pablo_Rub.story: Judges 14: a young Samson meets a lion on the road to Timnah and tears it apart "as one would tear a young goat." Rubens catches him mid-grapple, back muscles rippling, the beast's jaw pried open. Painted around 1628, it's an Old Testament set piece of the kind the Madrid court devoured during Rubens's second Spanish sojourn. Later, of course, Samson would find honey in the lion's carcass and get cocky — but that comes next chapter.

Sargent_-_Group_with_Parasols_(A_Siesta).title: Sargent - Group with Parasols (A Siesta), lot.7

source.canonical_title: File:Sargent - Group with Parasols (A Siesta), lot.7.jpg

Sargent_-_Life_Study_(Study_of_an_Egypti.title: Life Study (Study of an Egyptian Girl)

source.canonical_title: File:Sargent - Life Study (Study of an Egyptian Girl).jpg

Sargent_-_Life_Study_(Study_of_an_Egypti.story: Sargent traveled up the Nile in the winter of 1890 to 1891 gathering material for his Boston Public Library murals, and in a rented Cairo studio he painted this unnamed model from behind, weight on one foot, torso twisting. No bravura flicks here: he went back to his academic training, modeling the flesh slowly and carefully. He showed it at the Champ de Mars Salon in 1892, and it now lives at the Art Institute of Chicago.

Sargent_-_Madame_Ramón_Subercaseaux,_c._.title: Sargent - Madame Ramón Subercaseaux, c. 1880-81, nr. 41

source.canonical_title: File:Sargent - Madame Ramón Subercaseaux, c. 1880-81, nr. 41.jpg

Sargent_-_Madame_Ramón_Subercaseaux,_c._.story: Amalia Errázuriz, wife of the Chilean diplomat and amateur painter Ramón Subercaseaux, sits at a piano in a pale silvery dress, turning as if someone just spoke. Sargent painted her in Paris around 1880 to 1881 and sent it to the Salon of 1881, where it won him a second-class medal and real critical traction. The brushwork on the keyboard is almost careless, the face sharp as a photograph. Amalia would later become a close friend and patron.

Sargent_MonetPainting.jpg.title: Claude Monet Painting by the Edge of a Wood

source.canonical_title: File:Sargent MonetPainting.jpg

Sargent_MonetPainting.jpg.story: Monet at his easel at the edge of a wood, his wife Alice (or possibly Suzanne Hoschedé) reading in the grass behind him. Sargent tagged along to Giverny in the summer of 1885 and made this quick, affectionate sketch of his friend at work. You can see him trying on Impressionism for size, dashing little broken strokes into the meadow. He kept the painting his whole life. It now belongs to the Tate.
