Scène_des_massacres_de_Scio,_Eugène_De.story: A pile of survivors in the dust, a horseman above them with a captive girl lashed to his saddle, smoke drifting over a ruined island. Delacroix was twenty-five when he exhibited this at the Salon of 1824, and Paris was stunned: Gros called it "the massacre of painting." The subject was fresh news, Ottoman troops had slaughtered tens of thousands of Greeks on Chios in 1822. Delacroix repainted whole sections after seeing Constable's greens on the Salon walls just weeks before it opened.

Schongauer_Anthony.jpg.title: Schongauer Anthony
Schongauer_Anthony.jpg.description: The Temptation of St. Anthony by Martin Schöngauer c. 1480-90. Engraving. The Metropolitan Museum of Art, New York

source.canonical_title: File:Schongauer Anthony.jpg

Schongauer_Anthony.jpg.story: The desert hermit lifted off the ground by a pack of devils, each one a different anatomical nightmare — beaks, scales, tusks, tails, hooves, fur. They drag at his cloak, tug his beard, bite at his arms, while Anthony hangs in the air with unreadable calm. The young Michelangelo is said to have copied this engraving in paint, going to the fish market to study scales. Schongauer made it around 1470 and it set the European standard for demonic invention for a century. The discipline is extraordinary: chaos rendered with absolute control, every talon accounted for, the whole swarm pinned by the burin to a single blank sheet.

Scops_Owl,_Cherry_Blossoms,_and_Moon_by_.title: Scops Owl, Cherry Blossoms, and Moon by Shōson
Scops_Owl,_Cherry_Blossoms,_and_Moon_by_.description: Scops Owl, Cherry Blossoms, and Moon, woodblock print, ink and color on paper

source.canonical_title: File:Scops Owl, Cherry Blossoms, and Moon by Shōson.jpg

Sebastiano_Ricci_(Italian_-_Diana_and_He.title: Diana and Her Dog

source.canonical_title: File:Sebastiano Ricci (Italian - Diana and Her Dog - Google Art Project.jpg
source.credit: DAH5bsUIX48KXQ at Google Cultural Institute maximum zoom level

Sebastiano_Ricci_(Italian_-_Diana_and_He.story: The huntress rests. Bare-shouldered, leaning against a rock, quiver slung over her thigh, Diana looks off into the forest while her hound gazes up at her with a frankly adoring expression. Ricci works in the Venetian tradition of Titian and Veronese but filtered through the brightness and confectionary sweetness of the Rococo — the flesh almost rosy, the fabric loose and tumbling. He painted this around 1717-20, during his mature period when he'd already worked in London and Paris. The panel is at the Getty Museum in Los Angeles, one of several mythological cabinet pieces he produced for private collectors.

Sebastiano_Ricci_-_Venus_and_Satyr_-_Goo.title: Venus and Satyr

source.canonical_title: File:Sebastiano Ricci - Venus and Satyr - Google Art Project.jpg
source.credit: DQF-_OvOQfBgdw at Google Cultural Institute maximum zoom level

Sebastiano_Ricci_-_Venus_and_Satyr_-_Goo.story: She's asleep, or pretending to be. The satyr leans in, one goat-hoof crossing the other, lifting the drapery from her thigh with the practiced delicacy of a thief — the whole scene calibrated for voyeuristic charge. Ricci picks up the Venetian tradition of Titian's sleeping Venuses but speeds up the brushwork and sweetens the palette for eighteenth-century tastes. He painted this around 1716-20, after returning to Venice from his successful stay in London, where he'd decorated Burlington House. The painting is at the Getty Museum in Los Angeles, a companion in spirit to his other mythological cabinet works.

Self-portrait_as_the_Allegory_of_Paintin.title: Self-Portrait as the Allegory of Painting

source.canonical_title: File:Self-portrait as the Allegory of Painting (La Pittura) - Artemisia Gentileschi.jpg

Self-portrait_as_the_Allegory_of_Paintin.story: Artemisia leans across the pigment-grinding slab, brush raised, hair loose — her own face fused with Cesare Ripa's personification of Painting, a trick only a woman could pull off since Pittura is grammatically female. She signs the slab itself: A. G. F., 'Artemisia Gentileschi fecit.' Painted in London for Charles I around 1638-39, it was recovered for the Royal Collection at the Restoration in 1660.

Self-portrait_by_Sabine_Lepsius.jpg.title: Self-portrait

source.canonical_title: File:Self-portrait by Sabine Lepsius.jpg
source.credit: Selected work 33 from Self Portrait: Renaissance to Contemporary (Anthony Bond, Joanna Woodall, ISBN 978-1855143579 ).

Self-portrait_by_Sabine_Lepsius.jpg.story: Sabine Lepsius at twenty-one, palette in hand, looking out at us with the particular steady look young painters adopt when they know they're going to be studied. The brushwork on the grey-green smock and pink cuff is loose; the face is tighter, alert. She would go on to run one of Berlin's significant salons with her husband Reinhold and paint around 280 portraits, many of Jewish Berlin sitters in the Wilhelmine and Weimar years. Most of those later works were destroyed or lost in the Second World War, which gives this early self-portrait an afterlife it couldn't have anticipated in 1885.

Self-portrait_in_a_Straw_Hat_by_Elisabet.title: Self Portrait in a Straw Hat

source.canonical_title: File:Self-portrait in a Straw Hat by Elisabeth-Louise Vigée-Lebrun.jpg

title.pt: Autorretrato com chapéu de palha (Vigée Le Brun)
title.th: ภาพเหมือนตนเอง

Self-portrait_in_a_Straw_Hat_by_Elisabet.story: Vigée Le Brun saw Rubens's so-called Chapeau de Paille in Antwerp and couldn't let it go — she wrote about the double light, ordinary daylight plus the glow of the sun, and set out to match it. This is her reply: brushes and palette in hand, straw hat tilted to catch the sun, looking directly at us and refusing to choose between society lady and working professional. The original of 1782 caused a stir at the Salon de la Correspondance; this signed autograph version has hung in London's National Gallery since 1897.

Self-portrait_with_Her_Daughter_by_Elisa.title: Madame Vigée-Lebrun and Her Daughter

source.canonical_title: File:Self-portrait with Her Daughter by Elisabeth-Louise Vigée Le Brun.jpg
source.credit: own work, current photo taken by user Cybershot800i.

Self-portrait_with_Her_Daughter_by_Elisa.story: Painted in 1789 — the year the Bastille fell and Vigée Le Brun fled France with nine-year-old Julie. Mother and daughter in Grecian white, arms looped around each other, cheek to forehead, both smiling openly. That open smile was the scandal: portraiture convention kept mouths firmly shut, and showing teeth was something critics associated with peasants, children, or bad taste. She did it anyway. The painting is now at the Louvre, and reads as both tender domestic portrait and a very public defence of how she wanted to be seen.

SesshuShuutouTou.jpg.title: Winter Landscape
SesshuShuutouTou.jpg.description: Paysage d'automne et d'hiver , par Sesshû, Tôkyô National Museum

source.canonical_title: File:SesshuShuutouTou.jpg

SesshuShuutouTou.jpg.story: Sesshu in hard winter mode. A cliff splits the sky down the middle like a cracked slab, its edge left almost as bare paper; temple roofs huddle below, a lone figure picks along the path, and the near tree claws at the cold with a few black strokes. Everything is drawn with that angular, chopped brushwork he brought back from Ming China and made unmistakably his own. No atmospheric softness, no weather-poem prettiness, just rock and ink and the feeling that the air is very cold. One of the great late scrolls, Tokyo National Museum.

Seven_Sacraments_Rogier.jpg.story: A triptych painted around 1445-1450, probably for Jean Chevrot, bishop of Tournai and close advisor to the Duke of Burgundy. Three panels, one enormous Gothic church, and all seven sacraments happening simultaneously in its nave and aisles: a baptism at one font, a confession in a side chapel, a wedding at the screen, extreme unction in a far corner. In the foreground of the central panel towers a Crucifixion, with the Eucharist being raised at an altar directly behind it so that the Mass and the sacrifice become one image. Colour-coded angels with inscribed scrolls hover over each rite. It now hangs at the Royal Museum of Fine Arts in Antwerp.

Sharaku_(1794)_Ebisu.jpg.title: Ebisu

source.canonical_title: File:Sharaku (1794) Ebisu.jpg
source.credit: Yamaguchi, Keizaburō (1994). Sharaku no Zenbō 写楽の全貌 (in Japanese). Tōkyō Shoseki. ISBN 978-4-487-79075-3 .

Sharaku_(1794)_Ebisu.jpg.story: Sharaku is remembered for his cruelly honest kabuki actor portraits, but this one is different. It shows Ebisu, the chubby god of fishermen and good fortune, grinning as he hugs an enormous red sea bream, with more of the auspicious fish spilling out of a basket at his feet. Paper charms dangle from a cord above his head. It's cheerful, slightly clumsy, and almost nothing like the actor prints. He made it during the same ten-month burst of activity in 1794-95, and then he vanished, and no one has ever quite figured out who he was.

Shaw_John_Byam_Liston_Now_is_Pilgrim_Fai.title: Shaw John Byam Liston Now is Pilgrim Fair Autumn-s Charge
Shaw_John_Byam_Liston_Now_is_Pilgrim_Fai.description: "Now Is the Pilgrim Year Fair Autumn's Charge" // "The title of the work is an enigma. It appears to be a poetic quotation, but is from none of Shaw's preferred writers, including Christina and Dante Gabriel Rossetti, Tennyson, and Shakespeare."

Shipwreck_turner.jpg.title: Shipwreck of the Minotaur

source.canonical_title: File:Shipwreck turner.jpg

Shipwreck_turner.jpg.story: HMS Minotaur, a 74-gun ship of the line, went to pieces on the Haak Sands off the Dutch coast in December 1810 with heavy loss of life. Turner had been sketching a generic shipwreck since 1805; once Minotaur hit the news he slapped her name on the finished canvas and cashed in on the horror. Look at the huge wave rearing into the men in the boat and you can feel him inventing the vocabulary of all his later storm pictures. It's the painting that announces him as the great disaster artist of the Regency.

Shironeko_by_Takahashi_Hiroaki.jpg.title: Shironeko by Takahashi Hiroaki

source.canonical_title: File:Shironeko by Takahashi Hiroaki.jpg

Shironeko_by_Takahashi_Hiroaki.jpg.story: A plump white cat with ginger patches sits on a dark green ground, wearing an improbable red frilled collar studded with white dots. Yellow eyes, pink nose, tail tucked neatly around. Takahashi Shotei designed this for the shin-hanga publisher Watanabe Shozaburo in 1924 — the year after the Kanto earthquake had destroyed every single one of the woodblocks from his first career. He started over in his fifties and turned out prints like this one, flatter and bolder than his prewar work, with the decorative punch of a poster. Deeply popular with Western collectors and still is.

Siernetel_in_bloempot_-_s0185V1962_-_Van.title: Flame Nettle in a Flowerpot

source.canonical_title: File:Siernetel in bloempot - s0185V1962 - Van Gogh Museum.jpg

Siernetel_in_bloempot_-_s0185V1962_-_Van.story: A potted coleus, the kind of thing your grandmother kept on a windowsill — except Van Gogh used it as a colour lab. Rust-orange leaves against blue, with sly red and green flickers down the stem. He painted it in Paris around June or July 1886, weeks after arriving from Antwerp and moving in with his brother Theo. The complementary-colour pairings come straight from Delacroix's theory, which Van Gogh was then studying obsessively. The little canvas, just 42 by 22 cm, hangs at the Van Gogh Museum.

Sinite_Parvulos_-_A._Gentileschi.png.title: Christ Blessing the Children

source.canonical_title: File:Sinite Parvulos - A. Gentileschi.png

Sinite_Parvulos_-_A._Gentileschi.png.story: Christ bends toward a cluster of toddlers while a mother lifts her baby into the composition's light — a gentler register than Artemisia's usual severed heads. The painting was deaccessioned by the Met in 1979 as a Carlo Rosa and vanished; Gianni Papi stumbled on it in the Roman church of Sant'Ambrogio e Carlo al Corso in 2012, and restoration uncovered Artemisia's signature and the date 1626 on the back.

Sir_Anthony_Van_Dyck_-_Charles_I_(1600-4.title: Charles I (1600-49)
Sir_Anthony_Van_Dyck_-_Charles_I_(1600-4.artist: Sir Anthony Van Dyck (1599 - 1641) Details on Google Art Project

source.canonical_title: File:Sir Anthony Van Dyck - Charles I (1600-49) - Google Art Project.jpg
source.credit: BQHR9te2WWtyOA at Google Cultural Institute maximum zoom level

Sir_Anthony_Van_Dyck_-_Charles_I_(1600-4.story: Three Charleses for the price of one — face on, profile, three-quarter view. Van Dyck painted this triple portrait in 1635 to be shipped to Rome, where the sculptor Gianlorenzo Bernini would use it as a reference to carve a marble bust of the English king he'd never meet. The bust was duly made and delivered in 1637, only to be destroyed in the 1698 fire at Whitehall Palace. Van Dyck's canvas, however, survived; it belongs to the Royal Collection and usually hangs at Windsor Castle. Charles himself was beheaded on 30 January 1649, fourteen years after sitting for this.

Sir_David_Wilkie's_residence_in_Kensingt.title: Sir David Wilkie's Residence in Kensington, London
Sir_David_Wilkie's_residence_in_Kensingt.description: Sir David Wilkie's residence in Kensington London, by William Collins 1841 (painted just after Wilkie's death)

Sir_David_Wilkie_(1785-1841)_-_The_Defen.title: The Defence of Saragossa

source.canonical_title: File:Sir David Wilkie (1785-1841) - The Defence of Saragossa - RCIN 405091 - Royal Collection.jpg

Sir_David_Wilkie_(1785-1841)_-_The_Defen.story: Wilkie travelled through Spain in 1827-28 and came back with four pictures of Spanish resistance to Napoleon. This one shows Agustina de Aragón — the Maid of Saragossa — at the battery during the 1808 siege, stepping over her dead lover to touch a match to a cannon while the French closed in. She stands in white at the centre, a civilian woman leading soldiers and a priest in a fight that held the city for months. The canvas is now at Windsor.

Sir_David_Wilkie_(1785-1841)_-_The_Penny.title: The Penny Wedding

source.canonical_title: File:Sir David Wilkie (1785-1841) - The Penny Wedding - RCIN 405536 - Royal Collection.jpg

Sir_David_Wilkie_(1785-1841)_-_The_Penny.story: A 'penny wedding' was an old Scottish custom: guests each chipped in a penny to pay for the festivities, with anything left over going to the bride and groom. Wilkie painted this nostalgic reconstruction, set around 1770, for the Prince Regent (soon George IV) as a companion to his earlier Blind Man's Buff. The fiddler at the left is the real Niel Gow, Scotland's famous eighteenth-century reel player, sharpened from memory and print sources. Dozens of preparatory drawings survive — Wilkie choreographed the dancers like a stage director.

Sir_Henry_Raeburn_-_Colonel_Alastair_Ran.title: Colonel Alastair Ranaldson Macdonell of Glengarry (1771 - 1828)

source.canonical_title: File:Sir Henry Raeburn - Colonel Alastair Ranaldson Macdonell of Glengarry (1771 - 1828) - Google Art Project.jpg
source.credit: GgEDEPJ-LXa7Dg at Google Cultural Institute maximum zoom level

Sir_Henry_Raeburn_-_Colonel_Alastair_Ran.story: Macdonell poses as the last true Highland chief, kilted head to toe, pistol in belt, claymore and targe behind him. Raeburn painted him around 1812, and Walter Scott probably based Fergus MacIvor in 'Waverley' on him. The subtitle should be 'hypocrite,' though. While performing Gaelic authenticity for Edinburgh society, Macdonell was clearing his ancestral tenants off the land to make room for sheep. He died in 1828 after falling from a steamship he'd boarded to protest the new modernity. Macdonell's dates were actually 1773-1828, not 1771. National Galleries of Scotland.

Sir_Peter_Paul_Rubens_(Siegen_1577_-_Ant.title: Winter: The Interior of a Barn

source.canonical_title: File:Sir Peter Paul Rubens (Siegen 1577 - Antwerp 1640) - Winter, The Interior of a Barn - RCIN 401417 - Royal Collection.jpg

Sir_Peter_Paul_Rubens_(Siegen_1577_-_Ant.story: A barn at dusk in deep winter. A woman nurses an infant by the hearth, a crippled beggar has been waved over to the fire, children pile on top of each other, and beyond the open door the snow glows blue. Rubens is painting charity as a domestic scene, not an allegory in a toga. The pendant, a bustling summer market, also survives. Around 1618-19, Royal Collection, RCIN 401417.

Sir_Peter_Paul_Rubens_-_Milkmaids_with_C.title: Milkmaids with Cattle in a Landscape, 'The Farm at Laken'

source.canonical_title: File:Sir Peter Paul Rubens - Milkmaids with Cattle in a Landscape, 'The Farm at Laken' - Google Art Project.jpg

Sir_Peter_Paul_Rubens_-_Milkmaids_with_C.story: Two milkmaids in clean linen caps lug buckets and a basket of cabbages past a fat red cow; beyond them the steeple of Laeken church lifts above the trees. Rubens probably kept this panel for himself (an inventory of his estate lists a 'view of Laken'), and you can feel the affection. It's the Flanders of the Twelve Years' Truce, 1609-21, painted while peace was holding and the country was eating well. Around 1617-18, now in the Royal Collection.

Slave-ship.jpg.title: The Slave Ship
Slave-ship.jpg.description: Slavers throwing overboard the Dead and Dying — Typhoon coming on (" The Slave Ship ")

source.canonical_title: File:Slave-ship.jpg

Slave-ship.jpg.story: Turner hung it at the Royal Academy in 1840, the same season London hosted two big anti-slavery conventions. The full title twists the knife: Slavers Throwing Overboard the Dead and Dying - Typhoon Coming On. Behind it is the Zong, 1781, when the crew hurled more than 130 enslaved Africans into the Atlantic to claim insurance. Turner had read Clarkson's History and Abolition of the Slave Trade. John Ruskin's father gave him the painting in 1844 and Ruskin called it the noblest sea Turner ever painted.

Slovane_v_pravlasti_81x61m.jpg.story: This is canvas number one of Mucha's Slav Epic, finished in 1912 after he turned his back on Paris poster work to paint a twenty-panel history of the Slavic peoples. A terrified man and woman crouch in a field at night, the wreckage of a raid behind them; above, a pagan priest floats with two allegorical companions — a warrior for 'just war', a girl in white for peace. The canvas is enormous, 610 by 810 cm, and painted in egg tempera on linen. Mucha called this couple the Adam and Eve of the Slavs.

SmallLakewithBoatMunch.jpg.story: Munch was sixteen when he painted this, oil on cardboard, barely larger than a postcard at 12 by 18 centimeters. A small rowboat sits on a dark pond, trees leaning in. None of the screaming yet, none of the vampires, just a teenager figuring out what paint can do at dusk. Before art school, before Paris, before the breakdowns. It's kept at the Munch Museum in Oslo.

source.canonical_title: File:Sokokura by Hiroshige1.jpg

Sokokura_by_Hiroshige1.jpg.story: Sokokura was one of the Seven Hot Springs of Hakone — a wooden inn wedged into the gorge where the Haya River roars past. Hiroshige frames it tight: bathers behind sliding screens, a porter on the bridge, steam rising off the pools. The mountain walls press in close. Published in 1852 as part of his Hakone shichiyu zue, the series sold to travelers and armchair travelers alike. Sokokura's spring was said to be good for cuts and bruises — useful, after the climb to get there.

Song_of_the_Lark_Winslow_Homer_1876.jpeg.title: Song of the Lark (also known as „In the Field“)
Song_of_the_Lark_Winslow_Homer_1876.jpeg.description: A young farmer, holding a scythe, leaves his fields at sunset and is transfixed momentarily by the call of an unseen bird.

source.canonical_title: File:Song of the Lark Winslow Homer 1876.jpeg
source.credit: 1. The Athenaeum: Home - info - pic 2. Chrysler Museum of Art, search: 83.590 3. Google Art Project works from the Chrysler Museum of Art

Song_of_the_Lark_Winslow_Homer_1876.jpeg.story: A young farmer pauses at the edge of his field, scythe in hand, chin tilted to catch the call of a bird he cannot see. By 1876 most American farms had already traded the scythe for Cyrus McCormick's mechanical reaper, so Homer's choice was deliberate nostalgia, a hymn to the solitary hand-laborer. Sometimes called 'In the Field,' the painting is a small, stubborn monument to a vanishing way of work. It lives today at the Chrysler Museum of Art in Norfolk, Virginia.

title.es: La gran duquesa Sofía en el convento de Novodévichi

Sophia_Alekseyevna,_by_Ilya_Repin.jpg.story: Sofia Alekseyevna ruled Russia as regent for seven years, then her half-brother Peter the Great locked her in the Novodevichy Convent. Repin shows her a year later, in 1698, after her supporters' failed rebellion: fists clenched, jaw set, glaring out of a cell whose barred window frames the hanged body of a strelets swaying in the yard behind her. A nun cowers in the corner. Repin made his wife Vera sit for the pose and studied convent architecture on-site. The painting caused a sensation at the 1879 Peredvizhniki exhibition and hangs in the Tretyakov.

Spring_Flowers,_by_Claude_Monet,_Clevela.title: Spring Flowers
Spring_Flowers,_by_Claude_Monet,_Clevela.description: This early work reveals Monet's fascination with capturing the transitory effects that became the primary focus of his later innovations. Painted with almost scientific accuracy, this still life has a freshness and immediacy derived partly from its composition. Isolated against a dark background, the fully mature peonies, potted hydrangeas, and basketed lilacs spill downward and outward from the geraniums at the rear. At the same time, Monet's energetic brushwork conveys the sparkling play of light on leaves and petals.

source.canonical_title: File:Spring Flowers, by Claude Monet, Cleveland Museum of Art, 1953.155.jpg

Spring_Flowers,_by_Claude_Monet,_Clevela.story: Painted in 1864 in his first productive year, this is Monet before Impressionism - carefully set-up peonies, potted hydrangeas, basketed lilacs, all spilling forward from a pot of geraniums against a deliberately dark ground. The flowers are almost botanically exact, but the brushwork already has that quick flicker of light on leaf that would become his whole career. It hangs at the Cleveland Museum of Art.

Starry_Night_Over_the_Rhone.jpg.title: Starry Night Over the Rhône
Starry_Night_Over_the_Rhone.jpg.description: depicts the Rhône River at night

source.canonical_title: File:Starry Night Over the Rhone.jpg

Starry_Night_Over_the_Rhone.jpg.story: Painted in September 1888 from the east bank of the Rhone at Arles, about a ten-minute walk from the Yellow House. Van Gogh set up his easel with a crown of candles attached to his hat so he could see the canvas, a trick he described in letters to Theo. The gaslights along the quay leave long yellow reflections down the black water, the Great Bear glitters above, and a couple strolls arm in arm at the foreground edge. It hangs in the Musee d'Orsay, Paris.

Stieler-Jane_Digby.jpg.title: Lady Jane Elizabeth Digby
Stieler-Jane_Digby.jpg.description: daughter of Admiral Henry Digby of Trafalgar, leading beauty of her time, scandaliser, courtier to royalty across Europe, married 6 times, contributor to the Kama Sutra , originator of the word "cad". Finally found true happiness with a bedouin Arab Sheikh, buried in Damaskus . Painted in 1831 as Lady Jane Ellenborough by Joseph Karl Stieler for the Schönheitengalerie of King Ludwig I of Bavaria

source.canonical_title: File:Stieler-Jane Digby.jpg

Stieler-Jane_Digby.jpg.story: In 1831 she was Lady Ellenborough, wife of a future Viceroy of India, visiting Munich, already famously scandalous. Stieler painted her for Ludwig I's Gallery of Beauties with pale shoulders and a half-smile that suggests she knows exactly what she is doing. The life outran the portrait: six marriages, affairs across half the thrones of Europe, children by kings and counts, and finally a bedouin sheikh twenty years her junior in Syria. She is buried in Damascus. The picture caught her mid-flight.

Stieler_-_Alexandra,_Prinzessin_von_Baye.title: Portrait of Alexandra Amalie von Bayern (1826-1875)
Stieler_-_Alexandra,_Prinzessin_von_Baye.date_created: 1845, replica of a portrait painted in 1838

source.canonical_title: File:Stieler - Alexandra, Prinzessin von Bayern (Schönheitengalerie).jpg
source.credit: originally uploaded to de.wikipedia by Thyra ( talk · contribs ) on 20 December 2007, 19:16 under the file name Stieler - Alexandra, Prinzessin von Bayern (Schönheitengalerie).jpg . ( +/− )

Stieler_-_Alexandra,_Prinzessin_von_Baye.story: Alexandra was Ludwig I's favourite daughter, and it shows. Stieler's 1845 canvas is a replica of a portrait he had painted of her in 1838; the king wanted her in the Gallery of Beauties, and he got what he wanted. She is nineteen here, off the shoulder, coolly composed. The real Alexandra was stranger than the picture: a Bavarian princess who became an abbess, wrote novels and translations, and was convinced for years that she had swallowed a glass piano and must walk sideways through doors.

Stieler_-_Auguste_Strobl_(Schönheitengal.title: Portrait of Auguste Strobl (Gallery of Beauties)
Stieler_-_Auguste_Strobl_(Schönheitengal.description: Auguste Strobl (später verheiratete Auguste Hilber) aus der Schönheitengalerie ; Öl auf Leinwand in den Maßen 72,5 x 59,2 cm

source.canonical_title: File:Stieler - Auguste Strobl (Schönheitengalerie).jpg

Stieler_-_Auguste_Strobl_(Schönheitengal.story: One of the thirty-six panels Joseph Karl Stieler painted for Ludwig I's Schönheitengalerie at Nymphenburg, this 1827 portrait sets Auguste Strobl against a gusty blue-grey sky. The red-and-gold ribbon tied into fat bows above each ear is the same watered silk that cinches her waist — a detail of Munich dress-up 1820s style. Stieler keeps the face cool and pink-cheeked, the pearls understated, the gauze sleeves almost transparent. A bourgeois sitter held to the same specification as duchesses and dancers in the king's roster of favourite faces.

Stieler_-_Lola_Montez_(Schönheitengaleri.title: Lola Montez

source.canonical_title: File:Stieler - Lola Montez (Schönheitengalerie).jpg

title.ja: ローラ・モンテス、ヨーゼフ・スティーラー画.

Stieler_-_Lola_Montez_(Schönheitengaleri.story: Stieler did not want to paint her. Ludwig I had to ask repeatedly through 1846. When he finally sat her down in 1847, he put her in Spanish dancer's costume with a mask in her hand, shoulders bare, and the king took one look and demanded it be redone in black velvet. By then Lola was already upending Bavaria. Her naturalisation that year toppled the cabinet and brought rioters onto Munich's streets; the 1848 revolution cost Ludwig his throne. She outlasted the reign; the portrait outlasted her.

Stieler_-_Marianna_Marchesa_Florenzi,_18.title: Stieler - Marianna Marchesa Florenzi, 1831
Stieler_-_Marianna_Marchesa_Florenzi,_18.description: Marianna (1802-1870) was an Italian noble woman, translator, and lifetime friend of Ludwig I. von Bayern An Mariannina Siehe, Geliebte, das Meer, endlos da liegt´s vor den Blicken, endlos, wie solches, so ist unsere Anhänglichkeit auch.

source.canonical_title: File:Stieler - Marianna Marchesa Florenzi, 1831.JPG

Stieler_-_Marianna_Marchesa_Florenzi,_18.story: The Marchesa Florenzi was not in Munich to be pretty. She translated Leibniz's Monadology into Italian, pushed Kant and Schelling toward Italian readers, and studied natural sciences at Perugia when women simply did not. Ludwig I wrote her letters for forty years and asked her advice on matters of state. Stieler painted her in 1831 for the Gallery of Beauties with the dark-eyed calm of someone used to being listened to. The portrait hangs beside debutantes; Marianna had a mind the king kept consulting.

Stieler_-_Portrait_of_Caroline_Grafin_vo.title: Caroline von Holnstein from Fronberg

source.canonical_title: File:Stieler - Portrait of Caroline Grafin von Holnstein.jpg

Stieler_-_Portrait_of_Caroline_Grafin_vo.story: Ludwig I first noticed her at a court academy on 8 December 1833, and within months Stieler had her on canvas. Caroline, born 1815 at Fronberg Castle in the Upper Palatinate, was nineteen when she joined the Gallery of Beauties, and the result became one of the best-known pictures in the series. Soft shoulders, a gauzy white dress, a glance turned just past the viewer. She died at Fronberg in 1859, back where she had started, but the Munich portrait kept circulating on prints and miniatures long after.

Stieler_-_Portrait_of_Friederike_Freiin_.title: Portrait of Friederike Freiin von Gumppenberg

source.canonical_title: File:Stieler - Portrait of Friederike Freiin Von Gumppenberg.jpg
source.permission: PD

title.de: Bildnis der Friederike Freiin von Gumppenberg

Stieler_-_Portrait_of_Friederike_Freiin_.story: Stieler painted Friederike in 1845 in a red dress slipping off one shoulder, dark curls parted simply, a landscape opening behind her. She was twenty-two, born in Munich, and would soon marry her cousin Baron Ludwig von Gumppenberg, one of the king's ordnance officers. Of all the women in the Gallery of Beauties she had perhaps the longest run with the picture: Friederike lived to ninety-three, dying in 1916, long enough to see the Wittelsbachs lose Bavaria and the portrait outlive the kingdom that hung it.

Straße_mit_Kirche_in_Kandern.jpg.title: Street with church in Kandern

source.canonical_title: File:Straße mit Kirche in Kandern.jpg
source.permission: Author died in 1914, so the image is in the public domain.

title.ru: Улица в Кандерне во время дождя

Straße_mit_Kirche_in_Kandern.jpg.story: A Black Forest lane turned into a Fauvist crush of planes. The road curves uphill between whitewashed houses that Macke has repainted in lilac, cobalt and pumpkin, with black-bruised purple shadows stacking under every eave. A church tower caps the view in deep indigo. You can still read it as Kandern, but the rooftops have gone violet and the hillside yellow-green. Painted in 1911, the year Macke joined Kandinsky and Marc in founding Der Blaue Reiter.

Stuck,_Franz_von_-_Salome_-_Google_Art_P.title: Salome

source.canonical_title: File:Stuck, Franz von - Salome - Google Art Project.jpg
source.credit: zAFMUUYyQJazIg at Google Cultural Institute , zoom level maximum

Stuck,_Franz_von_-_Salome_-_Google_Art_P.story: Stuck's Salome doesn't dance for the king so much as strut for the viewer, arms lifted, belly bare, a cold grin catching the torchlight. In the lower corner a grinning servant hoists John the Baptist's severed head on a platter, almost as an afterthought. The night sky behind her is flat black, starless. Stuck, a Munich Secession founder, loved this cocktail of sex and menace, and the painting became something of a calling card. It hangs today in the Lenbachhaus in Munich, finished in 1906.

source.canonical_title: File:Stückelberg Sappho 1897.jpg
source.credit: "Von Anker bis Zünd, Die Kunst im jungen Bundesstaat 1848 – 1900", Kunsthaus Zürich, 1998, upload by Adrian Michael

Stückelberg_Sappho_1897.jpg.story: A late, private picture by the Basel painter better known for his Tellskapelle frescoes. Sappho stands barefoot on a ledge above a pale Mediterranean, lyre in one hand, dropping a rose into the water while another already drifts below her. The boat slipping across the bay and the distant fortress keep the suicide legend decorously offstage; Stückelberg is after the moment before, the stillness and the small red flower falling. Painted in 1897, six years before his death, it reads as a quiet farewell to the grand narrative style he had spent his career perfecting.

Sumida_River,_the_Wood_of_the_Water_God,.title: Sumida River, the Wood of the Water God, at Masaki
Sumida_River,_the_Wood_of_the_Water_God,.description: Japan, circa 1856-1858 Series: One Hundred Famous Views of Edo Prints; woodcuts Color woodblock print Gift of Dr. Harvey Eagleson (M.66.35.5) Japanese Art

source.canonical_title: File:Sumida River, the Wood of the Water God, at Masaki LACMA M.66.35.5.jpg
source.credit: Image: http://collections.lacma.org/sites/default/files/remote_images/piction/ma-18199982-O3.jpg Gallery: http://collections.lacma.org/node/190172 archive copy at the Wayback Machine

Sumida_River,_the_Wood_of_the_Water_God,.story: A branch of flowering cherry cuts the top of the frame; beneath it the Sumida River bends past Masaki, boats drifting, the Suijin shrine grove a dark hump on the far bank. Hiroshige loved this compositional trick — a close-up fragment pressed against a distant view — and uses it throughout his One Hundred Famous Views of Edo. This sheet came out around 1856, two years before his death. The Suijin shrine honored the water deity who kept the river from swallowing the neighborhood.

Sumō-wrestling_toads_by_Hōson.jpg.title: Sumō-wrestling toads by Hōson

source.canonical_title: File:Sumō-wrestling toads by Hōson.jpg

Sumō-wrestling_toads_by_Hōson.jpg.story: Four toads in a meadow, staged as a sumō bout. One raises an arm in triumph, two square off centre, a referee on the right holds up a maple leaf for a gunbai fan. A fourth hunches in the corner waiting his turn. The gag comes from an Edo tradition of anthropomorphic animal scrolls, but Koson, signing here as Hōson late in his career, plays it absolutely straight. The toads are drawn from observation, warty and correctly proportioned; only their postures give them away.

Sunset_across_the_Ryogoku_bridge_from_th.story: Dusk on the Sumida. A ferry poles its way across the river carrying merchants, a monk, a birdcatcher with his long rod. The passengers are sharply drawn; everything behind them — Ryogoku Bridge, the far shore, a squat Fuji on the horizon — dissolves into flat silhouettes of grey and mute green. Night is coming on. The trick here is the aizuri blue outline in the foreground giving way to lineless color beyond.

Sunset_at_Montmajour_1888_Van_Gogh.jpg.title: Sunset at Montmajour

source.canonical_title: File:Sunset at Montmajour 1888 Van Gogh.jpg

Sunset_at_Montmajour_1888_Van_Gogh.jpg.story: For a hundred years this picture sat in a Norwegian attic, dismissed as a fake. Van Gogh painted it on 4 July 1888, hiking out to the ruined abbey hill of Montmajour above Arles, and wrote to Theo the next day describing the oaks and the dying light. In 2013 the Van Gogh Museum reauthenticated it using that letter plus new x-rays: a major rediscovery, the first full-size painting added to his catalogue since 1928.

Surprised-Rousseau.jpg.title: Tiger in a Tropical Storm (Surprised!)

source.canonical_title: File:Surprised-Rousseau.jpg

Surprised-Rousseau.jpg.story: This was the first jungle. Rousseau had never left France, but in 1891 he hung a tiger among feathery reeds at the unjuried Salon des Indépendants and called it 'Surprised!' — though whether the tiger or the prey is the startled one, he never said. Lightning flashes; the grasses bend hard; the rain is a mesh of silver-grey diagonals Rousseau brushed across the finished surface. Most critics sniggered. The young Félix Vallotton wrote that the tiger was 'the alpha and omega of painting.' It hangs now in London's National Gallery.

Susanna_and_the_Elders.jpg.title: Susanna and the Elders

source.canonical_title: File:Susanna and the Elders.jpg
source.credit: 1. Moravian Gallery in Brno 2./3. Google Arts & Culture — rQH0ja0DwrR2tQ

title.avk: Susanna is toloye guazikye (3) (trutca ke Gentileschi)

Susanna_and_the_Elders.jpg.story: Susanna twists away from the leering elders, her shoulder catching a hard white gleam against the garden's olive shadow. The picture sat in the Azzolini collection as an Elisabetta Sirani until restoration unmasked Artemisia's hand and the collaborative touch of her pupil Onofrio Palumbo. Signed and dated 1652, it is her last known work, painted as she neared sixty at the Pinacoteca Nazionale in Bologna.

Susanna_and_the_Elders_(1610),_Artemisia.title: Susanna and the Elders

source.canonical_title: File:Susanna and the Elders (1610), Artemisia Gentileschi.jpg
source.credit: Web Gallery of Art : Image Info about artwork wga QS:P11807,"g/gentiles/artemisi/susanna"

Susanna_and_the_Elders_(1610),_Artemisia.story: Artemisia's first signed and dated painting, made at seventeen and now at Schloss Weissenstein in Pommersfelden, Germany. Susanna twists naked on the edge of a stone bath, arms crossed in a real flinch, while two elders lean over a low balustrade and whisper. Unlike most male versions of the subject, there is no flirtation in her body; her shoulders hunch up toward her ears. The '1610' date was long disputed until a 1970 x-ray confirmed it, settling the picture as the work of a teenager trained in her father Orazio's Roman studio.

Susanna_i_badet,_1879,_115_x_89,5_cm,_pr.story: Tuxen was twenty-six and fresh out of Paris training when he tackled this biblical set-piece — Susanna surprised at her bath by two elders — and it became his breakthrough. Critics singled out the modelling of the nude: firm academic draftsmanship, skin turned slightly toward the viewer, voyeurs shoved into the shadows. The Apocryphal story is a nasty one (blackmail, false accusation, last-minute rescue by the young Daniel), but Tuxen keeps it poised rather than lurid. He would return to the subject again and again across his career, never quite letting it go.

Suzanna,_Rembrandt_van_Rijn,_1636,_Mauri.title: Susanna

source.canonical_title: File:Suzanna, Rembrandt van Rijn, 1636, Mauritshuis, The Hague.jpg

title.ja: スザンナ (レンブラント)

Suzanna,_Rembrandt_van_Rijn,_1636,_Mauri.story: From the apocryphal Book of Daniel: two elders spy on Susanna bathing and threaten to accuse her of adultery unless she sleeps with them. Rembrandt shows the split second she realises she's been seen, one hand clutching a red robe, one foot still in the water, her face flushed with the understanding that she is trapped. The leering men are hidden in the dark trees behind her, almost invisible, which somehow makes it worse. The small panel, signed 1636, is in the Mauritshuis in The Hague.
