Suzanna_en_de_ouderlingen_Rijksmuseum_SK.story: The old Book of Daniel story, done in 1820 by a Ghent painter who'd studied in David's Paris studio: Susanna is bathing in her garden when two elders who've been spying through the shrubs step out to blackmail her. Sleep with us or we'll testify you met a lover here. Hanselaere gives her the classical contrapposto and cool skin David's pupils all learned to paint, and tucks the lechers into a properly shadowed thicket. She refuses, of course, and the prophet Daniel exposes them. The Rijksmuseum in Amsterdam keeps it under inventory number SK-A-1042.

Suzuki_Harunobu_(c._1760)_Ōmi_Hakkei_no.title: Suzuki Harunobu (c. 1760) Ōmi Hakkei no Uchi - Yabase Kihan
Suzuki_Harunobu_(c._1760)_Ōmi_Hakkei_no.description: print from the series Ōmi Hakkei no Uchi

source.canonical_title: File:Suzuki Harunobu (c. 1760) Ōmi Hakkei no Uchi - Yabase Kihan.jpg
source.credit: Museum of Fine Arts, Boston, via [ukiyo-e.org ukiyo-e.org] ( Search archive )

Suzuki_Harunobu_(c._1760)_Ōmi_Hakkei_no.story: From Harunobu's parody of the classical Eight Views of Omi, a landscape theme borrowed from Chinese painting and transplanted to the shores of Lake Biwa. 'Yabase Kihan' is the returning sails at Yabase — traditionally depicted as distant boats at dusk. Harunobu, typically, swaps sages and monks for young women and domestic interiors, turning a revered poetic subject into something intimate and slightly mischievous. The print predates his full-colour breakthrough, so the palette is restrained, but the wit is already fully his.

Suzuki_Harunobu_-_Woman_Admiring_Plum_Bl.title: Suzuki Harunobu - Woman Admiring Plum Blossoms at Night
Suzuki_Harunobu_-_Woman_Admiring_Plum_Bl.description: Ukiyo-e print by Japanese artist Suzuki Harunobu.

source.canonical_title: File:Suzuki Harunobu - Woman Admiring Plum Blossoms at Night.jpg

Suzuki_Harunobu_-_Woman_Admiring_Plum_Bl.story: Night in an Edo garden, rendered with almost no night. Harunobu lets a lantern's glow define the darkness, and a young woman leans toward branches of plum, the blossoms caught between silver and pink. It's a seasonal cliche he makes fresh — the faint chill, the reach of a sleeve, the deliberate hush. Like much of his work, it trades shock for attentiveness. This is the kind of print that made his brocade style a template for Kiyonaga and Utamaro: mood over incident, a single figure holding a whole evening.

Tab_V,_fetus_with_umbilical_cord_and_pla.title: Tab V, fetus with umbilical cord and placenta
Tab_V,_fetus_with_umbilical_cord_and_pla.description: Tab. V, fetus attached to umbilical cord and placenta. Wellcome Images Keywords: Bernhard Siegfried Albinus

source.canonical_title: File:Tab V, fetus with umbilical cord and placenta Wellcome L0034071.jpg

Tabi_miyage_dai_isshū,_Aki_no_Koshiji_b.title: Tabi miyage dai isshū, Aki no Koshiji by Kawase Hasui
Tabi_miyage_dai_isshū,_Aki_no_Koshiji_b.description: Autumn in the Koshiji Region (Aki no Koshiji), from the series Souvenirs of Travel I (Tabi miyage dai isshū). Note: "Koshiji" in the title of this picture is not about Koshiji-machi .

source.canonical_title: File:Tabi miyage dai isshū, Aki no Koshiji by Kawase Hasui.jpg

Tabi_miyage_dai_isshū,_Aki_no_Koshiji_b.story: Koshiji is the old poetic name for the Hokuriku coast along the Sea of Japan — not the modern town in Niigata, as the catalogue note flags. Hasui's scene is the autumn harvest: rice stalks hung on tall drying racks that stand like walls against the blue sea, an old woman crouched over a straw mat of red beans. The contrast he was after — blue water, yellow rice, the small red of the beans — is the whole reason for the print. From Souvenirs of Travel I, Watanabe, 1920.

Tabi_miyage_dai_isshū,_Bōshū_Iwai_no_.title: Tabi miyage dai isshū, Bōshū Iwai no hama by Kawase Hasui
Tabi_miyage_dai_isshū,_Bōshū_Iwai_no_.description: Iwai Beach in Awa Province (Bōshū Iwai no hama), from the series Souvenirs of Travel I (Tabi miyage dai isshū)

source.canonical_title: File:Tabi miyage dai isshū, Bōshū Iwai no hama by Kawase Hasui.jpg

Tabi_miyage_dai_isshū,_Bōshū_Iwai_no_.story: Iwai Beach sits on the Tokyo Bay side of the Bōsō peninsula in Chiba, in what is now Minamibōsō city — a summer escape within easy reach of the capital. Hasui spent part of the summer of 1920 there and came back with two designs for Souvenirs of Travel; this is the calmer of the pair. A horse stands on wet sand, a green cliff rises to the left, the water flat and cool under a soft sky. Signed and dated Taishō 9, summer, with the pre-earthquake Watanabe seal.

Tabi_miyage_dai_isshū,_Ishi_tsumu_fune_.title: Tabi miyage dai isshū, Ishi tsumu fune (Bōshū) by Kawase Hasui
Tabi_miyage_dai_isshū,_Ishi_tsumu_fune_.description: Loading Stone on a Boat, Awa Province (Bōshū), from the series Souvenirs of Travel I (Tabi miyage dai isshū)

source.canonical_title: File:Tabi miyage dai isshū, Ishi tsumu fune (Bōshū) by Kawase Hasui.jpg

Tabi_miyage_dai_isshū,_Ishi_tsumu_fune_.story: The second Bōsō print from Hasui's summer 1920 stay on the Chiba coast: a flat-bottomed boat being loaded with stone at the water's edge, bare-backed workers, the peninsula's low cliffs behind them. Not a famous place, not a set-piece view — just a small working scene he caught and decided was worth a sheet. Part of why Souvenirs of Travel reads so differently from Meiji-era landscape prints: Hasui picks the unmonumental corner and holds it. Watanabe, 1920, pre-earthquake blocks.

Tabi_miyage_dai_isshū,_Kanazawa_Asanoga.title: Tabi miyage dai isshū, Kanazawa Asanogawa by Kawase Hasui
Tabi_miyage_dai_isshū,_Kanazawa_Asanoga.description: The Asano River in Kanazawa (Kanazawa Asanogawa), from the series Souvenirs of Travel I (Tabi miyage dai isshū)

source.canonical_title: File:Tabi miyage dai isshū, Kanazawa Asanogawa by Kawase Hasui.jpg

Tabi_miyage_dai_isshū,_Kanazawa_Asanoga.story: The Asano is the quieter of Kanazawa's two rivers, winding past old teahouse districts on the north side of the city. Hasui worked it up from his 1920 trip to the Hokuriku coast. The original Watanabe blocks were among the many destroyed when the Great Kantō earthquake burned out the publisher's workshop in 1923, and were never recut — so first-state impressions like this one, bearing the pre-quake seals, are what survive. Part of the Souvenirs of Travel series.

Tabi_miyage_dai_isshū,_Kanazawa_nagare_.title: Tabi miyage dai isshū, Kanazawa nagare no kuruwa by Kawase Hasui
Tabi_miyage_dai_isshū,_Kanazawa_nagare_.description: Nagare Pleasure Quarter, Kanazawa (Kanazawa Nagare no kuruwa), from the series Souvenirs of Travel I (Tabi miyage dai isshū)

source.canonical_title: File:Tabi miyage dai isshū, Kanazawa nagare no kuruwa by Kawase Hasui.jpg

Tabi_miyage_dai_isshū,_Kanazawa_nagare_.story: Locals called the Kasube pleasure quarter of Kanazawa simply Nagare — the flow — because it backed onto the Asano River. Hasui wrote that at night the sound of the water and the shamisen inside the houses seemed to carry the same sadness. The print keeps the mood close: dark wooden façades, a wet street, the river suggested beyond. From Souvenirs of Travel I, Watanabe, 1920. Blocks lost in the 1923 earthquake; the pre-quake impressions in Chicago, MFA Boston, LACMA and the Freer are what remain.

Tabi_miyage_dai_isshū,_Mutsu_Mishimagaw.title: Tabi miyage dai isshū, Mutsu Mishimagawa by Kawase Hasui
Tabi_miyage_dai_isshū,_Mutsu_Mishimagaw.description: The Mishima River in Mutsu Province (Mutsu Mishimagawa), from the series Souvenirs of Travel I (Tabi miyage dai isshū)

source.canonical_title: File:Tabi miyage dai isshū, Mutsu Mishimagawa by Kawase Hasui.jpg

Tabi_miyage_dai_isshū,_Mutsu_Mishimagaw.story: Mishima isn't really a river. It's a short stretch of spring water running down to the sea between Hachinohe and Same, in what is now Aomori — close enough to the coast that the moon sits on both at once. By day, women come here to draw water and do the wash; Hasui holds his breath for a later hour, when moonlight turns the water silver and the dark village shoulders close around it. First sheet of the Souvenirs of Travel series, pulled from his 1919 northern sketching tour. Watanabe published it, and the MFA, LACMA and the Art Institute of Chicago all keep impressions.

Tabi_miyage_dai_isshū,_Mutsu_Tsutanuma_.title: Tabi miyage dai isshū, Mutsu Tsutanuma by Kawase Hasui
Tabi_miyage_dai_isshū,_Mutsu_Tsutanuma_.description: Tsuta Marsh in Mutsu Province (Mutsu Tsutanuma), from the series Souvenirs of Travel I (Tabi miyage dai isshū)

source.canonical_title: File:Tabi miyage dai isshū, Mutsu Tsutanuma by Kawase Hasui.jpg

Tabi_miyage_dai_isshū,_Mutsu_Tsutanuma_.story: Tsutanuma is a small, dense-banked marsh in the mountains of old Mutsu Province, the kind of place that swallows sound. Hasui sets it at early morning: two men in a narrow boat hauling in a net, reflections barely troubled, reeds crowding right to the water. He liked the marsh for its intimacy — a whole world you could almost reach across. It comes out of his 1919 trek through Sendai, Hachinohe, Towada and Aomori, the journey that seeded the first Souvenirs of Travel. Watanabe published it the same year.

Tabi_miyage_dai_isshū,_Sendai_yama_no_t.title: Tabi miyage dai isshū, Sendai yama no tera by Kawase Hasui
Tabi_miyage_dai_isshū,_Sendai_yama_no_t.description: Mountain Temple at Sendai (Sendai yama no tera), from the series Souvenirs of Travel I (Tabi miyage dai isshū)

source.canonical_title: File:Tabi miyage dai isshū, Sendai yama no tera by Kawase Hasui.jpg

Tabi_miyage_dai_isshū,_Sendai_yama_no_t.story: A hillside temple outside Sendai, moonlit, the buildings tucked into dark pines. Hasui came through here on his 1919 northern tour — the same trip that fed the first half of Souvenirs of Travel — and was drawn to the kind of site that only gives itself up after sundown. The design trades detail for stillness: a few roof lines, a suggestion of stone steps, and above it all that cool shin-hanga sky Watanabe's carvers and printers could render better than anyone. A print often reissued later, but the 1919 pull is the one collectors chase.

Tabi_miyage_dai_isshū,_Shiobara_Arayu_n.title: Tabi miyage dai isshū, Shiobara Arayu no aki by Kawase Hasui
Tabi_miyage_dai_isshū,_Shiobara_Arayu_n.description: Autumn at the Arayu Spa, Shiobara (Shiobara Arayu no aki), from the series Souvenirs of Travel I (Tabi miyage dai isshū)

source.canonical_title: File:Tabi miyage dai isshū, Shiobara Arayu no aki by Kawase Hasui.jpg

Tabi_miyage_dai_isshū,_Shiobara_Arayu_n.story: Shiobara is a string of hot-spring inns in the Tochigi mountains. In summer the Arayu spa at its heart is busy; by autumn, Hasui noted, it empties out and turns melancholy, and that emptiness was what he wanted. The print sets dark inn façades on either side of a narrow street, red and orange foliage burning overhead, indigo ridges in the distance. From Souvenirs of Travel I, Watanabe, 1920 — another of the pre-earthquake designs whose blocks were lost in 1923 and never recut.

Tabi_miyage_dai_isshū,_Shiobara_Yūhi_n.title: Tabi miyage dai isshū, Shiobara Yūhi no taki by Kawase Hasui
Tabi_miyage_dai_isshū,_Shiobara_Yūhi_n.description: Yūhi Falls at Shiobara (Shiobara Yūhi no taki), from the series Souvenirs of Travel I (Tabi miyage dai isshū)

source.canonical_title: File:Tabi miyage dai isshū, Shiobara Yūhi no taki by Kawase Hasui.jpg

Tabi_miyage_dai_isshū,_Shiobara_Yūhi_n.story: A waterfall in the Shiobara gorge, same 1920 trip to the Tochigi hot springs that gave him the Arayu print. Yūhi — evening sun — names the fall, and Hasui takes the name at its word: the water comes down in a narrow ribbon, the rock face catches a last warm light, everything around it already cooling into shadow. Small-format woodcut, part of Souvenirs of Travel I, Watanabe, 1920; a good impression lives in the Tokyo National Museum of Modern Art.

Tabi_miyage_dai_isshū,_Towada-ko_Senjō.title: Tabi miyage dai isshū, Towada-ko Senjōmaku by Kawase Hasui
Tabi_miyage_dai_isshū,_Towada-ko_Senjō.description: Towada-ko and Senjōmaku, from the series Souvenirs of Travel I (Tabi miyage dai isshū), woodblock print

source.canonical_title: File:Tabi miyage dai isshū, Towada-ko Senjōmaku by Kawase Hasui.jpg

Tabi_miyage_dai_isshū,_Towada-ko_Senjō.story: Senjōmaku — the Thousand-Fathom Cliff — is a sheer rock face plunging straight into Lake Towada, up in the volcanic highlands of old Mutsu. Hasui sketched it during his 1919 northern tour and thought enough of the composition to also work it up as a two-panel screen (now in the Weber collection in New York). The print pares the view down to the essentials: still water, the cliff's dark bulk, a cool sheet of sky. One of the opening sheets of Souvenirs of Travel, Watanabe, 1919.

Tabi_miyage_dai_isshū,_Wakasa_Kude_no_h.title: Tabi miyage dai isshū, Wakasa Kude no hama by Kawase Hasui
Tabi_miyage_dai_isshū,_Wakasa_Kude_no_h.description: Kude Beach in Wakasa Province (Wakasa Kude no hama), from the series Souvenirs of Travel I (Tabi miyage dai isshū)

source.canonical_title: File:Tabi miyage dai isshū, Wakasa Kude no hama by Kawase Hasui.jpg

Tabi_miyage_dai_isshū,_Wakasa_Kude_no_h.story: Hasui made his name by going places, sketching hard, and handing the results to the Watanabe workshop to translate into prints. Kude Beach sits on the Wakasa coast in Fukui, a few kilometres from Obama, and in 1920 it was exactly the kind of quiet rural inlet the shin-hanga market loved — fishermen's huts, thatch, gentle surf. This sheet opens his first Souvenirs of Travel series. The palette stays pale: wet sand, wash of sky, a low horizon doing most of the emotional work. A plain place, printed with unhurried attention.

Tabi_miyage_dai_isshū,_Wakasa_Kugushi-k.title: Tabi miyage dai isshū, Wakasa Kugushi-ko by Kawase Hasui
Tabi_miyage_dai_isshū,_Wakasa_Kugushi-k.description: Lake Kugushi in Wakasa Province (Wakasa Kugushi-ko), from the series Souvenirs of Travel I (Tabi miyage dai isshū)

source.canonical_title: File:Tabi miyage dai isshū, Wakasa Kugushi-ko by Kawase Hasui.jpg

Tabi_miyage_dai_isshū,_Wakasa_Kugushi-k.story: Lake Kugushi is a brackish lagoon in Wakasa, hooked behind a spit of sand on the Sea of Japan. Hasui visited in the summer of 1920 and brought back this horizontal oban, published by Watanabe that autumn. The composition is almost empty — flat water, a far shoreline, a boat or two. That restraint is the point. Early Souvenirs of Travel sheets like this one established the template Hasui would work for decades: a specific, under-famous place, observed at a quiet hour, cut and printed so the silence survives the translation.

Tabi_miyage_dai_nishū,_Ame_no_Kiyomizu-.title: Tabi miyage dai nishū, Ame no Kiyomizu-dera by Kawase Hasui
Tabi_miyage_dai_nishū,_Ame_no_Kiyomizu-.description: Kiyomizu-dera in rain (Ame no Kiyomizu-dera), from the series Souvenirs of Travel II (Tabi miyage dai nishū), woodblock print

source.canonical_title: File:Tabi miyage dai nishū, Ame no Kiyomizu-dera by Kawase Hasui.jpg

Tabi_miyage_dai_nishū,_Ame_no_Kiyomizu-.story: Kiyomizu-dera — 'pure-water temple' — is built out over a hillside in eastern Kyoto on the platform every visitor photographs. Hasui went on a wet day. A single figure with an umbrella stands at the balustrade looking into the rain, the valley beyond dissolved in grey. Extra shadow blocks around the wooden posts soften everything that should be sharp, reproducing the way a downpour flattens depth. 1921, Souvenirs of Travel II, published by Watanabe. A well-worn subject handled by weather rather than by composition.

Tabi_miyage_dai_nishū,_Echigo_no_Uraham.title: Tabi miyage dai nishū, Echigo no Urahama by Kawase Hasui
Tabi_miyage_dai_nishū,_Echigo_no_Uraham.description: Urahama in Echigo Province (Echigo no Urahama), from the series Souvenirs of Travel II (Tabi miyage dai nishū), woodblock print

source.canonical_title: File:Tabi miyage dai nishū, Echigo no Urahama by Kawase Hasui.jpg

Tabi_miyage_dai_nishū,_Echigo_no_Uraham.story: Urahama sits on the Echigo coast, facing the Sea of Japan — weather country. Hasui pitches the viewer offshore here, on the water with the fishing boats, as a squall rolls in. The perspective is unusual for him; he's usually on land looking out. Published by Watanabe in August 1921 as part of Souvenirs of Travel II. What sells it is the handling of the sky and the sea as one continuous grey mass, with the boats printed dark and small against it. Shin-hanga at its most unadorned.

Tabi_miyage_dai_nishū,_Etchū_Himi_Kōs.title: Tabi miyage dai nishū, Etchū Himi Kōshō-ji by Kawase Hasui
Tabi_miyage_dai_nishū,_Etchū_Himi_Kōs.description: Kōshō Temple in Himi , Etchū Province (Etchū Himi Kōshō-ji), from the series Souvenirs of Travel II (Tabi miyage dai nishū), woodblock print

source.canonical_title: File:Tabi miyage dai nishū, Etchū Himi Kōshō-ji by Kawase Hasui.jpg

Tabi_miyage_dai_nishū,_Etchū_Himi_Kōs.story: Kosho-ji is an old Jodo Shinshu temple in Himi, a fishing town on the Etchu coast (modern Toyama Prefecture). Hasui reached it in 1921 and dated the design September 6. He works the sheet low and quiet: temple roofline, trees, a strip of approach, not much else. The second Souvenirs of Travel set took him up and down the Sea of Japan side of the country, collecting subjects that weren't on the established picture-postcard circuit. Kosho-ji is a good example — a working provincial temple, printed without ceremony.

Tabi_miyage_dai_nishū,_Fuyu_no_Rankyō_.title: Tabi miyage dai nishū, Fuyu no Rankyō by Kawase Hasui
Tabi_miyage_dai_nishū,_Fuyu_no_Rankyō_.description: Arashiyama in Winter (Fuyu no Rankyō), from the series Souvenirs of Travel II (Tabi miyage dai nishū)

source.canonical_title: File:Tabi miyage dai nishū, Fuyu no Rankyō by Kawase Hasui.jpg

Tabi_miyage_dai_nishū,_Fuyu_no_Rankyō_.story: Arashiyama — the Arashi Gorge on the western edge of Kyoto — is usually drawn in spring, cherry blossoms over the Togetsukyo bridge. Hasui picked winter instead: bare branches, cold water, a hush. The sheet belongs to Souvenirs of Travel II, issued by Watanabe in 1921, and it's characteristic of the series' reluctance to go after postcard cliches. The gorge here is a real place in off-season weather, with no tourists and no blossom. A quiet print in a format Kyoto rarely gets.

Tabi_miyage_dai_nishū,_Getsumei_no_Kamo.title: Tabi miyage dai nishū, Getsumei no Kamo-ko by Kawase Hasui
Tabi_miyage_dai_nishū,_Getsumei_no_Kamo.description: Moonlight over Lake Kamo , Sado (Getsumei no Kamo-ko), from the series Souvenirs of Travel II (Tabi miyage dai nishū), woodblock print

source.canonical_title: File:Tabi miyage dai nishū, Getsumei no Kamo-ko by Kawase Hasui.jpg

Tabi_miyage_dai_nishū,_Getsumei_no_Kamo.story: Lake Kamo is a sea-lagoon on Sado, hooked behind a narrow neck of land. Hasui designed this sheet in August 1921 and printed it almost entirely in blues — an aizuri-e treatment, where one dominant pigment carries the mood. Moonlight picks out the still water and the ridge line behind it; nothing else moves. It's one of the more atmospheric prints in Souvenirs of Travel II, and a good example of how Hasui used limited palettes to do what watercolourists do with dilution. Quiet, cold, almost monochrome.

Tabi_miyage_dai_nishū,_Hamagoya_(Etchū.title: Tabi miyage dai nishū, Hamagoya (Etchū Himi) by Kawase Hasui
Tabi_miyage_dai_nishū,_Hamagoya_(Etchū.description: Beach shed at Himi in Etchū Province, from the series Souvenirs of Travel II (Tabi miyage dai nishū), woodblock print

source.canonical_title: File:Tabi miyage dai nishū, Hamagoya (Etchū Himi) by Kawase Hasui.jpg

Tabi_miyage_dai_nishū,_Hamagoya_(Etchū.story: Hamagoya means 'beach hut' — the kind of low wooden shed a fishing village builds to store nets and shelter from onshore wind. Hasui found this one at Himi on the Etchu coast in 1921 and made it the whole subject. No temple, no famous view, just a weathered structure against sand and sea. That willingness to spend a whole oban sheet on an anonymous beach shack is part of what keeps the Souvenirs of Travel series interesting nearly a century later. A plain building, printed as if it mattered.

Tabi_miyage_dai_nishū,_Kanazawa_Shimoho.title: Tabi miyage dai nishū, Kanazawa Shimohonda-machi by Kawase Hasui
Tabi_miyage_dai_nishū,_Kanazawa_Shimoho.description: Shimohonda-machi in Kanazawa (Kanazawa Shimohonda-machi), from the series Souvenirs of Travel II (Tabi miyage dai nishū), woodblock print

source.canonical_title: File:Tabi miyage dai nishū, Kanazawa Shimohonda-machi by Kawase Hasui.jpg

Tabi_miyage_dai_nishū,_Kanazawa_Shimoho.story: A shaded lane in Kanazawa's old samurai quarter, the kind of back street that once led to the residences of Maeda retainers and by 1921 held only the memory. Hasui keeps it almost empty: dappled greens along a wall, a lone figure in kimono walking away from us beneath the trees. Issued September 1921 in the Souvenirs of Travel II set published by Watanabe Shozaburo, it belongs to the prized pre-earthquake state, before the 1923 Kanto quake destroyed the original blocks. The whole effect is a held breath — heat, silence, a town getting on with its afternoon.

Tabi_miyage_dai_nishū,_Kōshū_Yanagawa.title: Tabi miyage dai nishū, Kōshū Yanagawa by Kawase Hasui
Tabi_miyage_dai_nishū,_Kōshū_Yanagawa.description: Yanagawa in Kai Province (Kōshū Yanagawa), from the series Souvenirs of Travel II (Tabi miyage dai nishū), woodblock print

source.canonical_title: File:Tabi miyage dai nishū, Kōshū Yanagawa by Kawase Hasui.jpg

Tabi_miyage_dai_nishū,_Kōshū_Yanagawa.story: The Yanagawa River threading through the mountains of Kai province (modern Yamanashi), sketched during Hasui's travels in 1921 and cut for Watanabe's Souvenirs of Travel II series. Kawase loved river bends like this — the bank dropping in layers, water catching a flat light, a wooded ridge closing the view. No drama, no famous landmark: just a stretch of country he passed through and wanted to fix on paper. The Toledo Museum of Art holds one of the early, pre-earthquake impressions.

Tabi_miyage_dai_nishū,_Mizuagetoi_(Sado.title: Tabi miyage dai nishū, Mizuagetoi (Sado shoken) by Kawase Hasui
Tabi_miyage_dai_nishū,_Mizuagetoi_(Sado.description: Irrigation, As Seen in Sado (Mizuagetoi ([Sado shoken]), from the series Souvenirs of Travel II (Tabi miyage dai nishū), woodblock print

source.canonical_title: File:Tabi miyage dai nishū, Mizuagetoi (Sado shoken) by Kawase Hasui.jpg

Tabi_miyage_dai_nishū,_Mizuagetoi_(Sado.story: A man works a wooden water conduit on Sado Island, lifting water to irrigate a patch of crop. Hasui sketched the scene on his August 1921 tour of Sado — the old exile island out in the Sea of Japan where emperors, poets, and the monk Nichiren had once been banished — and Watanabe issued it later that year as part of Souvenirs of Travel II. Karazuri (blind-printing) in the white clouds gives the sky a soft embossed texture. Rural labor treated without picturesque fuss: one of the least-sung prints in a crowded year.

Tabi_miyage_dai_nishū,_Nara_Kasuga-jinj.title: Tabi miyage dai nishū, Nara Kasuga-jinja by Kawase Hasui
Tabi_miyage_dai_nishū,_Nara_Kasuga-jinj.description: The Kasuga Shrine in Nara (Nara Kasuga-jinja), from the series Souvenirs of Travel II (Tabi miyage dai nishū), woodblock print

source.canonical_title: File:Tabi miyage dai nishū, Nara Kasuga-jinja by Kawase Hasui.jpg

Tabi_miyage_dai_nishū,_Nara_Kasuga-jinj.story: The deer-park approach to Kasuga Taisha in Nara, where stone lanterns line the path under old cryptomeria. Hasui dated the print February 12, 1921, near the start of the Souvenirs of Travel II series. He keeps the palette close — moss greens, damp grey stone, the red of the shrine just showing through — and lets the trees carry the mood. This is the kind of quiet shrine view Hasui made his signature: not the grand festival, just the walk in.

Tabi_miyage_dai_nishū,_Nara_Nigatsu-dō.title: Tabi miyage dai nishū, Nara Nigatsu-dō by Kawase Hasui
Tabi_miyage_dai_nishū,_Nara_Nigatsu-dō.description: Nigatsu-dō in Nara (Nara Nigatsu-dō), from the series Souvenirs of Travel II (Tabi miyage dai nishū)

source.canonical_title: File:Tabi miyage dai nishū, Nara Nigatsu-dō by Kawase Hasui.jpg

Tabi_miyage_dai_nishū,_Nara_Nigatsu-dō.story: Nigatsu-do, the hall on the Todai-ji hillside best known for the Omizutori fire-and-water rite each March, seen here in Hasui's more hushed register. From the 1921 Souvenirs of Travel II set, published by Watanabe Shozaburo. He lifts the viewpoint so the hall's veranda sits against a wash of sky, the wooden stage that gives the complex its nickname 'water-drawing hall' holding the light. A pre-earthquake design — the original blocks were lost in the 1923 Kanto disaster, making early impressions scarce.

Tabi_miyage_dai_nishū,_Ōsaka_Dōtonbor.title: Tabi miyage dai nishū, Ōsaka Dōtonbori no asa by Kawase Hasui
Tabi_miyage_dai_nishū,_Ōsaka_Dōtonbor.description: Morning at Dōtonbori , Ōsaka (Ōsaka Dōtonbori no asa), from the series Souvenirs of Travel II (Tabi miyage dai nishū)

source.canonical_title: File:Tabi miyage dai nishū, Ōsaka Dōtonbori no asa by Kawase Hasui.jpg

Tabi_miyage_dai_nishū,_Ōsaka_Dōtonbor.story: Dotonbori before the theatres open. Hasui signed the block Taisho 10, second month, fourteenth day — February 14, 1921 — and put a single boatman on the dark canal, the warehouses and teahouse windows mirrored in the water. The neon that now defines Dotonbori is a lifetime away; this is the older, quieter Osaka, sliding through first light. Part of the Souvenirs of Travel II series issued by Watanabe, and one of the prints most collectors rank among Hasui's best urban dawns.

Tabi_miyage_dai_nishū,_Sado_Aikawa-mach.title: Tabi miyage dai nishū, Sado Aikawa-machi by Kawase Hasui
Tabi_miyage_dai_nishū,_Sado_Aikawa-mach.description: Aikawa-machi in Sado , (Sado Aikawa-machi), from the series Souvenirs of Travel II (Tabi miyage dai nishū), woodblock print

source.canonical_title: File:Tabi miyage dai nishū, Sado Aikawa-machi by Kawase Hasui.jpg

Tabi_miyage_dai_nishū,_Sado_Aikawa-mach.story: Aikawa, the old gold-mining town on Sado's western flank. Hasui visited on August 18, 1921, and Watanabe published the resulting print in December. The composition works the way so many of his Sado views do — a cluster of weathered roofs tucked against a hillside, the sea or an estuary glimpsed beyond — nothing heroic, just a provincial town carrying on after its mining heyday. One of six Sado designs Hasui made for Souvenirs of Travel II, all now prized in their pre-earthquake state.

Tabi_miyage_dai_nishū,_Sado_Kamo-mura_b.title: Tabi miyage dai nishū, Sado Kamo-mura by Kawase Hasui
Tabi_miyage_dai_nishū,_Sado_Kamo-mura_b.description: Kamo-mura in Sado (Sado Kamo-mura), from the series Souvenirs of Travel II (Tabi miyage dai nishū), woodblock print

source.canonical_title: File:Tabi miyage dai nishū, Sado Kamo-mura by Kawase Hasui.jpg

Tabi_miyage_dai_nishū,_Sado_Kamo-mura_b.story: Lake Kamo on Sado Island, a shallow lagoon cupped between ridges on the island's eastern side. Hasui's daylight view of Kamo-mura is the gentler companion to his celebrated moonlight version from the same 1921 series — same water, same mountain spine, different hour. The color woodblock was pulled from Watanabe's Souvenirs of Travel II set that summer, after Hasui's August tour of the Hokuriku coast. An impression is held at the Toledo Museum of Art.

Tabi_miyage_dai_nishū,_Sado_Mano_wan_by.title: Tabi miyage dai nishū, Sado Mano wan by Kawase Hasui
Tabi_miyage_dai_nishū,_Sado_Mano_wan_by.description: Mano bay, Sado , (Sado Mano wan), from the series Souvenirs of Travel II (Tabi miyage dai nishū)

source.canonical_title: File:Tabi miyage dai nishū, Sado Mano wan by Kawase Hasui.jpg

Tabi_miyage_dai_nishū,_Sado_Mano_wan_by.story: Mano Bay on Sado's inner coast, looking out across still water to the low fold of Kosado. Hasui drew it during his August 1921 tour of the island and Watanabe published it that year as one of six Sado subjects in the Souvenirs of Travel II set. The bay has a pointed history — the exiled Emperor Juntoku lived out his last years nearby — but Hasui is not here for the history lesson. He wants the long evening water and the line of the far shore.

Tabi_miyage_dai_nishū,_Sado_Nishimikawa.title: Tabi miyage dai nishū, Sado Nishimikawazaka by Kawase Hasui
Tabi_miyage_dai_nishū,_Sado_Nishimikawa.description: Nishimikawa-zaka on Sado Island (Sado Nishimikawa-zaka), from the series Souvenirs of Travel II (Tabi miyage dai nishū), woodblock print

source.canonical_title: File:Tabi miyage dai nishū, Sado Nishimikawazaka by Kawase Hasui.jpg

Tabi_miyage_dai_nishū,_Sado_Nishimikawa.story: A solitary traveller in a yellow straw cape crosses a snowy coastal slope on Sado Island, the sea a flat grey below. Issued December 1921 in the Souvenirs of Travel II series, printed with bokashi gradations on the water and circular 'bare' passages where the snow falls — some of the finest craftsmanship out of Watanabe's workshop. Early versions even survive as a watercolor and intermediate states, giving a rare look at Hasui iterating on the same view. A pre-earthquake impression and one of the series' quiet highlights.

Tabi_miyage_dai_nishū,_Sado_Ogi_no_mina.title: Tabi miyage dai nishū, Sado Ogi no minato by Kawase Hasui 01
Tabi_miyage_dai_nishū,_Sado_Ogi_no_mina.description: Port of Ogi, Sado , (Sado Ogi no minato), from the series Souvenirs of Travel II (Tabi miyage dai nishū)

source.canonical_title: File:Tabi miyage dai nishū, Sado Ogi no minato by Kawase Hasui 01.jpg

Tabi_miyage_dai_nishū,_Sado_Ogi_no_mina.story: Ogi, the little southern port of Sado where tub-boats still ferry people between fishing coves. In Hasui's daylight version for Souvenirs of Travel II, small wooden boats line the shore and the village sits low against the water, a working harbor caught off-duty. The more famous companion piece shows the same port at dawn under fresh snow; this one is the plain, bright-weather face of the same place. Published by Watanabe Shozaburo in 1921.

Tabi_miyage_dai_nishū,_Sanuki_Takamatsu.title: Tabi miyage dai nishū, Sanuki Takamatsu-jō by Kawase Hasui
Tabi_miyage_dai_nishū,_Sanuki_Takamatsu.description: Takamatsu Castle in Sanuki (Sanuki no Takamatsu-jō), from the series Souvenirs of Travel II (Tabi miyage dai nishū), woodblock print

source.canonical_title: File:Tabi miyage dai nishū, Sanuki Takamatsu-jō by Kawase Hasui.jpg

Tabi_miyage_dai_nishū,_Sanuki_Takamatsu.story: Takamatsu Castle on Shikoku, one of the few Japanese castles with a moat fed directly by the sea. Hasui's 1921 print from Souvenirs of Travel II crops in on the surviving corner turret and the stone wall running into green water, the keep itself long gone — burnt in 1884, never rebuilt. A modest, almost offhand view of a castle most travelers barely noticed. Impressions are now in the Art Institute of Chicago and the Smithsonian's National Museum of Asian Art, both from the pre-earthquake state.

Tabi_miyage_dai_nishū,_Tango_no_Miyazu_.title: Tabi miyage dai nishū, Tango no Miyazu by Kawase Hasui
Tabi_miyage_dai_nishū,_Tango_no_Miyazu_.description: Miyazu in Tango (Tango no Miyazu), from the series Souvenirs of Travel II (Tabi miyage dai nishū)

source.canonical_title: File:Tabi miyage dai nishū, Tango no Miyazu by Kawase Hasui.jpg

Tabi_miyage_dai_nishū,_Tango_no_Miyazu_.story: Miyazu on the Tango coast, the port town whose inlet leads out to Amanohashidate, the famous pine-covered sandbar. Hasui picks the town itself rather than the tourist vista — roofs along the water, boats moored close in, mountains holding the bay. Published by Watanabe Shozaburo in 1921 as part of Souvenirs of Travel II. Copies are in the Harvard Art Museums and the Smithsonian, both in their early, pre-earthquake state.

Tabi_miyage_dai_nishū,_Teradomari_no_yo.title: Tabi miyage dai nishū, Teradomari no yosame by Kawase Hasui
Tabi_miyage_dai_nishū,_Teradomari_no_yo.description: Night rain at Teradomari (Teradomari no yosame), from the series Souvenirs of Travel II (Tabi miyage dai nishū), woodblock print

source.canonical_title: File:Tabi miyage dai nishū, Teradomari no yosame by Kawase Hasui.jpg

Tabi_miyage_dai_nishū,_Teradomari_no_yo.story: A figure in a straw cape and round hat leans into a hard evening rain in Teradomari, the small Niigata coast town (since absorbed into Nagaoka). Hasui dated the block August 27, 1921. The downpour falls in those long straight lines that openly nod to Hiroshige's Ohashi Bridge; glowing paper windows throw yellow puddles across the dark lane. A standout in Souvenirs of Travel II, and another scarce pre-earthquake design — one of the prints that made Hasui's name as the rain-and-snow master of shin-hanga.

Tabi_miyage_dai_nishū,_Yuki_no_akebono_.title: Tabi miyage dai nishū, Yuki no akebono (Sado Ogi minato) by Kawase Hasui
Tabi_miyage_dai_nishū,_Yuki_no_akebono_.description: Dawn snow at the port of Ogi on Sado Island (Yuki no akebono [Sado Ogi minato]), from the series Souvenirs of Travel II (Tabi miyage dai nishū), woodblock print

source.canonical_title: File:Tabi miyage dai nishū, Yuki no akebono (Sado Ogi minato) by Kawase Hasui.jpg

Tabi_miyage_dai_nishū,_Yuki_no_akebono_.story: Dawn over Ogi harbor on Sado, the fishing village muffled under fresh snow, sky washed a clean pink, not a footprint yet in the white. Small boats line the shore. Hasui pushes the composition almost flat — the village reads like a low frieze between the still water and the coloring sky — which gives it the faintly theatrical quality collectors love. From Souvenirs of Travel II, 1921, Watanabe Shozaburo. Pre-earthquake impressions are among the most sought-after prints in the series.

Tabi_miyage_dai_nishū,_Yuki_no_hashidat.title: Tabi miyage dai nishū, Yuki no hashidate by Kawase Hasui
Tabi_miyage_dai_nishū,_Yuki_no_hashidat.description: Snow at Hashidate (Yuki no hashidate), from the series Souvenirs of Travel II (Tabi miyage dai nishū)

source.canonical_title: File:Tabi miyage dai nishū, Yuki no hashidate by Kawase Hasui.jpg

Tabi_miyage_dai_nishū,_Yuki_no_hashidat.story: Amanohashidate — the pine-studded sandbar on the Sea of Japan coast, ranked for centuries among Japan's three great views — rarely gets drawn under snow. Hasui saw it that way in 1921 and made it the quiet centerpiece of Souvenirs of Travel II, the second of the sketchbook-style series he built from his prewar wandering. The Japanese title literally means 'travel gifts,' and that's the register: a print meant to feel like something brought home in a folded envelope, unhurried, weather-specific, true to a day.

Tabi_miyage_dai_nishū,_seiten_no_yuki_(.title: Tabi miyage dai nishū, seiten no yuki (Miyajima) by Kawase Hasui
Tabi_miyage_dai_nishū,_seiten_no_yuki_(.description: Snow on a clear day at Miyajima (seiten no yuki [Miyajima]), from the series Souvenirs of Travel II (Tabi miyage dai nishū), woodblock print

source.canonical_title: File:Tabi miyage dai nishū, seiten no yuki (Miyajima) by Kawase Hasui.jpg

Tabi_miyage_dai_nishū,_seiten_no_yuki_(.story: Miyajima's floating torii is the single most photographed gate in Japan, which makes Hasui's angle here the interesting move: snow on a clear day, the red of Itsukushima Shrine sharpened rather than softened by winter light. The print belongs to Souvenirs of Travel II (1921), the loose second sketchbook in which Hasui kept collecting the country as he found it. Shin-hanga cut prints like this one through the block carvers and printers of the publisher Watanabe Shōzaburō, who had set out to save ukiyo-e craft by pointing it at modern landscape.

Tabi_miyage_dai_nishū,_Ojiya_Asahi-bashi.title: Asahi Bridge in Ojiya
Tabi_miyage_dai_nishū,_Ojiya_Asahi-bashi.description: Asahi Bridge in Ojiya (Ojiya Asahi-bashi), from the series Souvenirs of Travel II (Tabi miyage dai nishū), woodblock print

source.canonical_title: File:Tabi miyage dai nishū, Ojiya Asahi-bashi by Kawase Hasui.jpg

Tabi_miyage_dai_nishū,_Ojiya_Asahi-bashi.story: Ojiya sits in Niigata's snow country, a textile town on the Shinano River; the Asahi Bridge crosses it. Hasui put the span into his second Souvenirs of Travel set in 1921, after a stretch of trips north. The subject is deliberately minor — not a famous view, just a working bridge in a working town — and that's much of the point of the series. Shin-hanga was trying to update ukiyo-e by taking it out of the theaters and red-light districts and dropping it into the weather of ordinary Japan.

Tabi_miyage_dai_nishū,_Uji_Byōdō-in_no_i.title: Part of the Byōdō-in Temple at Uji
Tabi_miyage_dai_nishū,_Uji_Byōdō-in_no_i.description: Part of the Byōdō-in Temple at Uji (Uji Byōdō-in no ichibu), from the series Souvenirs of Travel II (Tabi miyage dai nishū), woodblock print

source.canonical_title: File:Tabi miyage dai nishū, Uji Byōdō-in no ichibu by Kawase Hasui.jpg

Tabi_miyage_dai_nishū,_Uji_Byōdō-in_no_i.story: The Byōdō-in at Uji — the Phoenix Hall on the thousand-yen coin — is usually shown head-on across its reflecting pond. Hasui, in this 1921 contribution to Souvenirs of Travel II, takes only 'a part' of it, which is what the title says: a corner, an angle, a fragment of the eleventh-century temple glimpsed rather than monumentalized. The restraint is characteristic. Watanabe Shōzaburō's workshop carved and printed these with the full ukiyo-e technique, but Hasui had absorbed enough Western landscape sketching to keep the compositions close, partial, atmospheric.

Tabi_miyage_dai_sanshū,_Bōshū_Futomi_.title: Tabi miyage dai sanshū, Bōshū Futomi by Kawase Hasui
Tabi_miyage_dai_sanshū,_Bōshū_Futomi_.description: Futomi in Awa Province (Bōshū Futomi), from the series Souvenirs of Travel III (Tabi miyage dai sanshū)

source.canonical_title: File:Tabi miyage dai sanshū, Bōshū Futomi by Kawase Hasui.jpg

Tabi_miyage_dai_sanshū,_Bōshū_Futomi_.story: Futomi is a fishing village on the Boso Peninsula, what old maps called Boshu or Awa Province, an easy trip south of Tokyo. Hasui worked his way down the coast for Souvenirs of Travel III in 1925, sketching the inlets, boats, and weather-beaten houses. The print trades the drama of his snow scenes for something quieter: warm light, a working shoreline, the Pacific pressing against a country still largely shaped by the sea.

Tabi_miyage_dai_sanshū,_Hakubasan_yori_.title: Tabi miyage dai sanshū, Hakubasan yori mitaru Asahigadake by Kawase Hasui
Tabi_miyage_dai_sanshū,_Hakubasan_yori_.description: Asahi Peak Seen from Mt. Hakuba , (Hakubasan yori mitaru Asahigadake), from the series Souvenirs of Travel III (Tabi miyage dai sanshū)

source.canonical_title: File:Tabi miyage dai sanshū, Hakubasan yori mitaru Asahigadake by Kawase Hasui.jpg

Tabi_miyage_dai_sanshū,_Hakubasan_yori_.story: Mount Asahi seen from Hakuba, high in the Japanese Alps. This is Hasui out of his coastal comfort zone, up among the serious peaks that most travellers never reach. The print keeps its scale honest — snow, rock, the pale blue distances — without the theatrical flourishes earlier ukiyo-e piled on mountains. From Souvenirs of Travel III, 1924, the series he made by hiking with a sketchbook and sending the drawings back to Watanabe's block-cutters in Tokyo.

Tabi_miyage_dai_sanshū,_Hida_Nakayama-s.title: Tabi miyage dai sanshū, Hida Nakayama-shichiri by Kawase Hasui
Tabi_miyage_dai_sanshū,_Hida_Nakayama-s.description: Nakayama-Shichiri Road in Hida Province , (Hida Nakayama-shichiri), from the series Souvenirs of Travel III (Tabi miyage dai sanshū)

source.canonical_title: File:Tabi miyage dai sanshū, Hida Nakayama-shichiri by Kawase Hasui.jpg

Tabi_miyage_dai_sanshū,_Hida_Nakayama-s.story: The Nakayama-shichiri road in Hida, an old seven-ri stretch (roughly 28 kilometres) winding through the mountains of what is now Gifu prefecture. Hasui had a taste for roads: not the destination but the walking, the way a path folds around a ridge. From Souvenirs of Travel III, 1924. You can almost hear the straw sandals.

Tabi_miyage_dai_sanshū,_Iwami_Arifuku_o.title: Tabi miyage dai sanshū, Iwami Arifuku onsen by Kawase Hasui
Tabi_miyage_dai_sanshū,_Iwami_Arifuku_o.description: Arifuku Hot Springs in Iwami , (Iwami Arifuku onsen), from the series Souvenirs of Travel III (Tabi miyage dai sanshū)

source.canonical_title: File:Tabi miyage dai sanshū, Iwami Arifuku onsen by Kawase Hasui.jpg

Tabi_miyage_dai_sanshū,_Iwami_Arifuku_o.story: Arifuku hot springs in Iwami, a remote corner of what is now Shimane prefecture on the Japan Sea coast. Hasui liked onsen towns because they were already half-landscape — wooden inns clinging to a river valley, steam mixing with mountain mist. Souvenirs of Travel III, 1924: a working printmaker turning a weekend soak into something you want to frame.

Tabi_miyage_dai_sanshū,_Izumo_Hinomisak.title: Tabi miyage dai sanshū, Izumo Hinomisaki by Kawase Hasui
Tabi_miyage_dai_sanshū,_Izumo_Hinomisak.description: Hinomisaki in Izumo Province , (Izumo Hinomisaki), from the series Souvenirs of Travel III (Tabi miyage dai sanshū)

source.canonical_title: File:Tabi miyage dai sanshū, Izumo Hinomisaki by Kawase Hasui.jpg

Tabi_miyage_dai_sanshū,_Izumo_Hinomisak.story: Hinomisaki, the rocky cape at the western tip of the Izumo peninsula, home to one of Japan's oldest lighthouses and a shrine said to calm the sun itself. Hasui points his view out to the Japan Sea. Souvenirs of Travel III, 1924 — a print built out of cliff, water and sky, with almost nothing else in it, and all the better for the restraint.

Tabi_miyage_dai_sanshū,_Izumo_Matsue_(o.title: Tabi miyage dai sanshū, Izumo Matsue (oborozuki) by Kawase Hasui
Tabi_miyage_dai_sanshū,_Izumo_Matsue_(o.description: Misty Moonlight at Matsue in Izumo Province, (Izumo Matsue [oborozuki]), from the series Souvenirs of Travel III (Tabi miyage dai sanshū)

source.canonical_title: File:Tabi miyage dai sanshū, Izumo Matsue (oborozuki) by Kawase Hasui.jpg

Tabi_miyage_dai_sanshū,_Izumo_Matsue_(o.story: A second Matsue night for Souvenirs of Travel III — this time under an oborozuki, the hazy spring moon that Japanese poetry has been praising for a thousand years. Hasui treats the atmosphere as the subject: water, mist, a moon softened almost to a smudge. 1924. Proof that he could visit the same town twice and come back with something genuinely different.

Tabi_miyage_dai_sanshū,_Izumo_Mihogasek.title: Tabi miyage dai sanshū, Izumo Mihogaseki by Kawase Hasui
Tabi_miyage_dai_sanshū,_Izumo_Mihogasek.description: Mihogaseki Beach in Izumo Province, (Izumo Mihogaseki), from the series Souvenirs of Travel III (Tabi miyage dai sanshū)

source.canonical_title: File:Tabi miyage dai sanshū, Izumo Mihogaseki by Kawase Hasui.jpg

Tabi_miyage_dai_sanshū,_Izumo_Mihogasek.story: Mihogaseki beach, a fishing village on the Shimane peninsula looking out across Miho Bay. Izumo coast, 1924. Hasui keeps the palette cool and the composition low — boats drawn up, a pale strip of sand, the sea doing most of the horizon. Souvenirs of Travel III was the series where he settled into his mature style, and prints like this show why it held up for the rest of his career.

Tabi_miyage_dai_sanshū,_Kaga_Hatta_(aki.title: Tabi miyage dai sanshū, Kaga Hatta (aki no niji) by Kawase Hasui
Tabi_miyage_dai_sanshū,_Kaga_Hatta_(aki.description: Autumn Rainbow at Hatta in Kaga Province, (Kaga Hatta [aki no niji]), from the series Souvenirs of Travel III (Tabi miyage dai sanshū)

source.canonical_title: File:Tabi miyage dai sanshū, Kaga Hatta (aki no niji) by Kawase Hasui.jpg

Tabi_miyage_dai_sanshū,_Kaga_Hatta_(aki.story: An autumn rainbow over Hatta, in old Kaga province (now Ishikawa). Rainbows are rare in Japanese prints — too short-lived, too hard to design around without looking kitsch. Hasui builds the whole print around it anyway: wet fields, a low horizon, the arc coming through a washed sky. From Souvenirs of Travel III, 1924. A small gamble that pays off.

Tabi_miyage_dai_sanshū,_Suō_Kintai-kyo.title: Tabi miyage dai sanshū, Suō Kintai-kyō by Kawase Hasui
Tabi_miyage_dai_sanshū,_Suō_Kintai-kyo.description: Kintai Bridge in Suō Province, (Suō Kintai-kyō), from the series Souvenirs of Travel III (Tabi miyage dai sanshū)

source.canonical_title: File:Tabi miyage dai sanshū, Suō Kintai-kyō by Kawase Hasui.jpg

Tabi_miyage_dai_sanshū,_Suō_Kintai-kyo.story: Kintai Bridge in Suo (now Iwakuni, Yamaguchi), the famous five-arch wooden span over the Nishiki river. It had been rebuilt a dozen times since the 1670s and was already a tourist draw when Hasui arrived. He draws it more or less straight — the bridge does the work — with his usual attention to water, embankment and weather. Souvenirs of Travel III, 1924.

Tabi_miyage_dai_sanshū,_Tazawako_Gozano.title: Tabi miyage dai sanshū, Tazawako Gozanoishi by Kawase Hasui
Tabi_miyage_dai_sanshū,_Tazawako_Gozano.description: Gozanoishi Shrine at Lake Tazawa , (Tazawako Gozanoishi), from the series Souvenirs of Travel III (Tabi miyage dai sanshū)

source.canonical_title: File:Tabi miyage dai sanshū, Tazawako Gozanoishi by Kawase Hasui.jpg

Tabi_miyage_dai_sanshū,_Tazawako_Gozano.story: Lake Tazawa is the deepest in Japan, a near-perfect caldera in the Ou Mountains of Akita. Hasui traveled there in June 1926 and drew the torii gates of Gozanoishi Shrine standing in the shallows on the north shore. The water reads almost black in the print, with the red gate posts and a pale sky above — a composition that leans on ukiyo-e tradition but feels close to a plein-air painting. Published the same year in Souvenirs of Travel III.

Takiyasha_the_Witch_and_the_Skeleton_Spe.story: Kuniyoshi's 1844 triptych turns a scene from kabuki into pure theater: Princess Takiyasha, daughter of a defeated rebel, unrolls her scroll of sorcery in a ruined Soma palace and a giant skeleton crashes through the rafters to meet the warrior Mitsukuni. What's striking is the skeleton itself - ribs and jaw drawn with anatomical seriousness rather than cartoon menace, likely cribbed from Dutch medical plates circulating in Edo. The composition earns its scale by letting the specter span all three sheets while the humans crouch small and silhouetted at left.

Tempelskatten._Peter_finder_mønten_i_fis.title: The Ferry Boat to Antwerp

source.canonical_title: File:Tempelskatten. Peter finder mønten i fiskens gab.jpg

Tempelskatten._Peter_finder_mønten_i_fis.story: The Danish title — The Temple Tax. Peter Finds the Coin in the Fish's Mouth — is the giveaway: this is the Gospel story from Matthew 17, where Jesus tells Peter to go fishing and he'll find the tribute coin in the first fish he catches. Jordaens, early in his career, uses the episode as an excuse for a crowded ferry scene: dockhands, fishermen, passengers, a stocky boat pulled up to the Scheldt. It's a quintessentially Flemish move — turning a miracle story into a waterfront genre painting. Sometimes catalogued as The Ferry Boat to Antwerp.

Tentaciones_de_Cristo_(Botticelli).jpg.title: Temptations of Christ.

source.canonical_title: File:Tentaciones de Cristo (Botticelli).jpg

Tentaciones_de_Cristo_(Botticelli).jpg.story: Three devils, three refusals, one panoramic sweep. Botticelli folds all of Christ's temptations into a single fresco on the north wall of the Sistine Chapel, painted between 1481 and 1482 when Sixtus IV summoned Florence's best to Rome. Up on the rocky pinnacle the devil tumbles, his monkish robes flying to reveal claws and bat wings. Down below, a Jewish purification ritual unfolds in front of a building modeled on the newly completed Santo Spirito hospital in Rome. Sixtus's della Rovere oak appears in the foreground — Botticelli never missed a patron's heraldry.

source.canonical_title: File:The Antiques Seller by Rudolf Weisse, 1887.jpg

The_Antiques_Seller_by_Rudolf_Weisse,_18.story: Three men in a Cairo doorway haggling over a brass tray: a seated bearded merchant in a striped robe on a tiled stool, a customer in yellow with a red sash, and the shopkeeper in white on his rug, rifle across his lap. Around them — inlaid lanterns, an ornate ewer, a long-necked horn on the ground, a geometric Iznik-style carpet behind. Weisse, Austrian-born and Paris-based, was known for hauling props back from Egypt and arranging them in his studio, so the textures here are almost photographic. It's a staged tableau, but an honest one: the painter telling you exactly what he cared about.

The_Artist's_Garden_in_Argenteuil_(A_Cor.title: The Artist's Garden in Argenteuil (A Corner of the Garden with Dahlias)

source.canonical_title: File:The Artist's Garden in Argenteuil (A Corner of the Garden with Dahlias) A12382.jpg

The_Artist's_Garden_in_Argenteuil_(A_Cor.story: Renoir was there the day Monet painted this. The two friends set up easels beside the dahlia bed and worked side by side, Renoir's version now hanging at the National Gallery in Washington. A figure in a top hat drifts past the house, dwarfed by the fat red-and-orange blooms. It's the garden Monet rented with the house on rue Pierre Guienne in 1874, three years before a notice of eviction sent him packing.

The_Arts_Painting.jpg.title: Painting , part of the series The Arts

source.canonical_title: File:The Arts Painting.jpg

The_Arts_Painting.jpg.story: Painting is the morning-light panel of Mucha's 1898 series The Arts. Instead of handing her a palette, Mucha gave her a red flower held up to a disc of rainbows — the act of painting reimagined as looking hard at colour. Her gaze drops to a blossom in her lap; there are no brushes, no easel, no studio clutter. The series (Dance, Painting, Poetry, Music) was issued by Champenois as a set of decorative panels printed on vellum, with a small satin edition for luxury buyers, all produced at the height of Mucha's Paris fame.

The_Attack_by_Vereshchagin_(1887-1895,_G.story: Part of Vereshchagin's 1812 cycle, this canvas belongs to the sequence on the Russian counter-offensive against Napoleon's Grande Armee. Bayonets lowered, a ragged line of infantry surges forward under a cold, smoke-flat sky. No heroic halos, no waving colours on horseback — just men running into the muzzle of something unseen. Vereshchagin had walked real battlefields in Turkestan and the Balkans, and the mud-coloured palette here is the mud he actually knew. The painting now hangs in Moscow's State Historical Museum.

The_Bathing_Posts,_Brittany_by_James_McN.description: The Bathing Posts, Brittany by James McNeill Whistler, 1893, 16.6 x 24.3 cm, oil on wood, Hunterian Museum and Art Gallery, Glasgow

source.canonical_title: File:The Bathing Posts, Brittany by James McNeill Whistler, 1893.jpg
source.credit: Hunterian Museum and Art Gallery, Glasgow

The_Bathing_Posts,_Brittany_by_James_McN.story: Sixteen by twenty-four centimetres of oil on wood: smaller than a paperback. Whistler painted this on a Brittany summer in 1893, standing on the beach at Pouldu, looking out through three skinny wooden posts that marked the safe bathing zone. Everything is reduced to a haze of horizon and wet sand. He'd got so good at working this small that he could finish a picture in an afternoon and still make the sea feel cold. It lives at the Hunterian in Glasgow.

The_Beach_at_Trouville_1948.116.jpg.title: The Beach at Trouville

source.canonical_title: File:The Beach at Trouville 1948.116.jpg

The_Beach_at_Trouville_1948.116.jpg.story: One of five beach scenes Monet knocked out at Trouville in the summer of 1870, painted with Camille and Jean beside him on the sand. Grains of that sand are actually embedded in the paint surface, proof he worked right there at the water's edge. The quick, allusive touch almost skips past the figures to get at the wind, the glare, the striped parasols. A working sketch, very possibly meant to feed a larger Salon piece he never made.

The_Beheading_of_Saint_John-Caravaggio_(.story: The largest canvas he ever painted, and the only one he ever signed — the signature written in the pool of blood spreading from John's half-severed neck, reading 'f. Michelang.o,' the 'f.' for frater, brother of the Knights of Malta. He made it in 1608 for the oratory of St John's Co-Cathedral in Valletta, where it still hangs. Within months of finishing it he'd been arrested, imprisoned in the castle fort, broken out, and been expelled from the Order in this same room as a 'foul and rotten member.'

The_Blinding_of_Samson_(SM_1383).png.story: One of the most violent paintings in Dutch art. A Philistine has just driven a dagger into Samson's right eye; blood jets, the hero's body arches into a spasm, his fingers claw at nothing. Delilah flees toward the mouth of the tent clutching the shorn hair, half-turning to look at what she's done. A single shaft of sunlight rips through the canvas from behind her, a stage effect Rembrandt borrowed from Caravaggio. He finished it in 1636 and sent it to his patron Constantijn Huygens as a kind of strong-armed thank-you gift.

The_Christian_Martyrs'_Last_Prayer_GA&C..title: The Christian Martyrs' Last Prayer
The_Christian_Martyrs'_Last_Prayer_GA&C..description: William T. Walters commissioned this painting in 1863, but the artist did not deliver it until 20 years later. In a letter to Walters, Gérôme identified the setting as ancient Rome's racecourse, the Circus Maximus. He noted such details as the goal posts and the chariot tracks in the dirt. The seating, however, more closely resembles that of the Colosseum, Rome's amphitheater, in which gladiatorial combats and other spectacles were held. Similarly, the hill in the background surmounted by a colossal statue and a temple is nearer in appearance to the Athenian Acropolis than it is to Rome's Palatine Hill. The artist also commented on the religious fortitude of the victims who were about to suffer martyrdom either by being devoured by the wild beasts or by being smeared with pitch and set ablaze, which also never took place in the Circus Maximus. In this instance, Gérôme, whose paintings were usually admired for their sense of reality, has subordinated historical accuracy to drama. W. M. Brady & Co, New York, in "Drawings and Oil Sketches 1700-1900," 27 January 2009 - 12 February 2009, No. 21, offers "Study for the 'Death of Caesar," an oil on canvas with pen and ink underdrawing, measuring height: 19.5 cm (7.6 in); width: 33 cm (12.9 in) dimensions QS:P2048,19.5U174728 dimensions QS:P2049,33U174728 , which formerly belonged to Maurice Aiccardi, Paris. This sketch may be the one that Theophile Gautier alluded to during a visit to the artist's studio in 1858 (G. Ackerman, Jean-Leon Gerome: Monographie revisee 2000, pp. 240-241).

title.fr: La dernière prière des martyrs chrétiens
title.de: Das letzte Gebet der Christen im Circus Maximus

The_Christian_Martyrs'_Last_Prayer_GA&C..story: William Walters commissioned this in 1863. Gérôme took twenty years to deliver it. He told Walters the setting was the Circus Maximus, but he cheated freely: the seating looks more like the Colosseum, the hill behind nods to the Athenian Acropolis, and the pitch-smeared torches he paints never actually lit the Circus. A lion pads out of the shadows toward a huddle of praying Christians. Gérôme, usually the strictest of historical realists, traded accuracy for dread. The picture was finally exhibited in 1883.

The_Conspiracy_of_the_Batavians_under_Cl.title: The Conspiracy of the Batavians under Claudius Civilis
The_Conspiracy_of_the_Batavians_under_Cl.description: “Civilis summoned the leaders of the tribe and those prepared to fight for liberty to a sacred grove ostensibly for a banquet and when he beheld that their senses had been overcome by the nocturnal festivities he began to speak of the honour and glory of the tribe and went on to list the wrongs they had suffered. His words met with great acclaim and he bonded them together with patriotic oaths and barbaric rites.” This is how the Roman historian Tacitus describes the beginning of the revolt during the 2nd century by the Germanic Batavian tribe against the Romans under the leadership of their chief, Claudius Civilis. The Batavians’ struggle for liberty was used in the 17th century as an emblem for Dutch liberation from Spanish rule. In 1597 the northern provinces seceded from the empire of the Spanish Habsburgs and established a republic “the Seven United Provinces”. Tacitus’s account was chosen as the motif for some of the paintings decorating the walls of Amsterdam’s Town Hall. Begun in 1648, the Town Hall and was the Republic’s largest building project. It was intended to symbolise its power and wealth. The commission to depict the struggle for liberation by their ancestors originally went to Govaert Flinck, one of Rembrandt’s pupils. Flinck had hardly started the work before his sudden and untimely death. Rembrandt was then asked to complete the motif of the oath of loyalty, which was the only one Flinck had started. Following tradition, Flinck placed the Batavians and Romans on equal terms, painting them in classical armour. Rembrandt chose instead to follow Tacitus’s account more closely. In Rembrandt’s interpretation of Tacitus, Claudius Civilis dominates the scene in his costly garments and tall blue and orange headdress. He raises his heavy sword majestically to enable the men around the table to swear their oath of loyalty to him. According to legend, Claudius had lost an eye while prisoner of the Romans. Rembrandt defies tradition by depicting him full-face, so that the lack of one eye cannot be concealed. Rembrandt completed the work in 1662 and the monumental painting was hung in its intended place. Later in the same year it was removed for unknown reasons. There are no contemporary documents to explain why it was not allowed to remain, but a number of scholars believe that Rembrandt’s unconventional presentation did not please those who had commissioned the work. His style, with the use of light and shadow and thick layers of paint, was also somewhat old-fashioned at a time when history painting was increasingly characterised by austere classicism. Today a painting of the same motif by another of Rembrandt’s pupils, Jurian Ovens hangs on the same wall of Amsterdam’s Town Hall. The master’s own bold interpretation can now be seen here, somewhat smaller in size, at the Nationalmuseum, Stockholm, Sweden.

The_Conspiracy_of_the_Batavians_under_Cl.story: A one-eyed chieftain raises his heavy sword at a banquet table and his Batavian warriors cross their blades against his to swear the revolt against Rome. Amsterdam's new Town Hall commissioned it in 1661 as patriotic decoration, the tribe being a flattering national ancestor. Rembrandt painted Claudius Civilis full-face, missing eye and all, slathered the paint on thick, and lit the scene from below like a nightmare. The city hung it, then took it down within months. Rembrandt cut it up, probably to sell, and only the central fragment survives. It's the largest picture he ever made, now in Stockholm.
The_Conspiracy_of_the_Batavians_under_Cl.year_note: Source metadata lists 1597 (the year the Dutch Republic was established, referenced in the description). Rembrandt painted the work in 1661, installed it in Amsterdam's Town Hall in 1662.

The_Creation_of_Adam.jpg.story: The most reproduced square foot of paint in the world, and still a shock in the actual room. Adam lounges on the curve of the earth, arm outstretched, waiting; God sweeps toward him wrapped in a rose-coloured cloak that bulges with angels and unborn souls. Their fingers almost touch. Michelangelo painted it on the Sistine ceiling in 1511 or thereabouts, working on his back (despite the myth that he didn't), plastering one section at a time. The gap between the fingers is the whole point — not contact, but the instant before. Everything that follows in Western painting about yearning and animation traces back to that inch of sky.

The_Emperor_Commodus_as_Hercules_(B._144.story: Goltzius came back from Rome in 1591 with his sketchbook stuffed with antique statues, and this engraving is one of three he pulled from it. The vain emperor Commodus stands scowling in a lion skin, clutching a club almost as thick as his thigh, apparently convinced he really is Hercules reborn. Look at the swelling and tapering burin lines along the torso, the way each muscle seems to inflate under the light; that rope-like contour is the Goltzius signature his peers spent decades trying to copy. It was printed in 1592, alongside his Farnese Hercules.

source.canonical_title: File:The Fall of Man-1616-Hendrik Goltzius.jpg

The_Fall_of_Man-1616-Hendrik_Goltzius.jp.story: Goltzius paints Eden like a Saturday afternoon. Adam and Eve stretch out almost life-size, more lovers than sinners, the apple barely the point. In the distance an elephant plods by, a stock symbol for chastity, an ironic cameo given what's about to happen. The serpent has a sweet female face. Painted in 1616, late in Goltzius's career after he gave up engraving for brushes, this is him pushing classicism toward something that would soon be called baroque. It's at the National Gallery of Art in Washington.

The_Famous_Scenes_of_the_Sixty_States_55.story: The Naruto Strait between Awa and Awaji churns into whirlpools when the tide rips through, some of them four meters across. Hiroshige gives you the view from the cliffs — striated blue water spinning into white spirals, a skiff improbably small above the vortex. This is print 55 of his Famous Views of the Sixty-odd Provinces, published in 1855. The whirlpools still happen today, on a precise tide schedule; tour boats now nose right up to the edge.

The_Feast_in_the_House_of_Levi_by_Paolo_.description: Paolo Veronese, Dinner (even banquet or feast) in Casa Levi - Oil on canvas of Venetian Mannerism, at Galleries of the Academy of Fine Arts in Venice: - 1 architecture and sculpture (loggia in serliana, classical Palladian-Sanmichelina Renaissance architecture, Corinthian order, Doric-Tuscan in the right background, female bas-reliefs winged with victories ?, ideal city) - 2 at night - 3 table set (food, wine, goblet glasses, jugs, glasses) - 4 clothes (silk, ermine, turbans, fine fabrics) - 5 social classes (soldiers, patricians, bourgeois, servants, prelates, saints, jester, children, adults, men, waiters), multi-ethnic (Italians, Africans, Ottoman Turks, Germans) - 6 animals (dogs and cat in the centre, hawk with falconer on the right)

The_Feast_in_the_House_of_Levi_by_Paolo_.story: Originally a Last Supper for the Dominican refectory of Santi Giovanni e Paolo in Venice, until the Inquisition took exception in 1573 to the dogs, dwarves, drunken Germans, a fool with a parrot, and a servant with a nosebleed. Ordered to correct it, Veronese simply changed the title to 'Feast in the House of Levi' and left the party intact. The result is less a sacred image than a Venetian banquet spilling across three Palladian arches - silks, turbans, cats, a falcon - one of the great acts of cheerful defiance in art history. Gallerie dell'Accademia.

The_Fighting_Temeraire,_JMW_Turner,_Nati.story: The Temeraire had saved Nelson's Victory at Trafalgar in 1805. Thirty-three years later the Admiralty sold her, mastless and rotting, to a Rotherhithe shipbreaker named John Beatson for L5,530 - only the timber was worth anything. Turner shows her ghost-white and enormous, being dragged upriver by a squat black steam tug belching sparks, the sun setting behind them in an operatic smear of orange. He exhibited it at the Royal Academy in 1839 and refused every offer to buy it, calling it his 'darling.' It went to the nation in his 1851 bequest and now hangs in the National Gallery.

The_Fuji_from_Kanaya_on_the_Tokaido.jpg.story: The Oi River was the worst obstacle on the Tokaido: no bridge, by shogunal policy, so armies couldn't cross it in wartime. Travelers had to be carried. Hokusai shows the circus in full — coolies ferrying passengers piggyback through chest-deep water, whole teams of porters hoisting palanquins on a ladderlike platform. The river writhes in stylized swirls. Behind the chaos, a calm monochrome Fuji, unbothered.

The_Golden_Pavilion_(5759027207).jpg.title: The Golden Pavilion
The_Golden_Pavilion_(5759027207).jpg.description: Accession Number: 1998.101 Display Artist: Yoshida Hiroshi Display Title: The Golden Pavilion Series Title: Kansai District Creation Date: 1933 Height: 14 13/16 in. Width: 9 5/8 in. Display Dimensions: 14 13/16 in. x 9 5/8 in. (37.62 cm x 24.45 cm) Credit Line: Gift of Mr. and Mrs. Robert E. Paige Label Copy: "In the early Tokaido series created before Hiroshiges popular works of the 1830s to 1850s, stations of the Tokaido were depicted not as landscape scenes, but with an emphasis on figures, stories, or products associated with each region. In this print Hokusai depicts an interior scene, probably of an inn, with two women seated by an alcove and a large shoji lantern. One of the women appears to be trying to light the floor lantern while the other adjusts the bow of a large obi. In the vertical cartouche in the upper right corner the artist signed the print gakyojin Hokusai ga, which means, by Hokusai, who was crazy about art." Label Copy (Spanish): "En las series tempranas del Tokaid que se crearon antes de las populares obras de Hiroshige de los 1830 a los 1850, las estaciones del Tokaido se no se representaban como escenas de paisajes sino que enfatizaban las figuras, historias o productos asociados con cada regin. En esta impresin, Hokusai muestra una escena interior, probablemente de una posada con dos mujeres sentadas junto a una alcoba y una gran lmpara shoji. Parece ser que una de las mujeres intenta prender la lmpara mientras que la otra ajusta el moo de un gran obi. En la cartela en la esquina derecha superior el artista firm el grabado gakyojin Hokusai ga, que significa por Hokusai, quien estaba loco por el arte." Collection: The San Diego Museum of Art

The_Gorge_at_Varengeville_by_Claude_Mone.story: Varengeville-sur-Mer is a cliff-top village near Dieppe where chalky ravines tumble down to the Channel. Monet spent several weeks there in the spring and summer of 1882, setting up his easel along the gorges and customs paths that cut through the gorse. This canvas, on long-term loan to the Legion of Honor in San Francisco, is loose and sun-struck — green slope, blue sea, flecks of red and yellow in the scrub. The same gorge would later draw the painter Auburtin, who treated it as a reply.

The_Holy_Family_with_St._Elizabeth,_St._.story: A tiny panel, no bigger than a magazine. Mary lets the infant John wrangle a dove while Christ reaches, curious, for the fluttering wings. Elizabeth watches like any aunt who's seen this game end in feathers. Rubens painted it on oak, probably as a private devotional piece for an Antwerp patron after his 1608 return from Rome. It's at LACMA now, gift of the Denis fund in 1953.

The_Hookah_Lighter.jpg.story: A nude young woman crouches over a charcoal brazier, coaxing the hookah to life. Smoke curls, tile work gleams, embers glow. It's Gérôme in full Orientalist mode: a European fantasy of the Middle East, meticulously rendered down to the grout lines, untroubled by whether anyone actually lit a hookah this way. The paint is enamel-smooth, the anatomy academy-correct. Painted in 1898, six years before the artist's death.

The_House_on_the_River_Zaan_in_Zaandam.j.story: Zaandam, summer 1871. Exiled by war, Monet had wandered from London back through Holland and set up for some four months in this little town near Amsterdam, making roughly twenty quick views of its waterfronts and windmills. A house reflected in the river, brushed in fast; the point is the water's wobble, not the architecture. Part of what's sometimes called his Dutch interlude.

The_Ill-matched_Pair_(Jan_Massys)_-_Nati.story: A favourite Flemish joke turned into a painting: a young woman in an orange dress leans into a bald, bearded old man, her hand on his jaw, his on her breast. At right, a grinning procuress reaches for his purse while he is distracted; at far left, an older woman watches through a doorway, amused. On the table, gold coins in a dish, a plate of grapes, a loaf, and a monkey peeking up from behind the fruit — standard iconography for lust and greed getting their due. Jan Matsys, banished from Antwerp for years over his Protestantism, made this in 1566, the year the city fell apart in iconoclasm.

The_Incredulity_of_Saint_Thomas-Caravagg.story: Christ guides Thomas's finger into the wound — not a metaphor, not from a distance, but knuckle-deep, the skin puckering around it. Two other apostles lean in, foreheads almost touching, as if they're the ones who need convincing. Vincenzo Giustiniani, the Roman banker who already owned a pile of Caravaggios, commissioned it around 1601. It went to Prussia in 1816 when the Giustiniani collection was sold off and has hung in Sanssouci, outside Berlin, ever since.

The_Junction_of_the_Thames_and_the_Medwa.story: Where the two rivers meet off the north Kent coast, the water goes choppy and the shipping has to work for it. Four men bail out a rowboat in the foreground while a brig fights the wind behind. Turner showed it at his own Queen Anne Street gallery in 1807, not the Royal Academy, and the debt to 17th-century Dutch storm painters like Jan van de Cappelle is open and obvious. It's been at the National Gallery of Art in Washington since 1942.

The_Luncheon_by_Claude_Monet_-_Städel_-_.story: An interrupted meal: a soft-boiled egg in its cup, a half-peeled orange, the newspaper pushed aside, Camille waiting with little Jean in his high chair while a visitor hovers near the window. The canvas is enormous — 2.3 by 1.5 metres — a scale until then reserved for history painting, not a domestic table. Monet submitted it to the 1870 Salon, which rejected it; four years later it went into the first Impressionist exhibition. It hangs at the Städel Museum in Frankfurt.

The_Lute_Player_).jpg.story: An Arnaut soldier sits in a bare room, lute cradled against his chest, rifle and hookah at the ready. Gérôme had just returned from his first trip to Egypt in 1856, and the Balkan mercenaries he'd seen in Cairo's streets were already elbowing their way into his work. Look close and you can see where he lavished the attention: the silver butt of a pistol, the brass glint of the hookah stem, the blue shadows threading through the lute's belly. The canvas is small, barely larger than a sheet of paper. Signed and dated 1858.

An egg-shell torso, bare-branch arms, boat-like feet floating on water. Tiny people go about tavern business inside the hollow body. It's one of maybe ten surviving drawings confidently by him. The_Milk_Maid_by_Winslow_Homer,_1878.png.story: A barefoot milkmaid carries a wooden yoke across her shoulders, two buckets swinging, while a cow grazes behind her and a rooster pokes at the grass. Homer built the watercolor in 1878 from studies made at Houghton Farm in Mountainville, New York, where he spent that summer sketching farm children with a freshness that startled New York reviewers. Light dapples through the leaves and catches her striped shawl. The sheet, roughly 20 by 14 inches, is in the National Gallery of Art, Washington.

The_Muezzin,_1865,_Jean-Léon_Gérôme_(.description: The Muezzin, 1865, Jean-Léon Gérôme (French, 1824–1904), oil on canvas, Joslyn Art Museum

The_Muezzin,_1865,_Jean-Léon_Gérôme_(.story: Gérôme paints the muezzin mid-call: a solitary figure on a minaret balcony, his mouth just slightly open, a smear of birds wheeling past. Cairo stretches below in hazy ochre, other minarets rising from the sprawl like thin fingers. The wooden railing and cage-like cupola are rendered with almost pedantic precision, which was Gérôme's brand. There's no crowd, no response, no ritual spectacle: just one man, the city, and a voice you can't hear. It's atypical for nineteenth-century Orientalism in how quiet it is. The photograph is by Bruce M. White for the Joslyn Art Museum.

The_Old_Adam_and_Eve.jpg.title: The Old Adam and Eve
The_Old_Adam_and_Eve.jpg.description: Illustration By Edmund Joseph Sullivan for Sartor Resartus by Thomas Carlyle

source.canonical_title: File:The Old Adam and Eve.jpg

The_Old_Adam_and_Eve.jpg.story: A pen-and-ink illustration from Sullivan's 1898 edition of Carlyle's Sartor Resartus - the strange philosophical novel about a German professor of clothes. Sullivan gives us Adam and Eve stripped of everything except the tree and the serpent, scratched out in thick, nervous black lines that owe something to William Blake and something to Aubrey Beardsley. The couple stand on either side of the trunk like heraldic supporters; the snake coils between them in a long S. A tiny image, done for reproduction at book-page size, where every line has to carry weight.

The_Petit_Bras_of_the_Seine_at_Argenteui.title: The Petit Bras of the Seine at Argenteuil
The_Petit_Bras_of_the_Seine_at_Argenteui.description: The Petit Bras of the Seine at Argenteuil is a painting by Claude Monet currently in the national gallery

source.canonical_title: File:The Petit Bras of the Seine at Argenteuil.jpg

The_Petit_Bras_of_the_Seine_at_Argenteui.story: A backwater of the Seine, the side channel that slips behind the Ile Marante at Argenteuil. No boats, no bathers, just bare autumn trees doubled in still water. Monet is quieter here than in his regatta pictures, letting the reflections do the talking; the surface is so glassy the painting reads almost symmetrically. He was twenty-nine, newly installed in the town, and feeling out its quieter corners. The canvas entered the National Gallery in London in 1979 as part of the Hugh Beaumont bequest.

The_Pond_at_Benten_Shrine_in_Shiba,_Kawa.title: The Pond at Benten Shrine in Shiba, Kawase Hasui, MFAB 50.2885
The_Pond_at_Benten_Shrine_in_Shiba,_Kawa.description: The Pond at Benten Shrine in Shiba

source.canonical_title: File:The Pond at Benten Shrine in Shiba, Kawase Hasui, MFAB 50.2885.jpg

The_Pond_at_Benten_Shrine_in_Shiba,_Kawa.story: August 1929. Hasui sets you on the far side of the pond in Shiba Park, the red torii of the Benten shrine floating behind a screen of lotus pads, two women crossing the little bridge in summer kimono. He had lost almost everything - sketchbooks, blocks, his house - in the Great Kanto earthquake six years earlier and had spent the late 1920s rebuilding his archive of Tokyo views one print at a time. The shrine island itself wouldn't survive the war. The MFA Boston copy, accession 50.2885, is one of the early impressions before the original blocks were destroyed in the 1945 air raids.

The_Ragpicker_1869_Edouard_Manet.jpg.title: The Ragpicker

source.canonical_title: File:The Ragpicker 1869 Edouard Manet.jpg
source.credit: 1. The Athenaeum: Home - info - pic 2. The Norton Simon Museum

The_Ragpicker_1869_Edouard_Manet.jpg.story: A bearded old man in tattered brown rags stands nearly life-size against an empty background, a wine bottle at his feet and a hook in his hand. Manet called him a philosopher. He's the last and largest of four full-length figures Manet painted in homage to Velázquez, whose own ragged beggars he'd studied in Madrid. The canvas left Manet's studio in 1872 but he likely reworked it around 1876-77. The file says 1865 and the Norton Simon Museum dates it c. 1865-70.

The_Rising_Squall,_Hot_Wells,_from_St_Vi.title: The Rising Squall, Hot Wells, from St Vincent's Rock, Bristol

source.canonical_title: File:The Rising Squall, Hot Wells, from St Vincent's Rock, Bristol).jpg
source.credit: Sotheby's, London, 2 July 2025, L25033, lot 28 ( 2000 × 1609 pixel / 1,40 MB ) — with frame

The_Rising_Squall,_Hot_Wells,_from_St_Vi.story: Wind shoves rain across the Avon gorge; a small boat tilts below St Vincent's Rock. Turner was seventeen when he painted it in 1792, working up an oil from sketchbook drawings he'd made the previous summer near Bristol. It was his very first oil to be exhibited at the Royal Academy, shown in 1793 a few days before his eighteenth birthday. The picture vanished for 150 years, was mistaken for a lesser hand, then resurfaced at Sotheby's in 2024 and sold the following year for about 2 million pounds.
The_Rising_Squall,_Hot_Wells,_from_St_Vi.year_note: Dataset year 1775 is Turner's birth year. Painting was made in 1792 and exhibited at the Royal Academy in 1793, his first exhibited oil.

source.canonical_title: File:The Sea at Le Havre 1868.jpg

The_Sea_at_Le_Havre_1868.jpg.story: Choppy water, a hard wind tearing at the tops of the waves, sky the color of wet slate. Monet grew up in Sainte-Adresse, the suburb whose beach this view looks out from, and by 1868 he had been painting the Channel for years. The paint is laid on thick and fast, scraped and dragged — you can feel the weather in the surface. He showed it at the second Impressionist exhibition in 1876. The Carnegie Museum of Art in Pittsburgh bought it in 1953.

The_Seine_at_Bougival_1946_4.jpg.title: The Seine at Bougival

source.canonical_title: File:The Seine at Bougival 1946 4.jpg

The_Seine_at_Bougival_1946_4.jpg.story: Another look at that same 1858 road bridge near Bougival, painted in 1869 from a low, offhand vantage. Monet had settled in the hamlet of Saint-Michel that year with Camille and Jean, and he kept returning to this span over the Seine, working out how to set down moving water, overcast sky and riverbank trees without polishing any of it. The loose touch is the whole argument. The canvas is an oil, roughly 65 by 92 cm.

The_Sleepers_by_Gustave_Courbet.jpg.title: The Sleepers

source.canonical_title: File:The Sleepers by Gustave Courbet.jpg

The_Sleepers_by_Gustave_Courbet.jpg.story: Two women entangled in sleep after sex, pearls scattered, a broken hairpin on the sheet. Courbet painted it in 1866 for Khalil-Bey, an Ottoman diplomat with a taste for erotic commissions (he also owned Courbet's Origin of the World). It skipped the Salon entirely and hid in private hands. French authorities wouldn't permit public display until 1988. Today it hangs at the Petit Palais in Paris.

The_Tea_plantation_of_Katakura_in_the_Su.story: A full working day compressed onto one sheet. Women in bamboo hats pick leaves on the slope; others rest on benches; men haul baskets on their shoulders; at the bottom a man drags a reluctant horse across a plank bridge. A pine frames the right edge. Fuji's snow cone rises behind. Critics have always thought this one a bit busy for a single print — more like a page from an illustrated book.
