The_Triumph_Of_Christianity_Over_Paganis.title: The Triumph of Christianity over Paganism
The_Triumph_Of_Christianity_Over_Paganis.description: The Triumph Of Christianity Over Paganism (1868?). Oil in canvas. 118 x 79 in. Christ, carrying a Cross, surrounded by a host of angels, forming a circle, swords ready to attack, sweeping above pagan gods of every kind. The Joey and Tobey Tanenbaum Collection, 2002. Art Gallery of Hamilton, Ontario. Painted by Gustave Doré; Published in London on October 1st, 1899, by the Doré Gallery, 35, New Bond St. W. Copyright Registered, engraved by W.H. Simmons. Printed by Crowdy & Loud, 7, Pall Mall London, S.W."

source.canonical_title: File:The Triumph Of Christianity Over Paganism.Gustave Doré.jpg

title.fr: Le triomphe de Christianisme sur le paganisme

The_Triumph_Of_Christianity_Over_Paganis.story: Doré's huge canvas for the 1868 opening of his Doré Gallery on New Bond Street — roughly ten feet tall and painted to impress. Christ, cross in hand, leads a sword-swinging ring of angels that sweeps down through the clouds on top of Zeus, Venus, and the rest of the classical pantheon. It's propaganda on a grand scale, aimed at Victorian churchgoers who'd pay a shilling to see it. Now at the Art Gallery of Hamilton, Ontario, via the Tanenbaum gift.

The_Triumph_of_Bacchus;_oil_on_canvas,_1.title: The Triumph of Bacchus; oil on canvas, 1736 Charles-Joseph Natoire
The_Triumph_of_Bacchus;_oil_on_canvas,_1.description: The Triumph of Bacchus , oil on canvas painting by Charles-Joseph Natoire, 1736

source.canonical_title: File:The Triumph of Bacchus; oil on canvas, 1736 Charles-Joseph Natoire.jpg

The_Triumph_of_Bacchus;_oil_on_canvas,_1.story: A procession comes roaring out of the wine-dark: Bacchus enthroned on a cart, satyrs and bacchantes spilling grapes and cymbals, Silenus wobbling in the rear. Natoire painted this mid-1730s Triumph at the height of his powers, when contemporaries still ranked him beside Boucher. He liked the subject enough to return to it years later for a competition piece now in the Louvre. This earlier canvas is lighter on its feet — all garland and glissade, Rococo mythology as a dance figure, not a thesis.

The_Triumph_of_Death_by_Pieter_Bruegel_t.title: The Triumph of Death
The_Triumph_of_Death_by_Pieter_Bruegel_t.description: Obra moral que muestra el triunfo de la Muerte sobre las cosas mundanas, simbolizado a través de un gran ejército de esqueletos arrasando la Tierra. Al fondo aparece un paisaje yermo donde aún se desarrollan escenas de destrucción. En un primer plano, la Muerte al frente de sus ejércitos sobre un caballo rojizo, destruye el mundo de los vivos, quienes son conducidos a un enorme ataúd, sin esperanza de salvación. Todos los estamentos sociales están incluidos en la composición, sin que el poder o la devoción pueda salvarles.

source.canonical_title: File:The Triumph of Death by Pieter Bruegel the Elder.jpg

The_Triumph_of_Death_by_Pieter_Bruegel_t.story: An army of skeletons sweeps across a scorched landscape herding the living into a giant coffin. A king clutches his gold, a cardinal is led off by a skeleton in a mitre, lovers play a lute oblivious behind an overturned table. Bruegel painted it around 1562, a few years after a devastating plague in the Low Countries, and stuffed it with ways to die: hanging, drowning, fire, the blade. The Prado in Madrid acquired it in 1827 and finished a four-year restoration in 2018.

The_Triumph_of_Frederik_Hendrik,_by_Jaco.title: Triumph of Frederick Henry, Prince of Orange

source.canonical_title: File:The Triumph of Frederik Hendrik, by Jacob Jordaens (I).jpg

The_Triumph_of_Frederik_Hendrik,_by_Jaco.story: The centerpiece of Amalia van Solms' memorial hall for her husband — the enormous Oranjezaal at Huis ten Bosch. Frederick Henry, the stadtholder who'd turned the tide of the Eighty Years' War against Spain, rides in a triumphal chariot attended by Victory, bound captives, banners and a swirl of allegorical figures. Jordaens, a sometime-Protestant, got the main commission over Catholic Rubens partly for political reasons. The painting is still in situ — one of the few 17th-century decorative schemes in Europe never moved from the room it was designed for. Huis ten Bosch, The Hague.

The_Vision_of_The_Valley_of_The_Dry_Bone.title: The Vision of The Valley of The Dry Bones
The_Vision_of_The_Valley_of_The_Dry_Bone.description: Scan of a Gustave Doré engraving "The Vision of The Valley of The Dry Bones" - 1866

source.canonical_title: File:The Vision of The Valley of The Dry Bones.jpg

The_Vision_of_The_Valley_of_The_Dry_Bone.story: Ezekiel stands at the mouth of a valley littered with skulls and ribs, hand raised, waiting for the bones to knit. Doré cut the plate for his massive illustrated Bible, engraved by Charles Laplante — Doré's signature at bottom left, the engraver's at right. He piles the dead in deep perspective so the valley seems to keep going past the frame. The restraint is what's striking: no resurrection yet, just the prophet and the wreckage, the breath about to come.

The_Wailing_Wall_by_Bauernfeind.jpeg.title: The Wailing Wall by Bauernfeind
The_Wailing_Wall_by_Bauernfeind.jpeg.description: Gustav Bauernfeind: The Wailing Wall, Jerusalem

source.canonical_title: File:The Wailing Wall by Bauernfeind.jpeg

The_Wailing_Wall_by_Bauernfeind.jpeg.story: Jews at prayer along the base of the Western Wall, the enormous Herodian stones rising into afternoon shadow above them. Bauernfeind painted the site several times; this 1887 version, now in a private collection, is the best known. He is interested equally in the wall as architecture and in the individual figures, old men in black coats, younger ones in striped robes. The painting pre-dates mass tourism, electric light, and most of modern Jerusalem, and it feels it.

The_Water-Lily_Pond_-_Google_Arts_&_Cult.title: the-water-lily-pond
The_Water-Lily_Pond_-_Google_Arts_&_Cult.description: A high resolution scan of The Water-Lily Pond hosted on the Google Arts & Culture page

source.canonical_title: File:The Water-Lily Pond - Google Arts & Culture.jpg

The_Water-Lily_Pond_-_Google_Arts_&_Cult.story: Monet bought the marshy scrap of land across the road from his Giverny house in 1893, dammed the little Ru stream, and built a Japanese footbridge over the new pond. By 1899 the water lilies had taken and he began painting the bridge in earnest — twelve canvases that first summer from a single vantage point. Green on green on green, the bridge arcing like a drawn bow, lily pads floating like scattered coins. He'd return to this motif obsessively for the next twenty-six years, eventually producing roughly 250 water-lily paintings.

source.canonical_title: File:The White Horse by John Constable - Google Art Project.jpg

The_White_Horse_by_John_Constable_-_Goog.story: A workhorse being ferried across the Stour in a flat-bottomed boat, because the towpath has run out on its side of the river. Constable loved this ordinary piece of Suffolk logistics enough to make it the first of his six-footers actually to sell at the Royal Academy, in 1819. The sale, to his friend John Fisher, finally got him elected an Associate of the Academy after years of polite rejection. He later called it 'one of the happiest of my pictures.' It now lives in the Frick Collection in New York.

The_Zuiderkerk,_Amsterdam_by_Claude_Mone.title: The Zuiderkerk, Amsterdam (Looking up the Groenburgwal)
The_Zuiderkerk,_Amsterdam_by_Claude_Mone.description: The Zuiderkerk, Amsterdam (Looking up the Groenburgwal) at the Philadelphia Museum of Art.

source.canonical_title: File:The Zuiderkerk, Amsterdam by Claude Monet, 1874.jpg

The_Zuiderkerk,_Amsterdam_by_Claude_Mone.story: Looking up the Groenburgwal, the Zuiderkerk tower punches into a pale sky while a houseboat leans in the foreground. Monet had fled to the Netherlands in 1871 to dodge the Franco-Prussian war, and the Amsterdam canals gave him straight lines and flat light he rarely got at home. The canvas now hangs at the Philadelphia Museum of Art.

The_back_of_the_Fuji_from_the_Minobu_riv.story: Fuji seen from the west, which tradition calls 'ura-Fuji' — the back. Hokusai flanks it with two jagged peaks borrowed straight from Chinese landscape painting, making the sacred mountain look almost shy between its neighbors. Below, the Minobu River surges in curling waves, dotted dark blue. A man leads two horses one way; bearers carrying a palanquin come the other. They're on the pilgrim road to Kuonji, head temple of the Nichiren sect.

The_coast_of_seven_leages_in_Kamakura.jp.story: Shichirigahama — the Seven-League Beach — curving out into the Pacific between Kamakura and Fujisawa. A fishing village huddles at the bend, thatched roofs clustered. Beyond the promontory, across open water, snow-covered Fuji. The earliest impressions came out entirely in Prussian blue, an aizuri-e; later printings added green for the vegetation. In Hokusai's day the stretch was already a pleasure resort.

The_end_of_the_pose,_by_Jean-Léon_Géro.title: The End of the Session" Alternative title(s): The end of the pose The End of the Sitting [ 1 ]

source.canonical_title: File:The end of the pose, by Jean-Léon Gérôme.jpg

The_end_of_the_pose,_by_Jean-Léon_Géro.story: The session is over. A nude model, back to us, pulls on a robe while the sculptor — Gérôme himself, more or less — stands by his clay figure. The picture is a quiet studio joke about his own late-career shift into sculpture, and about the seams between the working day and the finished work: the plinth, the scraps of cloth, the posing stand. After decades painting other people's harems, Gérôme turns the camera around on his own workshop.

The_grand_canal_of_Venice_(Blue_Venice)_.title: The grand canal of Venice (Blue Venice)
The_grand_canal_of_Venice_(Blue_Venice)_.description: Manet made this painting during a trip to Venice in 1875. The work is different in mood from his North Atlantic seascapes. Manet had spent time painting alongside Claude Monet that summer and he employed brighter colors and broken brushstrokes to create the visual splendor of Venetian canals. This painting is part of the collections of the Shelburne Museum, Shelburne, Vermont.

source.canonical_title: File:The grand canal of Venice (Blue Venice) - Edouard Manet.png

The_grand_canal_of_Venice_(Blue_Venice)_.story: Manet spent the autumn of 1875 in Venice and came home with gondolas. The water here is not the muddy green of the real canal but a clanging ultramarine, slashed with white reflections and striped mooring poles in candy-cane red and white. He'd just been painting beside Monet and the broken brushwork shows. The Palazzo Barbaro sits in the distance, made almost weightless. It hangs at the Shelburne Museum in Vermont, which is not where you'd expect to find Venice.

The_lake_of_Hakone_in_the_Segami_provinc.story: A rare Hokusai landscape with no people in it, and no animals either. Morning fog slides across Hakone Lake, threading through the pines, softening the hills. A few thatched roofs sit among the trees on the right shore. Beyond the still blue water, Fuji. The restraint is almost startling after the crowded fishing scenes and ferry crossings elsewhere in the series — just weather, water, and the mountain.

Théodore_Géricault_-_Heroic_Landscape_.story: Another of the 1818 heroic landscapes, this one set at an invented waterside where fishermen go about their work under towering rocks and ambiguous weather. The scale is operatic; the human figures are small enough to feel almost incidental. Gericault builds the mood with massed shadow, rising cloud, and a sense that the real subject is the weight of the scenery pressing down on small lives. It's the same appetite for drama that, a year later, he'd pour into the Raft of the Medusa.

Théodore_Géricault_-_Portrait_of_a_Kle.story: One of Gericault's late series of ten portraits of psychiatric patients, painted around 1820 for the alienist Etienne-Jean Georget at the Salpetriere. Each sitter represents a diagnosed monomania; this one, a compulsive thief. Gericault gives him the same dignified, close-cropped, steady-eyed treatment a salon portraitist would give a banker — no caricature, no symbolism, no theatre. In an age that routinely mocked the insane, that neutrality was radical. Only five of the ten paintings are known to survive.

Théodore_Géricault_-_The_Kiss_-_WGA086.story: A late, intimate Gericault, painted in 1822 while his health was already failing from the riding injuries that would kill him two years later. The Kiss is small, private, and closer in feeling to a sketch than to his grand Salon machines — two lovers locked together, handled with the fleshy directness he brought to everything. After the public scandals of the Medusa and the psychiatric portraits, it's a reminder that his range was wider than his reputation: romantic in the other sense of the word.

Thomas-howard-rubensportrait.jpg.title: Portrait of Thomas Howard, 21st Earl of Arundel

source.canonical_title: File:Thomas-howard-rubensportrait.jpg

Thomas-howard-rubensportrait.jpg.story: Thomas Howard, 21st Earl of Arundel, was England's greatest collector of antique sculpture and Old Master drawings — his "Arundel Marbles" ended up at Oxford. Rubens met him during the London mission of 1629-30 and painted him around then, aged 44 or 45, in full armour with a gold baton: Arundel was Earl Marshal, ceremonial head of the English nobility. The portrait sat in private hands until Isabella Stewart Gardner paid £21,000 for it in March 1898, her priciest purchase after Titian's Europa. It now hangs in her Fenway palace in Boston.

Thomas_Eakins,_American_-_Portrait_of_Dr.title: Portrait of Dr. Samuel D. Gross (The Gross Clinic)
Thomas_Eakins,_American_-_Portrait_of_Dr.artist: Thomas Eakins, American, 1844 - 1916 (1844 - 1916) – Artist/Maker (American) Born in Philadelphia, Pennsylvania, United States. Died in Philadelphia, Pennsylvania, United States. Details on Google Art Project

source.canonical_title: File:Thomas Eakins, American - Portrait of Dr. Samuel D. Gross (The Gross Clinic) - Google Art Project.jpg
source.credit: tQFcdDEg20osqg at Google Cultural Institute maximum zoom level

Thomas_Eakins,_American_-_Portrait_of_Dr.story: Dr. Gross, scalpel bloody, pauses mid-lecture while his team operates on a patient's thigh. Behind them, the patient's mother cringes and hides her eyes. Eakins was thirty-one and painting his own teacher for the 1876 Centennial Exhibition; the jury rejected it as too gory and hung it in a medical pavilion with the army-hospital exhibits. Philadelphia kept it for 130 years, then nearly lost it to a Wal-Mart-funded buyer in 2006 before a public campaign raised $68 million to keep it. It lives at the Philadelphia Museum of Art.

source.canonical_title: File:Thomas Gainsborough - Cattle Watering by a Stream - Google Art Project.jpg
source.credit: xAEIetBVtfBolw at Google Cultural Institute maximum zoom level

Thomas_Gainsborough_-_Coastal_Landscape_.title: Coastal Landscape with a Shepherd and His Flock

source.canonical_title: File:Thomas Gainsborough - Coastal Landscape with a Shepherd and His Flock - Google Art Project.jpg
source.credit: uQExDZ9wUXdRhw at Google Cultural Institute maximum zoom level

Thomas_Gainsborough_-_Coastal_Landscape_.story: A shepherd and his dog drive sheep along a rocky shoreline while a fishing boat slides across a pale, silvery bay. By 1783 Gainsborough was sixty-one, living in London, painting for the King, and increasingly drawn to these hushed, almost moonlit coastlines, probably inspired by a summer tour to the Lake District. The palette is thinned down to grey-green and oyster; the flock almost dissolves into the cliff. It hangs in the Cincinnati Art Museum.

Thomas_Gainsborough_-_Hilly_Landscape_wi.title: Hilly Landscape with Figures Approaching a Bridge

source.canonical_title: File:Thomas Gainsborough - Hilly Landscape with Figures Approaching a Bridge - Google Art Project.jpg
source.credit: QQEt9B7ARFCb1A at Google Cultural Institute maximum zoom level

Thomas_Gainsborough_-_Hilly_Landscape_wi.story: Gainsborough made his living painting faces but loved landscape best. Here a peasant couple on donkeys picks its way toward a rickety plank bridge, sheep scattered on the slope, a ruined tower on the ridge. None of it was sketched outdoors: he built miniature stage sets on a tabletop from broccoli, moss, cork and broken mirrors, lit them with candles, and painted from those. The result is half Suffolk, half fantasy. Dated around 1763, it hangs in the Cincinnati Art Museum.

Thomas_Gainsborough_-_Mr_and_Mrs_Andrews.title: Mr. and Mrs. Andrews
Thomas_Gainsborough_-_Mr_and_Mrs_Andrews.description: Robert Andrews of the Auberies and Frances Carter of Ballingdon House after the marriage.

source.canonical_title: File:Thomas Gainsborough - Mr and Mrs Andrews.jpg

title.ca: El senyor i la senyora Andrews
title.es: El Señor y la Señora Andrews

Thomas_Gainsborough_-_Mr_and_Mrs_Andrews.story: Robert Andrews has a fowling piece under his arm and a slightly bored spaniel at his knee. Frances, newly his wife, sits on a rococo bench in a sky-blue silk dress that looks expensive even now. Behind them stretches the Auberies estate: clean stooks of wheat, pollarded oaks, a drilled field that was up-to-the-minute agriculture in 1750. Gainsborough, barely out of his apprenticeship, seems more interested in the stubble and the cloud bank than in the couple. Her lap is unfinished — the story goes she was meant to be holding a pheasant her husband had just shot.

Thomas_Gainsborough_-_Mrs._Richard_Brins.title: Portrait of Mrs. Richard Brinsley Sheridan

source.canonical_title: File:Thomas Gainsborough - Mrs. Richard Brinsley Sheridan .jpg
source.credit: National Gallery of Art pen Access Images Project. Link: https://www.nga.gov/content/ngaweb/Collection/art-object-page.99.html

title.my: မစ္စ ရစ်ချတ် ဘရင်းစလီ ရှယ်ရီဒန်

Thomas_Gainsborough_-_Mrs._Richard_Brins.story: Elizabeth Linley was a celebrated soprano who gave up the stage when she married the playwright Sheridan in 1773. By 1785 the marriage was fraying and her health was going. Gainsborough sits her outside, in a windblown park, her shawl and hair tugged by the same breeze that stirs the trees behind. No lute, no score, no nod to her famous voice. He treats the landscape and the sitter with the same loose, feathered strokes, so she half-dissolves into the weather. She died seven years later of tuberculosis.

Thomas_Gainsborough_-_Road_from_Market_-.title: Road from Market

source.canonical_title: File:Thomas Gainsborough - Road from Market - Google Art Project.jpg
source.credit: ugG16d2TvlRyYw at Google Cultural Institute maximum zoom level

Thomas_Gainsborough_-_Road_from_Market_-.story: Dusk on a lane cut through English woods: a girl rides pillion behind a farmhand, a boy trails with the dog, the horses pick their way home through gold light filtering between the oaks. Gainsborough painted this around 1767–68 for his own pleasure, not a patron, during his Bath years when he was the fashionable portraitist to the spa set. Reynolds called him a painter of landscapes forced into faces. The Toledo Museum of Art in Ohio has owned it since 1955.

Three_Friends_of_Winter_by_Zhao_Mengjian.title: Three Friends of Winter 歲寒三友
Three_Friends_of_Winter_by_Zhao_Mengjian.artist: Zhao Mengjian 趙孟堅 b. 1199 - d. circa 1264

Tintoretto,_Jacopo_-_Christ_at_the_Sea_o.title: Christ at the Sea of Galilee

source.canonical_title: File:Tintoretto, Jacopo - Christ at the Sea of Galilee.jpg
source.credit: 1. The Yorck Project (2002) 10.000 Meisterwerke der Malerei (DVD-ROM), distributed by DIRECTMEDIA Publishing GmbH. ISBN : 3936122202 . 2. National Gallery of Art

title.de: Christus am See Tiberias / Genezareth / Galilei

Tintoretto,_Jacopo_-_Christ_at_the_Sea_o.story: Long attributed to Tintoretto, now usually given to Lambert Sustris or another hand in his circle. Christ stands on the left shore in a pink-and-blue robe, beckoning; the disciples labor with a sail in a heaving green sea. The water is genuinely strange — churning in decorative, almost calligraphic whitecaps — and the figures feel stretched and Mannerist in a way that doesn't quite match Tintoretto's Venetian punch. Sustris, an Amsterdammer who spent most of his career in Titian's Venice under the name Alberto de Olanda, is the current best guess. The painting is in the National Gallery, Washington.

source.canonical_title: File:Tintoretto - Prayer in the Garden.jpg
File:Tintoretto - St Mary Magdalen.jpg
File:Tintoretto - The Baptism of Christ.jpg

Tintoretto_and_lukrecja.jpeg.title: Tarquin and Lucretia

source.canonical_title: File:Tintoretto and lukrecja.jpeg

Tintoretto_and_lukrecja.jpeg.story: Tintoretto seizes the worst moment: Tarquin, son of Rome's king, forcing himself on the matron Lucretia. A pillow tumbles mid-air, her pearl necklace snaps into a scatter of white beads, and the bed's carved canopy seems to buckle over them. Il Furioso paints the violence as architecture collapsing. Lucretia's suicide afterward will bring down the monarchy and birth the Roman Republic; Tintoretto does not show that part. He shows the split second no Renaissance decorum can glaze over. The canvas has hung at the Art Institute of Chicago since 1949.

Tintoretto_—_Deposition_(Accademia).jpg.title: Lamentation over the Dead Christ

source.canonical_title: File:Tintoretto — Deposition (Accademia).jpg

Tintoretto_—_Deposition_(Accademia).jpg.story: Painted near the end of Tintoretto's life for the church of San Giorgio Maggiore and now at the Gallerie dell'Accademia, this Lamentation is lit as if by a guttering candle. Christ's body sags in a diagonal slash of pale flesh; the Virgin collapses behind him, mourners dissolving into the dark. Gone is the theatrical bravura of the Scuola di San Rocco years. What is left is grief thinned almost to smoke, brushed in with the same urgency that earned him the nickname Il Furioso, now turned inward.

Titian_-_Self-portrait_(Museo_del_Prado).title: Self-Portrait
Titian_-_Self-portrait_(Museo_del_Prado).description: Self-portrait of the Italian painter Tiziano Vecellio (c. 1490-1576), better known as Titian.

Titian_-_Self-portrait_(Museo_del_Prado).story: Titian paints himself as he wants to be remembered: bearded, gold-chained, dressed in sober black, gripping a paintbrush like a man who still has work to do. He was probably in his seventies when he made this around 1562, though he often shaved a decade off his age for the Spanish court. There's no easel, no studio clutter, just the profile of a painter who outlived every rival. The canvas hangs in the Prado, across rooms from the mythologies he sent to Philip II.

Titian_-_The_Flaying_of_Marsyas.jpg.title: The Flaying of Marsyas

source.canonical_title: File:Titian - The Flaying of Marsyas.jpg
source.credit: 1./2. Scanned from the book The Complete World of Greek Mythology , ISBN 0500251215 (orginal uploaded by en:User:BorgQueen as en:Image:The Flaying of Marsyas.jpg ) 3. Bridgeman Art Library : Object 388734

Titian_-_The_Flaying_of_Marsyas.jpg.story: The satyr Marsyas lost a music contest to Apollo and the prize was his own skin. Titian paints the punishment in progress: Marsyas strung upside-down from a tree, Apollo kneeling with a knife, a small dog lapping at the blood. The brushwork is so loose it almost dissolves the figures into the forest gloom, and the seated figure on the right, chin on fist, is often read as Titian himself watching. He worked on it into his final years and it was still in his studio when he died in 1576.

Tizian_-_Danae_receiving_the_Golden_Rain.title: Danaë
Tizian_-_Danae_receiving_the_Golden_Rain.description: La obra representa a Dánae desnuda en su lecho y recibiendo a Zeus , que apareció en forma de lluvia de oro y la dejó embarazada.

source.canonical_title: File:Tizian - Danae receiving the Golden Rain - Prado.jpg
source.credit: Official gallery link Enlace a la galería oficial

title.es: Dánae recibiendo la lluvia de oro

Tizian_-_Danae_receiving_the_Golden_Rain.story: Zeus, forbidden to approach Danaë in the flesh, slips past her tower by becoming a shower of gold. Titian paints the moment the metal rain hits the bedsheets: a greedy nurse lunges with her apron to catch the coins while Danaë tilts back, lost in the clouds above her. Philip II of Spain commissioned this version as part of Titian's series of mythological 'poesie,' sensual pictures meant for his private gallery. It was painted in Venice around 1553 and shipped to Madrid, where it still hangs in the Prado today.

Tizian_-_Portrait_of_Federico_II_Gonzaga.title: Portrait of Federico II Gonzaga .

source.canonical_title: File:Tizian - Portrait of Federico II Gonzaga - circa 1525.jpg

Tizian_-_Portrait_of_Federico_II_Gonzaga.story: Federico II Gonzaga, Marquis of Mantua, in slashed blue silk, one hand resting on a small white Maltese spaniel that seems more alert than he is. Titian painted him around 1529, not 1525, during a diplomatic stop in Mantua; Federico liked the result enough to become a long-term patron, funnelling commissions to the painter for the next decade. The dog is a nod to courtly manners: loyalty, fidelity, domestic refinement. The portrait hangs in the Prado in Madrid.

Tizian_015_(2).jpg.title: Diana and Callisto

source.canonical_title: File:Tizian 015 (2).jpg

Tizian_015_(2).jpg.story: The nymph Callisto, pregnant by Zeus, has been hauled forward by her companions; Diana, enthroned on the right, jabs a finger and banishes her from the chaste troop. Water tumbles, dogs pant, pale bodies pile against dark trees. Titian delivered it to Philip II of Spain in 1559 along with its pendant Diana and Actaeon, the fifth and sixth of his Ovidian poesie. The two paintings were bought jointly by the National Gallery London and the National Galleries of Scotland in 2012, for £45 million.

Tizian_085.jpg.title: The Rape of Europa

source.canonical_title: File:Tizian 085.jpg

Tizian_085.jpg.story: Zeus has turned into a white bull and Europa is in trouble. Titian catches her mid-abduction: she's tumbled back across the bull's shoulders, one sandal dangling, a pink scarf ballooning overhead while cupids cartwheel through the sky. The surface is pure late Titian, smeared and fingered until the water looks wet. He finished it around 1562 for Philip II of Spain, the final 'poesia' in the series. Isabella Stewart Gardner bought it for her Boston museum in 1896 and it has never toured since.

Tizian_091.jpg.title: The Fall of Man

source.canonical_title: File:Tizian 091.jpg

Tizian_091.jpg.story: Adam recoils, reaching up as if to stop Eve; Eve, half-turned and glowing, takes the apple from a chubby, oddly smiling child-serpent coiled in the tree. Titian painted this around 1550 for a Spanish patron, possibly Mary of Hungary. Rubens saw it in Madrid sixty years later and made a near-copy, which now hangs beside the original in the Prado. The two Adams are a good way to feel the gap between Venetian warmth and Flemish muscle. Titian's version is the quieter, older one.

Torii_Kotondo_-_Kamisuki_(Combing_Her_Ha.story: Kotondo's 'Kamisuki' from 1929 - a woman crouched nude, drawing a wooden comb down a long slide of black hair. The back of the sheet is softened with a grey mica-like wash so she seems to kneel inside a dim room. Four years later a companion print, Asanegami, got seized by the authorities for being too erotic, and you can see the line Kotondo walked: ordinary, unglamorous intimacy - a morning chore - rendered with the shin-hanga publisher Sakai Kawaguchi's full register of delicate flesh tones, lacquer-black hair, near-invisible outline.

Torii_Kotondo_-_Woman_Before_a_Mirror_-_.story: A woman sits bare-chested before a low wooden mirror-stand, arms raised behind her head to gather her hair, a flowered pink juban tumbling off her hips into lilac underlayers. The mirror itself is barely a sliver at the edge of the frame - Kotondo gives us her reflection by implication only, the downward glance doing the work. Printed by Kawaguchi in 1930, three years before the authorities cracked down on the artist's nudes. The flat grey ground and the patterned robe show how far shin-hanga could push a simple bijin-ga toward something coolly modern.

Tōkyō_jūnidai,_Daikon-gashi_by_Kawase.title: Tōkyō jūnidai, Daikon-gashi by Kawase Hasui
Tōkyō_jūnidai,_Daikon-gashi_by_Kawase.description: Daikon-gashi, from the series Twelve Scenes of Tōkyō (Tōkyō jūnidai), woodblock print

source.canonical_title: File:Tōkyō jūnidai, Daikon-gashi by Kawase Hasui.jpg

Tōkyō_jūnidai,_Daikon-gashi_by_Kawase.story: Daikon-gashi — literally 'daikon embankment' — was a stretch of the Nihonbashi river where radishes used to be barged into the city. By 1920, when Hasui printed this sheet for his Twelve Scenes of Tokyo, it was a working waterfront of warehouses and piled goods. He takes the old Edo name seriously: low viewpoint, still water, buildings compressed along the bank. Three years later the Great Kanto Earthquake erased this Tokyo almost completely, which is why the pre-quake prints from this series now read as quiet reportage as much as art.

Tōkyō_jūnidai,_Fukagawa_Kaminohashi_b.title: Tōkyō jūnidai, Fukagawa Kaminohashi by Kawase Hasui
Tōkyō_jūnidai,_Fukagawa_Kaminohashi_b.description: The Kaminohashi Bridge in Fukagawa , from the series Twelve Scenes of Tōkyō (Tōkyō jūnidai), woodblock print

source.canonical_title: File:Tōkyō jūnidai, Fukagawa Kaminohashi by Kawase Hasui.jpg

Tōkyō_jūnidai,_Fukagawa_Kaminohashi_b.story: Kaminohashi spanned the mouth of the Sendai canal where it met the Sumida, in the old working district of Fukagawa. Hasui designed this sheet in the summer of 1920; he later admitted Hokusai had been in his head, and the composition — looking under the bridge across to the far bank — echoes Hokusai's Fukagawa view from the Thirty-Six Views of Fuji. But the mood is entirely Taisho: a yellow twilight sky against slow blue water, nobody hurrying. The bridge and most of the neighbourhood were gone by 1923.

Tōkyō_jūnidai,_Kiba_no_yūgure_by_Kaw.title: Tōkyō jūnidai, Kiba no yūgure by Kawase Hasui
Tōkyō_jūnidai,_Kiba_no_yūgure_by_Kaw.description: Evening at the Lumber Yards of Kiba (Kiba no yūgure), from the series Twelve Scenes of Tōkyō (Tōkyō jūnidai), woodblock print

source.canonical_title: File:Tōkyō jūnidai, Kiba no yūgure by Kawase Hasui.jpg

Tōkyō_jūnidai,_Kiba_no_yūgure_by_Kaw.story: Kiba was Tokyo's timber quarter — a grid of canals where huge rafts of logs were floated in from the provinces and stored on the water. Hasui catches it at dusk in 1920: the logs dark against a low sun, a bridge in silhouette, reflections breaking up across the channel. The shin-hanga technique lets the sky do real work here, with graded bokashi shifting from warm to cool overhead. It's a plainly industrial subject handled without fuss, one of the strongest sheets in the Twelve Scenes of Tokyo.

Tōkyō_jūnidai,_Samidare_furu_Sannō_b.title: Tōkyō jūnidai, Samidare furu Sannō by Kawase Hasui
Tōkyō_jūnidai,_Samidare_furu_Sannō_b.description: Early Summer Rain at the Sannō Shrine (Samidare furu Sannō), from the series Twelve Scenes of Tōkyō (Tōkyō jūnidai), woodblock print

source.canonical_title: File:Tōkyō jūnidai, Samidare furu Sannō by Kawase Hasui.jpg

Tōkyō_jūnidai,_Samidare_furu_Sannō_b.story: Early-summer rain on the gate of Hie Shrine — the old Sannō precinct on Tokyo's Akasaka hill — with a woman and her baby hurrying through. This is the city a few years before the 1923 earthquake flattened it, which makes the print a quiet document as much as a design. Watanabe took the unusual step of using mica to render the driven streaks of rain, something his workshop rarely did. From the 1919 Twelve Scenes of Tokyo, among Hasui's first sustained efforts to treat his own city the way he treated the provinces.

Tōkyō_jūnidai,_Shinagawa_oki_by_Kawas.title: Tōkyō jūnidai, Shinagawa oki by Kawase Hasui
Tōkyō_jūnidai,_Shinagawa_oki_by_Kawas.description: The Bay off Shinagawa (Shinagawa oki), from the series Twelve Scenes of Tōkyō (Tōkyō jūnidai), woodblock print

source.canonical_title: File:Tōkyō jūnidai, Shinagawa oki by Kawase Hasui.jpg

Tōkyō_jūnidai,_Shinagawa_oki_by_Kawas.story: Shinagawa was Tokyo's first post-station on the old Tokaido, and its bay was still thick with fishing boats in 1920. This sheet from the Twelve Scenes of Tokyo takes the offshore view — a low horizontal format, working sails on the water, a sky that's been block-printed rather than painted but behaves like weather. Published by Watanabe in the summer of Taisho 9, with Hasui's pre-earthquake 'Sui' seal. Shinagawa's waterfront would be reshaped repeatedly over the next century; the print preserves a version of it that barely outlasted the decade.

Tōkyō_jūnidai,_Toyama-no-hara_by_Kawa.title: Tōkyō jūnidai, Toyama-no-hara by Kawase Hasui
Tōkyō_jūnidai,_Toyama-no-hara_by_Kawa.description: Winter moon, Toyama Plain (Toyama-no-hara), from the series Twelve Scenes of Tōkyō (Tōkyō jūnidai), woodblock print

source.canonical_title: File:Tōkyō jūnidai, Toyama-no-hara by Kawase Hasui.jpg

Tōkyō_jūnidai,_Toyama-no-hara_by_Kawa.story: Toyamagahara was open ground on Tokyo's western edge, used as a military drill field and good for uninterrupted sky. Hasui loved it for the horizon. This pre-quake version, designed for the Twelve Scenes of Tokyo, pairs a winter moon with a row of bare trees — a subject he'd return to more than once over his career. The published 1931 reissue from a different publisher is better known, but the original from this series is the leaner, colder read. Cold light, thin branches, almost nothing else.

Tōkyō_nijū_kei,_Kanda_Myōjin_keidai_.title: Tōkyō nijū kei, Kanda Myōjin keidai by Kawase Hasui
Tōkyō_nijū_kei,_Kanda_Myōjin_keidai_.description: The Grounds of the Kanda Myōjin Shrine , (Kanda Myōjin keidai), from the series Twenty Views of Tōkyō (Tōkyō nijū kei)

source.canonical_title: File:Tōkyō nijū kei, Kanda Myōjin keidai by Kawase Hasui.jpg

Tōkyō_nijū_kei,_Kanda_Myōjin_keidai_.story: Kanda Myojin shrine had just been rebuilt when Hasui made this print. The 1923 Great Kanto Earthquake had flattened much of central Tokyo, and Twenty Views of Tokyo (1926) is partly a record of a city reconstituting itself. Here the shrine precinct is calm and ordered again: cherry or plum in bloom, visitors moving under the vermillion architecture, a sense that daily life has resumed. Published by Watanabe, whose own workshop had burned in the quake.

Tōkyō_nijū_kei,_Shin_Ōhashi_by_Kawas.title: Tōkyō nijū kei, Shin Ōhashi by Kawase Hasui
Tōkyō_nijū_kei,_Shin_Ōhashi_by_Kawas.description: Shin Ōhashi Bridge (Shin Ōhashi), from the series Twenty Views of Tōkyō (Tōkyō nijū kei)

source.canonical_title: File:Tōkyō nijū kei, Shin Ōhashi by Kawase Hasui.jpg

Tōkyō_nijū_kei,_Shin_Ōhashi_by_Kawas.story: The New Great Bridge over the Sumida, rebuilt after the 1923 earthquake with steel spans and electric lighting. Hasui put those modern elements front and center — this is not a nostalgic Tokyo. Twenty Views of Tokyo, published by Watanabe in 1926, tracks a city visibly shifting under Western influence, and Shin Ohashi is one of the series' clearest statements: the lanterns of old Edo have given way to cables, girders, and bulbs.

Transfiguration-Rubens.jpeg.title: The Transfiguration of Christ

source.canonical_title: File:Transfiguration-Rubens.JPG

Transfiguration-Rubens.jpeg.story: Commissioned in 1604 by Vincenzo Gonzaga, Duke of Mantua, as one of three huge altarpieces for the Jesuit church of Santissima Trinità. Rubens, then in his twenties and still in Italy, stacks the picture in two zones: Christ in dazzling light between Moses and Elijah at the top, and down below the apostles struggling to exorcise a possessed boy - the Gospel pairs the two scenes. French troops seized it during the Napoleonic wars in 1797; it passed briefly through the Musée Napoléon before being deposited in 1804 at the Musée des Beaux-Arts de Nancy, where it remains on state loan.

Triumphant_Cupid_among_Emblems_of_Art_an.title: Triumphant Cupid among Emplems of Art and War
Triumphant_Cupid_among_Emblems_of_Art_an.artist: Thomas Willeboirts Bosschaert / Paul de Vos
Triumphant_Cupid_among_Emblems_of_Art_an.description: In the seventeenth century there was a palpable desire to master and explain one’s surroundings. Reality was to be conquered, measured, calculated, and understood. But the understanding of the world, and humankind’s place in it, also brought with it a deep crisis when the religious worldview was shaken by new theories. In this painting the god of love is seated among scientific instruments, artistic attributes, and symbols of war. The image can be interpreted to mean that love conquers all.

source.canonical_title: File:Triumphant Cupid among Emblems of Art and War (Thomas Willeboirts Bosschaert & Paul de Vos) - Nationalmuseum - 17413.tif

title.sv: Amor triumferande bland symboler för konst, vetenskap och krig - Amor Triumphans
title.nl: Cupido omringd met voorwerpen die verwijzen naar oorlog en kunst

Triumphant_Cupid_among_Emblems_of_Art_an.story: A winged, red-draped Cupid plants his foot on a heap of suit-armor, trumpets and a painter's palette, a viola da gamba and lute nearby, a celestial globe and astrolabe on the right. He's bested soldiering, music, painting, astronomy - the lot. The theme is the old amor vincit omnia, but the treatment is Antwerp 1650: Willeboirts Bosschaert supplying the Van Dyckian boy, Paul de Vos laying in the still life of gleaming steel and instruments. What carries it is the juxtaposition of soft flesh and cold metal.

Triumphant_Entry_of_Constantine_into_Rom.title: The Triumphant Entry of Constantine into Rome

source.canonical_title: File:Triumphant Entry of Constantine into Rome by Peter Paul Rubens.jpg

Triumphant_Entry_of_Constantine_into_Rom.story: Not a finished painting but a working sketch — one of twelve Rubens whipped up around 1621 so weavers in Paris could turn his ideas into tapestry. Constantine parades in on a chariot after crushing Maxentius, laurel overhead, trumpeters blaring. You can see Rubens thinking fast: loose brushwork, bold silhouettes designed to read in wool. Louis XIII gave seven woven versions to Cardinal Francesco Barberini in 1625. The sketch now lives at the Indianapolis Museum of Art, part of the Clowes Collection.

Tsukioka_Yoshitoshi_-_The_moon_on_Musash.title: The moon on Musashi Plain (Musashino no tsuki) from the series 'One hundred aspects of the moon (Tsuki no hyakushi)' I/1892

source.canonical_title: File:Tsukioka Yoshitoshi - The moon on Musashi Plain (Musashino no tsuki) - from the series 'One hundred aspects of the moon (T... - Google Art Project.jpg
source.credit: jAHH0A04avBLOg at Google Cultural Institute maximum zoom level

Tsukioka_Yoshitoshi_-_The_moon_on_Musash.story: A fox slinking through tall pampas grass under a huge pale moon on the Musashi Plain, the flat country west of old Edo. Yoshitoshi keeps the whole print nearly monochrome, brown-gold grass, grey sky, just enough ink to trace the fox's spine. It belongs to his One Hundred Aspects of the Moon, 100 prints issued 1885-1892. This sheet is dated January 1892, the year Yoshitoshi died at 53.

Tsunami_by_hokusai_19th_century.jpg.title: The Great Wave off Kanagawa
Tsunami_by_hokusai_19th_century.jpg.description: Although it is often used in tsunami literature, there is no reason to suspect that Hokusai intended it to be interpreted in that way. The waves in this work are sometimes mistakenly referred to as tsunami (津波), but they are more accurately called okinami (沖波), great off-shore waves.

source.canonical_title: File:Tsunami by hokusai 19th century.jpg

Tsunami_by_hokusai_19th_century.jpg.story: Call it the Great Wave, not a tsunami. Hokusai's cresting claw is actually an okinami, a towering offshore swell, with three slender fishing boats pitched against it and tiny Mount Fuji holding still in the trough. The deep, saturated blue was new to Japan: Prussian blue pigment arrived in quantity around 1829, and Hokusai saturated his prints with it. Published around 1831 as the opening image of Thirty-six Views of Mount Fuji, it went on to become, by many counts, the most reproduced image in art history.

Turner,_J._M._W._-_The_Grand_Canal_-_Ven.title: The Grand Canal - Venice

source.canonical_title: File:Turner, J. M. W. - The Grand Canal - Venice.jpg

title.de: Venedig von der Terrasse von Santa Maria della Salute

Turner,_J._M._W._-_The_Grand_Canal_-_Ven.story: Turner first saw Venice in 1819 but only properly painted it after a second visit in 1833. This canvas, exhibited at the Royal Academy of 1835 under the title 'Venice, from the Porch of Madonna della Salute', looks across the mouth of the Grand Canal with palace walls dissolving into their own reflections. A gondola slides through the middle distance. It's been in the Metropolitan Museum of Art in New York since 1899, when Cornelius Vanderbilt II's widow gave it.

Turner,_Joseph_Mallord_William_(RA)_-_Li.title: Line Fishing, Off Hastings

source.canonical_title: File:Turner, Joseph Mallord William (RA) - Line Fishing, Off Hastings - Google Art Project.jpg
source.credit: -wG8RNgzDMZgIA at Google Cultural Institute maximum zoom level

Turner,_Joseph_Mallord_William_(RA)_-_Li.story: Turner knew this stretch of water. He'd sketched Hastings boats in 1816, drawn them again in watercolour in 1818, and by the time he worked them up as an oil for the Royal Academy's 1835 show, he could paint the handline fishery from muscle memory. The light is low, the sea chopping rather than storming, and the tackle does the talking. John Sheepshanks bought it, then handed it to the V&A in 1857 as part of his gift - which is where it still hangs.

Turner-deluge.jpg.title: The Deluge

source.canonical_title: File:Turner-deluge.jpg

Turner-deluge.jpg.story: Turner's go at Noah's flood, done around 1805 and shown at his own Harley Street gallery. Bodies tangle in the foreground muck, a leopard tries to climb a tree, and the light rakes in sideways like stage fire. He was reading Poussin hard at the time and wanted to beat him at his own apocalypse. The picture stayed with Turner his whole life and came to the nation in the 1856 bequest.

Turner_-_Antwerp_Van_Goyen_Looking_Out_f.title: Turner - Antwerp Van Goyen Looking Out for a Subject, 1833, 1901.1.118
Turner_-_Antwerp_Van_Goyen_Looking_Out_f.description: Joseph Mallord William Turner (1775 - 1851) Antwerp: Van Goyen Looking Out for a Subject, 1833 oil on canvas 36 1/8 in. x 48 3/8 in. (91.76 cm x 122.87 cm) Henry Clay Frick Bequest. Accession number: 1901.1.118

source.canonical_title: File:Turner - Antwerp Van Goyen Looking Out for a Subject, 1833, 1901.1.118.jpg

Turner_-_Antwerp_Van_Goyen_Looking_Out_f.story: Turner puts the 17th-century Dutch landscapist Jan van Goyen in a crowded rowing boat in Antwerp harbour, scanning the skyline for his next picture — a kind of self-portrait at one remove. The cathedral spire floats in soft grey behind a forest of masts. Turner showed it at the Royal Academy of 1833, the same year he himself returned to Venice hunting subjects. Henry Clay Frick bought the canvas in 1901; it's been at the Frick Collection ever since.

Turner_-_Fishermen_Upon_a_Lee-Shore_in_S.title: Turner - Fishermen Upon a Lee-Shore in Squally Weather, 1802
Turner_-_Fishermen_Upon_a_Lee-Shore_in_S.description: Fishermen Upon a Lee-Shore in Squally Weather

source.canonical_title: File:Turner - Fishermen Upon a Lee-Shore in Squally Weather, 1802.jpg

Turner_-_Fishermen_Upon_a_Lee-Shore_in_S.story: A lee shore is a sailor's nightmare - wind blowing you onto rocks you can't claw off of. Turner knew the vocabulary and painted it accordingly: a black squall rolling in, a fishing smack heeled over, breakers going white against an unseen coast. Shown at the Academy in 1802, it helped him sail straight into full Academician status that same year, at twenty-six. He was the youngest yet elected.

Turner_-_Newark_Abbey_on_the_River_Wey,_.title: Newark Abbey on the River Wey
Turner_-_Newark_Abbey_on_the_River_Wey,_.description: Newark Abbey on the River Wey

source.canonical_title: File:Turner - Newark Abbey on the River Wey, 5765910.jpg

Turner_-_Newark_Abbey_on_the_River_Wey,_.story: The second go at Newark Priory, done a year after the first. Same ruins, same river, lower sun. Turner shifts the viewpoint slightly downstream and warms everything up into a honey-coloured evening. He kept the first version and sold this one. Critics at the time picked it as the more resolved of the pair, though modern taste tends to prefer the earlier, scruffier canvas.

Turner_-_Peace_-_Burial_at_Sea.jpg.title: Peace - Burial at Sea
Turner_-_Peace_-_Burial_at_Sea.jpg.description: Painting showing burial of his friend the artist David Wilkie. Exhibited 1842, displayed alongside and contrasting with Turner's 'War'.

source.canonical_title: File:Turner - Peace - Burial at Sea.jpg

Turner_-_Peace_-_Burial_at_Sea.jpg.story: Turner's friend Sir David Wilkie died at sea returning from the Holy Land in June 1841 and was buried off Gibraltar. A year later Turner answered with this: the steamer lying to, black sails drinking the light, the whole picture pitched in cold blues and ashy whites. He hung it at the 1842 Academy next to its opposite number, War. The Exile and the Rock Limpet - Napoleon on St Helena, all strident reds and yellows. Peace and War, friend and emperor, mourned side by side.

Turner_-_Port_Rusdael.jpg.title: Port Ruysdael

source.canonical_title: File:Turner - Port Rusdael.jpg

Turner_-_Port_Rusdael.jpg.story: There's no such place as Port Ruysdael. Turner invented the name as a tribute to the Dutch marine painter Jacob van Ruisdael, then built a plausible storm-beaten harbour to put it in: one fishing boat shouldering through breakers, abandoned nets on the groins, sky the colour of wet slate. Exhibited at the Royal Academy in 1827, it didn't find a buyer until Elhanan Bicknell took it in 1844. It now lives at the Yale Center for British Art.

Turner_-_Rain,_Steam_and_Speed_-_Nationa.title: Rain, Steam and Speed - The Great Western Railway ; the painting depicts an early locomotive of the Great Western Railway crossing the River Thames on Brunel's recently completed Maidenhead Railway Bridge .The painting is also credited for allowing a glimpse of the Romantic strife within Turner and his contemporaries over the issue of the technological advancement during the Industrial Revolution (see below).

source.canonical_title: File:Turner - Rain, Steam and Speed - National Gallery file.jpg

Turner_-_Rain,_Steam_and_Speed_-_Nationa.story: A black locomotive charges straight out of the downpour toward you across Brunel's brand-new Maidenhead Railway Bridge. Turner was 68 when he painted it in 1844, and the story goes he'd leaned his head out of a carriage window in a storm to see what speed actually looked like. Look closely and there's a hare sprinting ahead of the train on the tracks, about to lose the race. It hangs in London's National Gallery.

Turner_-_Ships_Bearing_up_for_Anchorage_.title: Ships bearing up for Anchorage ('The Egremont Seapiece')
Turner_-_Ships_Bearing_up_for_Anchorage_.description: Ships Bearing up for Anchorage ('The Egremont Seapiece') exhibited 1802 Joseph Mallord William Turner 1775-1851 Accepted by HM Government in lieu of tax and allocated to the Tate Gallery 1984. In situ at Petworth House http://www.tate.org.uk/art/work/T03868

source.canonical_title: File:Turner - Ships Bearing up for Anchorage (‘The Egremont Seapiece’), exhibited 1802, T03868.jpg

Turner_-_Ships_Bearing_up_for_Anchorage_.story: The Earl of Egremont walked into the 1802 Academy, looked at this, and bought it. It was the first Turner he owned and the hook for one of the great collecting relationships of the century - a dozen more would follow, and Turner would eventually have his own painting room at Petworth. Dutch-inflected shipping in a lively green sea, a man-of-war standing off. It still hangs at Petworth House today, on long loan as Tate T03868.

Turner_-_The_Banks_of_the_Loire,_about_1.title: Banks of the Loire

source.canonical_title: File:Turner - The Banks of the Loire, about 1829, 1940.59.jpg

Turner_-_The_Banks_of_the_Loire,_about_1.story: Turner had tramped the Loire valley in 1826, filling sketchbooks from Nantes to Orleans. Three years later he worked this oil up for the Royal Academy of 1829, the scene glowing with that particular chalky French afternoon light he loved. Figures cluster on the riverbank under a sky that takes up two-thirds of the canvas. The Loire watercolours would eventually feed his engraved 'Wanderings by the Loire', published in 1833 as the first of his Annual Tour volumes.

Turner_-_The_Bright_Stone_of_Honour_(Ehr.title: Turner - The Bright Stone of Honour (Ehrenbreitstein) and the Tomb of Marceau, from Byrons Childe Harold, l17033
Turner_-_The_Bright_Stone_of_Honour_(Ehr.description: The Bright Stone of Honour (Ehrenbreitstein) and the Tomb of Marceau, from Byrons Childe Harold

source.canonical_title: File:Turner - The Bright Stone of Honour (Ehrenbreitstein) and the Tomb of Marceau, from Byrons Childe Harold, l17033.jpg

Turner_-_The_Bright_Stone_of_Honour_(Ehr.story: Turner loads the Rhine with ghosts. The fortress of Ehrenbreitstein towers over the river; below it stands the obelisk to General Marceau, the young French republican who fought the sieges here in 1795-96 and died at twenty-seven. Byron had already eulogised both in Childe Harold, and Turner stitched poem and place into a single golden haze. When the picture went up at the Royal Academy in May 1835, it was the hit of the room - the one painting critics and public actually agreed on.

Turner_-_The_Eruption_of_the_Soufrière_M.title: Turner - The Eruption of the Soufrière Mountains in the Island of St Vincent, 30 April 1812, 1815, FA.459
Turner_-_The_Eruption_of_the_Soufrière_M.description: Turner, Joseph Mallord William; The Eruption of the Soufriere Mountains in the Island of St Vincent, 30 April 1812; University of Liverpool; http://www.artuk.org/artworks/the-eruption-of-the-soufriere-mountains-in-the-island-of-st-vincent-30-april-1812-67007

source.canonical_title: File:Turner - The Eruption of the Soufrière Mountains in the Island of St Vincent, 30 April 1812, 1815, FA.459.jpg

Turner_-_The_Eruption_of_the_Soufrière_M.story: La Soufrière on St Vincent blew its top on 30 April 1812, throwing ash as far as Barbados. Turner, who'd never been to the Caribbean, worked from an on-the-spot sketch by the planter Hugh Perry Keane and turned it into this: a night sky ripped open by lava and flame, a tiny boat rowing for its life across the foreground. He showed it at the Royal Academy in 1815. It was given to the University of Liverpool in 1948 and hangs in the Victoria Gallery and Museum.

Turner_-_The_Evening_Star,_about_1830,_N.title: Turner - The Evening Star, about 1830, NG1991
Turner_-_The_Evening_Star,_about_1830,_N.description: Joseph Mallord William TurnerThe Evening Starabout 1830Oil on canvas, 91.1 x 122.6 cmTurner Bequest, 1856NG1991https://www.nationalgallery.org.uk/paintings/NG1991

source.canonical_title: File:Turner - The Evening Star, about 1830, NG1991.jpg

Turner_-_The_Evening_Star,_about_1830,_N.story: A boy wades out of the surf with a shrimping net; his dog waits on the shingle; above them, a single dab of thick white paint hangs in the dusk. That dab is why the picture is called The Evening Star — Turner never titled it, the name came later. Long dismissed as unfinished, curators now suspect he simply stopped when the mood was right. The canvas was found in his studio after his death in 1851 and entered the National Gallery with the Turner Bequest of 1856.

Turner_-_The_Trout_Stream,_1809,_1931.45.title: The Trout Stream

source.canonical_title: File:Turner - The Trout Stream, 1809, 1931.459.jpg

Turner_-_The_Trout_Stream,_1809,_1931.45.story: Anglers working a pool on the River Dee in North Wales, trees arching over the water, the whole scene slowed down to the speed of a float drifting. Turner showed this in his own Queen Anne Street gallery in 1809 rather than at the Royal Academy. The Earl of Essex bought it for Cassiobury Park, his Hertfordshire seat. It's now the star Turner at the Taft Museum of Art in Cincinnati.

Turner_-_The_Wreck_Buoy,_c.1849,_WAG_310.title: The Wreck Buoy

source.canonical_title: File:Turner - The Wreck Buoy, c.1849, WAG 310.jpg

Turner_-_The_Wreck_Buoy,_c.1849,_WAG_310.story: This is one of the last paintings Turner ever exhibited, shown at the Royal Academy in 1849, two years before his death. He actually reworked an older canvas by Chambers, repainting a rainbow arching over a scene of ships and a red wreck-buoy bobbing in the swell. Critics noticed the ghost of the original painting showing through. Turner was in his mid-seventies, mostly retreating from public view. It's held by the Walker Art Gallery in Liverpool.

Turner_-_Thomson's_Aeolian_Harp,_1809,_1.title: Turner - Thomson's Aeolian Harp, 1809, 1979.7

source.canonical_title: File:Turner - Thomson's Aeolian Harp, 1809, 1979.7.jpg

Turner_-_Thomson's_Aeolian_Harp,_1809,_1.story: A homage to the poet James Thomson, whose 'Ode on Aeolus's Harp' gives the picture its title. Turner plants an imaginary classical tomb above a soft arc of the Thames near Richmond, where Thomson is actually buried. Three barefoot dancers, the Graces, ring-dance in the foreground while the Four Seasons decorate the wind-harp. Shown at the Royal Academy in 1809 with verses Turner wrote himself, it's now at Manchester Art Gallery, a rare moment where he lets poetry drive the weather rather than the other way around.

Turner_-_Walton_bridges,_c._1806,_981-3..title: Walton bridges

source.canonical_title: File:Turner - Walton bridges, c. 1806, 981-3.jpg

Turner_-_Walton_bridges,_c._1806,_981-3..story: The twin-span bridge at Walton-on-Thames in late afternoon, with cattle wading and a barge easing through. Turner painted it outdoors, probably the first oil he ever finished en plein air, after moving to Sion Ferry House at Isleworth. Sir John Leicester paid him 280 pounds for it on 8 January 1807. It nearly left the country in 2018 but was saved for Norwich Castle Museum.

Turner_Cologne,_the_Arrival_of_a_Packet-.title: Cologne, the Arrival of a Packet-Boat, Evening
Turner_Cologne,_the_Arrival_of_a_Packet-.description: Oil on canvas 66 3/8 x 88 1/4 in. (168.6 x 224.2 cm) Henry Clay Frick Bequest Accession number: 1914.1.119

source.canonical_title: File:Turner Cologne, the Arrival of a Packet-Boat, Evening.jpg

Turner_Cologne,_the_Arrival_of_a_Packet-.story: A riverboat called Amitie noses toward Cologne's waterfront while the spire of Gross St. Martin catches the last gold of the day. The canvas is enormous, nearly seven feet across, and Turner made it as one of a trio of European port views exhibited at the Royal Academy in 1826. Henry Clay Frick bought it in 1914 and it hangs today at the Frick Collection in New York as accession number 1914.1.119.

source.canonical_title: File:Two Sisters (On the Terrace).jpg

Two_Sisters_(On_the_Terrace).jpg.story: Two girls perch on a terrace above the Seine at Chatou, a basket of wool balls between them in candy colors, like a small box of sweets. Renoir painted it in April 1881, quickly, over about a week. The elder model was Jeanne Darlaud, an eighteen-year-old aspiring actress; the little one in the hat trimmed with wildflowers is unknown. He sold it straight from the easel to the dealer Paul Durand-Ruel. It has hung at the Art Institute of Chicago since 1933.

Umegawa_in_Sagami_province.jpg.story: Dawn in Sagami. Five cranes wade a shallow stream while two more lift toward Fuji, wings spread against the pale sky. The whole print is rendered in cool blues, an aizuri-e made possible by the newly imported Prussian blue pigment that Hokusai had fallen for. Cranes carry a thousand years of longevity in East Asian lore, and Hokusai's hint is hard to miss: sacred mountain, sacred birds, same frame. It belongs to Thirty-six Views of Mount Fuji, published around 1830-32.

Unmatinapresledeluge.jpg.story: A square canvas, which is already unusual, and inside it Turner spins a golden vortex - light pouring out of the centre like the first day of a world starting over. The title is practically a sermon: Goethe's colour theory, the Flood receding, Moses sitting down to write Genesis. Turner had read Eastlake's 1840 translation of Goethe obsessively; yellow, in that system, is the first colour to come out of light. Exhibited 1843, paired with its dark twin Shade and Darkness.

Urteil_des_Paris.jpg.story: Marcantonio's engraving after a lost Raphael drawing, and one of the most influential prints of the sixteenth century. Paris hands the apple to Venus; river gods lounge in the foreground; in the corner sits the cluster of reclining nudes Manet would lift, three and a half centuries later, for the Déjeuner sur l'herbe. The engraving did exactly what it was designed to do — broadcast Raphael's composition across Europe, into studios in Antwerp and Fontainebleau and eventually into the long memory of French painting. Marcantonio's burin work is crisp, measured, almost sculptural. The print was the internet of its day, and this was its viral hit.

Utagawa_Hiroshige_(1857)_Awa_Naruto_no_f.title: Utagawa Hiroshige (1857) Awa Naruto no fuukei
Utagawa_Hiroshige_(1857)_Awa_Naruto_no_f.description: View of the Whirlpools at Awa , colour nishiki-e ukiyo-e print by Utagawa Hiroshige; Vertical ooban triptych; 37.7 x 76.2 cm; 1857, Ansei 4

source.canonical_title: File:Utagawa Hiroshige (1857) Awa Naruto no fuukei.jpg

Utagawa_Hiroshige_(1857)_Awa_Naruto_no_f.story: Hiroshige returned to the Naruto whirlpools and this time gave them a whole triptych — three vertical sheets of churning blue-green water, wave crests curling, spiral after spiral. No boats, no figures, just the sea doing its daily violence. Issued in 1857, the year of Ansei 4, the three panels measure about 38 by 76 centimeters assembled. It's one of his most abstract landscapes: nothing but pattern, current, and foam, pushed right up against the viewer.

Utagawa_Hiroshige_I,_published_by_Uoya_E.title: Horikiri Iris Garden (Horikiri no hanashōbu), from the series One Hundred Famous Views of Edo (Meisho Edo hyakkei)

Utagawa_Hiroshige_I,_published_by_Uoya_E.story: Push your face into the foreground and you're practically drowning in iris petals — purple, white, blooming taller than the tiny visitors out on the causeway beyond. Hiroshige loved this trick: a close-up plant almost blocking the view, then the wider world peeking through. Horikiri, on Edo's eastern edge, was iris country, and Edoites came by boat to gawk at the summer display. The print is sheet 64 in One Hundred Famous Views of Edo, issued in the fifth month of 1857, a year before Hiroshige's death.

Utagawa_Kunisada_(1857)_Imayō_mitate_sh.title: Utagawa Kunisada (1857) Imayō mitate shinō kōshō yori shokunin
Utagawa_Kunisada_(1857)_Imayō_mitate_sh.description: 三代歌川豊国『今様見立士農工商』より「職人」

source.canonical_title: File:Utagawa Kunisada (1857) Imayō mitate shinō kōshō yori shokunin.jpg

Utagawa_Kunisada_(1857)_Imayō_mitate_sh.story: A craftsman takes a break — pipe in hand, tools at his side, a young woman leaning in. The title translates roughly as "A modern parody of the four classes: the artisan." Kunisada riffs on the old Confucian hierarchy of samurai, farmer, artisan, merchant, restaging each as fashionable Edo genre scenes. By 1857 he was in his seventies and the reigning star of ukiyo-e portraiture; the publisher Uoya Eikichi — the same house issuing Hiroshige's famous views that year — put out the whole vertical ōban series.

Utagawa_Kunisada_I_(c._1832)_Dawn_at_Fut.title: Utagawa Kunisada I (c. 1832) Dawn at Futami-ga-ura
Utagawa_Kunisada_I_(c._1832)_Dawn_at_Fut.description: Dawn at Futamai-ga-ura , an ukiyo-e print from an unnamed series by Japanese artist Utagawa Kunisada I

source.canonical_title: File:Utagawa Kunisada I (c. 1832) Dawn at Futami-ga-ura.jpg

Utagawa_Kunisada_I_(c._1832)_Dawn_at_Fut.story: The same wedded rocks Hiroshige would return to decades later, but this is the earlier Kunisada version: dawn at Futamigaura, sun coming up between the two rocks, a boat on the near water. Kunisada is not a landscape specialist — his fame was in kabuki portraits and beauties — but the Utagawa school expected versatility, and he hands in a competent sunrise. The print is undated and the series unnamed; the rough year of 1832 comes from the publisher's seal.

title.da: Valley of Aosta: Snowstorm, Avalanche, and Thunderstorm

Valley_of_Aosta,_Snowstorm,_Avalanche,_a.story: Turner saw an avalanche come down in the Val d'Aosta in 1836 and spent the next year trying to paint the weather itself. The mountains are almost gone, dissolved into a swirling grey vortex of snow and thundercloud; only at the bottom right, tiny, do you pick out a scatter of figures and animals — a shepherd, a dog, red cloaks — caught in the path of the storm. The whole canvas is composition as centrifuge. This is the Turner of the 1830s, moving steadily past landscape into something closer to pure atmospheric event; the one Ruskin defended and Monet eventually studied very carefully.

VanGogh-starry_night_ballance1.jpg.title: The Starry Night

source.canonical_title: File:VanGogh-starry night ballance1.jpg

VanGogh-starry_night_ballance1.jpg.story: The same Starry Night of June 1889, painted at the asylum in Saint-Remy. Those swirls aren't invention for invention's sake — Van Gogh told Theo he'd been staring at the pre-dawn sky through his barred window and wanted to capture a Venus 'very big' above the cypress. The eleven stars, the crescent moon, the sleeping hamlet: all composed indoors, from memory. Since 1941 it has hung at the Museum of Modern Art in New York.

Van_Dyck_Pieter_Brueghel_the_Younger.jpg.title: Pieter Bruegel the Younger

source.canonical_title: File:Van Dyck Pieter Brueghel the Younger.jpg

Van_Dyck_Pieter_Brueghel_the_Younger.jpg.story: A sheet from Van Dyck's 'Iconography,' the print project he launched after returning to Antwerp from Italy, collecting likenesses of painters, scholars and statesmen. Pieter Brueghel the Younger, son of the great peasant-scene painter, appears in three-quarter profile, turned slightly away, one hand gathering a heavy cloak at the chest. The etched lines are loose and sketch-like around the face, tighter in the hair and collar. Van Dyck himself etched only eighteen of the series' hundred-odd plates; this is one of the earliest states of that group.

Van_Gogh_-Die_Brücke_von_Langlois_in_Ar.story: The first and most famous of the Langlois canvases, now in the Kröller-Müller. Washerwomen kneel at the canal edge beating laundry on stones while the drawbridge lifts behind them for a passing boat. Van Gogh loved the subject for its simple geometry — those black counterweights against the sky — and for the way it let him stage Provençal blues against the yellow ochre of the banks. He was freshly arrived from Paris, his palette just beginning to catch fire, and you can feel him working out the colour logic of everything that came after.

Van_Gogh_-_Abendstunde_(Nach_Millet).jpe.story: Saint-Remy, late 1889. Stuck in the asylum with no models to pose, Van Gogh asked Theo to mail him black-and-white prints of Jean-Francois Millet's peasant scenes so he could 'translate' them into colour — his word. This one reworks Millet's 'The End of the Day': a farmer shouldering his tools as dusk settles blue over the stubble. Van Gogh called them improvisations, not copies. It hangs today at the Menard Art Museum in Komaki, Japan.

Van_Gogh_-_Am_Stadtrand_von_Paris1.jpeg.title: On the outskirts of Paris

source.canonical_title: File:Van Gogh - Am Stadtrand von Paris1.jpeg

Van_Gogh_-_Am_Stadtrand_von_Paris1.jpeg.story: The raw edge of the city: factory chimneys smoking on the skyline, a lamppost, a couple walking along a dusty path through waste ground. Van Gogh painted this in the spring or summer of 1887, when he was walking out beyond the old fortifications — Asnières, Clichy, the banlieue — hunting motifs no academic would touch. The brushwork is looser now, the sky brightening toward blue. The canvas belongs to the Carnegie Museum of Art in Pittsburgh.

Van_Gogh_-_Die_Schäferin_(nach_Millet)..story: Another Saint-Rémy 'translation' after Millet, this time of a young shepherdess leaning on her staff while her flock grazes behind her. Van Gogh used the black-and-white print Theo had sent as a score and improvised the colour: the girl in a red bodice and blue apron against a spring field of acid yellow-green. Millet's peasants had been his first artistic religion back when he was preaching to Borinage miners, and copying them in the asylum was a way of going home in his mind during the months he couldn't go out.

Van_Gogh_-_Grünes_Weizenfeld.jpeg.title: Green wheat field

source.canonical_title: File:Van Gogh - Grünes Weizenfeld.jpeg

Van_Gogh_-_Grünes_Weizenfeld.jpeg.story: Painted at Saint-Rémy in the spring of 1889, one of the quieter asylum-garden pictures. A plain field of young wheat, stalks picked out in short vertical strokes, a strip of farmhouse and cypress at the horizon. No drama, no weather event, no blazing sun — just green on green on green, the kind of almost-boring subject he trusted to carry the emotion by itself. He believed wheatfields held a whole life in them: sowing, ripening, harvest, death, resurrection. This is the early-life version of the story.

Van_Gogh_-_Grünes_Weizenfeld1.jpeg.title: Green Wheat Fields, Auvers

source.canonical_title: File:Van Gogh - Grünes Weizenfeld1.jpeg
source.credit: 1. Copied from an art book 2. National Gallery of Art, Washington, D. C., online collection

Van_Gogh_-_Grünes_Weizenfeld1.jpeg.story: Painted in the last weeks of Van Gogh's life, after he had left Saint-Rémy for the quiet village of Auvers-sur-Oise. The wheat is still green, the sky bright, the brushwork looser and more horizontal than the furious swirls of the south. He worked at a ferocious pace that summer, often a canvas a day, trying to pin down the flat fields north of Paris before the harvest. A few weeks later he walked into one of them with a revolver.

Van_Gogh_-_Le_Moulin_de_la_Galette.jpeg.title: Dance at the Moulin de la Galette

source.canonical_title: File:Van Gogh - Le Moulin de la Galette.jpeg

Van_Gogh_-_Le_Moulin_de_la_Galette.jpeg.story: Not Renoir's famous dance hall but the same windmill, seen from the back lane — wood scaffolding, a couple of loungers, grey Paris sky. When Van Gogh moved to Montmartre in 1886 the Moulin de la Galette stood just up the hill from Theo's apartment, and he painted it at least seven times that year. The palette here is still dark, earthy, Dutch; the blaze of yellow is a year away. The canvas is in the Kröller-Müller Museum in the Netherlands.

Van_Gogh_-_Les_Alyscamps,_Allee_in_Arles.story: The Alyscamps is an old Roman necropolis at the edge of Arles, a long avenue lined with stone sarcophagi and poplars that was already a tourist postcard by 1888. Van Gogh painted it four times that October, most of them alongside Paul Gauguin, who had just moved into the Yellow House. The canvases are yellow, gold and rust: autumn leaves littering the tombs. Two months later the two men would fight, and Vincent would cut off part of his ear.

Van_Gogh_-_Seineufer_bei_der_Pont_de_Cli.title: Seine-shore at the Pont de Clichy

source.canonical_title: File:Van Gogh - Seineufer bei der Pont de Clichy.jpeg

Van_Gogh_-_Seineufer_bei_der_Pont_de_Cli.story: Summer 1887, just downstream from central Paris: Van Gogh has set up his easel on the Seine bank near the Pont de Clichy, where he often painted alongside Bernard and Signac. The water's full of broken reflections, the touch short and divided — he was studying the Pointillists without ever becoming one. Clichy was industrial, smelly, cheap; painters went there for light on water and room to work. This canvas is in the Saint Louis Art Museum.

Van_Gogh_-_Weißes_Bauernhaus_zwischen_Ol.title: The white cottage among the olive trees

source.canonical_title: File:Van Gogh - Weißes Bauernhaus zwischen Olivenbäumen.jpeg

Van_Gogh_-_Weißes_Bauernhaus_zwischen_Ol.story: A low white Provençal farmhouse tucked among the silver olives near Saint-Rémy, the whole scene vibrating with his 1889 handwriting — those tight comma-strokes that make the foliage shiver. He painted dozens of olive groves in his asylum year because he thought they were the true, unsentimental Mediterranean subject, the opposite of the Impressionists' sunny orchards. The house sits there quite calmly in the middle of all the painterly weather, roof a brick orange against the blue hills. Domestic life going on, seen by a man temporarily locked out of it.

Van_Gogh_-_Zwei_Bauern_beim_Umgraben.jpe.title: Two farmers digging over (after Millet)

source.canonical_title: File:Van Gogh - Zwei Bauern beim Umgraben.jpeg

Van_Gogh_-_Zwei_Bauern_beim_Umgraben.jpe.story: Saint-Remy, 1889. Another Millet translation — two peasants bent into the earth with spades, painted in Van Gogh's colour after Millet's black-and-white print. He worked these 'from a sickbed,' he told Theo, when he couldn't face going outdoors. The furrows churn violet and green; the figures almost dissolve into the ground they're working. Van Gogh saw it not as copying but 'as a musician plays Beethoven' — interpreting another man's score.

Van_Gogh_-_Zypressen_mit_zwei_weiblichen.story: Saint-Remy, February 1890, five months before his death. The cypresses here twist like green flame against a sky cooled down for winter; two small female figures walk past, almost incidental. Van Gogh had painted cypresses obsessively since arriving at the asylum, calling them 'as beautiful of line and proportion as an Egyptian obelisk.' The canvas is at the Kroller-Muller Museum in Otterlo.

Van_gogh_f1040_jh100.jpg.title: Van gogh f1040 jh100

source.canonical_title: File:Van gogh f1040 jh100.jpg

Van_gogh_f1040_jh100.jpg.story: Before the sunflowers, before Paris, there was this: Van Gogh working as a lay preacher in the Borinage coal district of Belgium, and sketching the miners he lived among. The sheet is dated 4 July 1879 — one of his earliest surviving drawings. Within months the mission board would refuse to renew his contract, citing his "excess of zeal." He kept drawing anyway. The catalogue numbers F1040 / JH100 mark it near the very beginning of the count that eventually runs to roughly 2,100 works.

Veld_met_klaprozen_-_s0033V1962_-_Van_Go.title: Field with Poppies

source.canonical_title: File:Veld met klaprozen - s0033V1962 - Van Gogh Museum.jpg

Veld_met_klaprozen_-_s0033V1962_-_Van_Go.story: June 1888, and Van Gogh is painting the countryside around Arles flat out, one canvas a day in the good weather. The poppies here aren't a tidy bouquet; they're scattered red dots across a windy green field, the horizon held down by a low line of trees. He kept telling Theo that Provence light made his earlier Paris palette look grey by comparison. The picture is in the Van Gogh Museum, Amsterdam, bequeathed from the family collection.

Velázquez_-_El_Triunfo_de_Baco_o_Los_Bor.title: The Triumph of Bacchus
Velázquez_-_El_Triunfo_de_Baco_o_Los_Bor.description: La obra, titulada El triunfo de Baco o Los Borrachos , es una de las obras mitológicas más conocidas del pintor sevillano Diego Velázquez .

source.canonical_title: File:Velázquez - El Triunfo de Baco o Los Borrachos (Museo del Prado, 1628-29).jpg

title.es: El triunfo de Baco o Los Borrachos
title.br: Los borrachos o el triunfo de Baco

Velázquez_-_El_Triunfo_de_Baco_o_Los_Bor.story: Nobody in Madrid called it The Triumph of Bacchus. They called it The Drunkards. A half-naked boy god crowns a grinning beggar with ivy while four flushed men squint at the viewer, letting us in on the joke. Velázquez painted it in 1628-29 for Philip IV, who paid him a hundred ducats and hung it in the royal bedroom. The grin on the right-hand drunk is one of the most honest laughs in Spanish painting.

Velázquez_-_de_Breda_o_Las_Lanzas_(Museo.title: The Surrender of Breda , or „The Lances“
Velázquez_-_de_Breda_o_Las_Lanzas_(Museo.description: La obra representa el momento en que Justino de Nassau rindió la ciudad de Breda , en 1625, a las tropas españolas al mando del general Ambrosio Spínola , que aparece recibiendo las llaves de la ciudad de manos de su enemigo.

Velázquez_-_de_Breda_o_Las_Lanzas_(Museo.story: The Dutch governor Justin of Nassau bends to hand over the keys of Breda. Ambrosio Spínola, Spain's general, stops him rising all the way, a hand on the shoulder that says no humiliation today. Behind them, the famous forest of vertical lances gives the painting its nickname. Velázquez finished it in 1635 for the Buen Retiro, nearly a decade after the siege itself ended in 1625.

Venus_and_Adonis_by_Titian.jpg.story: Adonis the hunter tears himself from Venus's embrace to go after the boar that will kill him; she clutches his waist, face pressed into his side, already losing. Titian shipped this to Prince Philip of Spain in 1554 as part of a series he called his poesie, paintings-as-poems drawn from Ovid. The composition, twisting Venus seen from behind, was copied, engraved and argued about for centuries. The Prado version is the prime one. Philip had it in his private apartments.

Venus_and_Mars_National_Gallery.jpg.story: Mars is out cold. Venus, fully dressed and wide awake, watches him snore while four satyr-children play with his abandoned armor — one cheekily blowing a conch in his ear. A swarm of wasps buzzes near his head, possibly a pun on the Vespucci family (vespa means wasp) who may have commissioned it around 1483. The wood panel's shape suggests a spalliera, a decorative backrest built into the paneling of a bedroom, likely for a wedding. Love has unstrung the god of war. It now hangs in London's National Gallery, acquired in 1874.

Venus_and_organist_and_little_dog.jpg.story: A richly dressed organist twists away from his keyboard to stare openly at a reclining nude Venus, who ignores him to fuss over a small lapdog. Cupid whispers in her ear; through the window, a formal garden recedes into Alpine blue. Titian and his workshop painted at least five versions of this scene for wealthy collectors in the late 1540s and 1550s. It's a sly little allegory about music, sight and desire, not necessarily in that order. This one, around 1550, is in the Prado.

Vereshchagin_Napoleon_near_Borodino.jpg.title: Napoleon near Borodino (1897)

source.canonical_title: File:Vereshchagin Napoleon near Borodino.jpg

Vereshchagin_Napoleon_near_Borodino.jpg.story: Napoleon on the morning of Borodino, 7 September 1812, in greatcoat and bicorne, field glass in hand. Vereshchagin places him on a low rise with his staff, studying the Russian lines across open country that will, within hours, become the bloodiest single day of the Napoleonic wars. The painter's interest is unglamorous: a middle-aged man looking at a map problem. Part of the 1812 series Vereshchagin worked on obsessively through the 1890s, researched from memoirs, uniforms, and the terrain itself.

Vermeer-view-of-delft.jpg.title: View of Delft

source.canonical_title: File:Vermeer-view-of-delft.jpg

Vermeer-view-of-delft.jpg.story: Vermeer set up across the harbour from his hometown on a summer morning, clouds still carrying the night's rain. The city wall glows; boats are moored; two women chat in the foreground. Proust called it the most beautiful painting in the world and put it at the centre of a death scene in his novel. Scholars now think Vermeer worked on it for years, possibly finishing as late as the early 1660s. It's one of the rare times he painted outdoors instead of his usual upstairs room. Hangs at the Mauritshuis in The Hague.

Veronese-persée-rennes.jpg.title: Perseus Freeing Andromeda
Veronese-persée-rennes.jpg.artist: Paolo Veronese / Formerly attributed to Francesco Montemezzano / Formerly attributed to Carlo Caliari

source.canonical_title: File:Veronese-persée-rennes.jpg

Veronese-persée-rennes.jpg.story: Veronese gives the Perseus rescue a workaday ferocity. Andromeda is chained to a stub of rock, twisting away from a barnacled sea-monster whose jaws open right at her ankles; Perseus drops from a stormy sky in rust-gold drapery, short sword raised, winged sandals visible. A pale Italian city gleams across the bay as if the whole myth were happening just outside Venice. The silver-on-red palette is pure Veronese, though authorship drifted to his pupil Montemezzano and his son Carlo Caliari before scholars handed it back.

Veronese_Allegory_of_Wisdom_and_Strength.title: Allegory of Wisdom and Strength

source.canonical_title: File:Veronese Allegory of Wisdom and Strength.jpg

Veronese_Allegory_of_Wisdom_and_Strength.story: Divine Wisdom, crowned and looking heavenward, stands beside a meaty Hercules who has put down his club to gaze, distracted, at a scatter of jewels. Down in the corner Veronese has written 'omnia vanitas' - all is vanity. The picture had an extraordinary afterlife: Emperor Rudolf II owned it, then Queen Christina of Sweden, then the Duke of Orléans, before it crossed the Channel and finally landed at Henry Clay Frick's house on Fifth Avenue, where it still hangs. A pendant 'Allegory of Virtue and Vice' lives on the opposite wall.

Vertumnus_årstidernas_gud_målad_av_Giu.story: Arcimboldo's flattery-as-still-life: Emperor Rudolf II rebuilt as Vertumnus, the Roman god of seasons and metamorphosis, every feature swapped for something edible. The nose is a ripe pear, the cheeks apples, the chin a chestnut, the moustache two wheat-stalks, the brow a vine-wreathed melon, the shoulders a cabbage and an artichoke. Painted late in the artist's life from his retirement in Milan, it reached Prague as a gift and stayed there until Swedish troops looted it in the Thirty Years' War, which is how it ended up at Skokloster Castle near Stockholm.

source.canonical_title: File:Vigee-Lebrun–Julie-Lebrun-as-Flora.jpg

Vigee-Lebrun–Julie-Lebrun-as-Flora.jpg.story: Vigée Le Brun's only child, Julie, sat for her mother constantly. Here she is Flora, goddess of flowers and spring, bride of the wind god Zephyr. The year is 1799 — and the same year Julie married Gaëtan Nigris against her mother's wishes, cracking a relationship that never fully mended. The mythology scarcely hides the tension: painted tenderness and domestic rupture, same canvas. Museum of Fine Arts, St Petersburg, Florida.

VigeeLeBrun_ViewOfTheLakeOfChallesAndMon.story: Two summers in Switzerland — 1807 and 1808 — saw Vigée Le Brun, now in her fifties, clambering into the Alps and writing home in breathless tones about the views. This pastel of Lake Challes with Mont Blanc looming behind is unusually dark and weather-thickened for her, and it is a landscape, rare in an output dominated by society faces. The sheet is actually two, joined together. Minneapolis Institute of Art.

Vigée-Lebrun,_Elisabeth-Louise_-_Charles.title: Portrait of Charles-Alexandre de Calonne (1734-1802)

source.canonical_title: File:Vigée-Lebrun, Elisabeth-Louise - Charles-Alexandre de Calonne (1734-1802) - Google Art Project.jpg
