Vigée-Lebrun,_Elisabeth-Louise_-_Charles.story: Calonne was Louis XVI's Controller-General of Finances when he sat for this in 1784, and he wanted the world to know it. He's in the robes of the Noblesse de Robe with the sash and star of the Order of the Saint-Esprit, holding a letter inscribed Au Roi; the charter on the table next to him is dated August 1784, the very document his enemies would later use to destroy him. Le Brun exhibited the portrait at the Salon of 1785. When Calonne was dismissed and fled to England he took it with him, and it passed into the British Royal Collection, where it still hangs.

Vigée-Lebrun_Marie_Antoinette_1783.jpg.title: Marie-Antoinette with the Rose

source.canonical_title: File:Vigée-Lebrun Marie Antoinette 1783.jpg

title.ja: バラを持つマリー・アントワネット

Vigée-Lebrun_Marie_Antoinette_1783.jpg.story: The repair job. Vigée Le Brun had just been forced to pull her portrait of Marie Antoinette in a simple white muslin chemise from the 1783 Salon — critics called the dress unpatriotic (imported cotton, not Lyon silk) and practically underwear. Within weeks she installed this replacement: same pose, same rose, but now in grey-blue silk with a striped bow and proper pearls, a pointed nod to the Lyonnaise weavers. The rose, her favourite flower, implies she's just picked it from the Versailles gardens. Politics disguised as a garden walk.

Vincent_Van_Gogh_-_Wheatfield_With_Cornf.title: Wheatfield With Cornflowers

source.canonical_title: File:Vincent Van Gogh - Wheatfield With Cornflowers - Google Art Project.jpg
source.credit: BwFKPHmzvqHGJw at Google Cultural Institute , zoom level maximum

Vincent_Van_Gogh_-_Wheatfield_With_Cornf.story: Early July 1890, the Auvers fields are shoulder-deep and spiked with blue cornflowers. Vincent wrote of losing himself in "vast stretches of corn under troubled skies" — this is one of those. The horizon is high, the sky a narrow band, your eye pushed down into the crop. It was painted only days before the gunshot in a wheatfield that killed him on 29 July. The Beyeler Foundation in Basel holds it.

Vincent_Van_Gogh_0013.jpg.story: A stocky man in a straw hat trudges down a road near Tarascon with his paintbox and stretched canvases on his back: a rare self-portrait in full body, half a caricature of himself. Van Gogh painted it in Arles in the summer of 1888. It used to hang in the Kaiser-Friedrich-Museum in Magdeburg and was destroyed in a fire during the Second World War, in 1945. Only photographs survive, which is why reproductions of it vary so wildly in color.

Vincent_Willem_van_Gogh,_Dutch_-_Rain_-_.title: Rain

source.canonical_title: File:Vincent Willem van Gogh, Dutch - Rain - Google Art Project.jpg

Vincent_Willem_van_Gogh,_Dutch_-_Rain_-_.story: Saint-Remy, early November 1889. Van Gogh painted the enclosed wheatfield he could see from his asylum window many times, but only once with weather like this: a screen of diagonal grey-blue slashes dragged across the wet field with a loaded brush. He was homaging the Japanese woodblock prints he collected, which rendered rain as straight lines. It has been at the Philadelphia Museum of Art since 1986.

Vincent_Willem_van_Gogh_030.jpg.story: Van Gogh climbed down to the Rhone embankment in October 1888 to paint this iron staircase in sharp diagonal perspective, all cold blues and lilac stone, people hurrying up the steps in the wrong direction. The Trinquetaille bridge itself was a wartime casualty, blown up in 1944, but the painting survived. It's now in a private collection and almost never exhibited. Van Gogh made it just weeks before Gauguin arrived at the Yellow House and the autumn unraveled.

Vincent_Willem_van_Gogh_037.jpg.title: Prisoners Exercising , also known as Prisoners' Round , (After Gustave Doré )

source.canonical_title: File:Vincent Willem van Gogh 037.jpg

Vincent_Willem_van_Gogh_037.jpg.story: Vincent copied this from a Gustave Doré engraving of Newgate Prison while he was himself a voluntary inmate at Saint-Rémy, in February 1890. The prisoners trudge in a hopeless circle between walls that rise forever; a pale blond figure in the front row, face turned out, is often read as the painter himself. He did not invent the scene — he translated black ink into blue-green oil. It belongs to the Pushkin Museum in Moscow.

Vincent_Willem_van_Gogh_128.jpg.story: August 1888, Arles. Van Gogh is painting sunflowers at speed, because they wilt fast, to decorate the guest room for Gauguin's arrival. Of the four he made that week this is the twelve-bloom version, flowers crammed into an earthenware jug on a blue-green table, yellow on yellow on yellow. He signed it 'Vincent' on the vase, lowercase, the way he signed the canvases he was proudest of. It hangs in the Neue Pinakothek in Munich.

Vincent_van_Gogh_(1853-1890)_Caféterras.story: Arles, September 1888, the Cafe du Forum still open after dark. Van Gogh painted it on the spot, at night, on a canvas set up in the street — no black used, he boasted to his sister, only blue, violet and green against the hot gas-yellow of the awning. The cobbles pulse, the stars are fat spinning discs, and a few late diners sit under the light like moths. One of the first of his great night pictures, and one of the happiest. Kroller-Muller Museum, Otterlo.

Vincent_van_Gogh_-_Bank_of_the_Oise_at_A.title: Bank of the Oise at Auvers

source.canonical_title: File:Vincent van Gogh - Bank of the Oise at Auvers - 70.159 - Detroit Institute of Arts.jpg

title.es: A orillas del Oise en Auvers
title.nl: Oevers van de Oise bij Auvers

Vincent_van_Gogh_-_Bank_of_the_Oise_at_A.story: Sunday boaters on the Oise, July 1890. Vincent rarely painted leisure — he mostly painted labourers, wheat, and cypresses — but here two rowboats are pulled up on the bank, a couple sits under a tree, and the river runs in thick horizontal strokes of blue and green. One of the last dozen canvases of his life. The Detroit Institute of Arts bought it in 1970 with funds from the Hawkins Ferry and City of Detroit funds.

Vincent_van_Gogh_-_De_oogst_-_Google_Art.story: June 1888, the plain of La Crau outside Arles. Van Gogh set up his easel and painted most of this in a single day, then wrote Theo that his brain was so tired he could barely think. A blue cart parks dead-centre among the stubble; a lone reaper works the background; the sky is that dry southern azure. He thought it 'killed all the rest' of his canvases. It's been at the Van Gogh Museum in Amsterdam since 1973.

Vincent_van_Gogh_-_Enclosed_Field_with_R.description: This picture was painted in the fall of 1889. Vincent and Theo van Gogh sent the painting to the 7th exhibition of Les XX in Brussels, where it was on display in the early months of 1890.

source.canonical_title: File:Vincent van Gogh - Houses at Auvers - Google Art Project.jpg

Vincent_van_Gogh_-_Houses_at_Auvers_-_Go.story: Orange-tiled and thatched roofs tumbling down a hillside, painted soon after Vincent arrived in Auvers-sur-Oise in late May 1890. He was delighted by the village — "profoundly beautiful," he told Theo, "real country, characteristic and picturesque." The paint is laid on in firm, separate tiles of colour, almost brickwork in itself. It's now at the Toledo Museum of Art in Ohio.

Vincent_van_Gogh_-_Irises_(1890).jpg.title: Irises

source.canonical_title: File:Vincent van Gogh - Irises (1890).jpg
source.credit: Metropolitan Museum of Art, online collection (accession number 58.187)

Vincent_van_Gogh_-_Irises_(1890).jpg.story: Another of the four great still lifes from Vincent's final week at Saint-Rémy, May 1890. Violet irises in a yellow vase on a yellow table against a yellow wall — he loved the complementary shock of purple against gold, and wrote to Theo that he was working at them "like a man in a frenzy" before his departure for Auvers. The Van Gogh Museum in Amsterdam holds this one.

Vincent_van_Gogh_-_Irises_-_Google_Art_P.title: Irises

source.canonical_title: File:Vincent van Gogh - Irises - Google Art Project.jpg
source.credit: ZQH2h7PBY47yXQ at Google Cultural Institute maximum zoom level

Vincent_van_Gogh_-_Irises_-_Google_Art_P.story: The companion piece: the same May 1890 frenzy at Saint-Rémy, but now the irises stand in a pale ceramic jug against a soft pink ground — quieter, almost tender. Vincent paired hot and cool versions on purpose; he thought in complements. Like the other three farewell bouquets, the pink has shifted over 130-odd years as the fugitive red lake pigment faded. This version belongs to the Metropolitan Museum of Art in New York.

Vincent_van_Gogh_-_Landscape_from_Saint-.title: Landscape from Saint-Rémy

source.canonical_title: File:Vincent van Gogh - Landscape from Saint-Rémy - Google Art Project.jpg
source.credit: AQGubXY-kY8jSg at Google Cultural Institute maximum zoom level

Vincent_van_Gogh_-_Landscape_from_Saint-.story: June 1889. Another view from Van Gogh's asylum window at Saint-Paul-de-Mausole — the walled wheatfield rising to the Alpilles hills, painted in the blazing first weeks of summer. He told Theo the field looked 'beautiful as the sea' when the wind moved through it. Thick green and yellow strokes, a sky pushed up to the top margin. The canvas is at the Ny Carlsberg Glyptotek in Copenhagen.

Vincent_van_Gogh_-_Landscape_with_Carria.title: Landscape with a Carriage and a Train

source.canonical_title: File:Vincent van Gogh - Landscape with Carriage and Train in the Background (1890).jpg

Vincent_van_Gogh_-_Landscape_with_Carria.story: June 1890, Auvers. A yellow carriage rolls along a country road while, far off, a toy-sized steam train trails smoke across the green plain. Vincent is watching modernity cross the fields — a carriage and a locomotive in one breath — but the whole thing is painted in his rolling, rhythmic strokes, not as reportage. It hangs at the Pushkin Museum of Fine Arts in Moscow.

Vincent_van_Gogh_-_Langs_de_Seine_-_Goog.story: Summer of 1887, and Van Gogh has walked out of Paris again with an easel strapped to his back. The riverbanks at Asnieres and Clichy were his open-air classroom that year, shared with Seurat, Signac and Bernard, where he started breaking color into little separate strokes instead of muddy Dutch browns. You can feel him trying things on. The paint sits loosely, almost tentatively, and he never quite finished it. The Van Gogh Museum in Amsterdam catalogues it as unfinished, probably meant to be worked up later in the studio.

Vincent_van_Gogh_-_Le_Moulin_de_blute-fi.story: The Blute-Fin was the last working windmill on the Butte Montmartre, standing on a ridge that in 1886 still felt half-rural — vegetable plots, rickety fences, a lamppost. Van Gogh walked up from Theo's flat on rue Lepic and painted it over and over. His brushwork here is thicker than in Antwerp, the sky brightening; you can feel him edging toward Impressionism without quite committing. The canvas lives at Museum de Fundatie in Zwolle, where it arrived as part of Dirk Hannema's collection.

Vincent_van_Gogh_-_Le_Moulin_de_la_Galet.title: Dance at the Moulin de la Galette

source.canonical_title: File:Vincent van Gogh - Le Moulin de la Galette.jpg

Vincent_van_Gogh_-_Le_Moulin_de_la_Galet.story: Theo's apartment on rue Lepic sat halfway up Montmartre, and the Moulin de la Galette was basically Vincent's backyard. While Renoir had turned the place into a glittering Sunday dance, Van Gogh kept painting the working windmill itself, its timbers weathered, the ground a scruff of dirt and fences. No top hats. Just the bones of a neighborhood. In 1887 he returned to the mill again and again in different weather and light, part of a whole Montmartre series he made during his two Paris years with Theo.

Vincent_van_Gogh_-_Le_moissonneur_(1889).title: The Reaper
Vincent_van_Gogh_-_Le_moissonneur_(1889).artist: Vincent van Gogh / After Jean-François Millet

source.canonical_title: File:Vincent van Gogh - Le moissonneur (1889).jpg
source.credit: Christie's , LotFinder: entry 6089477 (sale 14239, lot 6, London, 27 June 2017)

Vincent_van_Gogh_-_Le_moissonneur_(1889).story: Stuck in the Saint-Rémy asylum with no models and bad weather, Van Gogh worked from black-and-white prints of Millet, translating them into colour the way, he said, a musician plays another composer's score. Millet's reaper becomes a figure in gold and blue, scythe swinging through wheat the colour of fire. Van Gogh had revered Millet since his preaching days in the Borinage coal country, and these 'copies' are as much devotions as exercises.

Vincent_van_Gogh_-_Les_Vessenots_à_Auve.title: View of Vessenots Near Auvers

source.canonical_title: File:Vincent van Gogh - Les Vessenots à Auvers (1890).jpg

title.de: Blick auf den Ortsteil Vessenots in Auvers
title.avk: Wiks va Vessenots poke Auvers (trutca ke Van Gogh)

Vincent_van_Gogh_-_Les_Vessenots_à_Auve.story: Les Vessenots was a hamlet just outside Auvers-sur-Oise, thatched cottages set among wheat fields. Van Gogh painted this in May or June of 1890, soon after arriving under Dr Gachet's care. The brushwork is quick and nervous, the greens pushed almost to acid, the roofs a soft red glow in the middle distance. He told Theo he was finding the north gentler than Provence but no less beautiful. It is one of around seventy canvases he finished in the last two months of his life.

Vincent_van_Gogh_-_Montmartre-_molens_en.story: Behind the dance halls, Montmartre was still half countryside: allotment gardens, sheds, the occasional windmill creaking above the cabbages. Van Gogh painted this view in 1887 from the rue Lepic side of the butte, where Theo's apartment looked straight out onto vegetable plots. The brushwork has gone lighter and looser since Holland, the dirt rendered in pinks and lilacs he would never have used in Nuenen. It's in the Van Gogh Museum in Amsterdam, part of the dense Montmartre cycle he made while living with his brother.

Vincent_van_Gogh_-_Perzikbomen_in_bloei..title: Peach Trees in Blossom
Vincent_van_Gogh_-_Perzikbomen_in_bloei..description: The plain "La Crau" near Arles tree with blooming peach-trees

source.canonical_title: File:Vincent van Gogh - Perzikbomen in bloei.jpg

Vincent_van_Gogh_-_Perzikbomen_in_bloei..story: Arles, April 1889 — one of the last works Van Gogh finished before voluntarily entering the asylum at Saint-Remy. Peach trees in full pink bloom on the plain of La Crau, with the snow still dusting the Alpilles behind them. He told Theo the blossoms and distant mountain reminded him of cherry trees and Mount Fuji in his Japanese prints. It's at the Courtauld Gallery in London.

source.canonical_title: File:Vincent van Gogh - Road with Cypress and Star - c. 12-15 May 1890.jpg

Vincent_van_Gogh_-_Road_with_Cypress_and.story: One of the last things Vincent painted at Saint-Rémy before heading north, around 12-15 May 1890. A huge green flame of a cypress splits the sky; a crescent moon and a single enormous star burn on either side; two peasants walk the road below. He described it in a letter to Gauguin as a "last attempt" — a night effect with "an exaggerated star." It lives at the Kröller-Müller Museum in Otterlo.

Vincent_van_Gogh_-_Self-Portrait_-_Googl.title: Self-portrait

source.canonical_title: File:Vincent van Gogh - Self-Portrait - Google Art Project.jpg
source.credit: 9gFw_1Vou2CkwQ at Google Cultural Institute maximum zoom level

Vincent_van_Gogh_-_Self-Portrait_-_Googl.story: Saint-Remy, September 1889. Van Gogh painted this a month after recovering from a severe breakdown, and sent it to Theo with a note: 'You'll see, I hope, that my face is much calmer, though it seems to me my look is vaguer than before.' The background writhes in the same blue-green swirls as the jacket — the two almost fuse. It has hung at the Musee d'Orsay since 1986.

Vincent_van_Gogh_-_Self-Portrait_-_Googl.title: Self-Portrait

source.canonical_title: File:Vincent van Gogh - Self-Portrait - Google Art Project (454045).jpg

title.th: ภาพเหมือนตนเอง

Vincent_van_Gogh_-_Self-Portrait_-_Googl.story: Van Gogh painted himself roughly thirty-five times, and almost all of them happened because models cost money he didn't have. This one is from his Paris period, 1887, the phase where he's clearly been staring hard at Seurat and the neo-impressionists: the face is built from little parallel dashes of orange, green and blue, the beard practically vibrating. No ear bandage yet, no Arles yellow. Just a redheaded Dutchman testing out French color theory on the only sitter who'd hold still for free.

Vincent_van_Gogh_-_Self-portrait_with_pi.title: Self-portrait with pipe

source.canonical_title: File:Vincent van Gogh - Self-portrait with pipe - Google Art Project.jpg
source.credit: awGqjJSvEkyNwg at Google Cultural Institute maximum zoom level

Vincent_van_Gogh_-_Self-portrait_with_pi.story: Dark coat, felt hat, pipe clenched between his teeth — Van Gogh staring himself down in a mirror in autumn 1886, newly arrived in Paris. He painted roughly thirty-five self-portraits in his life, mostly because sitters were cheaper when they were himself. This one is still Dutch-dim, the brown-green gloom he brought from Antwerp. Within a year Impressionism and Japanese prints would blow the palette wide open. The little panel, about 46 by 38 cm, belongs to the Van Gogh Museum in Amsterdam.

Vincent_van_Gogh_-_Starry_Night_-_Google.title: The Starry Night
Vincent_van_Gogh_-_Starry_Night_-_Google.description: Vincent van Gogh - Starry Night on the Rhone, 1888

source.canonical_title: File:Vincent van Gogh - Starry Night - Google Art Project.jpg
source.credit: uQE3XORhSK37Dw at Google Cultural Institute maximum zoom level

Vincent_van_Gogh_-_Starry_Night_-_Google.story: Arles, September 1888. Van Gogh carried his easel down to the bank of the Rhône a minute's walk from the Yellow House and painted this outdoors, at night, under a gas lamp. A few days later he wrote Theo describing exactly what you see: the sky green-blue, the water royal blue, the Great Bear sparkling green and pink against it, the gaslights' reflections dropping into the river as red gold and green bronze. Down on the quay, a couple walks arm in arm. This is the first of his night pictures — the famous swirling one at Saint-Rémy came nine months later, from a different window, a different state of mind.

Vincent_van_Gogh_-_The_Bedroom_-_Google_.title: The bedroom

source.canonical_title: File:Vincent van Gogh - The Bedroom - Google Art Project.jpg
source.credit: rgHdFPzCeCfnxQ at Google Cultural Institute maximum zoom level

Vincent_van_Gogh_-_The_Bedroom_-_Google_.story: Saint-Remy, early September 1889. This is the second of the three bedroom paintings — Van Gogh made it at the asylum from memory, copying his own October 1888 Arles original after floodwaters damaged the first canvas. Same yellow bed, same red blanket, same tilted walls. He told Theo the flat colours were supposed to 'suggest rest, or sleep.' It lives at the Art Institute of Chicago.

Vincent_van_Gogh_-_The_Church_in_Auvers-.title: The Church at Auvers

source.canonical_title: File:Vincent van Gogh - The Church in Auvers-sur-Oise, View from the Chevet - Google Art Project.jpg

Vincent_van_Gogh_-_The_Church_in_Auvers-.story: Painted in early June 1890, a month before his death. The 13th-century church at Auvers leans and buckles as if the stones themselves were breathing; the sky behind it is a deep cobalt with no stars. Vincent wrote to his sister Wil that it was "almost the same thing" as the Nuenen church tower he'd painted years before — except the colour was now "more expressive, more sumptuous." It hangs at the Musée d'Orsay in Paris.

Vincent_van_Gogh_-_Tuin_in_Montmartre_me.story: This is Montmartre in its last rural gasp, 1887, before the funicular and the Sacre-Coeur crowds finished it off. A couple strolls between trellises in a pleasure garden on the butte, possibly the Auberge de la Bonne Franquette, with the city dropping away behind them. Van Gogh has borrowed the pointillists' broken color but not their discipline: strokes lean this way and that, blue shadows puddle on yellow paths. It hangs at the Stedelijk Museum in Amsterdam.

Vincent_van_Gogh_-_Veld_met_bloemen_bij_.story: Summer 1888. Van Gogh had fled grey Paris for the Provencal light and couldn't stop painting the wildflower strips at the edge of the Arles wheatfields. Crushed yellows, buttercup greens, a horizon shoved high so the flowers do most of the talking. He works thick and fast here, paint squeezed almost straight from the tube. The canvas lives at the Van Gogh Museum in Amsterdam.

Vincent_van_Gogh_-_Wheat_Field_with_Cypr.title: Wheat Field with Cypresses

source.canonical_title: File:Vincent van Gogh - Wheat Field with Cypresses (National Gallery version).jpg

Vincent_van_Gogh_-_Wheat_Field_with_Cypr.story: Saint-Remy, September 1889. Van Gogh painted three versions of this motif; this one he made in his asylum studio after the original, and kept for himself as a 'souvenir.' The cypresses are 'as beautiful of line and proportion as an Egyptian obelisk,' he told Theo — and he meant it literally. Churned clouds, a field bending in the mistral. It has been at the National Gallery in London since 1923.

Vincent_van_Gogh_-_Wheat_Field_with_Cypr.story: The plein-air original, painted late June 1889 in the fields just outside the asylum walls at Saint-Remy. Van Gogh stood in the mistral with his easel anchored, working the cypress and wheat straight from nature. He rated it one of his best summer canvases and made two studio copies afterwards. This first version lives at the Metropolitan Museum of Art in New York.

Vincent_van_Gogh_-_Wheatfield_under_thun.title: Wheatfield under thunderclouds

source.canonical_title: File:Vincent van Gogh - Wheatfield under thunderclouds - Google Art Project.jpg
source.credit: kAErTfh0dORNwQ at Google Cultural Institute maximum zoom level

Vincent_van_Gogh_-_Wheatfield_under_thun.story: Van Gogh stretched his canvas to an unusual 50 by 100 centimetres, flattening the horizon into a blade between green wheat and a bruise-blue sky. He painted it in Auvers-sur-Oise in July 1890, one of a run of wide-format fields he told Theo would say what he couldn't put in words, something about sadness and extreme loneliness. The clouds don't gather so much as loom, heavy and white-edged. Weeks later he shot himself in a field like this one. The picture was already with Theo in Paris by then.

Vincent_van_Gogh_-_Wheatfield_with_a_rea.title: Wheatfield with a reaper

source.canonical_title: File:Vincent van Gogh - Wheatfield with a reaper - Google Art Project.jpg
source.credit: BgFGcS3ucZqeRA at Google Cultural Institute maximum zoom level

Vincent_van_Gogh_-_Wheatfield_with_a_rea.story: From his barred window at the Saint-Paul asylum, Vincent watched a single reaper move through a yellow sea and saw, he told Theo, "the image of death, in this sense that humanity would be the wheat being reaped." Yet he insisted there was nothing sad in it — the sun poured everything with fine gold. He hacked out the first version through the bars, then painted this one in the studio in September 1889. It now hangs at the Van Gogh Museum in Amsterdam.

Vincent_van_Gogh_-_Wheatfield_with_crows.title: Wheatfield with crows

source.canonical_title: File:Vincent van Gogh - Wheatfield with crows - Google Art Project.jpg
source.credit: dwFdD5AMQfpSew at Google Cultural Institute maximum zoom level

Vincent_van_Gogh_-_Wheatfield_with_crows.story: Three paths fork into rolling green wheat under a sky the colour of a deep bruise, and a scatter of crows lifts off like punctuation. Van Gogh painted it in Auvers-sur-Oise in July 1890, on the same elongated 50-by-100-centimetre format he used that month. Legend wants it to be his last painting; scholars at the Van Gogh Museum no longer think so. What's not in doubt is the brushwork, gouged straight from the tube, and that he wrote to Theo the fields expressed 'sadness, extreme loneliness.' He died on 29 July.

Vincent_van_Gogh_-_Zeegezicht_bij_Les_Sa.story: Late May 1888. Van Gogh took a five-day trip by diligence from Arles down to the fishing village of Saintes-Maries-de-la-Mer — his first sight of the Mediterranean. He painted the water on the spot, in a wind so stiff grains of sand stuck in the wet paint. You can still find them if you look closely. The colour, he told Theo, was 'like mackerel — changeable.'

source.canonical_title: File:Vincent van gogh coin de jardin avec papillons).jpg

Vincent_van_gogh_coin_de_jardin_avec_pap.story: Six butterflies drift across the canvas: five small wood whites and a single red peacock. Van Gogh probably painted this in the Parc Voyer-d'Argenson at Asnieres, where he kept walking out to that summer of 1887. The dating was argued over for years; some catalogues pushed it to 1889, but Van Gogh Museum researcher Louis van Tilborgh made the case for spring 1887 in Paris, and Christie's agreed when they sold it in 2018 for $33 million.

Vue_du_val_d'Arco_dans_le_Tyrol_méridion.title: View of the Arco Valley

source.canonical_title: File:Vue du val d'Arco dans le Tyrol méridional - Musée du Louvre Arts graphiques INV 18579, Recto.jpg

Vue_du_val_d'Arco_dans_le_Tyrol_méridion.story: Coming home from Venice in the spring of 1495, Dürer stopped on the road near the town of Arco in the southern Tyrol and sat down with his watercolors. The castle crowns a crag; below it, terraced olive groves and cypresses descend toward the valley floor. He worked fast — the shadows on the rock are blocked in wet, the olive trees are little stippled clouds — but the geology is observed, crack by crack. This is one of the earliest pure landscapes in Western art, made not for a client or a church but because the place looked like something he'd never seen before.

WLANL_-_adagio808_-_Cloude_Monet,_Falais.story: Monet discovered Pourville in February 1882 — a sleepy Normandy village with cliffs that dropped straight into the Channel. He rented rooms, sent for Alice Hoschedé and the kids, and painted the chalk faces from every angle he could scramble to. In this view the cliffs bend away in chalky pinks and greens, the sea a scrubbed band below. He wrote to Durand-Ruel that the coast was 'so beautiful' he wished he'd come years earlier.

Wang_Meng_Dwelling_in_the_Qingbian_Mount.story: A narrow hanging scroll, almost a meter and a half tall, packed floor to ceiling with jostling peaks, knotted pines and tiny thatched huts. Wang Meng's brush never settles; the rocks swarm with his famous ropy, hair-like texture strokes. Painted in 1366 as the Yuan dynasty collapsed, it is less a view than a state of mind, a Daoist recluse's landscape of refuge. Wang would later be drawn into Ming court politics and die in prison on suspicion of treason. The scroll survived, and the Shanghai Museum treats it as one of the great monuments of Chinese ink painting.

Wassilij_Wassiljewitsch_Wereschtschagin_.title: Dervishes in Festive Attire

source.canonical_title: File:Wassilij Wassiljewitsch Wereschtschagin 001.jpg
source.credit: The Yorck Project (2002) 10.000 Meisterwerke der Malerei (DVD-ROM), distributed by DIRECTMEDIA Publishing GmbH. ISBN : 3936122202 .

Wassilij_Wassiljewitsch_Wereschtschagin_.story: Two Sufi dervishes in festival dress, painted during Vereshchagin's long Turkestan tour. The conical hats and patched cloaks are accurate to the Central Asian Sufi orders he encountered around Samarkand and Tashkent — wandering holy men who also worked as beggars, entertainers, and occasional rabble-rousers at the bazaar. Vereshchagin had a reporter's eye for costume, and pictures like this were partly ethnography, partly the raw material he would shape, back in his Munich studio, into the huge Turkestan Series.

Water-Lilies-and-Japanese-Bridge-(1897-1.title: the-water-lily-pond
Water-Lilies-and-Japanese-Bridge-(1897-1.description: Catalogue Entry: Water Lilies and Japanese Bridge represents two of Monet’s greatest achievements: his gardens at Giverny and the paintings they inspired. Monet moved to Giverny in 1883 and immediately began to develop the property. For him, the gardens were both a passion and a second artistic medium. His Asian garden was not part of the original estate; it was located on an adjacent property with a small brook, which he purchased and enlarged into a pond for a water garden in 1893. He transformed the site into an inspired vision of cool greens and calm, reflective waters, enhanced by exotic plants such as bamboo, ginkgo, and Japanese fruit trees and a Japanese footbridge. It was not until 1899, however, that he began a series of views of the site, of which this is one. A careful craftsman who reworked his canvases multiple times, Monet was committed to painting directly from nature as much as possible and for as long as he had the correct conditions; thus, he could work on as many as eight or more canvases a day, devoting as little as an hour or less to each. In this case, he set up his easel at the edge of the water-lily pond and worked on several paintings of the subject as part of a single process. Monet’s gardens and paintings show the same fascination with the effects of time and weather on the landscape. Both are brilliant expressions of his unique visual sensitivity and emotional response to nature. At Giverny, he literally shaped nature for his brush, cultivating vistas to paint. Gallery Label: Water Lilies and Japanese Bridge represents two of Monet’s greatest achievements: his gardens at Giverny and the paintings they inspired. In 1883 the artist moved to the country-town Giverny, near Paris but just across the border of Normandy. This was a time when he was enjoying increasing financial success as an artist, and he immediately began to redesign the property. In 1893, Monet purchased an adjacent tract, which included a small brook, and transformed the site into an Asian-inspired oasis of cool greens, exotic plants, and calm waters, enhanced by a Japanese footbridge. The serial approach embodied in this work—one of about a dozen paintings in which Monet returned to the same view under differing weather and light conditions—was one of his great formal innovations. He was committed to painting directly from nature as much as possible and whenever weather permitted, sometimes working simultaneously on eight or more canvases a day. Monet’s project to capture ever-shifting atmospheric conditions came to be a hallmark of the Impressionist style.

Water-Lilies-and-Japanese-Bridge-(1897-1.story: This is one of the twelve canvases Monet painted in the summer of 1899 from a single spot at the pond's edge, his easel planted where the bridge met the water. He'd sometimes work on eight canvases a day, devoting as little as an hour to each before the light moved on. The bridge curves cool against hot dapples of lily; bamboo and willow crowd the banks. Monet had dug the pond himself, or rather directed the digging, after buying the adjoining parcel in 1893. This canvas now lives at the Princeton University Art Museum.

Water_Lilies_(Agapanthus),_by_Claude_Mon.title: Water Lilies (Agapanthus)
Water_Lilies_(Agapanthus),_by_Claude_Mon.description: Monet spent the last thirty years of his life painting the lily pond at his home in Giverny, a small town on the river Seine, just north of Paris. While his initial exploration of the water lily theme (1902-8) produced smaller works more descriptive of a garden setting, the later paintings focus on the water's shimmering surface, indicating the surrounding trees and lush bank only through reflections. Here reflection and reality merge in strokes of blue, violet, and green. Fronds of water plants sway underwater and passing clouds are reflected above. By 1915 Monet had conceived a plan, called his Grande Décoration, for arranging a series of monumental water lily paintings in an oval room, thus creating a continuous panorama that would surround and enclose the viewer in an environment of pure color. That installation is located in two oval rooms in the Musée de l'Orangerie in Paris. Cleveland's painting is the left panel of a three-part variation on this water lily theme. Its companions are now in the St. Louis Art Museum and the Nelson-Atkins Museum in Kansas City, Missouri. The CMA painting was originally the left panel of a triptych titled Agapanthus (Nymphéas in French) that featured agapanthus growing in the foreground. At the end of World War I, Monet proposed a plan of installing the triptych together with several others in a building constructed on the grounds of the current Musée Rodin in Paris. However, the French government did not have the funds to finance such a project in the postwar era. A new idea was subsequently proposed of installing a series of these panoramic paintings in an existing building, the Orangerie near the Louvre. As the building was being prepared, Monet continued painting more works for the project and at some point repainted the Agapanthus triptych, during which the agapanthus were eliminated, leaving mostly water lilies floating in the water. Hence, the former Agapanthus triptych has become known as the Water Lilies (Agapanthus) triptych. When Monet died in 1926 none of his works had yet been installed in the Orangerie. A selection was placed there the following year, but it did not include Water Lilies (Agapanthus) triptych, which remained in the artist's studio under the care of his family until the 1950s, when the three panels were sold separately to American museums. The companion paintings are currently in the collections of the St. Louis Art Museum and the Nelson-Atkins Museum in Kansas City, Missouri. Water_Lilies_(Agapanthus),_by_Claude_Mon.story: Started in 1915 as the left panel of a triptych with agapanthus flowers blooming in the foreground, then reworked for years as Monet kept chasing his Grande Décoration. By the time he was done, the agapanthus had been painted out, leaving pure pond: strokes of violet, green, and blue where water, sky, and lily all share the same surface. Monet hoped the triptych would hang at the Orangerie with the others, but it stayed in his Giverny studio until the 1950s, when the three panels were sold separately to American museums. This one lives at the Cleveland Museum of Art.

Water_Lilies_by_Monet_(Yamagata_Museum_o.story: A quieter Nymphéas, paler, more tentative — a handful of pink blooms scattered across water that could be dusk or dawn. Monet painted more than 250 water lily canvases over thirty years, and the variations are endless: some are violent with color, some almost monochrome. This one traveled a long way from Giverny. It now hangs in the Yamagata Museum of Art in northern Japan, part of a collection built around French painting that opened to the public in 1964.

Waterloo_Bridge,_London,_at_Sunset_E1170.title: Waterloo Bridge, London, at Sunset

source.canonical_title: File:Waterloo Bridge, London, at Sunset E11705.jpg

Waterloo_Bridge,_London,_at_Sunset_E1170.story: Waterloo Bridge at dusk, finished in 1904, the span reduced to a dark horizontal across streaks of copper and mauve. Monet had watched this exact view from his Savoy suite during three winters — 1899, 1900, and 1901 — and kept the unfinished canvases in his Giverny studio for years afterward, tuning them from memory. He painted the bridge around forty times in all. The original Waterloo Bridge was demolished in the 1930s, so these canvases are now the best record we have of the granite arches Monet actually saw.

Watteau,_Antoine_-_Quellnymphe_-_1708.jp.title: Nymphe de fontaine

source.canonical_title: File:Watteau, Antoine - Quellnymphe - 1708.jpg
source.credit: 1. reproarte.com 2. Sotheby's New York, 26 January 2012, lot 63

Watteau,_Antoine_-_Quellnymphe_-_1708.jp.story: A spring nymph tips her urn and fresh water spills out onto the reeds. She's crowned with laurel and a few yellow blossoms, a pink drape slipping off one shoulder, a gilded staff in her other hand. The rosy flesh and dusty-blue sky are pure Watteau - the same cast he summoned for his fetes galantes, only here stripped of courtiers and set loose in a mythological garden. Painted around 1718, near the end of his short life. The cracks in the surface have aged with the paint; she looks faintly amused, as if she's heard the compliment before.

Wedding_of_Nicholas_II_and_Alexandra_Feo.story: The ceremony itself happened on 26 November 1894 in the chapel of the Winter Palace, barely a week after Nicholas's father was buried. Tuxen, a Dane who'd become the go-to painter for Europe's intermarried royals, worked up the scene the following year: robes, icons, candlelight, the young Alix of Hesse newly renamed Alexandra Feodorovna. Queen Victoria liked it so much she ordered her own version, which still hangs in the Royal Collection. Tuxen finished the Hermitage canvas in 1895.

Weyden_Christ_on_the_Cross_with_Mary_and.story: A stripped-down Calvary by van der Weyden's workshop: just three figures against a blood-red cloth of honour, the T-shaped cross planted on a narrow ledge. Christ is all bone and sinew; Mary and John, in chalk-white robes, flank him like carved pillars of grief. No landscape, no soldiers, no thieves — the painter wants you to meditate, not observe. The white on white against the red is startling, almost modern. Made for private devotion around 1457, it condenses van der Weyden's tear-streaked style into a single, hushed confrontation.

Weyden_Deposition.jpg.story: Painted for the crossbowmen's guild in Leuven around 1435 and reckoned the single most influential Netherlandish painting of its century. Ten near-life-size figures are compressed into a shallow gilded box barely deeper than a relief, the cross itself almost scraping the top edge. Mary, swooning, mirrors the curve of her son's body exactly, so grief and death share one silhouette. Every tear is an individually modelled drop. Philip II brought the panel to Spain in the sixteenth century; it now anchors the Flemish rooms at the Prado. Generations of Spanish, German and Italian painters learned how to stage grief from this one picture.

Whaling_off_the_Coast_of_the_Goto_Island.title: Whaling off the Coast of the Goto Islands
Whaling_off_the_Coast_of_the_Goto_Island.description: Whaling off the Coast of the Goto Islands by Hokusai, c. 1831–33

source.canonical_title: File:Whaling off the Coast of the Goto Islands.jpg

Whaling_off_the_Coast_of_the_Goto_Island.story: A swarm of small wooden boats rings an exhausted whale in the shallows off the Goto Islands, harpoon lines crossing the water like black threads. The print, from Hokusai's Oceans of Wisdom series of around 1833, documents the netted-whaling technique used by the Fukae whalers of western Kyushu, who drove the animal into coastal nets before killing it. Hokusai never travelled to the Goto; he worked from written accounts and earlier illustrations, which is why the whale's anatomy is a composite rather than a particular species.

Wheat_Field_with_Reaper_and_Sun_(F617),_.title: Wheat Field with Reaper and Sun

source.canonical_title: File:Wheat Field with Reaper and Sun (F617), 1889.jpg

Wheat_Field_with_Reaper_and_Sun_(F617),_.story: Vincent couldn't let the reaper go. After the Van Gogh Museum version, he painted this one in Saint-Rémy for his mother and sister — a smaller, tenderer restatement of the same yellow field and stooped figure under a blazing white sun. The paint is calmer, the ochre softer, the horizon mountains almost lavender. He catalogued it in a September 1889 letter to Theo as a repetition done "quite as good as the first time." It lives today at the Museo Nacional Thyssen-Bornemisza in Madrid.

Whistler-Nocturne_in_black_and_gold.jpg.title: Nocturne in Black and Gold: The Falling Rocket

source.canonical_title: File:Whistler-Nocturne in black and gold.jpg

Whistler-Nocturne_in_black_and_gold.jpg.story: Fireworks over Cremorne Gardens, Chelsea, reduced to a drift of sparks in wet black paint. John Ruskin saw it in 1877 and accused Whistler of 'flinging a pot of paint in the public's face.' Whistler sued for libel, won a farthing in damages in 1878, and went bankrupt paying court costs. He never regretted it. The painting entered the Detroit Institute of Arts in 1946, where it still hangs.

Whistler_-_Nocturne._Grey_and_Gold,_West.title: Nocturne: Grey and Gold, Westminster Bridge

source.canonical_title: File:Whistler - Nocturne. Grey and Gold, Westminster Bridge (1871-1872) y145.jpg

Whistler_-_Nocturne._Grey_and_Gold,_West.story: A foggy Thames swallows Westminster Bridge whole. Whistler rowed out with his brother William at dusk, memorising the smudged lights and the shape of the water, then painted back in the studio from memory. He wasn't after a view; he called this kind of picture a nocturne on purpose, borrowing from Chopin, so you'd listen to it as much as look. The bridge barely exists here, just a bar of grey lifted by a pinpoint of gold. The Burrells gave it to Glasgow in 1944.

Whistler_James_Symphony_in_White_no_1_(T.title: Symphony in White, No. 1: The White Girl

source.canonical_title: File:Whistler James Symphony in White no 1 (The White Girl) 1862.jpg
source.credit: National Gallery of Art, Washington, D. C., online collection

title.de: Symphonie in Wieß Nr. 1, Mädchen in Weiß
title.ja: 白のシンフォニー第1番 - 白の少女

Whistler_James_Symphony_in_White_no_1_(T.story: Whistler's lover Joanna Hiffernan stands on a wolfskin in a white dress holding a drooping lily, and nobody could agree what it meant. The Royal Academy rejected it in 1862; the Paris Salon rejected it in 1863; it ended up the scandal of the Salon des Refuses alongside Manet's 'Dejeuner sur l'herbe.' Whistler insisted it meant nothing at all, which was the whole point. He only attached the musical title 'Symphony in White' years later. It's at the National Gallery of Art, Washington.

Whistler_Selbstporträt.jpg.title: Arrangement in Gray: Portrait of the Painter .

source.canonical_title: File:Whistler Selbstporträt.jpg

Whistler_Selbstporträt.jpg.story: Whistler in his forties, a black hat pulled low, two brushes in one fist, watching himself watch himself. He called it an arrangement in grey because the colour mattered more to him than the face. His friend and patron Alexander Ionides bought it almost immediately. The brushwork is thin, almost scraped, the kind of surface Ruskin would soon accuse him of charging too much for. The panel lives now at the Detroit Institute of Arts, dated around 1872.

Whistlers_Mother_high_res.jpg.title: Portrait of the Artist's Mother
Whistlers_Mother_high_res.jpg.description: Depicted person: Anna McNeill Whistler place of creation: London

source.canonical_title: File:Whistlers Mother high res.jpg

title.es: Retrato de la madre del artista
title.fr: Portrait de la mère de l'artiste" Whistler's Mother

Whistlers_Mother_high_res.jpg.story: Whistler's proper title is Arrangement in Grey and Black, No. 1. The mother showed up late for a scheduled sitter; sixty-seven-year-old Anna posed instead, seated because standing tired her out. Her son fussed for weeks over the tonal balance, calling the picture an arrangement, not a portrait. The Royal Academy nearly rejected it in 1872. Then France bought it in 1891, made it the first American painting to enter the Louvre in 1925, and it's hung at the Musée d'Orsay since 1986.

Wilhelm_Alexander_Wolfgang_von_Kobell_00.title: The Siege of Cozel
Wilhelm_Alexander_Wolfgang_von_Kobell_00.description: Die Belagerung von Koźle/Cosel in Schlesien (Abwehr eines Ausfalls der preußischen Besatzung durch die Bayern im Dritten Koalitionskrieg am 15. März 1807)

source.canonical_title: File:Wilhelm Alexander Wolfgang von Kobell 001.jpg
source.credit: 1. The Yorck Project (2002) 10.000 Meisterwerke der Malerei (DVD-ROM), distributed by DIRECTMEDIA Publishing GmbH. ISBN : 3936122202 . 2. Bildergipfel

Wilhelm_Alexander_Wolfgang_von_Kobell_00.story: Bavarian officers and their mounts gather on a ridge above Cozel, in Silesia, watching a Prussian sortie being driven back on 15 March 1807. Kobell paints the scene with his usual clarity: bare trees silhouetted against a pale cold sky, the town floating on a band of river mist, the soldiers arranged like chess pieces along the road. No smoke, no scream, no heroics. The Third Coalition war reduced to a crisp sunlit tableau. Kobell was Munich's specialist in exactly this kind of orderly Napoleonic panorama, commissioned by Crown Prince Ludwig of Bavaria.

Wilhelm_von_Kaulbach_004.jpg.title: Schmetterlinge

source.canonical_title: File:Wilhelm von Kaulbach 004.jpg
source.credit: The Yorck Project (2002) 10.000 Meisterwerke der Malerei (DVD-ROM), distributed by DIRECTMEDIA Publishing GmbH. ISBN : 3936122202 .

Wilhelm_von_Kaulbach_004.jpg.story: A dark-brown ground scattered with butterflies and moths, some spreading full iridescent wings, others tucked along the bare branches of a tree. Titled simply Schmetterlinge, Butterflies. It's a curious piece from a painter best known for vast allegorical frescoes of the Tower of Babel and the Battle of the Huns. Here Kaulbach works small and zoological, closer to a naturalist's plate than a history canvas. The brown field makes the blues and pinks almost glow. Painted around 1860, late in his Munich years, when he could afford to indulge a quieter, more private kind of picture.

Wilhelm_von_Kobell_-_Cattle_Market_befor.title: Cattle Market before a Large City on a Lake

source.canonical_title: File:Wilhelm von Kobell - Cattle Market before a Large City on a Lake, 1820 - Google Art Project.jpg

Wilhelm_von_Kobell_-_Cattle_Market_befor.story: Kobell loved cold, clean light, and here he spreads it over a lakeside market like a freshly starched sheet. Cattle, dealers and idling horsemen cluster in the foreground; behind them a silvery city rises from the water under an impossibly clear Bavarian sky. He was court painter to the Bavarian royal family at the time, and by 1820 he'd perfected this bright, almost brittle clarity, figures pinned against distance as if on glass. No bustle, no dust. Just the cool pause before a sale.

Wilhelmine_Sulzer.jpg.title: Wilhelmine Sulzer

source.canonical_title: File:Wilhelmine Sulzer.jpg

Wilhelmine_Sulzer.jpg.story: A seventeen-year-old drama student at the Royal Court Theatre, Wilhelmine Sulzer caught Ludwig I's eye in 1837 and was on Stieler's easel within months. He painted her in 1838 with auburn hair loose around bare shoulders, a plain white gown, a heavy fur thrown across her arms, the theatrical hinted at but not performed. She had been hired the year before, barely a name on a cast list, and suddenly she was hanging at Nymphenburg beside princesses and countesses. That was how the gallery worked.

William_Holman_Hunt_(1827-1910)_-_The_Ha.title: The Haunted Manor

source.canonical_title: File:William Holman Hunt (1827-1910) - The Haunted Manor - T00932 - Tate.jpg

William_Holman_Hunt_(1827-1910)_-_The_Ha.story: An early Pre-Raphaelite landscape, painted when Hunt was only twenty-two, near Wimbledon Park. A still pond, dense ivy, the low sun setting fire to the upper windows of an abandoned house. Hunt worked outdoors on the spot, piling up leaf-by-leaf detail in the new Brotherhood manner. The title came later, prompted by viewers who found the empty windows unnerving. Hunt himself insisted there was no ghost, only light.

William_Holman_Hunt_-_Selfportrait.jpg.title: Self-portrait

source.canonical_title: File:William Holman Hunt - Selfportrait.jpg

title.th: ภาพเหมือนตนเอง

William_Holman_Hunt_-_Selfportrait.jpg.story: Painted in Florence in 1867, between trips to the Holy Land and at the moment Hunt was mourning his first wife Fanny, who had died in childbirth the year before. He shows himself bearded, direct, still the Pre-Raphaelite conscience in middle age. It was made for the Uffizi's collection of artists' self-portraits, placing him among the company he thought he deserved.

William_Holman_Hunt_-_The_Birthday.jpg.title: The Birthday
William_Holman_Hunt_-_The_Birthday.jpg.description: A Portrait Of The Artist's Wife, Edith

source.canonical_title: File:William Holman Hunt - The Birthday.jpg

William_Holman_Hunt_-_The_Birthday.jpg.story: A portrait of Edith Waugh, Hunt's second wife and the younger sister of Fanny, whose death had devastated him. English law forbade such a marriage, so the couple wed in Switzerland in 1875 and were cut by half of London society. The picture catches her in a soft domestic light, flowers at hand, more tender than Hunt's usual bristling Pre-Raphaelite finish.

William_Holman_Hunt_-_The_Finding_of_the.title: The Finding of the Saviour in the Temple

source.canonical_title: File:William Holman Hunt - The Finding of the Saviour in the Temple - Google Art Project.jpg
source.credit: qQEKNsHatzrphQ at Google Cultural Institute , zoom level maximum

William_Holman_Hunt_-_The_Finding_of_the.story: Hunt sailed to Jerusalem in 1854 determined to paint the twelve-year-old Jesus with actual Judaic detail, right down to the phylacteries and temple-floor mosaics. It took him six years. He hired local models, lost them, found others, sketched ancient rituals, paused to paint The Scapegoat, and finally finished back in England in 1860. Every robe pattern is researched; every elder's face is a portrait. The painting sold for 5,500 guineas, a record price for a contemporary British work at the time. Birmingham Museum has owned it since 1896.

William_M._Chase,_N._A.jpg.title: William M. Chase, N. A.

source.canonical_title: File:William M. Chase, N. A.jpg
source.credit: Metropolitan Museum of Art, online collection (The Met object ID 12471)

William_M._Chase,_N._A.jpg.story: Chase was one of America's busiest portraitists and its most charismatic teacher, and when his students clubbed together to commission a painting of him in 1902, they sent him straight to Sargent. Sargent put him in evening black with palette and brushes at the ready, moustache waxed, eyes sharp. It was a gift from the pupils to the National Academy of Design in New York, and the Metropolitan Museum of Art has owned it since 1905.

William_Merrit_Chase_-_Still_life_with_f.title: Still life with fruit

source.canonical_title: File:William Merrit Chase - Still life with fruit 1871.jpg

William_Merrit_Chase_-_Still_life_with_f.story: Painted the year Chase arrived in Munich to study under Karl von Piloty, this still life is darker and more old-masterly than the breezy plein-air pictures he would make a decade later. Ripe fruit tumbles across a cloth against a near-black ground — a young American trying on Dutch grandfathers before he found his own light.

William_Merritt_Chase_-_First_Touch_of_A.title: First Touch of Autumn

source.canonical_title: File:William Merritt Chase - First Touch of Autumn - Google Art Project.jpg
source.credit: twFSmkC99OhD0g at Google Cultural Institute maximum zoom level

William_Merritt_Chase_-_First_Touch_of_A.story: Half the canvas is sky. The other half is Shinnecock, the scrubby eastern end of Long Island where Chase ran his famous summer school through the 1890s, teaching a young Georgia O'Keeffe among others. By about 1898, when he painted this, the students had gone home, the dunes had emptied, and the first rust was coming into the grass. He flattens the whole thing into a slow horizontal hush. It hangs now at the Indianapolis Museum of Art.

William_Merritt_Chase_-_Girl_in_a_Japane.title: Girl in a Japanese Costume

source.canonical_title: File:William Merritt Chase - Girl in a Japanese Costume - Google Art Project.jpg
source.credit: zQFJS956MheMiw at Google Cultural Institute maximum zoom level

William_Merritt_Chase_-_Girl_in_a_Japane.story: A young woman turns in a loose kimono, meeting the painter's eye with unguarded directness. Chase kept a studio stuffed with kimonos, fans, screens and lacquer, part of the Japonisme craze sweeping 1880s New York, and he cycled models through the props. The sitter's identity is lost, the Brooklyn Museum records her only as 'young woman.' The face is sharply realist; the silks dissolve into impressionistic flicks. Painted around 1890, gifted to the Brooklyn Museum by Isabella Kurtz in memory of her husband Charles.

William_Merritt_Chase_-_Open_Air_Breakfa.title: Open Air Breakfast

source.canonical_title: File:William Merritt Chase - Open Air Breakfast - Google Art Project.jpg
source.credit: IwF0LR5CzDn15Q at Google Cultural Institute maximum zoom level

William_Merritt_Chase_-_Open_Air_Breakfa.story: Chase married Alice Gerson in 1887 and moved in with her parents in Brooklyn, and the next summer he painted their backyard as a kind of sun-dappled manifesto. Greyhound Fly naps in the grass, Alice's sister lolls in a hammock, baby Cosy props up in her high chair, and sister Hattie stands with a tennis racquet. The tablecloth almost glows. It's 1888, a casual American answer to Manet, and now belongs to the Toledo Museum of Art.

William_Merritt_Chase_-_Still_Life_with_.title: Still Life with Hummingbird

source.canonical_title: File:William Merritt Chase - Still Life with Hummingbird - Google Art Project.jpg
source.credit: IAHM9vQlxjlkuQ at Google Cultural Institute maximum zoom level

William_Merritt_Chase_-_Still_Life_with_.story: A hummingbird hovers stock-still at a tangle of flowers, wings a blur no paint can really catch and Chase doesn't try. He was about twenty-one, still in Indianapolis, years before Munich and Paris would sharpen his brush. You can feel the beginner's love of every petal here, the careful velvety dark behind the blooms. It's oil on canvas, dated 1870, and now hangs in the Indianapolis Museum of Art at Newfields, the city where the painter got his start.

William_Merritt_Chase_-_The_Song,_1907.j.title: The Song

source.canonical_title: File:William Merritt Chase - The Song, 1907.jpg

William_Merritt_Chase_-_The_Song,_1907.j.story: A late, plush interior: a woman at the piano, another listening, the whole scene wrapped in the amber light Chase loved for evening pictures. By 1907 he was out of fashion — the Ashcan painters were already sharpening their knives against his polished manner — but works like this show he could still summon the old Sargent-adjacent glamour when he wanted to. It's music as social ritual rather than performance: two figures, no audience, the song a private occasion sealed inside the velvet room.

William_Merritt_Chase_-_The_Young_Orphan.title: The Young Orphan

source.canonical_title: File:William Merritt Chase - The Young Orphan (1884).jpg

William_Merritt_Chase_-_The_Young_Orphan.story: Chase painted this solitary girl in mourning black slumped into a crimson settee — one of his first full-scale bids for serious recognition after returning from Munich. Originally titled 'At Her Ease,' it was renamed 'The Young Orphan' when it won him entry to the Society of American Artists, where sentimentality sold better than studio cool. The composition is nearly all red: the sofa swallows the figure, leaving only the pale oval of her face and her limp hands to register the grief. Now at the National Academy of Design in New York, a museum Chase once led.

William_Turner,_Bridge_of_Sighs,_Ducal_P.title: Bridge of Sighs, Ducal Palace and Custom House, Venice: Canaletti painting

source.canonical_title: File:William Turner, Bridge of Sighs, Ducal Palace and Custom-House.jpg

title.fr: Le pont des soupirs, le palais des doges et la douane, Venise. Canaletto peignant

William_Turner,_Bridge_of_Sighs,_Ducal_P.story: Look down in the bottom-left corner: a little figure in a dark hat is painting at an easel. That's Canaletto, dead for seventy years, dropped into Turner's own Venice as a tribute. This was Turner's first exhibited Venetian oil, shown at the Royal Academy of 1833, a decade after his first visit to the city. The Bridge of Sighs, the Doge's Palace and the Dogana stack up in pale sunlight. Robert Vernon gave the painting to the nation in 1847; it now hangs at Tate Britain.

William_holman_hunt-the_shadow_of_death..title: The Shadow of Death

source.canonical_title: File:William holman hunt-the shadow of death.jpg
source.credit: Originally from en.wikipedia ; description page is/was here . 2007-01-04 (original upload date). Original uploader was Paul Barlow at en.wikipedia

William_holman_hunt-the_shadow_of_death..story: The adolescent Jesus stretches after a day of carpentry, and the setting sun throws his silhouette on the back wall in the shape of a crucifixion, tools arranged where the nails will be. Mary, kneeling over the gifts of the Magi, looks up and sees it. Hunt painted the backgrounds in a real Bethlehem workshop and finished it in Jerusalem, with the Dome of the Rock visible through the window. Agnew's paid £10,500 for it, an astonishing sum at the time.

Wind_God_and_Thunder_God_Screens_by_Tawa.title: 風神雷神図屏風 (Wind God and Thunder God Screens)
Wind_God_and_Thunder_God_Screens_by_Tawa.description: Wind God Fujin (right) and Thunder God Raijin (left) by Tawaraya Sotatsu. These are deities (kami) in Shinto religion. This artwork is a National Treasure of Japan.

source.canonical_title: File:Wind God and Thunder God Screens by Tawaraya Sotatsu hi-res.png

Wind_God_and_Thunder_God_Screens_by_Tawa.story: Two deities crashing in from opposite edges of a sea of gold leaf. Fujin the wind god, green-skinned and grinning, drags a white sack of wind; Raijin the thunder god, pale and horned, rides a ring of drums. Sotatsu leaves the entire middle empty, which is the whole trick: the gods are pushed to the margins so the gold can do the work of sky. The screens became a Rinpa touchstone; Ogata Korin later copied them almost line for line, and Sakai Hoitsu copied Korin. National Treasure, now at Kennin-ji in Kyoto.

Windmill_and_Boats_near_Zaandam,_Holland.title: Windmill and Boats near Zaandam, Holland
Windmill_and_Boats_near_Zaandam,_Holland.description: Painting exhibited in the Ny Carlsberg Glyptotek, Dantes Plads 7, Copenhagen, Denmark.

source.canonical_title: File:Windmill and Boats near Zaandam, Holland, by Claude Monet, 1871 - Ny Carlsberg Glyptotek - Copenhagen - DSC09437.JPG
source.permission: This artwork is now in the public domain because the artist died more than 70 years ago.

Windmill_and_Boats_near_Zaandam,_Holland.story: Another from the Zaandam summer of 1871. A lone windmill, a cluster of masts, the slow-moving water of a Dutch canal — Monet, on the run from French politics, painting calm. The canvas is modest in scale (about 48 by 75 centimetres) and easy in mood: horizontal bands of sky, mill, boats, water, each answering the next. It was bought by the Danish brewing magnate Carl Jacobsen and has hung ever since in Copenhagen's Ny Carlsberg Glyptotek, where he parked a great deal of French nineteenth-century painting.

Winners,_by_Vasily_Vereshchagin_(1878).j.title: Winners

source.canonical_title: File:Winners, by Vasily Vereshchagin (1878).jpg

Winners,_by_Vasily_Vereshchagin_(1878).j.story: The other side of a Russian defeat at Plevna. Turkish soldiers move across a field of dead Russian infantry, pulling off boots, going through pockets, stripping uniforms for whatever the dead no longer need. Vereshchagin witnessed the assaults on Plevna himself. When he showed this canvas in Petersburg alongside the Requiem, officers were furious — Russian soldiers weren't supposed to lose, and they weren't supposed to be looted on the canvas. He painted it anyway. Victory in his Balkan series is always somebody else's.

Winslow_Homer,_American_-_A_Huntsman_and.title: A huntsman and dogs

source.canonical_title: File:Winslow Homer, American - A Huntsman and Dogs - Google Art Project.jpg
source.credit: fgGa0e8ULzplRw at Google Cultural Institute maximum zoom level

Winslow_Homer,_American_-_A_Huntsman_and.story: A boy on a ridge in the Adirondacks, slung deer pelt over his shoulder, two hounds panting beside him. The sky is bruise-colored; the pelt is the only warm thing in the picture. Homer wasn't sentimental about it: this was hounding, a practice so destructive to deer herds that New York State banned it four years later, in 1897. The Philadelphia Museum of Art holds the painting.

Winslow_Homer,_American_-_The_Life_Line_.title: The Life Line

source.canonical_title: File:Winslow Homer, American - The Life Line - Google Art Project.jpg
source.credit: xQE9eAXWkRGPUQ at Google Cultural Institute maximum zoom level

Winslow_Homer,_American_-_The_Life_Line_.story: A breeches buoy strung between a foundering ship and the cliff, two bodies lashed together, spray driving sideways. Homer hides the rescuer's face behind the woman's red scarf, smart move: the painting becomes about the rope, not the hero. He'd watched life-saving drills on the New Jersey coast the year before starting this. When it hung at the National Academy in 1884 it sold opening day for $2,500, a price that rescued Homer's finances after years of thin sales.

Winslow_Homer_-_After_the_Hurricane,_Bah.title: After the Hurricane, Bahamas

source.canonical_title: File:Winslow Homer - After the Hurricane, Bahamas - Google Art Project.jpg
source.credit: TAG7VpnWDiMTDQ at Google Cultural Institute maximum zoom level

Winslow_Homer_-_After_the_Hurricane,_Bah.story: A Black man sprawled on a beach beside his wrecked sloop, alive, maybe, unclear. The sky has already cleared to that bright post-storm blue. Homer painted it on his 1898-99 trip to Nassau, watercolor on paper, rapid washes for the sand and the bruised clouds. It's a quieter cousin to The Gulf Stream, painted the same winter. The Art Institute of Chicago has held it since 1933.

Winslow_Homer_-_Artists_Sketching_in_the.title: Artists Sketching in the White Mountains

source.canonical_title: File:Winslow Homer - Artists Sketching in the White Mountains.jpg
source.credit: 1. Unknown source Unknown source 2. antiquesandfineart.com 3. Portland Museum of Art

Winslow_Homer_-_Artists_Sketching_in_the.story: Three painters sit in a row on a New Hampshire ridge, easels up, turning their backs on us to face the same hazy valley, as if the mountain were posing for all of them at once. It's a sly little joke about the whole Hudson River scramble to paint the White Mountains. Homer, recently back from Paris and already restless with studio conventions, made it in 1868, nine and a half by nearly sixteen inches, oil on panel. Signed 'W. Homer 1868' lower left. Portland Museum of Art.

Winslow_Homer_-_Breezing_Up_(A_Fair_Wind.title: Breezing Up (A Fair Wind)

source.canonical_title: File:Winslow Homer - Breezing Up (A Fair Wind) - Google Art Project.jpg

title.fr: Le vent se lève (Un vent favorable)

Winslow_Homer_-_Breezing_Up_(A_Fair_Wind.story: A catboat heels hard in a stiff wind, three boys and a man at the tiller, a stringer of fish flopping at their feet. Homer started it in 1873 in Gloucester and kept reworking it until 1876, tightening the wave, repositioning the distant schooner. It became one of the most reproduced American paintings of the nineteenth century, a kind of maritime equivalent of Washington Crossing the Delaware. It's been at the National Gallery of Art in Washington since 1943.

Winslow_Homer_-_Clear_Sailing.jpg.title: Clear Sailing

source.canonical_title: File:Winslow Homer - Clear Sailing.jpg
source.credit: Philadelphia Museum of Art, online collection

Winslow_Homer_-_Clear_Sailing.jpg.story: Two boys lean against a post on a Gloucester wharf and watch a schooner head for open water under full sail. Homer spent the summer of 1880 living at Ten Pound Island lighthouse in Gloucester Harbor, Massachusetts, and the whole season went into watercolors like this one, loose, salt-bitten, built around harbor light. The title 'Clear Sailing' is literally the weather report: fair wind, no fog, a good day to be outbound on a fishing trip.

Winslow_Homer_-_Crab_Fishing.jpg.title: Crab Fishing

source.canonical_title: File:Winslow Homer - Crab Fishing.jpg
source.credit: 1. Bridgeman Art Library : Object 247063 2. The Athenaeum: Home - info - pic 3. Worcester Art Museum

Winslow_Homer_-_Crab_Fishing.jpg.story: A girl leans over the side of a flat-bottomed boat, line in hand, hauling in a crab from shallow green water. Homer painted the watercolor in 1883, the year he finally settled permanently at Prouts Neck on the coast of Maine after returning from England. Crabbing was a summer staple along the New England coast; all you needed was a length of twine, a chicken neck for bait, and a slow boat. The small sheet is pure Maine afternoon.

Winslow_Homer_-_Dad's_Coming!.jpg.title: Dad's Coming!

source.canonical_title: File:Winslow Homer - Dad's Coming!.jpg
source.credit: National Gallery of Art, Washington, D. C., online collection

Winslow_Homer_-_Dad's_Coming!.jpg.story: A woman stands barefoot on the sand with a baby on her hip. Her small son perches on the prow of a beached dory, staring out to sea. The title hopes; the postures don't. Homer painted this little nine-by-fourteen-inch panel in 1873, the same summer a gale off Gloucester sank nine fishing boats and killed 128 men. Harper's Weekly published an engraving of it that November. Paul Mellon bequeathed the original to the National Gallery of Art in 1999.

Winslow_Homer_-_Eagle_Head,_Manchester,_.title: Eagle Head, Manchester, Massachusetts (High Tide)

source.canonical_title: File:Winslow Homer - Eagle Head, Manchester, Massachusetts (High Tide).jpg
source.credit: Metropolitan Museum of Art, online collection (The Met object ID 20011474)

Winslow_Homer_-_Eagle_Head,_Manchester,_.story: Three young women have just come out of the surf at Eagle Head, on Massachusetts' North Shore, and the wet fabric and loose hair scandalised New York when Homer showed it in 1870. Critics called it indelicate. A reviewer in The Nation sniffed that the bathers were 'ugly and careless,' the skies 'quite pretty.' Homer didn't flinch, and the Metropolitan Museum of Art eventually bought it.

Winslow_Homer_-_Girl_and_Laurel.jpg.title: Girl and Laurel

source.canonical_title: File:Winslow Homer - Girl and Laurel.jpg

Winslow_Homer_-_Girl_and_Laurel.jpg.story: A girl in a wide straw hat stands among mountain laurel, the white and pink blooms crowding up around her skirt. Homer painted the watercolor in 1879, one of a cluster of laurel studies he worked on in the hills above the Hudson River Valley. Mountain laurel flowers in late June, which dates the scene tightly; the shrubs are notoriously hard to paint because the flower clusters read almost white in full sun. Homer solved it with a thin wash and reserved paper.

Winslow_Homer_-_Girl_in_the_Hammock.jpg.title: Girl in the Hammock

source.canonical_title: File:Winslow Homer - Girl in the Hammock.jpg

Winslow_Homer_-_Girl_in_the_Hammock.jpg.story: A young woman in a white dress stretches out in a hammock with a book, her shoes dangling off the edge as sunlight filters through the leaves and pools on her skirt. Homer painted it during the summer of 1873 and also titled it 'Sunlight and Shadow.' One New York critic called his canvases that year 'as fresh and full of nature as a breath of hawthorne on a May morning.' The 13 by 20 inch oil now lives at the Colby College Museum of Art in Maine.

Winslow_Homer_-_Long_Branch,_New_Jersey..title: Long Branch, New Jersey

source.canonical_title: File:Winslow Homer - Long Branch, New Jersey.jpg
source.credit: 1. The AMICA Library 2. Museum of Fine Arts, Boston, online database

Winslow_Homer_-_Long_Branch,_New_Jersey..story: Two young women in bright summer dresses stroll the bluff at Long Branch, parasols tilted, the Atlantic glittering below. Homer painted it in 1869 with a cool, sharp-edged light that owes a lot to the Manet he'd just seen in Paris. Long Branch was the Hamptons of its day, a resort where presidents summered and stylish visitors came to be seen. The Museum of Fine Arts, Boston bought it in 1941 for $2,800.

Winslow_Homer_-_Mink_Pond.jpg.title: Mink Pond

source.canonical_title: File:Winslow Homer - Mink Pond.jpg

Winslow_Homer_-_Mink_Pond.jpg.story: Watercolor, and Homer at his loosest. A bass rising under lily pads, a frog watching from a leaf, sunlight coming through the surface in broken stripes. He painted it at the North Woods Club in the Adirondacks, a sportsmen's retreat he visited most summers from 1889 on. Look at the frog's eye, a single dot of white gouache. Harvard's Fogg Museum has held it since 1928.

Winslow_Homer_-_Moonlight.jpg.title: Moonlight

source.canonical_title: File:Winslow Homer - Moonlight.jpg
source.credit: 1. The Athenaeum: Home - info - pic 2. Fenimore Art Museum

Winslow_Homer_-_Moonlight.jpg.story: A couple sits at the end of a pier, silhouetted black against a white track of moonlight laid across the Atlantic. Homer painted it in watercolor, gouache and graphite during a six-week stay on the eastern end of Long Island in the summer of 1874, and the alternate title spells out the spot: 'On the Beach, East Hampton, Long Island.' The air feels cool, the sea almost silent. The sheet is now held by the Arkell Museum in Canajoharie, New York.

Winslow_Homer_-_On_the_Beach.jpg.title: On the Beach

source.canonical_title: File:Winslow Homer - On the Beach.jpg

Winslow_Homer_-_On_the_Beach.jpg.story: Homer kept returning to the Jersey shore in 1869, and this is one of those small, sun-struck studies, figures pinned against wet sand and wide sky. You can feel the breeze in the women's skirts and the pause of an afternoon that is all leisure and no plot. His beach pictures from this year helped invent a new American subject: middle-class vacationers with nothing to do but exist in the light.

Winslow_Homer_-_On_the_Stile.jpg.title: On the Stile

source.canonical_title: File:Winslow Homer - On the Stile.jpg
source.credit: National Gallery of Art, Washington, D. C., online collection

Winslow_Homer_-_On_the_Stile.jpg.story: A girl pauses mid-step on a wooden stile cut through a rail fence, skirts gathered, looking back at the viewer. Homer worked up the small watercolor in 1878 from his summer at Houghton Farm in Mountainville, New York, the same Catskill-foothills retreat that fed a whole run of shepherdess and farm-child scenes that year. The subject is simple country geometry, a girl and a fence, but the light on her white sleeve is what carries it.

Winslow_Homer_-_Shark_fishing.jpg.title: Shark fishing

source.canonical_title: File:Winslow Homer - Shark fishing.jpg

Winslow_Homer_-_Shark_fishing.jpg.story: Two Bahamian men in a dinghy, a hooked shark thrashing alongside, the water that hard Caribbean turquoise Homer only found after his 1884 trip to Nassau. This is watercolor, not oil, and you can see him exploiting it: wet-into-wet for the spray, dry brush for the shark's hide. He'd return to these same waters and figures over and over through the 1890s. The composition reappears, rearranged, in the later oil The Gulf Stream of 1899.

Winslow_Homer_-_Sunlight_on_the_Coast_-_.title: Sunlight on the Coast

source.canonical_title: File:Winslow Homer - Sunlight on the Coast - Google Art Project.jpg

Winslow_Homer_-_Sunlight_on_the_Coast_-_.story: No figures this time, just a wave hitting ledge rock and the low, cold light of a Maine autumn. Homer painted it from his Prouts Neck studio, where he'd built a second-story balcony specifically to watch the sea. The steamer on the horizon is almost an afterthought. He was 54 and done with narrative: from here on it's mostly rocks, water, and weather. Toledo Museum of Art bought it in 1912.

Winslow_Homer_-_The_Adirondack_guide.jpg.title: The Adirondack Guide

source.canonical_title: File:Winslow Homer - The Adirondack guide.jpg

Winslow_Homer_-_The_Adirondack_guide.jpg.story: A guide named Rufus Wallace, probably, sitting in a guide boat with his pole, still water reflecting back the pines. Homer painted him repeatedly at the North Woods Club on Minerva Lake, New York. The boat is the classic Adirondack double-ender, light enough for one man to carry between ponds. Watercolor on paper, quick and confident. The Museum of Fine Arts, Boston has owned it since 1924.

Winslow_Homer_-_The_Blue_Boy.jpg.title: Cow Boys

source.canonical_title: File:Winslow Homer - The Blue Boy.jpg
source.credit: Ball State University Libraries: Digital Media Repository

Winslow_Homer_-_The_Blue_Boy.jpg.story: Two barefoot country boys in straw hats loaf on a grassy hillside, one stretched flat, one sitting up, both watching birds wheel through a soft-clouded sky. Homer worked this up in watercolor and graphite in 1873, the same summer he took up watercolor seriously at Gloucester, Massachusetts, and started sending the results to New York exhibitions. Despite the 'Cow Boys' label floating around, the piece is best known as 'The Blue Boy,' named for the blue shirt of the standing lad.

Winslow_Homer_-_The_Fog_Warning_-_Google.title: The Fog Warning / Halibut Fishing

source.canonical_title: File:Winslow Homer - The Fog Warning - Google Art Project.jpg
source.credit: GAEcgEvHorgctQ at Google Cultural Institute maximum zoom level

Winslow_Homer_-_The_Fog_Warning_-_Google.story: A lone dory, a halibut slung across the thwarts, and a schooner already half swallowed by the fog on the horizon. The fisherman turns his head to measure the distance against the weather. Homer painted it at Prouts Neck, Maine, the year he settled there for good. It's one of three Grand Banks pictures he made in 1885; the Museum of Fine Arts, Boston bought it in 1894 for $1,500.

Winslow_Homer_-_The_Four_Leaf_Clover.jpg.title: The Four Leaf Clover

source.canonical_title: File:Winslow Homer - The Four Leaf Clover.jpg
source.credit: 1./2. Bridgeman Art Library : Object 241624 3./4. Detroit Institute of Arts

Winslow_Homer_-_The_Four_Leaf_Clover.jpg.story: A girl in a long white dress and a cream hat with black embroidery sits beside an open window, holding up a tiny clover toward the light. Her orange stockings pick up the warmth of the flowers climbing the wall behind her. Homer painted the scene in 1873, a year he was leaning hard into children and rural leisure as subjects. The clover, of course, means luck. The oil now hangs at the Detroit Institute of Arts.

Winslow_Homer_-_The_Green_Hill.jpg.title: The Green Hill

source.canonical_title: File:Winslow Homer - The Green Hill.jpg
source.credit: National Gallery of Art, Washington, D. C., online collection

Winslow_Homer_-_The_Green_Hill.jpg.story: A lone figure rests on the slope of a green hill, the grass running up in long unbroken sweeps toward a pale sky. Homer made the piece in 1878, during the Houghton Farm summer that produced so many of his shepherdess and rural-child watercolors. The composition is unusually spare, almost a color-field experiment: a band of green, a band of sky, a single figure anchoring the seam. It marks the year Homer's watercolors began to thin out toward pure atmosphere.

Winslow_Homer_-_The_Gulf_Stream_-_Metrop.title: The Gulf Stream

source.canonical_title: File:Winslow Homer - The Gulf Stream - Metropolitan Museum of Art.jpg
source.credit: 1. The Yorck Project (2002) 10.000 Meisterwerke der Malerei (DVD-ROM), distributed by DIRECTMEDIA Publishing GmbH. ISBN : 3936122202 . 2. art database

Winslow_Homer_-_The_Gulf_Stream_-_Metrop.story: Homer had gone to Nassau the winter his father died, and when he got back to his studio in Prouts Neck, Maine, he painted this. A Black sailor on the canted deck of a dismasted sloop, rudderless, sugar cane spilling around him, sharks circling, a waterspout on the left and a distant ship on the far horizon that clearly isn't coming. Viewers kept writing to ask if the man survived. Homer, who hated explaining his work, eventually snapped at his dealer: tell them the boat and its occupant 'will be rescued and returned to his friends and home, and ever after live happily.' The Met bought it in 1906.

Winslow_Homer_-_The_Herring_Net_-_Google.title: The Herring Net

source.canonical_title: File:Winslow Homer - The Herring Net - Google Art Project.jpg
source.credit: ygF9ozok7GQIvA at Google Cultural Institute maximum zoom level

Winslow_Homer_-_The_Herring_Net_-_Google.story: A boy and a man hauling in a drift net heavy with silver fish, the schooner hull in the far distance barely a smudge. Homer piles the herring in the dory so densely you can almost smell them. He worked it up from sketches made off Gloucester, Massachusetts in the summer of 1884. The Art Institute of Chicago has had it since 1937, part of the Mr. and Mrs. Martin A. Ryerson Collection.

Winslow_Homer_-_The_Reaper.jpg.title: The Reaper

source.canonical_title: File:Winslow Homer - The Reaper.jpg

Winslow_Homer_-_The_Reaper.jpg.story: A young reaper stands in a field of tall grass, sickle lowered, pausing between strokes. Homer painted the small watercolor in 1878, the summer he based himself at Houghton Farm in Mountainville, New York, and filled sheet after sheet with farmworkers and shepherdesses in straw hats. Like 'Song of the Lark' two years earlier, the handheld blade is a deliberate anachronism; by then mechanical reapers had taken over most American grain fields, making the solitary figure already a kind of remembered image.

Winslow_Homer_-_Two_boys_watching_schoon.title: Two Boys Watching Schooners

source.canonical_title: File:Winslow Homer - Two boys watching schooners.jpg
source.credit: Art Institute of Chicago : online database: entry 16803

Winslow_Homer_-_Two_boys_watching_schoon.story: Two boys in rolled-up trousers sit at the edge of a wharf, heads turned toward a line of schooners working their way out of Gloucester Harbor. Homer painted the watercolor in 1880, the summer he lived on Ten Pound Island at the mouth of the harbor and cranked out some of the most atmospheric harbor studies of his career. The whole sheet is built from wet-into-wet washes, with the schooner masts picked out in a few darker strokes after the paper had dried.

Winslow_Homer_-_Warm_Afternoon.jpg.title: Warm Afternoon

source.canonical_title: File:Winslow Homer - Warm Afternoon.jpg
source.credit: National Gallery of Art, Washington, D. C., online collection

Winslow_Homer_-_Warm_Afternoon.jpg.story: A girl in a pale dress sits on sun-baked grass, hat tipped against the glare, the heat almost audible in the stillness. Homer made the watercolor in 1878 during his summer at Houghton Farm in Mountainville, New York, the Catskill-foothills property belonging to his friend and patron Lawson Valentine. That single season produced dozens of these pastoral sheets, and 'Warm Afternoon' is one of the quietest of the run: all light, grass, and the smell of hay.

Winslow_Homer_-_Watching_the_Breakers_(1.title: Watching the Breakers

source.canonical_title: File:Winslow Homer - Watching the Breakers (1891).jpg

Winslow_Homer_-_Watching_the_Breakers_(1.story: Three figures on a rocky Maine headland, coats flat against them, watching a wave break. Homer's signature move: turn the crowd's backs to us so we watch what they watch. The rocks are Prouts Neck ledge, the exact ones outside his studio window. No story beyond the weather. He subtitled it A High Sea in exhibition catalogues, and the Cleveland Museum of Art's holds the key sketches.

Woman_writing_a_letter,_with_her_maid,_b.title: Woman Writing a Letter, with her Maid
Woman_writing_a_letter,_with_her_maid,_b.description: Woman writing a letter, with her maid

source.canonical_title: File:Woman writing a letter, with her maid, by Johannes Vermeer.jpg
source.credit: Derived from National Gallery of Ireland
