He invented the slender-gold 'shoujin' calligraphy script, catalogued over 6,000 paintings at his academy, and insisted his court artists render birds and flowers with near-scientific literalness.
artist_briefings.sesshū tōyō: Japanese Zen monk and ink painter (1420-1506) generally regarded as the country's greatest master of suibokuga. Trained at Shōkoku-ji under Shūbun, he sailed with an envoy to Ming China in 1467 and returned to forge a muscular, uniquely Japanese landscape idiom, culminating in the sweeping Sansui Chōkan handscroll.
artist_briefings.alfons mucha: Czech Art Nouveau master (1860-1939) who shot to Paris fame overnight in 1894 with a poster for Sarah Bernhardt's Gismonda. His willowy women wreathed in flowers, stars and Byzantine arabesques defined the decorative style, though he regarded his true life's work as the vast nationalist cycle of canvases, The Slav Epic.
artist_briefings.andrea mantegna: Italian early Renaissance painter and engraver (c.1431-1506) from near Padua, obsessed with classical antiquity and vertiginous illusionism. Court artist to the Gonzaga at Mantua, he painted the Camera degli Sposi with its dizzying ceiling oculus, the shockingly foreshortened Dead Christ, and the great Triumphs of Caesar.
artist_briefings.artemisia gentileschi / orazio gentilesc: Caravaggesque father and daughter who trained together in Rome, reunited at Charles I's London court in 1638 to paint the Allegory of Peace and the Arts ceiling for the Queen's House in Greenwich. Orazio's lyrical idealism contrasts with Artemisia's naturalistic, often ferocious readings of heroines like Judith and Susanna.
artist_briefings.hokusai: Katsushika Hokusai (1760-1849), Edo-period ukiyo-e painter and printmaker who changed his name more than thirty times and kept reinventing his art into his eighties. His Thirty-six Views of Mount Fuji, including The Great Wave off Kanagawa, and the sprawling Hokusai Manga sketchbooks made him the most globally recognised Japanese artist.
artist_briefings.john byam liston shaw: British painter, illustrator and teacher (1872-1919), born in Madras and trained at the Royal Academy Schools. A late Pre-Raphaelite devoted to Rossetti and medieval subjects, he painted the much-reproduced Boer War memorial picture and in 1910 co-founded the Byam Shaw School of Art in Kensington.
artist_briefings.tsuchiya kōitsu: Japanese shin-hanga printmaker (1870-1949) from Hamamatsu who spent nineteen years as live-in pupil of the ukiyo-e artist Kobayashi Kiyochika. Only at sixty did he join Watanabe Shōzaburō's studio, producing the hushed, lamp-lit temple and snow scenes for which he is now prized.
artist_briefings.antonio da correggio: Italian High Renaissance painter (c.1489-1534), active mostly in Parma, who pushed illusionism and sensuous softness further than almost any contemporary. His dome frescoes in Parma Cathedral and San Giovanni Evangelista spin upward into vertiginous heaven, and his mythologies for Federico Gonzaga hum with erotic charge.
artist_briefings.ohara koson: Japanese kacho-e specialist (1877-1945), born in Kanazawa, who produced about 500 woodblock prints of birds, flowers and small animals under the successive names Koson, Shōson and Hōson. Published mainly by Daikokuya and Watanabe, his quiet herons, sparrows and prowling cats sold especially well in America.
artist_briefings.el greco: Doménikos Theotokópoulos (1541-1614), Cretan-born painter trained in the Byzantine icon tradition who passed through Venice and Rome before settling in Toledo around 1577. His elongated, flame-lit saints, storm-riven View of Toledo and the ecstatic Burial of the Count of Orgaz gave Spanish mysticism a wholly personal visual language.
artist_briefings.fernand khnopff: Belgian Symbolist (1858-1921), a founding member of Les XX in 1883, who abandoned law for painting after seeing Burne-Jones and Moreau in Paris. His enigmatic sphinxes, hushed portraits of his sister Marguerite and the medieval streets of Bruges embodied a cult of introspection; his Brussels studio bore the motto 'On n'a que soi'.
artist_briefings.fernand le quesne: French academic painter (1856-1932), born in Paris as son of the sculptor Eugène-Louis Lequesne and trained first by his father. He worked frequently in Brittany and briefly in London, producing polished salon allegories, mythological scenes and society portraits for late-nineteenth-century collectors.
artist_briefings.gerhard von kügelgen: German Romantic portraitist and history painter (1772-1820), born at Bacharach on the Rhine and twin brother of the painter Karl. After Rome and a spell portraying the Russian imperial family for Paul I, he settled in Dresden, teaching at the Academy and painting Goethe, Schiller, Herder and Caspar David Friedrich before being murdered by a robber outside the city.
artist_briefings.goyō hashiguchi: Japanese shin-hanga artist (1880-1921) who began as a book designer, most famously for Natsume Sōseki's I Am a Cat. After one uneasy collaboration with Watanabe Shōzaburō, he supervised every step of his own prints, producing only fourteen sheets, most of them luminous bijin-ga, before dying of meningitis at forty-one.
artist_briefings.doré: Gustave Doré (1832-1883), prolific French illustrator, painter and sculptor from Strasbourg whose wood-engraved visions defined how generations pictured the Bible, Dante's Inferno, Don Quixote and the slums of London. He worked at industrial speed with teams of engravers, and late in life turned to brooding oil paintings and monumental bronze sculpture.
artist_briefings.henri matisse: French painter (1869-1954) who co-founded Fauvism with his 1905 Salon d'Automne shock of pure, non-naturalistic colour. In his bedridden final years he invented the cut-out, wielding scissors through painted paper to produce works like 'The Snail' (1953) and the Vence Chapel.
artist_briefings.hugo van der goes: Flemish master (c.1440-1482) whose monumental Portinari Altarpiece, shipped to Florence in 1483, stunned Italian painters with its northern realism and emotional weight. A mental breakdown during his final years as a lay brother near Brussels was recorded in remarkable detail by the chronicler Gaspar Ofhuys.
artist_briefings.james abbott mcneill whistler: American-born expatriate (1834-1903) who titled his paintings 'Nocturnes' and 'Arrangements' to insist on art-for-art's-sake. He sued Ruskin in 1878 for reviewing his 'Falling Rocket' as flinging 'a pot of paint in the public's face' - won a farthing, went bankrupt.
artist_briefings.kanae yamamoto: Japanese artist (1882-1946) whose 1904 woodblock 'Fisherman' is widely credited as launching sosaku-hanga, the creative-print movement where one artist designs, carves and prints. He also founded the Nihon Nomin Bijutsu Kenkyujo to teach peasant crafts in rural Nagano.
artist_briefings.kitagawa utamaro: Edo ukiyo-e master (c.1753-1806) famed for bijin-okubi-e - large-head portraits of Yoshiwara courtesans rendered with unprecedented psychological nuance. Imprisoned and manacled in 1804 for a print depicting the warlord Hideyoshi, he died two years later.
artist_briefings.jean-antoine watteau: French Rococo inventor of the fete galante, whose reception piece 'Pilgrimage to Cythera' (1717) won him membership in a new Academy category created expressly for him. Tubercular and restless, he died at 36, leaving Boucher and Fragonard to inherit his dreamy park-and-parasol world.
artist_briefings.ma yuan: Southern Song court painter (c.1160-1225) nicknamed 'One-Corner Ma' for compositions shoved to a single edge, leaving vast washes of mist. With Xia Gui he defined the Ma-Xia school, whose asymmetric landscapes shaped Chinese and Japanese ink painting for centuries.
artist_briefings.paolo uccello: Florentine early-Renaissance painter (1397-1475) so obsessed with linear perspective that Vasari said his wife complained he wouldn't come to bed. His three 'Battle of San Romano' panels (c.1438-40) splay broken lances along vanishing lines like a geometry textbook in armour.
artist_briefings.parmigianino: Parma Mannerist (1503-1540) whose 'Madonna of the Long Neck' stretches anatomy into swan-like elegance. His astonishing 'Self-Portrait in a Convex Mirror' (1524), painted on a specially prepared hemispheric panel, won him entry to the papal court of Clement VII.
artist_briefings.henry raeburn: Scottish portraitist (1756-1823) who painted Edinburgh's Enlightenment elite - Walter Scott, Lord Newton, the Highland chiefs - with a bold, brushy technique he called his 'square touch'. The 'Skating Minister' on Duddingston Loch became an unlikely icon of Scottish cool.
artist_briefings.sebastiano ricci: Venetian decorator (1659-1734) who carried the late-Baroque manner to Vienna, London and Paris, frescoing Chelsea Hospital's chapel and Burlington House. His airy, Veronese-inspired style helped ignite the Venetian revival that Tiepolo would soon crown.
artist_briefings.torii kotondo: Shin-hanga printmaker (1900-1976), born Torii Kiyotada V, adopted heir to the theatrical-poster Torii line. His 1933 'Morning Hair' - a woman combing tangled locks - was confiscated by Japanese authorities as too erotic; surviving impressions are now prized bijin-ga classics.
artist_briefings.charles william bartlett: British painter and printmaker (1860-1940) who settled in Hawaii in 1917 and collaborated with Tokyo publisher Watanabe Shozaburo on shin-hanga views of India, Japan and the Pacific. His Hawaiian landscapes remain staples of Honolulu Museum of Art holdings.
artist_briefings.peter paul rubens / after jan cornelisz: Collaborative attribution: Rubens (1577-1640) reworked compositions by the earlier Dutch painter-tapestry designer Jan Cornelisz Vermeyen (c.1500-1559), who had accompanied Charles V on the 1535 Tunis campaign. Rubens owned Vermeyen's cartoons and mined them for costume and topographic detail.
artist_briefings.peter paul rubens / jan brueghel the you: A studio partnership where Rubens painted figures and Jan Brueghel the Younger (1601-1678) supplied the lush flowers, animals and landscape. The younger Brueghel inherited his father Jan the Elder's workshop in 1625 and kept the Rubens collaboration alive for another decade.
artist_briefings.anagoria: Not a historical artist but a Wikimedia Commons username - a prolific contemporary photographer who uploads high-resolution images of museum artworks across Europe, frequently credited when their photographs illustrate encyclopedia entries.
artist_briefings.eduard magnus: Berlin society portraitist (1799-1872) whose 1846 likeness of soprano Jenny Lind - the 'Swedish Nightingale' - became the definitive image of 19th-century operatic celebrity. A member of the Prussian Academy, he also painted Mendelssohn and traveled widely sketching in Greece and Spain.
artist_briefings.utagawa hiroshige ii: Pupil and son-in-law of the landscape master (1826-1869), who took the Hiroshige name in 1858 and completed the 'Hundred Famous Views of Edo' series. After a domestic split he dropped the name, signed himself Rissho, and ended his days painting lantern designs in Yokohama.
artist_briefings.shen zhou: Ming-dynasty literatus (1427-1509) and founder of the Wu School in Suzhou, who refused official posts to paint, write poetry and entertain scholar-friends. His album 'Twelve Views of Tiger Hill' and the Cloud-and-River landscapes made him a model of the amateur-gentleman ideal.
artist_briefings.after katsushika hokusai: Copies, reprints or pastiches in the manner of Hokusai (1760-1849), the Edo polymath behind 'The Great Wave' and the 'Thirty-six Views of Mount Fuji'. Later impressions from recut blocks and Meiji-era imitations circulate widely under this attribution.
artist_briefings.artist yoshitoshi tsukioka: Tsukioka Yoshitoshi (1839-1892), the last great ukiyo-e master, pivoted from gruesome 'bloody prints' of the 1860s to the luminous 'One Hundred Aspects of the Moon' series completed shortly before his death. He trained the printmakers who would cross over into shin-hanga.
artist_briefings.after peter paul rubens: Studio replicas, print reproductions and later copies of compositions by the Antwerp Baroque giant (1577-1640). Rubens himself ran a large workshop and authorised engraved versions of his paintings, so 'After Rubens' labels span everything from 17th-century shop copies to 19th-century academic exercises.
artist_briefings.albrecht altdorfer: Regensburg painter (c.1480-1538) and leader of the Danube School, whose 'Battle of Alexander at Issus' (1529) dissolves a classical clash into a cosmic Alpine panorama. He served as city architect and refused the mayoralty in 1528 to finish the painting for Duke Wilhelm IV.
artist_briefings.xia gui: Southern Song court painter (active c.1195-1230) paired with Ma Yuan as the Ma-Xia school. His long handscroll 'Pure and Remote View of Streams and Mountains', now in Taipei, sweeps through seasons with economical axe-cut brushstrokes that Japanese Zen painters later absorbed wholesale.
artist_briefings.attributed to anthony van dyck: Works plausibly but not certainly by the Flemish portraitist (1599-1641) - Rubens's most brilliant pupil and court painter to Charles I. 'Attributed' covers pieces that show his fluid brush and aristocratic poise but lack documentary proof or a fully autograph hand.
artist_briefings.after anthony van dyck / anthony van dyc: Anthony van Dyck (1599-1641) was the Flemish virtuoso who served as Charles I's court painter, inventing the elegant, long-limbed aristocratic portrait that shaped British painting for two centuries. Trained in Rubens's Antwerp studio, he died at 42, leaving works widely copied well into the 1700s.
artist_briefings.after giuseppe arcimboldo: Giuseppe Arcimboldo (c.1526-1593) was a Milanese Mannerist who served the Habsburg emperors in Vienna and Prague, famous for portrait heads ingeniously composed from fruits, vegetables, fish, and books. Revered as a curiosity, forgotten, then rediscovered by the Surrealists, who claimed him as an ancestor.
artist_briefings.giovanni baglione: Giovanni Baglione (c.1566-1643) was a Roman Late Mannerist and early Baroque painter better remembered today for his knock-down feud with Caravaggio, whom he sued for libel in 1603. He also wrote Le Vite, a biographical dictionary of Roman artists that remains indispensable source material.
artist_briefings.aubrey beardsley: Aubrey Beardsley (1872-1898) was the English illustrator whose sinuous black-and-white line scandalised late-Victorian London, most notoriously through his drawings for Oscar Wilde's Salome and the journal The Yellow Book. Tuberculosis killed him at 25, but his Art Nouveau graphic style reshaped book illustration.
artist_briefings.carl friedrich seiffert: Carl Friedrich Seiffert (1809-1891) was a German Late Romantic landscape painter trained at the Dresden, Düsseldorf and Berlin academies. He worked in the Carl Eduard Biermann atelier and made long study trips to Switzerland, Italy, Capri and Naples, producing luminous Alpine and Mediterranean views.
artist_briefings.daniel maclise: Daniel Maclise (1806-1870) was a Cork-born history painter who dominated Victorian London's Royal Academy and frescoed The Death of Nelson and The Meeting of Wellington and Blucher in the Palace of Westminster. A close friend of Dickens, he also caricatured literary celebrities for Fraser's Magazine as 'Alfred Croquis'.
artist_briefings.歌川国芳: Utagawa Kuniyoshi (1798-1861) was an Edo ukiyo-e master who made his name with the violent, tattoo-studded warrior prints of the 108 Heroes of the Suikoden. His work ranged from brawling samurai to cats dressed as courtesans and sly caricatures of the Tokugawa regime.
artist_briefings.chen rong 陳容 陈容: Chen Rong (c.1200-1266) was a Southern Song scholar-official from Fujian and the most celebrated dragon painter in Chinese art. His 1244 Nine Dragons handscroll, now in Boston, was reportedly painted drunk, ink splashed from a wine-soaked scarf onto the paper.
artist_briefings.pieter brueghel the younger: Pieter Brueghel the Younger (1564-1638) was the Antwerp painter nicknamed 'Hell Brueghel' and later 'Peasant Brueghel' who made a living replicating his father Pieter Bruegel the Elder's compositions. His large workshop, which trained Frans Snyders, produced hundreds of peasant scenes, winter landscapes and village feasts.
artist_briefings.cornelis de vos: Cornelis de Vos (1584-1651) was one of Antwerp's leading portraitists, a Guild of St Luke dean admired especially for tender, finely observed paintings of children and family groups. Brother-in-law of Frans Snyders, he also collaborated with Rubens and won commissions from Philip IV of Spain.
artist_briefings.jacques-louis david: Jacques-Louis David (1748-1825) was the austere Neoclassicist who set the visual tone of the French Revolution with The Oath of the Horatii and The Death of Marat, then became Napoleon's official painter. Exiled to Brussels after Waterloo, he died there, never returning to France.
artist_briefings.utagawa; hiroshige: Utagawa Hiroshige (1797-1858) was the last great ukiyo-e landscape master, author of The Fifty-Three Stations of the Tokaido and One Hundred Famous Views of Edo. His rain-swept bridges and snowbound temples reached Paris in the 1860s and directly shaped Whistler, Monet and Van Gogh.
artist_briefings.egbert van der poel: Egbert van der Poel (1621-1664) was a Delft-born Dutch Golden Age painter who specialised so intensely in nocturnal village fires that contemporaries called him Holland's best 'fire painter'. He painted the 1654 Delft gunpowder explosion, which killed his daughter, at least twenty times.
artist_briefings.dong yuan: Dong Yuan (c.934-962) was a Southern Tang court official in Nanjing who founded the Southern School of Chinese landscape painting. His 'hemp-fibre' brushstrokes rendered the soft rolling hills of Jiangnan and became the canonical model for literati painters through the Ming and Qing.
artist_briefings.after peter paul rubens / gustave doré: Peter Paul Rubens (1577-1640) was the Antwerp titan of the Baroque, whose fleshy, turbulent compositions dominated European courts; Gustave Doré (1832-1883) was the French illustrator of Dante, Cervantes and the Bible whose engravings reached millions. Each borrowed the other's muscular drama.
artist_briefings.edward hopper: Edward Hopper (1882-1967) was the American realist of solitude, whose late-night diners, empty hotel rooms and clapboard lighthouses distilled mid-century urban loneliness into hard geometric light. Nighthawks (1942), painted weeks after Pearl Harbor, is the most reproduced American canvas of the twentieth century.
artist_briefings.attributed to francisco goya: Francisco Goya (1746-1828) was the Spanish court painter whose work pivoted from rococo tapestry cartoons to the Black Paintings, the Caprichos and the unflinching Disasters of War. Deaf from 1793 and disillusioned by Napoleon's invasion, he died in self-imposed exile in Bordeaux.
artist_briefings.elisabeth louise vigee le brun: Elisabeth Louise Vigee Le Brun (1755-1842) was Marie Antoinette's favourite portraitist and one of the few women admitted to the Academie royale. Fleeing the Revolution in 1789, she painted her way across Rome, Vienna, Saint Petersburg and London before returning to France under Napoleon.
artist_briefings.hayami gyoshu: Hayami Gyoshu (1894-1935) was a Tokyo-born Nihonga painter who restlessly reinvented traditional Japanese painting, from meticulous realist studies of flowers to gold-leaf masterpieces like Dancing in the Flames and Camellia Petals Scattering. Typhoid fever killed him at 40, mid-career.
artist_briefings.after peter paul rubens / peter paul rub: Rubens (1577-1640), the Flemish Baroque master of Antwerp, ran the most productive studio of his age; Erasmus Quellinus II (1607-1678) was one of his closest collaborators in the 1630s and inherited much of that workshop's court business after Rubens's death.
artist_briefings.erasmus quellinus ii: Erasmus Quellinus II (1607-1678) was an Antwerp painter, draughtsman and tapestry designer, son of a sculptor and trained as a philosopher before entering Rubens's orbit. After Rubens's death in 1640 he took over much of his master's commissions, including the 1648 Joyous Entry of Archduke Leopold Wilhelm.
artist_briefings.rafael: Raphael (Raffaello Sanzio, 1483-1520) was the Urbino-born High Renaissance master who, alongside Leonardo and Michelangelo, completes the triumvirate of Italian painting. Working for popes Julius II and Leo X, he frescoed the Vatican Stanze and died in Rome at thirty-seven, mourned as a cultural catastrophe.
artist_briefings.attributed to louis le nain / antoine le: The Le Nain brothers (Antoine c.1600-1648, Louis c.1603-1648) were painters from Laon who worked in a joint Paris studio, rare in seventeenth-century France for their sober, empathetic depictions of peasants. Their works are so stylistically close that attributions between the brothers remain contested.
artist_briefings.félicien rops: Félicien Rops (1833-1898) was a Belgian printmaker and a founding member of Les XX, famed for brilliant dry-point and soft-ground etching technique and for Symbolist-decadent imagery of Satan, skeletons and eroticism. He illustrated Baudelaire, Mallarmé, Barbey d'Aurevilly and the fin-de-siècle Parisian avant-garde.
artist_briefings.follower of rogier van der weyden: A designation for Netherlandish painters working in the orbit of Rogier van der Weyden (c. 1399/1400-1464), Brussels' official city painter and the defining figure of mid-15th-century Northern panel painting. Followers echoed his emotionally charged compositions, slender figures and jewel-toned drapery without direct documented training under him.
artist_briefings.theodoor van thulden / frans snyders: A collaborative attribution pairing two Flemish Baroque specialists: Theodoor van Thulden (1606-1669), a pupil of Rubens from 's-Hertogenbosch known for altarpieces and mythological scenes, and Frans Snyders (1579-1657), Antwerp's virtuoso of game pieces, still lifes and hunt scenes. Such partnerships were common in 17th-century Antwerp, with figure painters and animal specialists dividing labour on a single canvas.
artist_briefings.frans snyders and workshop – creator bor: Frans Snyders (1579-1657) ran a busy Antwerp workshop producing muscular still lifes, market scenes and hunt pieces that dwarfed his figures with heaps of game, fruit and fish. A close collaborator of Rubens and Jordaens, he often painted the animals in their compositions while assistants replicated his signature kitchen and larder tableaux.
artist_briefings.tsukioka yoshitoshi: Tsukioka Yoshitoshi (1839-1892) was the last great master of the Japanese woodblock print, bridging the Edo and Meiji eras with violent warrior scenes, ghost stories and his celebrated series One Hundred Aspects of the Moon. Trained under Kuniyoshi, he fought depression and poverty to revitalise ukiyo-e just as photography threatened to eclipse it.
artist_briefings.sir david wilkie: Sir David Wilkie (1785-1841), a Scottish painter from Fife, made his name with The Village Politicians (1806) and rode a taste for vivid genre scenes of rural life into royal favour, succeeding Thomas Lawrence as Painter-in-Ordinary to the King in 1830. A later Continental tour pushed his style toward grander, looser history painting; he died at sea off Gibraltar.
artist_briefings.gerard van honthorst: Gerard van Honthorst (1592-1656), the Dutch Utrecht Caravaggist nicknamed 'Gherardo delle Notti' in Rome, specialised in theatrical candlelit scenes of musicians, card players and biblical night pieces. Back in the Netherlands he became a sought-after portraitist for the Stadholder's court and the exiled Stuart royals, eventually heading a thriving Hague studio.
artist_briefings.giorgione: Giorgione (c. 1477/78-1510), born Giorgio Barbarelli da Castelfranco, reshaped Venetian painting in barely a decade with mood-drenched, poetically ambiguous works like The Tempest and the Sleeping Venus. He died of plague in his early thirties, leaving so few securely attributed pictures that scholars still quarrel over which canvases are his and which belong to the young Titian.
artist_briefings.titian / giorgione: A joint attribution reflecting the famously entangled early Venetian output of Titian (c. 1488/90-1576) and Giorgione (c. 1477/78-1510). The two worked side by side on the Fondaco dei Tedeschi frescoes around 1508, and after Giorgione's early death Titian is thought to have finished several of his canvases, leaving connoisseurs to argue the boundary ever since.
artist_briefings.giuseppe bartolomeo chiari: Giuseppe Bartolomeo Chiari (1654-1727) was a Roman late-Baroque painter and the leading assistant of Carlo Maratta, succeeding him as Principe of the Accademia di San Luca in 1722. Clement XI was his major patron, commissioning the vast Glory of St Clement ceiling at San Clemente and prophet canvases for the Lateran; his lighter touch helped push Italian painting toward Rococo.
artist_briefings.after peter paul rubens / peter paul rub: A layered attribution centred on Peter Paul Rubens (1577-1640), the Flemish Baroque master, and Jacob Peter Gowy (c. 1610-after 1644), an Antwerp collaborator who executed The Fall of Icarus and Hippomenes and Atalanta in the Prado after Rubens' oil sketches. The sequence implies a Rubens design, a workshop realisation by Gowy, and a later copy.
artist_briefings.guercino: Giovanni Francesco Barbieri (1591-1666), nicknamed Guercino ('the squinter') for a childhood eye injury, was a self-taught Bolognese-school painter from Cento whose early work crackles with Caravaggesque light and diagonal drama. A 1621 stint in Rome for Pope Gregory XV yielded the Casino Ludovisi Aurora; after Reni's death in 1642 he inherited Bologna's leading studio.
artist_briefings.guo zhongshu: Guo Zhongshu (c. 928-977) was a Five Dynasties and early Song scholar-official famed for 'jiehua' boundary-line painting, using ruled lines to render pavilions and boats with astonishing architectural precision while keeping the brushwork atmospheric. He was also a pioneering paleographer of ancient Chinese scripts whose reputation for eccentric behaviour nearly rivals his reputation as a draughtsman.
artist_briefings.gustave doré / adam cuerden: Gustave Doré (1832-1883), the prolific French illustrator of Dante, Cervantes and the Bible, produced the original wood-engravings that shaped 19th-century visual imagination. Adam Cuerden is a contemporary Wikipedia restorer who digitally cleans and restores high-resolution scans of public-domain prints, including many Doré engravings now circulating through Wikimedia Commons.
artist_briefings.hasegawa tōhaku: Hasegawa Tōhaku (1539-1610) was a Momoyama-period Japanese painter who rose from provincial Buddhist icon work in Noto to challenge the dominant Kanō school in Kyoto. His ink-on-paper Pine Trees screens, dissolving into mist, are revered as a peak of Japanese monochrome painting, while his golden Maple Tree at Chishaku-in shows his equal command of lavish colour.
artist_briefings.hendrik martenszoon sorgh: Hendrik Martenszoon Sorgh (c. 1610-1670) was a Dutch Golden Age painter who spent his entire career in Rotterdam, rising to headman of the local Guild of St Luke in 1659. Trained under David Teniers the Younger and Willem Buytewech, he specialised in peasant interiors, kitchen still lifes and bustling market scenes.
artist_briefings.hendrick avercamp: Hendrick Avercamp (1585-1634), known as 'the Mute of Kampen' because he was born deaf, built an entire career around winter landscapes teeming with skaters, sledges and stranded ships under pale northern skies. His ice-bound panoramas are among the most vivid documents of the Little Ice Age in early 17th-century Holland.
artist_briefings.henri-julien-félix rousseau: Henri Rousseau (1844-1910), 'Le Douanier', worked as a Paris toll collector and took up painting seriously only in his forties, exhibiting at the Salon des Indépendants from 1886. His dreamlike jungle scenes, built from Jardin des Plantes visits and hothouse leaves, were ridiculed in his lifetime but adored by Picasso and the Surrealists.
artist_briefings.henri meunier: Henri Meunier (1873-1922) was a Belgian Art Nouveau lithographer, etcher and poster designer born in Ixelles and nephew of the sculptor Constantin Meunier. Trained in his father's engraving workshop, he adapted Japanese woodblock flat colour and bold outline into some of the Belle Époque's most admired Belgian posters, including the famous 'Rajah' coffee advert.
artist_briefings.ike no taiga: Ike no Taiga (1723-1776) was an Edo-period Japanese painter and calligrapher who, with Yosa Buson, defined the Nanga or bunjinga literati style that reinterpreted Chinese scholar-painting for Japan. A child calligraphy prodigy from Kyoto, he produced the celebrated Ten Conveniences album with Buson and was famed for painting with his fingers as well as brushes.
artist_briefings.workshop of jean-auguste-dominique ingre: The Paris studio of Jean-Auguste-Dominique Ingres (1780-1867), the French Neoclassical draughtsman supreme, trained a generation of Academic painters including Hippolyte Flandrin, Amaury-Duval and Théodore Chassériau. Works bearing this label are typically studio replicas or pupil-assisted versions of Ingres' tightly polished portraits and nudes.
artist_briefings.j.l. gerome: Jean-Léon Gérôme (1824-1904), French Academic painter and sculptor, became the late-19th-century face of Orientalism with slickly finished bazaar, harem and gladiator scenes such as Pollice Verso. A long-time professor at the École des Beaux-Arts, he taught Thomas Eakins and Odilon Redon while campaigning publicly against the Impressionists.
artist_briefings.jan cossiers: Jan Cossiers (1600-1671) was an Antwerp painter who trained with his father and with Cornelis de Vos, then travelled to Italy and France before returning to join Rubens' circle. He contributed mythological canvases to Philip IV's Torre de la Parada and settled into a prolific career of religious pictures, genre scenes and merchant portraits in his native city.
artist_briefings.jan van den hoecke / jacob jordaens / pe: A triple attribution from Rubens' Antwerp orbit: Peter Paul Rubens (1577-1640), the Flemish Baroque titan; Jacob Jordaens (1593-1678), his stocky, earthy successor; and Jan van den Hoecke (1611-1651), a leading studio assistant who later served Archduke Leopold Wilhelm as court painter in Brussels. Such canvases typically reflect a Rubens design executed with workshop help.
artist_briefings.jean-auguste-dominique ingres / after ti: A collaboration in which Ingres, the uncompromising French Neoclassicist (1780-1867), reworks a Titian composition - a common academic exercise that let him wrestle with Venetian color while imposing his famously taut, porcelain draftsmanship.
artist_briefings.jean-léon gerôme: Jean-Léon Gérôme (1824-1904) was a French academic painter and sculptor, a standard-bearer for the polished Salon style and a master of Orientalist scenes, gladiator arenas and Napoleonic tableaux rendered with near-photographic finish. He taught generations at the École des Beaux-Arts and loathed the Impressionists.
artist_briefings.jean-auguste-dominique ingres / paul fla: A joint work by Ingres (1780-1867) and his devoted pupil Paul Flandrin (1811-1902), the younger brother of Hippolyte. Flandrin often painted landscape backgrounds for Ingres, so such collaborations typically pair Ingres's crystalline figures with Flandrin's classical French countryside.
artist_briefings.hieronymus bosch or workshop: An attribution applied to Netherlandish paintings in the orbit of Hieronymus Bosch (c. 1450-1516), the 's-Hertogenbosch visionary famous for demon-haunted hellscapes like The Garden of Earthly Delights. Bosch's workshop and close followers replicated his grotesques so skillfully that scholars often hedge between master and shop.
artist_briefings.john atkinson grimshaw: John Atkinson Grimshaw (1836-1893) was a Leeds-born Victorian painter who made a specialty of gas-lit, moonlit streets - wet cobblestones, bare trees, lone figures in the fog. Whistler grumbled that he had considered himself the inventor of nocturnes until he saw Grimshaw's.
artist_briefings.kang: Kang Hui-an (1417-1464), art name Injae, was an early Joseon scholar-official who passed the gwageo exam under King Sejong in 1441 and excelled equally at poetry, calligraphy and ink painting. His intimate figure-in-landscape Scholar Contemplating the Water is a touchstone of Korean literati painting.
artist_briefings.torii kiyonobu: Torii Kiyonobu I (c. 1664-1729) founded the Torii school of ukiyo-e, the only ukiyo-e lineage still active today. He painted kabuki theater signboards in Edo and pioneered the bold, swollen-line "gourd-and-earthworm" style that defined the actor print for most of the 18th century.
artist_briefings.kaigetsudō ando: Kaigetsudō Ando (c. 1671-1743) founded the Kaigetsudō school, specializing in hand-painted hanging scrolls of solitary courtesans in boldly patterned kimono - hip thrust forward, head tilted back. His career ended abruptly in 1714 when he was exiled for his role in the Ejima-Ikushima scandal at Edo Castle.
artist_briefings.harada naojirō: Harada Naojirō (1863-1899) was a Meiji-era yōga painter who studied in Munich under Gabriel von Max and befriended the writer Mori Ōgai. His 1890 oil painting Kannon Bodhisattva Riding the Dragon - a Buddhist subject in full European realism - ignited one of modern Japan's fiercest debates about what national painting should be.
artist_briefings.kano hideyori: Kanō Hideyori, a mid-16th-century Kyoto painter probably descended from Kanō Motonobu, is known almost entirely through one screen: Maple Viewers at Takao (Tokyo National Museum), a designated National Treasure. Its candid depiction of ordinary people picnicking under autumn leaves anticipated the later genre-painting tradition by decades.
artist_briefings.kanō sansetsu: Kanō Sansetsu (1589-1651) led the Kyō-Kanō, the Kyoto branch of the Kanō school, after being adopted by his master Sanraku. While the main Kanō line decamped to Edo, he kept alive the jewel-bright Momoyama palette - his four-panel Old Plum at the Met is all gnarled black trunk and gold-leaf defiance.
artist_briefings.kenkō shōkei: Kenkō Shōkei (active c. 1478-1523), a Zen monk and secretary of Kenchō-ji in Kamakura, travelled to Kyoto in 1478 to study under Geiami, the shogun's house painter. He brought Chinese Southern Song ink-painting styles east and became the leading landscape painter of Kamakura, often signed "Kei Shoki."
artist_briefings.torii kiyonaga: Torii Kiyonaga (1752-1815) was the fourth head of the Torii school and the dominant ukiyo-e designer of the 1780s. His tall, stately bijin-ga - beauties in elegant groups, rendered in clear line and measured color - set a new standard of realism that shaped Utamaro and a generation of successors.
artist_briefings.konrad witz: Konrad Witz (c. 1400-1445) was a German-born painter active in Basel whose Miraculous Draft of Fishes (1444) depicts Lake Geneva with identifiable mountains - often cited as the first faithful topographical landscape in European art. His figures are stocky, sculptural and strikingly modeled in light.
artist_briefings.ogata kōrin: Ogata Kōrin (1658-1716), a Kyoto-born son of a wealthy textile merchant, became the defining figure of the Rinpa school. His gold-ground screens of irises and red-white plums turn nature into flat, rhythmic pattern, and the term "Kōrin style" still signifies that luxurious decorative manner in Japanese art.
artist_briefings.kuroda seiki: Kuroda Seiki (1866-1924), the "father of Japanese Western-style painting," went to Paris to study law in 1884 but was persuaded to paint instead, training under Raphaël Collin and working at Grez-sur-Loing. Back in Tokyo he championed plein-air light and the academic nude, founding the Hakuba-kai and leading yōga for a generation.
artist_briefings.paul berthon: Paul Berthon (1872-1909) was a French Art Nouveau lithographer and a pupil of Eugène Grasset who made his name with decorative panels rather than advertising posters. His muted, tapestry-like palette and long-necked, flower-wreathed women are often mentioned in the same breath as Mucha.
artist_briefings.jan brueghel the younger / peter paul ru: A collaboration between the Antwerp flower-and-landscape specialist Jan Brueghel the Younger (1601-1678) and Peter Paul Rubens (1577-1640). Following the model set by Rubens and Jan Brueghel the Elder, Rubens typically supplied the figures while Brueghel filled the composition with minutely observed blooms, fruit and beasts.
artist_briefings.giorgione and/or his disciple titian: A disputed attribution covering early-16th-century Venetian paintings begun by Giorgione (c. 1477-1510) and likely completed by the young Titian after Giorgione's plague death. The Sleeping Venus in Dresden and the Concert Champêtre in the Louvre are the canonical examples of this shared, twilit style.
artist_briefings.luca signorelli: Luca Signorelli (c. 1445-1523), born in Cortona and trained near Piero della Francesca, built muscled, almost sculptural nudes that pointed the way toward Michelangelo. His fresco cycle of the Last Judgment in Orvieto Cathedral (1499-1503) is an early High Renaissance tour de force of anatomy in violent motion.
artist_briefings.workshop of lucas cranach the elder: Paintings produced by the large Wittenberg studio run by Lucas Cranach the Elder (1472-1553), court painter to the Saxon Electors and friend of Martin Luther. The shop churned out Reformation portraits, slim Venuses and Judiths by the dozen, often indistinguishable from Cranach's own hand.
artist_briefings.franz marc: Franz Marc (1880-1916) co-founded Der Blaue Reiter in Munich with Kandinsky in 1911 and built a short, intense career around symbolically colored animals - blue horses, yellow cows, red deer - that he felt were purer than the human world. He was killed at Verdun at age thirty-six.
artist_briefings.mary stevenson cassatt: Mary Cassatt (1844-1926) was the Pittsburgh-born American who settled in Paris, befriended Degas and became the only American invited to exhibit with the Impressionists. Her tender mothers-and-children and sharp-edged, Japanese-influenced color prints helped persuade wealthy U.S. collectors to buy modern French art.
artist_briefings.matteo ripa: Italian priest (1682-1746) sent by Propaganda Fide to the Manchu court, where he served Kangxi as painter and engraver from 1711 to 1723. He produced the Thirty-six Views of Jehol, introducing copperplate engraving to Qing China, then founded Naples' Chinese Institute in 1732.
artist_briefings.millais: Sir John Everett Millais (1829-1896) was a Pre-Raphaelite Brotherhood co-founder who scandalised Victorian London with the hyper-detailed Christ in the House of His Parents. His Ophelia and Mariana set a new benchmark for botanical precision before he drifted toward lucrative society portraiture and the presidency of the Royal Academy.
artist_briefings.clause monet: Almost certainly a misspelling of Claude Monet (1840-1926), the French Impressionist whose series of haystacks, Rouen Cathedral facades and Giverny water lilies tracked light's shifts minute by minute. His 1872 Impression, Sunrise gave the movement its name.
artist_briefings.muqi: Muqi Fachang (c. 1210-1269) was a Southern Song Chan monk-painter from Sichuan who settled in Hangzhou. His spare ink works, above all the Six Persimmons and the Daitokuji Guanyin-Crane-Gibbons triptych, were dismissed in China yet revered in Japan, where most survive.
artist_briefings.william blake: English poet, engraver and visionary (1757-1827) who illuminated his own prophetic books in relief etching, marrying image and verse. Works like The Ancient of Days, Newton and illustrations for Dante and Job fused Christian mysticism with a hand-built private mythology largely ignored in his lifetime.
artist_briefings.utagawa kuniyoshi; utagawa kuniyoshi die: Utagawa Kuniyoshi (1798-1861) was a late Edo ukiyo-e master famous for explosive warrior triptychs, the 108 Suikoden heroes, ghost prints and sly political caricatures. Iseya Rihei was one of the Edo publishers who issued his woodblock designs.
artist_briefings.michael wolgemut: Nuremberg painter and woodcut designer (1434-1519) who ran the busiest workshop in late 15th-century Germany. He supplied the hundreds of illustrations for Hartmann Schedel's 1493 Nuremberg Chronicle and, most famously, trained the young Albrecht Dürer from 1486 to 1489.
artist_briefings.attributed to rembrandt: Rembrandt van Rijn (1606-1669), the Dutch Golden Age master of Amsterdam, whose etchings, biblical scenes and relentless self-portraits set the European standard for chiaroscuro drama. 'Attributed to' signals a work the connoisseurship community can only tentatively hang on his name rather than the studio.
artist_briefings.paul de vos / possibly cornelis de vos: Flemish brothers from 's-Hertogenbosch active in Antwerp: Paul de Vos (c. 1591-1678) was Frans Snyders' brother-in-law and painted roaring hunt and animal scenes, often for Rubens and the Spanish court. Cornelis de Vos (1584-1651) specialised instead in warm, dignified portraits of Antwerp burghers and their children.
artist_briefings.jan wildens / frans snyders / peter paul: A classic Antwerp collaboration: Rubens (1577-1640) composed figures, Jan Wildens (1586-1653) supplied the sweeping landscape backgrounds, and Frans Snyders (1579-1657) painted the animals, game and still-life elements. The division of labour let Rubens' studio churn out huge mythological and hunting canvases at court speed.
artist_briefings.peter paul rubens / after willem key: Peter Paul Rubens (1577-1640), Antwerp's Baroque powerhouse, here working from a prototype by Willem Key (c. 1516-1568), a Netherlandish portraitist who trained under Lambert Lombard and Pieter Coecke van Aelst. Such 'after' pictures were Rubens' way of studying or updating earlier Flemish masters.
artist_briefings.david rijckaert: David Rijckaert II (1586-1642) was an Antwerp painter and art dealer who became a master of the Guild of Saint Luke in 1607-08 and collaborated with the young Rubens on the Sleeping Silenus around 1611. Long misclassified, he was identified by Fred Meijer in 1995 as a specialist in sumptuous banquet still lifes.
artist_briefings.sailko: Sailko is the Wikimedia Commons username of Francesco Bini, a prolific Italian amateur photographer who has uploaded hundreds of thousands of images of European artworks, churches and museum interiors. He is a documentarian, not an artist whose own paintings appear in the collection.
artist_briefings.pierre auguste renoir: French Impressionist (1841-1919) who trained as a porcelain painter before joining Monet at the Salon des Refusés. His Bal du moulin de la Galette and Luncheon of the Boating Party made dappled sunlight on Parisian skin his signature, even after severe rheumatoid arthritis forced him to paint with brushes strapped to his hand.
artist_briefings.after pieter brueghel the elder: Pieter Bruegel the Elder (c. 1525-1569) was the Netherlandish painter of Hunters in the Snow, The Peasant Wedding and the Tower of Babel. 'After' indicates a later copy, print or workshop version of one of his compositions, often produced by his sons Pieter Brueghel the Younger and Jan Brueghel the Elder.
artist_briefings.marcantonio raimondi: Italian engraver (c. 1480-c. 1534) who trained in Bologna and became Raphael's printmaker in Rome, turning the master's designs into a pan-European currency of images. His 1524 suite I Modi, engraving Giulio Romano's erotic drawings, landed him in a papal prison and counts as the first pornography scandal of print.
artist_briefings.sabine lepsius: German Berlin-born portraitist (1864-1942), daughter of painter Gustav Graef and wife of Reinhold Lepsius. She ran a prominent salon with her husband and produced some 280 portraits, many of Jewish sitters in Wilhelmine and Weimar Berlin; most were lost or destroyed during the Second World War.
artist_briefings.sharaku: Tōshūsai Sharaku was an ukiyo-e designer active for just ten months in 1794-95, producing roughly 140 bust-length kabuki actor prints for the publisher Tsutaya Jūzaburō. His unflinching, near-grotesque likenesses baffled Edo audiences, he vanished without a trace, and his identity is still debated.
artist_briefings.shōtei takahashi: Takahashi Shōtei, later Hiroaki (1871-1945), was the first artist recruited by Watanabe Shōzaburō in 1907 for the shin-hanga woodblock revival. He designed roughly 500 atmospheric landscapes before the 1923 Great Kantō earthquake destroyed every block, then spent the next two decades recutting and designing anew.
artist_briefings.sir anthony van dyck: Flemish virtuoso (1599-1641) who assisted Rubens in Antwerp, spent six formative years in Italy, and from 1632 served Charles I of England as principal painter. His silvery, swagger portraits of the Stuart court set a template that Gainsborough and Reynolds were still copying a century later.
artist_briefings.ölgemälde: joseph karl stieler ; foto: l: Joseph Karl Stieler (1781-1858) was Bavarian court painter from 1820 and created Ludwig I's Schönheitengalerie at Nymphenburg, 36 Neoclassical portraits of Munich beauties from Lola Montez to a shoemaker's daughter. He also produced the canonical 1820 portrait of Beethoven; the credit here flags a Lempertz photograph of the oil.
artist_briefings.stuck: Franz Ritter von Stuck (1863-1928) was a Munich Symbolist, co-founder of the 1892 Secession and later professor at the Munich Academy, where he taught Kandinsky, Klee and Josef Albers. His brooding mythological pictures, above all Die Sünde of 1893, made him the 'painter prince' of Wilhelmine Germany.
artist_briefings.ernst stückelberg: Swiss painter from Basel (1831-1903) who won a 50,000-franc open competition in 1877 to redecorate the Tellskapelle on Lake Lucerne. He moved to Bürglen, painted 59 local villagers as models, and produced four frescoes dramatising Schiller's saga of Wilhelm Tell for the new chapel of 1879-80.
artist_briefings.pieter van hanselaere: Belgian neoclassical painter (1786-1862) who trained in Paris under Jacques-Louis David, then spent a decade in Italy as court painter in Naples before returning to Ghent as an academy professor. He specialised in portraits and biblical history, though his epic 24-foot Philip van Artevelde canvas flopped with critics and broke him.
artist_briefings.rudolf weisse: Austrian Orientalist painter (1869-c.1930), born in Usti on the Elbe and trained at Vienna's Akademie before settling in Paris. He specialised in photographically detailed Cairo street scenes, hauling tiles, robes and inlaid furniture back to his studio as props, and took a Médaille d'Honneur at the 1889 Exposition Universelle.
artist_briefings.michelangelo: Florentine sculptor, painter, architect and poet (1475-1564) whose terribilita shaped the High Renaissance. He carved the Pieta at 24 and David at 29, painted the Sistine Chapel ceiling over four backbreaking years, and capped his career designing the dome of St Peter's Basilica.
artist_briefings.hendrick goltzius: Dutch Mannerist engraver and painter (1558-1617) based in Haarlem, famous for a burin technique whose swelling lines dazzled patrons including Emperor Rudolf II. Despite a crippled right hand from a childhood fire, he produced virtuoso prints throughout Europe, then abruptly abandoned engraving at 42 to take up oil painting.
artist_briefings.jan matsys: Flemish Renaissance painter (c.1510-1575), eldest son of Quinten Matsys, trained in his father's Antwerp studio and entered the Guild of St Luke in 1531. Banished from Antwerp for eleven years over his Protestant leanings, he absorbed the School of Fontainebleau's sensuality and became known for sleek female nudes dressed up as Susannas and Bathshebas.
artist_briefings.edmund joseph sullivan: British book illustrator (1869-1933) who fused the pen-and-ink vigour of the 1860s school with Art Nouveau swagger. He cut his teeth at the Daily Graphic from age nineteen, then made his name with a sprawling 1898 edition of Carlyle's Sartor Resartus and a 1913 Rubaiyat of Omar Khayyam; he later taught illustration at Goldsmiths.
artist_briefings.possibly lambert sustris: Dutch painter (c.1515-after 1560), born in Amsterdam but active mainly in Venice, where he worked in Titian's studio and is often called Alberto de Olanda. His Mannerist-tinged mythologies and portraits took him to the Palazzo del Te in Mantua and eventually to the Habsburg court of Maximilian II in Vienna.
artist_briefings.thomas willeboirts bosschaert / paul de: Thomas Willeboirts Bosschaert (1613-1654), a Bergen op Zoom-born Flemish Baroque painter steeped in Van Dyck, collaborated here with Paul de Vos (c.1591-1678), Antwerp's virtuoso of hunts and animal fights and a regular partner to Rubens and Snyders. Together they combined Van Dyckian figures with de Vos's snapping hounds and tumbling game.
artist_briefings.marcantonio raimondi / after raphael: Marcantonio Raimondi (c.1480-c.1534), Bolognese goldsmith turned engraver, arrived in Rome around 1510 and joined Raphael's circle, producing roughly fifty plates after the master's drawings. His workshop effectively invented the reproductive print, broadcasting Raphael's designs across Europe and landing him briefly in jail over the scandalous I Modi series.
artist_briefings.utagawa hiroshige i: Japanese ukiyo-e master (1797-1858) born into an Edo firefighter's family, remembered as the last great designer of the tradition. Across some 8,000 prints - above all the Fifty-three Stations of the Tokaido and One Hundred Famous Views of Edo - he pioneered bokashi gradations that later floored Van Gogh, Monet and Manet.
artist_briefings.paolo veronese / formerly attributed to: Paolo Veronese (1528-1588), born Paolo Caliari in Verona to a stonecutter's family, became one of the cinquecento's 'great trio' alongside Titian and Tintoretto. Veronese is celebrated for sumptuous, silver-lit banquet scenes such as the Wedding at Cana; this work's authorship once drifted to pupils Francesco Montemezzano and Veronese's son Carlo Caliari before returning to the master.
artist_briefings.vincent van gogh / after jean-françois m: During his 1889-90 stay at the Saint-Remy asylum, Vincent van Gogh (1853-1890) translated black-and-white reproductions of Jean-Francois Millet's peasant scenes into vibrant oil 'copies,' calling it his way of making music from another man's score. Millet (1814-1875), a Barbizon founder, had provided the dignified labourers Van Gogh revered since his Borinage days.
artist_briefings.wang meng: Chinese Yuan-dynasty master (1308-1385) and grandson of Zhao Mengfu, counted among the Four Masters of the Yuan alongside Huang Gongwang, Wu Zhen and Ni Zan. His densely textured, ropy-brush landscapes like Dwelling in the Qingbian Mountains bristle with restless energy; wrongly tied to a Ming-era coup plot, he died in prison.
artist_briefings.wilhelm von kaulbach: German history painter and muralist (1805-1874) from the Dusseldorf school who became court painter to Ludwig I and directed the Munich Academy from 1849. He is best known for an ambitious cycle of six grand frescoes in Berlin's Neues Museum - including the Tower of Babel and the Battle of the Huns - that fed the nationalist imagination of mid-century Germany.
artist_briefings.俵屋宗達: Tawaraya Sotatsu (c.1570-c.1640) ran a Kyoto fan-painting atelier and, with calligrapher Hon'ami Koetsu, launched what became the Rinpa school. He rebooted classical yamato-e with bold outlines, lavish gold and silver grounds, and the tarashikomi 'pooling' technique, reaching a peak in the Wind God and Thunder God screens.
artist_briefings.fan kuan: Northern Song landscape master (c.960-c.1030) from Shaanxi who, scorning city life, retreated to Mount Hua to paint directly from nature. His monumental Travelers Among Mountains and Streams, roughly two metres tall, is widely considered the single greatest Chinese landscape painting.
artist_briefings.yamamoto kanae: Japanese artist (1882-1946) hailed as the father of sosaku-hanga, the 'creative prints' movement where one person designs, carves and prints. His 1904 woodblock Fisherman is taken as the movement's starting gun; he later studied in Paris, rode home across Siberia, and co-founded the Japan Creative Print Society in 1918.
artist_briefings.whistler: American-born painter and printmaker James McNeill Whistler (1834-1903), based mainly in London and Paris, championed 'art for art's sake' and titled works as Nocturnes and Symphonies to stress mood over narrative. After critic John Ruskin sneered at his Nocturne in Black and Gold, Whistler sued for libel, won a farthing, and went bankrupt.
